# Compendium Theologiae Positivae (1686)

## 1 Prolegomena: On the Nature and Constitution of Theology

### 1 Theology, by the force of the word

Theology, by the force of the word, denotes λόγον περὶ τοῦ Θεοῦ (a discourse or rational account concerning God). In common usage, however, it signifies a habit of knowing God and divine things, and of teaching, confirming, and defending them: a habit, moreover, that is conformed to its object and that falls within the capacity of human beings in the present state of life.

Notes. Θεολογία (Theologia) is an abstract noun and, if one considers its grammatical derivation, descends from the concrete form θεολόγος (theologos); although, attending to the logical denomination, the concrete or denominative term receives its appellation from the abstract, as from a denominating form. (Jacob Martini, Theological Disputations, disputation 1, thesis 9, p. 3.) One is called a θεολόγος (theologian) to whom pertains, or in whom resides, ὁ λόγος περὶ τοῦ Θεοῦ (the discourse concerning God). Thus the name "theologian" is employed in the superscription of the Apocalypse. So also in Lactantius (Lactantius, On the Wrath of God, ch. 11, p. 638) and in Augustine (Augustine, The City of God, book 18, ch. 14, p. 620, vol. 6 of the Works). Compare Musaeus (Introduction to Theology, p. 2).

Augustine, in the eighth book of The City of God, chapter 1 (p. 87), writes: "By the Greek word we understand a rational account or discourse concerning the divine nature to be signified." For although theology is not only λόγος περὶ τοῦ Θεοῦ (discourse concerning God) but also ἀπὸ τοῦ Θεοῦ (from God) and πρὸς τὸν Θεόν (directed toward God), the force of the word does not signify all these equally as it does the first. Rather, the noun Θεός (God), in composition with the noun λόγος (discourse), denotes the object, just as φύσις (nature), ἀστήρ (star), and ἀρετή (virtue) do in the compounds φυσιολογία (physiology), ἀρετολογία (aretology), and ἀστρολογία (astrology). Compare Jacob Martini (Martini, Theological Disputations, same place), Gerhard (Gerhard, Exegesis of the Theological Commonplaces, p. 1), and Musaeus (Musaeus, Introduction to Theology, §§ 12, 13, 14, pp. 3, 4, and Introduction, p. 1).

For it is not on account of any casual thought or discourse about God or divine things that people are customarily called theologians; rather, only those who from a settled habit are able and accustomed to reason or discourse about God receive this title.

This is so that theology may be a science, or a habit analogous to science. The knowledge of God that falls to simpler persons who are unskilled in teaching does not customarily confer the designation of "theologian." Thus the Blessed Theologians of Leipzig, in the Appendix to the Counsel of Dedeken (fol. 137a), caution that no one is properly called a theologian merely on account of some acquaintance with the Word of God; for theology properly so called, beyond apprehensive and judicative cognition, also comprehends the end, which is to instruct a person for attaining eternal salvation. Compare Meisner (Meisner, Philosophia Sobria, § 3, p. 104).

For a habit of the mind requires τὸ ἀληθεύειν (truth-telling), that is, to enunciate what is true concerning its object, whether by affirmation or negation. Therefore, we here set aside the various kinds of Gentile theology, full of lies and impious superstitions: the μυθικόν (mythical or fabulous), in which the poets were occupied; and the πολιτικόν (political or civil), in which the priests busied themselves. Indeed, even the φυσικόν (physical or natural), which the philosophers claimed for themselves, although it agrees in name with the natural theology that we commend in the following section, is nonetheless, as found among the Gentile philosophers, contaminated by not a few errors and not altogether worthy of the name of theology. Compare Gerhard (Gerhard, Exegesis of the Theological Commonplaces, §§ 13, 14, pp. 6, 7) and Musaeus (Musaeus, Introduction to Theology, pp. 3, 4).

For even though the most exact knowledge of God resides in God himself, and no less in Christ as man through the communication of divine attributes by virtue of the personal union; and even though the angels confirmed in goodness and the blessed in heaven know God more perfectly than any one of us; yet since common usage does not allow that God himself, or Christ, or the blessed should be called theologians, it is readily apparent that we leave aside that signification which otherwise obtains when, with a qualifier, we speak of "the theology of wayfarers." Meanwhile, that knowledge which God has of himself is called by the authors ἀρχέτυπος (archetypal) theology, since it does not depend upon any other knowledge of God in another subject as upon an exemplary cause. This archetypal knowledge is imitated, as a form and exemplar (though in a lesser degree of perfection, which is not unusual in ectypal copies), by that knowledge of God and divine things which angels and human beings possess from the divine bounty; and this latter knowledge is accordingly called ἔκτυπος (ectypal). Compare Martini (Martini, Theological Disputations, disputation 2, §§ 23 ff., p. 27), Gerhard (Gerhard, Exegesis of the Theological Commonplaces, § 15, p. 7), and Himmel (Himmel, Syntagma, pp. 2, 5, 10, 11, 12).

As for the knowledge of God and divine things that resides in Christ according to his human nature through the communication of attributes by virtue of the personal union: since it is the very infinite knowledge which Christ has from eternity according to his divine nature, considered in relation to God as its certain object, it is itself archetypal theology, not another or ectypal theology, even though it does not belong to the human nature subjectively but communicatively, not of itself but on account of the personal union. The habitual knowledge of God, however, which naturally inheres in Christ's human nature, is rightly called ectypal, just as it is rightly distinguished from the theology of the union. See König (König, Positive Theology, p. 2, § 15), and especially Musaeus (Musaeus, Introduction to Theology, ch. 1, §§ 4 ff. to the end, pp. 4 to 23).

### 2 This theology, according to a twofold mode of knowing

This theology, according to a twofold mode of knowing, is twofold: natural and revealed. The former rests upon the principles or light of nature; the latter upon supernatural manifestation or revelation. Both treat of God, not only as he is in himself, but as the end and supreme good of the human person.

Notes. The distinction of theology into natural and supernatural amounts to the same thing. We call this latter species "supernatural" from its origin, and "revealed" or "theology of revelation" from its gracious mode of communication, as Martini states (Martini, Theological Disputations, disputation 4, § 3, p. 80). Moreover, the distinction is such that among Christians, revealed or supernatural theology is called "theology" absolutely, while natural theology is scarcely named otherwise than with its qualifier, as "natural theology." Compare Musaeus (Musaeus, Introduction to Theology, ch. 3, § 1, p. 105).

For otherwise the word "to reveal," in a more general signification, pertains also to natural knowledge, as the Greek word φανερῶσαι (to make manifest) is taken in Romans 1:19. But here revelation in the stricter sense is understood, by which either hidden and concealed things, that is, things not naturally knowable, are made manifest and, as it were, uncovered or presented for view with the veil removed (to which the Greek word ἀποκαλύπτειν, "to reveal," corresponds, as in Luke 10:22), or a peculiar manifestation of any things whatsoever, including those that can be known by the guidance of the light of nature, is supernaturally made by God. See Musaeus (Musaeus, Introduction to Theology, ch. 3, § 25, n. 5, p. 155, and his Treatise on Conversion, disputation 6, ch. 2, § 29, p. 359).

Concerning revealed theology, more will become clear below in its proper place. Concerning natural theology, this much at least is certain: that no other discipline can claim for itself this distinguished task, and that the perfections of God cannot be sufficiently explained and known if this consideration is absent. See Musaeus (Musaeus, Introduction to Theology, ch. 2, § 1, pp. 23 ff.). Similarly, Martini, speaking of the theology of wayfarers, by which he embraces both natural and supernatural theology together, says that its internal (that is, intermediate) end is the contemplation of God and divine things and a pious life; while its external and ultimate end is an eternally blessed fellowship with God (Martini, Theological Disputations, disputation 3, § 37, p. 57; compare disputation 1, §§ 80 and 89, pp. 18, 20).

### 3 Natural theology is a science

Natural theology is a science, and indeed a practical science, in which the following elements occur: the end, the subject of operation, causes and means, as well as the material and formal object.

Notes. It is a science because it is an evident habit concerning a necessary object, deducing conclusions from necessary principles. Compare Musaeus (Musaeus, Introduction to Theology, ch. 2, § 3, p. 28). Or, as Martini puts it: "It proceeds from natural principles known in themselves, by the light of the natural intellect" (Martini, Theological Disputations, disputation 3, § 47, p. 53). Whence, as he adds in the same place (§ 54, p. 59), conclusions concerning God and divine things are truly and certainly gathered and established.

All its conclusions are practical, if not formally, then at least virtually. We call "formally practical" those conclusions that formally and directly prescribe some operation pertaining (so far as concerns the present matter) to the worship of God, and which must therefore be performed by a human being in this life: for example, "God is to be invoked," or "one's neighbor in necessities is to be helped." We call "virtually practical" those conclusions that, although they do not formally prescribe an operation pertaining to the worship of God, nonetheless bear upon and contribute, within the scope of this very science, to inferring formally practical conclusions. For example, "God is the cause of the goods of which we stand in need," and "Our neighbor is loved by God equally as we are": although these do not formally prescribe any operation to a person, they nevertheless contribute to the inferring of those formally practical conclusions mentioned above. Therefore, since they too are treated for the sake of practice, they are rightly regarded as practical. Compare Musaeus (Musaeus, Introduction to Theology, ch. 2, § 4, p. 29, and ch. 3, § 4, p. 125).

This is to say, insofar as theology is a practical habit, there first presents itself the end, by which the will of the agent is moved to act; then the subject, which is placed under the operation that the practical habit prescribes; further, the efficient cause of the end (if not of the thing as something to be effected or obtained through the operation, then at least of the operation by which we attain the thing that contains the highest goodness in itself); also the impulsive cause, moving the one who effects or bestows the end to effect or bestow it; and finally the means, which, even if they do not themselves have the character of causes toward attaining the end (when that end is obtained by another's undeserved or gratuitous benefit, as in the present case, as we shall presently indicate), are nonetheless conditions required on the part of the subject. Compare Musaeus (Musaeus, Introduction to Theology, pp. 29 ff. to 44). The distinction among means, some of which precede the thing as having the character of a cause upon which the thing depends, and others of which mark only a bare antecedence of order and are merely interposed between the causes of the thing and the thing itself, by necessity of presence rather than of efficiency, is also set forth by Hopfner (Hopfner, Disputation on Justification, disputation 2, § 25, p. 113).

That is to say, insofar as theology is a science, there occur both the thing to be known, or that about which conclusions are drawn, and that from which, as previously known, conclusions are deduced, or that which, as first known, is the ground of knowing the rest. The former is called the material object; the latter is called the formal object. Compare Musaeus (Musaeus, Introduction to Theology, ch. 2, §§ 14, 15, pp. 47, 48).

### 4 The end to which natural theology ultimately and of itself tends

The end to which natural theology ultimately and of itself tends, and to which it refers all that it teaches, is the final beatitude of the human person. By this name we comprehend God as the objective end, and the attainment and enjoyment of him, consisting in the most perfect operation of intellect and will, as the formal end.

Notes. It is not otherwise denied that the end of natural theology may rightly be said to be "to render the human person inexcusable and gradually to lead one by the hand to supernatural theology." On this, see Himmel (Himmel, Syntagma, disputation 1, § 20). But this end came about only after the Fall and the introduction of the corruption of the human race and the communication of supernatural theology for the restoration of humankind, and therefore accidentally. For in the primeval state, the Author of the light of nature and of natural theology did not intend this end, but rather the one we indicate in the thesis. See Martini (Martini, Theological Disputations, disputation 2, §§ 46, 52, 53, pp. 32, 33, 34).

Natural theology is 1. the noblest of the practical sciences, and therefore treats of the most perfect end; 2. it treats of God as the supreme good, and therefore as something to be obtained; 3. it treats of the human person as one to be made absolutely blessed. See Musaeus (Musaeus, Introduction to Theology, ch. 2, § 6, p. 30).

God contains all goodness in himself and alone can satisfy desire. Compare Musaeus (Musaeus, Introduction to Theology, same place) and Martini (Martini, Theological Disputations, disputation 2, §§ 55 ff., p. 34).

Beatitude is a good proper to the human person, and therefore is to be located in an operation of the rational soul. See Musaeus (Musaeus, Introduction to Theology, ch. 2, § 9, p. 35). By an act of the intellect we possess or are conjoined to God, attaining the character of good that is in God; by an act of the will we enjoy him or cling to him as our obtained good (Musaeus, same place, pp. 36, 37).

This operation must be such as to be able to satisfy desire. Therefore it must be a different operation from that which takes place in this life, where the knowledge of God is imperfect and the will has a desire for a more perfect union with God; although the human person cannot distinctly know by the light of nature what the future knowledge of God after this life will be, namely intuitive and clear. See Musaeus (Musaeus, same place, pp. 37, 38) and Martini (Martini, Theological Disputations, disputation 3, §§ 35, 36, 37, pp. 56, 57).

Both ends, taken jointly, constitute one complete end. For we are not made blessed through God or in God unless by a certain operation we possess and enjoy him; yet the operation of our soul, of whatever sort it may be, does not make us blessed unless it is directed toward God. See Musaeus (Musaeus, same place, § 9, p. 34).

### 5 The subject of operation is the human wayfarer

The subject of operation is the human wayfarer, that is, one tending toward eternal beatitude.

Notes. That is, the one who is placed under the operation which natural theology prescribes with respect to attaining beatitude. This subject is otherwise called the "end for whom" (finis cui). See Musaeus (Musaeus, same place, § 10, p. 41).

The "wayfarer" (viator) is opposed to the "comprehensor" (comprehensor), just as the "state of the way" and the "state of the fatherland" are elsewhere distinguished, from 1 Corinthians 9:24, where those who live on earth are compared to runners pressing toward a goal, and those who have departed this life in blessedness to those who have reached the goal; and from 2 Corinthians 5:6, 8, where those in this life are said to be absent (ἐκδημῆσαι) from the Lord, and to be moved by the desire to dwell with the Lord, where they might be at home (ἐνδημῆσαι). Compare Philippians 3:12, 13 and Musaeus (Musaeus, Introduction to Theology, ch. 1, § 8, p. 13).

We do not say "human sinner" here, but "wayfarer," because thus far we are treating of natural theology considered precisely and in itself, in which respect it abstracts from the state of integrity and the state of corruption. See Musaeus (Musaeus, Introduction to Theology, ch. 2, § 10, p. 41).

And indeed insofar as one is such, that is, chiefly with respect to intellect and will; for judgment concerning the subject of operation in practical sciences must be made from the end. See Musaeus (Musaeus, same place, § 30, p. 87).

### 6 Among the causes of beatitude are reckoned

Among the causes of beatitude are reckoned: 1. The efficient cause, which is God. 2. The internal impulsive cause, which is the goodness or gratuitous favor of God.

Notes. Not nature, nor doctrine, nor habituation. For by these nothing is at last acquired after this life; rather, that is received which corresponds to one's prior life, whether well or ill spent. And since beatitude consists in the most perfect knowledge of God, it is certain that no one can confer this upon a human person except God himself. See Musaeus (Musaeus, same place, § 11, p. 42).

Not justice, as contradistinguished from goodness. For a human being, who 1. depends upon God in being and in acting, and 2. whatever good one does, one does from obligation, has no right against God and no merit properly and strictly so called. See Musaeus (Musaeus, same place, § 12, p. 43).

### 7 The means of attaining beatitude

The means of attaining beatitude, in natural theology, are acts of the mind and will occupied with God, by which God is rightly acknowledged and worshiped. These are called by one name: religion. They are contained in the law of nature, or the moral law, and partly they are directly and immediately occupied with God, partly they directly order the human person in relation to oneself or to one's neighbor, yet consequently they order one toward God as well.

Notes. We understand "means" here in a more general sense, as equivalent to conditions required on the part of the subject who is to be made blessed, concerning which we spoke in the preceding § 3. Moreover, this is evident here from the fact that, as we stated in § 6, God is moved to bestow beatitude upon human beings by his own gratuitous favor; by which very fact a causal or meritorious means on our part is excluded. Nor does natural theology recognize an alien merit that, by being apprehended, might become our own. Hence the means given here must be mere conditions, and therefore means in a looser and less proper sense. Compare Musaeus (Musaeus, same place, § 13, pp. 43, 44).

Religion cannot be separated from wisdom, nor can wisdom be severed from religion, because the same God must both be understood, which is wisdom, and honored, which is religion. But wisdom precedes, and religion follows, because it is prior to know God, and consequent to worship him. See Lactantius (Lactantius, On True Wisdom, book 4, ch. 4, p. 176). Sometimes, however, the very acknowledgment of God is comprehended under the name of divine worship, namely, because knowing whom you worship is the principle of divine worship.

The name "religion" is derived from the bond of piety, because God has bound the human person to himself and constrained one with piety, since it is necessary for us to serve him as Lord and obey him as Father. So Lactantius (Lactantius, On True Wisdom, book 4, ch. 27, pp. 349, 351). The word "religion," in its stricter signification, denotes either the habit of the will by which we are inclined to devotion and to the honor and worship due to God on account of his excellence, or the very acts of honoring or worshiping God on account of his excellence; and it connotes, on the part of the intellect, right acknowledgment of God, and on the part of the will, other virtues or acts of virtues that are directed to the honor and worship of God. In its broader signification, it imports the entire complex of all virtues or acts pertaining to the worship of God. See Musaeus (Musaeus, Introduction to Theology, ch. 2, § 2, pp. 25, 27, and his Refutation of the Theologico-Political Treatise on the Liberty of Philosophizing, § 37, p. 19, and § 47, p. 28).

By the moral law, those things that befit a rational creature as such, and therefore pertain to morals or the manner of living, are defined and prescribed, while the opposite things, that is, those that are unfitting, are prohibited. This law is God's, as Author of nature, implanted by his finger, that is, by his influence, in the very soul of the human person at creation; concerning which we shall see more below in its proper place.

For example, on the part of the intellect: acts of meditating upon and knowing the essence, attributes, providence, works, and benefits of God. On the part of the will: acts of fear, love, trust, hope, patience, and the like, to which correspond external acts by which the internal ones are declared, such as prayers, invocation of God, and thanksgiving made through sensible signs, whether in a public assembly or privately; hymns and various celebrations of God, his perfections, and his benefits, and so forth.

For example, internal acts occupied in moderating the affections; acts of cultivating the mind with honorable arts and sciences; acts of rightly preserving life, body, reputation, wealth, and so forth, which are partly internal, partly external.

For example, acts of justice, by which to each is rendered what is due; acts of liberality; acts of fortitude for the defense of fatherland, kindred, and others, which are likewise either elicited in the mind or commanded and external.

These have the character of divine worship insofar as they are ultimately referred to God as their end, and are performed in obedience to him, for his praise and glory. See on all these matters Musaeus (Musaeus, same place, §§ 33 ff., pp. 88, 89).

### 8 With respect, however

With respect, however, to the sufficiency of the divine worship that natural theology prescribes for attaining beatitude after this life, the greatest diversity occurs and must be most diligently observed according to the diverse states of the human person: the primeval, or state of integrity, and the state of corruption, or sin. In the former state, the human person was able, by the guidance of natural theology and through the powers granted to oneself, to attain a sufficient acknowledgment of God and to render the worship due to God without deficiency or sin, and thus in this way to obtain eternal beatitude from God. In this latter state, however, through the very condition of corrupt nature, the human person is turned away from God and inclined to those things that displease God. And since one has God offended and angry on account of sins, one does not find in natural theology any means by which to make satisfaction to the offended God and to be restored to his favor. Indeed, one can neither perfectly know and prescribe for oneself those things that otherwise pertain to the worship of God, nor perform the worship that one understands by the force of the light of nature to be owed to God. Whence, for the present state, natural theology suffices for salvation for no human being.

Notes. Those diverse states are here presupposed. Below, however, in revealed theology, they will be set forth more clearly in their proper place.

In the primeval state, the human person had God favorably disposed and without difficulty inclined to confer beatitude upon one at some future time. Compare Martini (Martini, Theological Disputations, disputation 3, §§ 84 ff., pp. 66 ff.) and Musaeus (Musaeus, Introduction to Theology, ch. 2, § 13, n. 4, p. 45).

For although God is supremely good, he is also supremely just, and the most severe avenger of sins that contravene his most holy law, by virtue of his own immutable justice. Therefore, unless satisfaction is made to the offended divine justice, the goodness of God, which does not abolish God's justice, cannot be so known that the remission of sins and salvation to be conferred upon the sinner can be expected from it. Compare Musaeus (Musaeus, Special Disputation on the Insufficiency of Natural Theology for Salvation against Edward Herbert of Cherbury, annexed to the Treatise on the Eternal Decree of Election, § 64, pp. 36, 37).

This, however, is the chief point, in the absence of which no worship pleasing to God can be rendered. For it is necessary that the person first be pleasing to God (and this on account of Christ alone), if that person's works are to be pleasing and acceptable to God. These are the words of the Solid Declaration of the Formula of Concord (article 4, pp. 700, 701). "How, moreover, can the human heart love God when it perceives him to be terribly angry, and to be overwhelming us with temporal and perpetual calamities? The law, however, always accuses us and always shows God to be angry. God is therefore not loved until we have apprehended his mercy by faith; then at last he becomes an object worthy of love." These are the words of the Apology of the Augsburg Confession (pp. 83, 84; compare p. 66).

Although natural theology prescribes repentance to the human sinner, that one should grieve over sins, nevertheless this repentance neither extends to all sins, since many are committed by those who are ignorant or negligent, nor is original sin rightly acknowledged by a person left to oneself and destitute of supernatural revelation. Nor can that grief over sins wash away sins insofar as they import an offense against God and subject the human person to the wrath of God and the penalty of eternal punishment, even though it imports a certain retraction of them. See Musaeus (Musaeus, same disputation, §§ 37 ff., pp. 22 ff.).

This insufficiency is on account of the inborn obscurity of the intellect, even in natural things, concerning which more will be said below in the locus on original sin. Meanwhile, the words of Mylius are noteworthy, in which he shows that natural knowledge (theology) is deficient and incomplete. "Because," he says, "it inculcates only one part of heavenly doctrine, and that the smallest, namely the Law, and not even this in its entirety, but only by halves, while ignorance prevails both of true divine worship and of the evangelical knowledge of salvation, in both of which the very kernel of divine knowledge lies hidden" (Mylius, Positive Theology on God, thesis 13).

Because the whole of human nature has been corrupted, destitute of the good powers it ought to have had, and made prone to evil. Again, Mylius states beautifully: "It tinges and sprinkles the mind with knowledge, but subdues the disordered motions of the heart all too feebly" (Mylius, same place, thesis 12). Compare with these and the preceding remarks Martini (Martini, Theological Disputations, §§ 112, 113, p. 73), Musaeus (Musaeus, same place, pp. 45, 46, and the cited disputation, §§ 32, 33, pp. 18, 19, 20).

Whether or not someone has heard anything of supernatural revelation and of Christ the Mediator: for no one whatsoever is saved by the grace of God and the merit of Christ unless one apprehends by faith the satisfaction rendered by Christ for sins and appropriates it to oneself, so that it may be presented to the offended God as though it were one's own merit. See again Musaeus (Musaeus, same disputation, §§ 101 ff., pp. 6 ff., and Musaeus, Dissertation against Étienne de Courcelles on the Question: Whether the Gentiles without Faith in Christ Can Attain Eternal Salvation through an Extraordinary Grace of God, and so forth).

### 9 Meanwhile, natural theology

Meanwhile, natural theology, both with respect to its principles and with respect to the conclusions that depend upon them, is entirely true and certain, and does not truly conflict with revealed theology; although, as it is actually found to inhere in human beings after the Fall, it must be admitted to be contaminated by various prejudices and errors.

Notes. Natural theology is in itself one, and is not to be thought of as different in species on account of the diverse states of human beings, even though a diversity with respect to degrees of perfection and imperfection must be admitted. Compare Musaeus (Musaeus, Introduction to Theology, ch. 2, § 6, p. 32).

Its principles and conclusions depend, as constituting ectypal theology, upon God as their author, to whom falsehood is repugnant. And just as first principles concern things that cannot be otherwise and are therefore necessarily true, so the conclusions that have a necessary connection with those principles are likewise confirmed to be true and certain. Here the Leipzig Theologians refer, in the Appendix to the Counsel of Dedeken (fol. 143), to what Paul says of the Gentiles in Romans 1:18, that they hold fast the truth, and so forth, looking to natural knowledge as it inheres in them, as being a true science or cognition.

For truth is consonant with truth. Neither is there more than one truth. Although natural theology does not attain to those objects that are proper to revealed theology, it does not for that reason deny or attack any of them, or posit the opposite; rather, it suspends its judgment concerning them as matters placed outside its sphere. Indeed, if revelation be added, it is certain that the deficiency of our natural cognition is supplied by the addition of a higher knowledge. Compare Musaeus (Musaeus, Introduction to Theology, part 2, ch. 5, § 12, pp. 324 ff., and § 15, pp. 337, 338), and the treatise of Grauer (Grauer, On the One Truth). A fuller comparison of true natural theology with revealed theology was presented in 1676 under our presidency in the inaugural disputation by the late Heinrich von Lith, a most beloved relative by marriage.

Thus we removed above the physical or natural theology of the Gentile philosophers, together with the other kinds of Gentile theology, as erroneous (see note d to § 1). And that human beings destitute of true divine revelation also abused their reason and were carried off into various errors, we are taught from revelation itself (Romans 1:22 ff.). Hence it came about that, when they had not found the true revelation, they embraced false revelations as true rather than none at all. Compare Himmel (Himmel, Syntagma, disputation 1, §§ 23 ff. to 28).

### 10 The formal object of Natural Theology

The formal object of Natural Theology, considered as a practical science, is its End, and indeed its Objective End, namely God, insofar as He is known from the light of nature prior to demonstration, through a twofold knowledge: first, an innate knowledge, that is, a certain light implanted in the intellect and an instinct of nature; and second, a common or ordinary knowledge acquired from the inspection of creatures.

(a) That is, what is first known in Natural Theology, and which, once known, serves as the ground for knowing all the rest, in accordance with what we said at Section III, note d.

(b) For in any science, the end must be in some measure already known beforehand, since it is from this prior knowledge that a person is moved to undertake the practice or operation for its sake (Musaeus, Introduction, ch. 2, sect. 5, p. 29; sect. 15, p. 48).

(c) For the formal knowledge of the end, if not distinct then at least confused, depends on the objective end; and therefore it is not the formal end but the objective end that is first known (Musaeus, Introduction, sect. 15, p. 48).

(d) For insofar as God is made known through divine revelation, knowledge of Him belongs not to Natural but to Revealed Theology (Musaeus, Introduction, p. 49). By the expression "light of nature" we here understand those propositions which declare the existence, essence, and essential perfections of God, insofar as they are known either from the principles of nature and reason through discursive reasoning, or by the power of the agent intellect and phantasms, immediately and without discourse, from the apprehension of terms (Musaeus, Introduction, pp. 50, 51, 52). It should be noted that the formal object of Natural Theology is not constituted precisely by the light of nature, but by God as known from the light of nature. For the light of nature is not the proper and proximate ground of assent in Natural Theology, but rather a ground that is too general and remote (Musaeus, Introduction, sect. 28, pp. 85, 86).

(e) This knowledge is called "innate," not because an actual cognition of God or an express species is present in a human being by nature before the use of reason, but because, once the terms are apprehended, it is immediately present to the intellect without discursive reasoning, just as if it had been actually implanted together with nature itself (Musaeus, Introduction, sect. 19, p. 52).

(f) This light is not an impressed species existing in the intellect by nature before the use of reason; nor, therefore, is it a habit properly so called; nor again is it the bare dynamis (power) or potency of knowing. Rather, it is something superadded to or innate in the cognitive potency: namely, a certain perfection by which the intellect is rendered capable, or placed in proximate potency, for immediately eliciting the acts of knowing. Although this is not a habit properly so called, it is nevertheless analogous (analogon) to a habit. Musaeus taught this at length not only in several manuscript lecture courses but also in his Introduction, ch. 2, sect. 19, pp. 52 ff., up to p. 60, and again affirmed it in his Detailed Explanation, pp. 150 ff. Hülsemann likewise, in his Lectures on the Breviary, ch. 1, p. 1134, expressly acknowledges that he assents to the opinion which holds that natural knowledge is connate with the human being not in the manner of a habit but through a bare potency of knowing (by which he undoubtedly means a proximate potency). Having adduced the passages at Romans 1:19, 20 and Romans 2:14, he proves this opinion and concludes that natural knowledge inheres in the human being through a potency, not through an infused habit.

(g) This instinct is nothing other than the inclination of nature toward God as its end, which determines the intellect, already endowed with that connate light, as if by an added weight, to give assent, both to other common notions concerning God, and especially to that notion which concerns the existence of God, immediately and without discursive reasoning (Musaeus, Introduction, pp. 78, 79, 80; Detailed Explanation, pp. 161, 162, 163).

(h) Such knowledge as is commonly found in all persons, even the simpler sort who are not capable of demonstrations, and which is acquired either from the testimony of others, such as parents, teachers, magistrates, and the people, or from the inspection of creatures, by a consequence that is indeed inferential, yet easy and obvious even to the unlearned (Musaeus, Introduction, sect. 23, 24, p. 81).

(i) Natural Theology, therefore, as a demonstrative habit, presupposes both kinds of knowledge and from them, as from a principle of knowing, it derives the rule of right operation and draws its conclusions (Musaeus, Introduction, sect. 28, p. 86). And thus Himmel writes (Himmel, Systematic Disputations, disp. 1, sect. 19, p. 3): "Natural Theology has two principles: an internal one, namely the koinai ennoiai (common notions), the remnants or relics of the divine image; and an external one, namely the inspection of creatures."

### 11 To the material object belong the subject of operation

To the material object belong the subject of operation, the causes and means of attaining the end, and indeed, in its own way, the End itself, both formal and objective, insofar as the latter is known precisely through demonstration.

(a) By "material object" are understood the things to be known in Natural Theology considered as a science: namely, the things it considers and about which it draws its conclusions, for the purpose of explaining their nature and proving their truth, from some antecedent cognition or from certain more known and prior principles (Musaeus, Introduction, sect. 14, p. 47).

(b) For the subject of operation, insofar as it is placed under a certain operation for the sake of attaining the end, falls under the consideration of Natural Theology as a practical science. It must be admitted, however, that in the state of corruption, the full account of the subject and the depravity of its corruption cannot be sufficiently known through the light of nature, as much of it as still remains (Musaeus, Introduction, sect. 31, p. 87).

(c) For the relation of causes and means to the end is most evident; see what we said at Section VI and following.

(d) For knowledge of the formal end, if not distinct (which we said at Section IV, note e, cannot be investigated by the guidance of the light of nature with respect to its specific character), at least confused knowledge depends on the objective end and can be sought from it.

(e) Namely, the existence of God, together with His attributes and essential perfections, can indeed be demonstrated a posteriori from created things as divine effects and from their more careful consideration. The schools of the philosophers treat of these matters everywhere and may be consulted. In the meantime, see Musaeus, Introduction, sect. 26 ff., pp. 82 to 86.

### 12 The parts of Natural Theology are three

The parts of Natural Theology are three. The first concerns the End, the second the Subject of Operation, and the third the Principles and Means.

(a) These parts ought to be arranged according to the analytic method, just as is done in other practical sciences.

### 13 Natural Theology may be described as a practical science which

Natural Theology may be described as a practical science which, from the principles of nature, prescribes to the human wayfarer a worship fitting to God, and which explains, confirms, and defends that worship, for the sake of attaining eternal blessedness in God and from God.

Compare Musaeus, Introduction, sect. 41, p. 103. And so much for Natural Theology.

### 14 In order that we may be rightly informed concerning Revealed Theology

In order that we may be rightly informed concerning Revealed Theology, it must first of all be established that there exists a certain supernatural divine revelation. This, however, is evident not only to us who have been born in the Church, but also to the Gentiles.

(a) For once this has been shown, it is then without difficulty inferred that there exists a habit of Revealed Theology, by which certain persons are rendered capable of so knowing the things that have been divinely revealed that they can teach, explain, confirm, and defend them. For not only is the immediate divine revelation recognized as having been given to a few precisely so that through these divinely instructed persons others might be taught, but revelation itself expressly teaches that God gives teachers for the equipping of the saints (Ephesians 4:12), and elsewhere.

(b) For in part, the revelation contained in Scripture became known to us in early youth through the guidance of parents or teachers; and in part, that same revelation bore testimony concerning its own divine origin and engendered divine faith (Musaeus, Introduction, ch. 3, sect. 2, p. 106).

(c) This is what we noted at Section IV from Himmel: that Natural Theology itself gradually leads people toward supernatural Theology. To this end he cites Romans 1:19, 20 and Acts 17:27. Accordingly, when the Gentiles knew that God exists and that the human soul survives the death of the body; that there are diverse states after death for the good and the wicked; that human beings are most prone to sinning and daily offend God; and that they possess no means within Natural Theology by which they might appease God, they easily arrived at the thought that God, in His goodness, must have shown somewhere, through a special revelation, the way and means of salvation. Moreover, it is established through experience that no nation has ever remained content with Natural Theology alone (Musaeus, Introduction, and part 2, ch. 5, sect. 1, sect. 15, p. 387).

### 15 The habit of Revealed Theology is a science

The habit of Revealed Theology is a science, if not a science in the primary or strict sense, then at least in a broader signification. And indeed it is a practical science.

(a) That Revealed Theology, properly speaking, is a habit, was openly declared by the Wittenberg theologians on the occasion of the Magdeburg controversy between M. Andreas Cramer and his colleagues in 1623, so that they professed astonishment that this should be called into doubt by anyone. The Leipzig theologians likewise affirmed the same in 1624, as found in the Appendix to the Dedekenn Counsel, fol. 136, adding that if the name "theology" is taken to mean "doctrine," this usage arises through metalepsis. Other theologians also for the most part taught that theology considered ousiodos (essentially) denotes a habit of the mind, while considered symbebekotds (accidentally and relatively) it denotes a doctrine; that is, it is accidental to theology that it be taught or learned (Musaeus, Introduction, part 1, ch. 1, sect. 2, p. 3).

(b) Since it is established that theology is a habit of the mind, there is good reason to inquire to which species it may most properly be referred, so that we may grasp its nearest genus concept. Now among the habits that have hitherto been recognized, there is no species to which it can more properly be referred than to science. For by its very nature it tends toward teaching, explaining, and confirming the matters placed before it as a certain and determinate object, and therefore it draws certain conclusions from certain principles, that is, it constructs demonstrations, which is proper to science and belongs equally to no other habit (Musaeus, Introduction, ch. 3, sect. 4, pp. 112, 113). To the same end tend the words already written in 1598 by our own Georg Mylius (Mylius, Positions on the Word of God and Holy Scripture, thesis 1): "Just as every science emerges from its own principles through the conclusions of proofs and demonstrations, so too does theology have its own principle in the Christian religion," and so forth. The same author also set forth in a special disputation held in 1602 the method of tes theologikes apodeixeos (theological demonstration), and showed that apodeixis (demonstration), although it pervades all kinds of sciences, is nevertheless nowhere more perfect than in theology, in which, on account of divine revelation, there is such great certitude that no equal or greater can be given (see thesis 45 and following). Thus those who acknowledge Revealed Theology to be a habit of the intellect, and to be a habit of teaching and deducing certain conclusions about a peculiar and determinate object, such that the connection of the terms is necessary because the conclusions depend on necessary and certain premises, not without reason establish science as the genus of theology.

(c) Namely, if it be required for science simply and properly (as is commonly held following Aristotle) that it construct demonstrations from evident and self-evident principles. For it must be admitted that Revealed Theology, in the principal heads of Christian doctrine called Mysteries, deduces its conclusions from divine revelation alone, which is naturally non-evident (Musaeus, Introduction, pp. 116, 117). Meanwhile, retaining the name of science, it is better to express in the genetic concept of theology itself those features which belong to it as a habit, not only of the mind and indeed a practical one, but as a habit of conclusions, that is, a demonstrative habit, features which it shares with other habits of the mind but which are suited to designating the concept not of a more remote but of a nearer genus, rather than to omit all these and command students and teachers to be content merely with the name "habit," or "habit of the mind," or "habit of the practical intellect," or "divinely given habit," none of which expresses the nature of a demonstrative habit.

(d) For all conclusions are practical, if not formally, then at least virtually. Some formally prescribe something to be done or omitted, for example: "The Triune God is to be worshipped." Others, by their conjunction with other formally practical conclusions, yield a formally practical conclusion, for example: "Christ is true God," whence it is concluded: "Therefore, one must believe in Him" (Johann Olearius, Universal Theology, prooemium, pp. 8, 9). To the same effect is what Gerhard writes (Gerhard, Exegesis of the Theological Commonplaces, prooemium, sect. 12, p. 5): "All things that are taught in theology pertain to praxis, if not immediately and directly, then mediately and indirectly." That it is not repugnant for a science to be practical is shown by Jacob Martini (Martini, disp. 2, sect. 13 ff., p. 52 ff.; and disp. 4, sect. 22 ff., p. 86).

### 16 The end of Revealed Theology

The end of Revealed Theology, considered as a practical science, is twofold. The internal end consists in the acts of knowing the objects of theology, not in any manner whatsoever, but insofar as they must be accurately explained, confirmed, and defended, for the sake of the faith and salvation of human beings. The external end is faith itself and the salvation of human beings, together with those things that are conjoined with faith.

(a) Namely, as a practical science.

(b) For theology by its very nature attains these acts, and the theologian, by virtue of the science inherent in him, has them within his power (Musaeus, Introduction, ch. 3, sect. 6, p. 127; and Meisner, Philosophy of the Sacred, part 3, p. 112, where, having made a comparison between the theologian and the physician, he says the internal end of theology is "the theological healing, or working upon the human being who is to be saved," so that the theologian may be said to have rightly discharged his office if he has omitted nothing that lies within his power for healing and restoring human beings, even though he does not lead all to salvation).

(c) The external end lies outside the power of the theologian and is not always attained by virtue of the science that inheres in him, as is evident from experience (Meisner, Philosophy of the Sacred, sect. 17).

### 17 The external end is customarily distinguished into the ultimate and the intermediate

The external end is customarily distinguished into the ultimate and the intermediate. Each is further distinguished into the objective and the formal. The objective end is God, infinitely perfect and supremely good. The formal end is a certain operation directed toward God, by which we possess and enjoy Him as the supreme good. Thus the objective end is one and the same in both cases, but the formal end differs depending on whether one considers the ultimate or the intermediate end.

### 18 Namely, the formal ultimate end consists in the intuitive and clear knowledge of God

Namely, the formal ultimate end consists in the intuitive and clear knowledge of God, together with the most intense love of God thus intuitively known.

(a) Thus Christ in Matthew 5:8, when about to declare the blessedness of those who are pure in heart, says that they shall see God. And John (1 John 3:2), speaking of the future blessedness which has not yet appeared, places it in the fact that we shall see God (whose children we are) as He is. We are said in this way to possess God as the supreme good because God is apprehended through that act of the intellect and is rendered intimately present to us and united with us (Musaeus, Introduction, ch. 3, sect. 11, p. 130). We shall say more on this below in its proper place.

(b) By this love we cleave to God, clearly known or apprehended as our good, for His own sake. For it cannot happen that the will should not be drawn into the most intense love of God when the intellect perfectly knows Him as our supreme good (Musaeus, Introduction, p. 131).

### 19 The formal intermediate end is faith in Christ

The formal intermediate end is faith in Christ, as the cause of obtaining grace before God. To this end, therefore, there also pertains the love of God as reconciled to us; indeed also other acts by which we are made partakers of divine goodness, and in its own way the whole sanctity of life.

(a) For through faith we possess God as our good already in this life, insofar as Christ, whose merit we apprehend by faith, becomes our propitiation (Romans 3:25), so that we may have peace with God (Romans 5:1) and the right, or inheritance, of eternal life (John 3:16).

(b) Thus John conjoins the love of God with the true and saving knowledge of God (1 John 4:7, 8). And it is certain that by the act of love we already in this life cleave to God and enjoy Him as our good.

(c) For example, filial confidence, or the resting of the will in God as reconciled, as the cause of obtaining other goods; so that as children we cry out to God: "Abba, Father" (Romans 8:15). Whence there immediately follows also the hope of those goods, both spiritual and temporal, as in the same passage, verse 24, we are said to be saved by hope, that is, to expect salvation firmly by the act of hope; and in verse 28, being firmly persuaded and therefore also confidently hoping or expecting that all things work together for our good.

(d) Namely, theology tends altogether toward the whole sanctity of life, and in order to obtain it, is occupied in teaching and confirming conclusions that lead to this end and aim at it as at a target. It is certain, however, that sanctity of life does not have the character of a cause in the order toward the ultimate end in the same way as faith does. Rather, just as the term "means" is used broadly, so too the term "intermediate end" must be taken here in a broader signification. For this reason, some prefer here the term "secondary end" or "concomitant end." Meanwhile, Forster writes (Forster, Theological Problems, disp. 1): "The architectonic end of theology consists in praxis, which praxis is exercised either in faith or in life" (thesis 19 and following, up to 23). And Jacob Martini (Martini, sect. 34, p. 84) says that the external end of theology is piety, the true description of which is found in 1 Timothy 1:5: "The end of the commandment is charity out of a pure heart, a good conscience, and faith unfeigned." He adds the further passage of Hebrews 12:14: "Without holiness no one shall see God." Gerhard likewise (Gerhard, Exegesis, prooemium, sect. 12, p. 5) says that the praxis toward which theology tends as its end consists in doing the will of God, according to Matthew 7:21, Luke 6:46, and John 13:17.

If, therefore, the end of theology is the sanctity of life, yet one does not rest in it as the ultimate end but there is a further end, namely eternal salvation, in such a way that, although sanctity of life is not prescribed so that by it, as by a cause, we might attain eternal life, yet it is prescribed lest we fall away from it: why should the sanctity of life not rightly be called an intermediate end of theology? And if anyone should call it, with the qualification, a non-causal intermediate end (with respect to the ultimate end), we shall not object.

### 20 The subject of operation is the human being as sinner

The subject of operation is the human being as sinner, insofar as he is to be led to eternal salvation.

(a) That there is a subject of operation in Revealed Theology is acknowledged by our theologians who hold Revealed Theology to be a practical habit. And although the philosophers otherwise teach that the subject of operation in practical habits and sciences ought to bring a certain natural capacity (hikanotes) or aptitude for performing the operation that is prescribed, and although they further restrict praxis to things that are eph' hemin (in our power), while here the practice of faith depends on the supernatural grace and influence of God, and the human being is by nature unfit for it, like one who is dead: our theologians nevertheless judge it sufficient in this case that the end is to be introduced into the human being himself as the subject through certain means, or that the human being is to be led to the end through those means (Gerhard, Exegesis, sect. 28, p. 27; Meisner, Philosophy of the Sacred, part 3, pp. 114, 121). The subject of operation moreover coincides with the "end for whom" (Musaeus, Introduction, sect. 15, p. 136).

(b) That is, one who is corrupted or subject to sin, as every human being carnally begotten is throughout his entire life after the Fall. For we do not take the state of sin so strictly as to oppose it only to the state of regeneration; we rather acknowledge that even the regenerate person continues to stand in need of theological praxis as long as he is on the way or in this life.

(c) Namely, the sinful human being constitutes the material subject of operation, while insofar as he is to be formed and led to salvation, he constitutes the formal subject of operation (Gerhard, Exegesis; Meisner, Philosophy of the Sacred, part 3, p. 115).

### 21 The efficient cause of the formal ultimate end is the Triune God

The efficient cause of the formal ultimate end is the Triune God.

(a) That is, the efficient cause of that operation by which we perfectly possess and enjoy God Himself as our supreme good.

(b) For God alone can endow the human intellect with the light of glory and so elevate it to elicit that operation. God alone likewise can so perfect the will that the most intense act of love arises within it.

(c) For the bestowal of blessedness is an external work common to the three Persons.

### 22 The internal impulsive cause is the goodness of God

The internal impulsive cause is the goodness of God. The external, or meritorious, cause is the merit of Christ.

(a) Not only because blessedness is not owed to the human being by divine justice, but especially if one considers the blessedness to be given to a sinner.

(b) For since the justice of God, offended by sins, demands from the human being either satisfaction or punishment, the grace or goodness of God is not a complete principle of our salvation unless the merit that satisfies divine justice intervenes. And so Paul, in Romans 3:24, conjoins in the order of the sinner's justification the grace of God and the redemption that is in Christ Jesus. And in 1 Timothy 2:4, 6, having said that God wills all to be saved, he immediately adds the Mediator between God and human beings, who gave Himself as a ransom for redemption, so that we might be saved.

### 23 Faith in Christ is also rightly numbered among the causes of salvation

Faith in Christ is also rightly numbered among the causes of salvation.

(a) For thus faith is conjoined with the other causes, namely the grace or love of God and the merit of Christ (John 3:16). And elsewhere we are said to be saved dia tes pisteos, through faith (Ephesians 2:8), and to live ek pisteos, from faith (Romans 1:17; Galatians 3:11; Hebrews 10:38).

(b) Not, however, considered in itself and absolutely, as it is an act or quality, nor insofar as it is effective through love, but in its relation to its object, which is Christ the Mediator. If one must assign faith to some specific genus of cause, then just as it must be admitted that faith does not stand in relation to salvation and the beatific vision in the manner of an efficient, material, formal, or final cause, and that its causality consists in this, that while it presents to God the merit of Christ as apprehended by the human being, it thereby moves God to confer salvation on that person out of grace, so faith is rightly referred to the genus of impulsive cause. And because it moves God not by its own dignity but by that of Christ's merit, it may be called, in distinction from the merit of Christ itself, the less principal impulsive cause (Musaeus, Introduction, sect. 18, pp. 138, 139).

### 24 And because faith is conferred on human beings only by God

And because faith is conferred on human beings only by God, who works and confirms it through the Word and Sacraments as through instruments, these too are rightly numbered among the causes of salvation.

(a) For faith is not a work of human powers, but is supernaturally conferred on the human being who is by nature unfit to believe, as we shall see below.

(b) Thus in James 1:21, the Word of God is called the seed from which the faithful are born, and accordingly an active power and true causality in the order of producing faith in human beings is attributed to it. And Baptism, in Titus 3:5, is called the washing of regeneration, namely because regeneration depends on it as on a cause.

(c) For since the Word and Sacraments are causes of faith, which is a cause of salvation, they are also rightly regarded as causes of salvation itself.

### 25 The object of Revealed Theology is twofold

The object of Revealed Theology is twofold: material and formal. The material object consists of the things revealed, which are known in Revealed Theology. To this belong not only the subject of operation and the causes and means of attaining the end, but also the End itself, insofar as it is known by the habit of theology. The formal object, that is, the principle and ground of knowing on which depends the knowledge of the things set forth in Revealed Theology, is divine revelation.

(a) The things revealed are here understood as those things which have been supernaturally manifested by God, whether they could also have been known through the light of nature or not, as will be evident from what follows.

(b) In other respects, the end is indeed the principle of knowing in practical sciences. But the objective and likewise the formal end of Revealed Theology is not so well known that it need not be handed down and taught under some other previously known ground of knowing, namely divine revelation (Musaeus, Introduction, sect. 24, pp. 151, 152).

(c) This is otherwise called the First Truth revealing. By this single name, if we speak of theology as it exists today, is understood the divinely inspired (theopneustos) Scripture, which testifies of itself through the concurrence of God in the mind of the human being, and from which all theological conclusions are deduced, as will be taught in the following chapter.

### 26 The material object is distinguished into things to be believed and things to be done

The material object is distinguished into things to be believed and things to be done. "Things to be believed" are those which so pertain to faith that they are not formally operations directed by prior practical acts, yet they must be believed by those who are to attain salvation: for example, that God loves the human race; that Christ is the Son of God and the Son of Man; and so forth. By the name "things to be done" are understood the operations themselves, prescribed by the practical acts of theology, as well as the things to be applied to operation or acquired through operation, if not for the sake of attaining salvation, then at least lest we fall from it: for example, the actual or habitual apprehension of the merit of Christ; the actual or habitual love by which we love God, Christ, and our neighbor; the hope of eternal life; and so forth.

(a) If one considers the force of the terms, "things to be believed" and "things to be done" can coincide and sometimes are really the same. For "things to be done," by the very fact that they are supernaturally revealed, can rightly also be called "things to be believed." Conversely, if something is to be believed in such a way that it must be brought to bear on practice, it truly belongs to "things to be done" (Musaeus, Introduction, sect. 26, p. 156). How they are distinguished in common usage is clear from what follows in the thesis.

(b) For this reason it is evident that the foundation of this distinction is not the hypothesis that theology is a habit partly theoretical and partly practical. For even "things to be believed," although they are not formally praxeis (practices), are nevertheless treated for the sake of praxis, as we said above.

### 27 Things to be believed are otherwise called articles of faith

Things to be believed are otherwise called articles of faith, which in the broader signification are divided, first, into pure and mixed articles of faith, and second, into fundamental and non-fundamental articles.

Notes. Articles of faith are so called because from them, as from parts joined together in a close connection, faith, or the doctrine of faith that is to be believed, is constituted, just as the parts of fingers, fitted to one another and cohering in a close bond, are called articuli (joints) (Musaeus, Introduction, ch. 3, sect. 30, p. 163). Some prefer to call them articles not of faith but of the doctrine of faith. Yet it has long been the case that "faith" denotes not only that by which one believes, but also that which is believed, that is, the doctrine of faith.

It is certain that the term "article of faith" has sometimes been taken in a stricter signification, as it precisely denotes the mysteries of faith that are necessary to be believed for salvation, and therefore designates only pure articles, and those fundamental ones alone. Thus Luther, in his Commentary on Psalm 45 (Jena Latin edition, vol. 3, fol. 490), says: "Know this first, that articles of faith are truly propositions concerning such things as the eye has not seen, the ear has not heard, nor have they entered into the heart of man, and are taught and understood through the Word and the Holy Spirit alone. And it is the nature of all articles of faith that all reason recoils from them." Similarly, Conrad Schlüsselburg (Theology of the Calvinists, book 2, p. 13) declares that the customary definition of articles of faith handed down by our theologians runs as follows: "An article of faith is a proposition or doctrine, not known naturally but divinely revealed and delivered from the express Word of God, or constructed by an indubitable consequence therefrom, concerning God, His essence, will, Word, sacraments, and benefits, pertaining to the true worship of God and the salvation of human beings, to be apprehended by faith." It is also well known how Hunnius, at the Regensburg Colloquy (Session 11, pp. 351 ff.), contended at length that all articles of faith without exception must necessarily be known and believed by each and every Christian. To these positions correspond what Musaeus taught concerning the requisites of an article of faith strictly so called (Musaeus, Question 4 on Syncretism, sect. 13, pp. 28, 29). In common usage, however, the term "article of faith" is frequently taken in a broader signification, especially today, and admits the division indicated in the thesis. Musaeus discussed this at length (Musaeus, Introduction, ch. 3, sect. 30, p. 162 ff.; Detailed Explanation, p. 111 ff.; Question 4 on Syncretism, annotations, p. 38).

### 28 Pure articles of faith are those which are known solely from divine revelation

Pure articles of faith are those which are known solely from divine revelation, such as the article concerning the Most Holy Trinity, the article concerning the Incarnation of the Son of God, and others. Mixed articles are those which consist not only of revelation but also of the light of nature: for example, the article concerning the existence of God and the divine attributes.

(a) And concerning these mixed articles it is rightly said that they are not only believed but also known. They are called articles of faith, however, not insofar as they are evidently known from the principles of the light of nature, but insofar as they are believed, that is, insofar as they are received with the assent of faith on account of divine revelation.

### 29 The fundamental articles of faith are those which bear such a relation to the…

The fundamental articles of faith are those which bear such a relation to the foundation of faith and salvation that they cannot be either ignored or denied while that foundation remains intact. The foundation of faith is understood in two senses: first, as the thing itself upon which the faith and salvation of human beings rests, and this is Christ (1 Corinthians 3:11), insofar as He is the cause of our salvation; second, as the doctrine in which that thing upon which faith rests is contained, and this is a complex of several propositions divinely revealed which bear a certain relation to salvation. The former foundation is called by theologians the Real or Substantial foundation; the latter is called the Dogmatic foundation.

Notes. The term "foundation" is properly considered in architectural usage, where it denotes that which is first among the things that enter into the constitution of a building as its parts, and is the reason and cause why that which is founded, namely the building, exists or can exist. Hence, in this context, the foundation of faith and salvation is that which is primary in saving faith and in the salvation of human beings, and is the reason and cause why saving faith and salvation itself exist or can exist (Musaeus, Introduction, ch. 3, section 34, pp. 166-167).

Thus Paul declares that the foundation upon which the Church, that is, the assembly of the faithful and of those to be saved, insofar as it is such, and consequently the saving faith of human beings, rests, is Jesus Christ; nor can any other foundation be laid besides this one (1 Corinthians 3:11).

Now, just as Christ is the cause of our salvation by the fact that, through His merit satisfying divine justice, He moves the benevolent will of God to remit our sins and to confer eternal salvation, so God Himself is not excluded but included in the foundation of faith and salvation as the efficient cause, and His grace or philanthropia (love of humanity) as the internal impulsive cause of conferring salvation upon us (Musaeus, Introduction, p. 169).

So also in Ephesians 2:20, Paul says that the faithful have been built upon the foundation of the Prophets and Apostles, that is, the doctrine preached by them; indeed, the chief cornerstone being Jesus Christ Himself, to whom the reason of the foundation ultimately returns (Musaeus, Introduction, pp. 171- 172).

For the individual articles that are called fundamental do not, when considered separately, constitute the dogmatic foundation of faith; rather, all of them taken conjunctively do so. But when one or another fundamental article is removed, faith itself and salvation fail (Musaeus, Introduction, p. 172).

All of these articles certainly bear some relation to salvation, though not an entirely equal one, as will become clear from what follows. In the meantime, it is not necessary for a fundamental article that its relation to salvation be handed down in Scripture under an express necessity of believing unto salvation. For although this sometimes occurs, for example, with regard to the article concerning the one only true God and concerning the Son of God sent in the flesh (John 17:3), it nevertheless suffices if the relation of these articles to salvation is handed down in Scripture implicitly and by way of consequence, when those articles are proposed in such a manner, though not under an express necessity of believing, that their necessary connection with the foundation of salvation, Jesus Christ, can be understood from a deeper consideration of them and concluded by a ready and manifest consequence (Musaeus, On Syncretism, question 4, section 15, p. 30).

### 30 The fundamental articles of faith are distinguished into primary and secondary

The fundamental articles of faith are distinguished into primary and secondary.

Note. The reason for this distinction is grounded in the unequal relation and the unequal necessity of explicit knowledge of these articles for generating and sustaining faith.

### 31 Primary articles are commonly said to be those which cannot

Primary articles are commonly said to be those which cannot, while faith and salvation are preserved, not only not be denied but also not be ignored.

Note. That is, those whose explicit knowledge is necessary in order that saving faith be generated and exist (Hunnius, On the Fundamental Dissent, section 63, pp. 41-42; Musaeus, Introduction, pp. 176-177).

The a priori reason is that knowledge of them is necessary for apprehending or retaining the real foundation of salvation. For the foundation does not generate faith or cause salvation unless it is known (Musaeus, Introduction, p. 177).

### 32 The primary articles can in turn be distinguished into two kinds

The primary articles can in turn be distinguished into two kinds: first, those whose signified reality belongs to the intrinsic nature of the real foundation, for example, the article concerning Christ the Theanthropos (God-man), and likewise the article concerning the merit and satisfaction of Christ for our sins; and second, those whose signified reality, although it does not belong to the intrinsic nature of the real foundation, is nevertheless most closely connected with it, so that unless it is explicitly known, the remaining elements that enter into the constitution of that foundation will not be sufficient for generating and sustaining saving faith.

Examples of this second kind include: the article concerning God and Him as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; the article concerning the gracious will of God by which He wills all human beings to be saved; the article concerning sin, by which we are polluted, rendered hateful to God, and made worthy of punishment; the article concerning justification, that is, the remission of sins to be obtained through Christ; the article concerning faith, through which the remission of sins is obtained; and the article concerning the blessed life which those who have departed this life with God as propitious will attain.

Notes. Just as the real or substantial foundation of salvation is Christ, insofar as He is the meritorious cause of obtaining from God the remission of sins and eternal salvation (as stated in the note to Section 29), so the article concerning Christ the Theanthropos (God-man) presents Him who is the meritorious cause, and the article concerning the satisfaction of Christ for sins presents that by which He merits the remission of sins. Both, therefore, belong to the nature of the real foundation.

For in order that it may be known that Christ has made satisfaction for us, it is necessary to know that He underwent and performed something which human beings ought to have undergone or performed, and thus that He is a human being. It is also necessary to know that what He performed or underwent was sufficient, or had adequate worth and value, and thus that He is God: whether this, that Christ is the Theanthropos (God-man), be known directly through preaching, or indirectly, when one judges from the effect to the cause (Hunnius, On the Fundamental Dissent, p. 183, section 294).

For just as there is a most intimate connection between the meritorious cause and the efficient cause which, moved by the merit, bestows the effect, so if anyone is ignorant that there is a God who confers the remission of sins and salvation, that person cannot acknowledge Christ as the meritorious cause of salvation (Musaeus, Introduction, pp. 173- 174).

For it is necessary to know the Father, so that He who offers so great a grace to the human race may not be unknown. If the Father, then also the Son, for whoever is ignorant of the Father is also ignorant of the Son (and whoever does not have the Son does not have the Father either). Furthermore, by the same necessity by which the acknowledgment of the Father demands knowledge of the Son, the acknowledgment of the Father and the Son who spirate demands knowledge of the Holy Spirit (Hunnius, On the Fundamental Dissent, sections 272-273, pp. 172-173, and section 427, p. 270; cf. Musaeus, On Syncretism, question 4, section 9, p. 26). It should be noted, however, that it is one thing to consider the mystery of the Trinity formally and distinctly with the personal characters, that is, when the ternary numbering number is simply attended to and precisely three persons, no more and no fewer, are posited in the Trinity; and another thing to consider it materially, that is, according to the numbered number, when one believes in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit (Johann Meisner, Irenic Deliberation, section 2, sections 211 ff., p. 191; cf. Hülsemann, Apologetic Dialogue, p. 56).

The benevolent and gratuitous will of God is the proēgoumenē (antecedent) or internal impulsive cause of the remission of sins obtained for us, with which, therefore, the merit of Christ is most closely connected as the external impulsive cause, which would indeed have no place without it. For if God had not so loved human beings as to give His only-begotten Son for them, there would be no reason why God should accept the merit of Christ as something foreign on our behalf as though it were our own; for this entire matter depends upon the benevolent will of God toward us miserable human beings, as Musaeus writes (On Syncretism, question 4, section 9, p. 26).

Moreover, the dogma concerning the universality of divine grace (as well as that concerning the universality of the death of Christ), when taken literally and universally, as it absolutely ought to be taken, is so simply necessary for all to believe that no one, through the Word of God in the ordinary and customary manner (whatever may be said concerning simpler believers and the special mode of gracious operation by which the Holy Spirit works faith in them), can be certain concerning himself individually that God wills him to be saved (that Christ died for him) except through those parts of doctrine actually known and believed: as the aforesaid Musaeus expressly teaches (Musaeus, On Syncretism, pp. 66-67). With this Johann Meisner fully agrees (Irenic Deliberation, section 2, section 228, pp. 200- 201), where, discussing those universal propositions without which, he says, no one can certainly know and establish that the benefits won by the death of Christ pertain to him, he adds these words:

If, however, I should altogether concede that some person, for example Adam and Eve, could have conceived faith, or could still conceive it, who perhaps has never heard anything concerning the universal benevolence of God and the universal merit of Christ, or on account of weakness of intellect, defect of judgment, or some other cause could not penetrate it, I nevertheless deny that this can happen if the intellect is imbued with the contrary error of particularity.

The satisfaction of Christ for sins indeed implies a certain relation to sins (Musaeus, On Syncretism, p. 27). And unless someone knows that human beings sin, and each person in particular understands that he himself has sinned, no faith is to be hoped for: these are the words of Hunnius (On the Fundamental Dissent, section 340, p. 206; cf. section 454, p. 291).

For if there were no justification, the merit of Christ would profit us nothing (Musaeus, On Syncretism, p. 27). And Christ the Mediator stands in relation to the remission of our sins as the meritorious cause stands to the effect to be acquired or already acquired by meriting. Between the meritorious cause and the effect, however, there is this perpetual connection: that if the effect, of which the merit is the cause, is not granted, the meritorious cause would be null, or certainly its endeavor, labor, action, or suffering undertaken for the sake of meriting the effect would be vain and void (Musaeus, Introduction, p. 173).

For if there were no faith, the merit of Christ would profit us nothing (Musaeus, On Syncretism, p. 27). And just as it is necessary to know that Christ by His merit has acquired for all the grace of the remission of sins, so it is necessary to know that the merit of Christ actually benefits believers for the obtaining of the remission of sins.

What we have said in the note concerning the article of justification pertains in its own way here as well. For eternal life also stands in relation to Christ and His merit as an effect to a cause. And if anyone is ignorant that there exists a blessed life which those who depart this life with God as propitious will at length attain, that person can neither acknowledge Christ as the meritorious cause of our salvation nor fix upon Him the trust of obtaining eternal life from God (Musaeus, Introduction, pp. 173-174).

### 33 The secondary fundamental articles are commonly described as those parts of…

The secondary fundamental articles are commonly described as those parts of Christian doctrine which, although they can be ignored while the foundation of salvation is preserved, nevertheless cannot be denied while that foundation remains intact. Such are the articles concerning the characteristic properties of the divine Persons; concerning the personal union considered distinctly and the communication of attributes in Christ; concerning original sin; concerning the decree of election in view of final faith; concerning justification through faith alone, excluding the merit of works; and others. Although the explicit knowledge of these is not common to all simpler believers, nevertheless their denial on the part of the one who denies them cannot stand together with faith and salvation, unless a great simplicity and ignorance of the consequence (by which that denial is by consequence opposed to the very foundation of faith), and a mind abhorring the error that directly opposes the foundation of faith, and prepared to admit a better interpretation, intervene.

Notes. These are parts and declarations of the primary articles of faith themselves rather than constituting peculiar, complete, and distinct articles of faith in their own right, although in a more general signification they may rightly be called articles of faith insofar as they pertain to faith and cohere with the foundation of faith. For example, in the article concerning the Person of Christ, there are contained three parts concerning the three genera of the communication of attributes (Musaeus, On Syncretism, pp. 53-54; cf. Detailed Explanation, pp. 126 ff.).

In this respect they are called secondary and are contradistinguished from the primary. According to others, they are said to be necessary to believe, not in themselves positively and directly (which is proper to the primary fundamental articles), but by reason of another, negatively, indirectly (Hunnius, On the Fundamental Dissent, section 63, p.

42, and section 284, p. 178; Meisner, Irenic Deliberation, section 2, section 227, p. 199).

In this respect they merit and retain the name of fundamental articles.

The reason is that the denial of such an article necessarily and always implies an error indirectly opposed to the foundation of faith and salvation, and by which, through consequence, that foundation, or something without which it cannot be preserved, is destroyed (Musaeus, Introduction, p. 177).
