For just as the divine Persons are constituted in the being of certain persons through certain properties or hypostatic characters, and are distinguished from other persons by them, so when those properties are denied, the divine Persons themselves are denied in their being. In the meantime, those who have never even considered what distinguishes a person from an essence, or in what the personality of the Holy Spirit differs from the personality of the Son, that is, the Messiah, or what the proper and distinctive character of each is, and other such corollaries, can nevertheless believe in and worship the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit as the one true God (Hülsemann, Apologetic Dialogue, p. 56; Johann Meisner, Irenic Deliberation, pp. 191-192).

For the personal union and the communication of attributes are contained in the Person of Christ the Theanthropos (God- man), and His merit necessarily presupposes both. Therefore, whoever acknowledges and believes in the Person of Christ the Theanthropos (God-man) thereby also believes, if not explicitly, then implicitly, in the personal union and the communication of attributes. And conversely, whoever denies the personal union or the communication of attributes, or confuses the natures or the properties of the natures, by consequence denies Christ the Theanthropos (God-man) Himself, and imagines Him to be either only God, or only a human being, or two Christs (Musaeus, Introduction, pp. 175-176).

For generating trust in Christ, an explicit knowledge of original sin is not simply required, except for the purpose of guarding against the contrary opinion, which is the persuasion of innate holiness and the capacity to keep the divine commandments; for if anyone is deceived by this, he will never arrive at the acknowledgment of sin and salvation (Hülsemann, Calvinism Irreconcilable, p. 475; Johann Meisner, Irenic Deliberation, section 2, section 229, p. 201).

For just as the decree and its execution must accurately correspond to one another, so if it is denied that the decree of election was made in view of faith in Christ, it will by consequence also be denied that God in time saves human beings in view of faith in Christ: as Musaeus demonstrates (On the Eternal Decree of Election, especially ch. 5, sections 119 ff.). It is certain, however, that a simple ignorance of that decree does not obstruct the faith of simpler believers, who can nevertheless embrace the grace of God and the merit and satisfaction of Christ as the cause of salvation, even if they have not thought about the decree of election.

Indeed, Scripture itself opposes faith and works in justification in such a way that it argues from the positing of one to the destruction of the other, for example, from justification by works to the negation of justification by faith (Romans 3 and 4). In the meantime, one who has not thought about justification by faith alone and not by works can nevertheless believe in Christ and through this faith obtain the remission of sins. Hence also Johann Meisner reckons this dogma among those which become necessary only accidentally, and only so that the opposite error or false opinion might not creep into the intellect, which would undermine or destroy what has once been rightly established (Meisner, Irenic Deliberation, section 2, section 239, p. 205).

Indeed, whoever denies some secondary fundamental article in such a way that he can simultaneously see and does see that, with that article denied, some primary article of faith and consequently the very foundation of faith is overturned by consequence, such a person does not merely indirectly, by virtue of that denial, oppose the foundation of faith, but now, through the error deduced from that negation, directly destroys the foundation of faith itself, and prevents faith from being generated or existing in it (Musaeus, Introduction, p. 177).

For since the denial of a secondary article is not opposed to the foundation of faith except through consequence, and the one who out of simplicity embraces that negation does not grasp the consequence, therefore that denial can stand together with the foundation itself in such a subject. And because the express knowledge of the article that is denied is not simply necessary for generating faith and causing salvation, therefore the denial of it, proceeding from mere ignorance and simplicity, can stand together with knowledge of the other things that pertain to the foundation itself insofar as it needs to be known for causing faith and salvation. Neither, therefore, is faith itself and salvation necessarily removed and impeded (Musaeus, Introduction, pp. 177-178). Hülsemann agrees (Calvinism Irreconcilable, pp. 432 ff.), where he sets forth this axiom: "Not every dogma which by its nature asserts or destroys something necessarily presupposed by faith or consequent upon it produces the same effect in the mind of every person." And while he advises that the question returns to the understanding of consequences, he thinks a distinction must be made between those who are seduced and teachable and those who are seducers and pertinacious; and he illustrates this by the example of the article on the communication of attributes.

Hülsemann is then followed by Kromayer (Prooemium to Positive-Polemic Theology, p. 4).

### 34 Non-fundamental articles are those which

Non-fundamental articles are those which, while the foundation of faith is preserved, can not only be ignored but also denied or disputed on either side. For example, concerning the sin and perpetual rejection of certain angels; concerning the immortality of the first human being before the Fall; concerning the Antichrist; concerning the origin of the soul through creation or through propagation; and so forth.

Notes. Nevertheless, even in these matters one must take care not to sin rashly against divine revelation and God Himself by embracing or professing error, and especially not to establish anything against conscience and with the seduction of others, by which the supports and the truth of one or more fundamental articles of faith would be undermined. For in this way, as through mortal sin, the Holy Spirit and faith can indeed be, and customarily are, expelled (Johann Meisner, Irenic Deliberation, section 242, p. 207).

On these matters see Nicolaus Hunnius (On the Fundamental Dissent, section 65, p. 43).

Thus indeed Luther believed, when, even though Dr. Pomeranus urged and pressed him to determine with certainty what should finally be established, he resisted, and although inclined toward the view of propagation, he nevertheless preferred to think and contend with Augustine that it should not be held as an article of faith, against bold dogmatists who are too little attentive in these matters: as reported by Johannes Wigand, who says he remembers his discourse (On Natural and Intermediate Things, pp. 38-39), and Andreas Musculus in his Commonplaces Collected from the Fathers (book 1, pp. 39b ff.), where he presents excerpts from Luther's own mouth in a disputation held in the very year in which he died, 1546. Wigand himself, after adducing reasons on both sides, concludes that it is permissible to leave the entire matter undecided, and that it is not to be considered heresy to incline to either opinion. And within these boundaries there remained, besides Musculus, also other authors of the Formula of Concord: Martin Chemnitz (Theological Commonplaces, part 1, book on original sin, question 4, pp. 234-236) and David Chytraeus (Commentary on Revelation, ch. 3, p. 91; cf. Balduin, Commentary on the Epistle to Titus, ch. 3, question 1, p. 1519).

### 35 The formal object of theology

The formal object of theology, that is, divine revelation, exercises its function by affecting, impelling, and bending the human will, so that the will commands the intellect to give assent.

Notes. For divine revelation contains these two principles: the first, that whatever God says or reveals is true; the second, that this, or (when we speak of revealed theology and its formal object for the present state) whatever is contained in Holy Scripture, God says. The first principle is evident from the nature and attributes of God known through the light of nature. The second is inevident; and therefore, since the intellect cannot clearly perceive its truth, that is, the identity of the predicate with the subject, it is necessary that assent be commanded to the intellect by the will, and for this reason that the will be attracted or moved by revelation itself to determine the intellect to assent. Thus in Acts 16:14, the Lord is said to have opened the heart of Lydia, that is, to have efficaciously moved her will (which is frequently called by the name of "heart" in Scripture) so that she might attend to the things being spoken by Paul, that is, so that the will itself might apply the intellect to attention and to giving assent (Musaeus, Introduction, ch. 3, section 39, p. 184).

In the meantime, theology formally considered remains a habit of the intellect. For it does not cease to be a habit of knowing and assenting; however, it connotes or presupposes a certain habit of the will, which authors call pious affection (Musaeus, Introduction, section 40, p. 185).

### 36 And from this it is established that theology is a habit supernatural in its substance

And from this it is established that theology is a habit supernatural in its substance, acquired indeed by our acts, but through the powers of grace and the operation of the Holy Spirit.

Notes. That is, such as it is and ought to be in itself and by virtue of its genuine formal object, or, considered with respect to its genuine habit of assenting. For if one considers the habit of apprehending objects already revealed and of transmitting what has been apprehended to others, in this sense, if the supernatural habit of assenting is absent, as is the case with unregenerate and impious persons, it is only equivocally called theology (Musaeus, Introduction, sections 42-43, pp. 189 ff.; cf. Philipp Jakob Spener, The General Knowledge of God, part 1, question 5, pp. 185 ff., where consonant passages from many of our theologians are adduced).

That is, today and according to the common law, or ordinarily. For otherwise we do not deny that the habit of theology can be obtained in an extraordinary manner through the immediate illumination and inspiration of God, as happened for the Prophets and Apostles (Musaeus, Introduction, section 43, pp. 192-193; Gerhard, Exegesis of the Prooemium, section 17, p. 9).

For this reason some call theology a theodotos (God-given) habit: which, in this sense, that is, with respect to the gracious concurrence of God or illumination, Musaeus acknowledges is rightly said (Introduction, section 44, p. 169), although, if the word is taken in the Aristotelian sense, in which eudaimonia (happiness) is called theodotos (Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, book 1, ch. 9), in opposition to things which are acquired by our own study and labor, he not without reason denies that our theology is theodotos (Musaeus, Introduction, p. 194).

It is acquired successively, not without the labor and study of several years. In which sense also Scherzer says that theology is an acquired habit, because it includes the meditation of Psalm 1:2, for which the preparation of the arts and languages is a prerequisite, and the prayer of Psalm 119:18 (Scherzer, System of Theology, Prolegomena, section 8, p. 3; cf. Gerhard, Exegesis of the Prooemium, section 17, p. 9).

### 37 Theology is distinguished from faith as that which includes from that which is included

Theology is distinguished from faith as that which includes from that which is included. For theology, beyond faith, also imports the faculty of explicating and confirming those things which have been revealed.

Note. See Musaeus (Introduction, section 45, pp. 199 ff.), where he also teaches that theology is more perfect than faith, not intensively, but extensively (p. 206).

### 38 Theology can be defined as a practical science which teaches

Theology can be defined as a practical science which teaches, confirms, and defends from divine revelation all those things which are necessary for a sinful human being to know for faith in Christ and to do for the holiness of life, for the sake of attaining eternal blessedness in God.

Note. See Musaeus (Introduction, section 46, p. 206).

### 39 The parts of revealed theology are to be arranged according to the analytical order

The parts of revealed theology are to be arranged according to the analytical order, so that first those things are treated which pertain to the end, then those which pertain to the subject of the operation, and finally those which pertain to the causes and means.

Note. For although the end does not belong to the class of natural things, as is otherwise the case in practical sciences, nevertheless the knowledge of it, drawn from divine revelation, is by nature prior to the knowledge of the means, likewise drawn from divine revelation (cf. Musaeus, Introduction, section 47 ff., pp. 209 ff.).

## 2 Prolegomena: On the Principle of Revealed Theology, or on Sacred Scripture

### 1 The principle of knowing

The principle of knowing, or the formal object, of revealed theology is divine revelation; and indeed, for the present state of the Church, it is mediate revelation, which is contained in the Sacred Scriptures as in sensible signs.

Notes. These two concepts coincide in substance, though they differ in their formal rationale: insofar as it is called a principle of knowing, it is spoken of in relation to conclusions as things derived from a principle; but insofar as it is called a formal object, it is spoken of as something set before the intellect in such a way that it serves as the form or formal rationale directing toward the knowledge of other things (Musaeus, Introduction, part 2, ch. 1, §1, pp. 221–222). On the term "divine revelation," see what was said above in chapter 1, §2, p. 5, and §25, pp. 38–39. Others use the term "Word of God" in place of "divine revelation," which amounts to the same thing, for they understand by it the word of divine revelation (Gerhard, Exegesis, Prooemium, §18, p. 9).

Formerly, God made use of many and various modes for revealing those things that pertain to the salvation of human beings, according to Hebrews 1:1. Specifically: (1) By an address of articulate voice, formed in the air beyond the order of nature, as revelation occurred to the Patriarchs (Genesis 18:2; 19:1ff.; 22:24), to Moses (Exodus 3:2; Numbers 12:6), and to the Israelite people (Exodus 19:10ff.). (2) By dreams, or images presented to the imagination of those who sleep (Genesis 28:12; Daniel 2:1ff.). (3) By ecstatic visions of those who are awake (Ezekiel 1:4; Daniel 10:15; Acts 10:10). (4) Finally, by immediate illumination of the intellect apart from sleep and vision (2 Timothy 3:16; 2 Peter 1:21). But now, after God willed that those things which are necessary to know concerning revealed matters for salvation should be comprehended in definite books, and since new revelations have ceased, the habit of theology ordinarily rests upon those ancient revelations, which were made immediately to the Prophets and Apostles and thus committed to writing, as its sole principle.

### 2 By the name "Sacred Scripture" is understood that collection or volume of books…

By the name "Sacred Scripture" is understood that collection or volume of books which not only treat sacred matters and tend toward faith and holiness of life, but which were also set down by a peculiar operation of the Holy Spirit, and which we commonly call the Bible.

Notes. "Sacred Scripture," according to the force of the word and customary usage, properly signifies, in the strict sense, a writing or books rather than their meaning, although it connotes the sense and mind of God as that which the books exhibit and for the sake of exhibiting which they were set down (Hutter, Compendium, question 1, from Chemnitz, Examination of the Council of Trent; and Cundis, Notes, §3, p. 5). Similarly, Hunnius writes in his first disputation, thesis 1: "Sacred Scripture is a volume consisting of certain books of the Prophets, Apostles, and Evangelists, which are called Biblical and Canonical" (Hunnius, Disputation 1, thesis 1).

It is called "Sacred" from its object, which it nevertheless has in common with other writings. Likewise, it is called "Sacred" from its end, which it also shares with others. The designation drawn from the efficient cause, however, is most properly distinctive of Sacred Scripture, as will become clear from what follows.

The Bible is so called κατ᾽ ἐξοχήν (par excellence), and by the plural name τῶν βιβλίων (of the books), since many books, written in diverse places and times, appear in one codex; just as elsewhere not only ἡ γραφή (the Scripture, John 2:22) but also αἱ γραφαί (the Scriptures, Matthew 21:42), αἱ γραφαὶ ἅγιαι (the holy Scriptures, Romans 1:2), and ἱερὰ γράμματα (the sacred writings, 2 Timothy 3:15) are cited. Although it must be admitted that within the Biblical codex, besides books proceeding from divine inspiration, other books are also contained together which are indeed sacred with respect to their object and end but were nonetheless set down by human effort, and that the name "Sacred Scripture" has customarily been attributed to the entire codex by synecdoche, we here retain the specific and proper signification.

### 3 The principal efficient cause of Sacred Scripture is God

The principal efficient cause of Sacred Scripture is God, the Triune God; yet by appropriation, the Holy Spirit.

Notes. See Romans 3:2, where Paul calls Scripture λόγια τοῦ Θεοῦ (oracles of God), that is, proceeding from God. And 2 Timothy 3:16, where Scripture is called θεόπνευστος (God-breathed), and by this very fact it is indicated that it depends efficiently upon God. For Scripture is an external work and a λόγος προφορικός (uttered word) of God, according to the one essence, wisdom, and power. This is said according to the manner of speaking received in the Scriptures, whereby there is attributed to the Holy Spirit as His proper work that which is common to the entire Holy Trinity. Thus Peter in his second epistle (2 Peter 1:21) says that the Prophets in their writings, according to verse 20, spoke φερόμενοι ὑπὸ πνεύματος ἁγίου (carried along by the Holy Spirit). And Paul, writing to the Corinthians (1 Corinthians 2:12), says that he speaks in words taught by the Holy Spirit (compare 2 Samuel 23:2).

### 4 The causality of the principal efficient cause is θεοπνευσία (theopneustia)

The causality of the principal efficient cause is θεοπνευσία (theopneustia), or divine inspiration itself; that is, an action of such a kind whereby God supernaturally communicated to the intellect of the writers not only concepts of things conformable to the objects to be written about, but also the concepts of the very words and of all the words by which those things were to be expressed, and excited their will to the act of writing.

Notes. This is the formal rationale by which God is constituted in the being of its cause and exerts His influence upon Scripture. For just as in 2 Timothy 3:16, where Scripture is called θεόπνευστος, its dependence upon God as cause is indicated, so at the same time it is established that God is constituted in the being of the efficient cause of Scripture through the very θεοπνευσία from which Scripture is denominated θεόπνευστος (Musaeus, Introduction, part 2, ch. 2, §3, p. 245).

Indeed, it is not so much the things according to their real being, insofar as they exist outside the intellect of the writer, as the concepts of the things to be expressed in writing that are inspired into the intellect of the writer. Moreover, we believe that the concepts not only of sublime matters exceeding the capacity of human reason, but also of all other matters that Scripture contains as things to be committed to writing, were inspired by God to the sacred writers, since πᾶσα γραφή (all Scripture), not merely some part of it, is said to be divinely inspired. Inspiration, furthermore, imports not a bare assistance or governance for the prevention of errors, but the very communication or suggestion of concepts, in the manner in which things are dictated into the pen of an amanuensis that he must write (Musaeus, Introduction, part 2, ch. 2, §3, notes 4–5, pp. 246ff.).

For just as Sacred Scripture, from the characters of written words and letters, has the quality of being a writing, so when the whole of Scripture is called θεόπνευστος absolutely, simply, and without any restriction, as we have indicated in the preceding note, it must be acknowledged that the concepts of the words to be expressed in letters were also inspired to the sacred writers. This Musaeus proved at greater length and responded to the objections of dissenters (Musaeus, Introduction, part 2, ch. 2, §3, note 7ff., pp. 250ff.). That he always taught this, he most clearly showed in his Treatise on the Questions concerning Syncretism and Sacred Scripture (book 1, question 3, pp. 319ff.; compare his Detailed Explanation, question 6, pp. 42ff.).

To this pertains what is said in 2 Peter 1:20– 21: that prophetic Scripture (προφητείαν γραφῆς) was not brought forth of old by human will (that is, those men did not produce their prophecies by their own impulse and judgment), but that, carried (φερόμενοι) by the Holy Spirit, they spoke, and indeed applied themselves to the exercise of the act, both of speaking and of writing. For partly the divine inspiration itself, by which the things to be committed to writing are suggested, imports an influence toward the exercise of the act of writing; and partly it is certain that the holy writers were stirred to write by an express command of God, as for instance Moses (Deuteronomy 31:19), Isaiah (Isaiah 8:1; 30:2), and John (Revelation 1:11, 19; 2:1, 8, 12, 18), or that other occasions and incentives to write were set before them by God's particular providence, by which they were made certain of the divine will (compare Musaeus, Introduction, part 2, ch. 2, §8, pp. 257ff.).

### 5 The impulsive cause of Sacred Scripture

The impulsive cause of Sacred Scripture, committed to writing by divine will, is internally the goodness of God, and externally the need of those human beings who are to be saved.

Notes. It is necessary to recognize this cause for those who inquire into and set forth the reasons of the divine counsel as to why God willed that the heavenly doctrine, which had for some time been preserved through the tradition of the living voice without the aid of writings, should be committed to letters (Gerhard, Exegesis, book 1, §19, p. 36). For the communication of Scripture made to human beings is indeed an unmerited benefit of God. The external cause is commonly called προκαταρκτική (the antecedent cause), in the same way that our theologians elsewhere call the antecedent cause of God's will to send His Son the misery of the human race.

The reason is that: (1) as the human race multiplied, (2) and the span of human life was shortened, it was no longer possible for all to be instructed in person by the living voice of the Patriarchs, who had been equipped with the immediate revelation of God, as formerly; (3) moreover, various corruptions of doctrine had crept in; and (4) given the weakness and frailty of memory of those to be instructed, it seemed most advisable to divine providence that the chief heads of divine revelations should be comprehended in writing (Gerhard, Exegesis, book 1, §19, p. 37).

### 6 The less principal efficient cause of Sacred Scripture was holy men

The less principal efficient cause of Sacred Scripture was holy men, Prophets and Apostles.

Notes. For God did not reduce our Scripture to writing with His own fingers or by an immediate operation, as He once did with the Decalogue, but made use of the labor of men as amanuenses, who depended upon God the inspirer as their principal cause with respect to both the specification and the exercise of the act of writing, although with respect to the actual characters of letters and syllables to be inscribed with a pen on parchment or paper, they acted as a principal cause by virtue of the art of writing, whether natural or once conferred through a supernatural influence (Musaeus, Introduction, part 2, ch. 2, §9, p. 259).

These men were not entirely free from sin in other respects, but they were not exposed to the danger of erring in the act of writing, since they were then entirely subject to the Holy Spirit. Thus in 2 Peter 1:21 they are called "men of God," that is, men peculiarly and immediately called and chosen by God to commit divine revelations to writing (Gerhard, Exegesis, book 1, §18, p. 35). "Prophets" here means men who committed Scripture to writing before the Incarnation of Christ, the nucleus of which was the coming Christ (see Hebrews 1:1; compare Musaeus, Introduction, part 2, ch. 2, §4, p. 252). By "Apostles" are designated not only those whom Christ chose during the days of His flesh for teaching all nations, together with those added after His ascension, namely Matthew and Paul, but also apostolic men, nearest to the Apostles in office and dignity, who were to instruct the universal Church through public writings (Musaeus, Introduction, part 2, ch. 2).

### 7 The material cause of Sacred Scripture consists of words

The material cause of Sacred Scripture consists of words, phrases, and periods: in the Old Testament according to the Hebrew language, and in the New Testament according to the Greek language; these being set down in a style, that is, a selection and arrangement of words, that varies according to the diverse talents, characters, dispositions, and customary manner of speaking of the individual writers.

Notes. This is that from which Sacred Scripture is composed, and which Sacred Scripture may have in common with other writings as signs of certain things. Otherwise it must be acknowledged that Scripture is not so much a substance composed of matter and form as a unity formed by the aggregation of parts (Gerhard, Exegesis, book 1, §74, p. 73). Words considered absolutely in themselves may be called the remote matter of Sacred Scripture; the same words placed or construed in context may be called its proximate matter (Musaeus, Introduction, part 2, ch. 2, §10–12, pp. 259ff.). To this seems to amount what Gerhard writes, namely that the material cause of Scripture formally considered can not unsuitably be held to be the very structure and series of the Biblical books (Gerhard, Exegesis, book 1, ch. 4, §54, p. 73; compare his Disputation 4, §2, p. 11).

Regarding the Old Testament, that is, the books written before the birth of Christ (designated by the term "Old Testament" taken in the systematic or dogmatic sense): although certain Chaldaic passages also occur, for example in Jeremiah 11:11, Daniel 2:4ff. to 8:2, and Ezra 4:8ff. to 6:19, and from 7:11ff. to 27. It is evident that God, in employing a particular language, accommodated Himself to the condition of the people whom He had until then willed to make especially partakers of His gracious revelation as a people chosen for His own possession.

Regarding the New Testament (by which name, taken in the systematic sense, are designated the books written after the birth of Christ): it pleased God to use the Greek language, which for some centuries had been most commonly used among both the Jews and nearly all the nations in which the Church was to be planted through apostolic preaching, and was still in use at the very time when the New Testament Scriptures were committed to writing. And from this divine condescension (συγκατάβασις) it also came about that the Greek diction was ἑλληνιστική (Hellenistic), that is, mixed with Hebraisms (Musaeus, Introduction, part 2, ch. 2, §11, p. 261; compare Scherzer, System, book 1, §14, p. 14).

Nevertheless, we do not say that solecisms or barbarisms are to be attributed to Sacred Scripture, nor did Musaeus ever maintain this. When formerly, in his Philological Disquisition on the Style of the New Testament, delivered in 1641, he defended certain learned and well-deserving men (who, in attempting to show the difference of style between Scripture and other writers illustrious in the Greek language, had used those terms following the precedent of Jerome among the ancient Fathers) from the imputed charge of impiety and blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, and for that purpose examined the arguments of a certain writer and noted the faulty reasoning; he did so in the same manner in which Hülsemann also believed those Fathers and more recent writers who had spoken in this way should be excused, and cited Musaeus's disquisition and the subsequent vindications (Hülsemann, Lectures on the Formula of Concord, article 1, ch. 3, §5, p. 222). Yet Musaeus not only never made the opinion itself his own, namely that there are truly barbarisms and solecisms in the Scriptures, but also testified several times in that very disputation and throughout the entire vindication that he did not embrace it. In that entire affair, he obtained the approval of Johann Major, at that time Primary Professor of Theology, whose congratulatory poem, which is as it were an epitome and recapitulation of almost everything disputed in that disquisition, still adorns the disputation itself. The appendix of Musaeus to his vindication of the disquisition deserves to be read (pp. 457–458; likewise, his Treatise on Syncretism and Sacred Scripture, book 1, pp. 319–320). For this reason also Scherzer in his System (p. 143), although he denies that solecisms (importing κακίαν, that is, ugliness) and barbarisms opposed to ἑλληνιστική (Hellenistic) Greek should be attributed to Scripture, nevertheless commends Musaeus's Disquisition on the Style of the New Testament.

Furthermore, as to the dispute concerning the Gospel of Matthew and the Epistle to the Hebrews, namely whether those books were first committed to writing in the Hebrew language (as seemed the case to not a few of the Fathers): it suffices here that the Greek text of those books which survives today, whether it is original or translated from another language, is truly θεόπνευστος (God- breathed), and therefore rightly comes to be counted as part of the αὐτόπιστος (self- authenticating) principle of the things to be believed (compare Musaeus, Introduction, part 2, ch. 2, p. 261).

Indeed, the matter itself shows that the manner of expression in the Scriptures appears in some places gentler and more subdued, in others more weighty and vehement; again, in some places humbler and less polished, in others more grand and refined; sometimes purer with respect to the use of a single language, at other times mixed with the idioms of other languages. And since the primary Author of Scripture is one, and the whole of Scripture is θεόπνευστος, it must be acknowledged that the Holy Spirit Himself, in suggesting the concepts of words, accommodated Himself to the character and condition of the amanuenses (Musaeus, Introduction, part 2, ch. 2, §13, pp. 262–263). This property of style, which some call the external and accidental form of Scripture, is rightly referred to the material cause as a material affection, as is gathered from what has been said (compare Musaeus, Introduction, part 2, ch. 2, §18, p. 272).

### 8 The form, or formal rationale

The form, or formal rationale, of Sacred Scripture consists in the very concepts of things and words (of which the written words are signs) insofar as they were divinely inspired into the minds of the writers.

Notes. This is that by which Sacred Scripture is constituted in its specific being, as by a reason that is prior and proper, and by which it is distinguished from every other writing (Musaeus, Introduction, part 2, ch. 2, §15, p. 265). For this reason some say that the internal form, or the formal element of Scripture, is its sense (Cundis, Notes on Hutter's Compendium, question 1, p. 7). For the sense of the words of Scripture is nothing other than the concepts of the mind by which objects are represented to the intellect; and when the things themselves are understood under the name of "sense," it is certain that they are regarded not in themselves but as they are signified by words and concepts (Musaeus, Introduction, part 2, ch. 2, §15, p. 269).

For just as Sacred Scripture is constituted in the generic being of a writing by the sense signified by words, so it is constituted in its specific being, that is, in the being of Sacred Scripture, by its sense insofar as it is θεόπνευστος (God-breathed). And it amounts to the same thing if you say that the form of Scripture is θεοπνευστία (theopneustia), provided this is not taken precisely for the action of inspiring (for in that sense it pertains to the efficient cause, as Gerhard also observed in his Exegesis, book 1, §305, p. 322), but terminatively, that is, insofar as it terminates in the very concepts of things and words in the intellect of the holy men who were to express them in writing. Whence also Himmel writes in his Syntagma (disputation 2, §17) that the internal form of Scripture is θεόπνοια (divine breathing). Compare Musaeus (Introduction, part 2, ch. 2), who also shows (p. 266) how not only in the autograph codices of the sacred writers, but also in the copies of scribes, and thus even today, the form of Sacred Scripture remains one and the same: namely, because those copies were fashioned after the pattern of the original Scripture, either immediately or mediately; whence, although the codices have been multiplied with respect to external features, nevertheless the same θεόπνευστοι (divinely inspired) concepts of things and words remain.

### 9 The object of Scripture

The object of Scripture, generally speaking, is all sacred matters in the recounting of which Sacred Scripture is engaged. Specifically, however, and primarily, it is those matters that are by their very nature ordered to the salvation of human beings, and that pertain either to dogmas necessary to be believed or to a manner of life befitting one who is to be saved.

Notes. This is also called the "matter about which." For it is certain that Sacred Scripture, committed to writing in a historical style, contains various things which, although not all equally necessary to know, nevertheless all contribute in their own way to edification, and are therefore rightly called the object of Scripture (Musaeus, Introduction, part 2, ch. 2, §14, p. 264). Thus Gerhard says that the Law and the Gospel are the principal heads of divine revelation, to which all things taught in the Scriptures can be referred (Gerhard, Exegesis, book 1, §52, p. 72). And in this respect the object of Scripture and the object of revealed theology coincide, although those things that are treated in Sacred Scripture beyond the primary object also pertain in their own way to revealed theology, whether for the illustration of dogmas of faith and morals, or for the interpretation of Scripture itself (Musaeus, Introduction, part 2, ch. 2, p. 265).

### 10 The persons for whose benefit Sacred Scripture is destined are all human beings…

The persons for whose benefit Sacred Scripture is destined are all human beings without distinction of ecclesiastical and secular estate, as those to be instructed from the Scriptures not only through the labor of others but also through their own effort; and specifically those who are or will be teachers of the Church.

Notes. This is the subject for whose good Sacred Scripture has been destined (Musaeus, Introduction, part 2, ch. 2, §23, pp. 277–278). Some use the term "object" for this (but distinguished from the material object, which is otherwise called the "personal object"; see Gerhard, Exegesis, book 1, §480, p. 525). This will become clearer if one considers the final cause, about which we shall speak presently, which by God's intention pertains to all human beings.

Certainly, in both the ancient Israelite Church and the early Christian Church, not only was Scripture publicly read and the people thereby instructed, but the reading of Scripture was also freely permitted and commended to all without distinction. From the Old Testament: Deuteronomy 6:6–8, 31:11–12, and Isaiah 34:16, where not only the public use in sacred assemblies but also the domestic reading of Scripture is commended to all the faithful. And David in Psalm 1:2 pronounces blessed the one who is occupied in meditation on the Law, that is, on Sacred Scripture, day and night.

In the New Testament, Christ in Luke 16:29 and 31, not incidentally in a parable but by the very force and scope of the parable, says that the writings of Moses and the Prophets are to be diligently studied, consulted, and embraced by every individual. And in John 5:39 He commends to the Jewish people the searching of the Scriptures, by which the readers themselves might strive to penetrate into the sense of Scripture and thereby to recognize the Messiah for the sake of attaining eternal salvation. The Christians of Berea are also praised for their diligence in reading the Scriptures and searching out their meaning (Acts 17:11), as is Timothy (2 Timothy 3:15).

Those who are teachers of the Church are to be instructed from the Scriptures not only for their own benefit but also for the good of others whom they serve. Compare 2 Timothy 3:16–17, where Scripture is said to be profitable for the man of God, to equip him sufficiently for all the works of his office.

### 11 The final cause of Scripture

The final cause of Scripture, and indeed its ultimate end, is eternal salvation. The intermediate end, with respect to all human beings, is faith in Christ; with respect to the ministers of the Church specifically, the ends of Scripture are the ministerial operations that depend upon divine revelation.

Notes. The ultimate end spoken of here is with respect to us; otherwise, the end that is absolutely ultimate, and common to all things that God does or gives, is the glory of God (compare Gerhard, Exegesis, §§361–362). On eternal salvation, see what was said above concerning the end of revealed theology in chapter 1, §§17–18, pp. 31–32; for the ultimate end of theology and of the principle of theology is the same.

Thus John, at the close of his Gospel (John 20:31), indicates the intermediate end of Scripture and joins it with the ultimate end, saying: "These things have been written, proximately indeed to this end, that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God; and that, believing, you may attain the ultimate end, that is, have eternal life through His name." Furthermore, other acts conjoined with faith are not here excluded but are in their own way rather included, according to what was said concerning the intermediate end of revealed theology in chapter 1, §19, pp. 32ff.

With respect to ministers, the ends are all those πάντα ἔργα ἀγαθά (all good works) that Paul enumerates and for the accomplishment of which he says Scripture is profitable (2 Timothy 3:16): namely, for διδασκαλία (teaching), that is, the instruction of human beings in those things that are necessary to know regarding the articles of faith and the whole of Christian doctrine; for ἔλεγχος (reproof), that is, the demonstration and refutation of errors that conflict with heavenly truth; further, for ἐπανόρθωσις (correction), that is, the correction of disordered morals through rebukes and admonitions by which human beings are drawn away from sins; and finally, for παιδεία ἡ ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ (training in righteousness), that is, exhortation to a just and holy manner of life (2 Timothy 3:16; see Gerhard, Commentary on this passage, where he also teaches how παράκλησις, consolation, for the sake of which Scripture is said to have been committed to writing according to Romans 15:3, is comprehended either under teaching or under training). And thus it is also clear that these ends, although they are not ends of Scripture considered simply in itself, but rather of Scripture considered specifically in relation to the ecclesiastical ministry, nevertheless are consequently directed toward faith in Christ; because the ministers of the Church, in teaching, refuting, correcting, and instructing others, labor to bring human beings to faith in Christ and to the holiness of life that perpetually accompanies it, and to preserve those who have been brought thereto (Musaeus, Introduction, part 2, ch. 2, §22, p. 277).

### 12 Among the properties of Sacred Scripture

Among the properties of Sacred Scripture, the first place belongs to its authority, that is, its manifest dignity, which moves the human intellect to assent to its statements, and the will to render obedience to its commands.

Notes. For in this way it becomes apparent how Sacred Scripture discharges the office of the formal object of revealed theology. This authority may in Greek be called αὐθεντία (authenticity), in the same way that among jurists, instruments and writings are called "authentic" when they possess a certain and just authority such as to be able to oblige to assent or even to obedience (compare Cundis, Notes on Hutter's Compendium, book 1, question 1, p. 20). For no one is said to be in authority or to have authority unless his dignity, by which he deserves assent or obedience, is so known as to attract minds to it. In this respect, some call the authority of Scripture ἀξιοπιστία (worthiness of belief), and others αὐτοπιστία (self-authenticating credibility); that is, authority in speaking or testifying, so that it may be believed. To this corresponds the term ἐξουσία (power), that is, the power of one who commands, or authority in prescribing.

### 13 This authority of Scripture

This authority of Scripture, considered in itself and absolutely, that is, with respect to the thing itself, depends solely upon the Author of Scripture, God, and results from His supreme and infinite truthfulness and power.

Notes. Authority primarily and of itself belongs to the Author of any statement or writing, such as a law or command, and the remote foundation of authority is the perfection of the Author considered in himself, while the proximate foundation is his perfection as known. Thence, that is, on account of the dependence of a statement or writing upon one who possesses authority, authority also belongs to the statement or writing itself; and thus the authority of Sacred Scripture is founded in its very θεοπνευσία (divine inspiration), that is, in its dependence upon God as the Author whose supreme perfection is known to all (Musaeus, Introduction, part 2, ch. 3, §§1, 4, pp. 282, 288).

This authority does not derive from the less principal cause, just as other writings derive their authority not from the amanuenses but from the one who composed them or dictated them into the pen (Musaeus, Introduction, part 2, ch. 3, §3, p. 289). And from this it is evident that Sacred Scripture does not have its authority from the Church, since the Church was not its Author or efficient cause (Musaeus, Introduction, part 2, ch. 3, p. 290).

For just as God, on account of His infinite knowledge and goodness, is supremely truthful in speaking, so that He can neither be deceived nor deceive, and assent is therefore rightly to be given to Him when He speaks; so Sacred Scripture, through its truthful dependence upon God, is likewise worthy of the assent of all human beings. And just as God by right of creation has supreme dominion over human beings as creatures, by virtue of which He can oblige them to render obedience to Himself; so Scripture, by virtue of its being the Word of God, is also worthy that all human beings should render obedience to its precepts (compare Musaeus, Introduction, part 2, ch. 3, §§6, 13, p. 289).

### 14 With respect to us

With respect to us, however, that is, in order for it to be established for us that Sacred Scripture is worthy of being given faith and obedience, it is necessary that not only the very perfections of God be known, but also the dependence of Scripture upon God, that is, its θεοπνευσία (divine inspiration).

Notes. Compare §11, note c, above. This knowledge, although it is not a constitutive part of the authority of Scripture, nor its cause or foundation or part of its foundation, is nonetheless a condition, on the part of human beings whose minds ought to be moved to faith and obedience, that is necessary (Musaeus, Introduction, part 2, ch. 3, §11, p. 292).

### 15 The authority of Scripture

The authority of Scripture, insofar as it regards the assent to be given to its statements, can be considered in two ways: partly precisely in relation to causing the assent of the things to be believed, whereby Scripture possesses the quality of being the principle of knowing and the formal object of faith and of revealed theology; and partly in relation to distinguishing, from Scripture itself as θεόπνευστος (divinely inspired) and truthful, other writings and doctrines that treat of matters of faith and morals, whereby Scripture possesses the quality of being canonical, that is, of being the norm and rule for discerning the true from the false.

Notes. The former is that which theologians commonly understand simply by the term "authority of Scripture," and in explaining which they are almost exclusively occupied; and it must be acknowledged that this authority is prior in the order of doctrine to the other, which implies the force of binding to obedience to its commands, since the latter presents no difficulty once the former has been demonstrated (Musaeus, Introduction, part 2, ch. 3, §14, p. 294).

Although the authority of Scripture is one and the same, founded in the truthfulness of God and the dependence of Scripture upon God, by which it is constituted both in the capacity of a formal motive for causing the assent of faith and in the capacity of a norm for examining and judging all other writings and doctrines; nevertheless, since Scripture is to be employed somewhat differently as a formal motive for causing the assent of faith (in which capacity the doctrine of Scripture can function in any language) and as a norm for discerning the true from the false (which Scripture performs only in the original text), it is rightly necessary to treat the authority of Scripture distinctly in regard to each of these functions (Musaeus, Introduction, part 2, ch. 3, §15, p. 295). The former might perhaps be called the motive authority, causative of faith. The latter is otherwise called the canonical or normative authority of the true and the false (compare Musaeus, Introduction, part 2, ch. 3).

### 16 The authority of Scripture

The authority of Scripture, considered in relation to causing the assent of faith, requires the knowledge of two complex principles. The first is: "Whatever Scripture was committed to writing by God's inspiration is certainly and infallibly true." The second is: "Sacred Scripture was committed to writing by God's inspiration."

The truth of the first principle is scarcely in doubt, for it is naturally and evidently known from the very apprehension of its terms. Concerning the second, however, a somewhat fuller investigation is required, insofar as the discussion concerns either the knowledge of human faith, by which the divine origin of Sacred Scripture becomes known, or the knowledge of divine faith.

Notes. Compare what was said in §13 above. The first principle is naturally and evidently known from the very apprehension of its terms. By "human faith" is understood a kind of knowledge whose ultimate ground of assent is human testimony or another probable reason that generates an opinion, so that it is judged credible that Sacred Scripture is not an invention of human ingenuity but truly divine, proceeding from God Himself. By "divine faith" is meant knowledge that is simply certain and excludes all fear of the opposite, on account of the altogether infallible certainty of the divine revelation or testimony upon which it rests as the ultimate ground of assent.

SECTION XVII. The arguments which declare the divine origin of Scripture to be recognizable, or credible, by human faith are partly internal, that is, drawn from the intrinsic nature and properties of Scripture itself, and partly external, that is, derived from sources outside of Scripture.

Note. For although these arguments do not themselves produce divine faith in Sacred Scripture, they nevertheless render no small but indeed an excellent service: namely, that contempt and rash judgments concerning a doctrine not sufficiently known may be restrained, and rather, by means of a certain opinative or humanly credible knowledge of the divine origin of Scripture being implanted in the minds of men, they may be prepared and led to read, study, and meditate upon Holy Scripture with eagerness and a desire to learn. In this way, once obstacles have been removed, Scripture itself may thereafter, with the concurrence of God, produce the divine faith that is to be accorded to it, as will be evident from what follows.

### 18 Among the internal arguments

Among the internal arguments, some arise from the material aspect, that is, the style, and others from the formal aspect, that is, the θεόπνευστος (God-breathed) sense and the things signified (see Musaeus, Introduction, part 2, ch. 5, section 1, and following, p. 305).

### 19 To the first class belongs the simplicity of style

To the first class belongs the simplicity of style, combined with a gravity worthy of God alone, and the fact that not infrequently the things to be believed and done are set forth expressly under the very name of God Himself.

Note. The simplicity of style does not mean that the diction is confused and jumbled, without connection or order of words and subjects, for that is entirely false. Rather, it means that Scripture does not employ the allurements of words or the artifice of secular eloquence adapted to captivate minds.

The gravity worthy of God alone refers to the fact that the things to be believed, although supremely sublime and difficult, are nevertheless set forth without demonstrations, by bare assertions; and the things to be done or avoided, although themselves arduous and burdensome, are nevertheless proposed as if by authority, and indeed to all men, even to those who have no superior on earth, by way of command or prohibition (Musaeus, Introduction, same place).

As for the formulas of speech in which God is introduced as speaking or testifying that He Himself is the one who declares this or that through His ministers, such as the Prophets: although insofar as God Himself, joining His power with this part or doctrine of Sacred Scripture as He does with others, works efficaciously in the human soul, the faith that arises is not so much human as divine (as Musaeus also acknowledges in his Questions on Syncretism and Scripture, section 1, question 1, section 7, pp. 84 and 195; compare also the Detailed Explanation, p. 40), yet when the argument is considered precisely insofar as it pertains to style and forms of expression, it must be admitted that false prophets and deceivers can and do commonly produce such sayings. Hence Johann Schröder, in his Opuscule on the Principle of Theology, section 1, question 7, no. 1, also warns that this argument is one of those from which, taken individually, it is not easy to draw what is evident. Johann Müller likewise concurs (The Atheism Refuted, part 1, ch. 3, no. 3, p. 110), as does Hülsemann in his Commentary on Jeremiah, ch. 1, aphorism 3, theorem, p. 42. Nevertheless, it remains certain, and it contributes not a little to rendering the divine origin of the Scriptures credible, that when nothing can be presumed about the authors of Scripture from other sources, for instance that they were persons of ill repute or suspect, nor from the subject matter itself, nor from any failure of fulfillment of predictions, that they spoke falsely or deceitfully, then it is entirely fitting to hold that the Scripture which with such great asseveration declares God to be its Author is not a human invention but the true Word of God Himself (compare Musaeus, Introduction, same place, p. 309).

### 20 To the latter class of internal arguments belong those which are drawn from the…

To the latter class of internal arguments belong those which are drawn from the properties that any Scripture divinely destined for instructing men unto salvation would be expected to possess, even by the judgment of natural reason itself. Such properties are: the truth of its assertions, without any admixture of errors; perfect holiness, excluding everything that is dishonest or unseemly; and the sufficiency of those things which are set forth as to be believed or done by those who seek salvation.

Note. On these properties, see Musaeus (Introduction, same place, sections 6 and 7, pp. 317 and 318), and Hülsemann (Prolegomena to the Formula of Concord, article 1, ch. 2, section 4, pp. 216 and 317). The same point, as far as the substance is concerned, is made by others who present it in terms of the truly divine perfections of the Author of Scripture Himself: namely, His truthfulness, holiness, wisdom, and altogether perfect goodness, insofar as these shine forth from Scripture itself. This will be readily apparent upon comparison.

For just as true knowledge of God and the things pertaining to His worship is required of men who are to attain eternal salvation, so also the very light of nature would require that a Scripture or doctrine divinely granted for the saving instruction of men possess truth of doctrines pure from every error.

Likewise, just as a holy life, ordered in conformity with the divine laws, is required of those who are to be saved, so too the Scripture destined for true religion and the salvation of men must be holy, so that in delivering the things pertaining to holiness of life it puts forth nothing base or alien to what is honorable and fitting.

Otherwise, unless all things necessary for men to believe and do in order to be saved are delivered in such a Scripture without deficiency, the Scripture itself will be able to lead no one to salvation.

### 21 The truth of Scripture is proved partly by an induction of all the doctrines…

The truth of Scripture is proved partly by an induction of all the doctrines that are delivered in it for the sake of salvation, which either can be known from the light of nature itself, or exceed the light of nature (and none of which can be convicted of falsehood); partly from the agreement of the books of the Old and New Testaments and of all their parts among themselves; and partly by comparing the prophecies of future contingent events, especially those which depend precisely on the free will of God and of men, with their outcome or fulfillment, which corresponds to them exactly.

Note. On this point, see Musaeus (Introduction, same place, section 8, p. 319). Those doctrines which can be known from the light of nature, for example, concerning God, His essence, attributes, providence, worship, and the right ordering of life according to the will of God, are delivered in the Scriptures not only in full agreement with right reason in all respects, but also sometimes more perfectly than they could be known by reason left to itself in this corrupt state of nature. Hence the truth of Scripture with respect to these very doctrines is evident, and indeed a truth of such a kind as argues that God, whose perfection immeasurably surpasses the capacity of human nature and reason, is its Author. Moreover, an argument arises from this by which it may be inferred that this Scripture is likewise true and proceeds from God in the other things it teaches which exceed the light of nature (Musaeus, same place, section 11, pp. 321 and 322, and section 14, p. 334).

Among those doctrines that exceed the light of nature, some indeed fall under the light of nature according to a certain generic notion but exceed it according to their specific nature: for example, concerning the creation of this universe and of the first human beings, concerning the state of man both in integrity and in corruption, and concerning the ultimate end or blessedness of man. These not only do not truly oppose the light of nature, but also, when they have become known from the revelation contained in the Scriptures, can be recognized by the guidance of the light of nature itself as perfecting our natural knowledge and supplying its deficiency, as though a more sublime knowledge had been added. From this it may in turn be gathered that Scripture is not only true in such matters but altogether worthy of God as its Author, and indeed is to be ascribed not to men but to God as its revealer (see Musaeus, same place, section 12, pp. 324 and following, and section 15, pp. 336 and following).

Other doctrines, however, simply exceed the light of nature: for example, concerning the Trinity of divine persons in one essence, concerning the incarnation and the two natures and personal unity of Christ, concerning the redemption of the human race through the suffering and death of Christ, concerning justification through faith in Christ, concerning the resurrection of the dead, and concerning the intuitive vision of God and the glorification of bodies in which our blessedness will consist, and so forth. These, by the very fact that they are commended as mysteries revealed by God for our salvation, deserve to be held as true and certain, not devised by men but first known and committed to writing through God's supernatural revelation; and they argue that Scripture in its remaining parts as well, and therefore in its entirety, is true and proceeds from God (Musaeus, same place, section 16, pp. 338 and following). For although these mysteries may appear to corrupt reason, which follows the lead of its own principles and transfers by a μετάβασις εἰς ἄλλο γένος (transition to another genus) to divine things what is perhaps universally true only within the sphere of natural things, to involve a contradiction, it is nevertheless sufficient that a true contradiction in these mysteries, that is, that the same thing is simultaneously affirmed and denied of the same subject in the same respect and at the same time, cannot be demonstrated with the utmost evidence (see Musaeus, same place, pp. 341 and following).

Certainly the fact that so many writers of Scripture, most dissimilar in talent, education, and character, and sometimes separated by the greatest distances of place and time, lacking the opportunity to communicate with one another the thoughts they were to commit to writing, nevertheless conspire so splendidly and everywhere into one opinion on subject matter so weighty and sublime, touching the religion and salvation of men: this demonstrates the truth of Scripture in such a way that it simultaneously directs us to one and the same Author of the whole of Scripture, God, who inspired the ideas to be expressed in writing to each and all of them (Musaeus, same place, section 16, p. 345). For the more obscure or difficult passages that occur in some places and seem to conflict with others do not truly conflict with them, and have for the most part long since been reconciled through the labors of more learned interpreters (see Musaeus, same place, pp. 346 and following).

For future contingent events of this kind cannot be foreknown and predicted with certainty and infallibility except by God, whose knowledge is infinite, as we shall see below in the treatise on God. Accordingly, Holy Scripture, which is full of such prophecies confirmed by their fulfillment, for example concerning the things pertaining to the coming of the Messiah and its circumstances, as well as the fates of the Jewish people and so forth, is recognized to be so true that it must be believed to have proceeded from the omniscient and truthful God (compare Musaeus, same place, section 18, pp. 364 and following).

### 22 The holiness of Scripture is established by an induction of all the parts of…

The holiness of Scripture is established by an induction of all the parts of true religion by which man is directed both directly toward God, and toward himself, and toward other men, according to the will of God and His eternal law, and which are delivered in Sacred Scripture more perfectly than anywhere else (see Musaeus, same place, section 19, pp. 368 and following; see also what we said above at section 19, note). And thus at the same time it is recognized that the most holy God is the Author of that Scripture.

SECTION XXIII. The sufficiency of Sacred Scripture for salvation, given that the aforementioned properties hold true, must certainly be admitted, unless it can be shown that something necessary for a man to believe or do in order to be saved is not contained in it. Meanwhile, this sufficiency can be recognized from the fact that Scripture so clearly and perspicuously sets forth the way of reconciling sinful man with God, which no other religion or scripture teaches.

Note. And since no man can know and teach all those things that are necessary for a man to know and do in order to be saved, unless God reveals them (for we have shown above in chapter 1, section 8, p. 15, that natural theology is insufficient), it further follows that God is the Author of this Scripture which suffices for salvation (compare Musaeus, same place, section 20, pp. 373 and 377). For Scripture sets forth an altogether admirable way of expiating sins through the sacrifice of a Mediator appointed by God Himself, which the Gentiles, clumsily imitating through their κακοζηλία (misguided emulation), thereby unwittingly confirm its excellence (compare Musaeus, same place, pp. 374, 375, and 376).

### 24 Among the external arguments by which the divine origin of Scripture is proved

Among the external arguments by which the divine origin of Scripture is proved, first comes its antiquity, namely, that Scripture, with respect to the doctrine of faith and morals, partly began with the very origin of the world, partly became known to the first human beings shortly thereafter, and, with respect to written words, precedes in age the books of all the Gentiles.

Note. Antiquity could in its own way be referred to the internal marks, insofar as the duration of a thing differs from the thing itself only conceptually; here, however, it is considered with reference to time, by which the duration of a thing is measured, and which is extrinsic to the thing itself (see Musaeus, same place, section 2, section 1, p. 378).

If we consider that part of doctrine which, apart from the state of sin, man needed to know concerning God and His worship and concerning living justly and holily, and which was thereafter committed to the Sacred Scriptures by revelation (Musaeus, same place), this doctrine began with the origin of the world.

As for those things which are necessary for sinful man to know in order to be reconciled with God, the protevangelium of Genesis 3:15 pertains to this.

On the antiquity of Scripture in written form, see Justin Martyr (Exhortation to the Greeks, p. 18 and following), Tertullian (Apology, ch. 19, pp. 711 and 712), Eusebius (in the Preface to the Chronicle), Augustine (The City of God, book 18, ch. 34, vol. 5 of his works, p. 233). Compare also Philippe de Mornay (On the Truth of the Christian Religion, ch. 24, p. 405), Hugo Grotius (On the Truth of the Christian Religion, book 1, sections 15 and 16, pp. 28 and following), and J. H. Ursinus (Exercises on Zoroaster, and so forth, where he also endeavors to prove that Moses was the first writer of any book whatsoever).

### 25 A second argument can be drawn from the men who composed Sacred Scripture

A second argument can be drawn from the men who composed Sacred Scripture, both from their knowledge of the matters to be transmitted and from their sincere zeal for truth, without any bias of partisanship or personal affections; from which it is readily recognized that they are worthy of trust.

Note. For partly they recount the histories of things done by themselves or in their own time, events in which they themselves were present, or even of earlier times; and of all the events they recount, they demonstrate by their very work that they were knowledgeable. Partly they set forth doctrines knowable from the light of nature in such a way that one marvels at their knowledge, in which they surpass others. Partly, finally, they expound things that exceed the grasp of reason, where one perceives no less, indeed, if one considers that most of them were uneducated persons, untrained in letters, arts, and sciences, a knowledge altogether outstanding and to be esteemed as divinely bestowed (compare Musaeus, same place, section 2, pp. 383 and following; Grotius, On the Truth of the Christian Religion, book 3, section 5, p. 208).

So far were they from being moved to write, or while writing to conceal certain things or to present them otherwise than the matter itself required, by fear of danger or hope of gain or private advantage, that on the contrary their very writings testify that they had learned neither to flatter others or court favor, nor to conceal their own faults, nor to avoid hatred, persecutions, and the most extreme dangers at the cost of truth (see Musaeus, same place, pp. 387 and following, and the arguments adduced from Aegidius Hunnius, Treatise on the Majesty of Scripture, argument 10; add also Grotius, same place, section 6, p. 210).

For just as every falsehood proceeds either from ignorance or from ill will, so knowledge and zeal for truth make a writer ἀξιόπιστον (worthy of trust).

### 26 There is added a third argument drawn from miracles

There is added a third argument drawn from miracles, by which the sacred writers demonstrate both their own mission and the divine origin of the doctrine they set forth.

Note. By the term "miracles" are understood works or effects produced beyond the order of all created nature, which can only be produced by divine power. Concerning the miracles of Moses, which were performed before the people, were many and remarkable, were committed to memory by the clearest testimonies, and were truly divine and utterly unlike the deceptions of Satan, see Aegidius Hunnius (same place, argument 13, vol. 1 of his works, fols. 21, 22, and 23). The same account applies to the miracles that the Prophets, Christ Himself, and the Apostles performed, or that were divinely wrought to demonstrate their mission and the divine origin of their doctrine, the abundance of which the sacred Canon itself exhibits (see the same author, argument 14; compare Musaeus, same place, section 13, pp. 391 and following). That the miracles of Peter and others at the beginning of the New Testament also became known to the Gentiles is shown by Grotius (On the Truth of the Christian Religion, same place, section 7, pp. 212 and 213).

For God, by working miraculously, does not assist deceivers in order to deceive the minds of men, that is, so that men might be persuaded that they have been divinely sent to teach and therefore should be heard; but rather He assists those whom He has truly sent as men who will set forth true and saving things.

### 27 There follows the concordant and entirely unanimous testimony of the Church…

There follows the concordant and entirely unanimous testimony of the Church spread throughout the world, from the time of the Apostles onward, concerning the divine origin of the Scriptures.

Note. The Church constitutes the flower of the human race, and in it the liberal arts and disciplines, as well as honorable customs, flourish more than anywhere else. Nor is it credible that so innumerable a multitude of men surpassing others, dispersed throughout the whole world, could have conspired or been able to conspire in such a falsehood as to hold these books in such high esteem, however much they are abhorrent to the carnal sense and human self-love, and to testify as if with one mouth that they had been written by divine inspiration, if nevertheless each writer had composed them by mere human effort and judgment (compare Schröder, On the Principle of Theology, ch.

1, nos. 12 and 14; Musaeus, same place, section 4, pp. 423 and following).

### 28 Especially noteworthy is the constancy and more than human strength of the…

Especially noteworthy is the constancy and more than human strength of the innumerable martyrs, of both sexes, of every age and nation, distinguished also for their innocence and holiness, in bearing witness, even amid the most grievous torments, and in sealing with their own blood and death, their testimony concerning the truth and divine origin of that doctrine.

Note. These martyrs, although they were part of the Church, nevertheless bore a special testimony to the Christian doctrine, not merely verbal but supremely real, furnished on special occasions arising from persecutions (Musaeus, same place, section 5, pp. 444 and 445). For who would believe that these men, so many and so diverse, endowed with the use of reason and devoted to virtue, having despised and trampled underfoot all earthly things, honor, wealth, family, life itself, not only individually but in whole companies, and by the voluntary endurance of the most bitter evils from which they could easily have escaped, would have fought so tenaciously for the divine origin of that doctrine, unless they had been intimately convinced in their souls by the very power of God that it was such, and had been sustained and strengthened in those evils (Musaeus, same place, pp. 445 and following; compare Schröder, same place, no. 11; Grotius, On the Truth of the Christian Religion, book 2, section 22, pp. 196 and following).

### 29 There are added the remarkably swift and successful propagation of the…

There are added the remarkably swift and successful propagation of the Christian doctrine throughout the entire world, and its wonderful preservation amid so many persecutions.

Note. This becomes especially apparent if one considers the obstacles which seemed likely to impede that propagation: on the part of the men to be converted, who were already entangled in other religious practices and the cares of earthly things; on the part of the doctrine itself, which surpasses the grasp of reason and demands or foretells such difficult things; on the part of those who proposed that doctrine, men who excelled neither in eloquence nor in human wisdom and were rather held in contempt by the world; and finally on the part of other men, more powerful and more cunning, who strove against it. From all this it is easy to recognize the divine power which, superior to all those impediments, occupied the hearts of men and rendered them certain of the divine origin of that doctrine (compare Musaeus, same place, section 6, pp. 448 and 449; Hunnius, same place, argument 15, pp. 33 and following).

The case for preservation is much the same as for propagation: the divine power and efficacy must be acknowledged both in conferring and strengthening faith in the hearts of men and in checking and repelling, without human force, the assaults of so many and such great enemies (compare Musaeus, same place, section 7, pp. 449 and following, and Hunnius, argument 16).

### 30 Nor should the testimonies of the remaining peoples of the world be neglected

Nor should the testimonies of the remaining peoples of the world be neglected, who, although alien to the sacred writings, nevertheless bore witness, even unwittingly, to the deeds of the people of God and to the doctrine itself.

Note. On the Gentiles, see the extensive discussion by Hunnius (same place, argument 6, pp. 39 and following), and the summary provided by Schröder (same place, no. 15). On the Jews, who acknowledge the miracles of Christ (though they blasphemously ascribe them to sorcery), and on the Mohammedans, who celebrate Christ as a Prophet sent by God and renowned for miracles, the same authors may be consulted.

To this point also pertains the fact that pagan religion spontaneously collapsed as soon as human supports failed; that certain doctrines of the Christian religion are found to have been approved by the wise men of the Gentiles themselves; and that those doctrines which are found to be more difficult in Christianity are nevertheless superior to those things which the pagans hold as their own distinctive beliefs, no less difficult to credit and for the most part absurd; and further, that the pagans themselves imitate the sacred rites of the older and truer religion through a kind of κακοζηλία (misguided emulation) (see Grotius, On the Truth of the Christian Religion, book 4, nos. 10 and 12, pp. 282 and 287; Hoornbeek, On the Conversion of the Indians and the Gentiles). The Jews, moreover, can be convicted not only from the Scripture of the Old Testament which they retain, but also from their own traditions, that the Messiah has come and that He is Jesus of Nazareth, in whom accordingly one must believe, and by whose merit alone salvation is to be obtained (see Grotius, On the Truth of the Christian Religion, the entirety of book 3; de Mornay, On the Truth of the Christian Religion, chs. 29, 30, and 31; Hoornbeek, On the Conversion of the Jews). As for the Mohammedan religion, it is well known to be a medley pieced together from various religions, which overthrows itself and, when compared with the Christian religion, is forced to lower its standards (see Grotius, On the Truth of the Christian Religion, the entirety of book 6).

### 31 Finally, there also deserve to be counted the manifest and wonderful examples…

Finally, there also deserve to be counted the manifest and wonderful examples of divine vengeance against the persecutors and violators of this doctrine (on which see Hunnius, argument 21; Schröder, no. 13). For these demonstrate that God wills Scripture itself to be acknowledged and honored as proceeding from Himself, since He punishes so severely those who act otherwise.

### 32 Divine faith, by which the divine origin of Sacred Scripture on the part of its…

Divine faith, by which the divine origin of Sacred Scripture on the part of its formal aspect, that is, its sense or doctrine, is recognized, is produced by the doctrine of Scripture itself. This occurs insofar as that doctrine, when read with attention or set forth by the voice of a teacher, explained, and perceived by hearing, of itself and immediately, yet by the divine power which it has always and indissolubly joined to itself, and therefore with God concurring and exerting this power, on the one hand illuminates the intellect of man, that is, by arousing a holy thought suited to the object, inclines it to assent; and on the other hand attracts and moves the will, so that it commands the intellect to yield assent to the doctrine comprehended in the Scriptures as proceeding from God; and thus determines the intellect itself to assent under the formal aspect of divine revelation.

Note. For indeed, in order to yield the assent of divine faith to revealed doctrines, it is required that the very revelation of those doctrines be believed with divine faith (see Musaeus, Introduction, part 2, ch. 6, section 2, pp. 463 and following).

The ideas originally produced in the intellect of the sacred writers through the act of revelation are still today contained in the words of Scripture; and through the words of Scripture, transmitted to our intellect either by the voice of teachers or by the reading of the Scriptures, they are similarly produced in us today and move the intellect to a supernatural assent of its dependence upon God (see Musaeus, same place, section 12, pp. 468 and following).

This occurs in such a way that the ultimate ground of assenting with divine faith is the divine revelation itself as comprehended in the Scriptures, in which the assent rests and is not resolved into any distinct revelation or any further ground of assenting whatsoever (Musaeus, same place, section 2, p. 466).

For divine revelation, or Sacred Scripture, by itself alone, apart from the supernatural concurrence of God, is not the complete motive ground of the intellect for a supernatural assent to itself or to its dependence upon God. For words, as such, and prescinding from every supernatural concurrence of God, cannot move the intellect further than to a simple apprehension of the things they signify; and the things represented to the intellect by the words of revelation, even when they are apprehended, are in themselves inevident. And although they may possess a notable goodness by which they might seem able to draw the will into consent and to move it to command the intellect to assent, yet because the will in the order of spiritual things is by nature incapable and as it were dead, the will, in the absence of the supernatural concurrence of God, is not moved to command the intellect to assent (Musaeus, same place, section 5, pp. 481 and 482).

For although the authority of Scripture and its efficacy ought not to be confused, it is nevertheless certain that the latter is joined with the former insofar as the concurrence of God, or of His power, through which Scripture is efficacious, is required for the assent of faith by which Scripture's dependence upon God is recognized (Musaeus, same place, p. 490). Concerning this conjunction of divine power with the divine Word, we shall see more below, where the efficacy of Scripture is to be treated.

Otherwise the intellect of man, left to itself, when it fixes its thoughts upon the sacred doctrine set before it in writing or by the spoken word and known by simple apprehension through the force of the words, and when applying its judgment inquires into its truth or falsehood, that is, its human or divine origin, is rather incapable, like a blind man, of judging rightly, and is rather inclined to deny what is affirmed and to affirm what is denied there, according to 1 Corinthians 2:14. Therefore, in order to be inclined to judge rightly and to yield assent, it needs the concurrence of divine power (compare Musaeus, same place, section 8, pp. 492 and following, 509 and 510).

For because spiritual objects are inevident to us, therefore, in order to overcome the perverse judgments that customarily arise on the part of the intellect and to yield any supernatural assent whatsoever to the sacred doctrine, it is necessary that the will, which otherwise follows the condition of the intellect corrupted by nature and is dead to spiritual things, that is, alienated from them (Ephesians 2:1; Colossians 2:13), be divinely aroused and drawn into consent, and that by its command the intellect, notwithstanding whatever doubts may emerge from various quarters, be determined to assent (compare Musaeus, same place, section 9, pp. 516 and following).

What has been said is proved, first, from 1 Thessalonians 2:13, where Paul, with a glad heart and giving thanks to God, recalls that his hearers received the λόγον ἀκοῆς (the word of hearing), the message preached by him in the spoken word and perceived by hearing, not as the word of men but, as it truly is, as the Word of God; and thus they recognized that doctrine to be from God. He adds, however, that this happened because God ἐνεργούμενος (was working efficaciously) in those who believe; that is, by concurring supernaturally with the Word, He testified that this was His own Word and moved their minds to believe it with divine faith as the Word of God.
