Second, from 1 Corinthians 2:13, where Paul says: "My speech and my preaching were not in the persuasive words of human wisdom, but ἐν ἀποδείξει πνεύματος καὶ δυνάμεως (in the demonstration of the Spirit and of power), so that your faith might not rest in the wisdom of men but in the power of God." For this means nothing other than that the doctrine delivered by Paul, although it did not move to assent through arguments drawn from human wisdom, nevertheless moved through the power of God, or of the Holy Spirit, joined to it, and had the force of the most solid demonstration. Thus, although it was full of inevident mysteries (according to verse 7), it nevertheless made known its own dependence upon the Holy Spirit, to be believed with divine faith, and efficaciously moved their minds to the assent of faith (compare Musaeus, same place, section 4, pp. 475 and 476).

Moreover, how the Holy Spirit, while working through the Word a certain spiritual light on the part of the intellect, simultaneously produces on the part of the will a certain impulse and holy motions, is shown by Musaeus from the example of converts: the Eunuch (Acts 8:36 and 37), Lydia (Acts 16:14), and the hearers of Peter (Acts 2:37) (Musaeus, same place, section 9, pp. 522 and 523). Furthermore, it should be noted here that the same arguments by which hearers were originally persuaded to believe the apostolic preaching are the same arguments by which we are persuaded today to believe their writings: "For they wrote the same things they taught," as Gerhard says (Gerhard, Theological Commonplaces, vol. 1, on Sacred Scripture, section 31). For the Word of God preached by the Apostles from divine inspiration and the Scripture composed from divine inspiration do not differ except accidentally, insofar as the former consists in words uttered by the mouth and the latter in words committed to writing. In relation to the intellect of the believing person, however, the motive force of both for assent is one and the same (Musaeus, same place, p. 476).

### 33 And indeed this one argument is that by which divine faith concerning the…

And indeed this one argument is that by which divine faith concerning the divine origin of the doctrine contained in the Scriptures is engendered in individual persons, even if the use of arguments that generate merely human faith may not have intervened. Nevertheless, it must be acknowledged that, according to the common rule, for the purpose of converting others, those arguments ought to be set forth beforehand. Indeed, even for the faithful themselves, in cases of temptation, those arguments are not unprofitably employed for removing certain difficulties; indeed, they are in a certain manner necessary according to the condition of their state.

Notes. The remaining arguments are indeed useful both for urging and persuading, and for convincing an adversary, but not for producing persuasion in the proper sense, such that they either kindle, or nourish, or sustain that full assurance of faith by which, as by a heavenly ray, all the clouds of a mind deliberating within itself are dispersed. This full assurance is a benefit of the Holy Spirit, who, as Augustine says, "has His chair in heaven and teaches hearts inwardly." These are the words of the blessed Schröder (Schröder, the same work, no. 16), where he treats of the internal testimony of the Holy Spirit. Compare also Hülsemann (Hülsemann, Prelections on the Formula of Concord, art. 1, ch. 2, sec. 6, pp. 217–218), and those whom he, besides Schröder, instructs to be consulted: the blessed Hunnius (Hunnius, Commentary on 1 Corinthians 2:1) and Meisner (Meisner, Charges Written Against the Pontificals on the Crime of Calumny, theses 25–26). From this it is simultaneously clear how the argument drawn from the efficacy of Scripture, depending on the different senses of the term, is at one time to be referred to the class of those which generate only human faith, and at another time returns to this very one argument which generates divine faith. For insofar as we infer from the external and sensible acts of other people, such as confession of the doctrine of faith, a holier life, and even martyrdom itself, that these proceed from the very efficacy of Scripture, or that the doctrine which the Scriptures contain possesses a power to move, strike, kindle, and soothe minds, then, in the judgment of the blessed Schröder (Schröder, the same work, and no. 9), this argument does not kindle divine faith, namely before the intrinsic testimony of the Holy Spirit intervenes, forming in the mind of each individual believer this minor conclusion: "This word contained in these books is such; therefore it is divine." These are the words of the blessed Hülsemann (Hülsemann, the same work). Compare also Cundis (Cundis, Notes on the Compendium of Hutter, book 1, question 4, pp. 22–23). But when the efficacy of Scripture is considered insofar as it exerts itself inwardly in the hearts of individuals through spiritual acts of illumination, conversion, and the like, then it is nothing other than that very testimony of the Holy Spirit which He, through His concurrence with that doctrine, produces in the hearts of these people concerning the divine origin of that doctrine, and works assent. And thus we have said, in our remarks on section 32, note (d), that the efficacy of Scripture concurs in the recognition of Scripture's dependence upon God, which is required for the authority of Scripture. Compare Musaeus (Musaeus, Treatise on Syncretism and Sacred Scripture, question 1, book on Sacred Scripture, sec. 8, pp. 185 and 196 ff.; likewise Detailed Explanation, book 1, question 5, pp. 41–42).

See the example of Christian Gerson, a Jew who became a Christian, in the blessed Musaeus (Musaeus, Treatise on Syncretism and Sacred Scripture, question 2, book on Sacred Scripture, sec. 24, p. 244).

See what we have said at section 17 in the note, and compare Gerhard (Gerhard, Exegesis, book 1, on Sacred Scripture, sec. 22), where he advises that those who deny the authority of Scripture should not be told to wait until the Holy Spirit testifies in their hearts immediately concerning the authority of Scripture, but rather they should be led to arguments both external and internal. Add also Hunnius (Hunnius, Treatise on the Majesty of Scripture, near the beginning).

For if the faithful begin to doubt the authority of Scripture in temptations, they should be dealt with in the same way as those who deny it. For doubt is closely akin to denial; these are the words of the blessed Gerhard (Gerhard, the same work, sec. 20).

### 34 The canonical or normative authority of Sacred Scripture

The canonical or normative authority of Sacred Scripture, which it possesses not only with respect to its meaning but also with respect to the very words divinely inspired, that is, with respect to the original text, in relation to translations likewise produced by human effort and in relation to other writings and doctrines to be judged: just as this authority, considered in itself and absolutely, is founded upon the truthfulness of the inspiring God and upon the dependence of Scripture, with respect to the words of the original text, upon God; so also, in order that we may believe by divine faith that the books of Scripture, under the language or selection, sequence, and arrangement of words in a particular tongue in which they are presented to us, are divinely inspired and thus possess that normative force or canonical dignity, the testimony of the Church alone does not suffice. Rather, here too the internal testimony of the Holy Spirit, or His efficacious operation through Scripture itself, must concur.

Notes. Concerning which, see this book, section 15. The word κανών (kanon), that is, norm or rule, which is properly a mathematical term but is then transferred to designate civil laws, military orders and formations, and also the tongues of scales that merchants use (see Chemnitz, Examination of the Council of Trent, part 1, section on the canonical books, pp. 81–82; Cundis, Notes on the Compendium of Hutter, book 1, question 3, pp. 15–16), occurs, according to a similar analogy, in the Scriptures themselves (2 Corinthians 10:13; Galatians 6:16; Philippians 3:16) to designate a certain rule of faith and of Christian actions, so that what agrees with it may be admitted, while what is discrepant may be rejected.

The doctrine of Scripture indeed moves one to assent to it as divine, through the concurrence of God, in whatever language it is set forth and in whatever words, provided only that the doctrine itself, as it was revealed, is sincerely presented. But in order that the doctrine of faith and morals, which is here or there presented as divine, may be brought back to its authentic norm, and its either ὀρθοδοξία (orthodoxia, "orthodoxy") or truth, or its ἑτεροδοξία (heterodoxia, "heterodoxy") or falsity, may be accurately recognized, one must have recourse to the Scripture that is infallible with respect to its words, and therefore to the Scripture under that language in which the very words were employed by divine inspiration, without the intervention of human and fallible judgment. Compare Musaeus (Musaeus, the same work, p. 540).

For some of those translations are indeed liable to errors; and even if some should be found that correspond exactly to the authentic text, they nevertheless depend on the original text in terms of their certainty and truth, and therefore possess authority only after their agreement with the authentic text has been investigated and recognized (Musaeus, the same work).

Hence, when our symbolic books are sometimes called a Norm or come under the designation of normative books, this is not understood as a Norm in the absolute sense, but in a qualified sense or with an addition: a secondary norm, a normed norm, that is, a norm in a less proper sense. See Himmel (Himmel, On the Formula of Concord, disputation 1); Grauer (Grauer, On the Augsburg Confession, part 1, p. 5, and Supplement, ch. 4, p. 149).

For thus we have said at section 15, note (b), that the authority of Scripture is in reality one, which is both causative of the assent of faith and normative of doctrine.

Moreover, we confess that this can and ought to be believed by divine faith. Compare Musaeus (Musaeus, Introduction, the same work, p. 552).

Thus the blessed Musaeus expressly teaches (Musaeus, Introduction, part 2, ch. 7, sec. 3, p. 539).

For divine faith does not arise from any other source, by whatever causes the divinity of the Scriptures may be believed, not only as probably true but even as humanly infallible. Compare Hülsemann (Hülsemann, Prelections on the Formula of Concord, art. 1, ch. 2, p. 118).

### 35 Moreover, the Holy Spirit testifies concerning the particular language of the…

Moreover, the Holy Spirit testifies concerning the particular language of the books of Scripture, which is to be acknowledged as θεόπνευστον (theopneuston, "God-breathed"), not by excluding but by employing the testimony of the Church, yet not of just any church, but of the primitive Church. And indeed the discourse of faith comes roughly to this: In whatever language Sacred Scripture was originally set down, in that language it must be acknowledged as inspired by God Himself and thus also set down by divine inspiration. But the Sacred Scripture of the Old Testament was originally set down in that Hebrew which has been received in use up to now, and the Sacred Scripture of the New Testament was originally set down in that Greek which serves our use. Therefore the Sacred Scripture of the Old Testament was inspired by God Himself in that Hebrew which has been received in use up to now, and the Sacred Scripture of the New Testament was inspired by God in that Greek which serves our use, as the language for writing, and was thus also set down by divine inspiration. The major proposition, which is itself part of the doctrine contained in the Scriptures, is undoubtedly a matter of divine faith and, through the power of the Holy Spirit intimately conjoined with the whole of sacred doctrine, moves to the assent of divine faith. The minor proposition, which concerns a particular and sensible fact distinct from the doctrine of Sacred Scripture itself, depends on the testification of αὐτόπται καὶ αὐτήκοοι (autoptai kai autēkooi, "eyewitnesses and ear-witnesses"). This is as normally happens in proving matters of fact and sensible things. The conclusion, nevertheless, does not cease to be a matter of faith, just as in other cases a revealed conclusion, to be believed by divine faith, follows not only from two revealed premises but also from one revealed premise and another that is metaphysically or morally evident.

Notes. By the term "language" in this place is understood not only the tongue itself of a particular nation, distinguished from the tongues of other nations, but the very selection, sequence, arrangement, and so forth of words in a particular tongue. To this corresponds the term "document," which the blessed G. Zeamann used in this matter (Zeamann, Treatise on the Colloquy of Regensburg, ch. 9, or Exegesis of the Question on the Canonical Books, pp. 91, 108, 112).

For the internal illuminating power of Scripture, just as it is joined to the meaning in any language, does not precisely indicate the words of the original text as needing to be distinguished from other equivalent words of the same or any other language, text, or translation. Moreover, the remaining criteria that prove the θεοπνευσία (theopneusia, "divine inspiration") of the doctrine contained in the Scriptures either do not at all pertain to the material element, that is, the words of Scripture, but to the formal element or doctrine precisely, or, when in their own way they do pertain to the material element, that is, the words and their arrangement, they argue confusedly that God is the author of the material Scripture in some language or other, whatever it may be, but do not certainly indicate the specific and determinate language in which each book of Scripture was originally set down. There remains, therefore, the testimony of the Church, which indeed does not confer canonical or normative dignity upon the books of Scripture in any particular language, nor does it by its own power move one to the assent of divine faith by which the θεοπνευσία (theopneusia, "divine inspiration") of such a language would be believed; but nevertheless, insofar as it historically demonstrates a particular language as the original language of the books of Scripture, under which it received them as set down by their secondary authors, and produces moral certainty about this, it is, when conjoined with what Scripture itself teaches and with which the Holy Spirit has intimately united His power, operative within the discourse of faith, as is evident from the following argument. Meanwhile, see the blessed Musaeus (Musaeus, Introduction, the same work, sec. 6, pp. 542–544; likewise Treatise of Questions on Syncretism and Sacred Scripture, question 2, book 1, on Scripture, secs. 5–7, pp. 227–228 and 273; Detailed Explanation, p. 9 ff.).

By the designation "primitive Church" is understood that Church which flourished in those times when the writers of the sacred books lived: namely, with respect to the books of the Old Testament, the Jewish Church from Moses to Malachi; and with respect to the books of the New Testament, the Christian Church contemporary with the Apostles and their co-workers, to which the θεόπνευστοι (theopneustoi, "divinely inspired") books were delivered by their authors, and which, relying on the testimony of the senses, was likewise able to know and to testify with certainty which books it had received from the hands of their authors, and in what language and idiom they were written. See Musaeus (Musaeus, the same work, p. 445). The Church of subsequent times, however, in this question of fact pertaining to antiquity, can determine nothing except by relying on the testimony of the primitive Church (Musaeus, the same work, p. 551).

This argument is found in the blessed Musaeus (Musaeus, Introduction, the same work, sec. 7, p. 554). Compare also Detailed Explanation (p. 20) and Treatise of Questions on Syncretism and Sacred Scripture (book 1, question 2, sec. 18, p. 237).

For to this pertains what we read in 2 Timothy 3:16: πᾶσαν γραφήν (pasan graphēn), that the whole of Scripture is divinely inspired, which is the same as saying that when it was first written, even with respect to the language itself, that is, the words of a particular tongue and their selection, sequence, and arrangement, it proceeded from divine inspiration. Compare this book, section 10 and note (c).

That the testimony of the primitive Church, for recognizing with moral certainty the original language of the books of Scripture, was not only actually given in former times but also so survives that it suffices even today, although in the modern Church no one exists who has seen the πρωτότυπα (prōtotypa, "originals"), is lucidly demonstrated by the blessed Musaeus (Musaeus, Introduction, p. 545 ff.; and Treatise of Questions on Syncretism and Sacred Scripture, the same work, p. 247 ff.), who also adduces in support of this position the arguments of the blessed doctors Martin Chemnitz (p. 259), Jakob Andreae (p. 263), Aegidius Hunnius (p. 266), and G. Zeamann (p. 296). To these many others could be added, especially those who disputed against the Pontificals (whose well-known fraud is that by which they attempt to lead us away from the testimony of the primitive Church in examining and pursuing these matters): for example, the blessed Albert Grauer (Grauer, Inaugural Disputation on Sacred Scripture against Coster, with Piscator presiding, sec. 126); the blessed J. Major (Major, Treatise against Valerius M. on the Rule of Belief, response to the fourth consequence, ch. 3, sec. 7, p. 367); the blessed Gerhard (Gerhard, Exegesis, book 1, sec. 75 ff.); the blessed Solomon Glassius (Glassius, Glaubensgrund, ch. 2, pp. 38 ff., and ch. 7, p. 231); the blessed P. Haberkorn (Haberkorn, Against Valerius M., disputation 2, ch. 4, pp. 71, 79, 102, 107). Add also the blessed Georg Mylius (Mylius, Positions on the Word of God, sec. 70 ff.) and the blessed Kromayer (Kromayer, Positive-Polemic Theology, art. 1, p. 37). It must be acknowledged, however, that the aforementioned doctors treated in those places not only of the secondary authors of the books of Scripture but also of the language, and indeed chiefly of it, namely that the πρωτότυπα (prōtotypa, "originals") and αὐτόγραφα (autographa, "autographs") of the sacred writings were preserved in the custody of the ancient Church, and were seen, read, and faithfully copied by them. These are the words of the blessed J. Major (Major, the same work). The blessed Gerhard, as well as Glassius and Haberkorn, press that passage of Tertullian about the authentic letters of the Apostles, which were recited in the apostolic churches, "preserving the voice of the Apostles," and so forth. Kromayer likewise lists as the fourth criterion of a canonical book of the New Testament that it must have the testimony of the primitive Christian Church, which had seen, read, and recognized the αὐτόγραφα (autographa, "autographs"). Finally, the blessed Daniel Cramer (Cramer, Isagoge to the Prophetic and Apostolic Books, p. 15), where he treats of the distinction between the apocryphal and the canonical books, says: "This whole testification depends on the first inspection of the autograph by those into whose hands it came." Most manifestly of all, however, the blessed Zeamann (in the place which the blessed Musaeus cites in Treatise of Questions on Syncretism and Sacred Scripture, p. 266, namely in Theological and Scholastic Treatise on the Colloquy of Regensburg, ch. 9, or Exegesis of the Question on the Canonical Books, pp. 91 and 108) refers the historical tradition of the ancient Church not only to the question about the authors of the sacred books but also to the question about the document (as he calls what is otherwise termed the language), and affirms that the Church testifies about it as an αἰσθητόν (aisthēton, "sensible object"), and that one must rely upon its testimony.

For thus, for example, the conclusion is a matter of faith by which a regenerate person infers about himself individually: "I have been made a son of God and an heir of eternal life through baptism." The premises on which that conclusion rests are as follows: the major, which is revealed, states: "Whoever has been baptized has been made a son of God and an heir of eternal life through baptism," which is taught in Galatians 3:27. The minor, however, is not revealed, but rests either on the assertion of other trustworthy people, if one was baptized in infancy, or on one's own testimony of the senses, if one was baptized in adulthood, and is this: "But I have been baptized." Compare Musaeus (Musaeus, Introduction, the same work, pp. 554–555), who discussed this manner of reasoning at greater length in his Treatise on the Use of the Principles of Reason in Theology (book 2, ch. 13 ff., pp. 435 ff.) and his Treatise on Conversion (disputation 9, pp. 569 ff.).

### 36 Accordingly, the canonical books of the Old Testament

Accordingly, the canonical books of the Old Testament, which the ancient Jewish Church received and transmitted to the Christian Church, are the following: the five books of Moses, the book of Joshua, Judges, Ruth, two of Samuel, two of Kings, two of Chronicles, one of Ezra, one of Nehemiah (or the second of Ezra), the book of Esther, Job, the Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, the Song of Songs, the four books of the major prophets, which are Isaiah, Jeremiah (to whom also belong the Lamentations), Ezekiel, and Daniel; the twelve books of the minor prophets, which are Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi. All of these survive uncorrupted in the Church.

Notes. For they are mentioned by Christ as indubitably to be found among the Jews, and are divided into Moses and the Prophets (Luke 16:29, 31) and into Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms (Luke 24:44). With this division there agrees in a certain way that of the Jews, into הרות (Torah), that is, the Law; םיאיבנ (Nevi'im), that is, the Prophets, whom they further divide into ם ינושאר (Rishonim, "former") and םינורחא (Acharonim, "latter"); and םיבותכ (Ketuvim, "Writings"), which are otherwise called ἁγιόγραφα (hagiographa, "sacred writings"). Yet one must be careful not, after the manner of certain men, to attribute an inequality of perfection and dignity to writings equally divinely inspired. See the special dissertation of Frischmuth on this division of Scripture.

Concerning each of these individually, see the blessed J. Gerhard (Gerhard, Exegesis, book 1, ch. 7, sec. 118 ff.); the blessed Michael Walther (Walther, Biblical Workshop); the blessed Daniel Cramer (Cramer, Isagoge to the Prophetic and Apostolic Books); and the blessed Laurentius Fabricius (Fabricius, Partition of the Hebrew Codex).

That those books survived uncorrupted in the time of Christ cannot be denied; for otherwise He would surely not have said so absolutely: "They have Moses and the Prophets" (Luke 16:29); "Search the Scriptures, and they are the ones that testify of me" (John 5:39–40). And although He reproves the Jews' blindness and unbelief in maintaining true doctrine and in recognizing the exhibited Messiah, Paul nevertheless proclaims the faithful custody of the sacred Codex deposited with them (Romans 3:2; 9:4). After those times, moreover, with the multiplication of copies of that Scripture among Christians, no room was left for universal corruption, especially if one considers that God's providence watched over His word. See meanwhile on the purity of the Hebrew fountain in the Old Testament (Glassius, Sacred Philology, book 1, tract 1).

### 37 Those books which

Those books which, besides those already mentioned, sometimes appear in the Biblical Codex of the Old Testament, namely Judith, Wisdom, Tobit, Ecclesiasticus, Baruch, two (or three) of the Maccabees, (the third and fourth of Ezra,) the fragments of Esther, the story of Daniel concerning Susanna, the story of Bel and the Babylonian Dragon, the prayers of Azariah, of the three youths, and of Manasseh: just as they were held to be θεόπνευστοι (theopneustoi, "divinely inspired") neither by the ancient Israelite Church nor by Christ and the Apostles, nor by the Christian Church that immediately followed, and did not possess canonical authority among them, so they ought not to possess it today either. But so that they may be distinguished from the canonical books, they are rightly called apocryphal.

Notes. They are not only seen interspersed among the canonical books in the Vulgate translation, but are also found published in various other languages, since they were not entirely rejected but were considered useful for reading unto edification.

For the Jews did not hold as canonical any books except those which were set down in the language received by the people of God at that time, offered to the priests, and, with the divine calling and inspiration of the writers being recognized and the fact that these books had been composed by them in this sequence and arrangement of words being attested, were commended to the Church. Compare Gerhard (Gerhard, Exegesis, book 1, secs. 73–74).

Certainly nowhere in the New Testament is any of those books cited to prove any article of the doctrine of the faith. Compare this book, section 36, note (a).

For the early Church anxiously followed the canon of the Hebrews and did not dare to add any book to it. Witnesses are Melito of Sardis, as cited by Eusebius (Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, book 4, ch. 26); Origen, as cited by the same (Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, book 6, ch. 25); Eusebius himself (Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, book 3, ch. 9); and especially Jerome in the Prologus Galeatus, and many others cited by Gerhard (Gerhard, Catholic Confession, book 2, art. 1, ch. 1, p. 19). Compare also Gerhard's Exegesis (book 1, secs. 75 ff.).

That they are sometimes called "canonical," even by Augustine himself, cannot be taken in the proper and principal signification of the word; rather, it was said only in the sense, certainly more general and less proper, in which it was customary to call any book usefully read in the Church by that name (Gerhard, Exegesis, sec. 156).

See what we have said at section 35, note (c), near the end.

That is, "hidden," meaning that their origin from divine inspiration was not established for the Church of that time in which they appeared, and consequently is not established for the Church of subsequent ages either. Hence they are not to be brought forward when canonical Scripture is required, although they are not to be entirely hidden away but are to be read profitably. Compare Chemnitz (Chemnitz, Examination of the Council of Trent, part 1, p. 97).

### 38 The canonical books of the New Testament are all those which are contained in…

The canonical books of the New Testament are all those which are contained in the Biblical Codex, namely not only those about whose θεοπνευσία (theopneusia, "divine inspiration") there was never any doubt, which are the four Gospels of Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John; the Acts of the Apostles; the Epistles of Paul, namely one to the Romans, two to the Corinthians, one to the Galatians, one to the Ephesians, one to the Philippians, one to the Colossians, two to the Thessalonians, two to Timothy, one to Titus, and one to Philemon; the first of Peter and the first of John; but also the remaining writings about whose authors and consequently whose divine origin some formerly doubted, although today no dispute remains, namely the Epistle to the Hebrews, the second of Peter, the second and third of John, the Epistle of James, the Epistle of Jude, and the Apocalypse of John. All of these likewise survive uncorrupted.

Notes. They are therefore called πρωτοκανονικοί (prōtokanonokoi), that is, canonical of the first order.

Concerning these, see the blessed Martin Chemnitz (Chemnitz, Examination of the Council of Trent, part 1, section on the writings of the Evangelists, and on the writings and Epistles of the Apostles); the blessed Gerhard (Gerhard, Exegesis, sec. 243 ff.); the blessed Walther (Walther, Biblical Workshop); the blessed Cramer (Cramer, Isagoge), and others.

It certainly cannot be denied that the ancients doubted the secondary authors in such a way that they simultaneously denied the authority proper to θεόπνευστοι (theopneustoi, "divinely inspired") books. See Eusebius (Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, book 2, ch. 23; book 3, ch. 25; book 6, ch. 25). This, however, is to be understood not of the entire Christian Church but of certain particular communities which had not themselves inspected the autographs presented to them, as those same passages indicate.

And so even today they are called apocryphal by some, while others more suitably call them canonical of the second order, or δευτεροκανονικοί (deuterokanonokoi). See Gerhard (Gerhard, Exegesis, sec. 242).

See the blessed Glassius (Glassius, Sacred Philology, book 1, tract 2). Compare also Buxtorf's Anticritica and Hottinger's Thesaurus Philologicus (fol. 118 ff.), where it is shown that not even by accident and the injury of time have the modern codices been universally and fundamentally corrupted.

### 39 To the properties of Sacred Scripture there further pertains (2) its efficacy

To the properties of Sacred Scripture there further pertains (2) its efficacy, that is, that it has an active supernatural and truly divine power or potency for producing supernatural effects, namely for converting, regenerating, and renewing the minds of men, which power, by divine ordination, is intimately and indissolubly united to Scripture considered with respect to its meaning, even apart from actual use, in first act; and which, when the use of reading, hearing, or meditation supervenes, exerts itself in second act, so that those supernatural effects of grace, just as they proceed from God as the principal cause, so also from Scripture itself as the instrumental efficient cause, are efficaciously produced simultaneously and jointly, by one undivided influence.

Notes. We have said that this efficacy is to be joined with the authority of Scripture at note (e) to section 32, pp. 102–103. By the term "efficacy," which otherwise designates second act or actual operation, just as the Greek term ἐνέργεια (energeia) does, we understand in this place the δύναμις ἐνεργητική (dynamis energētikē) itself, that is, the active potency for producing spiritual effects (Musaeus, Introduction, part 2, ch. 8, sec. 2, p. 559).

Not a merely objective power, but an effective or productive power of supernatural forces and movements in the intellect and will of a human being who is by nature blind and dead with respect to embracing spiritual things (Musaeus, the same work, p. 560).

This power is certainly not to be sought in the elegance of speech, nor in the gravity of its sentences, nor in the oratorical weight of its arguments, but is superior to every created and finite power of acting, and is therefore not natural to Scripture, whether on the part of its words or on the part of the things signified, but supernatural, that is, intimately conjoined with the nature of Scripture by divine ordination, as is stated in what follows. Compare Musaeus (Musaeus, the same work, secs. 3–4, pp. 561–562). Thus also our predecessors, on the occasion of the Rathmannian controversy, taught in the Appendix of the Consilium Dedekenni (question 6, sec. 3, fol. 263b–264a) that the power of illuminating and converting belongs to Scripture not by physical or natural necessity, but in a supernatural manner; and that those theologians who perhaps said that the Word of God has that power "naturally" used that expression not in opposition to the ὑπερφυσικόν (hyperphysikon, "supernatural"), but in opposition to the παρὰ φύσιν (para physin, "against nature") of Rathmann; meanwhile, for the sake of avoiding ambiguity and disputes, one could abstain from that expression. Similarly, in the same place (secs. 9–10, p. 265b), they note concerning the term "essential" that although it can be said in a sound sense that the power of illuminating pertains to the essence of the Word, since otherwise not only constitutive but also consequential and necessarily connected properties are thought to pertain to the essence of a thing (the term "essence" being taken more broadly), yet because this term is ambiguous and liable to calumny, another may be substituted for it, and it may be said that the power of illuminating, converting, and so forth pertains to the whole perfection of the Word, because without indicating this power the Word of God cannot be perfectly described. Compare p. 225b.

That very same infinite power which is essentially, per se, and independently in God, and by which God illuminates and converts human beings, has been communicated to the Word and is to be considered here. Compare the Jena theologians (Jena theologians, Consilium, the same work, pp. 265b–267a, and the preceding p. 242b), whence some passages are cited by the blessed Musaeus (Musaeus, Introduction, the same work, ch. 5, p. 566). This assertion is proved from Ephesians 1:17, where the power or potency by which God, through the Word, illuminates and converts human beings is said to be the same as that surpassing greatness of divine power and might of strength which He exerted in raising Jesus from the dead. And for this reason it is said in Romans 1:16 that the Gospel is the power of God unto salvation for everyone who believes; not that the Word of the Gospel itself, properly speaking and in the nominative case, is the very power of God, which does not really differ from the essence of God (for then the Gospel would be God Himself), but that it is a powerful instrument, by a customary metonymy, concerning which Glassius writes (Glassius, Sacred Philology, book 5, tract 1, p. 25), whom the blessed Dannhauer cites and follows in these words (Dannhauer, Hodosophia Christiana, phenomenon 1, p. 95): Namely, according to Glassius, it is called δύναμις (dynamis), that is, an instrument or means through which God exerts His power in bringing believers to salvation and preserving them. And it amounts to the same thing when Glassius teaches elsewhere (Glassius, Sacred Grammar, tract 1, canon 7, p. 395) that in this passage the abstract is put for the concrete, or the substantive for the adjective, with notable emphasis and force, so that the Gospel is called "power," that is, remarkably powerful and efficacious for the conversion and salvation of human beings. Similarly, when in John 6:63 Christ says, "My words are Spirit and life," there is certainly indicated the divine force and efficacy of the divine Word (not only preached but also written), that is, its function not merely of signifying but of efficaciously conferring the gifts of the Holy Spirit and spiritual life. The expression, however, is metonymic: not of the thing signified for the sign, but of the effect for the cause, as our predecessors expressly taught in the Appendix (pp. 308b ff.): "This" (they speak of the words of Christ: "The words I speak are Spirit and life") "is a metonymic expression; the external and internal Word is called Spirit and life because it brings Spirit and life with it." And shortly after: "If one properly distinguishes cause and effect, then the life-giving Word, which is the cause of spiritual life, and life itself, which is the effect of the life-giving Word, must always be distinguished." Compare Glassius (Glassius, Sacred Philology, book 5, tract 1, ch. 1, no. 1, p. 3); Tarnow (Tarnow, Commentary on John, ch. 6, part 3, p. 555); Thummius (Thummius, On the Theanthropic Majesty of Christ, p. 252); and, following them, the blessed A. Prükner (Prükner, Vindications, on this passage, p. 624). Through this, however, the efficacy or active power of the Word is not denied but established. For when the Word is called the cause of the gifts of the Spirit and of spiritual life, it is necessary to attribute to it an active power as the ground of its causation. Furthermore, the efficacy of the Word both preached and written is proved also by Romans 10:17, where faith is said to be ἐξ ἀκοῆς (ex akoēs, "from hearing"), that is, from doctrine perceived by hearing (and the case is the same for reading). The particle ἐξ (ex) is causal and indicates the power of causing in what is heard (or read). Likewise John 17:20, where people are said to be going to believe διὰ τοῦ λόγου (dia tou logou, "through the Word"); and so by the force of the particle διά (dia), the power of exciting faith is attributed to the λόγος (logos) itself, or to the Word of God that was to be preached through the Apostles.

Concerning which we shall say more below in the chapters on Regeneration, Conversion, and Renewal.

For the power of illuminating is in the Word by the free will of God, or by voluntary divine ordination, as our predecessors write (the same work, p. 264a), and they repeat and emphasize this point, proving it also from 1 Corinthians 1:21: "It pleased God through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe."

Certainly that the power is not really conjoined and united to the letters and strokes of the words written on paper is admitted by the Jena theologians (the same work, fol. 200a, 240a, 265a, 270b). But they teach that the power is conjoined to the meaning of Scripture, whether it is in the mind of the Apostles, or is expressed by them through preaching, or is written in a book, or is in the mind of readers (pp. 240a, 267a, 273b).

Thus, against Rathmann, the blessed Musaeus taught that that divine power is communicated to Scripture not only in use, by a mere external juxtaposition and assistance, so that Scripture considered in itself and apart from use would be devoid of the power of illuminating and converting human minds, inefficacious and a dead letter; but that Scripture is in itself always efficacious and possesses the power of illuminating and converting human minds whether it is considered in use or in itself apart from use (Musaeus, Introduction, the same work, sec. 6, p. 567, and sec. 7, p. 571).

Namely, by the force of that ordination, freely made indeed, but never to be revoked, as the Jena theologians write (the same work, p. 264a): "By virtue of the voluntary ordination made by God Himself, the power of illumination, conversion, and salvation is always and indissolubly united with the Word."

For although that divine power, which on the part of the thing is the very essence of God, is not communicated to Scripture, as it is the λόγος προφορικός (logos prophorikos, "expressed Word") of God, in such a way that it would formally and subjectively inhere in it (for the formal element of divine Scripture is the meaning of the signs, not that archetypal meaning immanent in the divine mind, but the ectypal meaning, set forth, delineated, and represented through these signs as intelligible with respect to divine things, according to the mind and words of the blessed Hülsemann, Prelections on the Formula of Concord, art. 8, sec. 1, part 1, sec. 3, p. 432), and for this reason the Jena theologians frequently and carefully warned that the same power indeed belongs to God and to Scripture, but not in the same manner: for it belongs to God essentially, principally, originally, and independently, while it belongs to the Word of Scripture dependently, participatively, or by communication (the same work, pp. 225b, 264b, sec. 5, 267a, sec. 14, 270b); nevertheless, a conjunction of divine power with the Word must be acknowledged, concerning which our predecessors can be consulted (the same work, pp. 270a, 271a), where they also refer to the words of Luther (Luther, Works, vol. 4, J.L., fol. 530b): "Scripture has the Holy Spirit as an inseparable companion"; and likewise the words of the Wittenberg theologians in the Censure of Movius: "The Spirit is always conjoined with the Word" (compare pp. 246b, 264a, 265b, 266a). These words are also cited by the blessed Musaeus (Musaeus, Introduction, pp. 569–570), who finally (pp. 577–578) teaches how the divine power of illuminating and converting human minds is conjoined with the meaning of Scripture, both apart from the intellect and insofar as it has been apprehended by the intellect: namely, in the intellect by an actual conjunction or union of itself with the impressed and expressed species of the things signified; apart from the intellect, however, the power inheres in the meaning insofar as God by His most free will has so ordained that Sacred Scripture, even apart from the intellect, is always and everywhere attended by the Holy Spirit with His divine power and potency of illuminating and converting human minds, and that when Scripture is read or presented by the voice of a teacher, He simultaneously penetrates to the mind of the person, and there, united with the species of the things signified, partly impressed and partly expressed, exerts Himself through them unto conversion.

Unless, that is, its operation is impeded on the part of human beings, by the security of the flesh, the thorns of pleasures, or the cares of this age. Compare Musaeus (Musaeus, the same work, sec. 7, pp. 571, 574) and the predecessors (the same work, pp. 223b, 241a–b, 265a, sec. 7, 269a–b, 270b, 271a). In that last place, the words of the blessed J. Brenz are also explained (Brenz, Württemberg Confession, chapter on the Gospel, p. 407), where he states that the Gospel, when it is merely contained in letters or even pronounced by voice but apart from its legitimate use, is not efficacious of itself. These words are cited and adopted by Balduin (Balduin, Commentary on the First Epistle to the Thessalonians, ch. 1, part 2, question 1, p. 1127) and Dannhauer (Dannhauer, Hodosophia Christiana, phenomenon 1, p. 94). This is to be understood, that is, of efficacy considered in second act, which has no place apart from the use of hearing, reading, meditation, and so forth. See also pp. 349a, 350a.

This distinction between God and His Word as principal and instrumental cause was so carefully and frequently impressed by our predecessors in this matter and in the Rathmannian controversy that they could not have done so more emphatically. See the same work (pp. 225a at the end, 227b at the beginning, 228a near the end, sec. 20, 231b near the end, sec. 27 from the Formula of Concord, 236a in the middle, 240a–b, 242b at the beginning, 247b in the middle, 253a at the beginning and b in the middle, 254a at the beginning and in the middle from the Formula of Concord, 267b, sec. 17, 343b in the middle, 344a at the beginning and in the middle). Among these, the passages at pp. 240, 343, and especially p. 267b, sec. 16, are particularly to be observed. This last passage is also mentioned by the blessed Musaeus (Musaeus, Introduction, sec. 9, p. 593), where the distinction between a passive instrument and a cooperative instrument is presented, and it is shown that Scripture, although it is rightly distinguished from passive instruments, cannot simply be denied to be an instrument (namely a cooperative one), following the lead of the Symbolic Books themselves, especially the Augsburg Confession, article 5. Compare the same work (pp. 243b, sec. 37, 272a at the end). And the aforementioned doctors never abandoned or changed this position concerning the suitable use of the term "instrument" or "instrumental cause" in this matter, that is, concerning the Word of God in relation to supernatural effects; rather, as opportunity arose, they repeated and emphasized it, as is evident from the blessed J. Gerhard (Gerhard, Commentary on the First Epistle of Peter, ch. 1, verse 23, p. 136): "The Apostle describes Regeneration from its Instrumental Cause, which is the Word of God, etc."; the blessed Himmel (Himmel, Syntagma, disputation 18, sec. 20): "The Instrumental Cause of penitence is the Word of God, etc." (compare his Analytical Lectures on the Book of Concord, disputation 3, sec. 43); the blessed Glassius (Glassius, Sacred Philology, at the place cited above in note (d)); the blessed Gottfried Cundis, following the blessed Hutter (Hutter, Compendium, book 9, on free will, questions 16 and 21, p. 662, sec. 2): "The Word of God is the instrument of working conversion, etc." (and p. 671: "There are two causes of conversion: one is the principal efficient cause, the Holy Spirit; the other is the instrumental cause, the Word of God, which is the instrument of the Holy Spirit by which He effects the conversion of a person"); the blessed Christian Chemnitz (Chemnitz, Commentary on Romans, ch. 1, v. 16, pp. 38 and 43): "The Gospel is δύναμις τῷ Θεῷ (dynamis tō Theō), that is, a powerful and efficacious Instrument, etc."; and the blessed J. E. Gerhard (J. E. Gerhard, Isagoge to the Loci of his Father, book 18, on Penitence, thesis 9, p. 767): "The cause of penitence from which it is derived, that is, the instrumental cause, is the Word of God, etc." But if the Saxon theologians, in a German writing published in 1629 on the occasion of the Rathmannian controversy, titled On the Holy Scripture (pp. 141 ff.), do not seem equally to attribute the name and concept of "instrument" or "instrumental cause" to the Word of God, it should be observed that this is said with respect to instruments that are (as Rathmann alone acknowledged) passive, which have no power in themselves ("passive instruments that have no power in themselves," pp. 141–143), such as are commonly designated by the name "instruments," from whose class the Word of God is to be exempted ("the Word of God is not to be counted among the common passive instruments and tools," p. 146). Therefore, on the assumption that the term "instrument" without qualification seemed to designate passive instruments, those theologians added that the Word of God, in this stricter sense, is not an instrument, but if it is to be called by that name, the term "instrument" must be taken ἐν πλάτει (en platei, "in a broader signification"), p. 146, namely so as not to denote precisely passive instruments but to encompass active ones no less. And this very thing the blessed Musaeus also recognizes and emphasizes, when he accurately and carefully distinguishes between instruments of one kind, which are not conjoined with the principal cause except in use (and these coincide with those called passive), such as an axe, a hammer, and so forth, and instruments of another kind, which have the principal cause always conjoined with them even apart from use in subject and power, and consequently also always have in themselves the active power of the principal cause (and these are active instruments), such as the members of the human body, for example, the hand. And he refers Sacred Scripture not to the former but to the latter class of instruments, since just as it always has the Holy Spirit, even apart from use, conjoined with itself in subject and power, so it also has His power of illuminating and converting, as the principal cause's power, always in itself, even apart from use (Musaeus, Introduction, the same work, sec. 9, pp. 588–589). This is entirely in the manner in which their predecessors wrote (the same work, p. 224a): "An axe is an instrument that is not conjoined but separated; not living but inanimate; and it does not act by an intrinsic power but by one externally impressed; whence it is called, especially on Rathmann's assumption, a passive instrument, although in its own way it does act. On the contrary, a hand in a living body is a conjoined, living instrument, acting by an implanted and intrinsic power; whence it is called an active and cooperative instrument." Compare p. 267b, where the Word of God or Sacred Scripture is exempted from the class of passive instruments but reckoned among cooperative ones. Moreover, our theologians, when disputing against the Schwenckfeldians and similar enthusiasts (whose frequent objection is that by which they try to assail our teaching on the efficacy of Scripture, namely that by this reasoning there is attributed to the Word or Scripture what properly belongs to God), respond by means of the distinction between the principal cause and the instrumental cause: the former is God, the latter is the Word of God. See Schlüsselburg (Schlüsselburg, Catalogue of Heresies, book 9, on the Schwenckfeldians, pp. 301 ff.); Thummius (Thummius, Against the Errors of Weigel, error 12, p. 21); Gerhard (Gerhard, Academic Disputations, disputation 1 against Weigel, sec. 19, p. 827); and very recently the theologians of Lübeck, Hamburg, and Lüneburg (in The Doctrinal and Protective Writing Against the Guthmannian Patron of Revelation, part 2, pp. 273, 287, 311, 313, 506 ff.). But having admitted that Scripture is an instrumental cause of spiritual effects, since it seemed that, from the nature of instrumental causality, it would need to be explained how Scripture is elevated beyond its native power by the principal cause to produce supernatural effects, the blessed Musaeus taught (Musaeus, Introduction, the same work, sec. 11, pp. 595 ff.) that Sacred Scripture is indeed not elevated by a power of the principal cause supervening from without only in use (since it already has that power intimately conjoined with itself apart from use), but rather through this: that the Holy Spirit, with His power of illuminating and converting, communicated to Scripture, simultaneously actually flows into the illumination and conversion of a person, and assists Scripture in producing these nobler effects, which are beyond its own (that is, Scripture's) native and proper power (distinct from the power of the Holy Spirit), by the influx of a nobler (indeed truly infinite) power. In this manner also the blessed J. Gerhard writes (Gerhard, Loci Theologici, vol. 6, book on the Ministry of the Church, sec. 253, p. 406): "It pleased God to elevate the external Word, as an instrumentally acting cause, to that divine effect of conversion and the salvation of human beings." Nor did the blessed Christian Chemnitz hesitate to defend the same position (Chemnitz, Disputation on the Gratuitous Justification of the Sinful Person before God, sec. 18): that God uses the Word as an instrumental cause, and that the Word, although it does not attain the effect by itself and by its own proper power, is nevertheless elevated beyond its natural power to produce it by the principal cause. Compare, with what has been said so far, the blessed Musaeus (Musaeus, Detailed Explanation, book 1, question 10, pp. 57 ff. to 110).

See Musaeus (Musaeus, Introduction, the same work, sec. 9, pp. 580 ff.). Compare also the predecessors (the same work, p. 266), where they commend that saying of Movius: "The Holy Spirit and the Word of God are two distinct principles of conversion, but conjoined in the act of conversion they stand as if for one cause, whence only one, single, and undivided action of the Word and the Holy Spirit can result."

### 40 Furthermore, among the attributes of Holy Scripture belongs its Perfection

Furthermore, among the attributes of Holy Scripture belongs its Perfection, or Sufficiency, by which it is able to instruct us fully and perfectly concerning all things that a person seeking salvation must believe and do.

Notes. Indeed, this attribute flows from the fact that Holy Scripture is the first principle of theological knowledge; and it must therefore be adequate to all matters subject to the discipline of theology. To the same point belongs what we indicated above in Section XX and note (d), pages 87 and 88: namely, that the Scripture which has been divinely granted for the instruction of human beings in the true religion unto salvation must necessarily be sufficient (Musaeus, Introduction, part 2, chapters 5 through 7, pages 317 and 318).

At this point, Perfection and Sufficiency coincide. The concern here is not so much with the number of books that were ever written by holy men, some of which, as far as the names of authors or titles cited in the surviving books of Scripture are concerned, are thought to have perished. Rather, what is considered is the perfection of the surviving Scripture in relation to its end, as will be evident from what follows. Nevertheless, even concerning those books which some call lost, the following observations must be made. Some of them have not truly perished but still survive under other titles. For example, the words of Nathan and Gad, cited in 1 Chronicles 29:29, probably survive under the title of the books of Samuel. Likewise, the prophecy of Ahijah the Shilonite and the visions of Iddo, cited in 2 Chronicles 9:29, and finally the visions of Hozai, mentioned in 2 Chronicles 33:19, probably survive under the name of the books of Kings.

If, however, some writings of holy men have truly perished, it must be maintained that they were committed to writing not by divine inspiration but by human effort, and were historical rather than doctrinal in character. Indeed, even if one were to concede that divinely inspired books containing sacred doctrines had perished, the doctrines themselves nevertheless appear no less correctly and fully transmitted in the other surviving books. Certainly, no book that had once, by the intention of the Holy Spirit, entered into the body of the Canon or rule of faith, has perished to the detriment of Canonical Scripture, that is, in such a way that it would cease to be the adequate principle and norm of the doctrine of faith and morals. On this, see Gerhard (Catholic Confession, book 2, article 1, chapter 4, page 254 and following), to which correspond the things that Musaeus wrote in the Continuation of his Introduction, to be published, God willing (ean ho theos thelese), chapter 9.

The perfection of Scripture is to be considered in relation to its end; this is the constant opinion of our theologians. Those things are called perfect in relation to an end which lack nothing of what is necessary for attaining that end. The ultimate end of Scripture is our salvation; the intermediate end is faith in Christ, with which holiness of life is necessarily joined, as we said in Section XI, pages 77 and 78.

Scripture is perfect in such a way that no other principle or partial norm, such as unwritten traditions, need be joined to it alongside, since all doctrines of faith and morals without exception are contained in the Scriptures. Some are contained autotelei (sine kerypton), that is, according to the letter, explicitly and in so many words; others kata dianoian, virtually and implicitly, so that they can be gathered and known from those things that are expressly read, by a legitimate and easy inference (Gerhard, Exegesis, book 1, chapter 18, section 1, page 366, printed page 385). Gerhard also usefully notes that what was written at any given time of the Church exhibited a perfect Canon, since the divine revelation in those books was perfectly set forth with respect to that time. Thus, when only the books of Moses existed, Scripture was perfect, that is, with respect to that time of the Church when there did not yet exist further revelations which God willed to be committed to writing; to which may be referred that apostolic saying: "If in anything you think otherwise, God will reveal this also to you" (Philippians 3:15; Gerhard, Exegesis, book 1, section 266, page 386).

For it is expressly said in 2 Timothy 3:15 that the sacred writings, which Timothy had known from childhood, and therefore the Old Testament Scripture, which alone existed when Timothy was a child, were able to make him sophisai, that is, learned and wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus. Here the proportion of Scripture as a perfect principle to its end, which is common to all members of the Church, namely faith and salvation, is most manifest. For if even one of those things that pertain to faith and are necessary for a person to know for salvation were not contained in the Scriptures, then Scripture, with respect to this very doctrine omitted by it, would leave a person in ignorance or lead him into error, and could not make him wise unto salvation.

The Apostle continues in the same passage and shows in verses 16 and 17 that Holy Scripture is perfect in relation to the end proper to teachers. For he says that all Scripture, just as it is divinely inspired, so also all of it, that is, with respect to the whole body of doctrines it contains, is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness; and profitable for accomplishing these things not in just any manner, but in such a way that the man of God, the minister and teacher of the Church divinely called, may be artios, perfect (holding all the parts of his office, as Estius interprets it), for every such good work: that is, for teaching all things whatsoever are necessary to be believed, for solidly refuting all opposing errors, for persuading the avoidance of all vices and the cultivation of morals with respect to every species of virtue, he may be exertismenos, absolutely or perfectly instructed and equipped. This could not be the case unless Scripture itself contained and sufficiently demonstrated all these things.

Compare also John 20:31, where the things that John had written, not only about the deeds of Christ, but also about His doctrine, person, and office, are said to have been written for this end: that people, knowing the things that are written, might believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Savior of the world, and the Son of God, and that believing they might have life through His name. Therefore Scripture must contain and teach, without any deficiency, all the things that are necessary to know for saving faith and salvation itself.

### 41 Finally, among the attributes of Scripture a place belongs to Perspicuity

Finally, among the attributes of Scripture a place belongs to Perspicuity, or the fact that those things which are necessary for a person tending toward salvation to believe and to do are set forth in Scripture in words and phrases so clear and received in common usage, that any person who knows the language and possesses even moderate judgment, and who attends to the words, can grasp the true sense of the words with respect to those things necessary for him to know, and can embrace the very heads of doctrine by a simple apprehension of the mind; inasmuch as the human intellect is led by Scripture itself and its supernatural light, or the divine power conjoined to it, to give the assent of faith to the word apprehended and the things signified.

Notes. For it is required of a principle of knowing, and of the formal object of any intellectual habit, that it, being known first, should lead into the knowledge of the other things that are subject to that habit, according to what we said in Chapter 1, Section III, note (d), and Chapter 2, Section I, note (a).

Here we do not consider the general object of Scripture in its full breadth, but its special and primary object, which was treated above in Section IX, pages 74 and 75. For otherwise, if you were to survey all the things that occur in the Scriptures, it must be admitted that much obscurity would be found, for example, in proper names, chronological matters, genealogies, prophecies before their fulfillment, and so forth; but not equally in the elementary articles of faith (Cundisaeus, Notes on the Compendium of Hutterus, book 1, question 7, page 31).

The perspicuity of Scripture can indeed be established as threefold: one on the part of the things, another on the part of the words, and a third on the part of the supernatural light. But the first, which consists in the evidence of the things, or clarity in the order of distinct knowledge of them, either in themselves and from the apprehension of terms, or on account of principles that are known in themselves and with which those things have a necessary connection, is not considered here. For although it has a place in certain objects of Scripture that are subject to the natural light, yet with respect to the mysteries of faith, in the transmission of which Scripture is principally occupied, it does not have a place. When some of our theologians have said that the things of Scripture are not obscure, this must be understood in the sense that those things, although in themselves they are not self-evident (as those same theologians also said, that the things of God are obscure), are nevertheless perspicuously set forth in Scripture, so that the meaning of this expression reduces to the perspicuity of the words (Gerhard, Catholic Confession, book 2, special article 1, chapter 3, page 210).

Concerning the third kind of perspicuity, which in its own way pertains to the authority and efficacy of Scripture, discussion occurs at the end of this section and will be treated more fully in note (m). In the meantime, regarding the second, that is, the perspicuity of the words, it must be noted that it consists in the selection of the words themselves and their congruity with the things signified, and in their mutual connection and order according to common usage of speech. This is what Luther called the external clarity of Scripture (On the Bondage of the Will, volume 3, Jena Latin edition, folio 169a). Others call it grammatical perspicuity (Cundisaeus, from Höpfner, Notes on the Compendium of Hutterus, question 7, page 30). Musaeus discussed this threefold perspicuity of Scripture more extensively in the unpublished (anekdoto) Continuation of the Introduction, chapter 10.

At least in those passages where, as they say, a certain doctrine of faith or morals is treated expressly, or where its proper seat is contained, so that there is no article of faith and no precept of life that is not somewhere set forth in Scripture in proper, clear, and perspicuous words (Gerhard, Catholic Confession, book 2, article 1, chapter 3, page 209). For certainly in those things that are openly set forth in the Scriptures, all those things that pertain to faith and morals are found, as Augustine says (On Christian Doctrine, book 2, chapter 9), where he also adds: "The Holy Spirit has magnificently and healthfully so modified the Holy Scriptures, that by the plainer passages He might meet our hunger, while by the more obscure ones He might remove our disdain. For hardly anything is drawn from those obscurities that is not found most plainly stated elsewhere."

Not only the regenerate and faithful, but also the unregenerate and ungodly, by virtue of the clarity of the words signifying according to their established meaning, which extends equally to all readers, can attain a knowledge of the sense signified by the words, a literal or historical knowledge, though not a saving or faith-related knowledge, as will presently be stated. And indeed Musaeus taught this in his disputations on conversion held in 1647 and following years, and afterwards published again in 1658 at Halle in Saxony, Disputation 4, Section 27 and following, and in the Treatise on Conversionpublished in 1661, Disputation 4, chapter 2, Section 44 and following, page 272 and following, and again in his Detailed Explanation, question 44, pages 642 through 697.

He followed in the footsteps of his predecessors, the blessed doctors Johann Major and Johann Gerhard. The former, in 1630, in his Refutation of the Judgment Published by Valerianus Magnus on the Acatholic Rule of Faith, proposition 3, chapter 1, section 3, page 162, expressly disputes the opinion of Valerianus, who grants the true sense of Scripture to no one except one who is inwardly illuminated and taught by the Holy Spirit. Major himself, on the contrary, observes that the true and indubitable sense of the Sacred Letters is either conjoined with the assent of the heart and the fruit of conversion, or is destitute of the same. The latter can occur in unbelievers, such as the Jews; the former belongs to believers alone. And he pointedly adds: "Just as the Apostles, by the immediate and spontaneous gift of speaking in many languages (polyglottias), adorned by the Spirit, set forth the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven to various nations, so that they could be understood verbally by each, and through the working of the Holy Spirit be received by faith; although there were not lacking those who grasped the sense of the apostolic preaching yet, denying assent to what was said, derived no fruit from it" (Acts 13). "So many who are skilled in the languages in which God willed His oracles to be extant, extract and perceive from the words of Scripture a sense that is, nota bene, true and genuine, yet they impiously repel from themselves the fruit and effect of illumination, being lost in unbelief."

Further, in section 9, page 165, Major writes: "Things being thus, Valerianus should not have said so nakedly and crudely that no one certainly attains the true sense of the Sacred Letters unless he is inwardly illuminated and taught by the Holy Spirit." And in section 10: "Applying, therefore, the censor's distinguishing mark, let us correct and amend that proposition in this manner: Every person skilled in the biblical language certainly attains the true sense of the Sacred Letters, which the meanings of known words produce, even though he is neither taught nor illuminated inwardly by the Holy Spirit. On the other hand: No one attains the true sense of the Sacred Letters in those passages which treat of the articles of faith in such a way that he gives assent to what is said and derives fruit from it, unless the Holy Spirit inwardly moves and illuminates the heart."

Gerhard, moreover, in 1625, in his Exegesis, book 1, having distinguished in section 413, page 447, between the external clarity of Scripture and the interior clarity or illumination to be sought from the Holy Spirit, thereafter in section 424, page 461, responds to Bellarmine's objection against the perspicuity of Scripture, which Bellarmine drew from the necessity of prayers for attaining understanding of it, as indicated in Psalm 119:18. Gerhard responds by distinguishing between the knowledge of the letter and of the Spirit: namely, that for literal knowledge of the articles of faith, the external clarity of Scripture suffices, but for spiritual knowledge, the interior illumination of the Holy Spirit, to be obtained through pious prayers, is required.

Indeed, the entire Theological College of Jena, and together with it also the Theological Faculty of Wittenberg, in their Refutation of the Rathmannian Counterreport, number 69, page 365a, respond affirmatively to the question: "Whether an unconverted Jew, without antecedent and supervening grace and light, can understand Holy Scripture according to the letter and ascertain the literal sense from it." Having adduced the examples of Jerome, Graser, and Buxtorf, who consulted Jews in order to ascertain the true sense of the words of the Old Testament Scripture, they finally add: "It is one thing to understand the words and the meanings of terms, and to interpret them correctly. It is another thing to understand the realities themselves, and to take them in rightly, to apply them rightly, and to grasp them by faith. For this the gracious illumination and aid of the Holy Spirit is required; but for the investigation, explanation, and understanding of the literal sense, it is not." And in the following number 70, page 365b, past the middle: "If the Counterreport aims to say that no unconverted person can attain the proper meaning which the words in Scripture carry and convey, that is, the grammatical and literal sense, unless the Holy Spirit approaches with His gracious light, we do not hold with the Counterreport, but remain with our opinion, which we established firmly in the previous postal dispatch. For the vocabularies, and those who explain them and equip them for proper use, namely the lexicons, dictionaries, and also the grammar books, composed in Latin, Greek, Hebrew, Arabic, and other languages, are inventions of the human intellect and belong among the gifts of nature, not among the gracious gifts of the Holy Spirit. For He is not appointed nor poured out to deliver the precepts of grammar, to teach how to seek the roots in Hebrew, or to teach declension and conjugation, and in logic to form enunciations and syllogisms; but rather that He should set before us the articles of faith from Scripture and instruct us in the saving truth. Many a person has the right understanding of the words, but he does not have the saving understanding of the mysteries that belongs to faith. Therefore one must beware of equivocation here as well."

Furthermore, there could be adduced the concordant statements of Hunnius, Disputation 64, chapter 3, sections 6 through 8, volume 5 of his works, folio 631; Jakob Martini, Theological Disputations, Disputation 11, sections 29 and 30, sections 100 and following; Konrad Dieterici, in his Catechetical Institutes, on Sacred Scripture, question 30, response to objection 1 of the papists, page 45; the Marburg theologians, and in particular Johann Steuber, Disputation 7, on the Augsburg Confession, article 18, section 56, page 154; further, Justus Feuerborn, in his Anti-Ostorodus, Disputation 2, section 3; and Heinrich Kromayer, Positive and Polemical Theology, article 1, antithesis 6, page 70.

Thus Gerhard writes: "We by no means affirm that Scripture is clear and perspicuous to anyone whatsoever, but to those for whom there is no impediment either from age or from ignorance of the language in which they read Scripture" (Exegesis, section 413, pages 447 and 448). And Jakob Martini, in the same passage, sections 99 and following, observes that the reason not everyone understands Scripture arises from the privation of a twofold set of means, natural and supernatural; and among the natural means, the first is knowledge of the languages. As Musaeus teaches in his Disputations on Conversion, held in 1647 and following years, Disputation 4, Section 36: "For those who are unskilled in the languages in which the Word of God was originally written, that is, Hebrew and Greek, or who have not even learned to read, it suffices if they believe the doctrines of the faith, set before them in their vernacular language, to be true and revealed by God in the Holy Scriptures in the sense in which they have been set forth to them; which assent the Holy Spirit works in them, since He is efficacious in the hearts of people through the Word even when it is preached in the vernacular language, and He testifies of it that it is the divine Word. But for those who are to be instructed and converted through the Word of God read or preached in those languages in which it was originally written, it is altogether necessary that they be skilled in those languages; and if they are not absolutely certain about the sense of each passage of Scripture containing some doctrine of faith, they should at least believe that those doctrines which concern the foundation of salvation are each and every one contained in the Holy Scriptures, so that they do not doubt the sense of those passages, apprehended from the words themselves signifying according to their established meaning, through knowledge of that language. For otherwise they could not believe those doctrines to be true, since they are believed to be true for no other reason than that they have been revealed by God, that is, because they are contained in that sense in the Scriptures" (compare the predecessors, in the Appendix to Dedekennus's Counsel, at the same passage).

This is what Gerhard, in the same passage, requires: that there be no impediment from age, and therefore no deficiency of judgment arising from youthful age. The same reasoning applies if those who are more advanced in years possess the judgment of a child.

A person who does not attend to the words themselves but indulges his own prejudices and twists the words of Scripture to fit them, can err even in perspicuous passages and in the investigation of the genuine sense. Hence Gerhard, in his Catholic Confession, book 2, article 1, chapter 3, pages 209 and 210, requires that no impediment be presented by a preconceived opinion (Glassius, Foundation of Faith, chapter 3, page 103).

For although not all believers are teachers, nor do all interpret, according to 1 Corinthians 12:29, yet both theologians have that from which, as from a perspicuous principle, being learned, they are apt for teaching and refuting, according to 2 Timothy 3:16 and 17; and the remaining faithful likewise have that in which they may find eternal life, the way that leads to life having been perspicuously shown to them by the Scriptures themselves (John 5:39).

This is what they otherwise call literal or historical knowledge, distinguishing it from saving knowledge, which pertains to the second operation of the mind and involves a fitting judgment about the sense of the words as truly divine, and consequently a wholly certain assent of divine faith that the things signified truly are such as they are signified by the words to be (see Musaeus and the other authors cited in note (d), in their respective places).

The perspicuity of the words of Scripture is proved, first, from the efficient and final cause of Scripture itself. Since God, the Author of Scripture, caused it to be written so that people, from reading it, might be instructed unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus, according to 2 Timothy 3:15, and since He Himself, as the Artisan of mind and tongue, was undoubtedly able to speak plainly, it must be believed that He willed with supreme providence that divine things should lack deceit, so that all might understand what was spoken to all, in the words of Lactantius (Divine Institutes, book 6, chapter 21; Gerhard, Exegesis, section 415, page 449; Glassius, Foundation of Faith, chapter 3, pages 73 and 74). And just as in general the principal virtue of speech destined for the instruction of others is perspicuity, and perspicuous speech must be so constituted not only that it can be understood, but that it cannot possibly not be understood, as Quintilian says (Institutes of Oratory, book 2, chapter 2), so it must be acknowledged that Holy Scripture, which has been divinely given for teaching, instruction, and so forth, possesses in those things that are necessary to know a perspicuity that is owed to it by its very end.

To this is added, second, that Paul, in 1 Corinthians 14:8 and 9, where he most diligently urges upon the teachers of the Church that they should set forth the doctrines of the faith in a perspicuous and customary manner of speech so that they may be easily understood by all, gives this reason: "For if the trumpet gives an uncertain sound, who will prepare himself for battle? So also you, unless you utter by the tongue a significant speech, how will what is said be understood? For you will be speaking into the air." Therefore, unless we say, which cannot be said without impiety, that Scripture speaks not so much for the instruction of people as into the air, and that it is like a trumpet giving an uncertain sound from which no one will prepare for battle, and consequently that Scripture is futile, it must be admitted that the signification of the words employed in Scripture is known to readers according to the common usage of speech, and therefore that the language of Scripture is perspicuous (Musaeus, Disputations on Conversion, held in 1647 and following years, Disputation 4, Section 28).

Moreover, third, in Deuteronomy 30:14, it is said: "This word which I speak to you is near, in your mouth and in your heart," that is, it is committed to signifying words drawn from common usage in such a way that it can easily be understood. For in the preceding verses this nearness is explained by the fact that this word is not hidden, so that its understanding would need to be sought from heaven or from the abyss, as Kromayer interprets it (Positive and Polemical Theology, article 1, thesis 6, page 67). Hence, although the Law, of which God speaks through Moses and which is the rule of things to be done, constitutes only one part of Scripture, yet because Paul, being divinely inspired (theopneustos), transfers these very words that were once spoken by God about the Law also to the Gospel concerning Christ and the righteousness of faith (Romans 10:6, 8), it must certainly be admitted that Scripture, with respect to the Gospel as much as the Law, is clear and perspicuous on the part of the words. Compare what we shall say in the following note.

This is what is said in Psalm 19:8 and 9: the Law of the Lord (by which name is understood not precisely the Law specially so called and contradistinguished from the Gospel, but also the Gospel itself, as is evident from the comparison with Romans 10:18, and consequently the whole doctrine that is treated in Scripture as its primary object, and of which we are here speaking) illuminates the eyes and makes the simple person wise. And in Psalm 119:105, the Word of God is a lamp to one's feet and a light to one's path, namely so that one may be prudent and guard oneself from the way of falsehood, according to verse 104. Again, in 2 Peter 1:19, it is said that we should attend to the prophetic word (of prophetic Scripture, according to verse 20) as to a lamp shining (hos lychno phainonti) in a dark place, until the day dawns and the Morning Star rises in our hearts.

All these things tend to this, that we may understand that Scripture, in those things which must be manifest to a person in the state of this life (as they call it), lest being led into errors he fail to find salvation, and therefore with respect to the doctrine of faith and morals, provides to the intellect (as the eye of the mind) what a lighted and shining lamp provides to a traveler and to his bodily eyes for treading the right way, avoiding byways, and walking without stumbling. Therefore Scripture must be luminous not only in itself but also to others. And because two things are required for a person to know rightly the way of salvation: first, that he perceive by a simple apprehension of the mind those things necessary for him to know as one tending toward salvation; and second, that he embrace those things once apprehended as true and divinely revealed, and give the assent of faith; so Scripture, which in this matter must function as a light or shining lamp, must accomplish these two things. First, it must represent to the intellect, by words signifying according to their established meaning and that are perspicuous, the things that are to be known, so that they can be perceived by a simple apprehension of the mind. Second, when the thing signified is more sublime and the intellect itself is weaker or altogether corrupted, so that it cannot by its own powers rightly judge what is signified by those words, nor of itself give or produce the assent that it owes, Scripture itself, by its own power as an illuminator, must lead the intellect to that point and bestow the faculty of knowing and assenting.

### 42 In order that Scripture may be consulted by persons unskilled in the sacred languages
