In order that Scripture may be consulted by persons unskilled in the sacred languages, Hebrew and Greek, for the knowledge of the doctrine of faith and morals, it is useful that versions of Scripture exist in all manner of languages, and that people be encouraged to read them.

Notes. For these are the purposes of Scripture; see Section X and notes (a) and (c), pages 75 and 76. See also Section XLI and note (f), pages 154 and 155.

That is, translations of the words of Scripture from a less known language into another language or speech that is better known, which the Greeks call metaphrasin.

Versions should exist in all languages inasmuch as the Church was to be planted and preserved throughout all the nations of the earth and among peoples of every tongue (Matthew 28:19; Mark 16:15; Colossians 3:11).

The purpose is that the Word of Christ may dwell in them richly (plosios enoikeito), and that they may teach and admonish one another (Colossians 3:16). The arguments that we brought forward in note (c) to Section X, pages 75 and 76, are also valid here (Musaeus, Preface to the Treatise on Conversion, published 1660, pages 7 and following, page 21 and following). Although versions composed by human effort do not have canonical authority in the way that the divinely inspired (theopneustoi) texts do, nevertheless, insofar as they are conformed to those texts, they certainly serve for the attainment of faith and the advancement of faith, and for the exclusion of opposing errors.

### 43 But in order that the true sense of the words of Scripture

But in order that the true sense of the words of Scripture, especially the literal sense, which for any one passage is only one; and then also the mystical sense, wherever it has a place, may be rightly understood; and in order that not only the meaning of the clearer passages may be firmly held against the distortions of the heterodox, but also that the more difficult passages may be unfolded and understood for the advancement of spiritual knowledge: the rules of sound interpretation must be observed.

Notes. The sense of a passage is the concept of the mind which the author of Scripture intended and willed to signify by his words.

The literal sense is that which, absolutely speaking, is said to be signified by the words, and is proximately and immediately intended to be signified through them. If the words are taken in their proper meaning, it is called the proper sense; if they are modified by some figure of speech, it is called the figurative sense (Glassius, Sacred Philology, book 2, part 1, tract 2, section 1, page 269 and following).

For it is customary in every language and in every mode of expression that by one and the same words, set down once in one and the same context, an author intends to signify only one sense. Since God in Scripture speaks to human beings in a human manner, and with words signifying according to their established meaning and drawn from customary usage, it is rightly believed that in Scripture too the literal sense of any one passage is one, not many (Glassius, Sacred Philology, same passage, page 268).

The mystical sense is that which is not signified proximately by the words themselves, but by the things signified by those words, insofar as those things are types, shadows, figures, signs, or symbols of other things. It is also called the spiritual sense (Glassius, same passage, tract 1, section 1, page 249). From this it is also clear that the literal sense is prior to the mystical sense in nature and order (Glassius, same passage, tract 2, section 2, page 289, who also in what follows deserves to be read particularly on the allegorical, typological, and parabolic senses).

For a twofold sense, both literal and mystical, is not to be sought and embraced in every single text of Scripture and in every individual passage (Glassius, same passage, tract 1, section 1, page 248). A distinction must be drawn between, for example, innate allegories, which are expressly handed down in the Scriptures themselves and are properly speaking the mystical sense of Scripture, and imported allegories, or accommodations devised by interpreters, of things signified by the words to other things, which, properly speaking, are not the sense intended by the Holy Spirit in that place (Glassius, tract 2, section 3, article 3, pages 291 and 292).

For although from the words of Scripture that treat expressly of some doctrine, set forth in a known language, even the simplest persons can grasp a true and determinate sense without difficulty, it can nevertheless and often does happen that through the frauds of the heterodox, the sense even of clear words is perverted and rendered doubtful by contrived little arguments. This is manifest from the examples of the words of institution of the Lord's Supper, and of various passages that prove the deity of Christ. To meet this rightly, the rules of sound interpretation must be called in as an aid, and the true sense, conformable to those rules, must be distinguished from other false and fictitious senses.

See what we said in Section XLI, notes (b) and (d), pages 149 and 150. Some passages of Scripture are obscure in themselves and when considered in isolation; some are obscure in relation to other passages with which they seem to conflict. Both must be addressed with the help of legitimate interpretation (Gerhard, On the Interpretation of Scripture, section 64 and following).

For our theologians do not maintain that each person's private spirit is to be followed. Rather, they fully acknowledge rules of sound interpretation: both general rules, which right reason supplies as founded in nature and common to the interpretation of all writings, and special rules, which have been particularly observed in Sacred Scripture itself. That Luther was an observer of both kinds of rules is shown by Musaeus in the Preface to the Treatise on Conversion, page 37 and following, and in the Vindication of the German Glossed Bible, Disputation 2, thesis 35 and following, page 111 and following.

### 44 The rules for interpreting Scripture with respect to the literal sense are…

The rules for interpreting Scripture with respect to the literal sense are essentially reducible to these: I.The form and construction of the words and phrases must be diligently considered according to the custom of the language. II. From the antecedent and consequent context, from the occasion, scope, subject matter, and other causes, the intention of the speaker must be investigated. Concerning these, as well as other more specific rules that they contain under them, more ample treatment is given in the schools of exegetical theology.

Notes. Thus Franzius included in two precepts the things that pertain to the interpretation of Scripture, and Glassius follows him (Sacred Philology, book 2, part 2, section 1, page 351 and following).

Just as every language has its own genius and idioms, so also the Hebrew and Greek languages have theirs, for which the sacred grammar and rhetoric of Glassius in the Sacred Philology must be consulted, as well as lexicons, concordances, and the critical observations of scholars. For in this way not only the polysemy of words but also the emphasis, and not rarely the occasion and means for resolving apparent contradictions, is recognized.

This rule was formerly acknowledged and handed down by Hilary (On the Trinity, book 4, page 27, and book 9, page 116).

Beyond Gerhard, Franzius, and Glassius in the passages cited, one may also consult from among our theologians Flacius in his Key, Dannhauer in his Sacred Hermeneutics, Daniel Cramer in his Introduction to the Prophetic and Apostolic Books, Georg Grosshain in his Epitome of Sacred Hermeneutics, and others. To add more here is not consistent with the purpose of this work.

### 45 In particular, in order that the mysteries of faith transmitted in the…

In particular, in order that the mysteries of faith transmitted in the Scriptures may be rightly recognized, it must be observed that one must persist in the proper and customary signification of words, as long as no manifest circumstance of the text, or the condition of the subject matter, or some other pressing reason compels one to descend to an improper signification.

Notes. For this reason we thought this rule should be particularly emphasized.

This rule is founded in the natural manner of understanding, by which we are directed to attend to that sense which, according to the common usage and signification of the words, all people conceive or would conceive; for otherwise there would be no certainty of our understanding (Musaeus, Vindication of the Bible, Disputation 2, section 35, pages 111 and 112).

Although the thing signified may be more remote from human understanding and from the condition of other things to which we are accustomed, it must nevertheless be considered that this is proper to mysteries. See also Musaeus, Dissertation on the Lord's Supper against Vorstius, section 5, page 2.

If, however, the analogy of faith, or clearer parallel passages, or the antecedent and consequent context, or the scope of the speaker, or other circumstances, most openly conflict with the proper signification of the words, or if, upon admitting the proper signification, a manifest and unmistakable contradiction presents itself, then the necessity of departing from the proper signification of the words will be imposed upon the interpreter.

### 46 Finally, just as theological conclusions

Finally, just as theological conclusions, and things to be believed with divine faith, are rightly deduced from Holy Scripture as a perspicuous principle, so in arguments of this kind, even those whose conclusion is purely theological, not only the formal principles of reason are undoubtedly usefully employed, but also the material principles of reason are rightly used, provided that, when they are particular or singular, they are subjoined to a universal theological principle; and that no universal principles of reason are employed other than those of absolute necessity, such that the opposite involves a manifest contradiction.

Notes. For our theologians never denied this, even when they said that they would use Scripture alone as the principle, norm, or rule. Rather, they affirmed it every time they said they would prove their doctrines from the Scriptures, or that they wished controverted questions to be referred to Scripture as the norm. For to prove is to deduce something from another thing, as a conclusion from premises, by way of inference. To the norm, moreover, what needs to be referred is not so much what is formally affirmed or denied in that which serves as the norm, but rather that concerning which a doubt has arisen as to whether it agrees with those things that are formally contained therein (Musaeus, Treatise on the Use of the Principles of Reason, book 1, at the beginning, and book 2, chapter 13, section 30; also in the Treatise on Conversion, Disputation 9, chapters 2 and 3; and Disputation 1 against Masen, in which the Meditated Concord proposed by Masen is examined, section 29 and following, page 122 and following).

Concerning those matters that pertain to the mixed articles of faith and are treated not only in revealed theology but also in philosophy by the light of reason, there is less difficulty. On this distinction of theological questions, see Musaeus, On the Use of the Principles of Reason, book 1, chapter 6, section 6, chapters 13 and following, and book 2, chapter 1.

That is, those principles that pertain to the form of syllogisms, the disposition of terms in figure and mode, and the rules governing inferences (Musaeus, same treatise, book 2, chapter 2).

For although not all theological discourses need to be expressly set forth in syllogistic form, whenever the nature of a serious and solid disputation demands it, this labor should not be avoided. Otherwise it suffices that the discourses be such as can be reduced to syllogistic form.

By this name are understood propositions known by the light of nature and possessing metaphysical, physical, or moral evidence, which pertain to the matter of arguments and constitute the major or minor premise (Musaeus, same passage, book 2, chapter 2).

It follows indeed, if these are rightly conjoined with a theological proposition, that the conclusion is not only true and certain, but also one that pertains to the faith. This is demonstrated by Musaeus in the Treatise on Conversion, Disputations 8 and 9. Compare also what we said in note (g) to Section XXXV, page 116.

To this belongs the example we brought forward in the same passage, page 116. To which may be joined also this one, in which a person argues: "Every human being is seriously loved by God and has grace and salvation seriously offered to him. I am a human being. Therefore, etc." See Musaeus, Treatise on Conversion, pages 593 and 594.

For example: "Whoever has perfections proper to God alone is true God. But Christ has perfections proper to God alone. Therefore, etc." The minor premise must be proved from revelation. The major is known by the light of nature, but is of absolute necessity; and it involves a contradiction to say that someone has perfections that are really identical with the divine essence and yet does not have the divine essence, or is not true God.

For otherwise, if principles of reason that are not absolutely but only in a certain respect or in a certain class universal and necessary are employed, it easily happens that a conclusion is drawn which is repugnant to the mysteries or even the primary articles of faith. This is evident from the examples of the Anti- Trinitarians and others (Musaeus, On the Use of the Principles of Reason, book 2, chapter 14 and following, page 451 and following; and Treatise on Conversion, Disputation 9, sections 30 and 31, pages 595 and 596).

### 47 In establishing the doctrine of faith and morals according to the Scriptures

In establishing the doctrine of faith and morals according to the Scriptures, just as there is no need for a peculiar judge in the strict and proper sense of the term, one who would pronounce a sentence by his own authority and who would be visible, so nevertheless, in order that truth and falsehood may be rightly distinguished, it is partly necessary to examine carefully that which is proposed and brought forward for judgment, and to form the state of the question sincerely and accurately (to which end it is pertinent that ambiguities of words and phrases be diligently unraveled, that what is conceded or undoubted be separated and set aside from what is doubtful and controverted, and that the matter still in question be expressed in terms and phrases that are most proper and fitting).

Notes. It is partly necessary also to compare known opinions with the Scriptures in such a way that it becomes evident, either by the clear and express words of Scripture, or by necessary consequence deduced from the perspicuous and clear words of Scripture understood according to the rules of sound interpretation and with due observance of the laws of valid inference (and here there recur the matters we discussed above concerning the interpretation of Scripture and the deduction of conclusions, in Sections XLV and following), that a given doctrine is truly contained in the Scriptures, or is not contained therein, or that its opposite is contained therein. And indeed, just as this task belongs to the Doctors and Ministers of the Church, both individually (for it is their office to rightly divide, ὀρθοτομεῖν (rightly cutting), the word of truth (2 Timothy 2:15), and to reject profane and empty babblings, foolish and unlearned questions (2 Timothy 2:16, 22), and to be furnished not only for doctrine but also for reproof, ἔλεγχον (refutation) (2 Timothy 3:16, 17), so that they may be able to convict those who contradict, τοὺς ἀντιλέγοντας ἐλέγχειν (to refute the gainsayers) (Titus 1:9), and to stop their mouths, ἐπιστομίζειν αὐτούς (to silence them) (Titus 1:11)) and when assembled in council (indeed, the judgment of many gathered in a Synod, if they are learned and pious, is not without reason preferred to the judgment of one or another pronouncing sentence separately; and if a universal council could be had, exhibiting the concordant votes of absolutely all Christians, it would certainly avail a very great deal; meanwhile, such councils as we have, just as they do not possess the privilege of infallibility, so they bestow, equally with individual Doctors, a judgment of discernment, not of authoritative decision, for they cannot bind the intellect to assent and acquiesce in their decisions unless they have demonstrated the agreement of their decisions with the Scriptures), so also it belongs in its own manner to other Christians (for if they are equipped with the aids necessary for explaining the Sacred Scriptures and treating theological controversies, they can judge controversies with sufficient accuracy; for simpler folk, however, it suffices if, being informed from clear statements of Scripture concerning those things which are necessary to know, they remember that all things which deviate from those statements are to be avoided by them, even though they themselves are not equal to a more thorough examination of controversies; for in this matter the admonition of Philip Melanchthon must also be observed: "Let there be such modesty of minds that they modestly retain honorable opinions, and indeed those divinely handed down, even if they cannot destroy all the sophistries that are contrived against them"

(Melanchthon, Response to the Bavarian Articles, vol. 1, Works, p. 370; cf. Chemnitz, Examination of the Council of Trent, part 3, Loci, p. 82, and On the Foundation of the Holy Supper, ch. 10, p. 160)).

Our theologians, it should be noted, who have said that Scripture is the Judge of controversies of faith, have used the word "judge" in an improper sense, meaning the rule or standard of judging, that is, the norm according to which a sentence is to be rendered, just as it is elsewhere not unusual for the law to be taken in place of the judge (cf. Niemann, On the Principles of Revealed Theology, on Sacred Scripture, Section 161; Niemann, Disputation for a Position in the Faculty of Theology, on the Judge of Controversies of Faith, Section 5 and following, through Section 12). By a judge in the proper sense is meant what others call an authoritative judge, likewise a decisive, absolute, and principal judge, namely one who, by virtue of the authority he possesses, can oblige the litigants to acquiesce in the sentence he has rendered, without further inquiry or hesitation (cf. the same work, Section 18; Gerhard, Exegesis, book 1, Section 452). For otherwise our theologians would acknowledge that the Holy Spirit is the Judge of controversies, and indeed an authoritative one: especially in those matters which are contained in the clear and express words of Scripture, and in His own manner also with respect to those things which are deduced by consequence from the Scriptures (Niemann, same work, Sections 20 and following). That is to say, although He does not compel men by external force to acquiesce in His decision with respect to τὸν λόγον τὸν ἔξω (the outward reason), nevertheless, when the meaning of Scripture as the divine voice is clear, it is certain that the minds of men, with respect to τὸν λόγον τὸν ἔσω (the inward reason), are convinced, so that they can raise no objection except against a protesting conscience.

Indeed, all controversies concerning the dogmas of faith and morals could be judged and settled in this manner, provided that those who are about to dispute would bring to the occasion of the controversy pious minds, lovers of truth, and learned; for thus, with prejudices set aside, along with partisan zeal and depraved affections, and with the arguments of both sides weighed according to the norm of Scripture, it would easily appear which opinion is true and which is false. As for the remaining questions, however, which can be disputed on either side without prejudice to the faith, the adjudication and resolution of these ought not equally to be demanded or expected.

### 48 Sacred Scripture may be defined as a writing committed to record by God as the…

Sacred Scripture may be defined as a writing committed to record by God as the inspiring cause, through the Prophets and Apostles, partly in the Hebrew and partly in the Greek language, which instructs sinful man concerning all things that are necessary to be believed and done, so that he may obtain faith in Christ, and, being reconciled to God, may live holily, and at length, by the benefit of God, obtain eternal life.

Notes. By the term "Scripture" is indicated the generic concept, which Sacred Scripture shares in common with other writings, rightly established in this respect (cf. Musaeus, Introduction, part 2, ch. 2, Section 24, p. 278; and see above, Section 2, note (a), p. 63). Nor is it difficult to recognize that this generic concept is rightly constituted in that which is common to Sacred Scripture and other writings. If one prefers to substitute "Word of God" in place of the genus, it must certainly be understood as the external word and verbal sign (cf. Musaeus, same work, pp. 279, 281). The further specifications that follow pertain to the specific difference, drawn from the causes of Scripture, among which first occurs the principal efficient cause, namely God (see above, Section 3, p. 64). The term "inspiring" indicates partly the causality of the principal efficient cause, and partly the formal cause of Scripture (see Sections 4, p. 64, and 8, pp. 72, 73). The Prophets and Apostles are the less principal efficient cause (see Section 6, p. 68). The Hebrew and Greek languages pertain to the material out of which, or the material element of Scripture (see Section 7, pp. 69 and following). Sinful man is the final cause "for whom" Scripture exists (see Section 10, p. 75). The things necessary to be believed and done are the primary object of Scripture (see Section 9, p. 74). Faith is the intermediate final cause, "the end which" is aimed at (see Section 11, pp. 76 and following). Eternal life is the ultimate final cause (see the same place).

## 3 On God

### 1 By the name of God

By the name of God, we commonly understand the most excellent of all beings, than which nothing better can exist or be conceived; or, the first being, which exists of itself and is the cause of all other beings, and which preserves and governs all things.

Notes. That God must be treated first in theology is clear from the Prolegomena, ch. 1, sect. 17, p. 31, and sect. 39, p. 69.

The word "God" is here taken in its proper sense. For otherwise the word is improperly transferred to creatures that excel above others, for example angels and magistrates, and even to the idols of the Gentiles, which are held to be gods by the false opinion of men.

Indeed, it is established by experience that all human beings in their earthly pilgrimage conceive of God in no other way than in relation to created things (Musaeus, Introduction, ch. 2, sect. 22, no. 2, p. 76).

To this point it is also relevant that human beings, especially in calamities, take refuge in God, whom they commonly call the Best and Greatest. Compare Seneca (On Benefits, chs. 6 and 7). They sometimes invoke Him as Judge between themselves and others, and sometimes, being conscious of guilt, they fear Him as the most holy and most powerful.

### 2 Among the names of God

Among the names of God, of which many occur in the Scriptures of the Old Testament, that name הוהי (YHWH) stands out preeminently as the essential and incommunicable name.

Notes. The names are customarily numbered at ten, of which four are preeminent: הוהי, םיהלא ,ינדא, and לא (Jerome, Epistle 136, to Marcellinus; Gerhard, part 1, Loci on the Nature of God, sect. 21).

This name is thought to be derived from that passage in Exodus 3:14, היהא רשא היהא, "I am (or, I will be) who I am (or, who I will be)."

It denotes essence par excellence, namely that God is such a being as no other is or can be.

Moreover, it is incommunicable, for the following reasons: (1.) In the whole of Scripture no passage occurs in which the name הוהי in the nominative case is found attributed to any creature. And when an appearing angel claims this name for himself, the context shows that what is to be understood is not a created angel but the uncreated one, that is, the Son of God (for example, Exodus 3). (2.) Indeed, God Himself claims this name for Himself alone (Exodus 3:14; Numbers 6:24-26; Isaiah 42:8). (3.) Furthermore, Scripture attributes it to God as His proper name (Exodus 15:3; Isaiah 48:2; 54:5). (4.) Scripture also sometimes adds an exclusive particle (Psalm 83:19; Isaiah 37:20). (5.) To this is added the fact that all the marks of a proper name belong to this name: for instance, that it lacks a plural number, that it does not admit a demonstrative pronoun, that it admits no suffixes, and that it is never placed in the construct state. And so Musaeus taught in his manuscript lectures against the Socinians (Musaeus, Manuscript Lectures against the Socinians, Disputation 3, Question 2; likewise in his Manuscript Lectures on Illustrious Questions, on the locus on God, Question 2, of which the earlier ones on Syncretism and Sacred Scripture have been published in print).

### 3 Similarly, the Greek name θεός (theos)

Similarly, the Greek name θεός (theos), taken in its proper sense, is not so much a name of dignity as of the divine nature.

Notes. In Scripture itself, to be sure, it is sometimes applied to magistrates (John 10:34; 2 Thessalonians 2:4) and even to idols (1 Corinthians 8:5), but improperly.

For although the name θεός, by the force of its etymology, may seem to denominate God from some operation (whether it is derived ἀπὸ τοῦ θεᾶσθαι, "from contemplating," according to John of Damascus, On the Orthodox Faith, book 1, ch. 12; or ἀπὸ θέειν, "from running," in the sense that He pervades, cherishes, and preserves all things; or ἀπὸ αἴθειν, "from burning," because He is, as it were, a consuming fire, as in Deuteronomy 4:24), it must nevertheless be admitted that just as upon hearing the abstract noun θεότης (theotes, "divinity") we first conceive of the divine nature or essence, so upon hearing the name θεός we first and foremost conceive of the supposit that possesses the divine essence or nature. So also Musaeus taught in his manuscript lectures against the Socinians (Musaeus, Manuscript Lectures against the Socinians, at the cited place, Question 1). To this point also pertains what Scripture distinguishes between θεοὶ φύσει (theoi physei), gods "by nature," and θεοὶ λεγόμενοι (theoi legomenoi), gods "by name" only, not in reality or by nature (1 Corinthians 8:5; Galatians 4:8).

### 4 That God exists can be proved

That God exists can be proved: 1. from the contemplation of this universe; 2. from the testimony of conscience; 3. from the consensus of peoples, both Gentile and Christian.

Notes. Indeed, among Christians the existence of God might seem to need to be presupposed rather than proved; but since we must contend not only with atheists but also, on account of the corruption of nature, with the doubts of our own minds, the arguments that prove the existence of God are not to be neglected (Gerhard, Exegesis, book 2, sect. 58).

As for the first argument, Paul writes (Romans 1:20) that "the invisible things of God, as of one who exists, are clearly perceived from the things that have been made, being understood by the intellect" (τοῖς ποιήμασι νοούμενα καθορᾶσθαι). And it is otherwise evident how, when we turn our eyes upon this universe, we are led to the knowledge of its cause and conceive of some first being upon which it depends for its existence (Musaeus, Introduction, ch. 2, sect. 22, p. 74; sect. 24, pp. 81-82; sects. 25 and 31, pp. 82-83). There also is noted how a precise and careful knowledge of the existence of God is demonstrated by arguments drawn from a more exact consideration of this universe, for example: from movers subordinate to one another to a single First Mover; from causes subordinate to one another to a First Cause; from the governance of this universe to a supreme Governor, and so forth.

As for the second argument, Paul teaches (Romans 2:14-15) that τὸ ἔργον τοῦ νόμου (to ergon tou nomou), "the work of the law" (that is, those notions concerning the distinction between honorable and base things, with reference to a supreme Lawgiver) is written, as if by the finger of Nature or of God, on the hearts not only of the Jews but also of the Gentiles who do not have the written Law; "their conscience bearing witness and their thoughts mutually accusing them" (so that the wicked are convicted of their crimes and pronounce divine vengeance upon themselves) "or also excusing them" (so that the good are encouraged by the rectitude of their good deeds) (Musaeus, Introduction, ch. 2, sect. 22, pp. 57-58; Musaeus, Dissertation on the Insufficiency of the Light of Nature against Lord Herbert, sects. 71-72, pp. 43-44). To this point also pertains, in its own way, what was said above in the Prolegomena, ch. 1, sect. 10, pp. 20-21, concerning the innate knowledge of God. For the fact that human beings by nature prescribe to themselves, as if from the authority of some superior, what is to be done and what is to be avoided, and consequently, if they act otherwise, the result is that they hold captive (κατέχουσι, katechousi) the truth, that is, the true knowledge of what is to be done according to the will of a superior, in unrighteousness, and prevent it from exercising itself unto moral uprightness and the true worship of God (Romans 1:18); and the fact that after performing good deeds they rejoice, and after evil deeds they are struck with fear, without thinking of human rewards or punishments: all these things argue an inward and naturally implanted sense of the Deity (Musaeus, Introduction, at the cited place, pp. 57-58).

As for the third argument from the consensus of peoples, this applies not only with respect to the acquired knowledge that God exists, but also with respect to the innate knowledge (Musaeus, Introduction, at the cited place, pp. 58-60).

### 5 In order, however

In order, however, that what God is and who He is may be rightly known, first those things that pertain to the divine essence and attributes, and then those things that pertain to the divine persons, must be distinctly examined and proved from the Scriptures.

Notes. By the name of the divine essence is understood that which is first conceived in God, and by which God is adequately distinguished from all other things, and which, according to our manner of conceiving, is the principle and root of all the perfections that are attributed to God by way of properties.

By attributes are understood those perfections which, according to our mode of understanding, follow upon the essence of God, that is, upon what we first conceive in Him, and are thus attributed to God by way of adjoining forms, although in reality they are not accidents nor do they differ really from the divine essence. They are distinguished from the divine essence and from one another, however, on account of the infinite perfection of God and the imperfection of our intellect.

As for the persons, Scripture presents several who are really distinct from one another, each of whom bears Himself in the manner of an intelligent supposit, and each is taught to possess that divine essence and those divine properties, as we shall see below.

Those things that pertain to the essence and attributes of God, just as they are known in some measure from the light of nature in addition to the Scriptures, so also the consideration of these rightly precedes the treatment of the persons, which can be known only from divine revelation (on which more will be said below).

Insofar as some of these matters are known from the principles of reason, as we have just indicated, their consideration belongs to philosophy or natural theology.

### 6 The essence of God

The essence of God, as distinguished from the attributes, can be described as follows: God is a spiritual being subsisting of Himself; or more briefly: God is an independent Spirit.

Notes. No one should demand or expect a definition in the strict sense.

For it must be admitted that in this life we do not possess a quidditative, proper, and adequate knowledge of the divine essence, according to 1 Corinthians 13:12. So also Musaeus taught (Musaeus, Manuscript Lectures against the Socinians, Disputation 1, Question 5, sect. 12; compare Hafenreffer, Locus on God, p. 27; Franz, On the Interpretation of Scripture, Oracle 103, pp. 226-227, and also Disputation 5, On Sacrifices, thesis 119; Cundisius, Notes on the Compendium of Hutter, book 2, Question 2, pp. 70-71).

The word "spiritual" holds the place, as it were, of a genus or broader concept. For just as a complete being is immediately distinguished into material and immaterial, that is, spiritual, so God is rightly considered to be an immaterial or spiritual being. Compare John 4:24, where it is expressly said, πνεῦμα ὁ θεός (pneuma ho theos), "God is Spirit."

By the phrase "subsisting of Himself," God is adequately distinguished from all other things. There is nothing that you can conceive in God as a prior and determinate concept before this, namely that He is not from another and therefore subsists of Himself. This also is what Scripture says when it calls God "the first" (Isaiah 41:4; 44:6; 48:12). For to be first is to acknowledge nothing prior upon which one depends, that is, from which one has one's being. What is such, accordingly, subsists of itself. Compare Exodus 3:14, where God says that He is "the one who is," and thus, just as He attributes to Himself a wholly unique mode of existing, so He indicates that He does not exist from another, as all other beings exist, but from Himself.

### 7 The divine attributes are divided into negative and positive

The divine attributes are divided into negative and positive. The negative are: unity, simplicity, immutability, infinity, immensity, and eternity. To the class of positive attributes belong: life, knowledge, wisdom, holiness, justice, truthfulness, power, goodness, and perfection.

Notes. The common description of the attributes may be seen in the note to Section 5 above.

The negative attributes are so called because, either by the force of the words or by the force of their signification, they imply a certain negation or removal of some imperfection found in creatures.

The positive attributes are those that are conceived with respect to perfections that we discern in creatures, and in the manner of those perfections, though in a more eminent degree.

Each of these will be treated in its own order.

### 8 Unity belongs to God both in an absolute sense

Unity belongs to God both in an absolute sense, which denotes the undivided essence of God, and in an exclusive sense, by which we know God as the sole God, besides whom there is no other.

Notes. The absolute unity virtually coincides with the simplicity of God, which we are about to treat.

In its exclusive sense, unity denotes the negation of several beings of the same nature or kind.

This is proved partly from those passages of Scripture where God is expressly called one, for example, Deuteronomy 6:4, "Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is one"; 1 Corinthians 8:4, "There is no God but one" (compare Ephesians 4:6; 1 Timothy 2:5); and partly from those passages in which it is denied that any other God exists besides Him, for example, Deuteronomy 4:35, "The Lord Himself is God, and there is no other besides Him" (compare Isaiah 44:6).

### 9 Absolute simplicity belongs to God

Absolute simplicity belongs to God, by which God is free from every true and real composition.

Notes. This refers not only to composition of matter and form (which is already implied by the spiritual nature of God), and consequently also to composition of integral parts, but also to the kind of composition whereby something consists of subject and accident, or of nature and subsistence, really distinct from one another.

The composition of reason, however, for example when we conceive of God as just, and wise, and good, and so forth, does not conflict with even the highest simplicity, nor with God Himself.

To this point Exodus 3:14 is customarily referred, for there it is indicated that whatever is in God is God Himself. When, however, Sacred Scripture sometimes attributes human members and other features that occur in creatures, especially in human beings, and that imply composition in them, this is done through metaphor, namely that which they call ἀνθρωποπάθεια (anthropopatheia, "attribution of human passions to God") or συγκατάβασις (synkatabasis, "condescension"), and it must be interpreted θεοπρεπῶς (theoprepos), that is, in a manner befitting God.

### 10 The immutability of God consists in this

The immutability of God consists in this, that God is subject to no change, neither according to His being, nor according to accidents, nor according to place, nor according to will or purpose.

Notes. With respect to being, God is immortal and incorruptible (Romans 1:23, where He is called ἄφθαρτος, aphthartos, "incorruptible"; 1 Timothy 1:17, where He is called βασιλεὺς ἄφθαρτος, basileus aphthartos, "the immortal King"; and 1 Timothy 6:16, where He alone is said to possess immortality, ἀθανασία, athanasia).

With respect to accidents, James 1:17 says that with God there is no παραλλαγή ἢ τροπῆς ἀποσκίασμα (parallage e tropes aposkiasma), "variation or shadow of turning."

With respect to place, see Jeremiah 23:24, "Do I not fill heaven and earth? says the Lord." He who fills all things does not change His place, nor is He able to do so.

With respect to will and purpose, see Numbers 23:19, "God is not a man, that He should lie, nor a son of man, that He should repent. Has He said and will He not do it? Or has He spoken and will He not fulfill it?" And Malachi 3:6, "I the Lord do not change; but I have fulfilled and will fulfill what I have decreed and promised."

When, however, repentance is sometimes attributed to God in Scripture, and when local motion, descent or ascent, is sometimes ascribed to Him, this is said ἀνθρωποπαθῶς (anthropopathos), after the manner of human experience, as we said concerning immutability above. Similarly, affections are attributed to God; those, indeed, which in their formal concept imply imperfection are attributed only metaphorically, but those which do not formally imply imperfection truly belong to God, yet without any change.

### 11 Infinity of essence belongs to God

Infinity of essence belongs to God, inasmuch as the essence of God is contained by no limits.

Notes. In other respects, infinity is not a particular attribute of God but extends to various positive attributes, inasmuch as the knowledge, goodness, and power of God are said to be infinite, and so forth.

This is proved from Psalm 145:3, "Great is the Lord and greatly to be praised, and of His greatness there is no end (or investigation)." What is understood here is not greatness of mass or of quantity, which does not apply to God, but greatness of essence.

### 12 The immensity of God consists in this

The immensity of God consists in this, that the divine essence cannot be measured or enclosed by any spatial boundaries.

Notes. Rather, since other things exist, God according to His substance is omnipresent, in such a way that He is circumscribed by no place, yet is present without extension of Himself to all creatures without distance. Thus, with immensity as a negative attribute, omnipresence is customarily joined as a positive attribute. The immensity and omnipresence of God are proved from Jeremiah 23:24. For He who fills heaven and earth, although He is repletively in heaven and on earth, is nevertheless not here or there circumscriptively. And similarly, "He whom the heavens of heavens cannot contain" (1 Kings 8:27) is rightly said to be incapable of being measured by any spatial boundaries, since heaven, the highest, is so described that beyond it nothing created is indicated to exist.

When, however, God is sometimes said in Scripture to draw near to human beings and to withdraw from them, this is not to be understood as though He begins or ceases to be circumscribed according to His essence in some place, but as spoken through ἀνθρωποπάθεια (anthropopatheia), as we said concerning immutability above at Section 10. For even the fact that the Scriptures teach a certain special habitation and nearness of God in the saints, although it presupposes the indistant presence of God with respect to substance (or ἀδιαστασία, adiastasia), formally signifies a certain particular mode of modified presence, whereby God is said to be present where He manifests His presence through certain operations, namely that He confers upon and increases in the regenerate the more excellent spiritual gifts. However, whether, beyond the special gracious operation of God (who by the force of His immensity is already intimately present to all things), there is also a special approximation of His essence itself, has not yet been sufficiently clearly demonstrated. For the letter of Scriptural expressions such as "we will come to him" and the like cannot be pressed, since a rigid interpretation would signify some distance of the divine essence from the human essence, or that God had previously been absent before He came, and by this reasoning it would be necessary to deny the immensity of the divine essence. Moreover, it is certain that not only throughout the preceding century to its end, when Johann Wigand published his Systematic Consideration on the Ubiquity or Omnipresence of God (printed at Jena in 1591), and therein treated expressly of ubiquity in the Church and of the indwelling in the regenerate, but also at the time when our Gerhard began to write his Theological Loci (which was in the year 1610), the opinion concerning diverse degrees of the divine presence, to be described by diverse approximations of the divine essence to the substances of created things, was not yet known or received in our churches. Rather, Gerhard taught that the diverse degrees differ only in their effects, and that the distinction of manifold presence consists in the diversity of effects alone (Gerhard, Theological Loci, volume 1, sect. 219). Indeed, even after Gerhard had published his Exegesis fifteen years later, and in the meantime the opinion concerning the approximation of the divine essence to the substance of the human being had begun to appeal to some and become known, he himself was found not to subscribe to it but, having set forth arguments on both sides, to suspend his judgment. And so also his colleagues and successors refrained from embracing that opinion (Musaeus, Detailed Explanation, Question 74, p. 601 and following).

### 13 The eternity of God

The eternity of God, taken in the absolute sense, signifies the permanent existence or duration of God, without beginning and end and without all succession or vicissitude.

Notes. For it is not taken here for a long period of time, nor for a duration that has a beginning and merely lacks an end, but in the strictest sense, which Boethius defined as "the whole, simultaneous, and perfect possession of interminable life."

Thus it implies the negation of boundaries, that is, interminable life.

As the "whole, simultaneous possession of life," it excludes before and after, past and future, and consequently a beginning not only with respect to being but also with respect to motion and operation, so that it is rather a uniform duration.

The eternity of God is proved from Psalm 102:27, where, in contrast to heaven and earth, which exist for a long time but not without beginning or end, God is said to endure, as one exempt from all decline, fall, or ruin; He is said to be the same always, without any alteration or vicissitude. Compare Psalm 90:2, where God is said to be "from everlasting to everlasting," so that no boundary, neither beginning nor end, can be assigned to God. In Genesis 21:33 and Isaiah 40:28 He is called םלוע לא (El Olam), "the God of eternity." Likewise in 1 Timothy 1:17 He is called βασιλεὺς τῶν αἰώνων (basileus ton aionon), "the King of the ages," namely superior to all time, coexisting with all ages, yet not measurable by ages or by time. Finally, in Revelation 1:4 and 8, 11:17, and 16:5, He is described as "the one who is, who was, and who is to come," namely that before He is conceived by us to exist, He had already existed and could be conceived as existing infinitely, and that He can also be conceived as existing hereafter infinitely.

### 14 The life of God

The life of God, considered in the first act, signifies the essence or nature of God itself, insofar as it moves itself in a certain manner, or can be conceived as the principle of vital or immanent operation. In the second act, it denotes the immanent operation itself, proceeding from the divine nature.

Notes. God is called "the living God" (Genesis 16:14; Joshua 3:10; Psalm 42:3; 84:3; Isaiah 37:4; Acts 14:15). He is said to have life "in Himself" (John 5:26). He swears by His own life (Deuteronomy 32:40; Ezekiel 33:11), and human beings swear by the living God (1 Kings 17:1).

Life is taken in a double sense. In the first act, it signifies the nature of each thing that moves itself in some way; in the second act, it signifies the motion or immanent operation itself proceeding from such a nature, which is either material (namely vegetative or sensitive) or immaterial (that is, rational or intellectual). In God, however, life in the first act and in the second act are, from the side of reality, entirely the same, since the very being of God is His living.

Moreover, since this life must be the most perfect, it is necessarily immaterial and therefore intellectual. Whence we must proceed at once to treat of the intellect and will of God.

### 15 The knowledge of God consists in this

The knowledge of God consists in this, that God knows Himself and all other things distinct from Himself, both those that are and those that can be, all of them according to their own proper being, which each has in itself outside of God, by one singular act, through Himself immediately, without an intelligible species or discursive reasoning. Moreover, God understands exactly not only those things that truly exist or will exist, whether by necessity of nature or contingently through the free determination of the human will, but also those things that would have been future if some condition had been fulfilled which in fact is not fulfilled.

Notes. The knowledge or intelligence of God, whether taken for the power of understanding or for the act or actual cognition, is really the same and most simply one with the divine essence, since no accident can befall God, according to Section 9 and its note.

Hence the knowledge of God is distinguished into natural and free. Natural knowledge belongs to God by nature and necessarily, inasmuch as God knows from eternity, and antecedently to every decree of the free will, both Himself as necessarily existing and all other possible things as such (in which latter respect it is also called "knowledge of simple intelligence"). Free knowledge belongs to God consequently upon the free decree concerning things to be produced at some time, and in this way God knows from eternity all things as future after His free decree, and what each and all will do with the divine concurrence (in which respect it is called "knowledge of vision," because through it God knows things according to their own proper existence, as it were beholding them face to face).

It is called omniscience, and is proved from 1 Samuel 2:3, where God is called "the Lord of knowledge," that is, possessing all knowledge; and from 1 John 3:20, where it is expressly stated, "God knows all things." Especially noteworthy are those passages in which God is said to know the secret thoughts of all human beings, which no one else knows or can know (1 Kings 8:39; Psalm 7:10; 34:15; 139:1 and following; Proverbs 15:3).

God does not know created things only insofar as they have their being eminently in Him, but also in such a way that His intellect terminates at their being which they have in themselves. Nor are the acts of understanding in God really multiplied with respect to the diversity or number of objects.

Intelligible species, where they have any place, serve in lieu of objects and are really distinct from the intellect, constituting with it one complete principle of understanding. But in God, where there are no acts of intellect really produced, the divine intellect itself represents the object in the manner of an expressed species.

Although the word "knowledge" elsewhere implies knowledge of a thing through its cause, and therefore a progression from the cause as something better known to the effect as something less known, nevertheless, because God, to whom nothing is unknown, does not proceed from the known to the unknown, neither can knowledge through demonstration or discursive reasoning be attributed to God.

As for future contingent things and conditional future things: these are known immediately in themselves, as having in themselves a determinate truth (since of contradictory opposites, for example "Adam will sin" and "Adam will not sin," one must be true and the other false), and are therefore truly knowable. That God knows future contingent things of the kind whose existence depends on a free cause, that is, one indifferent to acting and not acting, namely on the choice of the created will, is what is peculiarly called the foreknowledge of God. This is proved partly by the many predictions of things future among human beings that have been divinely made, and partly by the fact that God distinguishes Himself from false gods by this very characteristic (Isaiah 41:22-23; 42:9; 43:9-12).

Hence arises the knowledge of the conditional future, that is, of such a kind where the condition has a connection with the effect or the future thing, but only a contingent one. This is otherwise called "middle knowledge," namely because its object lies between things considered under the aspect of bare possibility and things absolutely future. That the knowledge of conditional future things belongs to God is proved from Matthew 11:21, where Christ, as the God-man (θεάνθρωπος, theanthropos), testifies that He knows that the citizens of Tyre and Sidon would have repented in sackcloth and ashes, given a certain condition, namely if such miracles as occurred in His time in the cities of Chorazin and Bethsaida had been performed before them; yet since that condition was not fulfilled, they were not in fact converted. See also 1 Samuel 23:11 and following. Compare also the special academic dissertation on the knowledge of God by Friedrich Bechmann.

### 15 The wisdom of God denotes the most exquisite counsel of God

The wisdom of God denotes the most exquisite counsel of God, by which He knows how to dispose and order all causes and effects in a wholly admirable manner toward their end.

Notes. Although wisdom may seem to be included under the knowledge of God, since it is customarily distinguished and treated separately both in common usage and by Scripture itself, which accommodates itself to common understanding, it was proper to indicate it here separately.

This is proved from Job 12:13 and 28:20. Compare 1 Timothy 1:17, where God is called μόνος σοφός (monos sophos), "alone wise," and Romans 11:33, where the astonishing and inscrutable wisdom of God is celebrated.

### 16 Before we proceed to the consideration of the remaining attributes

Before we proceed to the consideration of the remaining attributes, something must be said about the will of God, that is, insofar as the divine essence bears itself in the manner of an appetitive power, tending toward the good known by the intellect as something to be willed, and toward the evil known as something to be rejected.

Notes. For the attributes of holiness, justice, and truthfulness pertain to the divine will.

By "will" is understood the principle of the act of willing an appetible object and of rejecting or turning away from an object that is disagreeable or evil, although the essence of God, and His will, and the act of that will, do not differ from each other or from the divine intellect in reality, but are really one and the same.

### 17 Of the acts of the divine will there are no causes that formally cause them

Of the acts of the divine will there are no causes that formally cause them; there are, however, causes that virtually cause them: an efficient cause, an internal impulsive cause, an external impulsive cause, and a final cause.

Notes. There are no formally causing causes, for otherwise it would be necessary to posit within God something really produced and really diverse from the divine essence, since a formally causing cause and the thing caused differ as one thing from another. But on the contrary, it would imply a contradiction if we were to posit that the divine essence is independent and yet that something which in reality is the same as the divine essence is dependent, as truly and really produced by another (Musaeus, Treatise on the Eternal Decree of Election, ch. 1, sect. 4 and following, p. 2 and following).

Nevertheless, there are reasons of being a priori which, according to our manner of conceiving, bear themselves in the manner of causes, so that if that of which the cause is said were actually caused, they would really exist as its causes in that genus (Musaeus, at the cited place).

Thus God Himself is the efficient cause of the acts of His will.

Some acts are said to proceed from the divine goodness as their internal impulsive cause, others from the divine justice.

As for the external impulsive cause, the act of the will by which God decrees to confer salvation upon certain human beings acknowledges as its external impulsive cause the merit of Christ, to be apprehended by final faith and thus foreseen, as we shall see below in the locus on predestination.

And the final cause is this: God is said to will and to do whatever He does for the sake of His glory as the final cause.

### 18 The will of God is distinguished into natural and free

The will of God is distinguished into natural and free. By natural will, God is said to will that which He cannot not will. By free will, He is said to will that which He could also not will, or will the opposite.

Notes. In the former respect, He is said to will Himself, as that in which every aspect of goodness without deficiency appears, so that He is the primary object of the divine will, bearing a necessary relation to the will of God.

In the latter respect, He is said to will created things, which, since they are contingent and possess only a finite goodness, do not bear a necessary relation to the divine will. To this pertains what is said in Psalm 115:3, that God does whatever He wills, and therefore wills freely and acts according to His free will in whatever He does.

### 19 The free will of God is distinguished in the following ways

The free will of God is distinguished in the following ways.

(1.) Into efficacious and inefficacious. The efficacious will is that by which God wills something as to be brought about. The inefficacious will is that by which something pleases God in itself, although He does not intend to bring it about. Thus the will by which Christ as the God-man willed to give Himself to death, or to lay down His life, and to offer Himself as a victim for sinners (John 10:18; Hebrews 9:27), was indeed efficacious, because Christ intended to accomplish this very thing. According to the thesis, however, the efficacious will is said to be that by which something is intended to be accomplished, whether or not the effect follows or the intended end is obtained. In this sense, God, although He intends the salvation of all human beings, does not obtain it in the case of all. Compare Musaeus (Disputation on the Antecedent and Consequent Will of God, appended to the Treatise on the Use of the Principle of Reason, sect. 14, p. 697). Conversely, Christ as the God-man willed the preservation of human life and the avoidance of impending death (Luke 22:42), inasmuch as these pleased Him in themselves, yet without changing His will to die for humanity. Some define the inefficacious will as that which is not fulfilled even though something is intended to be accomplished, an opinion we leave to its authors.

The efficacious will is further divided into absolute, by which God wills something without a condition, and conditioned, by which He wills something under a condition. The word "absolute" is used in various senses; the specific meaning must be derived from the respect in which it is called absolute. Here it is said to be absolute in relation to some condition, and in opposition to the conditioned will. In this sense, God is rightly said to have willed absolutely from eternity to create the world, for He willed it without a condition. He is also rightly said to will absolutely that those whom He has foreseen as finally believing should be saved, for He wills this too without a condition, since final faith foreseen has the character of a condition already fulfilled, not one still to be fulfilled. The conditioned will pertains to that by which God wills all human beings to be saved, namely if they shall have believed; likewise, that by which God willed many good things for the Israelites, namely under the condition of sincere and constant obedience (Deuteronomy 28). That this will is not fulfilled (since God foreknew that the condition could fail to be fulfilled and would not be fulfilled) is not absurd (Musaeus, Disputation on the Antecedent and Consequent Will, sect. 31, p. 710).

(2.) Into absolute and ordained. The absolute will is that by which God wills something to be accomplished by His absolute power, that is, power not bound to secondary causes. Thus God willed the sun to stand still (Joshua 10:13; compare Musaeus, cited Disputation, sects. 28-29, p. 703). The ordained will is that by which God wills something to be accomplished by His ordained power, that is, power bound to secondary causes and to a certain order of means established by Himself. In this way God wills to save the elect through the means of grace. Hence it is also evident that the conditioned and the ordained will do not entirely coincide, although at first glance they may appear to do so. Moreover, it is certain that it is not absurd that the ordained will of God can be resisted (Musaeus, at the cited place, sects. 30 and following, pp. 708 and following; sect. 42, p. 719).

(3.) Into first (or antecedent) and second (or consequent). The antecedent will is that by which God wills something from Himself alone, that is, from His native inclination precisely, without yet taking into account the circumstances. The consequent will is that by which He wills something after considering the circumstances, that is, in view of some cause or condition on the part of the creature to which He wills something. Thus Chrysostom, in his homily on Ephesians chapter 1, and John of Damascus, in On the Orthodox Faith, book 2, chapter 26, called the will of God by which He wills the salvation of all πρώτη ἢ προηγουμένη (prote e proegumene), "first" or "antecedent," although this is not understood in the same way by all (Musaeus, at the cited place, sects. 2-3, pp. 689-690; sects. 10 and following, pp. 695 and following).

Some explain the consequent will precisely as that which arises from our fault, that is, by which God wills to punish, condemn, and so forth, on account of sin. Others take it more broadly as referring to whatever has its cause or occasion in us, whether from sin or from some other source. Our theologians, in this latter sense, refer to the consequent will not only that which pertains to the damnation of unbelievers but also that which terminates at the salvation of those who finally believe as such, that is, with final faith in Christ foreseen (Musaeus, cited Disputation, sects. 2-3, and 10 and following).

Both of these, the antecedent and the consequent will of God, are clearly taught in Matthew 23:37, where Christ as the God-man testifies that His will was first, or antecedently, directed toward the salvation of the Jewish people, and that from His native paternal inclination and affection; but then, or consequently, after first taking into account their incorrigible impiety, it was directed toward the destruction and ruin of the Jews.

### 20 In a particular sense

In a particular sense, a decree of God is called absolute in order to exclude any reference to an impulsive cause outside of God; to this is opposed the non-absolute decree, for which there exists an external impulsive cause outside of God, and indeed one that is virtually causative.

Notes. The word "will" has a broader scope than "decree." For we are said to will whatever things are desirable in themselves, even if, when all circumstances are considered, we do not actually will them. But we are properly said to decree only those things which, after all circumstances have been considered, we efficaciously will. Hence the antecedent will (discussed in the preceding section) cannot properly be called a decree. Compare Aegidius Hunnius at the end of the Admonition to the Reader prefixed to his Treatise on Providence and Predestination.

Not only in the sense of formally causing (for in that case every decree of God would be absolute), but also in the sense of virtually causing; see Section XVII, note (a).

For this reason our theologians say that the decree of Predestination and Reprobation is not absolute, since it acknowledges an external impulsive cause or reason: the former, indeed, the merit of Christ apprehended by final faith; the latter, final unbelief. We shall see more on this in its proper place.

### 21 There also occurs the distinction of the divine will into the will of sign and…

There also occurs the distinction of the divine will into the will of sign and the will of good pleasure. The former is spoken of when the name "will" is attributed to an effect of the divine will, namely as a sign of some will in God. The latter denotes the very act of the divine will by which He wills or does not will something. From this it is clear that the distinction is analogical. One must take care, however, not to fabricate a will of sign to which the will of good pleasure, which the sign ought by its institution to signify, would be repugnant.

Notes. This distinction is found not only in Peter Lombard (Sentences, book 1, distinction 45, chapters 3 and following, and distinction 47, chapter 2) and in Thomas Aquinas (Summa Theologiae, part 1, question 19, article 12), but also among our own theologians, such as Balthasar Meisner (Anthropology, disputation 12, question 1, thesis 1) and Johann Gerhard (Exegesis, locus on God, section 269), and others.

To this category belong passages such as Matthew 6:15, 12:30, and 1 Thessalonians 4:3, where the will of God is taken to mean the commandment of God, which is an effect and sign of the divine will; although authors refer not only the commandment but also other things to this heading, such as counsel, prohibition, operation, and permission.

That is to say, there is such an inequality between the members of the distinction that one claims the name "will" properly, while the other claims it improperly, according to a figure of speech (as they say).

For example, if one should say, with the Reformed theologians who follow in the footsteps of the Scholastics, that God wills the salvation of all by the will of sign but does not will this very thing by the will of good pleasure; or that He commands man to be converted, yet does not seriously will that he be converted. For such assertions are repugnant to the divine wisdom, goodness, and equity, and would destroy the certainty of Scripture. Compare Conrad Müller (Treatise on the Articles of the Elective Decrees, chapter 11, sections 316 and following, pages 253 and following).

### 22 Among the attributes of the will of God

Among the attributes of the will of God, Justice comes first. By this attribute God is partly just in Himself, which we call by the particular name Holiness, and it denotes the rectitude of the divine will by which He wills all things that are right and good in conformity with His eternal law; and partly just in relation to others, so that He prescribes fitting laws for creatures, directs and governs them, keeps and fulfills the promises made to human beings, and finally rewards the good and punishes the wicked.

Notes. Thus in Leviticus 19:2 God says, "Be holy, because I am holy." Compare also 1 Peter 1:15, 16, 17.

See Deuteronomy 32:4: "All His ways are justice. God is truth and there is no iniquity in Him; He is just and upright." And Psalm 92:16: "The Lord is upright, and there is no unrighteousness in Him." This justice of God bears a certain analogy to what philosophers call Universal Justice, yet it must not be understood with the rigor with which they employ the term, but in a manner befitting God (θεοπρεπῶς). For God is Himself His own law, and to this is customarily referred that passage in Hebrews 2:10: ἔπρεπε τῷ θεῷ (it was fitting for God), that is, it was congruent with His most perfect nature.

The rectitude of the will is indeed the same in substance as the former, but it is considered with relation to creatures who are to be led to their end, and to whom a manner of living congruent with them is to be prescribed.

To fulfill or discharge promises is customarily ascribed to justice, even though it is otherwise referred to truthfulness, of which we shall speak presently. Meanwhile, what is relevant here is that in Isaiah 45:23 God says: "Righteousness has gone forth from my mouth, a word that shall not be revoked." And in Romans 3, the justice of God is mentioned (verse 4, 5) insofar as it coincides with truth (verse 7), by which God gives credibility to His words (verse 2).

Hence it is customarily called by the particular name Remunerative Justice. On this see Romans 2:5, 6, 7, where it is referred to the δικαιοκρισίαν (righteous judgment) of God that He confers eternal life on those who persevere in doing good; and 2 Thessalonians 1:6, 7, where it is said to be just before God to repay with relief those who are afflicted. Nevertheless, one must not therefore suppose that a human being has any right or merit in the proper sense before God, by the force of which God would owe something good to the human being; since rather whatever good exists in a human being comes from the grace of God, and God crowns His own gifts in the human being, or rewards out of sheer grace. Therefore, just as it is founded in the love of God and in the divine promises, so it is not so much called justice in an absolute sense, but is rather referred to the goodness or truthfulness of God.

This is the justice which is commonly called Vindicative or Avenging. On this, see the passages cited: Romans 2:5, 8, 9, where God is said to be about to render, out of righteous judgment, indignation, wrath, and affliction to contentious persons who do not obey the truth but obey unrighteousness; and 2 Thessalonians 1:6, 7, where it is just before God to repay with affliction those who afflict others, and thus to inflict vengeance on those who do not know God, and so forth. Compare also Genesis 18:20 and Psalm 5:5.

### 23 There follows the Truthfulness of God

There follows the Truthfulness of God, by which God is constant in declaring what is true and in keeping His promises.

Notes. It is otherwise called truth in speaking or testifying, and is distinguished from truth in being and truth in knowing; both of which, however, also belong to God.

Namely, just as through the infinite perfection of His intellect, or omniscience, He cannot be deceived, so through the infinite perfection of His will He cannot deceive. See Numbers 23:19 (referred to in this locus, Section X, note d) and Hebrews 6:18: "It is impossible for God to lie."

### 24 Next comes the Power of God

Next comes the Power of God, by which the divine essence is efficacious for working and producing something outside of itself, and indeed everything whatsoever that is in any way possible and does not on the part of the one working imply an imperfection.

Notes. This power is either the very will of God directed by His practical knowledge, which is believed to be so efficacious in itself that whatever He wills, He can produce simply by willing, without any executive faculty or power as if distinct from the will; or it is the very Being of God insofar as it is subordinated to the divine knowledge and will for working outside of Himself, according as God is conceived to work through power those things which He has freely willed, and thus to work through a power directed and applied by a free act of the will.

From this it is clear that active power is meant, just as it is otherwise certain that God is entirely devoid of all passive power.

It is commonly called Omnipotence, or power extensively infinite, because it has no limit in the range of its effects. This is proved from Matthew 19:26: "With God all things are possible." And Luke 1:37: "With God nothing shall be impossible" (πᾶν ῥῆμα, everything that He signifies by words He will do). To the same point belongs the fact that God is called παντοκράτωρ (omnipotent), exercising strength or dominion over all things (2 Corinthians 6:18; Revelation 4:8), and that all power and might (δύναμις καὶ ἰσχύς) is ascribed to Him (Revelation 7:12).

For it is not absurd that God cannot lie, be hungry, or sleep, since to be able to do these things belongs not to perfection but to imperfection, and they are therefore repugnant to God as the most excellent Being. For the power of God is also intensively perfect, or of infinite perfection in itself, as David in Psalm 145, having said that there is no end to the divine greatness, adds: "Generation after generation shall declare Your works and shall announce Your strength (power)."

### 25 The power of God is customarily distinguished into ordained and absolute power

The power of God is customarily distinguished into ordained and absolute power. Ordained power is that which has been determined by a decree or some law of God to operate in a certain manner. Absolute power is that which belongs to God in Himself and has not been determined by any prior decree or law. The former can be resisted; the latter cannot.

Notes. It is indeed one and the same infinite power of God, but it exerts itself in different ways, and accordingly is called ordained and absolute in different respects. Compare what we said about the absolute and ordained will of God in Section XIX, page 188.

That is, the power by which God acts in conformity with His law or with a decree instituted by Himself, concurring with secondary causes and operating according to their requirements: for example, when He sustains human beings through food, or when He regenerates through the means He has instituted, namely the word and baptism.

For example, when He causes a virgin to give birth, raises the dead, and so forth.

Namely because secondary causes can be resisted and their influence can be impeded.

For otherwise the finite power of a creature would prevail over the infinite power of God.

### 26 Goodness belongs to God both absolutely and in Himself

Goodness belongs to God both absolutely and in Himself, which is His very Perfection, that is, the essence of God insofar as it contains in itself all perfections, either formally or eminently; and also relatively, that is, in relation to creatures, to whom God is good insofar as He efficiently produces all created goodness, and does so according to His own perfection as the idea or exemplar of created perfection; and He also attracts or moves creatures to the love and desire of Himself as the highest good.

Notes. For the Goodness and Perfection of God differ only in this respect: that God is called perfect absolutely and in Himself, but good not only in Himself and absolutely, but also relatively.

Thus in Matthew 5:48 Christ says: "Be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect," that is, emulate, as far as is permitted, the perfection set before you in the example of God. And in Luke 18:19 He says: "No one is good except God alone." For creatures are indeed perfected by things that are superadded to their essence; but God, in whom no accident inheres, is perfect through His very essence.

This pertains to perfections that are simply such, which in their formal concept do not include imperfection.

This pertains to perfections in a qualified sense, that is, those which in their formal concept involve perfection mixed with imperfection. These, therefore, do not exist in God according to their proper nature, but through something more excellent, or through an eminent power to produce them in other subjects. Compare Psalm 94:9.

Hence He is said to be good in the genus of efficient cause. To this belongs the fact that He is said to give to all life and breath and all things (Acts 17:25), and that in Him we live and move and have our being (Acts 17:28).

In this respect He is said to be good in the genus of exemplary cause, as we shall see in the loci on Creation and the Image of God.

In this respect He is said to be good in the genus of final cause. Compare Psalm 73:25, 26, where David, despising heaven and earth and all that is in them, though his flesh and his heart fail, declares that God is the strength of his heart and his portion (as of a desired inheritance, and therefore the good in which he rests) forever. To this also pertains what we demonstrated above, that God is the ultimate end of the human being and of Theology, both Natural and Revealed (Prolegomena, chapter 1, section 4, pages 8, 9; section 17, page 51).

### 27 As for the Divine Persons

As for the Divine Persons, it must be held most simply that the essence and all the divine perfections are, without division or multiplication, common to these three distinct ones whom Scripture calls the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

Notes. The consideration of these Persons follows in the order of doctrine; see above Section V, page 170, and page 171, notes c, d, e.

The sum of this mystery is demonstrated by the passages 1 John 5:7 and Matthew 28:19. For in the former it is said: "There are three who testify in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit, and these three are one" (ἕν εἰσι). And just as the authenticity of this passage, as part of divinely inspired Scripture, was acknowledged by Jerome, who used the most accurate codices, and by Cyprian, who cited these words before the Arian controversy (Cyprian, On the Unity of the Church), and afterwards also by Fulgentius in his response to the last objection of the Arians (Fulgentius, Responses to the Arian Objections, final objection); and it is confirmed also by the Complutensian, Antwerp, British, Robert Stephanus, and Vatican Library codices (compare Johann Gerhard, Academic Disputations, part 3, page 1306 and following): so it is manifest that those three, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, are presented as really distinct from one another, yet at the same time as testifying in heaven, endowed with heavenly or supreme and truly divine authority, and as being among themselves (not merely thinking or willing alike, but being) one, and therefore one God.

In the other passage, moreover, where Christ commands the Apostles to baptize in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, these three are again joined together as distinct, yet in such a way that baptism must be administered in their name, as in a common name, and therefore with equal authority, the baptism by which human beings are consecrated to God and made capable of His grace and of the remission of sins (according to John 3:5, Acts 2:38, and Titus 3:5). And since there is no name of such great dignity in which so grave and salutary a rite can and ought to be administered except that of God alone (according to 1 Corinthians 1:13 and Luke 20:4 and following), it is evident that the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit are that true, one, and eternal God.

### 28 For a fuller declaration of this mystery it must be observed

For a fuller declaration of this mystery it must be observed: first, that the Father differs really from the Son, the Son from the Father, and the Holy Spirit from both, so that the Father is truly one, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another.

Notes. Thus Christ expressly says that the Father is ἄλλον (another) from Himself (John 5:32, 37), and that the Holy Spirit, the παράκλητον (Comforter or Advocate) of the faithful, is ἄλλον (another) from Himself and the Father (John 14:16). The same is clear even from the names Father and Son, and from the fact that the former is described as begetting and the latter as begotten (Psalm 2:7; John 1:14, 18; 3:16), and that the Son is said to be sent by the Father (John 10:36; Galatians 4:4), the Holy Spirit to proceed from the Father (John 15:26), to be sent by the Father (John 14:26), and to be sent by the Son (John 15:26). For no one is Father or Son of himself; no one begets himself or is begotten by himself; no one proceeds from himself or is sent by himself. Compare Peter Müller (Academic Disputations held in 1649, disputation 3, sections 11, 12, 13, pages 57, 58, 59).

### 29 Second, it must be observed that not only the Father

Second, it must be observed that not only the Father, but also the Son and the Holy Spirit, are the true and eternal God.

Notes. That He whom Scripture calls the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ is the true and supreme God is today conceded by all who accept Scripture.

The following various arguments prove that the Son is the true God by nature:

I. Scripture expressly calls Him GOD. (Now the name of God, properly taken, is the name of the divine nature; see above, Section III, and note b, pages 167, 168.) See Acts 20:28, where God is said to have redeemed the Church with His own blood; Christ, the Son of God, is meant. Elsewhere, epithets are added that confirm the proper signification: for instance, that Christ the Son of God is called "True God" (1 John 5:20); that the same One, who will one day appear visibly, is called "the great God" (Titus 2:13); that He is called "God over all, blessed forever" (Romans 9:5), a formula by which the supreme God is described (Romans 1:25).

II. From the comparison of passages of the Old and New Testaments, namely that what is expressly said of the supreme God in the Old Testament is explained of Christ the Son of God in the New. For example, let the argument be thus: He whom the Israelites tempted in the wilderness besides Moses is the true and eternal God, which is proved from Numbers 21:5, 6. But Christ is the One whom the Israelites tempted in the wilderness, according to 1 Corinthians 10:9. Therefore Christ is the true God. Similarly: He whose glory Isaiah saw (Isaiah 6:1 and following) is the true God. But Christ is the One whose glory Isaiah then saw, which is proved from John 12:40, 41. Therefore He is the true God.
