In this manner the following passages may also be compared: Psalm 68:19 with Ephesians 4:8; Psalm 97:7, Psalm 45:7, Psalm 102:26, and Psalm 110:1 with Hebrews 1:6, 8, 9, 10, 13; and finally Isaiah 40:3 and Malachi 3:1 with Matthew 3:3, Mark 1:3, Luke 3:4, and John 1:23. Moreover, to fabricate in this matter some subordination, dependence, or resemblance, or I know not what else under the name of Accommodation that must be admitted so as to avoid conceding identity and equality, is alien to the Christian religion. Compare Johann Friedrich Hackspan (Disputation on Accommodation, in his Sylloge, page 417).

III. From the generation of the Son from God the Father, the argument arises in this way: Whoever is begotten of the substance of God the Father is the true and eternal God. But Christ, the Son of God, is begotten of the substance of God the Father. Therefore He is the true and eternal God. The major premise is evident from the light of nature, by which we are taught that the one begetting and the one begotten, if the terms are used properly, are of the same essence, so that it would be a contradiction for one to be begotten from another, properly speaking, and yet not have the same essence. The minor premise is proved from John 1:14, 18 and 3:16, where Christ is called the Son μονογενής (only- begotten), that is, begotten without trope; not merely beloved, or improperly begotten, adopted, and so forth. Compare Romans 8:32 and John 5:18, where He is called the Son of God ἴδιος (His own proper Son).

IV. From the divine attributes (which do not differ really from the divine essence, as we saw in Section V, note b, page 171) assigned to Christ, such as: (1) Eternity, described in John 1:1, that His existence is ἐν ἀρχῇ (in the beginning), not in a qualified sense with respect to creation or the restoration of the human race, but absolutely, so that before the λόγος (the Word), or the Son of God, nothing at all existed; and He Himself existed from the beginning πρὸς τὸν Θεόν (with God the Father), in such a way that neither did the Father exist before the Word, but the Word coexisted with Him from eternity. Compare Revelation 1:8, where in the same manner in which God eternal was previously described in verse 4 (see Section XIII, note d, page 180), it is said of Christ: ὁ ὢν καὶ ὁ ἦν, καὶ ὁ ἐρχόμενος (who is, and who was, and who is to come); and there is added in the person of Christ: ἐγώ εἰμι τὸ Α καὶ τὸ Ω, ἀρχὴ καὶ τέλος (I am the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end), and in verse 11: ὁ πρῶτος καὶ ὁ ἔσχατος (the first and the last), lacking a beginning because He is the beginning of all things that are, and having no end because He is Himself the end of all things. Compare Hebrews 1:11, where the eternity of God described in Psalm 102 is attributed to Christ. (2) Omniscience (John 21:17): "Lord, You know all things." Also, that in Christ are "all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge" (Colossians 2:3), and that Christ is the Searcher of hearts (which belongs only to omniscience; see Section XV, note e, page 183): Matthew 9:4, John 2:24, 25, 1 Corinthians 4:5. (3) Omnipotence (John 10:28), where He Himself says that no one is able to snatch His sheep (His faithful ones) from His hand, and therefore that His power surpasses all finite power; and Revelation 1:8, where He is expressly called παντοκράτωρ (Omnipotent).

V. From truly divine works (which argue for the divine nature and perfections in the one who performs them) ascribed to Christ as their principal cause, such as: (1) The creation of this universe, of all things (τῶν πάντων), John 1:1 and Colossians 1:16, so that not only are all things said to have been produced through Him (just as Paul says he was called through the Father, but not as a less principal cause, Galatians 1:1), but also He Himself is said in the nominative case to have created all things (Hebrews 1:10, from Psalm 102:26): "You, Lord (Son of God, verse 8), in the beginning laid the foundation of the earth," and so forth. (2) The preservation of this universe, as in Colossians 1:17, where all created things are said to hold together through Him and to be sustained by His power lest they fall apart and perish; and in Hebrews 1:2, 3, where He is said to be φέρων τὰ πάντα (upholding all things) lest they perish. (3) The resurrection of the dead, even of those long buried, and that by His free will (John 5:21, 28, 29). And here also belongs (4) the crushing of the head of the serpent, or the destruction of the kingdom and power of the Devil, which is ascribed to the seed of the woman, that is, the promised Messiah (Genesis 3:16). For this is truly a divine work, and it was necessary that He who was to accomplish it be God omnipotent; as Peter Müller also taught, and showed that the mystery of the Trinity can be demonstrated from several arguments drawn from the Old Testament (Peter Müller, Manuscript Colloquium on Illustrious Questions, locus on God, question 1).

VI. From the fact that truly divine worship (which God denies He will give to another who is not the true God, Isaiah 42:8 and 48:11) is ascribed to Him as equal with God the Father. For instance, in John 5:23, all are commanded to honor the Son "just as" (καθώς) they honor the Father, that is, with no other kind of worship. Compare Hebrews 1:6 and 8.

That the Holy Spirit is the true and eternal God is likewise proved:

I. From passages of Scripture in which He is expressly called God. Thus Peter in Acts 5:3 says that the One to whom Ananias had lied besides the Apostles, and on whom he had dared to impose his falsehood as truth, is the Holy Spirit, and in verse 4 he calls Him God. And Paul in 1 Corinthians 3:16, 17 says that the faithful are the temple of God by this very fact, that the Spirit of God dwells in them as in a temple; he therefore indicates that the Holy Spirit is God. Compare also 2 Samuel 23:2, where David says: "The Spirit of the Lord spoke in me, and His word was upon my tongue." He then adds in verse 3: "The God of Israel said, the Rock of Israel spoke to me," and so forth. He therefore teaches that the same One whom he calls the Spirit of the Lord is the Lord Himself.

II. From the comparison of Old and New Testament passages. For example, in this way: He who spoke to Isaiah and commanded him to go to the people (Isaiah 6:9) is the true and supreme God. But the Holy Spirit is the One who spoke to Isaiah, according to Acts 28:25. Therefore the Holy Spirit is God. Similarly: He who spoke through David in Psalm 95:8, 9, 10, 11 is the true and supreme God, according to verses 1 and following to verse 7. But the Holy Spirit is the One who spoke those words through David, as is expressly stated in Hebrews 3:7, 8, 9, 10. Therefore He is the true and supreme God. Here also the remarks made above under point two concerning accommodation must be recalled.

III. From truly divine attributes, for example: (1) Immensity, which is ascribed to the Holy Spirit in Psalm 139:7: "Where shall I go from Your Spirit?" and so forth; that is, wherever I go, Your immense Spirit is there. (2) Omniscience, which is attributed to Him in 1 Corinthians 2:10, namely that He searches (ἐρευνᾷ), that is, thoroughly penetrates, and without anyone else revealing them, nevertheless knows by Himself accurately the depths of God, all the secret thoughts and counsels of the divine mind, so that nothing is hidden or remains obscure.

IV. From truly divine works, for example: (1) Creation, which Job mentions in chapter 33:4: "The Spirit of God made me, and the breath of the Almighty gave me life." And David in Psalm 33:6 proclaims that by the breath of God's mouth the entire host of heaven was made. (2) The voluntary distribution, as from a principal efficient cause, of spiritual gifts for ministry, and at that time miraculous ones, which is attributed to the Holy Spirit in 1 Corinthians 12:11. (3) The governance of the Church and the appointment of bishops, that is, ministers of the Church (Acts 20:28).

### 30 Finally, third, it must be observed that the Father

Finally, third, it must be observed that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are not three Gods, but one God.

Notes. We have already shown above in Section VIII, pages 173, 174, that God is one and that there is no other besides Him. Therefore, once it has been demonstrated that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are the true God, it immediately follows that they are one God, not several Gods.

### 31 In order to express this mystery more distinctly and to exclude the sophistries…

In order to express this mystery more distinctly and to exclude the sophistries of heretics, the ancient Christians spoke as follows: the Western or Latin theologians said that there are three Persons in one divine essence; the Eastern or Greek theologians said that there are τρεῖς ὑποστάσεις καὶ μίαν οὐσίαν (three hypostases and one essence). In particular, the Nicene Fathers determined regarding the Son that He is, or ought to be acknowledged as, ὁμοούσιον (coessential or consubstantial) with the Father.

Notes. That is, so that while the unity of God stands firm, the real distinction between the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, as being of the same nature and equal dignity, might be signified in clear terms.

Of these heretics, some said that the Father alone is the true God, the Son is a creature, and the Holy Spirit is a creature made through the Son, or a gift of God in human beings. Others maintained that only different names are attributed to the one eternal God on account of different respects, and that in reality the Father is the very same as the Son and the Holy Spirit, having devised various evasions by which they might withdraw from the clear light of Scripture and defend and commend their errors.

Although the Greeks and the Latins for some time contended with one another (the Greeks thinking that by the Latin term "person" was designated an office or external bearing, and that therefore three persons did not convey or express a real distinction of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; while the Latins thought that ὑπόστασις denoted in the nominative case the very essence, so that with the admission of three ὑποστάσεις, three essences would have to be posited), afterwards, when they had better understood one another, it came about that the Greeks also said τρία πρόσωπα (three persons) and the Latins said three hypostases.

That is, one who is of one and the same essence with another, not specifically but numerically. See what I have discussed in the Disputation on the Council of Nicaea, sections 72 and following to 78, and in the Disputation on Paul of Samosata, chapter 4, final section, pages 55, 56.

### 32 By the term Essence

By the term Essence, or οὐσία, is understood the divine Nature itself as it is in itself and absolutely considered, which together with the attributes is most simply one and singular, and thus is also but one essence of the three Persons.

Notes. According to what we said in Sections V and following.

In such a way that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit have also one intellect by which they understand, one will by which they will, and one power by which they work outside the divine essence. Compare John 5:19.

### 33 By the term Person

By the term Person, or ὑπόστασις, just as elsewhere it signifies an intelligent supposit, so in this context it indicates that there are three subsistences or personalities in the one divine Essence, and therefore three supposits: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

Notes. By which term we embrace the nature as the material element and its subsistence as the formal element. But if you further ask what the Latin word "person" or "supposit" signifies in the nominative case, whether the nature itself or the subsistence, a difficulty arises on either side. For if the former is said, it does not appear how, once three persons are admitted in the one Essence of God, it can subsequently be denied that there are three natures or three divine essences. If the latter is admitted, this would seem to be the same as if one were to say that "blackness" in the nominative case denotes the very quality of being black. Therefore it is perhaps to be said that "person" in the nominative case signifies something constituted from the nature and the subsistence, just as otherwise in the concept of a material composite, neither matter nor substantial form is posited in the nominative case as the composite itself. See Peter Müller (Introduction to the Locus on the Person of Christ, section 43 and following). As for the Greeks, the word ὑπόστασις denoted for them sometimes the subsistence itself precisely, and sometimes the supposit or Person. In the same way, certain Latins also used the word "substance" when they defined the person through substance, although otherwise we are accustomed to designating the nature itself by the name of substance.

These subsistences are relative, not absolute. For they are founded in the divine relations, about which more will be said presently. The one and simple divine essence does not admit of several absolute subsistences, but we acknowledge relative subsistences in God according to revelation, although reason left to itself would know nothing of such things.

In such a way that no Person and no subsistence differs really from the divine Essence, but only by a distinction of reason (which is clear from the simplicity of God); but the Persons differ from one another really and apart from any operation of the mind, on account of the relative opposition between them.

### 34 Although the Father

Although the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are not expressly called in the Scriptures three ὑποστάσεις, Persons, or three supposits, the reality itself signified by these words is nevertheless contained in the Scriptures.

Notes. Certainly the Father and the Son cannot be denied to be Persons by those who are unwilling to twist the meaning of words, but acknowledge that the terms are grounded in a true and real generation. Furthermore, the attributes mentioned above, especially those which have reference to operation, such as omniscience and omnipotence, and above all those actions, creation, preservation, and resurrection (which we discussed above), belong to supposits or persons as their Principles of Which, according to the well- known axiom. And of the Holy Spirit no less properly than of the Son and the Father are predicated works proper to Persons: for example, that He distributes to each one individually as He wills (1 Corinthians 12:11); that He comforts, convicts, and teaches (John 14:16, 26; 15:26; 16:8, 13). Here it is not permitted to invent tropes as a means of evading the mystery.

### 35 Although in this life we cannot sufficiently understand or explain how three…

Although in this life we cannot sufficiently understand or explain how three Persons of one most simple Essence, distinguished from that Essence itself only by reason, yet really distinguished from one another, can exist, nevertheless, because both truths have been revealed, we rightly believe both.

Notes. Indeed, if our reason should dare to determine anything here (which, however, it ought not to do in a matter that exceeds its proper bounds), so far is it from being able to bring forward from its own principles a firm demonstration of this doctrine, that it would rather either adduce matters foreign to the question or fall into manifest absurdity (as the Blessed Musaeus showed by the example of Bartholomaeus Keckermann in a special disputation, through a counter-demonstration opposing Keckermann's false proof, which is appended to his treatise On the Use of the Principle of Reason, p. 661 ff.), or else it would end up denying or attacking the mystery itself (as is evident from the example of the Socinians and others like them).

And we are certain that these truths do not involve a contradiction, even though they may appear to do so to the reason of certain men who argue improperly from the nature and condition of finite things. For every thought must be led captive to the obedience of Christ, according to 2 Corinthians 10:5.

### 36 Furthermore, the divine Persons are distinguished by personal Acts

Furthermore, the divine Persons are distinguished by personal Acts, personal Properties, and personal Notions.

Notes. These acts are otherwise called works ad intra, because they terminate within the divine essence upon a certain Person, who regards another Person (or the remaining Persons) as producing (or as producers). And these are divided works, that is, not common to all Persons of the Godhead but proper to this or that Person. In this respect they are opposed to works ad extra, which, proceeding from the active power common to the three Persons, terminate in an effect really produced outside of God (cf. Musaeus, Disputation on God, which is the third of those held in 1649, section 42, p. 70).

Nevertheless, it must not be denied that a certain external work, or opus ad extra, is customarily ascribed in a special manner to each individual divine Person, by which that Person has peculiarly manifested Himself. Thus Creation is customarily ascribed to the Father, Reconciliation to the Son, and Sanctification to the Holy Spirit, even though each of these proceeds from all three Persons. Authors call this Appropriation (see Musaeus, same work, section 54, p. 75).

Those Properties are called by some constitutive Notions (νοτιόνες συστατικαί), constituting each Person in its being as such a Person; for they are relations founded upon the personal acts.

Notions are certain grounds of knowing by which we conceive the divine Persons and by which they are distinguished among themselves and internally, that is, within the divine essence. These notions, taken broadly, also comprehend the personal properties themselves; but taken more strictly, they are distinguished from those properties and are called, with the added qualifier, significative and indicative notions (νοτιόνες σημαντικαὶ καὶ γνωριστικαί).

### 37 The personal acts are two

The personal acts are two: Generation and Spiration.

### 38 Generation is an action ad intra by which God the Father from His own substance…

Generation is an action ad intra by which God the Father from His own substance has from eternity produced the Son.

Notes. This generation is not tropical or modified, but truly and properly so called, just as Father and Son in the Godhead are not said improperly but properly (cf. Sections XXVIII and XXIX, pp. 202, 204).

One may call it a real action insofar as it has a term really produced and distinct from the producer, although that term is not an effect that acknowledges an efficient cause from which it differs as one thing from another. If you inquire more precisely about this action, it must be admitted that both the action itself and the active power of generating are inscrutable to us. For thus Gregory of Nazianzus says: "Let the divine generation be honored by silence" (Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration I on the Son of God, p. 209 middle). Compare also Cyril of Jerusalem, Catechetical Lecture XI, p. 118 E.

This indeed pertains to the formal concept of generation. However, this divine generation did not occur by means of a seed detached from the substance of the begetter; nor is the divine essence a material principle out of which the Son was produced. Rather, it consists solely in this: that the very same essence which belongs to the Father who begets has been perfectly communicated to the begotten Son (cf. Musaeus, same work, p. 70).

Thus in Psalm 2:7 God the Father says to the Messiah, that is, to Christ (see Acts 13:33): "You are my Son; today I have begotten you," where the word םוֹיּהַ (today) denotes the most present and single moment of eternity, in which there is nothing past and nothing future. Compare also Micah 5:2, where the Prophet says that the goings forth (the nativity) of the Messiah are from of old, from the days of eternity: םלָ וֹע ימֵ ימִ םדֶּ קֶּ מִ (from of old, from the days of eternity).

That the Father produced the Son by an act of intellect reflected upon Himself (God as understanding), or by the act of speaking, cannot be demonstrated or defended (see Musaeus, Disputation cited against Keckermann, section IX ff., p. 662 ff.).

### 39 Spiration is an action ad intra by which God the Father and the Son together

Spiration is an action ad intra by which God the Father and the Son together, from Their own substance, have from eternity produced the Holy Spirit.

Notes. 1. Just as the Son is said to send the Holy Spirit (John 15:26; Luke 24:49), so it must be acknowledged that the Son also spirates the Holy Spirit, since the Mission of a divine Person is founded upon the substantial procession of that Person from the sending Person; and no other mode of proceeding than spiration can be attributed to the Holy Spirit. 2. It is further confirmed by the fact that the Holy Spirit is called not only the Spirit of the Father (Matthew 10:20) but also the Spirit of the Son (Galatians 4:6; Romans 8:9; 1 Peter 1:11). For He is called the Spirit of that Person from whom He is spirated. 3. Otherwise the relative opposition between the Son and the Holy Spirit would be destroyed, and consequently also their real distinction.

Thus, although the Father and the Son are in truth two supposita, they nevertheless produce the Holy Spirit by one and the same spirative power. In this sense the Doctors have said that the Father and the Son have themselves as one principle spirating the Holy Spirit.

Spiration agrees with divine generation in this respect: that it denotes the emanation of the spirated Person from the spirating Person within the divine essence. And just as generation is eternal, so also is spiration.

However, we do not dare to say that the Holy Spirit is spirated by an act of the will or of love (cf. Musaeus, Disputation cited, section X ff., p. 664 ff.).

### 40 It is certain that the generation of the Son and the spiration of the Holy Spirit differ

It is certain that the generation of the Son and the spiration of the Holy Spirit differ; but we cannot more fully define the manner in which they differ.

Notes. They differ not only with respect to the principle, since the principle of Generation is the Father alone (for He alone is said to have begotten the Son), while the principle of Spiration is the Father and the Son (according to the preceding Section, notes a and b), but also with respect to the term produced. For we do not say that the Holy Spirit is begotten or is a generated being, nor that the Son is spirated. And although in the Scriptures the Son is said ἐξέρχεσθαι (to go forth), He is nevertheless not said ἐκπορεύεσθαι (to proceed); this latter is believed to be proper to the Holy Spirit alone.

See (cf. Gerhard, Locus on the Holy Spirit, section 71; also Augustine, Against Maximinus, book 3, ch. 14; Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration on the Holy Spirit, and elsewhere).

### 41 The personal Properties are three

The personal Properties are three: Paternity, Filiation, and Procession strictly so called, or passive spiration.

Notes. These are three in number, corresponding to the number of the Persons, each of which is constituted in its being as a certain Person by a relative subsistence.

Paternity is founded upon generation viewed actively.

Filiation is founded upon generation viewed passively, or terminatively.

Passive spiration is so called not because any passion befalls God, but speaking grammatically, or because the Holy Spirit is said to be spirated, not to spirate. Yet on God's part, spiration is a pure act, devoid of all passion (cf. Musaeus, Disputation cited on God, section VI, pp. 73-74).

### 42 The Notions specially so called are two

The Notions specially so called are two: Innascibility and active Spiration.

Notes. That is, notions distinguished from the properties. For otherwise, if the word "notion" is taken more broadly and the properties are also included, there are five notions.

By innascibility (ἀγεννησία) the Father is made known insofar as He is not from another, neither begotten nor proceeding. By active Spiration, the Father and the Son, though not from each other, are nevertheless distinguished from the Holy Spirit. Nor are the Persons thereby multiplied, because according to the rules of the theologians, in the Godhead all things are one except where a relative opposition intervenes. On the part of the Father, Paternity, Innascibility, and active Spiration are not relatively opposed to one another; just as, on the part of the Son, Filiation and active Spiration are not.

### 43 The Father is the first Person of the Godhead

The Father is the first Person of the Godhead: not begotten, nor proceeding, but from eternity begetting the Son from His own substance, and together with the Son from eternity spirating the Holy Spirit.

Notes. He is first, however, not in time, nor in nature (such as the priority of a cause in relation to an effect), nor in dignity. For all the divine Persons are coeternal, really identical with the independent divine essence, and coequal with one another. He is first only in order, which some call the order of natural enumeration, inasmuch as it is founded upon the origin or emanation of one Person from another. Hence the Father, who is not from another but from Himself, and who is the one from whom another proceeds, namely the Son and the Holy Spirit, holds the first place.

### 44 The Son is the second Person of the Godhead

The Son is the second Person of the Godhead, begotten from eternity by the Father, from whom together with the Father the Holy Spirit proceeds from eternity.

Notes. He is second because, although the Son is not from Himself, yet from Him another proceeds, namely the Holy Spirit.

### 45 The Holy Spirit is the third Person of the Godhead

The Holy Spirit is the third Person of the Godhead, not begotten, but proceeding from eternity from the Father and the Son.

Notes. He is third because He is not from Himself, nor does another, that is, another Person of the Godhead, proceed from Him.

### 46 God, considered simultaneously with respect to His essence and His Persons

God, considered simultaneously with respect to His essence and His Persons, may be described as a spiritual Being subsisting of Himself in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

Notes. Other, more prolix descriptions are customarily adduced, in which the Persons are also described from their works ad extra: the Father from Creation, the Son from Redemption, the Holy Spirit from Sanctification. But because these works are not coeternal with God and the divine Persons, we have preferred to retain the description that pertains to God and the divine Persons as they are in themselves from all eternity (cf. Musaeus, Disputation III cited, final section, p. 76).

## 4 On Creation

### 1 Among the works by which God displayed His supreme goodness

Among the works by which God displayed His supreme goodness, creation is to be considered in the first place.

Note. (see Chapter I, Section 21; and thus the rationale for the order of this topic, immediately joined to the preceding one, becomes clear),

### 2 The word "creation," speaking properly and in the language of Scripture

The word "creation," speaking properly and in the language of Scripture, denotes the production of a subsisting thing, either from nothing, that is, a production that occurs independently of any subject, or dependently upon a subject, that is, from some subject, but one so unsuitable and undisposed that the effect cannot be produced from its potency by the power of any created agent.

Notes. For in other uses, magistrates, consuls, generals, and the like are also said to be "created." And Scripture itself says that a new heart is "created" in a person, that is, that new spiritual powers are conferred upon the person: this they call metaphorical creation. Philosophers, however, take the word "creation" more strictly, as meaning precisely the production of a thing from nothing.

Both of these senses of the word "creation" occur in Genesis, chapter 1: the former indeed at verse 1, and the latter at verses 21 and 27. Further details will become clear from what follows.

### 3 Production from nothing also occurs in two ways

Production from nothing also occurs in two ways. In the first way, an effect is produced independently of every subject, whether preexisting or coexisting: in this manner immaterial substances, that is, the angels and the soul of Adam, were produced. In the second way, an effect is produced independently of a preexisting subject, yet dependently upon a coexisting subject: in this manner the simple bodies were produced, for example, the heaven and the elements.

Notes. For substances that do not depend on matter for their being were fittingly produced, in accordance with their nature, independently of all matter as well.

For material things, even the simple ones, just as they consist of matter and form with respect to their being, so also the matter of these things did not exist separately prior to all form, nor did the material form exist apart from matter. Thus in their coming into being they depend, as composites, on matter, yet not on preexisting matter.

### 4 The remaining works of creation

The remaining works of creation, that is, the mixed bodies, were produced dependently upon preexisting matter, namely from the simple bodies that had first been produced.

Notes. For although God, by His absolute power, could have produced even mixed bodies independently of any preexisting subject, it nevertheless pleased God to carry out the work of creation in accordance with the order of nature, and to produce mixed bodies from the preexisting simple bodies.

Thus plants were produced from the earth, and fish from the water, as we shall presently see.

### 5 According to the history of creation

According to the history of creation, God completed the production of this universe within the space of six days.

Notes. Which is carefully described in Genesis chapters 1 and 2.

See chapter 1, final verse, and chapter 2, verse 2.

### 6 On the first day

On the first day, when until then no created thing existed but God alone (Genesis 1:1), God produced the heaven and the earth, as well as light, which would establish the alternation of day and night.

Notes. Regarding the word bereshith in Genesis 1:1, it is to be expounded adverbially and negatively.

As for "heaven," this means the heaven itself under the substantial form of heaven, and "earth" means the earth under the substantial form of earth. This is proved partly by the literal, or proper, signification of the words "heaven" and "earth" (which ought not to be abandoned without significant necessity, according to the rule of interpretation of Scripture given above in the Prolegomena, Chapter II, Section 45), and partly by the fact that Moses adds the emphatic or demonstrative particle on both sides, as if pointing with outstretched finger to signify "this heaven" and "this earth."

As for what is added, that the earth was tohu vavohu, empty and void, this indeed denies the cultivation and adornment of the earth (which in this sense, and because it was enveloped in waters, could be called a formless, rough, and undigested mass), but it does not deny the substantial form of the earth (compare Isaiah 34:11; Jeremiah 4:23). Further discussion may be found in Musaeus (Musaeus, Theological Disputation V on Creation, Sections 26ff., pp. 140ff.; and Detailed Explanation, Questions 23, 24, 25, pp. 183ff.).

In exactly the same manner, Hutterus taught (Hutterus, Theological Commonplaces, on Creation, Question 3, p. 201) that by the designation of heaven and earth one should not understand those parts of the universe as they later became or are now beheld by the eyes, elaborated with wondrous and astonishing workmanship, but rather a formless, rough, and in a certain way confused mass, which God afterward distinguished and elaborated by a definite plan. Thus by the name "heaven" is meant the entire celestial body, encompassing all the spheres, perfect and complete indeed with respect to substance and magnitude, but nevertheless without light, without motion, and without the distinction of stars, which were only added later. Likewise, by the name "earth" in Genesis 1:1, one should understand the very element of earth, which was afterward on the third day distinguished and separated from the waters. And Hutterus notably adds these words: "For unless it is established that in the beginning the earth was created insofar as it is considered with respect to its substance, it does not appear from Moses when it was finally created. For what some object concerning the third day is too weak an argument, since Moses does not say that on that third day the earth was created, but that God commanded the dry land, or earth, to appear from the waters." Gesnerus similarly taught (Gesnerus, Commentary on Genesis, p. 11), as did Selneccerus (Selneccerus, Exposition on Genesis, p. 43) and Scherzerus (Scherzerus, System, Book 3, Section 10, p. 90), who also commends the disputation of Musaeus on creation cited here.

Furthermore, that water, produced together with the earth, was not from preexisting matter can be gathered from Genesis 1:1 (compare Hutterus and Musaeus at the places cited). As for air and elementary fire, if such exists, the probable opinion is that they were similarly created along with the other elements on the first day.

Regarding the light (Genesis 1:3), it appears to be understood as a certain ethereal and luminous body, produced dependently upon the substance of the heaven, serving in place of the sun (compare Hutterus, Theological Commonplaces, on Creation, Question 8, p. 211; and Musaeus, Theological Disputation on Creation, Sections 27, 28, pp. 142, 143, 144).

### 7 On the second day

On the second day, God divided the elemental waters (which on the first day had not been separated by location from the earth, but together with it had constituted one confused globe, so that the earth lay hidden in them as in an abyss; for the same waters are meant in Genesis 1:2 and 1:6) into lower and upper waters, by interposing an aerial expanse (Musaeus, Theological Disputation on Creation, Section 30, p. 14).

The expanse is called by Moses raqia in Genesis 1:6, which properly signifies an expanse, as Chytraeus, Osiander, Gesnerus, Gerhard, and others acknowledge.

It is to be understood as aerial, a view held not only by the Rabbis but also by Marbach (Marbach, Commentary on Genesis, p. 10). For although on the first day both the elemental waters and perhaps also the element of air had been produced, because at that time the watery mass surrounded the earth on every side, and the thinner parts of the water, mixed with the air, extended all the way up to the heaven like a denser fog, it pleased God on the second day to cause the air to have the function of an expanse and of a medium intervening between both parts of the elemental water (compare Musaeus, Theological Disputation on Creation, Section 30, pp. 145, 146; and Detailed Explanation, p. 196).

The expanse was so arranged that from its upper part it touched the more subtle waters, gathered in the clouds, and from its lower part it touched the denser waters, surrounding the surface of the earth. For the Hebrew words lemaalah and mittachath should not so much be translated "above and below," but rather "from above, from the upper part" and "from below, from the lower part." This accordingly confirms the view that by the raqia one should understand not the ethereal heaven (which certainly does not reach down to the lower waters), but the aerial heaven, which, even though not according to its entirety (as the words of the text do not require), nevertheless truly according to some part of itself lies between the upper and lower waters and touches both (see Musaeus, Theological Disputation on Creation, Section 37, pp. 150, 151; Detailed Explanation, pp. 198, 199, 204, 205). Thus also Marbach considers that God in this passage of Genesis assigns the middle region of the air to rain clouds and pluvial waters, so that they may be held there for the irrigation and fertilization of the earth. And Grauer, to the question "Are there true and natural waters above the starry heavens?" responds: "It is doubtful" (Grauer, Illustrious Questions, Disputation 8, Corollary 1, p. 336).

For in Psalm 104:3, clouds are understood by the name of "waters" (compare Geier in his Commentary). And Marbach believed that in Genesis 1:7, 8, pluvial waters are indicated. Moreover, the region where clouds exist is not infrequently called "heaven" (see Genesis 1:26, 28, 30, where birds are said to fly through the heaven, which certainly fly not in the ether but in the air; compare Deuteronomy 4:18). And the cataracts of heaven, namely the aerial heaven, are said to be opened and closed (Genesis 7:11; 8:2). And in Psalm 148:4, hammayim asher meal hashamayim, Luther translates: "the waters that are above the heaven," and the glossators added: "in the rain clouds." So the expanse of the heavens encompasses both the ethereal and the aerial expanse, of which now the one, now the other, now both together, must be understood depending on the diversity of the predicates and the context (see Musaeus, Theological Disputation on Creation, Sections 33ff., pp. 148ff.; Detailed Explanation, pp. 200ff.).

### 8 On the third day

On the third day, the lower waters bathing the earth were gathered into certain bays or channels, which God called seas. The remaining parts of the earth appeared dry, and from them there immediately sprang forth herbs, trees, shrubs, and the like.

Note. Genesis 1:9, 10.

(Genesis 1:11, 12). The earth, however, had the function not of an active or efficient principle, but of a passive and material one (see Musaeus, Theological Disputation on Creation, Sections 53, 54, p. 166). Furthermore, it is not unreasonably believed that stones, metals, and the very garden of Eden, that is, Paradise, were produced on this same day (see Musaeus, Theological Disputation on Creation, Section 40, p. 153).

### 9 On the fourth day

On the fourth day, God made the sun, the moon, and the remaining stars, and He bestowed upon them a definite motion and a power of influencing, so that they might measure times and by their influence produce various effects upon the earth.

Notes. Concerning the sun: God added fuller light and perfection to the imperfect luminous body that had been fashioned on the first day, so that it might then at last fully obtain the character of the sun.

The moon and the remaining stars were made either directly from the substance of the ethereal heaven, or from that luminous body which we have mentioned (Musaeus, Theological Disputation on Creation, Section 42, p. 155).

See Genesis 1:14ff., to verse 17.

### 10 On the fifth day

On the fifth day, aquatic animals were produced from the water, and flying creatures from the earth.

Notes. (Genesis 1:29). The waters brought forth swarming creatures not as an efficient principle but as a material one, just as we said of the earth with respect to plants in Section 8. And indeed it was fitting for the nature of these animals that they be produced from water, though not from water alone or pure (Musaeus, Theological Disputation on Creation, Section 44, p. 155).

See (Genisis 2:10) Likewise, earth is more suited to the nature of flying creatures than water is.

### 11 On the sixth day

On the sixth day, God produced terrestrial animals, both quadrupeds and reptiles, from the earth.

Note. See Genesis 1:24.

And in these animals, it is manifest that earth is the predominant element.

### 12 On the same day

On the same day, God created the human being, forming his body from the dust of the earth. His soul, however, God produced from nothing and joined it to the body (Genesis 2:7).

Note. See Genesis 1:26ff.

See Genesis 2:7. Whence the name "Adam" was derived.

The insufflation denotes nothing other than the immateriality of the action, namely that the effect produced is a spirit distinct from body and from all matter.

And in such a way that at the same moment the body was produced from the dust and the soul was breathed into it.

### 13 God made in the beginning only one human individual

God made in the beginning only one human individual, namely a male. The female He afterward produced from a rib of the sleeping man.

Notes. And it is of this one Adam that mention is made in both chapters 1 and 2 of Genesis. That Adam was for some time alone, without a female companion, is clear from Genesis 2:18, 19, 20.

At least as to her body (Genesis 2:21, 22).

### 14 In what place, or in what part of the earth

In what place, or in what part of the earth, God produced Adam and Eve, we do not determine. However, it is rightly affirmed that they were formed outside of Paradise and afterward introduced into it.

Note. See Genesis 2:15 and 21.

### 15 When these works were completed and the six days had elapsed

When these works were completed and the six days had elapsed, God rested. Nor did He create any further species of creatures, although He could have added innumerable ones.

Notes. See Genesis 2:2.

In other respects, however, God does not entirely rest or cease from working, as we shall see in the chapter on Providence.

### 16 As to the causes of creation

As to the causes of creation, it is readily established that God, the Triune, is the principal efficient cause.

Notes. (Genesis 1 and 2; compare Isaiah 45:12; Jeremiah 10:11; Psalm 146:6; Acts 4:24; 17:24; Revelation 4:11, where it is shown that God alone is the cause of creation), For creation is a work ad extra. In Genesis 1:1 and 1:26, the plurality of Persons is indicated, not only by the plural noun Elohim, but also by the verb and the two plural suffixes in the words naasseh betsalmenu kidmuthenu, "let us make in our image (as of several), according to our likeness (of several)." To these are added the passages by which it was proved above (Chapter I, Section 29, pp. 206, 208) that creation belongs equally to the Son and the Holy Spirit as to the Father.

This is, moreover, one cause, not three associated causes, for the power of creating belonging to the three Persons is one and the same (compare Musaeus, Theological Disputation on Creation, Section 15, p. 113, where the question "whether the three Persons may rightly be called three creators" is decided with the observation that this expression was never adopted in the usage of ecclesiastical writers, and that those who entirely abstain from it seem to act more safely, even though the expression might perhaps be defensible by the force and signification of the words).

### 17 The exemplary cause of creation consists in the ideas of the individual…

The exemplary cause of creation consists in the ideas of the individual creatures expressed in the divine intellect.

Notes. For in Genesis 1, Moses almost invariably prefixes to each work the formula "God said," and then adds "God saw what He had made, and it was very good." By this it is indicated that the forms of the individual things to be produced were present to the divine intellect, that the things produced truly imitated those forms by the intention of God, and that they were thus approved by God. Furthermore, it is the nature of causes that act through intellect to produce effects in imitation of some form preconceived in the mind. That the world and all things in it were made not by chance but by the counsel of God is, up to this point, certain.

### 18 The impulsive cause of creation we seek in the goodness of God alone

The impulsive cause of creation we seek in the goodness of God alone.

Note. (Psalm 136:1ff). And this will be recognized without difficulty if we presuppose that the world was made by the free will of God.

### 19 We acknowledge no instrumental efficient cause of creation

We acknowledge no instrumental efficient cause of creation.

Note. For whether angels, or anything else distinct from God, could even be an instrument of creation in the sense of producing something from nothing is an uncertain and speculative question. But that there was in fact any such cause of the creation of this universe, or of its parts, can by no means be said. The Son of God, through whom all things are said to have been made (with respect, of course, to the order which He has in relation to the Person of the Father by reason of origin), is nevertheless not properly speaking an instrument of the Father, since the power of creating that belongs to Him is the same as the Father's, not an inferior one. The improper manner of speaking used by certain ecclesiastical writers may indeed be excused, but it ought not to be imitated (compare Musaeus, Theological Disputation on Creation, Section 11, p. 129).

### 20 The matter of the creation of immaterial things is nothing

The matter of the creation of immaterial things is nothing. The matter of simple bodies is given, but it did not exist before the form. The matter of mixed bodies is to be sought in the simple bodies Note. See above, Sections 3, 4, and 5; Musaeus, Theological Disputation on Creation, Sections 24, 25, pp. 139, 140.

### 21 The mode of the creation of this universe

The mode of the creation of this universe, although congruent with the order of nature, was nonetheless entirely different from physical or natural generation, and it was an argument of the infinite wisdom and power of God.

Notes. Regarding its congruence with nature: God first produced the simple bodies, which are the principles of mixed bodies, and from these He then produced the mixed ones. Again, He produced imperfectly mixed things, such as clouds, first; afterward the mixed ones, and from the class of mixed things He produced first the plants, then the fish, the birds, and the terrestrial animals, all indeed from that element which is most suited to their nature, in which they exist, live, and are preserved. Finally, He produced the human being, the most perfect of corporeal creatures and their future lord (see Musaeus, Theological Disputation on Creation, Sections 28ff., pp. 143ff.).

Regarding the difference from natural generation: first, physical generation always requires preexisting matter, but here, as far as the production of heaven and earth is concerned, matter did not exist before the form, as we saw in Section 2. Second, in natural generation a suitable subject and a passive potency that is not too remote are required, which must be altered and successively disposed to actually receive the form. But here, even the mixed bodies were produced from an unsuitable and undisposed subject in such a way that the dispositions toward the form and the forms themselves were produced in the matter instantaneously (Musaeus, Theological Disputation on Creation, Sections 49, 50, pp. 161, 162, 163).

That this was an argument of divine wisdom and power is evident from what has just been said, and it must be recalled what we stated in Section 17: that God created all things by speaking, that is, by the command of His will, directed by the practical knowledge of His intellect. He applied His effective power to action, or, as others teach, God by willing, that is, by the very act of His will (which has the character of a productive power), accomplished in the work of creation whatever He willed (compare what we said concerning the power of God, in the preceding chapter, Section 24, p. 127; Musaeus, Theological Disputation on Creation, Sections 51, 52, pp. 263, 264, 265).

### 22 So that the world might endure

So that the world might endure, God produced the simple bodies on the condition that they should never entirely perish. For the heaven is incorruptible, to be destroyed only by the power of God. The elements, although they are subject to changes insofar as they enter into the constitution of mixed bodies, nevertheless never perish entirely in themselves. Mixed bodies, however, when they are corrupted, are resolved into the elements of which they consist.

Notes. To mixed things, which have a life subject to corruption, God communicated the power of generating or multiplying themselves, for the preservation of the species.

Thus God created "the herb yielding seed" and "the tree making fruit of its kind, whose seed is in it" (Genesis 1:11, 12, 29). Likewise, blessing the aquatic and flying creatures, He said: "Be fruitful and multiply" (Genesis 1:22). Hence He also simultaneously produced two individuals of each kind of animal, of both sexes.

In contrast to the other animals, Adam alone is said for some time not to have found a helper like himself (Genesis 2:20).

To the first human being likewise God soon joined a female companion and bestowed upon them the power of generating (Genesis 1:27, 28, where mention is made of male and female, and of the blessing by the power of which they could multiply and fill the earth). But whether, just as brute animals possess the power of multiplying themselves through generation, by which, with the general concurrence of God, they produce both seed and from altered and disposed seed the form and thus the whole animal, so also by virtue of the divine blessing a human being is generated by a human being with respect to the soul equally as the body, with only the universal concurrence of God; or whether in human generation the effect is nobler than what can be produced by human parents entirely by themselves with the general concurrence of God alone (namely, because the rational soul is by its nature immaterial and demands a mode of production congruent with its mode of being, that is, that it be produced independently of matter, or from nothing, for which secondary causes with the general concurrence of God do not suffice), and therefore by virtue of that blessing God, as the first cause, where secondary causes fall short, concurs by a special influence and supplies the deficiency of the human generators: this is an ancient and difficult question, in which we prefer to suspend judgment (epechein). See what we said in the Prolegomena, Chapter I, at Section 34, note c, p. 56.

### 23 The ultimate end of creation is the glory of the divine wisdom

The ultimate end of creation is the glory of the divine wisdom, goodness, and power. The intermediate end is the benefit of the human being.

Notes. That is, that through creatures the goodness, wisdom, and power of God might become known, inasmuch as from the contemplation of them the human being can and ought to be moved to celebrate the goodness, wisdom, and power of God (see Psalms 19:1; 104:1, 2; 136:1ff.; 148:1ff.).

See (Genesis 1:27). As Gerhard states (Gerhard, Introductory Disputation XI, Section 6, On Creation, Section 6): "God would not have commanded the other things to be made unless He had decreed to make the human being." For some creatures serve the necessities of human life, others its delight; some serve as remedies for diseases, others as safeguards of health; some as aids for conducting affairs, others for example and imitation (compare Lactantius, On the Wrath of God, ch. 13; John of Damascus, On the Orthodox Faith, Book 2, ch. 10; Musaeus, Theological Disputation on Creation, Sections 56, 57, pp. 167, 168).

### 24 Creation is defined as an action of the Triune God directed outward

Creation is defined as an action of the Triune God directed outward, by which God, moved by His goodness, produced this world and all things that are in it: first the simple bodies from no preexistent matter; then from the simple bodies, as from unsuitable and undisposed matter, the mixed bodies; and also, independently of all matter, the immaterial substances. He did this in such a way that He powerfully effected each of these things according to the idea of His mind, by the sole command of His will, and completed the entire work within the space of six days, for the glory of His wisdom, power, and goodness, and for the benefit of humankind.

Notes. On the efficient cause, see Section 16, p. 232.

On the impulsive cause, see Section 18, p. 234.

On the series of the works of creation, see Sections 6ff.

On the exemplary cause, see Section 17, p. 233.

On the mode of creation, see Section 22, p. 236.

On the end of creation, see Section 23, p. 238.

## 5 On the Angels

### 1 Among creatures

Among creatures, all of which participate in the divine goodness, the most perfect are those which Scripture calls angels.

Note. Thus in the Epistle to the Hebrews 1:4, when it was necessary to prove that Christ is more excellent than every creature, he is said to be superior to the angels.

### 2 Although the word "angel" (ἄγγελος) is a name of office and denotes a minister or legate

Although the word "angel" (ἄγγελος) is a name of office and denotes a minister or legate, nevertheless by this appellation a certain species of creatures is specifically signified, distinct by its very nature from human beings and all other creatures.

Notes. Just as among the Hebrews the word ךאלמ carries the same meaning, so Hilary says that Scripture, when it calls the heavenly spirits "angels," testifies to the signification of their office (Hilary, On the Trinity, book 5). And Augustine says: "Angel is the name of the office, not of the nature" (Augustine, Exposition on Psalm 104; see also Musaeus, Disputation VI on the Angels, section 2, p. 169).

Hence also by this name are called any human beings who discharge the function of legates (Genesis 32:3, 6; James 2:25), and especially the heralds or ministers of the divine Word (Malachi 2:7; Matthew 11:10). Indeed Christ himself is preeminently called the Angel of the Covenant (Malachi 3:1), namely as one sent to consummate and announce the covenant of grace established by God with humanity. He was sent, however, not as an inferior by a superior, but on account of a special operation through which he began to exist in a new manner in a certain place, or with a new effect, conceived in relation to God the Father, from whom he proceeded by eternal generation (Musaeus, Disputation on the Angels, section 5, p. 171).

This species of creature is itself also divinely destined for ministries and embassies, for they are called πνεύματα λειτουργικὰ ἀποσταλμένα (ministering spirits sent forth) (Hebrews 1:14).

### 3 That such natures

That such natures, or angels, exist, Scripture most explicitly indicates.

Note. (Hebrews 1:4, 5, 6, 7, 13, 14; Psalm 91:11; Psalm 104:4; Matthew 4:6, 11, and elsewhere). From the light of nature, however, this can scarcely be demonstrated with certainty, although it may be supported by probable arguments.

### 4 The efficient cause of the angels is God

The efficient cause of the angels is God, who produced them out of nothing, in time, although when exactly they were created is not established with sufficient clarity.

Notes. Thus in Psalm 148:2 and 5, and in Psalm 104:4, and in Colossians 1:16, the angels are numbered among creatures.

They are indeed simple substances, and just as in their being, so also in their coming to be, they are independent of matter.

See Proverbs 8:22, where the substantial Wisdom or Son of God is said to have been with God before his works). And so it is gathered that, just as with the rest of God's works or creatures, so also the angels did not coexist eternally with God and his eternal Son, although it is also otherwise established that eternity belongs to God alone (see Part 1, Chapter 1, section 13, p. 179).

They were not created before heaven and earth (Genesis 1:1), and it is moreover well known that the existence of God before the creation of the world describes his eternity (Psalm 90:2; Isaiah 43:13). That the angels were created before humanity is usually proved from Job 38:7. Indeed, some believe that from this very passage it can be understood that the angels were created on the first day, because when God laid the foundation of the earth, the angels are said to have immediately praised God. But these matters are not sufficiently clear, nor is it necessary to say that the angels are indicated metaphorically by the names of either "heaven" or "light" in Genesis 1.

### 5 The angels are by their nature spirits

The angels are by their nature spirits, that is, spiritual or incorporeal substances, not composed of matter and form.

Notes. See Hebrews 1:14.

The term "spirit" is here taken not for a subtler corporeal substance, such as wind, but in adequate opposition to body, in that sense in which it is taken in James 2:26, and in which it ought to be understood when attributed to a living and intelligent nature (see also Ephesians 6:12; Musaeus, Disputation on the Angels, section 24, p. 182).

Among those bodies, however, which the angels are sometimes read to have assumed, whether fashioned from the surrounding air or of whatever other nature, and the spiritual substance of the angels themselves, there obtains only an accidental union. For they were present in those bodies by way of an assisting form, not an informing one. Hence it is not permissible to call this a natural or essential union (Musaeus, Disputation on the Angels, sections 38 ff., pp. 196 ff.).

### 6 Just as the angels have a spiritual essence in common with God and the human soul

Just as the angels have a spiritual essence in common with God and the human soul, so they differ from God in that their essence is not infinite but finite, and from the human soul in that their substance is complete.

Notes. For since the angels have their being not from themselves but from God, they did not receive being except as finite and limited.

Their substance is not ordered by its nature to another thing with which, as with another component part, it would constitute a single being per se (Musaeus, Disputation on the Angels, sections 35 ff., p. 194).

### 7 The angels are furthermore intelligent substances

The angels are furthermore intelligent substances, such that intellect, understood as the power of understanding, belongs to their essence.

Notes. For operations proceeding from the intellect are everywhere in Scripture attributed to them: for example, praising God (Isaiah 6:3), worshipping (Hebrews 1:6), and knowing what is preached in the Church (Ephesians 3:10).

The second act of understanding that proceeds from this power, that is, intellection or cognition, is indeed a really produced act and an accident, as is clear from the following distinctions.

### 8 The cognition of the angels is established as threefold

The cognition of the angels is established as threefold: natural, revealed, and beatific.

Notes. For although the power of knowing in the angels is one, nevertheless the acts of understanding vary according to the diverse manner of knowing, whether in the same subject or in different ones (Musaeus, Disputation on the Angels, sections 52, 53, 54, pp. 206 ff.).

Natural cognition is equally common to good and evil angels. Revealed cognition was common to all before the fall of some; after the fall, however, it was taken away from those who fell as a punishment for their lapse. The good angels, having been transferred into the state of glory, do not need it as formerly, although in their own manner they can still be said to be partakers of it. Beatific cognition belongs uniquely to the angels confirmed in goodness.

### 9 Natural cognition is that by which the angels know both themselves and the…

Natural cognition is that by which the angels know both themselves and the angels coexisting with them, as well as the essences of heaven and earth and all things contained in them, and finally God himself.

Notes. They know the former things, indeed, with clear cognition, so that they know themselves without an intelligible species, through their very own essence, while they know other things through species concreated with them, that is, impressed upon them by God himself at their first production. God, however, they know only abstractively, that is, a posteriori and from created things, yet more perfectly than is our abstractive cognition (Musaeus, Disputation on the Angels, section 56, pp. 210 ff.).

### 10 Nevertheless, particular things distinct from themselves

Nevertheless, particular things distinct from themselves, especially material things that exist at one time and another, as well as the accidents that belong to individual things, they begin to know successively and in time.

Notes. For we cannot attribute omniscience to them, and it is relevant here that it is said: "so that NOW the manifold wisdom of God might be made known to the principalities and powers in the heavenly places through the Church" (Ephesians 3:10).

### 11 Future contingent events that depend on their free will they do not know with…

Future contingent events that depend on their free will they do not know with certainty and infallibility, although we cannot deny a conjectural knowledge to their sagacity.

Notes. Those future events that proceed from determinate causes and from things that always operate in the same manner according to the order of nature, for example, the constellations of the stars, eclipses, and the like, they know with certainty in their causes and in this way foresee the future; yet what God may do by his absolute power, having altered the order of nature, they do not know.

To know future contingencies with certainty and infallibility belongs to God alone, by which characteristic he willed to be recognized by human beings (Isaiah 41:12; see also Part 1, Chapter 1, section 15, p. 184).

This limitation applies by virtue of their natural cognition; that God can reveal to them, and sometimes does reveal, such contingent future events so that they know them with certainty is not denied, but it does not pertain to the present discussion.

By way of conjecture, the angels know future wars, seditions of peoples, sins, and remarkable deeds of individual human beings, namely from the temperaments, characters, habits of people, and from past and present circumstances carefully observed. Yet this knowledge is only a probable and uncertain, and often fallacious, opinion.

Similarly, future contingent events of another kind, which arise from natural causes that are subject to various changes, or from causes concurring accidentally and by chance, and which therefore happen in different ways, now this way, now that, such as storms, diseases, and the like, they foreknow only probably.

### 12 Likewise concerning the hidden thoughts of human beings

Likewise concerning the hidden thoughts of human beings, the angels possess only an opinion gathered from signs or effects.

Note. For God claims for himself alone the accurate and infallible knowledge of the human heart (1 Kings 8:39; Romans 8:27; see also Part 1, Chapter 1, section 15, p. 183).

### 13 With the intellect in the angelic nature is conjoined a free will

With the intellect in the angelic nature is conjoined a free will, that is, a power of desiring good things and turning away from evil things.

Notes. For never is the power of understanding without the will. The angelic will is indicated by the act of joy attributed to the angels (Luke 15:10) and by the act of desire, concerning which see 1 Peter 1:12 and 1 Peter 5:8.

This freedom of the angelic will in the state of probation was such that the angel could indifferently desire good or evil. What the freedom of the will of the good and evil angels is today will be taught below.

### 14 There belongs also to the angels a faculty of speaking

There belongs also to the angels a faculty of speaking, that is, of manifesting to others the concepts of their mind, so that they can speak to God, to other angels, and to human beings.

Notes. What they speak to themselves through internal concepts of the mind does not differ from the cognition of the angels itself.

That they speak to God is indicated by their being said to praise God (Isaiah 6:3).

That they speak to one another is evident from the same passage, where one is said to have cried to another.

That they speak to human beings is clear from many texts (Luke 1:13, 19, 28, 30, 35; Luke 2:10, 14; Zechariah 2:3).

The question arises, however, concerning the mode of angelic speech. For although they can speak to God through thoughts alone directed, for example, to praising or petitioning God, since there is no need of other signs to manifest those thoughts to the omniscient divine intellect, nevertheless how they converse among themselves is difficult to explain. The more probable opinion among others is that one freely impresses intelligible species upon the intellect of another (Musaeus, Disputation on the Angels, sections 67, 68, pp. 216 ff.). Similarly, they appear to be able to speak to human beings through species impressed upon their intellect, and furthermore through phantasms presented to the human imagination. Most often, however, in the Scriptures they are read to have spoken with a sensible and distinct voice, formed in the air in imitation of the human voice, which nonetheless cannot be called natural to the angels in the same way as it is to human beings, since it is not produced by the organs naturally required for forming a natural voice that inherently belong to the speaker.

### 15 There also belongs to the angels a certain power of operating outside themselves

There also belongs to the angels a certain power of operating outside themselves, which is indeed great but limited and finite.

Notes. Since the will is attributed to them, the faculty of executing or effecting what they will in accordance with their nature and original state ought not to be denied (Musaeus, Disputation on the Angels, section 70, pp. 219, 220). To this faculty or power belongs the fact that they can assume bodies and that they can speak to human beings with a sensible voice.

Hence they are called "mighty in strength" (Psalm 103:20), "the hosts of the Lord" (Genesis 32:2), "the strong one" (Matthew 12:29), and "a strong armed man" (Luke 2:21), and marvelous effects are everywhere ascribed to them in Scripture.

Their power, however, being created and subject to divine authority and omnipotence, cannot be denied (see Job 1 and 2). Therefore it does not extend to those things that exceed finite power (for example, the angels cannot produce something out of nothing or raise the dead), nor to all things that otherwise fall within finite power to be effected immediately through their own power, but only to those things that are proportionate to their nature and power. Hence, although they can produce a spiritual quality, that is, an intelligible species, outside themselves in another angel or in a human being, they cannot immediately and of themselves produce or alter corporeal substances, but only by means of natural causes, applying active things to passive ones (Musaeus, Disputation on the Angels, sections 71, 72, pp. 220, 221).

### 16 From the essence of the angels flow the following properties

From the essence of the angels flow the following properties.

First, simplicity, namely that they are not composed of the essential parts of matter and form, nor of integral parts, unless perhaps the very spirituality of their essence formally implies simplicity opposed to physical composition. Through this, however, it is not denied that they are composed of essence and subsistence, and likewise of subject and accidents (see section 8 above).

Second, incorruptibility, namely that they do not have in themselves a principle of corruption. That they can, however, be destroyed and annihilated by God, by whom they were created, and thus, even though they do not have a form that could be cast off while the subject remains, they can nevertheless be simply changed from being to non-being, is certain (Musaeus, Disputation on the Angels, section 27, p. 185). In the meantime, aeviternity, that is, a duration having a beginning but lacking an end, is rightly ascribed to them.

Third, non-locality, namely that they are not in a place. For since they lack matter, they are not, properly speaking, quantitative, nor can they be circumscribed by a place. We do not say, however, that they are everywhere, but in a certain definite "where," as it is called, so that they can also move themselves from one location to another and move material things elsewhere (Matthew 8:32, where the demons, cast out of the possessed man by Christ and migrating into a herd of swine, drove the whole herd headlong into the sea; Musaeus, Disputation on the Angels, sections 34 ff., p. 193, and sections 72 ff., pp. 221, 224).

### 17 The number of angels is exceedingly great

The number of angels is exceedingly great.

Notes. Thus thousands of thousands and ten thousand times a hundred thousand angels are mentioned who serve God (Daniel 7:10). And Christ teaches that if he were to ask, the Father would easily send more than twelve legions of angels to him (Matthew 26:53). Moreover, in one man a whole legion of unclean spirits is read to have been present (Mark 5:9). A legion among the Romans was commonly a multitude of six thousand soldiers, although the number otherwise varied. Innumerable angels (μυριάδων) are mentioned in Hebrews 12:22. And in this great number the angels were created by God, not multiplied through generation of some from others as with human beings.

### 18 That the angels differ among themselves in certain orders or degrees is not in doubt

That the angels differ among themselves in certain orders or degrees is not in doubt. Whether, however, they also differ in species and essence is not certain.

Notes. As is gathered from the diverse names, such as Cherubim (Genesis 3:24), Seraphim (Isaiah 6:2), θρόνοι (thrones), ἀρχαί (principalities), κυριότητες (dominions), ἐξουσίαι (authorities), δυνάμεις (powers) (Colossians 1:16; Ephesians 1:21), and Archangels (1 Thessalonians 4:16), and from the fact that they are described elsewhere as having an order among themselves, such as that of those commanding and those obeying (Luke 11:25; Matthew 25:41).

Indeed, the blessed Augustine, speaking of the distinction among the angels, says: "Let those who can, explain these things; I confess that I am ignorant of them" (Augustine, Enchiridion to Laurentius, chapter 28).

### 19 The angels, considered with respect to the nature common to all

The angels, considered with respect to the nature common to all, may be defined as spiritual, intelligent, complete, and finite substances.

Note. See sections 5, 6, and 7 above.

### 20 To the angelic nature God at the first creation bestowed certain habitual…

To the angelic nature God at the first creation bestowed certain habitual perfections for the purpose of eliciting acts befitting them and of attaining a supernatural end through God's grace.

Notes. These perfections the authors call by the name of grace. For no state of pure nature, as some call it, is to be imagined; rather, it must be acknowledged that God, who made all things very good, made the angels at their very beginning such as they needed to be in order to attain a supernatural end (see Jude 6, where the angels who became evil are said not to have kept their own origin, τὴν ἑαυτῶν ἀρχήν). It is therefore necessary that they were first good.

The states of the angels are distinguished into the state of grace and the state of glory, concerning which one must treat separately.

### 21 Just as the angels

Just as the angels, tending toward their end, were obliged rightly to know God, to love him above all things, to believe his truthfulness, to trust in his goodness, to obey his commands, and to hope for eternal life, so the grace divinely granted to the angels for performing these acts entailed, on the part of the intellect, a certain habitual light, by the benefit of which the angels could know those things that needed to be known for attaining the supernatural end but could not be known by the light of nature. Some call it faith or the light of faith; the blessed Gerhard calls it a supernatural habit of faith (Gerhard, Theological Commonplaces, Disputation 13, Chapter 9, section 7, p. 557). That is, distinguishing faith from evident knowledge, they held that the angels believed through faith what they knew under the aspect of truth, not however through the evidence of the object, but through the authority of God who speaks and reveals.

Notes. This light seems to have consisted in divinely impressed species, by which God, as it were, spoke to the angels, and supernatural things to be known were presented to their intellect, so that those things could be recognized, not indeed evidently and as they are in themselves, but with reference to the God who speaks, and the angelic intellect in this manner became a sufficient principle for supernatural acts of knowing and assenting. For example, they were to know the ultimate end itself, that is, the beatific vision of God to be expected at some future time, as a motive for constant obedience to be rendered in the meantime. At the same time also the mystery of the Most Holy Trinity, which surpasses the limits of natural intelligence, was to be known by the angels, so that God might be worshipped as he truly is with respect to the persons. The mystery of the Incarnation, however, since Christ did not assume the nature of angels (Hebrews 2:16), and the other free decrees of God, we do not say were known to the angels in the state of probation through the light of grace.

On the part of the will, the grace entailed habitual justice and holiness, that is, a complex of supernatural virtues constituting a complete or universal justice. To this pertains the ἀλήθεια (truth), or truthfulness, faithfulness, integrity, and sincere holiness from which the Devil is said to have fallen away (John 8:44). The authors call this hope and charity (Gerhard, Theological Commonplaces, Disputation 13, Chapter 9, p. 557). The angels in the state of probation had hope by which they embraced the future beatitude as a good that was absent and arduous, yet possible and truly to be obtained unless they themselves should stand in their own way. This hope presupposed confidence placed in God as the cause of attaining beatitude, by which their will rested in God as a present good and cause of another good.

Charity, for its part, had as its object both God, for whom they desired to do something pleasing, and their fellow angels, to be loved for God's sake as sharers in their nature and future co-heirs of salvation. They were not, however, necessitated to perform their actions in a holy manner, but retained the freedom of acting otherwise and of falling away, as is evident from the subsequent fall of some.

### 22 And so it is clear that it cannot altogether be denied that the angels were…

And so it is clear that it cannot altogether be denied that the angels were created in the image of God.

Notes. It must be admitted that this is not expressly stated in the Scriptures, unless perhaps one might refer here to the fact that the angels are called sons of God (Job 1:6; 2:1; 38:7), and that the Son is commonly called the image of the Father.

Certainly that the angels were in this respect conformed to the divine Being, and received this conformity from the intention of God who bestowed it upon them, is assuredly certain (Gerhard, Theological Commonplaces, Disputation 12, Chapter 6, section 26, p. 523).

### 23 Although the gifts of grace were conferred upon all the angels by God

Although the gifts of grace were conferred upon all the angels by God, nevertheless not all, but only some, rightly used the grace granted to them; and from this arose the distinction of the angels into good and evil.

### 24 Those are called good who persevered in the goodness

Those are called good who persevered in the goodness, that is, the justice and holiness in which they had been created, and who were confirmed in good by God, who was graciously to reward their obedience, so that they can no longer lose their goodness, sin, or become evil.

### 25 Those are called evil who voluntarily departed from their original goodness

Those are called evil who voluntarily departed from their original goodness, and who, with grace justly withdrawn by the judgment of God, are so confirmed in evil that they cannot return to goodness, do well, or refrain from sinning.

Notes. For this is what it means not to keep their own origin but to undergo a change from the first state for the worse (Jude 6). The ἀρχή (origin) in this passage denotes not the substance itself received in the first creation, which always remains the same, but the concreated perfections that could be lost. And for the same reason, the one who is said not to stand in the truth (John 8:44) is presupposed to have formerly been in it.

### 26 How long the state of grace lasted

How long the state of grace lasted, that is, before some of the angels were confirmed in good while others, departing from good, became evil, is not established with sufficient clarity.

Notes. Some suppose that the fall of the evil angels occurred on the second day of creation, indicated by the fact that the narrative of the works of that day does not add: "God saw that those works were good." But this is plainly weak, and one should rather note the general conclusion in Genesis 1:31: "God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good." From this one may rather gather that the angels had not yet fallen when the entire hexaemeron was completed.

It is, however, certain that the distinction of the good and evil angels took place before the first human beings fell. For thus Christ calls the Devil a murderer ἀπ' ἀρχῆς (from the beginning) and the father of lies (John 8:44), and it is evident that the Devil gave a specimen of consummate malice in seducing Eve (Genesis 3:1 ff.). On the other hand, the angel who guarded Paradise when the fallen humans were cast out from it was beyond doubt already confirmed in good (Genesis 3:24; see Gerhard, Commentary, p. 124).

### 27 The good angels were confirmed in good through their very beatitude

The good angels were confirmed in good through their very beatitude.

### 28 Namely, after they had constantly rendered their obedience to God in the state…

Namely, after they had constantly rendered their obedience to God in the state of probation, even while other angels were falling, it pleased God to fill them with the light of glory, so that they might be able to know God himself clearly and intuitively.

Notes. Some assign to these angels a particular operation consisting in combat against the evil angels and resistance opposed to their assaults.

For this is what it means to see the face of the heavenly Father (Matthew 18:10). And rightly the blessed Gerhard says: "βλέπειν πρόσωπον Θεοῦ (to see the face of God), precisely in the sacred Scriptures, does not signify to await God's command (although it connotes this), but the beatific vision" (Gerhard, Theological Commonplaces, Disputation 13, Chapter 9, section 9, p. 558).

### 29 Upon this vision of God there followed an intensely burning love

Upon this vision of God there followed an intensely burning love, by which the will of the angels began to cling to God in such a way that it could not be turned away from him.

Notes. see Part 1, Prolegomena, Chapter 1, section 4, note d, p. 10.

### 30 And thus their confirmation in good was accomplished
