And thus their confirmation in good was accomplished, that is, a determination of the will toward good, so that whatever they do, they do it in relation to God as a good infinitely perfect and perfectly known, without any blemish or defect.

Notes. And this is the ἀναμαρτησία (sinlessness) or impeccability customarily ascribed to the blessed angels. For sin implies ἀνομία (lawlessness), that is, illegality. The sum of the Law is to love God above all things. Therefore those who always love God, clearly known, above all things, and incessantly embrace him as the supreme good, by this very fact cannot act ἀνόμως (lawlessly), since it implies a contradiction that someone, while loving God above all things, should be conformed to the Law and at the same time, by sinning, wander from the Law.

### 31 Nor, however, is all freedom of the angelic will thereby removed

Nor, however, is all freedom of the angelic will thereby removed. For although it is no longer indifferent to good and to evil, it is nevertheless indifferent with respect to created goods, so that whichever of them it wills, it can also not will, or in place of one it can will another.

Notes. Nor indeed did that freedom of willing evil as well as good imply a perfection.

Thus it is free with the freedom of contradiction or exercise.

And with what the authors call the freedom of contrariety or specification.

### 32 To that beatitude

To that beatitude, moreover, the good angels were destined by the eternal decree of God, and were thus elected.

Notes. For it cannot be said that God confers upon the angels in time what he had not from eternity decreed he would one day confer. And Paul makes express mention of the "elect angels," τῶν ἐκλεκτῶν ἀγγέλων (1 Timothy 5:21), indicating that a few were chosen from the many, that is, from the entire company of spirits, upon whom the beatitude of which all could have become partakers would be conferred.

This decree was not, however, absolute, that is, one that excluded every foreseen condition on the part of the subject, to be fulfilled freely yet certainly. For just as God in time conferred beatitude only upon those who persevered in good, so the eternal decree concerning the angels to be saved at some point rested upon the foresight of that condition to be fulfilled in time. The election of the angels acknowledges an internal impulsive cause or reason in the electing God, namely his goodness, but not an external impulsive cause. And although on the part of the divine intellect it presupposes an act of cognition directed toward the constant obedience of the angels themselves, nevertheless this obedience, owed to God the Creator and temporal in nature, does not have the force of merit before God, or the force of impelling his will to decree or bestow the good of eternal beatitude.

We do not, however, say that the angels were elected in the sense in which Scripture describes the election of human beings, which has regard to the merit of Christ and to faith to be placed in him (Gerhard, Theological Commonplaces, Disputation 13, Chapter 9, section 13, p. 561).

### 33 In their blessed life the good angels discharge various operations

In their blessed life the good angels discharge various operations, of which some pertain to their beatitude itself, while others are ministerial, by which the angels serve God and Christ the God-man, and promote the salvation of human beings.

Notes. For beatitude does not consist in idleness, but partly implies a certain ἐνέργεια (activity) in itself, and partly admits of further operations to be exercised by those who are blessed.

Nor are the angels ashamed, in the state of glory, to discharge this office, which they can render to God and to Christ the God-man as their Lord, and to faithful human beings on account of the Lord's will and out of an affection of charity, as to friends and co-heirs of salvation (Psalm 103:20; Matthew 4:11; Hebrews 1:14). God, however, uses their ministry by his free will and by the gentle disposition of his providence.

### 34 Operations of the first kind are partly those in which the essential beatitude…

Operations of the first kind are partly those in which the essential beatitude of the angels consists, namely the acts of intuitively knowing God and of most intensely loving God clearly known, and partly those which add a certain accidental beatitude to the angels. These additional operations include acts of understanding other objects specially revealed by God or perceived through experience in the Church, such as the mystery of the Incarnation, the conversion of a sinful human being. To which likewise on the part of the will are added acts of love and joy.

Notes. See sections 28 and 29 above.

For the beatitude of the angels does not refuse an accidental increase, just as on the part of human beings to be made blessed there are also degrees of glory, as will be taught below.

See Luke 1:26, 31; Luke 2:13.

See Luke 15:7, 10.

### 35 Operations of the latter kind concern partly individual pious persons

Operations of the latter kind concern partly individual pious persons, and partly the hierarchical orders themselves, which are to be guarded.

Notes. Regarded generally as human beings without consideration of a specific state or order.

That is, the sacred classes or orders of human beings within the Church, where some preside and others are subject.

### 36 The angels minister to individual pious persons when they protect them at the…

The angels minister to individual pious persons when they protect them at the very beginning of life and in infancy, guard those who are more mature in every honorable function. As well as attend upon the dying.

Whether a certain angel has been assigned to each individual person for guardianship has long been debated. This much is certain: the custody of a person is not to be assigned to one angel in such a way as to deprive that person of the help of the others. Ordinarily, however, it can be said with probability that one angel is destined for the guardianship of each pious individual; extraordinarily, several angels are sent to individual believers (Gerhard, Theological Commonplaces, Disputation 13, section 7).

See Matthew 18:10.

"the angel of the Lord encamps around those who fear him and delivers them," Psalm 34:7; "he has given his angels charge over you, to guard you in all your ways," Psalm 91:11, 12.

As the soul of Lazarus is said to have been carried by the angels into Abraham's bosom (Luke 16:22).

### 37 With respect to the ecclesiastical state

With respect to the ecclesiastical state, it pertains to the office of Angels that they advance the ministry of the Word. In particular, they were present as ministers at the promulgation of the Mosaic Law, they announced the coming of Christ in the flesh, they prevent the introduction of idolatry into the Church, they attend the sacred assemblies.

Notes. Deuteronomy 33:2; Galatians 3:19, where the Law is called ὁ νόμος διαταγείς, "the law ordained through angels," which our theologians explain as referring to the sound of trumpets produced by the Angels; see also Acts 7:53.

See Luke 1:26; Luke 2:9.

(Jude 9) For it is believed that the dispute of the angel with Satan over the body of Moses arose from the fact that Satan was striving to bring to light the body of Moses, which God had concealed, in order to furnish the Israelites with an occasion for idolatry, and that therefore a good angel opposed him.

1 Corinthians 11:10, where Paul draws an argument for more easily persuading women to observe modesty of dress in the sacred assemblies from the presence of the angels, who are lovers of good order and propriety; and it is certain that Angels are present with us and together celebrate God, and that they remove not a few hindrances.

### 38 Angels serve the political state in such a way that they prevent the bonds of…

Angels serve the political state in such a way that they prevent the bonds of the commonwealth from being broken. They assist and defend the magistrate and his ministers, and they ward off dangers and afflict unjust enemies.

Notes. Daniel 10:13, where it is said that God sent an angel into the court of the King of Persia at the time when, through the zeal and activity either of evil angels or of wicked officials and counselors, religion and justice seemed about to be overthrown, so that by suppressing their efforts, public tranquility and safety might be preserved.

Daniel 6:22, where we read that an angel sent by God shut the mouths of the lions so that they could not harm Daniel, a chief minister of the kingdom, who was undergoing danger for the glory of God.

2 Kings 19:35; Isaiah 37:36, where it is narrated that the angel of the Lord came to the aid of the pious King Hezekiah, who had been attacked in an unjust war by the Assyrians, and delivered the enemy army to destruction.

### 39 They minister to the household by promoting the marriages of the godly

They minister to the household by promoting the marriages of the godly, by guarding the family's property, and by protecting the children of the family.

Notes. As Abraham, when arranging his son's marriage, testified that he hoped for this; Genesis 24:7.

Job 1:10, where God is said to have hedged about or surrounded his house with a wall, in the sense in which Psalm 34:7 says that God sends His angel round about those who fear Him.

See Matthew 18:10.

### 40 Finally, there will be a special office of the angels which they will discharge…

Finally, there will be a special office of the angels which they will discharge on the last day, when they will accompany Christ as He comes to judgment and will proclaim His advent with the sound of trumpets. They will gather human beings from all parts of the world, separate the godly from the ungodly, place the former at the right hand of Christ, having led them into the air to meet Him, and station the latter at the left hand of the Judge, soon thereafter casting them down into hell.

Notes. Matthew 25:31; 1 Thessalonians 4:15, 16.

Matthew 24:31; Mark 13:27.

Matthew 13:41, 49.

Matthew 25:32.

1 Thessalonians 4:17.

Matthew 25:32.

Matthew 13:47.

### 41 On account of those perfections with which we have seen that the good Angels are endowed

On account of those perfections with which we have seen that the good Angels are endowed, and because they greatly favor and benefit us, it is certainly fitting that we hold them in high regard. We should love them and take care not to offend them by wicked deeds.

Notes. For what the Augsburg Confession teaches is owed to the departed saints in Article 21, the same may rightly be rendered to Angels as well, especially since it is otherwise established that Angels take an interest in our actions.

See 1 Corinthians 11:10, as discussed above.

### 42 However, it is not fitting to direct our prayers to Angels

However, it is not fitting to direct our prayers to Angels. For this is either impious and idolatrous, or at the very least useless and ill-advised.

Notes. Namely if we direct religious prayers with trust to them as bestowers of spiritual goods.

For whatever kind those prayers may be, it must nonetheless be acknowledged that Scripture furnishes us with no commandment, no example, and no promise in this regard. And whence, one may ask, shall it be possible to know whether angels understand our prayers or take delight in them? Indeed, in Revelation 19:10 and 22:8, 9, the Angel simply and steadfastly refuses the worship of adoration, adding the reason that he is a fellow servant of John and of the companions in the faith, and that God alone (in opposition to all who are not God but are fellow servants among themselves, and therefore God alone) is to be worshipped. And it is clear that the angel does this not out of feigned humility but seriously and for solid reasons, nor does he distinguish between degrees of religious worship, of which some higher degree might belong to God alone while another might be appropriate to himself.

### 43 As for the fall or first sin of the evil Angels

As for the fall or first sin of the evil Angels, by which they departed from their created goodness and became evil, what exactly it was is not sufficiently clear.

Notes. It is commonly thought to have been pride, that is, an inordinate self-complacency and an aspiration to divine honor and dominion. For the spirit lurking in the serpent (Genesis 3:5) seduced Eve with the vain promise of a singular likeness to God. And he who wished to be worshipped by Christ (Matthew 4:9), as he thereby displayed a specimen of consummate pride, so he is believed to have first polluted himself with this sin. Because, moreover, the beginning of all sin is said to be pride (Sirach 10:14), it is inferred from this that the origins of the Devil's sin, which was the first of all, are likewise to be found there (Gerhard, Introduction, Disputation 11, ch. 9, §§ 8, 9).

### 44 The company of evil Angels fell under a certain leader or prince whom Scripture…

The company of evil Angels fell under a certain leader or prince whom Scripture calls the Devil, who induced the rest into a partnership in the same sin either by his example or by his persuasion.

Notes. See John 8:44.

Hence it is that Scripture makes mention of "the angels of the Devil" (Matthew 25:41; Revelation 12:7).

### 45 Having committed sin

Having committed sin, all those Angels lost the grace that was created with them and thus fell into the most bitter misery, without hope of restoration.

Notes. For God did not grant to angels, as He did to human beings, a time and place for repentance, but utterly denied the help of grace. For the reasons of this divine counsel as handed down by the Church Fathers, see Gerhard (Gerhard, Introduction, Disputation 14, ch. 9, § 17).

### 46 Their intellect

Their intellect, deprived not only of the light of Grace but also of the light of Glory, and fixed upon the contemplation of the divine wrath and of their own misery, is as it were dulled and lacks a right judgment concerning good things to be done.

Notes. This is what is said in John 8:44, that the truth is not in the Devil. For just as the truth in which Satan was first created but did not stand was a full integrity and a δύναμις (power) and perfection created together with him for the right exercise of actions befitting him, which above all entailed a right judgment concerning things to be done, so by falling from the truth, and when truth is denied to be in him, he is thereby recognized as lacking a true and sound judgment concerning things to be done. Hence also in speaking he is not truthful but a liar, a deceiver, and a slanderer. Moreover, the corruption of the Devil's intellect is also customarily demonstrated from the fact that Satan promoted the death of Christ with such great zeal, not perceiving that the greatest adversity would thereby be brought upon himself. Whatever natural knowledge remains in the evil angels, however, adds nothing to their happiness.

### 47 Their will, deprived of the supreme love of God and of the joy drawn from it

Their will, deprived of the supreme love of God and of the joy drawn from it, and thus turned away from God, is hardened in evil and is therefore wretchedly tormented and afflicted.

Notes. This hardening occurs not from any special influx or determination on God's part, nor from an absolute decree of God, but on account of the withdrawal of those perfections of intellect and will that was merited by the preceding offense.

For knowing that there is a God, an idea which they cannot fully expunge from their mind, and that this same God is supremely powerful and indeed supremely good toward Himself and toward the other good angels, yet irreconcilably opposed to them and always threatening and severe, they not only do not love Him but abhor and oppose Him. And since they recognize that they brought this evil upon themselves by their own yoke, as the saying goes, they are angry with themselves and quarrel, as it were, with themselves, thus pursuing both God and themselves with hatred. Whence, since they perceive that others fare better than they, there necessarily arises envy of another's happiness and perpetual grief over the continual presence of their own evils.

### 48 Therefore the freedom of the will of the condemned Angels does not entail an…

Therefore the freedom of the will of the condemned Angels does not entail an indifference to good or evil, or to multiple goods, but is exercised with respect to particular evils, insofar as they are able to choose and not choose this one from among many, and likewise to choose another.

Notes. They do so, to be sure, under the appearance of good, but of what is not truly good, their own corrupted judgment deceiving them.

### 49 The operations which evil Angels carry out are varied

The operations which evil Angels carry out are varied. Above all, however, those should be noted which tend toward the destruction both of individual human beings and of the hierarchical estates.

### 50 They attempt to do harm partly to the bodies of human beings

They attempt to do harm partly to the bodies of human beings, so as to inflict diseases, partly to external goods or wealth, so as to corrupt or take them away, and partly to the soul itself, so as to turn it away from God and drag it through sins into damnation.

Notes. Luke 13:11, where a crippled woman, bent over, is said to have a spirit of infirmity, and in verse 16 it is said that Satan had kept her bound until then.

See Job 1:12 and following.

Ephesians 6:11, 12, where Paul commends spiritual armor in the battle against evil spirits, which presupposes their assaults by which the salvation of souls is put in jeopardy; and Peter in 1 Peter 5:8, 9 says that the enemy, who seeks whom he may devour, that is, whom he may bring to the utter ruin of the soul, must be resisted by faith and Christian vigilance.

### 51 Especially relevant here are spiritual possession

Especially relevant here are spiritual possession, by which Satan efficaciously impels the minds of ungodly people to the worst crimes, and bodily possession, by which Satan according to his substance dwells within the bodies of human beings and operates in them by divine permission.

Notes. Luke 22:3, where Satan is said to have entered the heart of Judas; see also John 13:27, where he is said to have put it into his heart to betray Jesus, verse 2; likewise Ephesians 2:2, where the prince of this world, the evil spirit, is said ἐνεργεῖν, "to work efficaciously," in the sons of disobedience, that is, unbelieving people; and 2 Corinthians 4:4, where the god of this age is said to blind the minds of unbelievers, lest the light of the Gospel should shine upon them.

He is said not merely to be present but κατ᾽ οὐσίαν καὶ αὐτοπροσώπως (essentially and in his own person) to be within the bodies of human beings. Examples of δαιμονιζομένων (demoniacs), that is, those possessed by an evil demon, are many in Scripture (Matthew 8:28, 31, 32; Mark 7:25 and following; Luke 4:35, 36).

This occurs not only to the ungodly but sometimes also to the godly, as experience shows. Our theologians infer this from the analogy of similar afflictions, for example Job 2:12, whose body Satan most wretchedly afflicted, and 2 Corinthians 12:7; for if Paul, so great an Apostle, was buffeted by an angel of Satan lest the greatness of his revelations should exalt him, what wonder if power over the bodies of the godly is also granted to Satan for a time (Gerhard, Introduction, Disputation 14, ch. 8, § 13).

The demon torments the body of the person and performs various, extraordinary, and sinful actions through his members, from which, if not individually then at least taken together as signs, a true bodily possession, distinct from epilepsy and other diseases or bewitchments, is recognized.

This occurs when God permits, either immediately or mediately through the agency of people, whether good (for example, ministers of the Church through the greater excommunication of those guilty of enormous sins, on which see 1 Corinthians 5:3; 1 Timothy 1:20) or evil (those who seek to harm others, for instance through sorcery or curses), that certain people be subjected to Satan. God, in permitting these things and either punishing more grievous sins, contempt of the Word, carnal security, blasphemies, or conspiracy with the Devil by a severe judgment, or chastening and testing the godly by bodily affliction, intends the manifestation of His power, justice, and goodness, and the repentance, faith, and salvation of people, if not of the possessed themselves, then at least of others who observe or hear of it.

### 52 Similarly relevant here is the fact that demons deceive people through specters…

Similarly relevant here is the fact that demons deceive people through specters and strive to destroy or afflict either the soul or the body.

Note. See Wisdom 17:3 and following.

### 53 In particular, they oppose the ecclesiastical state when they devote themselves…

In particular, they oppose the ecclesiastical state when they devote themselves to spreading heresies. They hinder the godly and salutary endeavors of the ministers of the Church. They draw hearers away from pious meditation upon the Word, so as to subvert their conversion and salvation.

Notes. Matthew 13:27, where the Enemy is said to sow tares in the field of the Church; Paul in 1 Timothy 4:1, 2 calls heresies "doctrines of demons"; and the fact that Antichrist inflicts so much evil on the Church is said in 2 Thessalonians 2:9 to occur through the working of Satan.

As happened to Paul, according to 1 Thessalonians 2:18.

Luke 8:12, for this is to take the Word from the hearts of hearers.

### 54 In political life

In political life, Satan suggests unjust and destructive counsels to rulers, and he otherwise disturbs the harmony of the commonwealth in many ways.

Note. Such as the counsel to number the people which he supplied to David, 1 Chronicles 21:1, and that given to Ahab to make war upon the Syrians, 1 Kings 22:21, 22.

### 55 In the household

In the household, they lie in wait against spouses themselves, their children, and the family's goods.

Notes. For example, by sowing quarrels or inciting to lust, 1 Corinthians 7:5.

Job 1; Matthew 15:22.

As in the histories of Job and Tobias.

### 56 Meanwhile, God Himself also makes use of the ministry of evil angels to…

Meanwhile, God Himself also makes use of the ministry of evil angels to chastise the godly in this world and to punish the ungodly, both in this life, and after death.

Notes. As seen again in the history of Job.

Psalm 78:49; for the "angels of evils," whether they are called angels intent upon inflicting evils or harms, or angels of evil people in opposition to those destined for the heirs of salvation, are in either case rightly understood as evil spirits; see the note to § 51 above.

Matthew 18:34; for although the words appear to be parabolic, nevertheless, because it is added, "So also will my heavenly Father do to you," it is rightly understood as referring to torturers sent against irreconcilable people, by whom they are afflicted without end, and under this designation none are more aptly signified than the evil angels.

### 57 Moreover, the Devil and his angels also have prepared for them torments and…

Moreover, the Devil and his angels also have prepared for them torments and pains from the fire of hell.

Note. (Matthew 25:41 and elsewhere). To explain in detail how fire, if it is corporeal, acts upon spirits is more a matter of curiosity than of usefulness or necessity.

### 58 The punishments by which the evil Angels are afflicted will be eternal

The punishments by which the evil Angels are afflicted will be eternal.

Note. Matthew 25:41, 46; Mark 9:43.

## 6 On the Image of God Bestowed upon Man at the First Creation

### 1 After the angels

After the angels, human beings hold the most eminent place among creatures. Concerning them it is most clear from the history of creation that God created them in His own image.

Notes. The order of the doctrine is thus evident: we must treat here of man insofar as the divine goodness of the Creator shines forth in him, before he, as a sinner requiring restoration to salvation, is subjected to the operation of revealed theology.

For the triune God says (Genesis 1:26), "Let us make man in our image, according to our likeness." And just as God decreed, so He accomplished, and truly created man in His own image; in the image of God He created him; male and female He created them (Genesis 1:27).

That is to say, God bestowed upon man a certain form excellently expressed after His own likeness; hence, notably, in the cited passage the word "likeness" is added to "image," so that we may understand it as a most faithful image. Moreover, it is established that the other creatures, although fashioned according to a certain idea present to the divine intellect, are indeed called very good, but are not said to have been made in the image of God.

### 2 Now, that which God willed to bestow

Now, that which God willed to bestow, and did bestow, upon man when fashioning him after His own likeness or image, must be sought not in any single person, but in the triune God as the exemplary cause.

Notes. For thus in the cited passage (Genesis 1:26), not only the verb but also a double plural suffix occurs. The sense of the words is: "We, who are multiple persons, let us make man in our image," that is, in the one common image of us who are many.

### 3 And this image of God in man ought not and cannot be referred to everything…

And this image of God in man ought not and cannot be referred to everything that exists in God. Neither does it exist in man at the same degree of perfection as it exists in God.

Notes. For example, that God exists of Himself, that He is immutable, immense, eternal, and infinite, is not found in a similar manner in man.

Likewise, since knowledge and wisdom are infinitely perfect in God, in man they were only finite. Since the holiness of God is conjoined with impeccability, in man, however, holiness was not so conjoined.

For it is otherwise well established that it is not required of an exemplar that whatever perfection exists in it should also be expressed in the copy (Musaeus, Introduction to Theology, ch. 1, §5, pp. 7f.).

### 4 The divine image which man obtained is

The divine image which man obtained is, however, taken in two senses. First, generally and without restriction, insofar as it contains everything in which a certain conformity of man with God as archetype obtains. Second, specially, that is, with restriction and κατ᾽ ἐξοχήν (par excellence), insofar as it denotes a certain preeminent likeness of man with God, by virtue of which man, absolutely speaking, can be called the express image of God.

### 5 The divine image taken in its general sense

The divine image taken in its general sense, in addition to the righteousness and wisdom concreated with the first man, includes within its scope also the very spiritual being of the human soul and its faculties, namely intellect and will, as well as the immortality of the body and dominion over the other creatures.

Notes. Thus Gerhard writes (Gerhard, Catholic Confession, book 2, part 3, article 20, ch. 2, p. 348):

The image of God and original righteousness stand as whole and part. For the image of God in the first man was an excellent conformity with God as the archetype. This conformity was twofold: one primary, the other secondary or less principal. The primary conformity was situated in the soul, partly in the intellect, partly in the appetite, both rational and sensitive. These three excellences are expressed by the single name of original righteousness. The less principal conformity of man with God was situated partly in the condition of the body, partly in external dominion. Or, as others proceed, the less principal conformity consists first in the soul, both as to substance and as to attributes; second in the body, with respect to impassibility and immortality; third in the whole man, with respect to external dominion over all things.

Wigand, speaking of the passage in Genesis 1:26, says (Wigand, Syntagma of the Body of Doctrine, p. 402):

The image of God there is to be understood of the whole substance of man, for Scripture says "He created man in His own image"; it does not say that only the soul of that first being was capable of this good. We believe, moreover, that this general expression refers to all the ornaments and gifts in the soul and body of man, by which he represented a certain likeness to God, albeit finite and suited to a creature, according to the judgment of almighty God.

See also Chytraeus (Commentary on Genesis, ch. 1, p. 57).

Since there is a certain congruence between the spiritual being of God and the spiritual being of the human soul, and between the intellect and will of God and the intellect and will of man, then, unless we say it happened by some chance that man is in these respects similar to God, it must be admitted that man was fashioned by God who, looking upon Himself as the exemplary cause, so constituted him, and that in this very respect man bears the image of God. And this is why man, even after the Fall and outside the state of renewal, is called the image of God (Genesis 9:6; James 3:9). For when in Genesis 9 it is decreed that homicide must be punished by death, not only the murder of a faithful man renewed according to the image specially so called, but the murder of any man whatsoever who is rashly killed, and the reason for the commandment is drawn from the fact that any homicide involves a violation of the divine image present in the slain person, and God so grievously resents this violation of His image that He wills it to be avenged by the death of the violator: certainly, when in the slain person there was no original righteousness as the image of God specially so called, the concept of the divine image must extend more broadly and reach to those things which have been stated in the thesis. For if one were to say that the image of God in this passage is regarded not as that which was in the slain person, but as that which once was in the first man, the common parent of all, even though it did not reach to the person who is killed, this would indeed be far-fetched and would undermine the connection between the divine commandment and its foundation. The reasoning for the latter passage (James 3:9) is the same, because cursing directed against a man, not precisely one who is reborn, but any man whatsoever, is condemned on the ground that it is a dishonoring of the divine image, namely because this image exists in the very person who is cursed and can be recognized there (Musaeus, Comprehensive Explanation, question 28, pp. 210ff.; cf. Graver, Lectures on the Augsburg Confession, article 2, member 2, in the response to the arguments of the Photinians; Hafenreffer, in his books On the Image of God; Gerhard, Commentary on Genesis, ch. 9, p. 243; the Leipzig Theologians, in the appendix to Dedekenn, Counsels, p. 139, and the authority they cite, Tilemann Heshusius).

The immortality of the body corresponds in a certain way to divine immortality, and more will be said about it at §12.

In the dominion over creatures, a certain ray of the divine majesty displays itself, as will be shown below at §13.

### 6 The divine image taken in its special sense denotes certain accidental…

The divine image taken in its special sense denotes certain accidental perfections concreated with the intellect and will of the first human beings, conformable to the perfections that exist in God, and bestowed upon men for the purpose of rightly ordering and completing their actions, for the sake of attaining the ultimate end.

Note. Thus from Genesis 1:31, where all creatures are said to have been very good, it is rightly inferred that man also was very good, and therefore furnished with the perfections necessary for attaining the end appointed for him.

### 7 Namely, on the part of the intellect

Namely, on the part of the intellect, God bestowed upon the first human beings, in imitation of Himself as the exemplary cause, a certain wisdom, that is, a habitual light or perfection of the intellect, directed toward an excellent knowledge of divine, human, and natural things, and sufficient for the primeval state.

Notes. This means that the intellect of man knew the essence and will of God to the extent necessary for the intellect to prescribe the worship proper to God, or to the extent sufficient for living justly and holily. Thus in the Epistle to the Colossians (Colossians 3:10), the divine image is said to be restored in man in the act of renewal by this, that he is brought to a saving knowledge of God.

The acts of cognition could in all respects be rightly conducted, that is, in conformity with the things themselves and without error.

This knowledge pertained to those things which it was necessary for man, created in such a state and tending toward the end divinely appointed for him, to know.

Yet it was such wisdom as could increase with the progress of time, but not so perfect and extensive as to reach even to the knowledge of God's free decrees, nor did it impart the most exact science of all natural things.

### 8 On the part of the will

On the part of the will, God bestowed upon man spiritual powers, that is, a habitual inclination and readiness to love God above all things, to do all things according to the prescription of the rightly illumined intellect, to omit whatever the intellect judged should be omitted, and likewise to govern the lower faculties so that they would by no means break forth into disordered and sinful acts.

Note. This is that righteousness and holiness of truth, that sincere, genuine, and steadfast virtue, concerning which, as pertaining especially to the divine image, see Ephesians 4:24 and Ecclesiastes 7:30.

### 9 Moreover, the sensitive appetite was then so perfected that it submitted itself…

Moreover, the sensitive appetite was then so perfected that it submitted itself promptly and without struggle to the right judgment of the intellect and the holy command of the will, nor did it give place to any disordered motion as though it were unavoidable.

Notes. For just as it is otherwise evident that the sensitive appetite in man is not entirely incapable of reason and morality, so also it needed to be equipped so that it could constantly obey the higher faculties and not tend toward objects pleasing to the senses except in conformity with right reason, so that man might be truly and perfectly just, holy, and very good (Genesis 1:31).

This is what is meant by the fact that the first parents in the state of integrity did not know that they were naked, nor were they ashamed, that is, they were not touched even slightly by any disordered desire (Genesis 2:25).

### 10 And this wisdom

And this wisdom, righteousness, and holiness of the first human beings so possesses the character of the divine image that it alone is that by which man, absolutely speaking, can be called the image of God.

Note. This is certainly more true than of the spiritual substance of the soul itself with its essential faculties, considered precisely in themselves. For without that wisdom, the mind of man would have been blind in comparison with the most wise divine mind; without holiness, the will, depraved and infected by the rebellion of the sensitive appetite, would have been more unlike than like the most pure and most holy will of God (Musaeus, Comprehensive Explanation, question 28, pp. 215 and 221).

### 11 This divine image was therefore also a natural gift

This divine image was therefore also a natural gift, that is, one owed to man by nature for the right exercise of his natural acts, in the absence of which nature would have been not pure but impure.

Notes. It can also be called natural in another sense, insofar as it was received with man's nature, inhered in the natural or essential faculties of man, adorned and perfected them, and was due to be propagated to posterity together with nature itself through carnal generation. It is not, however, called natural as though it constituted the essence of man or necessarily followed from that essence, for it is certain that it was taken away while the essence of man remained.

Indeed, for man to lack those perfections without which the intellect, will, and sensitive appetite cannot rightly perform their office surely imports a certain blemish and impurity in man. For although it is natural to man, insofar as he consists of body and soul, to have a sensitive appetite tending toward its objects, nevertheless, since man is by nature ordained to a life led εὐσεβῶς, δικαίως καὶ σωφρόνως (piously, justly, and temperately), as to acts natural to him and requisite for the attainment of the ultimate end toward which man tends, it is also natural to man to have a sensitive appetite obedient and exactly responsive to the higher faculties, and with respect to all his faculties to possess perfections of such magnitude as are necessary so that man, laboring under no deficiency of powers, should never need to stumble or sin, but rather could rightly and constantly discharge his office without blemish or enormity. Hence, in the absence of such perfections, the natural endowments of man cannot be said to be whole or pure; they are rather corrupt and therefore impure.

### 12 Furthermore, God bestowed upon man also on the part of the body a certain image of Himself

Furthermore, God bestowed upon man also on the part of the body a certain image of Himself, inasmuch as not only did the perfections of the soul manifest themselves through the external acts of the body, but moreover the very members of the organic body bear a certain analogy to the divine attributes, and the countenance raised toward heaven bears an appearance of divine majesty. Above all, the immortal body, that is, one that could endure perpetually and remain free from all corruption, bore by the intention of God a likeness to divine immortality.

Notes. And thus the divine image, which formally was in the soul, belongs to the body by participation.

For thus Scripture by anthropopathy ascribes to God eyes, ears, and hands.

For just as man thereby departs from the likeness of the other animals, so he in a certain way approaches the likeness of God, and is seen as an heir of the heavenly life.

For although a remote potency for dying would indeed fall upon the body of man, since it was material, nevertheless the necessity of dying and the proximate potency for death were absent, since the elemental qualities, although contrary in themselves, were nevertheless tempered with the most exact harmony, so as to give no place to any deterioration tending toward destruction. That the body of man in the state of integrity was immortal in this sense is clear especially from Genesis 2:16, Romans 5:12, and Romans 6:23, where the origin of death is ascribed to sin, and accordingly it is denied that in the first state, where sin had no place, death or the necessity of dying had place either. The first man is said to have been immortal on the part of the body by nature, not in the sense in which God is immortal by nature, for whom it is essentially repugnant to be mortal or to be destroyed; nor in the sense in which the angels, being immaterial by nature, are also said to be naturally immaterial, even though they could be annihilated by God; but insofar as the very nature of the first man's body was so constituted that it could live perpetually and was not subject to death to be undergone sooner or later.

### 13 Finally, God added to man dominion over the creatures

Finally, God added to man dominion over the creatures, by which he likewise bore a certain likeness to God, the Lord of this universe.

Notes. This dominion consisted not only in the right and power of man over the beasts and other creatures, but also in the force and ability to bend them to obedience, without difficulty and without fear of suffering harm from them (Genesis 1:26, 28; Genesis 2:16).

And indeed, if you take the image of God in its general sense, it cannot be denied that part of it was situated in this dominion, according to what has been said from Gerhard and Wigand in the note to §5. If you take it in its special sense, it can be called not a part but a certain consequence or appendage of the divine image. See Genesis 1:27, where God, blessing the human beings already fashioned in His own image, says: "Have dominion over the fish of the sea and over the birds of the heavens and over every living thing that moves on the earth."

### 14 The subject "which" was not Adam alone

The subject "which" was not Adam alone, but also Eve, especially insofar as the image was situated in original righteousness. However, with respect to those things which were not equally necessary for attaining the end appointed for each, we do not assert complete equality between the two parents.

Notes. That is, the supposit or person who is denominated as bearing the divine image.

For it is expressly stated (Genesis 1:27; Genesis 5:1f.) that the human being whom God fashioned in His own image was not an individual of one masculine sex alone, but male and female.

Indeed, the passages in Colossians 3:10 and Ephesians 4:24, where mention is made of the image of God κατ᾽ ἐξοχήν (par excellence) so called, to which human beings must be renewed or which they must recover, speak not of males only but also of females. And the matter itself teaches that the woman stood in need of the perfections of the soul, that is, of original righteousness, no less than the man, for rightly exercising the acts natural to her.

In regard to the knowledge of natural things, Eve seems to have been inferior to Adam. And it is commonly taught that Satan preferred to attack Eve as the weaker one in temptation, to which end is adduced the statement that Adam was not deceived, but Eve (1 Timothy 2:14). Nor was equal dominion granted to both, since the man was also the head of the woman, and she was subject to him (1 Corinthians 11:7). The immortal body, however, and whatever else pertains to the essence of a human being, the woman possessed no less than the man.

### 15 The subject "in which" of the divine image specially so called were the…

The subject "in which" of the divine image specially so called were the faculties of the human soul: the intellect, the will, and the sensitive appetite.

Notes. That is, the parts of man according to which he bore the divine image.

As has been discussed above (§7, 8, 9).

### 16 The end of the divine image specially and principally so called is the holy…

The end of the divine image specially and principally so called is the holy life of human beings, pleasing to God, and the consequent eternal blessedness. The end of the divine image taken in its general sense is the glory of God's wisdom, power, and goodness.

## 7 On the Providence of God

### 1 The most manifest proof of divine goodness after creation is divine providence

The most manifest proof of divine goodness after creation is divine providence.

### 2 The word "providence," derived from "to provide," by its native force seems to…

The word "providence," derived from "to provide," by its native force seems to denote a foreknowledge or foresight of future things before they occur. However, in common usage, and especially in this context, "to provide" means the same as "to take care for the welfare of creatures". And divine providence denotes not only an act of the intellect by which God knows how to arrange and bestow those things that are conducive to preserving created things in their being and guiding them to their ends, but also an act of the will by which, in accordance with that knowledge of His, He wills and decrees to preserve and govern creatures.

Notes. For the preposition "pro," as frequently elsewhere, so also in composition with the verb "to see," is known to signify the same as "before" or "in advance"; thus Cicero in his speech for Murena uses "to foresee the future," and Caesar pairs "to provide" with "to foresee".

For one who merely sees the future in some manner is not called "provident," but rather one who, having taken account of present circumstances and of future events foreseen to occur, takes care for his own needs or those of others; and when we consider divine providence, the word has reference to things other than God, that is, to things distinct from Him and created, for whose care God is responsible and whose benefit He promotes.

Opinions do indeed vary on this point, inasmuch as some contend that the name "providence" signifies not so much the immanent acts of the divine mind and will as the external acts themselves of preserving and governing. Others teach that an immanent act is indeed denoted by this name, but believe it pertains formally to the intellect and consequently to the will; still others hold the reverse. Yet this entire controversy is easily recognized as being about words rather than about the substance of the matter. For all concede that providence, considered in its full breadth, encompasses both πρόγνωσιν (foreknowledge), that is, the act of the intellect by which God foreknows what is conducive to creatures; and πρόθεσιν (purpose), that is, the act of the will by which He wills to ordain and arrange those things He has foreseen to be conducive; and finally διοίκησιν (administration), that is, the actual preservation and governance of creatures. Meanwhile, if we attend to the proper force of the terms, providence seems to denote not so much the external acts, as if belonging to an executive power, but rather the very care for creatures in God, and thus acts of the intellect and will from which those external acts proceed. And the order of those internal acts is such that the act of the intellect precedes, followed by the act of the will, that is, the purpose of bestowing, in accordance with the dictate of the intellect, whatever benefits creatures; although this act of the will does not so much follow upon providence itself as, together with the prior act of the intellect, intrinsically constitutes it. If, however, we consider common usage, it must be acknowledged that the name "providence" is not infrequently ascribed, by a well-established metonymy, to the acts of preservation and governance, which are the effects, signs, and marks of providence.

### 3 That divine providence exists

That divine providence exists, besides being evident from the light of nature, is most clear from Scripture.

Notes. For once the existence of God is granted, along with the dependence of creatures upon a God who is wise, powerful, and good, providence cannot be denied.

For not only is the whole of Scripture, communicated to humanity for their salvation by the provident hand of God, an effect and indication of providence, but especially Psalm 104 in its entirety and Matthew 6:26 and following declare it.

### 4 The efficient cause of providence is the entire Holy…

The efficient cause of providence is the entire Holy Trinity

Notes. That is, the cause in a virtual sense; although if you take the word "providence" to mean the external acts themselves, a formally efficient cause must indeed be admitted.

Just as of the other immanent acts and all external works. See specifically concerning the Father, as the one who provides for creatures, Matthew 6:26 and 32, where our heavenly Father is said to care for the birds and for human beings. Concerning the Son, it is taught in Hebrews 1:3 that He upholds all things. Concerning the Father and the Son together, the saying of Christ in John 5:17 applies: "My Father is working until now, and I am working." Concerning the Holy Spirit, it is said in 1 Corinthians 12:11 that He distributes spiritual gifts for the preservation and governance of the Church.

### 5 The impulsive cause of providence is the goodness of God

The impulsive cause of providence is the goodness of God.

Notes. That is, the reason for acting, and an internal one at that.

See Luke 11:13, where Christ, from the fact that in human affairs fathers provide for their children, moved by the love with which they cherish their offspring, concludes that much more does the heavenly Father, out of His supreme goodness and love for humanity, provide for our affairs. And David in Psalm 136, occupied with celebrating the works of divine providence, continually interjects: "For the Lord is good, and His mercy endures forever."

### 6 The object of divine providence is all creatures

The object of divine providence is all creatures, each and every one, both inanimate and animate, and among the animate, both plants, brute animals, and human beings

Notes. That is, the object for which God provides, whose care He undertakes, and whose advantage He promotes.

Thus in Hebrews 1:3 the Son of God is said to uphold all things, as having been created through Him; and in Colossians 1:17 it is taught that all things hold together through Him.

Regarding inanimate things, this pertains to what Job in chapter 28, verse 25, declares: that God gives weight to the winds, measures out the waters, sets a law for the rain, and appoints a way for the thunderstorm.

Regarding plants, for example, David in Psalm 104:14, 15, and 16 mentions that God causes grass, grain, oil, and wine to be produced from the earth.

Regarding brute animals, for example, God is said to give food to the beasts and to the young ravens in Psalm 147:9, to feed the birds of the air in Matthew 6:26, and to care for each individual sparrow in Matthew 10:29 and Luke 12:6.

Regarding human beings, in Acts 17:28 we are said to live, move, and have our being in God.

### 7 With respect to human beings in particular

With respect to human beings in particular, providence is so engaged that it extends to the origin of their life, its progress, and its end, as well as to all their actions.

Notes. Concerning their origin, Job in chapter 10, verses 8 and following, addressing God, says: "Your hands," using the Hebrew ינִ וּבצְּ עִ (fashioned me), "with the utmost diligence, care, and as it were anxiety, wrought me and made me with precision on every side; as clay You made me," and so forth. And David in Psalm 71:6 says to God: "Upon You I have leaned from the womb; You are He who drew me from my mother's bowels."

Concerning the progress of life, for example, with respect to supplying food, clothing, and other necessities of this life, see Matthew 6:25 and following; with respect to warding off dangers encountered in any affairs, see Psalm 91:1 and following, and compare Deuteronomy 30:20 and Job 10:12.

Concerning the end of life, that is, with respect to the determined time or number of days and months of this life, see Job 14:5.

Concerning actions, both secret thoughts, and speech, and outward deeds, and dealings with others, see Psalm 139:1 and following.

### 8 The acts to which providence is directed

The acts to which providence is directed, as exercised toward creatures, are the preservation or sustaining of each creature in existence, and governance. Governance involves partly a universal concurrence with secondary causes, and partly a special and manifold operation and direction of created agents.

Notes. See Section II above and its notes.

Preservation is what is otherwise called a continuation of creation, for it involves an unceasing influx suited and necessary to each created thing according to its own nature, so that it may persist in its being and in its power to act. And to this belong those expressions:

φέρων τὰ πάντα (bearing or carrying all things), lest they collapse, perish, or be reduced to nothing (Hebrews 1:3), and πάντα αὐτῷ συνέστηκε (all things hold together in Him) (Colossians 1:17). As Theophylact says: "Not only did He create these things, but He also sustains them, so that if they were withdrawn from His providence, they would necessarily perish at once."

Regarding universal concurrence, in Acts 17:25 and 26, God is said to give to all life and breath in all things, and from one blood (by concurring with those who generate) to have made every race of humankind.

Regarding special governance, for example, secondary causes not yet constituted in act by nature are divinely applied to action, as in 1 Kings 18:44 concerning the hastening of rain. Sometimes God confers upon secondary causes a power of acting that is either entirely supernatural, or else restores and strengthens a natural power that had been lost or weakened, as in Judges 16:28 and 29 concerning the restoration and increase of Samson's strength, and in Genesis 17:16, 17, and 19 concerning the power of procreation bestowed upon Abraham at one hundred years of age and upon Sarah at ninety, who had previously been barren. Finally, God sometimes prevents secondary causes that would naturally be constituted in act from producing their effect, as in Deuteronomy 28:23, where He threatens to withhold rain from a disobedient people. For by such works God makes it manifest that He is not bound to physical causes and the order freely established by Himself, as Blessed Gerhard states (Gerhard, Theological Commonplaces, disputation 16, ch. 5, on providence, paragraph 12, p. 654).

### 9 Divine providence also has its degrees

Divine providence also has its degrees, and although it extends to all creatures, it especially regards human beings, and within the human race, the company of the faithful, that is, the Church.

Hence arises the division of divine providence into universal and particular, or general and special, to which some add a most special or singular providence, which Gerhard, however, judges can be reduced to special providence (Gerhard, Theological Commonplaces, on providence).

God has subjected the remaining creatures to human beings and created them for their sake (see the chapter on creation, Section 23, p. 236).

As it is said in Romans 8:28, for those who love God all things work together, πάντα συνεργεῖν εἰς ἀγαθόν (all things cooperate for good).

### 10 With regard to the origin of a human being

With regard to the origin of a human being, it appears that God concurs in producing a human being not only by a general influx but also by a special one.

Note. As Blessed Gerhard writes (Gerhard, On Providence, ch. 8, paragraph 71, p. 67): the entrance into human life is governed peculiarly by divine providence. And for this reason it is rightly maintained that God bears the character not only of a universal cause but also of a particular one, and supplies the deficiency of secondary causes, or at least directs and governs them in their action.

Some explain this in such a way that, partly in view of the variety of bodily members and their wonderful connection and structure, a particular efficient cause acting with knowledge is required; and thus they maintain that some power other than what resides in the seed (commonly called δύναμις πλαστική, the formative power), indeed a higher power that can only be conceived as belonging to God Himself, concurs by a special influx. Partly also, considering the immateriality of the soul and the fact that it must therefore be produced independently of a subject, that is, from nothing, and that such production demands an infinite power of acting and thus belongs to God alone, they infer from this that God provides a special and determinate influx for the production of the human soul.

Others, however, even though they believe that the body as well as the human soul is produced by the parents themselves as secondary causes with the concurrence of God as universal cause, nevertheless, since they recognize in the production and birth of a human being various hazards, dangers to be averted, and many singular evidences of God's particular care and favor, attribute to God a special or particular concurrence in addition to the universal one, and refer to this the passage in Job 10:8, 9, 10, and 11.

### 11 Among human actions to which God concurs

Among human actions to which God concurs, those that are good must be distinguished from those that are evil; and within the category of good actions, those that are civilly good must be distinguished from those that are spiritually good.

Notes. Otherwise called natural, insofar as they can be performed by human beings through the powers of nature.

Called by another name supernatural, because they exceed the natural powers of human beings and cannot be accomplished through them, but require higher powers to be conferred by God.

### 12 Divine providence regards civilly good actions not only with respect to…

Divine providence regards civilly good actions not only with respect to imparting a general concurrence, but also with respect to commanding them, assisting them, and approving them. It relates to spiritually good actions in the same manner, but in addition God Himself concurs with them by a particular influx.

Notes. Regarding the commanding of civilly good actions, the work of the law is written in the hearts of human beings, whence the Gentiles do by nature the things of the law (Romans 2:15).

Regarding assistance, for example, by adding courage or exciting heroic impulses, as God is said to have called King Cyrus and to have grasped his right hand (Isaiah 45:1, 3).

Regarding approval, it especially pertains that God also rewards such actions, as is evident from the example of the Egyptian midwives, to whom God is said to have done good and to have built houses, after they had assisted the Israelite women in childbirth and their offspring (Exodus 1:20, 21).

Regarding the special influx for spiritually good actions, we are otherwise not competent of ourselves, as of ourselves, to think anything of this kind, much less to do it (2 Corinthians 3:5).

### 13 Divine providence is directed toward evil actions in such a way that

Divine providence is directed toward evil actions in such a way that, when they occur, a general concurrence is indeed imparted to them. However, many actions that would otherwise have occurred are prevented, and those that are permitted to happen are nevertheless so directed that they tend toward a good end.

Notes. For in Him we move, whatever we do; Acts 17:28; but at the same time it is clear that evil actions are considered in this respect only as actions, not as evil.

Thus God prevented the adultery of Abimelech with Sarah from being completed (Genesis 20:6). And in Psalm 33:10 the Lord is said to frustrate the counsel of the nations and to bring to nothing the thoughts of the peoples.

God, by permitting the sins of those who seem to excel above others, admonishes the sinners themselves of their weakness, lest they be too pleased with themselves and despise others; to this pertains the fall of Peter (Luke 22:32). Sometimes He intends to correct others through the losses of sinners and, having dispelled their complacency, to make them more attentive (Luke 17:32).

When He permits the pious to be afflicted by the wicked, He exercises the humility and patience of the afflicted, as in the example of Job, chapter 1 (compare James 5:10, 11). Sometimes He turns the affliction of the pious into an occasion of better fortune and desires that even the afflicters themselves be helped and amended through their efforts, as Joseph testifies by his own example (Genesis 50:20).

### 14 In neither case

In neither case, however, whether in good actions or in evil ones, does the providence of God abolish the freedom of the human will.

Note. For general concurrence does not determine secondary causes or impose a necessity of acting. Likewise, to permit or not to prevent an action, and to direct one that is permitted toward a certain end, is not to determine the agent to perform this action. Moreover, that spiritual actions are so wrought in a human being by God that the person can nevertheless resist God and cause them not to take place, we read expressly affirmed by Christ and shown by the example of the Israelites (Matthew 23:37; compare Acts 7:51).

### 15 Divine providence regards the end of human life not only insofar as

Divine providence regards the end of human life not only insofar as, by the common law, each person is endowed with his own constitution, by virtue of which he can reach a certain span of life with God's general concurrence. But providence also regards the end of life insofar as the life of certain persons is prolonged beyond the term to which they would have arrived by the powers of nature, and insofar as for others the end of life comes sooner than it ought to have according to the course of nature.

Notes. Namely after the fall, since originally the human being in the primeval state was immortal, as we saw in the preceding chapter.

This is otherwise called the natural term of life, concerning which Blessed Hunnius writes: "God leads a human being to the goal of human life for the most part through the mediation of nature. For when the radical moisture fails, along with the innate heat, when the κρᾶσις, the constitution, of the human body is disturbed and its powers are overthrown, the human being comes to die. God, however, concurs in establishing this term not only by reason of His foreknowledge, but because He Himself sustains and governs nature and the secondary causes. And thus through these means God, as the first cause, appoints the term of which we speak"; Hunnius, Questions and Responses on Providence, vol. 1, of his works, folio 714). And to this is usually referred what is said in Psalm 90:10: "The days of our years in them are seventy years; if by reason of strength" (if the power of nature prevails, according to Kimchi; or according to others, if the number of years increases) "they are eighty years.".

A manifest example is provided by the history of Hezekiah, 2 Kings 20:1 and following.

Thus men of blood and deceit are said not to live out even half their days, Psalm 55:23; and in Psalm 102:24, David prays to his God not to cut him off in the midst of his days.

### 16 Divine providence alters the natural term of human life with respect to both…

Divine providence alters the natural term of human life with respect to both pious persons and impious ones.

Notes. Hence arises the hyperphysical, or as some call it divine, term of life (see Gerhard, Theological Commonplaces, on providence, ch. 6, disputation 16, paragraph 23, p. 667).

The term applied to the pious is called the term of grace.

While the term applied to the wicked is called the term of wrath.

### 17 God prolongs the life of the pious either as a reward for their obedience

God prolongs the life of the pious either as a reward for their obedience, or on account of the public good. He shortens their life partly lest they be corrupted by the wicked examples of others, and partly lest they see coming calamities and be distressed.

Notes. To this pertains the promise of the fourth commandment, Exodus 20:12; compare Proverbs 3:1 and 4:10.

Which is inferred to have happened to Paul from 2 Corinthians 1:8 and following, and to Epaphroditus from Philippians 2:27, 30.

As the author of the Book of Wisdom teaches, Wisdom 4:10, 11.

As the example of Josiah testifies, 2 Chronicles 34:28; compare Isaiah 26:20 and 57:1.

### 18 God by His just judgment cuts short the life of the wicked sooner

God by His just judgment cuts short the life of the wicked sooner, either when He Himself inflicts a lethal disease or death upon them, or when He commands death to be inflicted, or when He allows them to bring diseases or violent death upon themselves either through intemperance, or through other crimes.

Notes. For example, when pestilence is sent, or as Scripture says, when God strikes people so that they die; compare the divine threat in Deuteronomy 28:21 and 22, and the examples of Er, Onan, and Nabal, Genesis 38:7 and 10, 1 Samuel 25:38.

For example, upon murderers, Genesis 9:6, Exodus 20:12 and 14 and following; upon sorcerers, Sodomites, idolaters, and those guilty of incest, Exodus 22:18 and following, Leviticus 18 and 20.

See the example of Ben-Hadad, 2 Kings 8:15, although daily experience abounds with such cases; compare Hunnius in the same place, p. 715.

Here are referred the fates of Absalom, 2 Samuel 18:14, and of Ahithophel, 2 Samuel 17:23. And this last term of life God is said not so much to have positively established, and to have Himself ordained the means by which it is reached, as rather not to have prevented it, or to have permitted it.

### 19 And thus it is also established that it is not absolutely necessary

And thus it is also established that it is not absolutely necessary, that each person die at the time of death at which he or she does die.

Notes. That is, it has not been decreed by God absolutely and immutably, without any and prior to all regard for causes and circumstances to be found outside of God; for otherwise the prayers and vows of the pious, and the promises and threats of God, would be in vain; compare Hunnius in the same place, p. 713. And Blessed Gerhard writes in his Introductory Disputations (Gerhard, Theological Commonplaces, on providence, p. 667): "The hyperphysical or divine term is always hypothetical, including the condition of piety or impiety or contempt of the means of preservation.".

Meanwhile, we are not permitted to investigate too curiously the reason that divine providence regards concerning the term of life of individual persons, according to that saying in John 21:22, where Christ says to Peter, who was anxious about the term of John's life: "If I wish him to remain until I come, what is that to you?".

### 20 The proximate end of divine providence is the benefit of human beings

The proximate end of divine providence is the benefit of human beings, especially of the pious. The ultimate end is the glory of God's wisdom, power, and above all His goodness.

Notes. Thus in Psalm 33:18 and 19 the eye of the Lord is said to be upon those who fear Him and who hope in His mercy, to deliver their souls from death and to keep them alive in famine. And in Romans 8:28, for those who love God all things work together, συνεργεῖ (cooperate), for good (compare what we have said concerning the end of creation).

Let Psalms 104 and 136 be consulted in their entirety. And God always attains this end, even though human beings sometimes by their own fault bring it about that the benefit God intends does not redound to them.

### 21 Divine providence may be defined as the benign purpose of the divine will

Divine providence may be defined as the benign purpose of the divine will, directed by the practical knowledge of God, concerning the preservation and governance of all creatures, especially human beings, and among human beings the faithful, for the benefit of human beings themselves and for the glory of God's wisdom, power, and goodness.

## 8 On Eternal Beatitude

### 1 Since it has been established that God is our highest Good and the objective…

Since it has been established that God is our highest Good and the objective end of theology, we must now proceed to examine from the Scriptures that operation by which we fully and perfectly possess and enjoy God as the highest Good, as our ultimate formal end.

Notes. See above, Prolegomena, ch. 1, §4, p. 9, and §16ff., p. 31.

Our beatitude consists in the most perfect vital operation, which derives its perfection partly from the perfection of the object and partly from the perfection of the mode by which the object is attained.

This is the end which, once obtained, completely satisfies our appetite.

And although a human being in the present state, by the guidance of natural light, can know that after this life there will be another, and that in it things will go well for the good, since God will reward their benefactions, and that the beatitude of souls will consist in the knowledge of God, nevertheless a more distinct understanding of that beatitude and of the clear knowledge of God cannot be attained by the guidance of natural light alone, but must be learned from divine revelation (compare Musaeus, Introduction, ch. 2, §9, no. 9, pp. 38-39).

### 2 Now, a human being possesses God as the highest Good through this

Now, a human being possesses God as the highest Good through this: that God is rendered intimately present to the intellect by a most perfect act of knowing, occupied with God. This is commonly called the beatific vision.

Note. That is, the clear and intuitive knowledge of God. It is called "vision" by a metaphorical expression, because by it we shall know God as distinctly and clearly as we know a thing that we see with our eyes. It is called "beatific" because it is the formal reason by which we are constituted blessed. To this pertains what is said in Matthew 5:8: "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God." Concerning these words, Gerhard writes in his commentary (Gerhard, Commentary, p. 259): "Most interpreters," he says, "understand this of the beatific vision of God in eternal life." And he adds: "They shall see God, that is, they shall dwell with God in eternal life and shall perfectly know Him." Compare also 1 Corinthians 13:12, 1 John 3:2, and Hebrews 12:14.

Indeed, in Matthew 5 an intellectual or spiritual vision of God is manifestly indicated, corresponding to the spiritual purity of heart. And thus also the passage in Hebrews 12:14 is understood. As for what is said in 1 Corinthians 13:12, namely that those things which we now see through a mirror in an enigma we shall one day, once the imperfection of this life has been abolished, see face to face, Balduin also explains this in his Analysis or Exposition as referring to a more exact knowledge by which we shall know God intimately and perfectly. For the phrase "face to face" is a Hebraism, since God does not otherwise have a face. And those things which Paul has hitherto taught through similitudes he now sets forth more clearly, as the summary of the whole matter, when he says: "Now I know in part, but then I shall know even as I also am known."

Compare the paraphrase of this passage, and Questions 2 and 3, as well as Aphorism 8.

The matter itself shows that within the genus of intellectual vision, opposite members are exhibited for the state of this life and of the life to come. As for what is said in 1 John 3:2, "Beloved, now we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be; but we know that when He appears, we shall be like Him, because we shall see Him as He is," this was long ago expounded by Hunnius in his Commentary as referring to the knowledge of God, whose children we are, and indeed a perfect knowledge, as great as can belong to a creature, which is to be expected in the age to come. On these and other passages compare Chytraeus (On Death and Eternal Life, part 1, pp. 172ff.).

### 3 For a better understanding of this operation of the intellect

For a better understanding of this operation of the intellect, a comparison must be drawn between the knowledge we have of God in this life, and that which is to be expected after this life. In this life we can form only inadequate concepts of God through intelligible species drawn from created things and from the revealed Word. After this life, however, we shall know God and all things that are formally in Him by a single and simple act, without any intelligible species.

Notes. As Scripture itself leads us in 1 Corinthians 13:12, comparing what happens to us νῦν καὶ τότε (now and then) with respect to the knowledge of God and divine things.

This is commonly called abstractive knowledge, and is otherwise described as the knowledge either of an object not actually existing (which description does not apply here, since God always and necessarily exists) or of an object that does exist but is not known through a proper species, nor immediately and through its own substance conjoined with the intellect (compare Musaeus, On Eternal Beatitude, §19, pp. 8- 9).

As we said above, ch. 1, §6, note (b), p. 172, that in this life we do not have a proper and adequate quidditative knowledge of the divine essence grasped and understood.

The divine essence, persons, and attributes will be known, but the free decrees of God, which are directed toward things outside God to occur in time, and the perfections of creatures, are not equally attained by the blessed by virtue of that knowledge. To this pertains what is said in Matthew 24:36 and Mark 13:32, that the angels, though blessed, are said to be ignorant of the day of the last judgment. And concerning Abraham and Israel, though blessed and clearly seeing God, Isaiah says (Isaiah 63:16): "He does not know us, he is ignorant of us." Nevertheless, it is not denied that the blessed can know certain things from a special manifestation of God that they do not know by virtue of the beatific vision of God, as we shall say in §6 and its notes.

This is commonly called intuitive knowledge, and is usually described as knowledge not merely of an actually existing object, but of one that is moreover conjoined with and present to the intellect either through a proper species or immediately through its own substance. It is the latter description that applies in this case. Scripture in 1 Corinthians 13 calls it the vision "face to face," and in 1 John 3:2 the vision "of God as He is." The term "comprehensive knowledge" is also well known, from which the blessed are also called "comprehensors." This must not, however, be understood as though the intellects of the blessed will comprehend God in the same manner as God comprehends Himself, but only that nothing of those things that are formally in God will be hidden from the glorified intellect (compare Augustine, Epistle 112, ch. 9).

### 4 Therefore, for this knowledge or beatific vision of God

Therefore, for this knowledge or beatific vision of God, it is necessary that there concur, besides the human intellect, also the light of glory and the divine essence and persons themselves with their perfections.

Notes. The intellect is required because that vision is a vital act formally pertaining to the intellect.

The light of glory is required because otherwise our intellect is not proportioned and suited to know God perfectly, inasmuch as all our natural knowledge depends in some way upon the senses. The light of glory is, as to its substance, a certain spiritual habit supernaturally infused into the intellect, elevating it beyond its natural powers to know God clearly in Himself, and determining it in place of an impressed species to elicit the act of intuitive knowledge. It is called "light" because it accomplishes for the intellect, as the eye of the mind, what light in the proper sense, for instance that of the sun, accomplishes for the bodily eye by illuminating the air and lighting up colors, enabling the eye to see and know the species received from them. It is called the light "of glory" because it comes to our intellect for beholding God, who is our Glory, in the state of glory or of the future life, according to 1 Corinthians 15:40, and makes us glorious.

The divine essence and persons are required inasmuch as that knowledge is not of just any object, but of God, and indeed is a clear knowledge of God (compare Musaeus, On Eternal Beatitude, §32, pp. 17-18).

### 5 This same beatific vision is not a free act but a necessary one

This same beatific vision is not a free act but a necessary one, both as to the exercise and as to the species of the act, and therefore the blessed will never cease from it, nor will they be able to cease.

Notes. For while the acts of faith that depend on the light of grace are freely elicited, so that they can also not be elicited, and the intellect, being negligent in its duty, can form another concept about spiritual objects, the case is different in glory.

The intellect, since it is not a free power but a necessary one, once all the prerequisites for acting are in place (on which see §4), cannot fail to act. The will, moreover, cannot divert the intellect from the exercise of that act, because it can neither remove the influx of the light of glory nor impede the conjunction of the divine essence with the intellect. Nor does the will wish to divert the intellect from the contemplation of that object which is the highest Good, perfectly represented to it by the intellect.

### 6 Although the beatific vision is occupied solely with contemplating God and…

Although the beatific vision is occupied solely with contemplating God and those things that are formally in Him, nevertheless in that state the blessed will also possess knowledge of other things, so that each one will perfectly and clearly know his own condition or felicity, as well as his companions in beatitude.

Notes. For it is the vision of God, not of other objects.

See Matthew 17:1 and 3, where the Apostles, having only a foretaste of eternal life, recognized Moses and Elijah; compare Chytraeus, On Death and Eternal Life, part 1, pp. 65ff.; Hunnius, Marburg Disputations, vol. 1, disp. 43, p. 543; Hutter, Compendium, locus 34, question 5; Gerhard, vol. 8, last locus, §147, p. 1002.

This knowledge will come through proper species, whether infused or acquired, and likewise through the power of the light of glory, which perfects the intellect and supplies its natural deficiency, so that it can penetrate more intimately the nature not of one object only but of many (compare Musaeus, On Eternal Beatitude, §42, p. 25.

And thus also the intellect of the blessed will be able to know the free decrees of God, not through the beatific vision itself, but by means of a special revelation, should God will to communicate one to them, the light of glory at the same time rendering the intellect capable of giving assent without any hesitation (see Musaeus, On Eternal Beatitude, §41ff.).

### 7 Meanwhile, that vision of God is truly beatific

Meanwhile, that vision of God is truly beatific, and just as it makes a human being a participant of the highest Good, so it leads him into that condition of being made as similar to God as possible.

Note. So it is expressly said in 1 John 3:2. And to this pertains that participation in the divine nature of which Peter speaks in 2 Peter 1:4, which is in some manner begun in this life and perfected in the next (compare Gerhard, Commentary on this passage, p. 39).

### 8 Furthermore, the same vision of God

Furthermore, the same vision of God, although it formally pertains to the intellect, necessarily draws the will of the blessed person to the most intense love of God. And thus it comes about that a human being enjoys God as the highest Good.

Notes. For by the very fact that the highest and infinite Good is clearly known, there is no place in the intellect for either indifference of knowledge (see the note to §5) or comparative knowledge, as some say, that is, such knowledge by which other goods might be known as more excellent than this Good, or as preferable and more desirable than it. Moreover, Scripture most closely connects the knowledge of God with love of Him, as we read in 1 John 4:7-8: "Everyone who loves is born of God and knows God. He who does not love does not know God, because God is love." Therefore the more perfectly the blessed know God, the more they love Him. And Paul says that love will never fail, that is, it will have a place not only in this life but also in the next, and in this respect is more excellent than faith (1 Corinthians 13:8).
