The principal object of love is God (compare Chytraeus, On Death and Eternal Life, pp. 173-174, where he also refers to the fact that, according to the most common usage in Sacred Scripture, the words "knowledge" or "sense" embrace not merely bare recognition or apprehension of an object in the mind or sense, but also genuine affections in the will and heart, and effects or actions following from that knowledge and vision).

To enjoy a good is nothing other than to cling to it with love for its own sake, as Augustine says (Augustine, On Christian Doctrine, book 1, ch. 3, §9).

### 9 Therefore also the will

Therefore also the will, perfectly determined to the love of God, will not be able to fall away from God and to sin.

Note. This is the ἀναμαρτησία (sinlessness) that is commonly ascribed to the blessed. And to this pertains what is said of the Church as ἔνδοξος (glorious) or triumphant, that it has neither spot nor wrinkle (Ephesians 5:27), which is most rightly understood of inherent and most perfect holiness.

### 10 Although through that determination of the will to embrace the highest Good constantly

Although through that determination of the will to embrace the highest Good constantly, freedom or indifference toward good and evil is removed, nevertheless some true freedom will still have a place, since with respect to many goods that are finite and particular, the blessed will be able to act or not act, to do this or to undertake doing something else.

Notes. This removal of indifference toward evil is not an imperfection absolutely speaking, but only in comparison with a power that is determined solely toward evil and cannot do good.

The highest and infinite Good cannot be indifferently desired or loved by the blessed, as was said at §8.

Among particular goods, however, comparative knowledge does have a place. Meanwhile, it is certain that whatever the blessed do with respect to diverse particular goods, they refer it all precisely to the glory of God. And such freedom is freedom in the truest sense and is a perfection absolutely speaking; therefore it also belongs to the angels (see above, ch. 3, §35), and indeed to God Himself in His own manner.

### 11 Finally, from the vision of God there arises pleasure or ineffable joy

Finally, from the vision of God there arises pleasure or ineffable joy, with which human beings are affected as they behold and love God.

Notes. This arises as something ἐπιγινόμενόν τι τέλος (a supervenient end), or an end that supervenes and accrues of its own accord, as Aristotle elsewhere speaks when he teaches that from every perfect operation there arises delight or pleasure (Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, book 10, ch. 4).

By its power the mind of the blessed peacefully rests in the possession and enjoyment of the present Good. See Isaiah 35:10, where, under the figure of those returning from the Babylonian captivity, the joy of the blessed is vividly described: "The redeemed of the Lord shall return and come to Zion with jubilation, and everlasting joy shall be upon their heads; they shall obtain gladness and joy, and sorrow and sighing shall flee away." Christ calls it the joy of the heart (John 16:22) and the joy of the Lord (Matthew 25:21). Compare Chytraeus (On Death and Eternal Life, pp. 207ff.).

### 12 Moreover, that beatific vision

Moreover, that beatific vision, together with the love and joy arising from it, will be equally perfect in all the blessed.

Notes. For not only does Scripture make no distinction here that would obtain among different subjects (see the passages cited, 1 John 3:2 and 1 Corinthians 13:12), but the matter itself shows that when God is seen as He is, that knowledge cannot be intensified or diminished while still remaining clear and intuitive. And if the vision is the same in all, the love and joy arising from it will likewise be equal.

It is clear, however, that we are speaking of the perfection of knowledge considered intensively. For we do not deny that extensively, not indeed the beatific vision of God itself, but nonetheless the knowledge of other objects, can be greater or lesser among the blessed (see the preceding §6).

### 13 Besides those things that pertain to the essence of beatitude

Besides those things that pertain to the essence of beatitude, and which furthermore formally consist in the soul, it pleases God also to add other gifts by which the bodies of the blessed may be most greatly perfected and blessed.

Notes. The first concept of beatitude, prior to which no other is given (inasmuch as it entails the attainment and possession of the highest Good, and is to be sought for its own sake, and primarily belongs to an intelligent nature), consists in the very vision of God conjoined with perfect love.

In addition, the knowledge of other objects, by which the intellect is perfected, also pertains here (on which see §6 and notes).

Furthermore, just as beatitude is otherwise described as a state perfect through the aggregation of all goods, when such a state is to be given to a human being, all the faculties of the soul and the body itself must be perfected.

### 14 The beatitude of the bodies of the blessed will consist primarily in this

The beatitude of the bodies of the blessed will consist primarily in this: that the bodies will be spiritual, that is, subject to the soul, which is a spirit, in the most perfect manner, partly as an informing form, partly as a moving principle.

Notes. (1 Corinthians 15:44) This is not to be understood as a change of the body into a spirit that is essentially immaterial.

The subjection to the soul as informing form constitutes the subtlety of the bodies, by virtue of which the bodies will so subsist under their souls without imperfection, as if they themselves were spirits; and thus they will also be able to penetrate other solid bodies (see Philippians 3:21, compared with John 20:19 and 26, and also Luke 24:37 and 39). The proof is this: if Christ, with His glorified body, penetrated through doors that were truly closed at the time and could be seen as substantially present, and if our bodies in the state of the future life will be conformed to the glorious body of Christ, it follows that our bodies likewise will be so subtle as to be able to penetrate another solid body without any new change of themselves or injury to themselves or to the body penetrated. The first premise is proved partly from the cited passages of John and Luke, and partly from Philippians 3; and the second premise is also true (compare the Detailed Explanation, locus 6, question 21, pp. 175- 176).

The subjection to the soul as a moving principle constitutes the agility of the bodies, by virtue of which the bodies will be able to move most easily and swiftly wherever they please (see 1 Corinthians 15:43, where it is said that the bodies of the pious, which are sown in weakness, shall rise in power, ἐν δυνάμει (in power), because, whereas in this life the human body is heavy, slow, sluggish, and inert, in the resurrection it will receive a special δύναμιν (power) and agility, so that it can move most swiftly). Compare the Detailed Explanation at the same passage, p. 176. To this same power of the bodies of the blessed is referred what is said in 1 Thessalonians 4:17, that the faithful will be caught up to meet the Lord in the air.

### 15 Therefore also the bodies of the blessed will be impassible

Therefore also the bodies of the blessed will be impassible, subject to no corrupting passion, whether proceeding from internal or external causes, and consequently they will be immortal.

Notes. This impassibility will perhaps come through that same supernatural quality by which they are rendered spiritual (see §14).

For example, they will be able to be harmed neither by heat nor by cold, and thus will have no need of garments to protect them against injuries of the air; they will not be afflicted by hunger and thirst, and accordingly will not need food or drink; they will be subject to no bodily distemper, nor to any internal and adverse disturbance of the mind (compare Revelation 7:16). To this is also customarily referred the ἰσαγγελότης (equality with angels) of the blessed, of which Matthew 22:30 speaks.

Incorruptibility and immortality, ἀφθαρσία καὶ ἀθανασία, are expressly attributed to the bodies of the blessed (1 Corinthians 15:42, 50, 52, 53, 54).

### 16 Nevertheless, the blessed will be able

Nevertheless, the blessed will be able, when they themselves wish, to present their bodies to be touched and seen.

Note. Just as Christ presented His glorious body to His disciples to be seen and touched whenever He wished (see John 20:20 and 27; Luke 24:39; compare Philippians 3:21).

### 17 There will also be added to the bodies of the blessed a great clarity or splendor

There will also be added to the bodies of the blessed a great clarity or splendor.

Note. So that they will shine like the sun (Matthew 13:43; compare 1 Corinthians 15:41ff.; Daniel 12:3). And from this is also gathered an elegant proportion and beauty of the bodies of the blessed in all their individual parts.

### 18 And because the soul

And because the soul, insofar as it is sensitive, uses certain parts of the body as organs, the beatitude of the pious will be augmented in this respect as well, so that the eyes may delight themselves by beholding the incarnate Son of God, their Savior, and the blessed. And perhaps also the ears may delight themselves with most elegant hymns.

Notes. Thus Job hoped that he would see his Redeemer with his own eyes, Job 19:25-26). That the blessed will see the divine essence itself with the clarified eyes of the body, we do not dare to affirm. For not only does God, who is an infinite Spirit, not fall among the proper objects of sight as a corporeal power, with respect to His essence and persons, but also, even if it could be shown that sight, considered as a creature of God, could be assumed through obediential potency as an instrument for producing a vision of God, nevertheless God has nowhere in the Scriptures promised that this will actually take place. The passages in Matthew 5, 1 Corinthians 13, 1 John 3, and Hebrews 12 speak of intellectual vision, as we have seen above. Balduin holds that the essence of God is invisible to the eyes of the body, however clarified (Balduin, Commentary on 1 Corinthians 13, part 3, question 4, p. 490). And lest you think this slipped from him, he repeats and shows it more extensively in his Commentary on Colossians 1 (part 2, question 2, pp. 1054-1055): that between the essence or face of God and the bodily eye there is absolutely no proportion. He also appeals to the agreement of the Fathers: Ambrose, Jerome, Gregory of Nazianzus, Augustine, and others. Again in his Commentary on 1 Timothy 6 (part 2, question 3, pp. 1383-1384), he says that the epithet by which God is called invisible is perpetual and will not cease even in the other life, and having repeated four arguments from the earlier passage on Colossians 1, he directs the reader to consult Chrysostom, Tertullian, Gregory of Nazianzus, Hilary, Basil, and Irenaeus, all of whom show at length that the nature of God cannot be attained by the eyes of the human body either in this life or in the future life. Whatever may be said about these matters, it is certain that the opinion which holds that the beatific vision will be only intellectual is probable, even if the opposite opinion is not therefore immediately rejected as false, which Gerhard also acknowledged (Gerhard, vol. 8, last locus, §144, p. 997). Compare the Detailed Explanation(locus 4, questions 20 and 22, pp. 172ff.) and Cundis (Notes on Hutter's Compendium, pp. 1385- 1386).

For that mutual recognition of the blessed, in the state of restored bodies, appears also to extend to the bodily sight of them; compare the authors cited there. (see §6 and note (b).

So it is gathered from Revelation 7:10 and 19:4. Concerning the further perfections and operations of the other senses in the state of eternal life, it is scarcely possible to determine anything definitive in this life.

### 19 According to these accidental gifts of beatitude

According to these accidental gifts of beatitude, especially the clarity of the bodies, a certain inequality among the blessed will be found, insofar as one person will have produced more specimens of Christian virtues than another in this life.

Notes. (See 1 Corinthians 15:41; Daniel 12:3). As for the inequality of other gifts, although it is not equally easy to determine anything, the passages in Matthew 19:28 and Luke 22:30 may be consulted, where a certain special honor and glory on the day of judgment is promised to the Apostles, described in the language of this age as a table furnished with every delight and a sitting as upon thrones.

We also read in Matthew 10:41-42 and Luke 19:17 and 19 of differing rewards. But these must not be understood as pertaining to the merit of works. For it is one thing for God, out of His generosity or unowed favor, to render unequal rewards to those who have labored unequally; it is quite another for God to render to those who have merited unequally a wage owed to each by virtue of meritorious works, and a diverse or unequal one to different persons.

### 20 And just as those things which we have said thus far concerning eternal…

And just as those things which we have said thus far concerning eternal beatitude are rightly held according to the Scriptures, so no one will have found in this life a full and perfect declaration of it.

Note. For it has not yet appeared what we shall be (1 John 3:2). And in Isaiah 64:4, and thence in 1 Corinthians 2:9, it is said that eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love Him.

## 9 On Eternal Damnation

### 1 Damnation is set over against blessedness

Damnation is set over against blessedness, partly in a privative sense, insofar as it entails the absence of all the goods that constitute the felicity of the blessed, and partly in a contrary sense, insofar as it denotes not merely the bare absence of blessedness but involves positive adversities and torments, together with the most acute sensation of evils.

Notes. And for this reason the doctrine of damnation is here appended to the doctrine of blessedness, so that opposites placed side by side may shine forth more clearly. It must also be acknowledged that those who are not easily moved by the goodness of the End of theology (being corrupted, as they are, by love of earthly things) can in the meantime be terrified by the consideration of the misery that otherwise awaits them. For there is no third possibility: those who do not attain the highest good will not escape the greatest evil. This is established from the force of those propositions in which the final destinies of all human beings are reduced to two classes (Daniel 12:2; John 5:28; Matthew 25:32, 33, and 46).

It is customarily observed in this connection that the state of the damned is called the "second death" (Revelation 2:11; 20:6). For death is the privation of life, and it is called "second" because it entails the privation of that other life which, upon the completion of this present life, we might have attained. Ecclesiastical writers call this the "penalty of loss."

Thus the same state is sometimes designated by the name of reproach or ignominy, and sometimes by the name of eternal fire. See the passages cited above from Daniel and Matthew. Otherwise it is called the "penalty of sense."

### 2 In the first place

In the first place, the damned will lack, on the part of the intellect, the beatific vision of God, nor will they be endowed with the light of glory that is divinely bestowed upon the blessed.

Notes. It is customarily referred to in this connection that the damned are said to be cast into darkness (Matthew 8:12; 22:13), as though expelled from the Lord, who is the light of minds, according to Prosper (Prosper of Aquitaine, On the Contemplative Life, book 3, ch. 12; cf. Gerhard, Theological Commonplaces, vol. 8, On Hell, §. 42, p. 590). They are also said to depart from Christ (Matthew 25:41) and to be left behind (Luke 17:34).

Indeed, they will also lack the light of grace, which they despised in this life, and they will be deprived of right judgment concerning divine matters and their own condition.

### 3 And thus it is also readily apparent that love of God as the highest good clearly known

And thus it is also readily apparent that love of God as the highest good clearly known, and the joy resulting therefrom, will be entirely absent from the damned.

### 4 The endowments of the blessed bodies

The endowments of the blessed bodies, by which they are glorified, will likewise be denied to the damned.

Notes. For although the bodies of the damned will be incorruptible, nevertheless that incorruptibility will not proceed from impassibility or spirituality as from an intrinsic perfection, nor will it redound to the glory of those bodies, but rather to the increase of their misery, as will be discussed below.

### 5 Among the positive punishments

Among the positive punishments, the first to present itself is that knowledge of the intellect by which the damned will know God abstractively and from their punishments: partly as the Lord of supreme majesty, but one whom they have most grievously offended; partly as a just judge, and by that very fact the most bitter avenger of their sins; and partly as a most benign Father, though not to themselves, but to others who believed and have been made blessed.

Notes. Thus in Revelation 6:17, the damned are described as recognizing the one seated upon the throne, that is, God possessed of supreme majesty, whose face, threatening the utmost, they cannot endure.

### 6 Similarly, they will contemplate themselves in such a way that they will…

Similarly, they will contemplate themselves in such a way that they will reflect in their minds upon the multitude and gravity of their sins, as well as the desert, bitterness, and perpetuity of the punishments with which they are afflicted.

Note. So at the beginning of Wisdom 5, the lament of the damned is set forth, in which they accuse their own folly and confess that they went astray from the way of truth, that they were filled with the paths of iniquity and perdition, and that they wandered through trackless deserts, meditating upon the vanity of pride, riches, and boasting.

### 7 They will behold other human beings who are blessed

They will behold other human beings who are blessed, as partakers of that felicity of which they themselves are destitute, and free from the calamities by which they themselves are oppressed.

Note. In the same chapter of Wisdom they are described as seeing the righteous standing with great confidence before them, and being astonished at the unexpected salvation of the righteous.

### 8 Therefore, on the part of the will

Therefore, on the part of the will, there will arise hatred of God, inasmuch as He is hostile and implacable toward them; hatred of themselves, since they have been the cause of their own misery; envy resulting from the sight of another's blessedness; grief, sorrow, and anguish on account of the immense mass of present evils; and perpetual impatience and despair.

Note. See Revelation 6:16, 17, where a great aversion to God is indicated, whose sight they cannot endure.

The accusation that the damned bring against themselves indicates displeasure and detestation of themselves (Wisdom 5:4, 6, 7).

Likewise, in that same passage, beginning at verse 3, they are said to speak of the blessed righteous one: "This is the one whom we once held as an object of mockery and as a common reproach. How has he been numbered among the children of God, and how is his lot among the saints?"

To this belongs the θλῖψις καὶ στενοχωρία (affliction and anguish) spoken of in Romans 2:9. Compare Wisdom 5:3, where they are said to groan on account of anguish of spirit.

They will seek and desire to die, that is, to cease to exist altogether, or to be utterly destroyed (Revelation 9:6).

### 9 By this very fact

By this very fact, moreover, the will of the damned, entirely turned away from God, will be determined toward evil, so that whatever they do displeases God, and they sin incessantly in thoughts, words, and deeds.

Note. For just as love of God above all things is the sum of the divine law, so the absence of divine love and perpetual hatred of God cannot but entail ἀνομία (lawlessness) and a perpetual discordance with the law in the faculties and operations of the damned.

### 10 The bodies of the damned will be tormented by hellfire that is real and properly so called

The bodies of the damned will be tormented by hellfire that is real and properly so called, and inextinguishable.

Notes. For it is certain from Matthew 10:28, where bodies are said to be destroyed in Gehenna, that they will indeed be truly punished (cf. Gerhard, Theological Commonplaces, On Hell, §. 83, pp. 683, 684).

See especially Matthew 25:41, where Christ the judge, about to pronounce sentence from the tribunal, is read as one day declaring this kind of punishment upon the damned. We believe that He spoke properly, not figuratively or obscurely. And it is otherwise most frequent in Scripture that the punishments of the damned are designated by the name of fire. From this it is also established that that fire will not be spiritual (for then it would not be fire properly so called) but material and corporeal. To wish to explain its nature more precisely, however, is a matter more of curiosity than of profit.

See Matthew 3:12; 25:41 and the final verse.

### 11 Moreover, it is not improbable that the organs of the senses

Moreover, it is not improbable that the organs of the senses, and indeed the senses themselves, will be tormented by particular punishments, so that those who sinned through the organs of the senses may also be punished through the same.

Notes. Concerning touch, at any rate, there can be no doubt, given the accepted doctrine of fire properly so called, as stated above.

As for the punishments of the remaining senses, there are those who hold that with respect to sight there will be horrible spectacles of demons appearing in certain forms, as well as the sight of other damned persons; with respect to hearing, one's own groans and those of fellow sufferers, weeping and gnashing of teeth; with respect to taste, foul flavors and thirst; and with respect to smell, the stench of sulfurous fire. Others, however, take those passages from Scripture that are adduced in this connection metaphorically and parabolically, as depicting the most grievous pains by means of things that are the most bitter that can befall a person in this life (Gerhard, Theological Commonplaces, On Hell, §. 71, pp. 665, 666, 667).

### 12 That there will be degrees of infernal punishments cannot be denied

That there will be degrees of infernal punishments cannot be denied, but to define those degrees more precisely, in view of the diversity of all the various subjects, is not equally easy.

Notes. Thus Christ in Matthew 10:15; 11:22 and 24, and Luke 10:12 threatens the Jews of His time, and especially the inhabitants of the cities Chorazin, Bethsaida, and Capernaum, with heavier punishments than those due to the citizens of Sodom, Gomorrah, Tyre, and Sidon.

Indeed, it is probable that the pangs of conscience will be found to be more vehement in those who sinned more frequently and more gravely against conscience, and that more intense bodily pains will be inflicted upon those who were more industrious in exercising sins through their bodies in this life. Concerning the infants of the Gentiles, however, it is customarily debated whether their punishment, beyond the lack of the beatific vision, also consists in real infernal torments. On this question, Musaeus preferred to withhold judgment (Musaeus, Detailed Explanation, final question, pp. 704, 705). In agreement with this is what Hülsemann wrote (Hülsemann, Lectures on the Formula of Concord, article 8, section 2, mem. 1, §. 3, p. 444, proposition 9): concerning the infants of the Gentiles we can indeed pronounce that, according to the norm of the revealed Word, they will have no share in eternal blessedness (John 3:36; 2 Thessalonians 1:8), but concerning the quality and quantity of their punishment we can determine nothing.

### 13 To seek or attempt to define in this life the location of hell is a matter of…

To seek or attempt to define in this life the location of hell is a matter of useless curiosity, but that a definite place has been appointed for the damned is not to be doubted.

Notes. Compare Gerhard (Gerhard, Theological Commonplaces, On Hell, §. 84, pp. 686 ff.). And indeed it is easier to demonstrate the difficulty of each of the opinions that attempt to define something here than to confirm any one of them sufficiently.

For Scripture itself makes very frequent mention of hell, prison, and the like.

### 14 That the punishments of the damned will be eternal is most certain

That the punishments of the damned will be eternal is most certain.

Note. Thus Daniel 12:2 mentions eternal ignominy; Matthew 25:46 speaks of eternal punishment; 2 Thessalonians 1:9 speaks of eternal destruction. Compare also Jude verses 6 and 13, and what was said above at §. X, note c.

## 10 On Death

### 1 Since the highest or ultimate blessedness is found not in this life but in the…

Since the highest or ultimate blessedness is found not in this life but in the life to come, and likewise the opposite, namely the greatest misery, occurs only after this life, we must now examine those things which, according to divine revelation, pertain to the end of this life and to the entrance into the life or state beyond.

Notes. See Prolegomena, chapter 1, section 4, note e, p. 10; and Part 1, chapter 6, sections 3 and 20, pp. 313 and 329.

See chapter 7, section 1, note a, p. 330.

These matters are otherwise called the "Last Things," in Greek τὰ ἔσχατα (the final things), and they are distinguished as follows: some are "last" with respect to individual human beings, while others are "last" with respect to all people universally and the whole world. To the former class belong death and the state of the soul after death. To the latter class belong the resurrection of the dead and the analogous transformation of the living, the final judgment, and the conflagration of the world. Each of these must be treated separately.

### 2 First, then, death must be considered

First, then, death must be considered. Death is the privation of the natural life of human beings, arising from the dissolution of soul and body.

Notes. Death is opposed to life only privatively, and it signifies the absence of life in a subject suited to possessing life. Or, as others express it, it is the privation of animal life.

For we are not here considering spiritual death, whether of believers or unbelievers, nor eternal death, but that which is otherwise called temporal death or the death of the body.

### 3 Strictly speaking

Strictly speaking, there is no efficient cause of death in the proper sense. Nevertheless, we must consider the causes of the dissolution of soul and body, and these causes are partly physical and partly moral.

Notes. For death is a privation, as we have seen, and efficient causes properly pertain to real and positive effects.

For the causes of privations are said to be whatever produces some effect with which the privation is necessarily and intrinsically connected.

Physical causes are those which really act upon the union of soul and body and destroy it.

Moral causes are those which do not actually destroy such a union but nevertheless contribute something to its destruction, so that the destruction is rightly imputed to them.

### 4 Among the moral causes of death

Among the moral causes of death, the Devil must be numbered first, inasmuch as by his persuasion he led Eve into sin, and thus brought upon her and her companions in sin the guilt of death.

Notes. John 8:44, where he is therefore called a murderer.

See Genesis 3:1 ff.

Genesis 3:3, 4; compare Wisdom 2:24, where it is said that death entered the world through the envy of the Devil; and Hebrews 2:14, where the Devil is said to hold the power of death, in the manner of a tyrant who consigns to death those whom he has conquered.

### 5 Next, the first parents are rightly called the cause not only of their own…

Next, the first parents are rightly called the cause not only of their own death but also of the death of their descendants. Eve, because she not only sinned by obeying the persuasion of the Demon, but also enticed Adam into partnership in sin, and thus brought the guilt of death upon both herself and Adam. Adam, however, by hearkening to his wife and violating the law of God, both incurred the necessity of dying himself and became the cause of both sin and death for all who would descend from him according to nature.

Notes. Although they did not directly intend death, but rather supposed that all other outcomes would follow (Genesis 3:3, 4).

Genesis 3:16; 1 Timothy 2:14.

Genesis 3:6, 17, 19; Romans 5:12),

### 6 God, however, is not the cause of death

God, however, is not the cause of death, except insofar as, acting as a just judge, He took away from the first parents the gift of immortality on account of their neglect of the prohibition and the severe warning, and thus subjected human beings to the death they had merited.

Notes. For God created the first human beings ἐν ἀφθαρσίᾳ (in incorruption), and He takes delight not in death but in the preservation and life of human beings. (Wisdom 1:13; 3:23).

Death is here considered as a penal evil, to be inflicted in view of an intervening moral fault. (Psalm 90:7, where the wrath of God is said to consume us).

Attached to the law itself (Genesis 2:17).

Namely, this is the meaning: that man, once the gift of immortality has been withdrawn, ought to return to the earth from which he was taken (Genesis 3:19).

### 7 The physical causes are divided into natural

The physical causes are divided into natural, preternatural, and violent causes.

Note. Some authorities establish only two classes, but in nearly the same sense, for what are here called preternatural causes are referred by them either to the natural or to the violent category.

### 8 The natural cause of death is the consumption of the radical moisture and the…

The natural cause of death is the consumption of the radical moisture and the extinction of the innate heat, arising from the primary qualities gradually acting upon one another.

Notes. This cause arises proximately from the necessity of a corrupted, not an intact, nature.

Such a death occurs in persons who are long lived and have enjoyed firm health, with no intervening serious illness.

Specifically, the vigor of the innate heat, which does not have sufficiently pure nourishment, gradually languishes and converts the food it takes in less and less successfully; thus, as suitable fuel fails, the innate heat is more and more weakened and finally extinguished.

In this way, there is properly only one natural cause of death.

### 9 Among the preternatural causes are more severe diseases

Among the preternatural causes are more severe diseases, by which the innate heat together with the radical moisture is likewise extinguished, but in a manner contrary to nature.

Notes. These causes, although they occur within the human body, do not arise from the common necessity of nature but from some other source, such as a faulty diet.

Examples include fevers, dropsy, consumption, plague, and other diseases that are excited by powerful causes and overturn the substance, temperament, and remaining constitution of the bodily parts, and so dissipate or suffocate the spirits that nature has no means left to defend itself or to return to its former state.

### 10 Among the violent causes are reckoned external things

Among the violent causes are reckoned external things, by which such force is inflicted upon the body or upon a nobler part of the body, or upon a part simply necessary for life, that the generation and distribution of nutritive blood and vital spirits is impeded or destroyed.

Notes. Such as a lethal weapon, fire, water, and the like.

For without these, the body itself is rendered unfit for the functions of the soul, and life cannot continue.

### 11 The subject of death is human beings

The subject of death is human beings: not only the first parents after the fall, but also all others propagated from them through carnal generation.

Notes. Or that which is subject to death, and is therefore said to die. Others call it materiam in qua (matter in which).

In accordance with the divine warning (Genesis 2:17; 3:19) and the event corresponding to it (Genesis 5:5).

For Christ, who was conceived ἐκ πνεύματος ἁγίου (of the Holy Spirit), was not subject to the necessity of death.

Thus death is said to have passed upon all human beings (Romans 5:12), and it is said that it is appointed for all people to die once (Hebrews 9:27). As for the fact that Enoch and Elijah were translated alive into heaven, and that those people whom the last day of the world will find alive will not undergo death (although they too are mortal and would truly have died if the last day had not anticipated the end of life, that is, the death they would otherwise have undergone), this is something peculiar and extraordinary. The Apostle testifies that these will undergo a transformation analogous to death (1 Corinthians 15:51).

### 12 The final cause of death

The final cause of death, considered in itself, is the vindication of sins and thus the declaration of divine justice.

Notes. That is, insofar as death, such as it is by its own nature and as it was first sent upon the human race by God, is considered.

However, by accident and by the grace of God it has come about that for certain subjects, namely those who believe in Christ, who have been reconciled to God and freed from the guilt of sins, death is not punishment in the proper sense, but the end of temporal misery and a passage to a better life (John 5:24). It is called a sleep (Matthew 9:24; John 11:11), a deliverance from this body of death (Romans 7:24), a desired dissolution (Philippians 1:23), and an entrance into rest from labors (Isaiah 57:2; Revelation 14:13).

### 13 When the dissolution of soul and body has taken place

When the dissolution of soul and body has taken place, and death has accordingly occurred, the soul nevertheless remains in existence and continues to exercise its operations.

Notes. Thus Solomon says that the dust, that is, the body of a human being, returns to the earth as it was, but the spirit returns to God who gave it (Ecclesiastes 12:7). And Christ says that those who kill the body are not able to kill the soul (Matthew 10:28).

The operations that remain are those which formally pertain to the intellect and the will as essential faculties of the soul insofar as it is human or rational. It is rightly believed that these faculties survive and are not idle, but that the intellect retains the intelligible forms it possessed while in the body, and is thus able to elicit further acts of cognition, to which in turn certain acts of the will correspond regarding objects presented by the intellect. To this end it is customarily noted that in Revelation 6:10, knowledge of their former state and a certain desire are ascribed to the souls of the martyrs.

However, we do not say that the souls of the departed know distinctly and determinately the actions and affairs of individual living persons which occurred after their departure from the body.

### 14 Indeed, we believe that the souls of the pious

Indeed, we believe that the souls of the pious, immediately after they have been separated from their bodies, attain essential blessedness, while the souls of the impious undergo their damnation.

Notes. For Paul desires dissolution so that he might more quickly be with Christ, that is, in the glorious kingdom of Christ, so that to be with Christ is to enjoy blessedness with Christ (Philippians 1:23). And thus Christ Himself said to the penitent thief, "Today you will be with Me in paradise," that is, "You will enjoy heavenly glory with Me" (Luke 23:43). What Christ also says, that those who believe in Him pass from death into life (John 5:24), indicates that believers who die are immediately made partakers of eternal life. And in Revelation 7:4, 15, the souls of the blessed martyrs are said to be before the throne of God and to serve Him day and night, which is certainly a description of blessedness (see Musaeus, Extended Explanation, book 19, question 92, p. 700 ff.).

For the reasoning concerning opposites is similar. And in 1 Peter 3:19, Christ, descending to the underworld, is said to have preached to the spirits who were in prison, namely those who were disobedient in the time of Noah. Now, the souls that are in that prison are without doubt cast out from the face of God and are afflicted with the punishments connected therewith.

Certainly, no intermediate Purgatory ought to be invented.

## 11 On the Resurrection of the Dead

### 1 Just as the soul of a human being survives after death

Just as the soul of a human being survives after death, so also the body, which was destroyed through death, will rise again and return to life. This is most clear from the Scriptures, though it cannot be known by natural reason, even if it is not repugnant to reason.

Notes. Thus Job believed and confessed (Job 19:25). Isaiah also foretold (Isaiah 26:19, Daniel 12:2). Christ Confirmed (John 5:28; 11:23; 1 Corinthians 15:12ff.; 1 Thessalonians 4:16).

For natural reason, although it may attain to the immortality of the soul, nevertheless remains ignorant as to whether the soul will live without the body, or whether it will at some point be reunited to a body, and to which body (Musaeus, Introduction, ch. 2, §9, p. 1).

However, when Scripture reveals the doctrine of the resurrection of the dead, then reason, which acknowledges God as the avenger of crimes and the rewarder of the good, finds it more agreeable than contrary to itself that bodies should be raised up for a share in punishments or rewards. And although one may not discover how bodies numerically the same, which have been dissolved into ashes, can be raised again, it is nevertheless so far from being able to demonstrate the impossibility of this by an invincible argument, that it is rather compelled to leave the matter to divine power (Musaeus, Introduction to Theology, part 2, ch. 5, §12, pp. 330–331).

### 2 The resurrection of the dead consists in this

The resurrection of the dead consists in this: that the body, destroyed through death, is reproduced from the matter into which it was converted, and is reunited to the soul, or, in a single word, rises again, and so together with the soul arrives either at the blessedness or at the damnation destined for it.

Notes. For in these two acts the formal nature of the resurrection consists, insofar as it is spoken of transitively, that is, as a resuscitation. And thus we believe that the ἀνάστασιν (resurrection) and the ζωοποίησιν (vivification), as far as the substance of the matter is concerned, are one and the same action.

Accordingly, just as death, so also the resurrection of the dead, is a condition or means, broadly so called, without which, according to the common law, the full blessedness or misery of the entire person does not come to pass (John 5:28; Daniel 12:2).

### 3 The efficient cause of the resurrection is the triune God

The efficient cause of the resurrection is the triune God, and Christ the God-man (θεάνθρωπος).

Notes. That is, the cause which by its own power, and therefore by a power that is infinite in accordance with the demands of the work and its effect, will restore bodies and give them life.

For the resuscitation of the dead is an outward work (opus ad extra).

Christ accomplishes this through the omnipotence which, as God, He possesses essentially, and which, as man, He possesses through the communication of attributes. As it is written: "the Son gives life to the dead, just as the Father raises and gives life" (John 5:21). It is also said that the dead who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of God and come forth to judgment (John 5:25, 28). Moreover, just as the power to judge, so also the power to raise the dead for judgment was given to Him "because He is the Son of Man" (John 5:27), that is (when the particle ὅτι is understood specificatively), insofar as He is the Son of Man, or according to that nature by which He is the Son of Man or a human being.

### 4 The internal impulsive cause of the resurrection of the dead in general is divine justice

The internal impulsive cause of the resurrection of the dead in general is divine justice. Specifically, with respect to the pious, it is remunerative justice; with respect to the impious, it is vindictive justice.

Notes. Thus the dead are said to be raised and made manifest so that each one may receive τὰ διὰ τοῦ σώματος (the things done through the body), whatever he has done through the body, whether good or evil.

That is, God, moved by His goodness, wills to transfer the bodies of the blessed, which were the instruments of holy actions, into a share in blessedness (2 Thessalonians 1:5). Scherzer calls this distributive justice, which absolutely demands that that very body in which the pious fought should be crowned.

And God, by that perfection of His by which He is inclined to avenge sins, is also impelled to punish the sins of the impious in their restored bodies (1 Thessalonians 1:5).

### 5 The external impulsive cause

The external impulsive cause, with respect to the resurrection of the pious, is the merit of Christ apprehended by final faith; with respect to the impious, it is final impenitence.

Notes. As Christ says: "I am the resurrection and the life; whoever believes in me, even if he has died, will live" (John 11:25). And in 1 Corinthians 15:22, all who descend from Christ through spiritual birth are said to be made alive through Christ, just as all who descend from Adam through carnal birth die through Adam. Now to be made alive through Christ is to be made alive by the power of His merit; hence Christ is also called the meritorious cause of the resurrection of the pious.

With respect to the impious, the evils which each person has committed in the body move God to will that he be made manifest in the body, to receive punishments in the body (2 Corinthians 5:10). However, we have no reason to call the merit of Christ the impulsive or meritorious cause of the resurrection even with respect to the impious. For the merit of Christ, rendered by the Mediator in our place and for our benefit, is called a meritorious cause in relation to some good to be obtained for us; but the resurrection of the impious does not have the character of a good with respect to them (Gerhard, On the Resurrection of the Dead, 1, §55ff.).

### 6 The subject "which" (subjectum quod) of the resurrection consists of all dead human beings

The subject "which" (subjectum quod) of the resurrection consists of all dead human beings.

Notes. That is, those who are ultimately designated as rising, or, in a single word, the persons (supposita) that will rise.

For those who are found alive on the last day will not, properly speaking, rise again, since they have not fallen through death; nevertheless, they will be changed and will put off the mortal condition of the body (1 Corinthians 15:51ff.).

Indeed, it is expressly stated: "all who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of God and will rise again in one hour" (John 5:28). As for the fact that some are read to have been raised not only at the universal resurrection, but already long ago when Christ rose (Matthew 27:53), and are believed to have ascended with Christ into heaven, this was extraordinary. Those, however, who in the Old Testament were raised by the prophets, and in the New Testament were raised by Christ before His passion and by the apostles after Christ's ascension, from the dead to this natural life, are rightly judged to have died again, and therefore to be due to be raised at the final resurrection to immortal life.

### 7 The subject "by which" (subjectum quo) is the body numerically the same that…

The subject "by which" (subjectum quo) is the body numerically the same that each person had in this life.

Notes. That is, that essential part of a human being according to which he is said to rise, or which, having been previously destroyed, is reproduced through the resurrection and reunited to the other part that survived.

Indeed, the very word ἀνάστασις (anastasis), or resurrection, implies a repeated standing of that which previously stood and had fallen. Hence, if you were to suppose that one body had stood in this life and fallen through death, while a different body were to be produced hereafter, there would be no true resurrection. Compare 2 Corinthians 5:10, where the identity of the body is clearly indicated: the body in which each person did good or evil in this life, and in which he will receive rewards or punishments at the last judgment.

In the Old Testament, Job, about to utter a confession of faith worthy of eternal remembrance, said that he knew that after the passage of a very long time, or in the last time (ןורחא), in his own flesh, previously corrupted and consumed by worms, with these very eyes which he had in this life, he would see his Redeemer (לאוג), who was joined to him by kinship or consanguinity as one who redeems (and no one other than the Messiah can be understood here), living and appearing in visible form, and, like a mighty conqueror, coming to rule over the dust (Job 19:25).

The risen will also retain the sex and all the parts or members that they had in this life. Moreover, the bodies of the pious will be rendered glorious in the resurrection itself. And if perhaps they were deprived of certain members in this life, they will then receive them.

In what stature, however, the bodies will rise, we do not determine.

### 8 The proximate end of the resurrection of the dead

The proximate end of the resurrection of the dead, with respect to the faithful, is the full participation in blessedness; with respect to the unfaithful, it is the consummation of damnation. The ultimate end is the glory of divine justice, both remunerative and vindictive.

Notes. For they will rise so that they may receive τὰ διὰ τοῦ σώματος (the things done through the body), and so forth (2 Corinthians 5:10). And in John 5:28, the resurrection is said to be either of life or of condemnation, the designation being drawn from its end.

For just as God is moved to raise human beings by that justice of His, so He is rightly said to intend the glory of that same justice.

## 12 On the Last Judgment and the Consummation of the Age

### 1 Since the universal resurrection of the dead has this purpose

Since the universal resurrection of the dead has this purpose, that human beings might receive either rewards or punishments, we must now treat of that judgment by which rewards and punishments will be assigned to them.

### 2 That there will be a certain solemn judgment is most clearly attested by the Scriptures

That there will be a certain solemn judgment is most clearly attested by the Scriptures. It is also certain that the last judgment and the resurrection of the dead will occur on one and the same day. However, God did not wish for us to foreknow with precision when that day will come.

Notes. Matthew 25:31 and following; Acts 17:31; 2 Thessalonians 1:6 and following.

Ses 1 Thessalonians 4:16, 17.

(Mark 13:32). And experience has shown hitherto how greatly those have erred who believed they could determine something by divination.

### 3 In the meantime

In the meantime, there are signs by which God exhibits the approaching judgment so that it may in some measure be recognized, just as summer is known to be drawing near from the tender branches of the fig tree and from its sprouting leaves (Matthew 24:3 and 33; Mark 13:29; Luke 21:29, where they are also expressly called "signs"). These signs are generally divided into common signs, that is, such as occur not merely in one age but recur frequently or continue over time, and proper signs, which are to be observed only as the judgment draws nearer and not equally in earlier ages.

Among the common signs are heresies, for thus Christ makes mention of false prophets who will lead many into error (Matthew 24:24), and Paul predicts that in the last times there will be deceitful spirits and doctrines of demons (1 Timothy 4:1; cf. 2 Timothy 3:8, where mention is made of men resisting the truth, corrupt in mind, reprobate concerning the faith, seducers of the simple, and the like). The faithful, therefore, beholding these things, ought at the same time to remember the last judgment, by which truth will triumph over defeated heresies. Likewise, wars and similar public calamities are included among these common signs (Matthew 24:6 and following), as well as the carelessness of human beings, such as was characteristic of those before the Flood (Matthew 24:37, 38, 39), and an enormous catalogue of vices prevailing in the last times is enumerated (2 Timothy 3:1 and following).

Others distinguish these signs into remote and proximate, in nearly the same sense. Namely, the common and more remote signs, although they may not seem to indicate the precise time of the judgment, nevertheless do signify it by the institution and intention of God, and ought to admonish Christians that a certain solemn judgment is to be expected, by virtue of divine justice and the truth of the prophecies. Among the proper or more proximate signs, the difference is that some precede the judgment by a longer interval and some by a shorter one, and therefore not even these indicate a determinate time with certainty, except that certain of them (or at least the one to be discussed in § IV below) are believed to be conjoined with the very beginning of the judicial solemnity.

Among the proper signs are the following. First, the revelation of the Antichrist. This is what Paul describes (2 Thessalonians 2:3 and following): the adversary of Christ (τὸν ἀντικείμενον, "the one who opposes") sitting in the temple of God, that is, in the Christian Church, as though he were its head or monarch, after he has, through the working of Satan, with signs and lying wonders, deceived a great number of people and erected and established his kingdom, so that for a time and by very many people he is not recognized for what he is, namely that he is the Antichrist. Yet in his own time he will be revealed and recognized as the Antichrist, although even then the day of the Lord will not come immediately; rather, the Antichrist himself, now made manifest, will continue to persist until he is abolished by the splendor of Christ's coming. The unmasking of the Antichrist, therefore, ought to serve as a sign to the faithful, signifying that the judgment is to follow, by which the Antichrist, now revealed, will at last be destroyed.

Second, extraordinary eclipses of the heavenly bodies and the falling of stars to the earth (Matthew 24:29). For although we do not have a revealed account of the precise manner and determinate nature of these celestial signs, and especially of the falling of stars to earth, it is nevertheless better to retain the literal sense of Scripture in these matters and to leave the manner of the thing to divine wisdom and power, than to abandon the literal sense and seek or embrace a metaphor, especially since elsewhere express mention is made of celestial signs, distinguished from earthly ones (Luke 21:25).

Third, according to the opinion of some, a notable conversion of the Jews, such that in their public assemblies the doctrine of the Gospel, hitherto rejected by them, will be preached, and entire congregations will subscribe to it, and thus very many will be saved through faith in Christ (Romans 11:25 and following). For that "Israel" to which blindness has hitherto happened is the same one described in the same chapter under the image of the natural olive branches, in contrast to the wild olive, and it denotes Israel according to the flesh, in contrast to the Gentiles, the same people whom Paul had also described above (Romans 9:3, 4, 5) as his kinsmen according to the flesh. Furthermore, the desolation of the seven- hilled city of Rome is customarily referred to here (Revelation 18), as well as the destruction of Gog and Magog (Revelation 20).

### 4 When the judgment itself is at hand

When the judgment itself is at hand, a special sign will be seen, which is called the sign of the Son of Man. What this sign will be, however, is difficult to explain.

Notes. See Matthew 24:30.

Nevertheless, the more probable opinion among the rest is that which teaches that this sign will consist in the brightness of the very body of Christ, in the splendor of the clouds and the angelic retinue, in accordance with (Matthew 24:30 and 25:31), and likewise in the mighty sound of which we read (1 Thessalonians 4:16).

### 5 The Judge will be Christ himself

The Judge will be Christ himself, who, appearing gloriously in the assumed human nature and sitting as it were upon a tribunal, visible to all, will pronounce sentence by divine authority.

Notes. Matthew 25:31 and following, where the Son of Man sitting on the throne of glory and about to judge all the nations gathered before him is described at length; cf. Acts 17:31; John 5:22.

This authority is one and the same as that of the entire Holy Trinity, and it belongs to Christ as man by way of communication. In this respect, the efficient cause of the judgment is said by others to be the whole Holy Trinity. For when it is denied that the Father judges anyone, namely by appearing in his own person (αὐτοπροσώπως) and pronouncing sentence, it is nevertheless added that the Father has given all judgment and the power of judging to the Son (John 5:22 and 27). And in Acts 17 it is said that God will judge the world "by a man" (ᾧ ἀνδρί, "by a man"). The persons distinct from the Son are therefore not excluded, but they bestow their divine authority upon that act together with him. To this belong also the passages where "the judgment of God" and "God the judge of all" are mentioned (Romans 2:2, 3, 5, 6, 16; Hebrews 12:23).

### 6 The internal impulsive cause is partly the remunerative justice

The internal impulsive cause is partly the remunerative justice, or goodness, of God, and partly the vindictive justice, which is otherwise called justice absolutely.

Note. See 2 Thessalonians 1:6, 7.

### 7 The external impulsive cause is

The external impulsive cause is, on the one hand, faith in Christ, and on the other, the sins and final impenitence of those who are to be judged.

Notes. For faith, by virtue of the merit of Christ which it apprehends, moves God to adjudicate to believers at the last judgment not only eternal life but also, in proportion to the diversity of works proceeding from faith, degrees of glory with respect to accidental rewards.

With regard to sins (2 Corinthians 5:10; and cf. the discussion at Chapter IX, § V above), Christ also says (John 12:48): "He who rejects me and does not receive my words has one who judges him: the word that I have spoken will judge him on the last day." This amounts to saying that the unbelieving person, by the very fact that he does not believe, moves the Judge to condemn him at the last judgment.

### 8 Christ will have

Christ will have, in part, assessors and, in part, ministers of the judgment: holy human beings and good angels.

Notes. Thus the Apostles are said to be about to judge the twelve tribes of Israel (Matthew 19:28; Luke 22:30). And Paul says (1 Corinthians 6:2): "Do you not know that the saints will judge the world?"

The angels are likewise mentioned (Matthew 25:31).

### 9 The office of the angels will be not only to accompany Christ as he comes to…

The office of the angels will be not only to accompany Christ as he comes to judgment and to make his arrival known by a mighty sound, but also to gather together, from all parts of the world, both those raised from the dead and those found alive, then to separate the godly from the ungodly, placing the former on the right and the latter on the left, and finally to cast the condemned into hell.

Notes. Matthew 25:31.

1 Thessalonians 4:15.

Matthew 24:31; Mark 13:27.

Matthew 13:41, 49.

Matthew 25:32.

Matthew 13:42, 50.

### 10 The holy human beings

The holy human beings, however, will be witnesses and approvers of the judgment of Christ.

Notes. Even though they themselves must first be judged, as will be discussed shortly.

They appear to be stationed in a higher place (1 Thessalonians 4:14), and nearest indeed to Christ, appearing in visible form, will be the Apostles (Matthew 19:28; Luke 22:30). After them will come the Patriarchs, Prophets, Martyrs, Doctors, and the rest of the faithful, in their proper order, who will look upon the ungodly, stationed in a lower place, and will approve their condemnation (cf. Revelation 19:1 and following).

### 11 The object of the last judgment is twofold

The object of the last judgment is twofold: material, which consists of the persons to be judged, and formal, that is, the standard according to which each person is to be judged.

### 12 To the material object belong all human beings

To the material object belong all human beings, both the godly and the ungodly, and indeed also the evil angels.

Notes. 2 Corinthians 5:10: "For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each one may receive what is due for what he has done in the body, whether good or evil"; Romans 14:10: "We shall all stand before the judgment seat of Christ".

See 2 Peter 2:4, where it is said that the angels who sinned are kept for judgment; cf. Jude 6; Matthew 25:41.

### 13 The formal object

The formal object, on the part of the godly, is faith; on the part of the ungodly, unbelief, insofar as each is recognized from works.

Note. For Christ the Judge will exercise judgment in such a way that he will render to each according to their works, as clear testimonies of either faith or unbelief (2 Corinthians 5:10; cf. Romans 2:6 and following; Matthew 25:35, 36, 42, 43; Revelation 20:12, 13). Care must be taken, however, not to confuse the formal object (especially on the part of the godly, who will receive that joyful sentence of the Judge according to their works, but not on account of their works) with the external impulsive cause.

### 14 The judgment itself is customarily distinguished into the judgment of…

The judgment itself is customarily distinguished into the judgment of investigation and the judgment of retribution.

Note. For although the Judge, Christ, who is the knower of hearts (καρδιογνώστης), has no need of an investigation of cases or of an inquiry to be instituted only at that time, and could also, without so solemn a process, lead the godly whom he knows to eternal life and cast the ungodly, no less distinctly known to him, into hell, nevertheless, in order that the rationale of a just judgment may be most clearly manifest to those who are judged, he freely enters into that judgment of investigation.

### 15 The judgment of investigation is that by which the works of all persons

The judgment of investigation is that by which the works of all persons, hidden and manifest alike, will be brought to light. Chiefly so that each one may sufficiently understand what pertains to himself and what bears upon his salvation or damnation.

Notes. Romans 14:12, where Scripture calls this "giving an account to God," that is, to God as Judge, calling the life and actions of all into examination.

This applies not only to those whose faith or unbelief could be doubted in this life, but also to the rest, whose faith or unbelief was established by public testimonies. For the Apostle's assertion is universal, where he declares concerning all the dead and living over whom Christ has dominion that all will give an account to God.

The good works of the godly will be brought to light to manifest their faith, and to show how great is the difference between them and the unbelievers; the evil works of the ungodly will be brought to light for their shame, and so that it may be evident that they are justly punished.

Some also think that the sins of the godly will be brought back to their memory, not indeed so that they might be put to shame, but so that, recognizing their own unworthiness, they might celebrate all the more the greatness of divine grace toward them (cf. Matthew 25:37 and following).

### 16 The judgment of retribution consists in the pronouncement of the sentence that…

The judgment of retribution consists in the pronouncement of the sentence that is fitting for each one's case, by which some will be sent to life and others to eternal damnation; and the execution of the sentence once pronounced will follow immediately.

Notes. Matthew 25:34 and 41 See Matthew 25:46.

### 17 Once the judgment has been completed

Once the judgment has been completed, the consummation of the world will immediately follow, in which the heaven and the earth, together with the remaining elements and bodies composed of elements, will perish as to their substance by means of fire.

Notes. See Psalm 102:26, 27; Hebrews 1:10, 11, where it is said of the earth and the heavens: "They will perish, they will grow old like a garment, they will be changed like a cloak." What is contrasted here is the immutability of God according to his being, and the mutability and mutation of heaven and earth: first, when through creation they passed from non-being to being, and then that final mutation by which they will pass from being to non-being, which is indeed a substantial change; cf. 2 Peter 3:10, 12.

As Peter expressly states: "The heavens and the earth that now exist are stored up for fire against the day of judgment," 2 Peter 3:7, 10; concerning the nature of this fire, however, the dispute is more curious than useful.

In the meantime, the godly will also have new heavens and a new earth, that is, a glorious habitation (2 Peter 3:13; Revelation 21:1 and following), while the ungodly will have the prison and hell destined for them (Revelation 20:14, 15).

## 13 On Sin in General

### 1 Since the subject of the operation of revealed theology is the human sinner

Since the subject of the operation of revealed theology is the human sinner, therefore, with respect to the end of theology and what pertains to it, we must now speak of sin.

Notes. See Prolegomena, ch. 1, §20, p. 34.

(See the same work, ch. 1, final §, p. 60). For just as in the other practical disciplines, when we must treat of the manner of introducing the end into the subject, the subject must first be considered as lacking the end, and whether, and to what extent, it is capable of the end; so too in theology, after blessedness has been treated, the human being must be considered not only as lacking blessedness, but also as turned away from God through sin and lacking the powers to obtain blessedness from God: namely, so that, having been freed from sin and reconciled to God, he may be led to blessedness (compare Musaeus, Introduction, ch. 3, §1, p. 214, §11).

### 2 Now sin is taken in this place partly in an abstract sense

Now sin is taken in this place partly in an abstract sense, as the very lack of conformity with the law that pertains to the life and actions of a rational creature, in which respect it is a mere privation and not something positive; and partly in a concrete sense, inasmuch as, besides the absence of conformity with that law, it also encompasses some subject to which that privation attaches, whether it be an innate quality, an acquired habit, or an act that is otherwise than it ought to be according to a certain law, that is, one that deviates from the law or does not agree with the law; in which respect it is certain that sin is something positive.

Notes. In other contexts, sin is spoken of more generally in relation to any rule prescribing a definite mode of operation; in which sense there is a sin of nature (which is called a monstrosity), and likewise a sin of art. But here, with the word taken in its special and proper sense, sin is understood in respect to the rule of morals, and is called moral sin.

So John expressly states: ἡ ἁμαρτία ἐστὶν ἡ ἀνομία (sin is lawlessness) (1 John 3:4).

For it imports nothing beyond the negation of a positive entity, namely of that rectitude or conformity with the law which ought to be present. But no substance and no positive accident is formally a privation, for this would be a contradiction.

Thus depraved concupiscence, vicious habits, and all acts that conflict with the law are customarily and rightly called sins.

For even though that from which, as from a form, a thing has its being and is denominated sin is not something positive but a mere privation, nevertheless, because in sin taken concretely, besides that formal element, some material element is also involved, therefore, as far as the material of sin is concerned, it can indeed involve a positive entity (compare with the remarks on this section in Musaeus, Theological Theses on Sin, published and publicly debated in 1651, near the beginning).

### 3 Moreover, by "law" must be understood the eternal and immutable wisdom and…

Moreover, by "law" must be understood the eternal and immutable wisdom and judgment of God concerning those things which are fitting or unfitting for a rational creature as such, conjoined with the will that those things be done or not done.

Notes. For since the law is the norm or rule from which sin deviates, a norm of this kind must be sought that is primary and adequate to all sins.

And thus it exists formally in God himself, although it is directed toward creatures and what pertains to them.

It is otherwise called the law of nature, because it deals with those things that are by nature or in themselves honorable and base, that is, things that are fitting or unfitting for a rational nature as such. It is also called the moral law, insofar as it pertains to morals, that is, the manner of living that becomes or disgraces a rational creature.

### 4 That law was first promulgated in creation itself

That law was first promulgated in creation itself, when the knowledge of practical principles was conferred upon human beings, together with the faculty of applying them to individual actions and the circumstances of actions.

Notes. (See what was said above concerning the image of God with respect to the intellect, part 1, ch. 4, §7). For the law of nature, implanted in the minds of human beings, is a certain expressed image of the eternal law existing in God himself, that is, a communication or promulgation of the divine law, by which those things that God himself would judge to be fitting for the human being, things to be done and things to be avoided, were made manifest to the human being, as things to be observed by the authority of God the Creator.

These principles prescribe universally what is to be done and what is to be omitted. The Scholastics call that knowledge synteresis (συντήρησιν).

And thus it would be established what, according to those general precepts, is to be done and not to be done here and now. The Scholastics call this phronesis (φρόνησιν).

### 5 Afterward, when those perfections previously received by virtue of the divine…

Afterward, when those perfections previously received by virtue of the divine image were lost through the fall, that law was indeed greatly obscured, but nonetheless some vestiges or traces of it remained. But God, besides other revelations, especially in the Decalogue, repeated the sum of the law by voice and in writing, and explained individual precepts more clearly in various places throughout Sacred Scripture.

Notes. As will be explained more distinctly below in the section concerning original sin.

As it is said (Romans 2:15): the Gentiles, who do not have the law (set before them externally through a special revelation), are a law unto themselves, showing the work of the law written in their hearts, and so forth; inasmuch as they possess a certain knowledge of discerning honorable and base things inscribed on their hearts as if by the finger of nature, by whose force also, when after performing various actions they descend into themselves, they now accuse themselves as violators of a law imposed by a superior, and now, finding that they have acted rightly, excuse themselves and (at least in some measure) defend themselves.

That came to the Patriarchs and through them to others on more than one occasion (compare Gerhard, On the Law, §15 and following, to §24, where he shows that the practice of the moral law, comprehended in the Decalogue, had its place even before Moses).

(See Exodus 20:1 and following). And it is indicated (Exodus 31:18) that God, after he had finished speaking with Moses on Mount Sinai, gave him two tables of testimony, containing the sum of the statutes, tables written by the finger, that is, by the immediate operation of the power of God (compare Deuteronomy 4:13; 9:10).

(See what Gerhard, On the Law, section 9, taught concerning the individual precepts of the Decalogue, with other passages of Scripture adduced for explanation). It is especially to be noted how Christ purged the old law from the corruptions of the Pharisees (Matthew 5:20 and following; 19:3 and following). He also showed that the sum of the law is comprehended in the precepts of loving God and neighbor (Matthew 22:37 to 40).

### 6 And thus the most great and most universal binding force of this law can be recognized

And thus the most great and most universal binding force of this law can be recognized, which no human being can escape.

Notes. For it concerns things good and evil in themselves, and has as its author God, who is most wise, most holy, and most powerful.

For it is contradictory that a being should be human and yet not be obligated by the authority of the Lawgiver, who is the Creator and Lord of all, to do those things which are fitting for a rational creature as such.

### 7 Moreover, that which is committed against any positive law

Moreover, that which is committed against any positive law, whether divine or human, is also truly a sin, provided that the human law does not conflict with the divine law.

Notes. For since these principles, "the things which the magistrate, who is an ordinance of God, prescribes are to be done," are of eternal truth and are implicitly contained in the Decalogue, no one can act against a positive law imposed by a superior without also simultaneously acting against the eternal law of God.

Otherwise, if human law conflicts with divine, that apostolic principle holds (Acts 4:19): "Judge whether it is just in the sight of God to listen to you rather than to God." And (Acts 5:29): "It is necessary to obey God rather than men." Furthermore, it is established that the commands of inferior magistrates cannot derogate from the laws of the superior magistrate, and that he who observes the latter and does not comply with the opposing commands of the former does not sin.

### 8 The physically efficient cause of sin considered in the abstract

The physically efficient cause of sin considered in the abstract, properly speaking, does not exist. But of the acts and habits to which sin attaches, insofar as they are acts and habits, the physical cause may rightly be inquired into.

Notes. Or by a real influx producing it as a true and real effect.

For sin, as such, is a privation (see this chapter, §2, note c), and it is repugnant for a privation to be really produced by a physically efficient cause.

Since they constitute the material element in sin taken concretely and are distinct from the formal element. (see note c to §2).

Thus, of Cain's sinful action by which he killed his brother (that is, of the sin called fratricide or parricide), insofar as it is a positive action, the physically efficient cause was Cain himself, who struck his brother. Of a vicious habit, for example of intemperance, the cause is the one who acquired it for himself by repeated acts.

### 9 Meanwhile, a moral cause may rightly be assigned to sin as such

Meanwhile, a moral cause may rightly be assigned to sin as such. And this cause is always some nature endowed with intellect and will.

Notes. That is, a cause which, although it does not provide a real influx into that which is a mere privation as something truly to be produced by it, nevertheless contributes something in view of which that thing (or the ἀνομία, lawlessness, itself) is imputed to it as an effect, no less than if it really exerted an influx. Others prefer to call it a "deficient" cause, following Augustine (The City of God, book 12, ch. 7), namely, because if the agent is considered precisely in relation to lawlessness, it is called its cause not by reason of any influx but by reason of a certain defect in causing, that is, because it does not act in conformity with the law (compare Musaeus, cited Theses, no. 9).

See 1 John 3:4, where it is expressly said that he who commits ἁμαρτίαν, sin, also commits ἀνομίαν, lawlessness, namely by the very fact that he does what is ἄνομον, unlawful.

For indeed brute animals and other agents devoid of reason, when they do what would be considered sin if a human being did it, are nevertheless not properly said to sin, just as they are not considered to act in conformity with the law when they do such things as the law prescribes for rational creatures, since they are utterly destitute of the faculty of knowing what the law commands and forbids.

### 10 God, however, can rightly be called the cause of sin neither morally

God, however, can rightly be called the cause of sin neither morally, nor physically.

Notes. Not morally, for he who is supremely good and perfect cannot intend sin either directly or indirectly.

Nor physically, for although God, in the manner of a universal cause, concurs with all actions of secondary causes, and therefore with evil actions equally as with good ones, nevertheless, because those actions are sins not by reason of their positive entity but by reason of their ἀνομία (lawlessness), and because God does not provide a special influx into their positive entity (for he neither wills nor decrees that they be done, nor does he determine the will of the sinner to sinful acts, but particular agents themselves determine themselves by their own will to that species of action), it is manifest that God can in no way be called the cause of sins.

And as for the fact that God does not prevent sins, which he could but was not obligated to prevent, and that he sometimes, by the force of his justice and supreme majesty, withdraws from sinners the grace necessary for avoiding sins (a grace of which they themselves have rendered themselves unworthy), sins do not on that account become effects of God and his actions, but rather their objects.

### 11 The devil, however

The devil, however, and other rational creatures not determined to the good, can indeed become, and do become, the efficient cause of sin.

Notes. As it is said (John 8:44), where the devil is called a murderer, one who did not stand in the truth, one who speaks lies from his own resources, a liar and the father of it (that is, of lying): by all of which predicates, sins, for example murder and lying, are attributed to him as to an agent that is deficient in acting.

For those creatures that are determined to the good, for example by the light of glory, cannot fail in acting but are incapable of sin, as we said in the chapters on the angels and on eternal blessedness.

### 12 Furthermore, that sin does not exist unless it is voluntary

Furthermore, that sin does not exist unless it is voluntary, with respect to the one who is thereby considered a sinner, is not universally true.

Note. For the philosophers indeed include nothing under the name of sins except that in which some aspect of the voluntary appears, so that things done contrary to the law are called sins only insofar as they partake of the voluntary. But in the Scriptures, sin is taken in a much broader signification, as John (1 John 3:4) is content to define sin by ἀνομία (lawlessness) without expressing the aspect of the voluntary (compare what we shall teach in the following chapter 2, on original sin).

### 13 The consequence of every sin is the guilt of fault and of punishment

The consequence of every sin is the guilt of fault and of punishment, both temporal and eternal.

Notes. Some call this the formal element, and certain others call it the formal consecutive element of sin. The former indeed consider sin not absolutely and in itself (for thus it must be acknowledged that the formal element of sin is ἀνομία, lawlessness) but relatively and in relation to the subject which it affects and to which it gives its denomination. And thus guilt can be called the formal element of sin, for through this guilt a human being is constituted before God as unjust, a child of wrath, and liable to eternal damnation (see Musaeus, On Sin, thesis 14). The latter opinion, however, agrees more openly with our own.

Guilt is spoken of insofar as sin is unfitting for a rational nature and renders it culpable.

And insofar as sin imports a violation of the law and an offense against God, the supreme Lawgiver and Lord, it thus constitutes the offending human being as deserving of punishment.

As it is said (Matthew 12:36): on the day of judgment, where their ultimate justification or salvation and condemnation are at issue, human beings will give account for every ἀργόν (or ἀέργον, idle) word, that is, every word that lacks either the reason of just necessity or the intention of pious usefulness, as Gregory the Great explains in his Moralia (compare Jerome, and from both of them, Gerhard, at this passage, p. 648).

### 14 The sins by which the human race is stained are customarily distinguished into…

The sins by which the human race is stained are customarily distinguished into original and actual, inasmuch as a certain sin has its origin from the carnal origin or birth of each individual human being, while others arise in a human being already existing, only with the subsequent addition of one's own proper acts.

Note. I say "carnal origin," not from the origin of the first human being, but of the rest, who descend from the first through carnal birth. That the fall of the first parents is otherwise called originating original sin, and is distinguished from originated original sin, does not pertain to the present discussion, but has its place in its own way among actual sins, even though it was the cause of original sin, as will be said shortly. Others distinguish between the first sin and the sin arising from the first. They subdivide each: the former indeed into the first sin absolutely so called, which is the apostasy of the angels, and the first sin in the human race, which is the fall of the first parents; and they distinguish the sin arising from the first into original and actual.

## 14 On Original Sin

### 1 Original sin, although reason cannot know it with certainty and distinctness…
