Original sin, although reason cannot know it with certainty and distinctness from its own principles, is nevertheless most clearly indicated in Scripture.

Notes. For reason will either suspend its judgment, or, if it ventures to determine anything, will deny it, supposing that human beings are born indifferent by nature, even though it may detect a certain inclination of the sensitive appetite that is at variance with the judgment of reason; see Musaeus, Dissertation on the Insufficiency of the Light of Nature against Lord Herbert, section 27, pp. 22–23; and Heinrich von Lithe, Inaugural Disputation held under our presidency, in which he presented a Synopsis of Natural Theology compared with Revealed Theology, section 5, sections 33 ff.).

See especially Romans 5:12, where it is said that death passed to all human beings because in one man, Adam, all sinned or were constituted sinners. For although the word ἁμαρτάνειν (to sin) elsewhere denotes the actual act of sinning, it must be acknowledged that it is taken in this passage also of those who, by reason of age and the lack of the use of reason, do not actually sin in that manner, and indeed of those who did not even exist when the first man fell. Hence, that all sinned in Adam does not mean the same as that all imitated Adam's sin by similar acts, since in verse 14 it is expressly stated that death (which entered the world through sin) prevailed even over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam's transgression. Accordingly, it must be said that all sinned in one man insofar as, when he sinned, it came about that all who were to descend from him naturally contracted the necessity of being born with sin, and thus each person, on account of his own sin present at birth itself, became subject to death.

Compare Ephesians 2:3, where, when all human beings are said to be by nature children of wrath, the cause of this guilt is presupposed, namely that all are sinners by nature. For to be a child of wrath is the same as to be subject to the divine wrath and worthy of the punishment to be inflicted by God the vindicator of the law on account of the violation of the law. Therefore, one cannot be a child of wrath by nature unless one is polluted with sin by nature or through the corruption of nature. Furthermore, in Genesis 6:5 and 8:21 it is said that every imagination of the thoughts of the human heart is only evil all the day long, from youth onward. Although this may seem to denote actual acts or actual sins, yet the universality both of the subject and of the time indicates that the very faculty of thinking which is in human beings has been so depraved through the corruption of nature itself that it cannot even exercise an act of good or holy thought, but is most inclined to evil acts of thinking.

### 2 Original sin involves partly the privation of original righteousness

Original sin involves partly the privation of original righteousness, and partly the inclination of the whole nature toward evil.

Notes. The nature of original sin cannot be more correctly understood than from the opposite image of God, in whose place it has succeeded.

To the privation belongs that death, or the lack of spiritual life and of all powers for exercising vital acts in conformity with the divine law, which is attributed to human beings insofar as they are by nature children of wrath (Ephesians 2:1, 5). And in Romans 3:10 ff. it is said that Jews and Greeks are all subject to sin, as it is written (Psalm 14:3 ff.): "There is no one righteous, not even one" (all therefore lack the righteousness which they ought to have); "there is no one who understands, no one who seeks God" (thus a right understanding of God and of divine things, and the pursuit thereof, is denied to all); "there is no one who does good, there is not even one" (all therefore lack moral goodness, and the exercise and powers of exercising morally good acts).

Thus in Romans 7:17 and 20 there is mention of sin dwelling in us; in verse 21, of evil lying close at hand (κακὸν παρακείμενον, evil lying close at hand); in verse 23, of a law which is in the members, rebelling against the law of the mind, and so forth, which in verses 7 and 8 was called ἐπιθυμία (concupiscence). By this is understood not only the lower power of desiring, which belongs to the sensitive appetite, but also the inclination of the will toward evil, and indeed the rash proneness of the intellect itself to judge perversely concerning spiritual things, and it encompasses the evil thoughts that suddenly arise. Hence also the Apology of the Augsburg Confession, article 2, p. 55, among other things understands by concupiscence that which seeks not only the pleasures of the body but also carnal wisdom and righteousness, and trusts in these goods while despising God, and so forth (see Musaeus, Detailed Explanation, thesis 44, on sin).

That the theologians of Jena do not teach that original sin, properly and strictly speaking, is a mere privation, nor do they exclude depraved concupiscence from original sin, is shown by the same author in the Detailed Explanation, question 31, pp. 229–230.

Both elements, moreover, have the character of sin: both because a human being is destitute of those powers which he ought to have for exercising acts befitting him, and thus is unfit for doing what the law commands; and because his faculties are inclined toward those things which the law prohibits or which are repugnant to the law.

### 3 Specifically, on the part of the intellect

Specifically, on the part of the intellect, original sin involves a total privation of spiritual light, so that one can neither rightly know God, nor therefore perfectly prescribe the manner in which God is to be worshipped, nor embrace with firm assent those things which have been divinely revealed, and at the same time a proneness of the intellect to make rash and false judgments concerning spiritual things.

Notes. See Ephesians 5:8, where human beings, such as they are by nature before regeneration, or such as they are born, are called σκότος (darkness). The abstract is used for the concrete in order to intensify the meaning, so that they are called darkness, that is, greatly or fully darkened, lacking all spiritual light. Compare chapter 4, verse 18, where they are said to be ἐσκοτισμένοι τῇ διανοίᾳ (darkened in their understanding), namely on account of the ignorance which is in them, as it is immediately explained.

See 1 Corinthians 2:14, where concerning the natural man, that is, such as he is according to the condition of the soul left to itself (who is opposed to the spiritual man, that is, one who has the Spirit of God, which is conferred only through a special operation of God, according to verses 10 and 12), it is said: "He does not perceive, he cannot understand the things of the Spirit of God," that is, the mysteries which God has revealed through his Spirit, according to verses 7 and 10. Thus it is said in the same passage that spiritual things are foolishness to the natural man, that is, they are judged by him to be foolish, absurd things, and so forth.

### 4 On the part of the will

On the part of the will, original sin consists in the lack of original holiness, that is, of the powers of loving God above all things, and of carrying out what the intellect rightly dictated, and likewise of rightly restraining the appetite; and that the will, on the contrary, is inclined toward sinful works.

Notes. This is the inability of willing and accomplishing spiritual things, according to Philippians 2:13. For when both of these things are attributed solely to God, and we are therefore commanded to work out our salvation with fear and trembling, it is certain that this is denied to our natural powers, and we are warned lest, when we have been endowed with grace that is not our own, we render ourselves unworthy of it and be deprived of it. The same inability of the will is indicated by death through trespasses, opposed to spiritual life (Ephesians 2:5; compare section 2 above).

This is that πώρωσις (hardening), or a certain callous hardness of heart (Ephesians 4:18), by which human beings are inclined to carnal security, to contempt and hatred of God, to distrust of God and trust in temporal things, as the blessed Gerhard interprets it (Gerhard, Isagogical Disputations, disputation 24, ch. 3, on original sin, section 7, p. 879).

### 5 On the part of the sensitive appetite

On the part of the sensitive appetite, there is the privation of the obedience due to the higher faculties, and the fact that the appetite, on the contrary, rushes with a certain impetus, as it were, toward those things which are pleasing to the senses, even though they are prohibited by divine law.

Notes. See Romans 7:18–19, where Paul says that in his flesh there dwells no good, and that therefore he does not do the good that he wills.

See also Romans 7:8. For although depraved concupiscence, when the term is taken more broadly, diffuses itself through all the faculties of the human being, it is nevertheless specifically referred to the sensitive appetite, and in this respect it is rightly said in verse 23 to exert itself in the members against the law of the mind.

### 6 Although the power of acting or tending toward objects belonging to each faculty

Although the power of acting or tending toward objects belonging to each faculty, when considered precisely and in itself, is not sin, nevertheless, because it is borne toward objects in a lawless manner (ἀνόμως), it is rightly called sin.

Notes. For in that respect it is something positive and merely the material element of sin; for we call that corruption of nature which encompasses the proneness and impulse of all the powers of the soul toward evil a positive quality, not as though some power of acting were in itself and by itself sin, but because that power of acting in the human being is only prone and ready for sin; meanwhile we do not forbid a subtle distinction to be drawn between the power of acting itself and the defect of that power, just as a distinction is drawn between an action itself and the defect of the action; these are the words of Gerhard, Theological Commonplaces, volume 2, section 88, p. 402; compare Isagogical Disputations, disputation 24, ch. 3, thesis 15, pp. 880–881).

This is speaking concretely. Hence, if some refer concupiscence to the formal element of original sin, it should be understood as the form of the whole, or as the entire essence, as it were, of original sin. Thus, taken concretely, original sin is something positive on account of the connatural habitual proneness toward the object toward which it is inordinately borne, which it connotes by way of subject; but taken abstractly and formally, it is a mere privation. This is taught in the Detailed Explanation, question 31, pp. 231 ff. This, moreover, was the ancient opinion of our theologians. In the year 1619, there were published, in two quires, the testimonies of Philip Melanchthon and Martin Chemnitz, likewise of Aegidius Hunnius and Leonhard Hutter, to the effect that every sin, although it is not a pure privation only but, with respect to its material element, is often also a corrupt habit, a positive quality, and so forth, as the Apology of the Augsburg Confession most correctly teaches, nevertheless with respect to its formal element declares it to be not something positive but a privation.

Among other things cited from Chemnitz's Theological Commonplaces, chapter 5, on the cause of sin, in the response to the argument of the Manichaeans, after the distinction between the material and the formal has been emphasized and applied to the present matter, he says: "These things seem to be thorny and to suit the subtleties of dialecticians rather than theological simplicity; but because the things created by God must necessarily be distinguished from sin, which is the disturbance of the divine order, such things are rightly and usefully taught."

From Hutter's Commonplaces, moreover, the following among other things should be noted: that in defending the Philippian definition, by which sin is defined through privation, he adduces in the third place this argument of the adversaries: "Whatever extenuates the atrocity of sin ought not to be taught. Privation extenuates the atrocity of sin. Therefore it ought not to be taught." He responds, however, that in the minor proposition a false hypothesis is assumed as certain and indubitable, whence a begging of the question emerges. "For," he says, "by the word 'privation,' the atrocity of sin is not extenuated but rather exaggerated: it is shown what great destruction and how immense a loss the human race has suffered from this privation." He continues: "There are, moreover, weighty reasons why the term 'privation' should be retained in the definition of sin, namely, so that the distinction may be clearly seen between created things and the privation of things, which was not created but derives its origin from the Devil." These and further matters can be seen in the Theological Commonplaces of Hutter, published in the same year with a preface of the theological faculty of Wittenberg, pp. 308–309.

If conforming testimonies of others are desired, one may consult those which Musaeus adduced from Grauer, Gerhard, Himmelius, and Hopfner in the Detailed Explanation, pp. 234 ff. Grauer and Kromayer repeated the positions set forth in those passages also elsewhere. Grauer indeed in the Century of Illustrious Questions, corollary 1 of the final disputation, whose words are these: "Original sin formally is not something positive, but materially it is, when these terms are rightly and not vulgarly employed." Kromayer, for his part, writes in Aphoristic Theology, locus 8, aphorism 10: "The Apology of the Augsburg Confession retains the definition of Anselm that sin is the lack of original righteousness, but adds concupiscence. Yet concupiscence itself is considered either as an inclination toward its object, or as a deviation from the norm. If by the lack of original righteousness is understood the privation of a connatural good that ought to be present, involving great corruption (whereas the Pontificals would have original righteousness be some supernatural good, and in this way the pious confessors perceived that original sin was being extenuated), then we could be content with Anselm's definition. Be that as it may, we acquiesce in the distinctions laid down from the beginning of the discussion: namely, that if sin is considered metaphysically and in the abstract, it is something privative; but if ethically and in the concrete, it may be called something positive." In the preceding passage he had said that those who maintain that original sin is something positive press concrete expressions, such as that the heart is called a heart of stone (Ezekiel 36:26), and that which is born of flesh is flesh (John 3:6), but that this opinion concerning the positive, properly so called, is called by some a small branch or offshoot of Flacianism, because it is defended with the same arguments that labor under a confusion of the concrete and the abstract. So says Kromayer.

### 7 The efficient cause of original sin

The efficient cause of original sin: the remote cause is the Devil; the proximate cause is the first parents, Eve and especially Adam.

Notes. Indeed, no physical efficient cause of original sin, formally considered, can be given, since in this respect it is a privation, as we have seen. What is sought is the deficient cause, that is, the one who by failing or sinning brought it about that human beings are born without original righteousness and with depraved concupiscence (see Musaeus, Detailed Explanation, question 35, p. 305).

That the Devil is the remote cause means what is expressed when the Devil is called a murderer and the father of lies (John 8:44). For he could not have been the cause of the death or destruction of humanity unless he were the cause of the sin introduced into the human race, since human beings before sin were immortal, and death entered the world through sin. He is also the father of lies, who by lying drew human beings away from the faith and obedience due to God, and thus gave occasion to the corruption that followed.

Eve, having been seduced by the Devil, became a transgressor, so that in memory of the first woman deceived by Satan, who by sinning induced her husband to sin by her persuasion (whence that corruption of the entire human race arose), no woman should be admitted to preach publicly in the Church (1 Timothy 2:14).

See Romans 5:12, where one man, Adam, as the common parent of the whole human race and the root and active principle thereof, is declared to be the cause of sin, inasmuch as through him sin entered the world.

### 8 The first parents

The first parents, and especially Adam, are the cause of original sin by means of their fall. For by this act they rendered themselves unworthy of God's continuing to bestow upon them the influx necessary for preserving in them and propagating to their posterity original righteousness; rather, God by a just judgment withdrew it. And thus it was impossible for original righteousness, which had been lost in the first parents themselves, to be born together with their posterity, who descended from parents deprived of original righteousness; instead, the lack of that righteousness and the proneness of all faculties toward evil would be born with them.

Notes. This fall some call the proximate and adequate cause of original sin; others call it the causality, that is, the reason through which the first parents actually became the cause of original sin.

That is, they forfeited their claim, or moved and impelled God as judge.

For God had, as it were, entered into a covenant with the first human beings, to whom in his undeserved goodness he had created together with them the divine image, that they should use it not merely as a personal gift but as a natural one; and that through their continuing obedience they should both preserve it themselves and, with God's concurrence, propagate it to their children and subsequent posterity.

As for the more subtle question of how God could have imputed the fall of the first parents to their posterity, who did not yet exist, in such a way that they too would necessarily be born destitute of original righteousness and as sinners, it is neither necessary nor perhaps advisable to pursue this matter further.

### 9 The fall of the first parents was completed by the external act of eating from…

The fall of the first parents was completed by the external act of eating from the fruit of the forbidden tree, contrary to the express law of God, yet this act was preceded by several internal sinful acts: In the intellect, doubt concerning the truth of the divine threat, and soon a fuller unbelief; in the will, an inordinate inclination toward a greater likeness to God; in the sensitive appetite, an inordinate motion tending toward an object pleasing to the senses, though forbidden.

Notes. For the Lord God had commanded the man, saying: "From the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat," Genesis 2:17; but in Genesis 3:6 and 11 it is written: "The woman took of the fruit of that tree and ate, and gave also to her husband with her, and he ate").

See Genesis 3:3 ff., where we are taught that Eve first indeed recalled the divine law and the appended threat, but soon listened to and believed the crafty serpent (ὑπερχόμενον, insinuating) teaching otherwise, for example: "You will not die. Your eyes will be opened," and so forth. The man, however, obeyed the voice of his wife (verse 17), that is, he preferred the persuasive voice of his seduced wife to the divine prohibition, and despised the authority of God.

Namely, Satan in Genesis 3:1 had promised through the serpent that the first parents would become םיהִ לֹאכֱּ (like God); and the woman, seeing that the tree was desirable for gaining understanding, thus took of the fruit (verse 6). Accordingly, the will of the woman more eagerly desired that apparent good promised by Satan, which was nevertheless false and not to be attained by this means.

In the same passage (verse 6), the woman saw that the tree was good for food and that it was desirable to the eyes. Thus, inflamed with desire for enjoyment, she took and ate.

### 10 God, however, although as a just judge he denied to the fallen first parents…

God, however, although as a just judge he denied to the fallen first parents the influx necessary for preserving and propagating original righteousness, nevertheless cannot be called the cause of the fall or of original sin.

Notes. For just as all evils of punishment, according to Amos 3:6, so also the lack of original righteousness, considered as an evil of punishment, could be said to have been inflicted by God; for God was indeed able to take away by the force of his vindicatory justice that gift which by the force of his goodness he had given to human beings in the first creation, after human beings had rendered themselves unworthy of that gift and of all divine benefits through their subsequent transgression.

For he severely prohibited the fall; he gave powers for guarding against sin; but he neither impelled nor determined the first parents to fall, although as a universal cause he could not fail to concur with the material element of that act. And thus it is established that God intended neither the fall of the first parents nor the original sin that followed from it, by either a direct or an indirect intention.

### 11 The subject "which" of original sin

The subject "which" of original sin, is all human beings descending from the first parents through carnal generation, and in their own way the first parents themselves.

Notes. That is, that which is denominated a sinner by this sin and contracts the guilt of both culpability and punishment.

See Romans 5:12, where it is expressly said that all human beings have sinned, and thus through sin (with which all are polluted) death has passed to all.

And thus we exclude Christ the man from the fellowship of those who are stained with original sin, namely because he was not carnally begotten. And notably the angel says to Mary (Luke 1:35): "The holy one who will be born of you will be called the Son of God." Similarly, in Hebrews 7:26, Christ is called ὅσιος, ἄκακος, ἀμίαντος, κεχωρισμένος ἀπὸ τῶν ἁμαρτωλῶν (holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners).

As for the first parents themselves, the corruption which is in us and is called original sin truly had its place in them after the fall (see Genesis 3:7). For that knowledge of their nakedness implies a sense of inordinate and shameful concupiscence recently contracted, from which the lack of original righteousness can certainly be inferred. It must be admitted, however, that this corruption could not properly be called original sin with respect to the first parents themselves, because it was not present in them from the origin of their nature and from the beginning of their existence.

### 12 The primary subject "in which" of original sin

The primary subject "in which" of original sin, is the soul with its faculties: the intellect, the will, and the sensitive appetite. Secondarily, however, and consequently, the members of the body are also rightly referred to this subject.

Notes. That is, that by means of which original sin belongs to a human being, or in which it formally and immediately inheres, otherwise called the proper subject, in Greek πρῶτον δεκτικόν, the primary receptive.

Just as the opposite original righteousness was, in whose place, once it was removed, original sin succeeded (compare what was said above in sections 3, 4, 5, and 6; and Musaeus, Detailed Explanation, book 7, question 40, pp. 312 ff.). Thus also Balduin writes (Balduin, Commentary on the Epistle to the Ephesians, ch. 4, part 2, aphorism 7, p. 923): "The subject of original sin is indeed the whole human being with all his powers. Nevertheless the primary seat of it is the sense of the mind, which the Apostle also commands in particular to be renewed (verse 23). For the mind rules the whole body, and from its corrupt dominion the corruption of the remaining parts in the human being easily follows." Similarly, Eckard says (Eckard, Giessen Disputations, volume 2, disputation 12, section 90, p. 435), having stated that the whole human being according to himself wholly and entirely, that is, both the body and the soul of each individual, is the proximate subject (he means the subject "in which") of original sin. To the objection of some that the body, being a brute thing, is not capable of sin and therefore cannot be its subject, he responds: "To those who object thus, this one saying of a certain philosopher may easily give satisfaction, namely that sin cannot reside in the body by itself, but only insofar as it has communion with the soul. The body, I say, is not guilty of sin when considered by itself, but as constituting the other part of human nature."

Again, in section 94, p. 438, in order to show that the soul is the primary subject of original sin, he argues thus: "What was the subject of original righteousness is also the subject of original unrighteousness. For a habit and the privation opposed to it refer to the same subject. But not only the body, but principally the soul was the subject of original righteousness. For the whole human being was created in the image and likeness of God, of which, however, the soul held the principal parts, being most illustrious by the light of knowledge, wisdom, and learning, and by the zeal of holiness and the love of truth. Therefore the same applies to original sin." In the same manner, Cundisius (Cundisius, Notes on Hutter's Compendium, locus 8, question 6, section 3, p. 579) and König (König, Compendium of Positive Theology, part 2, sections 84–85, pp. 78–79) expressly taught that the πρῶτον δεκτικόν (primary receptive), or the primary subject of original sin, is the rational soul, and the secondary subject is the animate body.

Namely, just as in the state of integrity the body was made a participant in original righteousness in that it served the soul as an instrument for the works of holiness and righteousness, so also original sin extends itself to the members of the body as weapons of unrighteousness. Thus Cundisius writes in the same place: "The secondary subject of original sin is the body, whence St. Paul says in Romans 7:18: 'In my flesh there dwells no good.' Hence it is that the members of a sinful person are called members of a harlot (1 Corinthians 6:15). Thus to sinners are attributed eyes full of adultery (2 Peter 2:14), and in Romans 3:13–15, mouth, lips, throat, feet, and eyes are named, all of which are instruments of that original wickedness."

As for the fact that, just as in the state of integrity impassibility and immortality belonged to the bodies of the first parents, so now a certain morbid quality appears in our bodies through which they have been made subject to various diseases and calamities and to death itself: this does not so much pertain formally to the essence of original sin itself as it follows upon it as its effect. As Cundisius also notes in the same place, question 7, p. 580, he reckons bodily diseases and temporal death among those effects of original sin which are punishment only, not punishment and sin at the same time. Compare Gerhard, Isagogical Disputations, disputation 25, ch. 8, section 3, p. 896.

### 13 The effects of original sin are the various evils of the soul and body

The effects of original sin are the various evils of the soul and body, both temporal and eternal.

Notes. That is, the consequence which follows that sin, as an evil of guilt, by the just judgment of God, by way of punishment.

Among the evils of the soul are the privation of the grace of God, and the opposite wrath of God (Romans 3:23; Ephesians 2:3).

The afflictions that befell the first parents themselves, Adam and Eve, after the fall, according to Genesis 3:16 ff., have in their own way also been transmitted to their posterity. Specifically concerning temporal death, which through sin pervaded all human beings, see Romans 5:12, 14. And in Romans 6:23 it is said that θάνατος ὀψώνια τῆς ἁμαρτίας (death is the wages of sin): namely, that just as soldiers formerly used to be paid rations in both food and money, so sinners, having followed the camp of Satan, receive death in place of their wages.

The eternal effect is damnation or eternal death, which was discussed above in Part 1, chapter 7 (compare Romans 5:18). And this eternal damnation is brought upon all by original sin, as a sufficient and adequate cause, in whom it is not expiated unless through faith in Christ (compare Musaeus, Detailed Explanation, question 38, p. 307).

### 14 The properties of original sin are

The properties of original sin are: first, tenacity, or persistent inherence throughout the whole of life; and second, natural propagability from parents to children.

Notes. As for the first property, Paul, already converted, confesses that sin dwells in him (Romans 7:17). He means the concupiscence of which he had spoken in verses 7 and 8. And he openly attributes to it both the name and the formal concept of sin properly so called. Compare Hebrews 12:1, where it is called ἁμαρτία εὐπερίστατος (the sin that so easily entangles), that is, the sin that firmly adheres to us and surrounds us on every side.

As for the second property, this is what Christ says in John 3:6: "What is born of the flesh is flesh," that is, because one is begotten by carnal or sin-corrupted parents, one is also carnal and corrupted by sin. To this correspond the words of Job (Job 14:4): "Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean? No one," that is, no one will show a clean person begotten from an unclean parent. And the words of David (Psalm 51:5): "Behold, I was formed in iniquity, and in sin my mother conceived me," indicating the contagion of sin transmitted into him through carnal generation in the very act itself.

Moreover, although the propagability of original sin from those who beget to those who are begotten is rightly maintained, it may suffice to know that the first parents by their fall merited that, such as they themselves were after the fall in body and soul, such should all thereafter be procreated. But how the soul contracts that evil may, without harm to faith, remain unknown. "For the Holy Spirit did not wish to make this known through certain and clear testimonies." These are the words of Chemnitz (Chemnitz, Theological Commonplaces, part 1, on original sin, fol. 236). He followed the footsteps of Augustine, who, having treated the question of the origin of the soul and the contracted stain of original sin in letter 28 to Jerome, makes mention of the earlier letter in the following letter 29, and says:

It is reported that someone said something elegant which fits this matter quite aptly. When a certain man had fallen into a well where the water was deep enough to catch him so that he would not die, yet enough to choke him so that he could not speak, another came along, and seeing him, said in amazement: "How did you fall in here?" And the man replied: "I beg you, think about how to get me out of here, and do not ask how I fell in." Therefore, since we confess, and hold by the catholic faith, that the soul even of a little infant must be freed from the guilt of sin, as from a well, by the grace of Christ, it is enough for such a person that we know the manner in which he may be saved, even if we never know how he fell into that evil.

So says Augustine. Now, just as the question of the origin of the soul has begun to be investigated somewhat more carefully in the schools of theologians, so it has come about that those who held the opinion of the propagation of the soul by transmission explained the propagation of original sin through carnal generation in one way, and those who embraced the opinion of the creation of the soul explained it in another.

When it is held that original sin, considered in itself, abstractly and formally, is a privation or lack of original righteousness, and consequently, by the very fact that it is not a positive entity but a mere privation, does not acknowledge an efficient cause by whose real and positive influx it would be produced, it simultaneously appears that the mode of propagation is established negatively, namely, consisting in the non- production of the opposite form, that is, of original righteousness; or in the fact that when the soul is efficiently produced, original righteousness is not simultaneously produced in it and with it.

Accordingly, those who hold the propagation of the soul by transmission seem to indicate that since parents, as secondary causes, produce and bestow upon their offspring a rational soul as from their own resources, with God as the first cause providing general concurrence, therefore these same parents, whose souls have already lost original righteousness in the first parents, cannot in the act of generation together with the soul transfer to their children or propagate the original righteousness which they themselves lack; rather, they bestow a soul destitute of original righteousness and thus corrupted by sin, just as God also provides his concurrence for the propagation of the soul into the offspring, but not for the propagation of original righteousness.

Those, however, who hold the creation of souls believe that original sin is thus propagated: since the first parents by their fall contracted the guilt of having original righteousness removed, and truly lost it through their own fault and by the just judgment of God, in view of this fall and guilt, God now denies in the production of the souls of their offspring the influx for co- producing original righteousness. Otherwise, if human beings had remained in the state of integrity, God would always have concurred in the act of generation by creating the soul with original righteousness. But after the fall committed by the common parent of the human race, each human being in the generation of offspring, as an effect connatural to himself, does not require the concurrence of the first cause for producing original righteousness together with the soul of the offspring, since a connatural effect is not more perfect than its cause.

If, however, original sin, considered in itself, abstractly and formally, is said to be not a mere privation but a positive entity which requires the real and positive influx of an efficient cause in order to be produced and propagated, then a notable difficulty appears on both sides, lest one establish God as the cause of propagated original sin, whether one holds that the soul is propagated from the parents by transmission with God nevertheless concurring as the first cause, or that it is immediately created by God. Compare Musaeus, Detailed Explanation, questions 30 and 35, pp. 301 ff. On this very difficult and doubtful matter, the modesty of Augustine, who prefers to suspend judgment (ἐπέχειν), is pleasing.

### 15 Original sin may be described as the lack of original righteousness

Original sin may be described as the lack of original righteousness, propagated through the fall of Adam to all human beings through carnal generation, intimately corrupting human nature itself and all the faculties of the soul, rendering them unfit for pursuing spiritual goods and inclined toward all manner of evils, and thus subjecting them to the divine wrath and eternal death, unless there intervenes the remission of sins on account of the merit of Christ apprehended by faith.

Notes. For the lack of original righteousness, see section 2, above. For the fall of Adam as its cause, see sections 7 and 8, above. For its extension to all human beings, see section 11, above. For its propagation through carnal generation, see section 14, above. For the corruption of all faculties, see sections 2 ff. and section 12, above. For the effects of wrath and eternal death, see section 13, above.

## 15 On Actual Sins

### 1 Actual sin, by the force of the word

Actual sin, by the force of the word, is a sin that is accomplished by some actual deed or by acting. But as to the matter itself, it must be admitted that actual sins ought to be reckoned not only those that are committed by acting, but also those that are committed by not acting.

Note. For just as certain laws concern things to be done, and others concern things to be omitted, so sins, which are opposed to laws, are perpetrated in some cases by doing what is prohibited by law, and in other cases by not doing, that is, by omitting the act prescribed by law.

### 2 Accordingly, actual sin is described as an action

Accordingly, actual sin is described as an action, or an omission of action, that conflicts with the eternal law of God.

### 3 The efficient cause of actual sin is the human being who sins

The efficient cause of actual sin is the human being who sins, inasmuch as, while he is the physically efficient cause of the positive act to which ἀνομία (lawlessness) adheres, he by that very fact becomes the moral cause of the adhering lawlessness; and inasmuch as, by not doing what he ought to have done, he by that very fact claims entirely for himself the ἀνομία (lawlessness) of that omission.

Notes. We consider here actual sin not of every kind whatsoever, but that which falls upon the subject of theology, that is, upon a human being who is still a wayfarer in this life.

On the efficient cause, see above, chapter 1, sections 8 and 9.

For although an omission of a prescribed act, considered in itself, is nothing but a negation, and accordingly is not considered something positive and really producible, nevertheless a human being is judged to be its cause, partly because he is the cause of some action that is incompatible with the action prescribed by law which ought to have been performed here and now, and partly because sometimes a person elicits within himself an act of the will concerning the omission of a prescribed act, especially an external one.

### 4 God is in no way the cause of actual sin as such

God is in no way the cause of actual sin as such, nor can He be called so.

Note. As we noted above concerning sin in general, chapter 1, section 3, pages 377 and 378. Indeed, we judge that one ought also to abstain from that scandalous phrase by which God is said to be the cause of sin per accidens (Musaeus, Detailed Explanation, question 39, page 310).

### 5 Other causes of actual sin

Other causes of actual sin, however, occur both outside and within the human being. Outside him are the Devil and the world, that is, the things and people contained in this world. Within him are ignorance of the intellect, the affections or passions or motions of the sensitive appetite, and malice of the will.

### 6 The Devil is a cause of human sin inasmuch as he partly presents to the human…

The Devil is a cause of human sin inasmuch as he partly presents to the human being objects that invite him to sin, partly persuades him directly or supplies counsel for accomplishing a crime, and partly arouses certain imaginations in the phantasy, or even, by altering the humors, stirs up passions in the sensitive appetite by which human beings are led into sin.

Notes. See John 8:44 and 1 John 3:8. For when evil men and slanderers, as such, are said to be of the Devil as their father, and to comply with the desires of their father when they sin, the Devil is certainly said to contribute something, and indeed a great deal, to those sins by way of a cause. Compare 2 Corinthians 4:4, where the god of this age is said to blind the minds of unbelievers, lest the light of the Gospel should shine upon them. And Ephesians 2:2, where the same spirit is said ἐνεργεῖν (to work efficaciously) in the sons of unbelief, that is, in unfaithful people.

Thus in Genesis 3:6, Satan, hiding in the serpent, is read to have displayed to Eve the fruit of the forbidden tree, by which her appetite might be moved objectively to desire it, and so that the external act of eating might follow.

Likewise in verse 4 and 5 of the same passage, by an argument drawn from utility, that is, from the greater conformity with God and the more excellent dignity that would follow, Satan commended to Eve the act of eating that fruit and persuaded her to perform it. Compare 1 Chronicles 21:1, where it is recorded how Satan incited David to number the people.

See John 13:2, where it is indicated how the Devil not only led Judas by arguments suited to persuasion so that he would wish to betray Christ, but also taught him by what method the act could be accomplished without hindrance and conveniently, εὐκαίρως (at the opportune moment), which is the role of a counselor. Compare Luke 22:3 and 6.

The example of Saul also pertains here (1 Samuel 16:15 and 18:10, 11).

### 7 Meanwhile, the Devil does not necessitate or immediately determine the human will to sin

Meanwhile, the Devil does not necessitate or immediately determine the human will to sin, but human beings voluntarily consent to the deceiver.

Note. See James 4:7, where it is said that people can resist the Devil when he incites them to sin, so that he flees from them. He who can thus be resisted does not himself necessitate anyone to sin. Compare Ephesians 6:11, 12, 13 and 1 Peter 5:9.

### 8 Human beings, who are called by the name of the world

Human beings, who are called by the name of the world, become the cause of another's sin by counseling, persuading, and inviting by their own example.

Notes. Hence they are also called instruments of the Devil. See Proverbs 1:10 concerning their seductions. Compare the examples of Jeroboam (1 Kings 15:24) and the concubines of Solomon (1 Kings 11:3).

And thus scandals are said to come (Matthew 18:6, 7), by which people are offended so that, with respect to the actions of this life, they are either drawn away from good, so that they act more sluggishly or not at all, or they are led to evil they would not otherwise have committed, whether willingly or through imprudence. Compare chapter 4, verses 11 and 12.

### 9 The things of the world

The things of the world, which are subject to our senses, move the sensitive appetite and the will objectively toward sins.

Note. See 1 John 2:15 and following, where we are forbidden to love the things that are in the world, because from this arises the lust of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life. Compare the example of David, inflamed with lust at the sight of Bathsheba (2 Samuel 11:2).

### 10 Within the human being

Within the human being, the efficient cause of actual sin is the corrupt nature of the person itself, or, speaking abstractly, the perversity innate to the human being, consisting in the lack of original righteousness and the depravity of concupiscence.

Note. Thus from within, from the heart of human beings, evil thoughts, adulteries, fornications, murders, and the like are said to proceed (Mark 7:21, 22, 23). And in Romans 7:17, Paul says that it is not he himself who perpetrates what is done against the law, but original sin dwelling in him, that is, depraved concupiscence. Compare Galatians 5:19, where various works of the flesh, which proceed from carnal concupiscence, are enumerated.

### 11 Specifically, on the part of the intellect

Specifically, on the part of the intellect, ignorance is a cause of sins, inasmuch as it excludes the knowledge that would otherwise have prevented the act of sinning.

Note. And this ignorance is not that which is antecedent to the will, but either concomitant or consequent; and if consequent, whether affected or supine, it is itself also a sin.

Accordingly, it operates as that which removes a hindrance, just as Paul says (1 Timothy 1:13) that he became a persecutor because he lacked knowledge of the true religion, which, had he possessed it, he would not have allowed himself to be induced to persecute true believers.

### 12 On the part of the sensitive appetite

On the part of the sensitive appetite, the causes of sins are the passions or affections, inasmuch as they partly distract or hinder the will so that it tends either more remissly or not at all toward the objects commended to it by the intellect; partly disturb the imaginative faculty, and thus the judgment of the intellect itself, and through that medium draw the will toward sensible goods; and partly, if they are exceedingly vehement, cast down the will by their weight, as it were, toward sensible good, contrary to the dictate of reason.

Notes. See James 1:14. For concupiscence in that passage denotes the sin innate in us, but when it is said to conceive, the disordered motions or passions proceeding from it are signified, from which in turn arise sins so called κατ᾽ ἐξοχήν (par excellence), that is, external sinful acts, and indeed graver ones, casting a person down from the state of grace into the guilt of death. And to this topic belong the things that the philosophers discuss concerning incontinence and its species, namely precipitancy and weakness.

For example, when a sudden fear prevents a person from performing an act of courage or a confession of faith.

Likewise, the affection of love is said to blind the intellect of the wise.

To this also pertains what is taught in the schools of the philosophers concerning the very close connection of the sensitive appetite with the rational appetite, that is, the will. And experience teaches how a more vehement love or anger sometimes degenerates into madness or insanity.

### 13 On the part of the will

On the part of the will, the cause of sin is habitual malice, by which a person knowingly and willingly girds himself for sinning.

Notes. This malice is acquired by sinful acts more frequently repeated, or when, apart from ignorance of the intellect or passion of the sensitive appetite, and rather by wicked deliberation, what is evil is freely chosen; nor does sorrow and repentance immediately follow the perpetrated action.

For otherwise, evil persons can also commit sins from some passion. But here they are considered inasmuch as, although they sin with affections, they do not equally sin from passion or a more vehement affection.

See 2 Timothy 3:1 and following, where the Apostle presents a lengthy catalog of sins of malice.

### 14 But also preceding sins are customarily the cause of subsequent sins

But also preceding sins are customarily the cause of subsequent sins, partly inasmuch as they incline one toward similar sinful acts, and partly inasmuch as they drive out grace, upon the removal of which human beings rush into graver sins.

Notes. For thus acts commonly leave behind them certain dispositions inclining toward other similar acts, and if repeated more often, they generate a habit.

Accordingly, preceding sins are said to be a cause inasmuch as they remove a hindrance.

### 15 The subject of actual sins in the sense of "that which" (the subject of…

The subject of actual sins in the sense of "that which" (the subject of denomination) is the human being himself who sins.

### 16 The subject "by which" sins affect the human being consists of the faculties of…

The subject "by which" sins affect the human being consists of the faculties of the human soul that are the principles of human actions: the intellect, the will, and the sensitive appetite.

Notes. That is, the medium through which sins, as sins, affect the human being.

And thus the ἀνομία (lawlessness) adhering to the act is referred to the same subject upon which the act itself depends as its efficient principle.

With respect to what is voluntary, however, all sins subjectively pertain to the will, inasmuch as they are either commanded by it or approved by it. Some also say secondarily that the members of the body are the subject of certain actual sins, though others more suitably call these members the instruments of those sins.

### 17 The effect of actual sin is partly a certain disposition of the will

The effect of actual sin is partly a certain disposition of the will, by which it is inclined to perform other similar acts, and, if these are repeated more frequently, a hardening of the will in evil. It is partly the guilt of fault and punishment, both temporal and eternal.

Notes. This is the case if actual sins are considered with respect to their material aspect. Compare what we said in section 14 and its note.

Inasmuch as actual sin implies a disagreement with rational nature and with the law of God, it not only stains the human being and renders him culpable, but also moves God, whom it offends, to inflict punishment.

And this applies to every sin, even if it appears most trivial. See Matthew 12:36, and compare chapter 1, section 13, pages 379 and 380 of this work. That certain sins are venial, however, is per accidens, as will presently be stated.

### 18 Actual sin is divided

Actual sin is divided, first, with respect to the efficient cause, into voluntary and involuntary. Voluntary is that sin whose cause is the full and deliberate will, determining itself from its own malice to the act of sinning, not hindered either by ignorance of the intellect or by a more vehement passion. Involuntary is that sin whose cause is not the full and deliberate will, but rather unaffected ignorance or a more vehement passion, which nevertheless has not entirely removed the use of reason and befalls the person without culpability.

Notes. See above, section 13, page 412. These are hence called sins committed from deliberate choice, sins of malice, and so forth. Otherwise, every actual sin pertains to the will as its subject, according to what we said in section 16 and its note, and in this sense every actual sin could be called voluntary; but here voluntary is understood κατ᾽ ἐξοχήν (par excellence).

See above section 10. These are called by the particular name sins of ignorance, to which belong the words of David in Psalm 19:12: "Who can discern his errors? Cleanse me from my hidden faults," that is, from those things that are unknown to my intellect or memory, which I did not regard as sins. Such are especially those cases when one acts out of ignorance either of the strict demands of the divine law or of certain circumstances of the action, things which, if we knew what we are ignorant of, we would not do.

See section 11. These sins are called sins of weakness, not in opposition to sins of precipitancy, but in a somewhat broader sense, having regard to the feebleness of our powers both to prevent the affections that arise in us and to overcome those that have arisen and with which we have struggled for some time.

Moreover, to distinguish involuntary sins from voluntary sins always and accurately in practice is extremely difficult (Musaeus, German Treatise on Repentance against Stenger, part 2, chapter 2, page 173, and part 3, chapter 4, pages 499 and following).

### 19 Actual sins are divided

Actual sins are divided, second, on the part of the material element, into sins of commission and sins of omission. The former are those that consist in positive acts conflicting with a negative precept. The latter consist in the negation or omission of an act prescribed by an affirmative precept.

Note. See above, sections 1 and 2.

### 20 Furthermore, third

Furthermore, third, sins are divided on the part of the object into sins against God, against one's neighbor, and against the sinner himself. The first are those that immediately and directly concern God. The second are those that immediately regard one's neighbor. The third are those that are directed directly against the person of the sinner himself.

Notes. Just as the Apostle divides the opposite good acts that conform to the law, saying that some are done εὐσεβῶς (piously), others δικαίως (justly), and others σωφρόνως (temperately) (Titus 2:12). Some refer here to the distinction of actual sins into carnal sins, by which those committed against oneself and against one's neighbor are comprehended, and spiritual sins, which are committed against God.

The first category coincides with the sins of the first table of the Decalogue, just as the latter two species taken together correspond to the sins of the second table. To sins against God, therefore, belong acts of idolatry, blasphemy, superstition, and the like.

Sins against one's neighbor are those by which the person, reputation, or goods of fortune of one's neighbor are harmed.

Sins against oneself include, for example, fornication, drunkenness, αὐτοχειρία (self- murder), and the like.

### 21 With respect to degree

With respect to degree, fourth, sins are divided into sins of the heart, of the mouth, and of deed.

Note. According to others, they are divided into inchoate sins (in the heart) and consummated sins (of the mouth and of deed), or into internal and external sins. On sins of the heart, mouth, and deed, see Matthew 5:21, 22, 28 and 15:19.

### 22 With respect to the consequence

With respect to the consequence, fifth, sins are divided as follows. First, into mortal or deadly sins, which are actually imputed to the sinner unto death, and venial sins, which, although they are worthy of death, are nevertheless not imputed to the sinner unto death. Second, into crying sins, that is, those which, even when human beings are silent, customarily move God to public vengeance, and non-crying sins, that is, those which God in His longsuffering often tolerates and overlooks. Third, into remissible sins, that is, those which, just as they do not by their nature exclude repentance, so also can be and customarily are remitted, and the irremissible sin, that is, one which is by its very nature such that it is never remitted.

Notes. For otherwise every sin is in itself mortal, and none is venial.

To the category of mortal sins belong those sins of the regenerate that drive out faith; but for the unregenerate, all sins whatsoever belong here.

Venial sins are so called because the one who sins does not thereby cease to be a believer, and accordingly remains in the state of grace. And such sins are partly the indeliberate motions of faithful people, partly sins of the same people committed from ignorance or passion, which are accompanied by sorrow and repentance.

Four crying sins are especially enumerated: homicide (Genesis 4:10), sodomy, that is, lust most alien to human nature (Genesis 18:20), oppression of the innocent (Exodus 3:7), and the withholding of due wages (James 5:4), though other graver sins are not excluded.

See Acts 17:30 concerning sins that God tolerates.

To the category of remissible sins belong all sins except that which is called the sin against the Holy Spirit.

The irremissible sin is so called because it is by its very nature conjoined with final impenitence. And this is what is called the sin against the Holy Spirit, which must now be discussed somewhat more distinctly.

### 23 The gravest of all actual sins

The gravest of all actual sins, which is called the sin against the Holy Spirit, consists in the malicious denial of heavenly truth already acknowledged, and in its blasphemous and obstinate attack.

Notes. The denomination is taken from the object, which is the Holy Spirit, here considered metonymically with respect to the office that He exercises through the ministry of the Word in converting the souls of human beings. Such an acceptance of the term is also found in 2 Corinthians 3:8. Accordingly, the sin against the Holy Spirit is a sin committed against the office and ministry of the Holy Spirit and against the heavenly truth made manifest through that ministry. It is also otherwise called the sin unto death, a denomination taken from the effect, because it most certainly brings death, that is, eternal damnation (1 John 5:16).

The doctrinal basis for this sin is found in Matthew 12:30 and following, Mark 3:28, and Luke 12:10.

The heavenly truth in question is either doctrine that has been approved by the assent of divine faith and public confession, or doctrine so clearly perceived that the mind, though convicted, has nothing that it can oppose to the matter. In the former manner, apostates sin against the Holy Spirit, who deny and assail with insults the truth once acknowledged and believed; such persons are described by the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews (Hebrews 6:4 and following). To the latter class belong the Pharisees and Scribes, who had never approved the doctrine of Christ by their own confession, yet were so convinced in their minds of its truth from the Scriptures and miracles of Christ that they had nothing to oppose but insults. See the cited passages in Matthew 12:24, Mark 3:22, Luke 12:10, and compare John 11:47 and 48, John 15:12, Acts 4:16 and 17, and Acts 7:51.

The denial and attack of heavenly doctrine occurs ἑκουσίως (willfully) (Hebrews 10:26), so that the principle of the denial and attack is pure and utter malice. Those who deny the faith from ignorance or fear of danger, however, are not therefore sinners against the Holy Spirit, but can obtain remission of their sin. See the examples of Paul (1 Timothy 1:13) and Peter (Matthew 26:70 and following).

For in the cited passages it is called a word that someone has spoken against the Holy Spirit, and blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, and therefore formally it involves a contumelious utterance by which the office of the Holy Spirit is assailed, for example, when His doctrine or His miraculous work, performed for the confirmation of doctrine, is ascribed to the power and operation of Satan, which is what the Pharisees did (Matthew 12:24 and Mark 3:22).

And accordingly this sin is by its very nature such that it cannot be remitted and is never remitted to anyone, according to the cited passages of Matthew and Mark, namely because by its very nature it closes off the way to repentance. The reason why final impenitence is so closely conjoined with this sin is that such persons directly oppose themselves to the means of conversion, and therefore God withdraws His grace from them and delivers them over to a reprobate mind. Nevertheless, it is difficult to pronounce concerning a person still living, as if from prior causes, that he sins against the Holy Spirit (Musaeus, Special Disputation on This Sin, held in the year 1668).

## 16 On Christ, the Beginning and Foundation of Our Salvation

### 1 In order that sinful human beings may be led to eternal salvation

In order that sinful human beings may be led to eternal salvation, they need a mediator, by whose benefit they may obtain from God the blessedness of which they are in themselves unworthy. And this mediator is none other than the one whom Scripture calls Jesus Christ.

Notes. For God is indeed the cause of the conferral of blessedness, yet He will not bestow it upon a sinner unless satisfaction is rendered to His justice. And the goodness of God is indeed the internal impelling cause of our salvation, but in such a way that an external or meritorious cause must also be added, namely the merit of Christ (see above, Prolegomena, ch. 1, section 22, p. 36).

Acts 4:12; 1 Timothy 2:5.

### 2 The doctrine concerning Christ can most conveniently be set forth so as to treat

The doctrine concerning Christ can most conveniently be set forth so as to treat, first, of the Person of Christ, who is the mediator; second, of His states of humiliation and exaltation; and third, of His mediatorial office, and those things connected with it. Let us therefore begin with SECTION I.

ON THE PERSON OF CHRIST.

### 1 In the Person of Christ the following must be considered

In the Person of Christ the following must be considered. First, that Christ is true God, consubstantial with the Father, coeternal and coequal. Second, that the same Christ is true Man, consubstantial with us.

Notes. See what we said above, Part 1, ch. 1, section 29, p. 203, which is here presupposed.

For Scripture expressly calls Him a man, 1 Timothy 2:5; John 8:40; the title "Son of Man" is applied to Him eighty-two times in Scripture. To this belong also the designations "seed of the woman" (Genesis 3:15), "seed of Abraham" (Genesis 17:7; Galatians 3:16), and "branch of David" (Jeremiah 23:5). Moreover, the essential parts of human nature are attributed to Christ: a soul (Matthew 26:38; Luke 23:46) and a human body (John 2:14). Finally, His genealogy is recorded, in the ascending line in Luke 3:23 and following, and in the descending line in Matthew 1:1 and following.

This is what is said in Hebrews 2:14: just as children share in flesh and blood, so the Son of God Himself παραπλησίως (in altogether the same manner), at least as far as substance is concerned, became a partaker of the same.

### 2 From the fact, moreover

From the fact, moreover, that the same Christ is the one whom Scripture describes now as God and now as Man, it is concluded that the Person of Christ is one, subsisting in two natures.

Notes. For instance, the same one who is made of the seed of David is said to be the Son of God (Romans 1:3); the same one who is born of Mary is called the Son of the Most High (Luke 1:35); the same one who is the Word of God and God is said to have become flesh (John 1:14; cf. John 20:28, 31; Galatians 4:4).

For the terms "Son of God" and "Son of Man" in the nominative case denote the Person who possesses either the divine or the human nature.

While the nature itself is signified by the Person in an oblique case.

And this is that greatest mystery, as Paul himself calls it (1 Timothy 3:16; cf. Matthew 16:16-17), which must be examined here above all.

### 3 Once the unity of Person is admitted

Once the unity of Person is admitted, it is necessary further to confess that the human nature of Christ does not possess its own proper subsistence, but subsists by an alien subsistence, namely that of the divine nature.

Notes. For a Person is formally constituted by subsistence in its essential being, and from the unity of subsistence the person must be judged to be one.

It is necessary that one or the other of the natures that coalesce into one person lack its own proper subsistence. And since the divine nature, which is most simply one with its subsistence, cannot lack that subsistence, it is evident that the lack of a proper subsistence must be attributed to the human nature.

Nor does the human nature of Christ thereby become more imperfect than our own nature, since the perfection of a thing is judged from its essence itself, not from its subsistence; and moreover, the lack of its own personality in the human nature of Christ is supplied by the divine subsistence.

### 4 Next, because two natures exist in the one Person of Christ

Next, because two natures exist in the one Person of Christ, through which the same Christ is Son of God and Son of Man, a twofold generation must be considered: eternal and temporal.

Notes. For the relation of being a Son is grounded in generation. Yet through a twofold generation and the twofold filiation grounded in it, there do not come to be two Sons, since both relations inhere in one subject, just as one father can be and customarily is the father of many children, and one lord the lord of many servants, to each of whom he stands in a distinct relation.

By the eternal generation Christ has that He is the Son of God (see Part 1, ch. 1, section 29, no. 3, p. 204).

By the temporal generation He has that He is Man, or the Son of Man (Galatians 4:4, and the passages cited at section 1 above), which teach that Christ truly derives His human nature from other human beings already existing, through a generation that, though not entirely natural, is nonetheless real. And it is the temporal generation that is primarily in view at present.

### 5 Presupposing the eternal generation of Christ

Presupposing the eternal generation of Christ, the temporal generation must be treated in such a way as to explain, in part, the production of the human nature, and in part, its union with the divine nature.

Notes. Our intellect first conceives that the human nature is produced, and then that it, as though already existing, is united to the other nature; although, if one attends carefully, both actions occur simultaneously and at the same time, or perhaps in reality there is only one action.

The production terminates in the human nature considered in itself.

The union terminates in the same human nature insofar as it constitutes one supposit together with the divine nature.

This is called by a single name "incarnation," from the words of John 1:14, ὁ λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο (the Word became flesh), and also "assumption of the human nature," from Hebrews 2:16, where the Son of God is said to have assumed the seed of Abraham. The incarnation and the assumption, although grammatically they are not predicated of the Son in the same way (for the Son is said to be incarnated passively, but to assume actively, that is, to assume the other nature and not to be assumed by it), are nevertheless not in reality two actions but one. For by the very fact that the Son of God becomes flesh, or is incarnated, the human nature is assumed by Him, or He Himself assumes the human nature; and conversely, when He assumes the human nature, He is incarnated.

### 6 The efficient cause of the production of the human nature of Christ is the Holy Spirit

The efficient cause of the production of the human nature of Christ is the Holy Spirit, yet not to the exclusion of the other Persons.

Notes. See Luke 1:35, where the Holy Spirit is said to come upon Mary with respect to producing in her the human nature of the Son of God, that is, as the one who would bring it about that she herself should conceive a human child; and Matthew 1:18, 20, where the preposition ἐκ (from) in the words ἐκ πνεύματος ἁγίου (from the Holy Spirit) is causal and denotes the efficient cause.

For this is a work ad extra. And to this pertains what is said concerning "the power of the Most High," that is, the omnipotence common to the three Persons, which would overshadow Mary (Luke 1:35). For although elsewhere the Holy Spirit Himself is believed to be called "power from on high" (Luke 24:49), it cannot be denied that the very word δυνάμεως (power) denotes potency, and the word ὑψίστου (of the Most High) denotes the supreme God. Hence, literally, "the power of the Most High" is the potency of God, and with respect to an effect really produced outside of God, it assuredly denotes a potency common to the three Persons, even though the work itself may be attributed to one particular Person, namely the Holy Spirit, by way of appropriation, and thus the same Person of the Holy Spirit may be called by the name of divine power.

### 7 The matter is the blood-substance of the Virgin Mary

The matter is the blood-substance of the Virgin Mary, from which the human nature of Christ was made or produced.

Notes. For to be born of a woman, and therefore to derive one's substance from a woman who contributed something of her own to this generation, is what is meant in Galatians 4:4; likewise in Luke 1:42, the child is pointedly called the "fruit of Mary's womb," as drawing thence substance, nourishment, and blood.

And thus the subject or matter of our generation and of the human nature of Christ is, at least in part, the same (Hebrews 2:14).

### 8 The impregnation of Mary itself

The impregnation of Mary itself, and the production of the human nature of Christ effected in her, can be described as a supernatural action by which the Holy Spirit sanctified the blood-substance of the blessed Virgin, and, having conveyed it to the customary place of generation, disposed and elevated it so that from it a perfect human fetus would be formed.

Notes. Scripture calls this an ἐπέλευσις (a coming upon) and ἐπισκιασμός (an overshadowing) (Luke 1:35). For that coming upon is an act by which the Holy Spirit, who is otherwise omnipresent everywhere according to His infinity and immensity, here in Mary manifested His presence by some new and singular effect. And that overshadowing is believed to bear an analogy to that action by which the Holy Spirit in the work of creation, brooding over the waters and as it were warming them, was efficacious for the production of creatures.

Whether, however, the organic body of Christ was fully formed in a single moment and the soul united to it, we do not here dispute.

### 9 It is therefore evident that this conception was most greatly distinct from…

It is therefore evident that this conception was most greatly distinct from that which occurs according to the course of nature, that is, it was miraculous, although Christ the God-man received through it a nature consubstantial with our own.

Notes. Luke 1:34, 37, for not only does Mary there acknowledge that it is naturally impossible for her, who knows no man, nevertheless to conceive and bear a child, but the angel also concurs in this and teaches that one must simply look to the omnipotence of God.

See Hebrews 2:14, 17; cf. section 1 above.

### 10 The union of the human nature with the divine consists in this

The union of the human nature with the divine consists in this, that those natures have been so conjoined as to become one Person. The terminus of the union is either Christ the God-man; or the human nature considered as personally united to the Son of God.

Notes. The Greeks call such a person σύνθετον (composite), where one nature is compounded with the other.

And this is called the terminus "who," or the adequate terminus, and the act of uniting terminates in him in the sense in which actions and passions are said to belong to supposits); or the union itself.

And this is called the formal terminus, or the terminus "by which".

And thus this terminus of the union coincides with the union itself, which exists subjectively in the human nature, for only this nature is perfected through the union, while the divine nature cannot equally be perfected by the human nature or receive anything from it.

### 11 The union itself

The union itself, resulting from the act of uniting, is not just any conjunction of the two natures, divine and human, but rather such a union whereby the divine nature, insofar as it is the nature of the Son of God, or insofar as it subsists in the hypostasis of the λόγος (the Word), has within this very hypostasis the human nature most closely and indissolubly conjoined with itself, and together with it constitutes one ὑφιστάμενον (subsisting being), which is both true God and true man.

Notes. Which is a state or mode of united extremes.

For God is also joined with faithful human beings when He dwells in them as in temples, 1 Corinthians 3:16, whence the one who clings to the Lord is said to be one spirit with God, 2 Corinthians 6:17; but this union or conjunction differs greatly from the personal union.

The ancients, on the occasion of the controversies with Nestorius and Eutyches, declared this union in the following manner: that the two natures in Christ are united, first, ἀσυγχύτως (without confusion), so that a union by mixture is excluded, in which the things united cease to be what they were and are united with one another to constitute a third thing called a mixture; second, ἀτρέπτως (without conversion), so that it is distinguished from that union in which one or the other extreme is absorbed or converted into the other (hence these two terms indicate that each nature, even after the union was effected, retained its essence and properties); third, ἀδιαιρέτως καὶ ἀχωρίστως (inseparably), with respect to intervals of times and places. For this reason the union is called not only most close but also indissoluble, since neither does God by His absolute power ever will to destroy it, nor can anything else destroy it. Therefore we believe that even in the three days of death, although the natural union of body and soul ceased, the personal union nonetheless remained intact, so that the body lying in the tomb was truly the body of the Son of God, and the soul separated from the body was truly the soul of the Son of God.

### 12 And thus it is established that this union is neither a natural or essential union

And thus it is established that this union is neither a natural or essential union, nor, properly speaking, an accidental one.

Notes. For it is indeed a union of two natures, but not a natural one, because neither nature is of itself, or by virtue of being such a nature, ordered toward the other or toward constituting with the other extreme a single third nature; hence it is also not essential, because the united extremes are not essential parts, nor do they coalesce so as to constitute one essential being or one essence.

For the bond and ground of the union is not some accident, but the ὑπόστασις (hypostasis), or personality, which is a substantial mode.

### 13 From the personal union flows the communication of natures

From the personal union flows the communication of natures, through which it comes about that the human nature is the nature of the Son of God, and the divine nature is the nature of the Son of Man.

Notes. To designate this communication the word περιχώρησις (perichoresis), which by its native signification denotes a penetration or the existence of one in the other, began to be employed: the divine nature is said actively to penetrate (to permeate, to perfect) and the human nature is said passively to be penetrated (to be permeated, to be perfected). This must be understood with the removal of all imperfections, however. For the divine nature does not so penetrate the human nature that it successively occupies one part of it after another and extends itself through it in a spatial manner; rather, because it is spiritual and indivisible, it simultaneously as a whole actuates and perfects every part of the human nature and the whole nature, and is and remains whole in the whole human nature and whole in each of its parts. To this pertains the passage in Colossians 2:9: when all the fullness of the Godhead is said to dwell in Christ σωματικῶς (bodily), it must be understood that the divine nature together with all its perfections so exists in the human nature that it permits no part of it to be without itself, and thus intimately penetrates it. This indwelling of the Deity in Christ differs most greatly both from that by which God formerly dwelt in the temple and from that by which He dwells in the saints.

The communication of natures is said to flow from the personal union according to our mode of conceiving; that it really differs from the personal union, however, does not appear.

### 14 Upon the unity of person and the communion of natures are founded

Upon the unity of person and the communion of natures are founded, and serve to declare them, those propositions which are called "personal propositions," in which the concrete of one nature is predicated of the concrete of the other nature: for example, "God is man," "man is God," and the like. These propositions are not merely verbal but in the highest degree real.

Notes. For thus the mode of predication follows the mode of being effected.

The formal ground of predication follows the mode of being, and these propositions are also called "unusual predications," because in all of nature there is no example in which two disparate terms can properly be predicated of one another in the nominative case, or could be so predicated without manifest falsehood. Hence they are not safely called accidental either. For although they might seem to be referable to the accidental mode of predication insofar as in them the predicate falls outside the primary concept of the subject and does not flow from it as a property, one must take care lest, if these predications are called accidental, the union itself, which this mode of predication follows as a mode of being, should be believed to be accidental (see what we said at section 12 above).

By "concrete" is understood a word that signifies the supposit in the nominative case and the nature in an oblique case. Thus "God" denotes a supposit having the divine nature, and "man" denotes a supposit having the human nature. And these, on account of the unity or identity of the supposit, can rightly be predicated of one another. Abstracts, however, which signify natures in themselves without connoting a hypostasis, cannot equally be predicated of one another, since the natures, although conjoined within one person, are nevertheless diverse among themselves. For one cannot say "the divine nature is the human nature," or vice versa.

In the Scriptures, to be sure, we do not read these propositions expressed in so many words; but just as the same thing is signified for the present purpose by the names "God" (understanding the second Person of the divinity), "Son of God," ὁ λόγος (the Word), "Son of the Most High," and likewise by "man" (understanding Jesus of Nazareth), "Son of Man," "Son of Mary," "born of Mary," and so forth, so personal propositions are rightly stated when in Matthew 16:13 (with Christ's approval in the following verse) Peter says, "You, O Son of Man, are that Son of the living God," and in Luke 1:31 it is said, "What will be born of Mary (that is, the Son of Mary) is that Son of the Most High."

For although the predicate does not belong to the subject as such, or according to that nature from which the subject is expressly denominated (as, for example, when it is said "God is man," the sense is not that being a man formally belongs to that supposit or person according to the divine nature), it is nevertheless sufficient that between what is denoted in the subject and what is denoted in the predicate, both in the nominative case, there is a real identity, so that one may rightly say: He who is the Son of God is truly the very same one who is the Son of Mary, and conversely. For in both cases, in the nominative, the person is signified, which is one and the same whether it is denominated from the divine or the human nature.

### 15 Those propositions also in which a concrete of one or the other or both natures…

Those propositions also in which a concrete of one or the other or both natures is predicated of the concrete of the Person can in their own way be referred here, but they are rightly distinguished from the personal propositions properly so called.

Notes. A "concrete of the person" is a word or name that formally signifies the person constituted of both natures: for example, "Christ," "Messiah," "Emmanuel," which names in the nominative case signify the supposit, and in the oblique case signify not either nature alone but rather both.

For example, "Christ is God" or "the Son of God"; "Christ is man" or "the Son of Man".

For example, "Christ is the God-man," or "is God and man at the same time."

These propositions also have something unusual about them, since in the place of the subject stands an individual comprehending equally two natures, divine and human, and therefore the predicate does not belong to it in the way that a species is predicated of an individual (whose entire essence it contains under itself), nor as a genus of a species or individual, nor as a specific difference, property, or accident is predicated, but in a peculiar mode.

Since both natures are contained in the formal concept of "Christ" and "Messiah," the predications by which the concrete of one or both natures is stated of such a subject are judged to be formal.
