Thus Balduin Mentzer, in his Exegesis of the Augsburg Confession(article 3, section 10), advises that predications of this kind be conveniently and usefully distinguished from the personal propositions, as their very definition clearly shows. Cf. the same author (Disputations, vol. 5, Giessen Disputations, disp. 9, pp. 205- 206, section 17), where he says: "When it is said, 'God is man,' or 'Christ is man,' the latter proposition, strictly speaking, is not personal, describing the union itself, but is a description of the whole composite person from one of the natures."

### 16 From the communication of natures there further flows the communication of…

From the communication of natures there further flows the communication of attributes (communicatio idiomatum), through which it comes about that those things which, when the two natures are compared with one another, belong to one of them per se and formally, truly belong also to the other nature.

Notes. The communication of attributes is said to flow from the communication of natures according to our mode of understanding; as to the reality, the communication of attributes does not seem to differ from the communication of natures.

The word "idiom" is here taken broadly, not in the strict sense of what is called a "property in the fourth mode," but for everything that belongs to one or the other nature per se and formally, yet outside its primary concept. Thus the idioms of the divine nature are to be omnipotent, eternal, immortal, and the like; the idioms of the human nature are to be born, to suffer, to thirst, to sleep, to be wounded, to die, and so forth.

This communication pertains either to the concretes, or to the nature itself considered in the abstract, as will appear from what follows.

### 17 Three genera of the communication of attributes are customarily established

Three genera of the communication of attributes are customarily established. The first is called that genus by which God claims for Himself what belongs to man, and man what belongs to God.

Notes. Although it is commonly described through predications, the formal ground is to be located not in the predications themselves but in the real communication that provides the foundation for the predications.

This communication is mutual, whence it is also called ἀντίδοσις (mutual giving) and τρόπος ἀντιδόσεως (the mode of mutual giving).

### 18 The predications pertaining to the first genus of the communication of…

The predications pertaining to the first genus of the communication of attributes are those in which a human idiom is predicated of the concrete of the divine nature, and conversely, a divine idiom is predicated of the concrete of the human nature.

Notes. For example, when from Acts 3:15 it is said, "The Author of life was killed": in the place of the subject stands the supposit having the divine nature, which is of itself and gives life to all others, while the predicate is "to be killed," which does not formally apply to the divine nature (which is of itself impassible and immortal) but belongs to the human nature. Likewise, according to Romans 8:32, "being delivered over to death" is predicated of "God's own Son" as the subject, and in 1 Corinthians 2:8, "being crucified" is predicated of "the Lord of glory."

Conversely, when in John 6:62 it is said, "The Son of Man will ascend to where He was before," our theologians elicit the proposition: the Son of Man was already of old, before the ascension of the human nature into heaven, in heaven. Here the subject is the concrete of the human nature, but the predicate does not belong to it formally according to the human nature, but pertains in this respect to the divine nature.

And these predications are real, although, as our theologians acknowledge, the predication is to be understood κατ᾽ ἄλλο (according to another), not formally according to that nature which the subject denotes in the oblique case, but according to the other nature. For this reason, too, discriminative particles, such as κατά (according to), ἐν (in), κατά (in respect of), and the like, are frequently added, indicating to which nature the predicate formally pertains. See Romans 9:5, where concerning Him who is "God over all," and therefore concerning the concrete of the divine nature, "being born from the fathers" (which is an idiom of the human nature) is predicated; yet the qualifying phrase "according to the flesh" is added, so that you may understand that the predicate belongs to the subject not according to that nature from which the subject is here denominated, but according to the other nature, which consists of flesh and blood.

### 19 Those predications

Those predications, however, in which either the subject is the concrete of the nature to which the predicate formally pertains, or in which the subject is the concrete of the person and the predicate is an idiom of one or the other nature, differ indeed from those that properly pertain to this genus of the communication of attributes, yet they can in their own way be referred here.

Notes. For example, "the Son of God is immense," "the Son of God is eternal"; "the Son of Man suffered," "the Son of Man died".

For example, "Christ is the splendor of the Father's glory"; "Christ was born from the fathers".

Indeed, Leonhard Hutter, writing on Christ (ch. 3, p. 157), after saying that "some describe the first genus of the communication of attributes thus: the first genus is that by which the property of one nature is predicated of the other in the concrete in Christ," and that "others describe it somewhat differently, thus: the first genus is when that which is proper to one nature is attributed not to that nature alone separately whose property it is, but to the whole person who is God and man simultaneously, and then through a discriminative particle it is shown according to which nature this belongs to the person," then offers his own judgment: "Those who hold the former definition seem to have observed more properly the nature of the communication of attributes and to have looked to those expressions of Scripture that show that the λόγος or Son of God so appropriated to Himself the human nature together with its idioms that now the idioms of one nature are predicated of the other in the concrete." And on the preceding page (p. 155), where he likewise treats of those propositions in which "the idioms of both natures are predicated of the whole person of Christ" (on account of which some had established a fourth genus of the communication of attributes), he states his own view in these words: "Since these propositions do not predicate by some communication the idioms of one nature concerning the other nature, either in the concrete or in the abstract, but predicate of the whole person what is attributed to the whole person with respect to one nature, therefore in these propositions, properly speaking, there does not seem to be a communication of attributes." So Hutter in the cited passages, and Schertzer concurs (Schertzer, System of Theology, book 8, p. 198).

The former type of propositions are referred here insofar as the name of the Person stands in the place of the subject, a Person who truly is σύνθετος (composite), that is, constituted of another nature besides the one from which it is denominated, even though it is not distinctly expressed as such. And especially the propositions of the latter class are reduced to this heading, in which, first, the fact that the attributes of both natures can be predicated of the concrete of the person of Christ is due to the fact that the subject is neither a mere man nor merely God, and so that mode of predication arises from the personal union. Second, if one more carefully considers the relation of the predicate to both natures comprehended in the subject and its signification, it will appear that the predicate is formal only by reason of one nature comprehended in the subject, not by reason of the other. Hence, third, in those propositions the use of discriminative particles also has its place; for example, "Christ was born from the fathers according to the flesh" (Romans 9:5). Cf. Johann Musaeus (Detailed Explanation, question 53, pp. 528-529).

### 20 The second genus of the communication of attributes is that by which truly…

The second genus of the communication of attributes is that by which truly divine perfections, and the authority and power resulting from them, as well as the highest honor and glory, are communicated to the human nature of Christ in the abstract.

Notes. With the more modern theologians, we place this genus in the second position, although formerly it generally held the third. It is, however, a declaration of the first genus, and it comes down to this: just as on the part of the natures, although the divine nature is personally united to the human and the human to the divine, this distinction nevertheless exists, that the divine nature intimately penetrates and perfects the human nature, while the human nature does not conversely penetrate and perfect the divine but is penetrated and perfected by it, so also in the communication of attributes this distinction exists on the part of the natures, that the divine nature, penetrating the human, makes that same nature, even abstractly conceived, a participant in its divine perfections in its own manner, whereas the human nature, which neither permeates nor perfects the divine nature, cannot equally make the divine nature, abstractly conceived, a participant in its own properties, nor does it do so. Hence, that each nature in the concrete claims for itself the idioms of the other nature belongs to the first genus; but that the divine nature also bestows its divine properties upon the human nature itself considered in itself (though within the personal union) is referred to the second genus of the communication of attributes.

And indeed all divine perfections have been communicated to the human nature, insofar as on God's part they are simply one; nor can it happen that one is communicated without the rest being communicated. Not all, however, can be predicated of the human nature in the same manner, as we shall presently say. To this pertains what is said in Colossians 2:9: πᾶν τὸ πλήρωμα τῆς θεότητος (all the fullness of the Godhead), and therefore the entire complex of divine attributes, dwells in Christ σωματικῶς (bodily), that is, as in a man, and by the grace of the union. Cf. Matthew 11:27, where Christ Himself says, "All things have been delivered to Me by the Father." What Scripture affirms Christ received in time it does not say He received according to His divinity (according to which He possesses all things from eternity), but that the Person of Christ with respect to the human nature received them in time, according to the most common rule approved by the consensus of the entire orthodox Church, which the Solid Declaration of the Formula of Concord repeats (p. 776).

Specifically, that omniscience has been communicated to Christ according to the human nature is established from John 3:34, where Christ, whom God sent as a man to men, is said to speak the words of God, with the added reason that God gave this one the Spirit of wisdom "not by measure," which is the same as saying that immense or infinite wisdom was given to Him (cf. John 2:24-25). That omnipotence also has been communicated to the same nature is proved from John 5:19, where the power of doing all things that the Father does is said to be given to the Son in time. And in the following verses (5:21, 28), the power of giving life to human beings, both those spiritually dead and those bodily dead, is particularly attributed to Him. To the same point belongs what is said in Matthew 28:18: that all ἐξουσία (authority) in heaven and on earth has been given to Christ. Although this formally denotes the supreme right, the authority, and all power of acting than which no higher exists, nevertheless, since Christ cannot exercise that authority according to the human nature unless omnipotence is also given to it and manifests itself in it and through it, omnipotence is thereby really understood to have been communicated to Christ's human nature; although moreover ἐξουσία (authority) elsewhere customarily denotes δύναμιν (power) or effective force itself.

Indeed, we believe that omnipresence also has been communicated to the human nature of Christ, according to what Christ Himself says in Matthew 28:20: "Behold, I (to whom all power has been given in heaven and on earth, v. 18, and who have now sent ministers to teach and baptize, v. 19) am (according to that same nature according to which all power has been given to Me) with you (wherever in this world you shall be) always." We believe, however, that by this testimony of Scripture it is declared that Christ, according to that assumed nature of His, both can be present with it and is in fact present wherever He wills; and especially we hold that He is present with His Church on earth as Mediator, Head, King, and High Priest. These are the words of the Solid Declaration of the Formula of Concord (article 8, p. 783; cf. p. 387, no. 4), and they clearly describe that omnipresence not as absolute, consisting in a bare and unqualified proximity to all creatures without effective operation, but as qualified, that is, conjoined with effective operation and corresponding to the requirement of that universal dominion which Christ exercises according to both natures, just as the Electoral Saxon theologians also declared in their Solid Decision and its Apology. Cf. Johann Musaeus (Detailed Explanation, questions 56ff., pp. 542ff.).

See also what has just been said concerning the ἐξουσία (authority) communicated to Christ according to the human nature from Matthew 28:18. To this can also be referred the fact that all things are said to be placed "under His feet" (1 Corinthians 15:27-28; Ephesians 1:22). Specifically, there pertains here the power of remitting sins, which is truly divine, yet communicated to Christ insofar as He is man (Matthew 9:6); and the power of executing judgment, given to Christ ὅτι υἱὸς ἀνθρώπου ἐστί (because He is the Son of Man), that is, according to that nature by which He is the Son of Man (John 5:22, 27).

So that all must honor the Son just as (καθώς) they honor the Father: that is, with precisely the same honor that is given to God the Father on account of the supreme excellence of the divine nature and perfections, and not with any other, dissimilar, or inferior degree of worship must Christ, insofar as He is man, be venerated (John 5:23). Hence the adequate object of divine worship ("the object who," or the adequate object) is said to be the supposit itself, Christ; the inadequate object ("the object by which") is said to be not only the divine nature but also the human nature.

The communication pertains to the human nature itself, not only to the concrete or to the person denominated from the human nature and perhaps to be regarded with respect to the divine, but to the human nature itself; not, however, insofar as it is conceived precisely and outside the hypostatic union, but by virtue of the union and insofar as it is considered within that union.

That communication, however, was not made through an essential or natural effusion of the properties of the divine nature into the human nature, as if the humanity of Christ possessed them by itself and separated from the divine essence, or as if through that communication the human nature in Christ had entirely laid aside its natural properties, or been converted into the divine nature, or been made equal in itself to the divine nature by those communicated properties, or as if both natures had the same or at least equal natural and essential properties and operations. The terms and phrases "real communication" and "really communicated" are employed in opposition to a merely verbal communication. See the Solid Declaration of the Formula of Concord (pp. 777-778).

### 21 To this genus of the Communication of Idioms

To this genus of the Communication of Idioms, therefore, belong those predications in which perfections that are truly divine, namely those which in their formal concept have regard to some operation, yet do not involve anything that is altogether repugnant to the truth of the human nature, are predicated. In this way, divine power and glory are also predicated denominatively and immediately of Christ according to His human nature. The remaining divine perfections, however, which of themselves and formally do not have regard to operation, but involve something repugnant to the human nature, are not predicated immediately, but are nevertheless enunciated denominatively of Christ according to His human nature by means of another attribute of the prior kind.

Notes. These are called ἐνεργητικά (operative) attributes, and such are, for example, omniscience, omnipotence, and omnipresence. For omniscience has regard to the act of knowing or understanding; omnipotence to the act of working outside itself or in another; and omnipresence (that is, modified presence) has regard to the exercise of dominion over creatures who are present.

These perfections, namely power and glory, result from those divine perfections; and whoever is a partaker of the latter, and is said to be so, cannot but also be a partaker of, and be said to possess, the divine authority and glory that results from them.

So that, for example, I may say: Christ, as man, is omnipotent. Concerning those propositions, however, whose subject is the abstract term of the human nature itself, which are specifically called "abstractive propositions," the question is customarily raised, for example: "The human nature of Christ is omnipotent," or "The human nature of Christ is omnipresent." The foundation of such propositions is certainly contained in the Scriptures; and one may consider especially the passage where it is stated nearly in these very terms: "The flesh of Christ is the living bread," or "The flesh of Christ is truly food, having the power of conferring life" (John 6:51 ff.), which is the same as if one were to say: the human nature of Christ, to which the word "flesh" corresponds, is life-giving. Concerning the sober and timely use of abstractive propositions, see the theologians assembled at Smalcald in the year 1578 (Hutter, Concordia Concors, ch. 21, p. 680).

Such are simplicity, eternity, and immensity: of which simplicity imports the negation of composition; eternity the negation of a beginning; and immensity the negation of measurability. These cannot stand together with the truth of the human nature, which by its essence is something composite, has a beginning of existence, and is measurable by place.

Namely, although I cannot say, "Christ according to His human nature is eternal," I can nevertheless rightly say, "Christ according to His human nature is omnipotent with an eternal and immense omnipotence," and so forth. Compare Scherzer (Systematic Theology, book 2, p. 200), where he teaches that only those idioms have been immediately communicated to the human nature of Christ which are necessary for the end of the union (that is, for actual use in His office), and which do not overthrow the origin and truth of the human nature. Whence, for example, eternity has not been immediately communicated (that is, not in such a way that it could be immediately predicated of Christ according to His human nature), because it would abolish the origin of the humanity, and so forth.

### 22 The third genus of the Communication of Idioms consists in this

The third genus of the Communication of Idioms consists in this: that the operations pertaining to the office of Christ are not the operations of one nature alone, but are common to both natures, inasmuch as each contributes what is its own, and thus each acts with the communication of the other.

Notes. This genus is placed in the second position by others, and is called κοινοποιΐα or κοινοποίησις (communication or communion of operations). When, however, it is called the Communication of Idioms, it is certain that the word "idioms" is taken more broadly, so that the works of the office, which embrace something proper to the divine nature and something proper to the human nature, are comprehended under that term.

These are commonly called ἀποτελέσματα (completed works), that is, works produced from the actions of both natures, coordinated toward a single end. They are likewise called θεανδρικαί (theandric), or God-manly operations, because Christ operates according to both natures, as θεός (God) and as ἀνήρ (man), in such a way that one supposit or person of Christ is the principle "which" of such a work, while the principles "by which" are the two natures, divine and human, which act distinctly, yet not separately, in that work.

That is, inasmuch as each nature is left to its own powers and properties with respect to its part of the common work. For otherwise, even the human nature, through the majesty communicated to it, performs the same things that the divine nature performs; but this pertains to the second genus of the Communication of Idioms, that is, to the Communication of Majesty.

Thus, for example, in the work of satisfaction or redemption, which includes partly the endurance of the most bitter suffering and death, and partly the addition of infinite value (so that it is not a bare suffering, but a satisfactory one), the former pertains of itself to the human nature, and the latter to the divine nature. Similarly, in the miraculous work by which Christ, to prove His office as Messiah, restored sight to a man born blind (John 9:6 ff.), the human nature of Christ contributed what was its own with respect to the act of spitting on the ground, making clay from the spittle, anointing the clay upon the eyes of the blind man, and finally saying to him, "Go, wash in the pool of Siloam." The divine nature, however, contributed what was its own, namely by infusing powers into those means for the production of that supernatural effect.

Our theologians were preceded in this by Leo the Great, in his tenth epistle, with these words: "Each form," that is, each nature in the person of Christ, "performs with the communication of the other what is proper to itself: the Word, namely, working what belongs to the Word, and the flesh carrying out what belongs to the flesh" (Leo the Great, Epistle 10).

### 23 To this genus, therefore

To this genus, therefore, belong those propositions whose predicate is an operation pertaining to the office of Christ, and whose subject is a concrete name designating the person of Christ either from both natures or from one nature; indeed, even those propositions in which the very name of the office in the concrete is predicated of the person of Christ.

Notes. Such is the proposition: "Christ died for our sins" (1 Corinthians 15:3), where the subject, "Christ," is a name of the person designated from both natures, and the predicate, "to die for our sins," is a work of the mediatorial office, which embraces partly the act of dying, which is a property of the human nature, and partly the addition of infinite value, so that that death might have the character of a ransom for sins. To this correspond the following: "Christ Jesus gave Himself" (namely, unto death) "for our sins" (Galatians 1:4); "Christ gave Himself for us, an offering and a sacrifice to God for a sweet- smelling fragrance" (Ephesians 5:2).

Here belong the following: "The Son of God" (which is a concrete name of the divine nature) "destroys the works of the Devil" (by rescuing men from his power through the merit of His obedience, and by gathering them into the kingdom of grace) (1 John 3:8). "The seed of the woman" (the Messiah, designated from His human nature) "shall crush the head of the serpent" (that ancient serpent, the Devil, whose kingdom and power He will destroy) (Genesis 3:15). "The Son of Man came to save souls" (Luke 9:56).

It is noted that the person of Christ stands in the place of the subject. For the fact that of the human nature in the abstract, beyond those things which are proper to it, those things which are truly divine are also rightly predicated, we have said pertains to the second genus of the communication.

For example: Christ is our Mediator, Savior, King. For it amounts to the same thing, as far as the present matter is concerned, whether you say that Christ operates according to both natures in virtue of His office, or that there belongs to Him a function by virtue of which He operates in a certain manner.

## 17 On the States of Humiliation and Exaltation

### 1 Although the communication of attributes followed the personal union by an…

Although the communication of attributes followed the personal union by an indissoluble bond, and consequently also the communication of majesty, nevertheless that majesty did not always manifest itself in the same manner. Rather, it came to pass that Christ was first humiliated and then exalted.

Notes. See above, Section I, §§ XVI and XX; from which it is clear that just as the divine nature was inseparably united to the human nature, so through that same perpetually enduring union the divine majesty, considered in the first act, always remained communicated to the human nature.

Philippians 2:6ff., especially verse 7, where it is expressly said of Christ ἑαυτὸν ἐκένωσε (he emptied himself), and verse 9, ὁ θεὸς αὐτὸν ὑπερύψωσε (God highly exalted him, or raised him to the highest sublimity).

### 2 The humiliation of Christ therefore pertains to his human nature

The humiliation of Christ therefore pertains to his human nature. This humiliation consists in the fact that Christ, for a time, renounced the full use of the divine majesty which the human nature received as communicated to it in the personal union, and, as a lowly man, endured things that were far beneath the divine majesty.

Notes. For the fact that the Son of God assumed human nature does not mean that the divine nature was properly speaking emptied, nor did it divest itself of its own majesty or become inferior, since it is utterly immutable and ceaselessly exercising its own perfections.

By this divine majesty we understand the μόρφωσις θεοῦ (form of God), in which Christ is said to have existed (Philippians 2:6), where it is added that he did not consider it robbery, that is, he held it as a firm conviction that it was by no means alien to him, nor seized by force, but rightly belonging to him, to be equal with God; and yet he emptied himself.

This renunciation was not such that the use of majesty was perpetual and full but exercised secretly or in a hidden manner; nor as though Christ produced no evidences of divine majesty during the state of humiliation. Rather, he used that majesty more rarely and, as it were, in an extraordinary fashion, but not ordinarily and incessantly. To this pertains what is said in Luke 2:52, that Christ increased in wisdom just as he increased in age and stature.

The "form of a servant" that Christ is said to have assumed (Philippians 2:7) corresponds to what is attributed to him as σχῆμα ὡς ἄνθρωπος (the outward appearance and likeness of men), namely with respect to his external condition.

To this belongs that humiliation even unto death, and indeed the death of the cross.

### 3 In particular, the following must be considered here

In particular, the following must be considered here: the conception and nativity of Christ, his upbringing, his visible life among men, and finally his passion, death, and burial.

Notes. Regarding the conception and nativity, these are to be considered not in themselves precisely, but insofar as the flesh of Christ, although not from the seed of a man, was nevertheless formed in the womb of a woman and from her bodily substance, carried through the customary months, and only then brought into the light. For the opinion held by some, that Mary gave birth to her son with her womb remaining closed, is uncertain.

Regarding his upbringing, this took place in the house of a carpenter (Matthew 13:55), and in such a manner that he was subject to untimely correction (Luke 2:48).

Regarding his visible life among men, he was subject to the magistrate, regarded as equal to or inferior to others, ate and drank to satisfy hunger and thirst, slept when weary, and endured the hardships of labor and travel, dangers, temptations, sorrow, poverty, insults, and the like.

Regarding his passion, there was above all that confluence of afflictions which Christ endured in the two days before his death. To this especially belongs the abandonment mentioned in Matthew 27:46. Christ was indeed abandoned, yet not as if the bond of the personal union was broken, nor as if he had been utterly cast away from the face of God never to be received back into grace, nor did he truly and properly speaking despair. Rather, in the greatest convergence of evils, on account of the sins of mankind imputed to him, he so felt the wrath of God, or God as estranged from him who bore the person of all sinners, that he perceived within himself no consolation from the fullness of the indwelling divinity. In this sense also one should understand what is otherwise said, that Christ endured the pains of hell.

Regarding his death, Christ truly underwent it, so that his soul was separated from his body and his body was deprived of life.

Regarding his burial, by it the reality of his death was confirmed and his lifeless body was given over to rest. And thus, if one adds the time spent in the tomb up to the resurrection, the state of humiliation is concluded.

### 4 The state of exaltation is that in which Christ

The state of exaltation is that in which Christ, according to his human nature, having laid aside the infirmities of the flesh, assumed the full use of the divine majesty.

Notes. For it is opposed to the state of humiliation, and it is readily apparent that exaltation in the proper sense cannot pertain to the divine nature; and as for the fact that the assumption of the human nature into the hypostasis of the Son of God was called by some an exaltation, that does not pertain to the present discussion, where we are considering the exaltation that followed after the state of humiliation.

Thus in Romans 6:9, death is said no longer to have dominion over Christ after the completion of the state of humiliation; and the same reasoning applies to the other infirmities with which the human nature of Christ formerly contended, so that it is denied that Christ is any longer subject to them or can be oppressed by them.

Accordingly, now not only as God but also as man, he knows all things, can do all things, is present to all creatures, and has all things that are in heaven, on earth, and under the earth beneath his feet and in his hand, as the Formula of Concord teaches (Formula of Concord, Article VIII, § XI).

From this it also clearly follows that the adequate foundation of the omnipresence of Christ according to the human nature, that is, an equal and modified omnipresence (or one received in accordance with the majestic dominion which Christ exercises most intimately over all things according to both natures), is established in his exaltation itself (Detailed Explanation, p. 541ff.).

### 5 To the beginning of the state of exaltation must be referred the descent into hell

To the beginning of the state of exaltation must be referred the descent into hell, together with the true and glorious resurrection from the dead. There followed the ascension into heaven, and finally the session at the right hand of the Father provided its completion.

Notes. Regarding the descent into hell, Christ did not undergo some difficult, bloody, or uncertain struggle with Satan, but rather appeared to him, already overcome through the passion and death, in the manner of a victor and triumphator. Present in both soul and body, he displayed himself to the devil and to all the hosts of hell as Lord possessing the highest majesty. In this sense it is said of Christ in 1 Peter 3:18 that, having been put to death in the flesh but made alive by the Spirit, that is, by divine power, by the force of that same power he also went, or truly betook himself, to the underworld, and there preached to the spirits who were in prison (on which see also 2 Peter 2:4 and Jude 6), that is, he showed openly and by deed itself that he is the one who has crushed the head of the serpent and destroyed the works of the devil.

Regarding the time of the descent into hell, although it is not sufficiently clear, we nevertheless do not dare to place it before the moment of the resurrection from death to life, according to what we have just seen from 1 Peter 3:18-19.

Regarding the resurrection, Christ was raised not only by the Father but also by himself, according to what is read in John 10:17-18, that he himself has ἐξουσία (authority), that is, power conjoined with effective capacity, to take up again his soul, or life, which he had freely laid down.

He received the same body that he had before, but now glorified, according to Philippians 3:21, for σῶμα τῆς δόξης (body of glory), by a Hebraism, denotes a glorious body, and of such a kind whose properties are described at length in 1 Corinthians 15:40ff. Hence also he came forth powerfully from the sealed tomb (see Matthew 28:2, 6, where it is recounted that the angel of the Lord removed the stone from the tomb, not to open an exit, but to show others the place already left behind by the risen Christ).

Regarding the ascension, it was indeed true and real, with his body being lifted upward from the earth (Acts 1:9). Yet it should not be scrutinized too closely or defined according to a natural mode so as to deny the presence on earth of the body carried into heaven, for he is said to have ascended not only into heaven but also above all heavens (Ephesians 4:10).

Regarding the session at the right hand of the Father, the right hand of God is not a certain definite place, but the very omnipotent power of God, which fills heaven and earth, according to the sound declaration of the Formula of Concord, Article VIII. Accordingly, he who powerfully and providently governs the whole world, and especially the Church, and rules over all his enemies, is said to sit at the right hand of God (Psalm 110:1-2; Acts 2:34-35).

## 18 On the Office of Christ

### 1 It is certain that the Son of God assumed human nature not out of any necessity…

It is certain that the Son of God assumed human nature not out of any necessity nor in vain, but for the sake of a definite purpose: namely, that in the assumed human nature and through it he might save sinful human beings.

Notes. See Matthew 1:21, 25, where the name of Jesus, the incarnate Son of God, is said to be derived from the act or office of saving, which he performs; moreover, the very name of Christ, which denotes "the anointed one," simultaneously indicates a reference to an office for the undertaking and exercise of which Christ as man was anointed, inasmuch as in the Old Testament and among the people of God, prophets, priests, and kings were customarily anointed and in this manner each was inaugurated into his own office, so also Christ was anointed for the sake of such offices.

That Christ would have assumed human nature even if Adam had not sinned cannot be proven.

### 2 Therefore, in order to attain that end

Therefore, in order to attain that end, Christ the God-man willed to carry out three principal functions. (1). To show sinful human beings the way of escaping from the state of sin and of attaining salvation: this is called the prophetic office. (2). To pay the price of redemption for the fallen human race to God himself and to reconcile him: this is the priestly or, in the strict sense, the mediatorial office. (3). To govern those who adhere to him, to defend them, and finally to make them blessed: this is customarily called the royal office.

### 3 That these may be understood more distinctly

That these may be understood more distinctly, it should be known that Christ was a prophet more excellent than all others, and that He most clearly manifested to human beings the will of God concerning their salvation.

Notes. Thus Peter in Acts 3:22, according to the prophecy of Moses in Deuteronomy 18:15, says that Christ is that prophet like Moses, namely in this respect: that just as Moses excelled above all other prophets with regard to more intimate fellowship with God and the fact that he was not only a teacher but also a leader of the people, so Christ is a prophet κατ' ἐξοχήν (par excellence); although it must be admitted that Christ is not thereby made merely equal to Moses, but surpasses him, as will be clear from what follows.

No longer through types and obscure prophecies but in clear words setting forth the matter to be understood by men so that what was being said could be perceived openly and distinctly. For to be a prophet, whom the Hebrews call איבנ (nabi), is to be an interpreter of God among men, or to convey to men what has been divinely spoken or revealed to oneself. This formerly occurred in the Old Testament in such a way that the prophets, since they themselves were taught through dreams and visions having some degree of obscurity, also taught others about divine matters under such signs, according to the measure of knowledge which God then imparted. A fuller clarity, however, was signified long ago as reserved for the times of the Messiah himself.

Christ instructed people concerning those things that were necessary for belief and action, purified the law of God from Pharisaic corruptions (Matthew 5, 6, 7, and elsewhere), and showed the impenitent and unbelieving the gravity of sins and the wrath of God (Matthew 23; Luke 19:41ff.).

Thus it is said in Matthew 7:29 that Christ taught ὡς ἐξουσίαν ἔχων (as one having authority), that is, that in his own name and on his own authority, as they say, he set forth things to be believed and done alike, and bound and moved the minds of men to give him their assent and obedience (cf. Mark 1:27; Luke 4:32).

### 4 Furthermore, in the prophetic office of Christ one must observe how both the…

Furthermore, in the prophetic office of Christ one must observe how both the human and divine natures each contributed what was proper to them. According to the human nature, Christ taught with a living voice for a full three years and more, He instituted the sacraments to be celebrated in the Church and called to himself ministers of the word and the sacraments. According to the divine nature, however, he conjoined infinite power and authority with the word and the sacraments instituted by him.

Notes. See Luke 4:21; for the act of speaking with a living, articulate voice through the organs naturally designed for forming speech is in substance a human act, which Scripture elsewhere describes by the phrase "opening his mouth," Matthew 5:1; the period of three years that Christ devoted to the office of preaching can be known from the history of his life and the number of Passovers he celebrated after his baptism.

Matthew 26:26; 28:19.

Matthew 28:19; John 20:21.

Mark 16:20; John 20:23.

### 5 Now, however, in the state of exaltation

Now, however, in the state of exaltation, where Christ no longer personally and visibly carries out the ministry of teaching but teaches through his ministers, the prophetic office seems to coincide with the Kingdom of Grace.

Notes. For He certainly causes the divine will to be proclaimed to us and leads people to the knowledge of the truth through the word and the sacraments.

This view indeed appears more suitable than flatly denying that Christ is a prophet in the state of exaltation, for whatever is accomplished through those ministers depends entirely upon Christ, who is with them all days even to the consummation of the age (Matthew 28:20). Compare what will be said below concerning the Kingdom of Grace.

### 6 The priestly office consists in this

The priestly office consists in this, that Christ holds the middle ground between God and men who are at variance with one another, in such a way that he offers sacrifice and prayers on behalf of men to be reconciled with God.

Notes. Christ as a priest is treated especially in Hebrews 4, up to 10.

For the mediatorial and the priestly office of Christ coincide, according to 1 Timothy 2:5- 6, although otherwise not every mediator is also a priest, since arbiters, guarantors, sureties, and others sometimes claim the name of mediator; the prophets themselves could also be called by this name, cf. Galatians 3:19.

This sacrifice is an expiatory offering for the sins of men, as the antitype of the ancient piacular sacrifices (Hebrews 7:27-28; 9:7, 12-14, 25-26, 28; 10:4, 10; See also Hebrews 5:7.

### 7 Moreover, the sacrifice of Christ surpasses the sacrifices of the priests of…

Moreover, the sacrifice of Christ surpasses the sacrifices of the priests of the Old Testament in that those sacrifices were types and shadows of it, and had to be repeated frequently, whereas the sacrifice of Christ is the antitype and contained in itself an expiatory power, and indeed an infinite one, and needed to be performed only once.

Notes. See Hebrews 3, 7, 9, 10.

Those former sacrifices were profitable to men only in virtue of the perfect sacrifice to be rendered by Christ in due time. For it was necessary that the man on whose behalf a piacular sacrifice was offered in the Old Testament confess his guilt and acknowledge that he had merited the wrath of God and punishment, and that in his place a certain animal be slaughtered according to divine ordinance, while he at the same time looked in his mind toward the future Messiah who would be slaughtered and die as a victim for the sins of all men; in consideration of whom God in the meantime permitted that typical act, in which a brute animal is slaughtered and offered, which he himself had instituted or prescribed, to be so pleasing to him that the man on whose behalf the sacrifice was offered by the priest would be deemed worthy of grace and mercy on account of the value of the antitype.

And thus that sacrifice, although not yet performed in the Old Testament, was nonetheless foreseen by God and moved him as an impulsive or meritorious cause to receive sinners into grace (Hebrews 9:12, 14).

### 8 Furthermore, whereas in the other sacrifices the victims offered were distinct…

Furthermore, whereas in the other sacrifices the victims offered were distinct from the priests, Christ sacrificed himself when he voluntarily subjected himself to suffering and death, and thus offered himself to God as a victim for the expiation of the sins of the human race.

Notes. For a sacrifice requires, first, the destruction of the offering, and indeed the slaughter if it is a living being, and second, its oblation or consecration in honor of God.

See Hebrews 9:12, 14; Ephesians 5:2.

Although Christ did not inflict violent hands upon himself, he nevertheless intended his own passion and death when he delivered himself to his enemies (cf. John 10:18). Christ was able to do this because, even though as man he seemed to be bound by the natural law to preserve his own life, as God he had supreme power over all things, and consequently power over the life and death of his human nature; and because it had already been decreed by the eternal counsel of God that he should, at the appointed time, endure death in the place of sinners for their salvation.

And so the killing of Christ, which, with respect to the Jews and Gentiles, was a horrifying crime, was nonetheless, with respect to Christ, a priestly act most acceptable to God (Ephesians 5:2; Hebrews 9:12, 14).

### 9 By that sacrifice

By that sacrifice, that is, by his passion and death, Christ is commonly said to have made satisfaction for us, satisfaction in a strict priestly sense includes also the most perfect fulfillment of the entire divine law performed by Christ on our behalf.

Notes. This term is common among ecclesiastical writers, although Scripture employs the terms "redemption" (Romans 3:24) and "reconciliation" (2 Corinthians 5:18ff.). For that redemption denotes the payment of a price that is sufficient for a captive, and that reconciliation of God with men is so described in the Scriptures that it is clear it was not made without a λύτρον (ransom) which divine justice demanded from the mediator or conciliator (cf. 1 Timothy 2:5-6).

For Christ our mediator truly made satisfaction for us, not only insofar as he took our punishments upon himself, or in our place, but He also paid the λύτρον (ransom) by his suffering, so that we might be freed from the punishments to be endured on account of sins, but also insofar as he rendered perfect obedience to the will of God the lawgiver in our place, and obtained rewards from God for us as if we ourselves had fulfilled the law. The former is called passive obedience; the latter, active obedience.

See Matthew 5:17, where Christ says that he came to fulfill the law, that is, to do fully all that the whole law commands and to abstain fully and completely from all that the law forbids; and to this pertains Christ's entire life in the days of his flesh, with its most holy and most illustrious works conformed to the divine law.

### 10 Christ made satisfaction to the entire Holy Trinity for human beings

Christ made satisfaction to the entire Holy Trinity for human beings, and indeed for all human beings, the elect and the reprobate alike.

Notes. As the offended party, or the supreme lawgiver and Lord of men whose majesty had been violated. Therefore Christ in a certain sense also made satisfaction to himself; for insofar as Christ made satisfaction, he is regarded precisely as mediator, but insofar as he himself also demanded the satisfaction, he is to be regarded precisely as God, the author and avenger of the law, supremely just in his essence, equal with the Father and the Holy Spirit.

But not for himself or for angels; for he himself was not a sinner and therefore not an offender. As for the angels, whether one considers those who did not sin or the rest who fell, just as he did not assume their nature, so neither did he, as mediator, make their cause his own, cf. Hebrews 2:16.

Not only insofar as the value of the satisfaction extends to all, but also insofar as the intention of Christ in making satisfaction extends to all. 1 Timothy 2:6; for he who gave himself as ἀντίλυτρον ὑπὲρ πάντων (a ransom for all), not only for the elect but for all men for whom prayer is to be made, according to verse 1, must be acknowledged both to have been able and to have willed to pay on behalf of all, that is, in the place of each and every sinful human being as those to be redeemed.

For we will show below that election itself rests upon the foreseen satisfaction of Christ, and that notwithstanding the acceptance of another's satisfaction, both salvation and election remain gratuitous.

The reprobate are nevertheless justly rejected and condemned by God, both on account of other sins and especially because they themselves spurn the satisfaction of Christ; God, however, neither wills nor is bound to impute the alien satisfaction of Christ to anyone who does not believe in Christ.

### 11 As for prayers, or intercession

As for prayers, or intercession, Christ our priest offered them indeed for all human beings, but in such a way that in praying for the ungodly, he procured their conversion, while in interceding for the godly, he promoted their constancy and growth in faith and holiness.

Notes. He prayed not only for those who were subsequently converted, but also for those who were not in fact converted. See Luke 23:34, where Christ prayed for those who crucified him without exception; and without doubt among them some, perhaps not a few, persisted in their ungodliness. Yet Christ, in praying for them, showed that as far as it was in his power, he did not wish them to be deprived of the fruit of his death, but rather to be converted and saved.

In this sense Christ had earlier denied (John 17:9) that he was praying for the world, as opposed to the company of the faithful, that is, for the wicked, so that that denial should be understood not absolutely but in a qualified sense (John 17:11).

### 12 Both natures of Christ concur in his priesthood

Both natures of Christ concur in his priesthood, with respect both to the sacrifice and to the intercession. As for the sacrifice, the human nature contributed what was proper to it when Christ went forth to meet his enemies and endured his passion and death; the divine nature contributed the infinite value and power added to the passion and death, so that it sufficed for the expiation of human sins and the appeasement of God. As for the intercession of Christ, the acts of praying themselves, considered in themselves, formally pertain to the human nature, but the dignity and value of those acts derives from the divine nature.

### 13 In the state of exaltation

In the state of exaltation, it must be admitted that Christ no longer offers a sacrifice on our behalf, nevertheless he presents the sacrifice once performed to God, and even now intercedes on our behalf.

Notes. For he is no longer slaughtered or dies: Romans 6:9-10; and in Hebrews 9:12, 25 it is said that Christ the priest differs from the priests of the Old Testament in that they offered sacrifice frequently, whereas he offered it once, namely through his own blood; once offered to take away the sins of many, verse 28; and that with one offering for sins he has sat down at the right hand of God, Hebrews 10:10, 12, 14.

Hebrews 7:24-25, where Christ is said to hold a perpetual priesthood, living so as to intercede for us. And Christ is called the παράκλητος (advocate) of sinners with the Father, 1 John 2:1.

Whether that intercession is verbal, consisting in words and prayers made either by thought alone or also by voice, or whether it is merely real, consisting in this, that Christ by the power of his merit and satisfaction once rendered, and of the prayers once made, moves God to remit our sins, it is not necessary to define (see what is collected from the German Biblical Gloss, Nuremberg edition, and from the writings of Aegidius Hunnius, Balduin, Brochmand, and Gerhard by Musaeus in the Detailed Explanation, book X, question LV, pp. 535ff.; Romans 8:34).

### 14 The royal office of Christ is threefold

The royal office of Christ is threefold: the Kingdom of Power, the Kingdom of Grace, and the Kingdom of Glory.

Notes. That Christ is King is clear from Psalm 2:6 and Luke 1:33.

This threefold distinction arises from the different manner in which Christ the King regards and governs in different ways those who are subject to him. For although, if one considers the words themselves, the Kingdom of Grace and the Kingdom of Glory might seem to be comprehended under the Kingdom of Power, insofar as both truly depend upon the divine power communicated to Christ's human nature, nevertheless the customary usage of speech requires that the Kingdom of Grace be spoken of in relation to spiritual goods in this present age, and the Kingdom of Glory in reference to the glory of the age to come, while the Kingdom of Power signifies universal dominion.

### 15 The Kingdom of Power is that by which Christ powerfully rules over this universe

The Kingdom of Power is that by which Christ powerfully rules over this universe, and both preserves and most providently governs it. Therefore, the subjects in this kingdom are all creatures

Notes. See Daniel 7:14; Matthew 28:18; Ephesians 1:21.

To this pertains what we said about power to be attributed to Christ not only as God but also as man in Section I, § XX, pp. 443, 445.

See Psalm 8:7; 1 Corinthians 15:27; Ephesians 1:20. In particular, the enemies of Christ, whom Christ holds under his feet, are referred to this kingdom (Psalm 110:2; Hebrews 1:13).

### 16 The Kingdom of Grace is that by which Christ gathers

The Kingdom of Grace is that by which Christ gathers, preserves, and abundantly endows with spiritual goods the Church Militant through the word and the sacraments.

Notes. Jeremiah 23:5; Zechariah 9:9; John 18:36-37; 1 Corinthians 10:4.

Matthew 28:19.

Matthew 28:20; Matthew 16:18).

These spiritual goods include both sanctifying and ministering gifts, John 10:9- 10; 1 Corinthians 12:4-5. Therefore to this belongs the institution of the ministry, its preservation, and its concurrence with the labor of the ministers. See Ephesians 4:11; 1 Corinthians 3:7, 9. More will be said in the section on the Church, where the headship of the Church must be treated.

Accordingly, the subjects in this kingdom are the faithful. See John 17:6, 14, 16, where Christ says that his subjects are not of this world but were given to him out of the world. And in 1 Peter 2:9 they are called a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people acquired for God's own possession.

### 17 The Kingdom of Glory is that by which Christ gloriously rules the Church…

The Kingdom of Glory is that by which Christ gloriously rules the Church Triumphant and fills it with eternal felicity. Accordingly, the subjects in this kingdom are the blessed.

Notes. See Matthew 25:31, where a throne of glory is attributed to Christ as King.

See John 17:24. To this belongs the resurrection of the faithful to life and their solemn introduction to glory in the last judgment (Matthew 25:34; Luke 22:29-30).

However, because in the next life Christ will exercise dominion not only over the blessed but also over the damned, some distinguish between the Kingdom of Glory and the Kingdom of Justice, referring to the latter the resurrection of the ungodly from the dead and their condemnation (Matthew 25:41ff.). Others, referring both to the same Kingdom of Glory, say that the glorification of the elect pertains to it in itself, while the damnation of the reprobate (which in itself would belong to the Kingdom of Power) is referred to the Kingdom of Glory in the manner in which opposites are customarily referred to the same faculty.

### 18 And although Christ was made King by the power of the personal union from the very womb

And although Christ was made King by the power of the personal union from the very womb, nevertheless he only began to use the royal majesty fully in the state of exaltation.

Notes. For he received the divine majesty communicated to him at that very moment according to the human nature, as discussed above in Section I, §§ XVI and XX, pp. 437, 442), cf. what we said in Section II, § I, pp. 444- 445.

## 19 On Faith in Christ

### 1 In order that sinful human beings may attain eternal salvation through Christ the Mediator

In order that sinful human beings may attain eternal salvation through Christ the Mediator, faith in Christ is required, that is, they must believe in Christ as Mediator.

Notes. Although through the passion and death of Christ there was truly rendered whatever satisfaction could be demanded from all human beings in the world for the abolition of the debt contracted through their offenses, and thus for the appeasement of God and for reconciling them to Him, God nevertheless willed that sinners should acknowledge that satisfaction rendered on their behalf by the Son of God, and by faith apprehend it and make it their own. Thus He willed that whoever embraces the Mediator by faith should enjoy His merit, and should have God actually reconciled to himself and wholly favorable for the conferring of salvation; but conversely, if anyone does not apprehend the Mediator by faith, that person should likewise be deprived, through his own fault, of His satisfaction and of the grace of God, and should remain under the offense of God, according to John 3:16, 18, 36 (Musaeus, On Conversion, disputation 3, ch. 2, § 91, p. 144).

Faith in Christ is called by Paul "faith in his blood," that is, faith fixed upon the merit and satisfaction of Christ, which He rendered for us by the shedding of His blood; by which reasoning He is also set forth to us as a hilasterion (propitiatory sacrifice or means of appeasement) (Musaeus, On Conversion, same place). It is also called "the faith of Christ," that is, faith whose object is Christ (Galatians 2:16). Otherwise, indeed, the doctrine of faith itself is also called "faith," as in Galatians 1:23, 3:2, 5, and Ephesians 4:5. But here what is to be considered is not faith which is believed, but faith by which one believes.

See especially John 3:14, 15, 16, 36.

### 2 To faith in Christ there pertains

To faith in Christ there pertains, first, knowledge, and indeed explicit knowledge of the things to be believed, especially concerning Christ and His merit, and the grace of God, that is, the remission of sins and salvation to be obtained from God through that merit.

Notes. For we cannot believe what we do not apprehend with the mind or have not come to know by simple apprehension. Hence knowledge is commonly called the first degree of faith, or the first part or beginning of faith (see Detailed Explanation, pp. 575, 576).

By "explicit" knowledge is meant the kind by which the thing to be believed, even if it is not known evidently, or even if all the knowable aspects contained in it are not actually attained by the act of cognition, is nevertheless known distinctly, that is, in such a way that it can be distinguished from other objects. To this is opposed "implicit" knowledge, by which someone is thought, for example, to believe that Christ is the Mediator when he believes that whatever the Church believes is true, even though he himself has no knowledge at all of what it is that the Church believes (Musaeus, On Conversion, disputation 3, ch. 2, § 96 and following, pp. 146, 147).

On the things to be believed, see the Prolegomena, chapter 1, § 27 and following, p. 40 and following; and § 31, 32, pp. 45 and following.

From this it is clear that when faith is named "faith in Christ" from its object, other things are not thereby excluded but rather included, namely the grace of God and the gratuitous divine promises concerning the remission of sins and salvation on account of Christ (Musaeus, On Conversion, disputation 3, ch. 2, § 101, p. 148, and § 142 and following, pp. 177 and following).

That such knowledge is required for faith in Christ is proved from John 6:69: "We have believed and have come to know that you are the Christ, the Son of God"; and from John 17:3: "This is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent." So also in Luke 1:77, saving faith is described through "the knowledge of salvation," and so forth. And the opposite, unbelief, is called ignorance (Acts 17:23, 30; Ephesians 4:18).

### 3 Second, to faith in Christ there pertains assent

Second, to faith in Christ there pertains assent, that is, a judgment of the intellect by which those things that are handed down in the Scriptures, especially concerning Christ the Mediator and the grace of God and salvation to be obtained through Him, are judged to be truly declared; and this on account of divine revelation, that is, the truthfulness of the revealing God, and grace working inwardly in the heart in a supernatural manner, that is, concurring with the word of Scripture.

Notes. This is otherwise called the second degree or second part of faith, and it is certain that faith in its formal concept involves assent resting upon the authority of the one who speaks or testifies.

Thus Paul says that the things of the Spirit of God are "spiritually discerned," anakrinesthai (1 Corinthians 2:14, 15).

Although it is necessary for a person who is to be saved to believe that all things contained in the sacred Scriptures are true, nevertheless in this place, when we are treating of faith as a cause of salvation, it is to be considered in relation to that special or particular object which has the power of recovering the salvation lost through sin, and in view of which faith itself can be reckoned among the causes of salvation.

Thus the eunuch, in Acts 8:37, after Philip's discourse in which he had preached Jesus to him, when Philip asked whether he believed with all his heart, responded: "I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God."

The teaching of Scripture itself, moreover, must be en apodeixei pneumatos kai dynameōs (in demonstration of the Spirit and of power), according to 1 Corinthians 2:13 (see Prolegomena, ch. 2, § 32, pp. 101 and 104).

### 4 Moreover, it is also required for faith in Christ

Moreover, it is also required for faith in Christ, considered with respect to assent, that a person should descend from the universal propositions concerning Christ the Mediator and the grace to be obtained through Him to himself as an individual, and believe that Christ suffered and died for him. Hence this is also customarily called "special faith."

Notes. For example, "Christ gave himself as a ransom for all" (1 Timothy 2:5); "He died for all" (2 Corinthians 5:15); "He is the propitiation for the sins of the whole world" (1 John 2:2).

For such is the force of universal signs that, when added to some common term (for example, "human being"), they signify that what is said of the common term applies to all the individuals contained under it. These universal signs are also read in Scripture as having been so frequently added and impressed upon this present matter, so that sinners who are anxious and troubled about their sins might raise themselves up by the universality of the satisfaction rendered by Christ for the sins of all, and by the grace thereby restored and the remission of sins, and might safely and firmly believe that these things pertain to them also as individuals. Without this universality, if it did not exist, the sinner would have no ground from which to raise himself up amid the terrors of conscience and the sense of divine wrath on account of sins. For one cannot argue from a particular, nor from the fact that Christ died for some and merited the grace of God and the remission of sins for certain persons, can any sinner infer determinately and as an individual, and conclude that Christ also made satisfaction for him, and so forth (Musaeus, On Conversion, disputation 3, ch. 2, § 107, 108, pp. 153, 154; compare also Prolegomena, ch. 1, § 32, p. 48).

Thus Job, making a profession of his faith, said: "I know that my Redeemer lives" (Job 19:26). And Paul says in Galatians 2:20: "The life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me."

And so it is clear that faith is not called "special" on account of promises or revelations that have been made specially and in particular to each believer, but both from the special object toward which it is directed, namely Christ the Mediator and the promises concerning the grace of God and the remission of sins and salvation on account of Christ, and from its special application to the one who believes (Musaeus, On Conversion, § 110 and following, pp. 155 and following; and On the Church, part 1, disputation 1, § 61, pp. 38, 39).

### 5 Besides knowledge and assent on the part of the intellect

Besides knowledge and assent on the part of the intellect, faith in Christ also includes, on the part of the will, trust, that is, an act of such a kind by which the will rests in Christ the Mediator as in a present good that is ours, and as the cause of obtaining another good, namely the remission of sins and eternal life.

Notes. For just as Christ the Mediator is set forth in the Scriptures not for the sake of bare or speculative knowledge, so that He might be understood merely as something that is truly so, but rather so that He might have the character of our good, and might be presented to us as the meritorious cause of obtaining salvation, so it must be acknowledged that the will of human beings can and ought to be moved by Him toward the pursuit of Him, that is, so that by an act of trust it may rest upon Him and raise and comfort itself against the wrath of God and the stings and terrors of conscience.

For trust, speaking generally, is thus defined and is distinguished from hope: trust has for its object a present good, upon which the will relies as the cause of another good; hope, however, has for its object an absent good, which the will expects and anticipates as attainable and to be obtained (Musaeus, On Conversion, disputation 3, ch. 3, § 121 and following, pp. 164 and following).

Those goods are called "present" with respect to trust not only which are really and physically present, but also which are morally present by reason of some merit and value, or are apprehended as present. Accordingly, the faithful in the Old Testament could rightly place their trust in the coming Messiah and in the satisfaction for sins to be rendered by Him at some future time; and we trust in that same satisfaction once rendered through His passion and death. For Christ and His passion and death extend themselves morally and by reason of their merit to all past ages, and likewise to present and future ones, and at every time were the cause for believers of obtaining the remission of sins and salvation, so that in this respect also we may say with the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews: "Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever" (Hebrews 13:8) (Musaeus, On Conversion, disputation 3, ch. 3, § 127, p. 166).

For goods, however present they may be, will not be of assistance to us so that we may trust in them, unless they are ours, or at least pertain to us in some way on account of a friendship and covenant that we have with the one to whom they belong, and are in this regard reckoned as ours. And so, although the merit and satisfaction of Christ were not rendered by us but by Christ, yet because they were rendered by Him on our behalf and in our place, and God regards them just as if they had been rendered by us ourselves, we rightly reckon them among things that are ours or that pertain to us (Musaeus, On Conversion, disputation 3, ch. 3, § 128, p. 167).

Trust in Christ differs from love of Christ in this: that love has Christ absolutely as its object, whereas trust has Him as its object under the relation of a known cause for obtaining another good (Musaeus, On Conversion, disputation 3, ch. 3, § 129, p. 167; § 139, 140, pp. 174, 175).

Indeed, inasmuch as the goods obtained through Christ are many and varied, according to Ephesians 1:3, 2 Corinthians 1:20, and John 16:23, trust in Christ generally has for its object Christ as related to obtaining various goods, both bodily and spiritual, by way of cause. Here, however, we are treating not of any trust whatsoever, but of that trust by which a sinful human being strives to attain the grace of God and eternal salvation; just as it must also be acknowledged that all trust in Christ as the cause of obtaining other goods is ultimately resolved into trust in Him as the cause of reconciliation with God and of the remission of sins (Musaeus, On Conversion, disputation 3, ch. 3, § 141, pp. 175, 176).

That faith in Christ includes, beyond the act of believing in the intellect, also trust in Christ on the part of the will, is proved from Romans 3:24 and following, where the object of faith is constituted as Christ set forth as a hilastērion (propitiatory sacrifice), a means of appeasing divine wrath, set forth in His blood, that is, inasmuch as through the shedding of His blood, that is, through His passion and death, He is the meritorious cause for appeasing divine wrath and obtaining the remission of sins before God. From this it is immediately evident that this faith is not a bare assent without any act of the will concerning Christ (for in that case it would be dead faith); and because it has conjoined to it some act of the will concerning Christ, this act is itself the act of trust, since it is occupied with Christ as the cause for obtaining some good, namely the grace of God (Musaeus, On Conversion, disputation 3, ch. 3, § 161 and following, p. 194, where, by the example of Abraham believing in Him who justifies the ungodly, that is, believing in God who, although just and an avenger, nevertheless for the sake of the Messiah the Mediator grants grace to sinners, and so forth, he demonstrates the same at length). Moreover, it is clear from other passages that to pisteuein eis ton huion (to believe in the Son), as it is stated in opposition to apeithein tō huiō (to disobey the Son) in John 3:36, is the same as to confide in the Son, that is, to place one's trust in Him (Musaeus, On Conversion, § 171, 172, pp. 214 and following).

### 6 This, therefore

This, therefore, is that faith which is said to apprehend Christ, or the merit of Christ: namely, as it is assent conjoined with trust, or trust conjoined with assent; from which acts, as it were united, it consists and is sometimes called by the name of the one, sometimes of the other, with the other always being connoted.

Notes. To this is referred the phrase labōn ton Christon (receiving Christ) in John 1:12 and Colossians 2:6. It is understood, however, that this is not a bodily but a spiritual apprehension, which takes place by the mind or soul, and is therefore metaphorical, drawn from the likeness of a hand grasping a friend or some other thing, such as alms (Musaeus, On Conversion, disputation 3, ch. 4, § 189, p. 222).

Otherwise, apprehension pertains to the first operation of the mind and is almost always called, with a fitting qualifier, simple apprehension or apprehension of simple things. But in this place, to apprehend is the same as, on the part of the intellect, to transfer a thing to oneself by knowing it, and on the part of the will, to be carried by desire toward the thing known as toward one's own good and the cause of other goods to be obtained; and to hold it, as it were, clasped in one's hand lest it be snatched away (Musaeus, On Conversion, disputation 3, ch. 4, § 200, p. 220, and § 206, pp. 233, 234). And here belongs the plērophoria (full assurance) of faith, of which Romans 4:18 and following speaks: namely, that the mind of the believer is fully carried toward the object, that is, according to every respect in which the object is presented to it; by the intellect, indeed, insofar as it is presented under the character of the true, and by the will, insofar as it is presented under the character of the good and the desirable (Musaeus, On Conversion, § 183, p. 207).

Hence it is clear how faith exists in diverse faculties, the intellect and the will: namely, as an aggregate or complex composed of diverse acts terminated at the same object, and having a certain order among themselves and toward that one and the same object (Musaeus, On Conversion, disputation 3, ch. 3, § 179, p. 210).

Thus faith is described through the act of believing that Jesus is the Christ (John 6:69; 1 John 5:1, and so forth), in which manner assent is formally signified, though trust is to be understood as implied. At other times, however, it is described through the act of believing in Christ, that is, resting upon Him by an act of trust, with the assent of the intellect connoted or presupposed (John 3:36; compare § 6 above, notes a and g). Similarly, pepoithēsis (confidence), which is ascribed to faith, sometimes signifies a firm persuasion of the mind, as in Romans 8:38, 39 and 2 Timothy 1:12, and sometimes trust fixed upon someone, as when it is said pepoitha en Kyriō (I have confidence in the Lord) in Philippians 2:24; and so it signifies persuasion of mind together with trust, or trust together with a firm persuasion of the soul.

### 7 It is also clear at the same time how the merit of Christ itself

It is also clear at the same time how the merit of Christ itself, and the remission of sins and eternal life acquired for all human beings by Christ, are applied to believers through faith, so that they are truly made partakers of them.

Notes. On the acquisition of merit by Christ, see above chapter 1, section 3, § 2, p. 455.

Just as the merit of Christ, so also the promises concerning the gratuitous remission of sins on account of Christ are of themselves indeterminate and extend to all human beings; but when they are actually to benefit this or that particular person, it is necessary that there be some means of uniting between that person and those things, by which the merit of Christ, indeterminate in itself, and the gratuitous general promises may be referred to this or that individual, or may become his own (Musaeus, On Conversion, disputation 3, ch. 4, § 215, p. 240). Hence even the promises of grace and of the remission of sins themselves include faith (John 3:16; Acts 10:43). Yet it does not follow from this that one who believes in Christ must also believe that he believes in Christ, as Musaeus demonstrates (Musaeus, On Conversion, disputation 3, ch. 2, § 115 and following, pp. 159 and following).

For otherwise that saying of Christ holds: "No one comes to the Father," that is, to obtain grace before Him, "except through me," that is, through the Mediator between God and human beings, acknowledged and believed (John 14:6; Musaeus, Disputation on the Salvation of the Gentiles, against Curcellaeus, § 22).

Meanwhile, God applies the merit of Christ to a person in one way, and the believing person applies it to himself in another. For the application that is made by the person through faith does not differ, as to the thing itself, from faith in Christ itself, that is, from the acts of assent and trust by which one is directed toward Christ. But the application by which God applies the merit of Christ to a person consists in this: that God accepts that merit of Christ, even though it is not the person's own proper merit but an alien one, just as if it were his own, namely because it was rendered in his place and has been apprehended by him through faith. More will be said on this in the section on justification.

### 8 Faith in Christ therefore holds a place among the principles and causes of salvation

Faith in Christ therefore holds a place among the principles and causes of salvation, not of itself, and not as it is an act or habit of believing, but by reason of the object toward which it is directed, and which it apprehends and applies to the believer.

Notes. For the dignity, power, and value of faith itself, considered absolutely in itself, is not and cannot be so great before God that we might suppose God to be moved by it to confer salvation upon us (compare Prolegomena, ch. 1, § 23, note b, p. 37; and Musaeus, Introduction, ch. 3, § 48, pp. 138, 139; more will be said in the sections on justification and predestination).

That object, namely, is the merit of the God- man (theanthrōpos), and through this it is a merit of infinite price, weight, and value; and it suffices for this purpose, that in view of it the divine will should determine itself to receive us into grace and to bestow salvation upon us.

The reason, therefore, why salvation is attributed to faith, just as to the merit of Christ, as to a cause, is precisely this: that faith is intimately conjoined with the merit of Christ, not only as an act with its object, but in such a way that it unites the thing itself with which it is concerned to us, so that it becomes ours. Hence it is also clear how faith, or fiducial assent, can accomplish this, whereas love cannot equally do so (Musaeus, On Conversion, disputation 3, ch. 4, § 215, p. 240).

### 9 A property of faith in Christ is certainty

A property of faith in Christ is certainty, both on the part of the object that is believed, to which falsehood cannot belong, and on the part of the subject, that is, the one who believes, who most tenaciously adheres to and relies upon the divine promises as those in which deception cannot reside.

Notes. For this certainty flows into the assent of faith from the formal object, which is revelation founded upon the supreme truthfulness of God (see Prolegomena, ch. 1, § 35, p. 57).

This is what they call the certainty (others call it the firmness) of adhesion, which consists in this: that the intellect, notwithstanding the lack of evidence of the object, nevertheless by divine power, without fear of error and without hesitation, assents to those promises; and the will adheres to them with trust; and so, with doubts overcome, and with the impulses of the flesh and various temptations surmounted, the mind of the person, with the help of God's grace, enjoys a most efficacious consolation.

The passages of Scripture that prove this certainty of faith are those in which there is attributed to faith pepoithēsis (confidence), that is, the most firm adhesion of the soul to the divine promises (Ephesians 3:12); plērophoria (full assurance), meaning that we are carried by the full impulse of the soul toward those promises (Romans 4:18 and following; hence Abraham is said to have "believed against hope in hope, not to have wavered through unbelief, but to have grown strong in faith," Romans 4:18, 20). Faith itself is also called hypostasis elpizomenōn (the substance of things hoped for), insofar as those things that are hoped for as future are, as it were, made present through faith; and elegchos pragmatōn ou blepomenōn (the conviction of things not seen), insofar as those things that are not perceived by the eyes are nevertheless presented to the intellect through faith, as though known with certainty by demonstration (Hebrews 11:1).

### 10 Faith in Christ has necessarily conjoined with it hope and love

Faith in Christ has necessarily conjoined with it hope and love, although these do not equally have the character of a cause of salvation.

Notes. Although trust and hope differ in that trust is concerned with a present good that is ours and is the cause of another good, while hope is occupied with a future or absent good so that it may become ours, and arises from the will's resting in a present good that can be a cause or aid for obtaining another good (Musaeus, On Conversion, disputation 3, ch. 3, § 130, p. 168), yet insofar as faith in Christ looks toward salvation to be obtained through Christ, it is a certain security of the will concerning salvation to be obtained through Christ, which cannot but be conjoined with the hope of obtaining it (Musaeus, On the Church, part 1, disputation 1, § 80, p. 55).

Indeed, the faith by which we desire Christ and the other goods to be obtained through Him for ourselves involves a different act from that by which we love Christ, that is, by which we wish well to Christ Himself or desire good for Him (Musaeus, On Conversion, disputation 3, ch. 3, § 140, p. 175, and § 158, p. 193; ch. 4, § 207, p. 235). Yet that trust is not without love. For when our will regards Christ as a present good, and God as appeased and made propitious to us on account of Christ, it not only pursues Him with the love of complacency, but it is also moved to wish Him well, that is, to desire to render what would be good and pleasing to Him (Musaeus, On Conversion, same places; and On the Church, part 1, disputation 1, § 76, p. 51, and § 80, p. 55). More will be said in the section on Renewal.

Neither hope nor love possesses meritorious power such that by some dignity of its own it could move God to give salvation to a person; nor do they unite the merit of Christ to us or make it ours so that it might benefit us.
