Rather, faith, insofar as it involves the apprehension of the merit of Christ through assent and trust, accomplishes this (Musaeus, On Conversion, disputation 3, ch. 4, § 215, p. 240). More will be said in the section on Justification.

### 11 It also happens to faith in Christ that it can be lost by human beings through…

It also happens to faith in Christ that it can be lost by human beings through sins against conscience, and that it is sometimes lost, not only for a time, but also in such a way that it is never recovered.

Notes. On account of the demerit of such sins, the Holy Spirit, by virtue of divine justice, can withdraw that undeserved influence upon which supernatural habits depend for their being; hence, just as grace and love, so also supernatural faith (to which it is natural that it cannot exist without grace and love) can be expelled morally and by way of demerit (Musaeus, On the Church, part 1, disputation 1, § 82 and following, pp. 58 and following).

To this belong those who are proskaroi (temporary believers), who believe for a time (Luke 8:13; Matthew 13:21, 22; Mark 4:17, 19; compare also 1 Timothy 1:5 and 19). Examples of those who lost faith for a time are David and Peter. For those who lost it permanently, see Hebrews 6:4 and following, and 2 Peter 2:20.

### 12 Therefore, just as a person through the act of believing in Christ immediately…

Therefore, just as a person through the act of believing in Christ immediately obtains the grace of God and the inheritance of salvation, so in order actually to attain eternal salvation after this life, it is necessary that faith be final.

Notes. According to what we have said above in §§ 1 and 6, and as will appear more distinctly from what is to be said in the section on Justification, in the meantime see Romans 8:1, 16, 17, 24.

That is, it is necessary that a person either never lose through his entire life the habitual faith born from acts of believing (which will be explained more clearly in the section on Conversion), or if he has perhaps lost it through sins, that he recover it before death and preserve it; certainly he must take care lest death overtake him while he lacks both the act and the habit of faith. Hence it is said in Revelation 2:10: "Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life" (compare also Revelation 3:11, 14:13, and Matthew 24:13).

## 20 On Regeneration and Conversion

### 1 Since it is established that Christ profits no one unto salvation unless that…

Since it is established that Christ profits no one unto salvation unless that person believes in Christ, we must consider by what action faith in Christ is conferred upon human beings, which action is commonly called regeneration or conversion.

Notes. Thus in Titus 3:5 παλιγγενεσίας (regeneration) is mentioned in relation to obtaining justification through the grace of Christ, and so that we might be made heirs according to the hope of eternal life. And Christ in John 3:3 and following says that a birth from above, or from the Spirit, which must follow birth from the flesh, is so necessary that unless someone is born in this manner, he cannot see the kingdom of God or enter into it. And so, since that inheritance and entrance into eternal life is not obtained except through faith in Christ (to which the words of John 3:15, 16, 17, 18 also point), it is readily established that regeneration consists in this: that faith is generated in human beings, and accordingly human beings are changed from unbelievers into believers. Furthermore, in 1 John 5:1, "Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ" is said to be "born of God." To be born of God, however, is to be reborn; and so it is plainly established that a person is reborn by the very fact that faith is kindled in him (cf. Musaeus, Disputations on Conversion, Halle edition, Disputation 1, section 15). In other respects, regeneration is indeed taken more broadly, insofar as it encompasses conversion, justification, and renovation; but here the stricter signification is intended (cf. Musaeus, same work, and Disputation 2, sections 9 and 10; Disputation 5, section 61).

In Acts 15:3, the ἐπιστροφὴ τῶν ἐθνῶν (conversion of the Gentiles) is mentioned, which Peter then explains by saying that the Gentiles believed the word of the Gospel (verse 7), and that God purified their hearts by faith (verse 9). Compare verse 19 and Acts 26:18.

### 2 Moreover, infants are regenerated equally with adults

Moreover, infants are regenerated equally with adults: the former through baptism, the latter through the word and baptism, although what the nature of infant faith may be can scarcely be defined with sufficient clarity.

Notes. For what is said in John 3:3 and Titus 3:5 concerning regeneration is common to human beings of every age, since all are able to be baptized; on which we shall see below in the chapter on Baptism. In the meantime, see Musaeus (same work, section 17).

Infants are not yet capable by reason of age of hearing the word.

To adults pertains what Peter says (1 Peter 1:23), where he tells the faithful (on whom see verses 21 and 22) that they have been "born again, not of mortal seed but of immortal, through the living and abiding word of God." And James says that "God brought us forth by the word of truth" (James 1:18).

That is to say, although faith is generated through the word in adults before baptism, it is nevertheless sealed through baptism.

Concerning infant faith, however, together with Chemnitz (Chemnitz, Examination of the Council of Trent, Part 2, on Baptism, at Canon 13, according to the Formula of Concord established among the theologians of Saxony and Upper Germany in the year 1536), we judge that when infants are said to believe, one must not imagine that infants understand or feel the movements of faith; rather, the error of those is rejected who imagine that baptized infants please God and are saved without any action of the Holy Spirit in them, since Christ clearly says, "Unless one is born again of water and the Spirit," and so forth. Therefore it is necessary that the Holy Spirit be efficacious and operative in infants who are baptized, so that they might be able to receive the kingdom of God, which is offered and bestowed in baptism, in their own manner, one neither sufficiently known to us nor explicable. See further in the same place.

### 3 And so, since regeneration implies a certain spiritual change

And so, since regeneration implies a certain spiritual change, the terms "from which" and "to which" must be noted.

### 4 The terminus from which is the lack of spiritual powers for faith and other spiritual acts

The terminus from which is the lack of spiritual powers for faith and other spiritual acts; and accordingly, on the part of the intellect, an inability to know spiritual objects; on the part of the will, an inability to pursue spiritual goods; on the part of the sensitive appetite, an unfitness to obey the Spirit and to restrain the desires of the flesh.

Notes. This is just as in other cases, where through generation one passes from non- being (for example, of a human being) to the being of a human being. Here, however, that from which regeneration begins and which is removed through it is called the death of sin (see Ephesians 2:1; cf. Musaeus, Disputation 2 on Conversion, Halle edition, sections 5, 6, and 12).

Hence it is evident that what was said above concerning original sin pertains here. And it should be noted what Christ says (John 6:65): "No one can come to me (that is, believe in me) unless it has been given to him by my Father."

Thus the Ephesians, such as they were before they were reborn, are called "darkness" by Paul (Ephesians 5:8), that is, lacking spiritual light, or the powers of knowing spiritual things.

Furthermore, the will, such as it is through the carnal condition, "is not subject to the law of God, nor indeed can it be" (Romans 8:7).

For in that state, sin has not yet ceased to reign in the body, whence human beings rather obey it through its lusts (Romans 6:12).

### 5 The terminus to which of regeneration is spiritual powers

The terminus to which of regeneration is spiritual powers, or spiritual life, which indeed on the part of the intellect imports spiritual light, or the powers of rightly judging concerning spiritual objects or assenting to them; on the part of the will, powers of pursuing spiritual goods, especially of trusting in Christ; on the part of the sensitive appetite, a certain faculty by which it begins to be brought under the obedience of the Spirit.

Notes. This is considered in first act, which relates to actual spiritual life as a principle. Hence regeneration is also otherwise called vivification (cf. Musaeus, Disputation 5 on Conversion, Halle edition, sections 2 and following).

Thus the Ephesians, once reborn, are called "light in the Lord," that is, endowed with spiritual light (Ephesians 5:8). Elsewhere those who are reborn are said to be "in the light" (1 John 2:9) and "enlightened" (Hebrews 6:4).

Accordingly, the spiritual person is said to judge spiritual things differently from the natural person, who regards them as foolishness and cannot understand them (1 Corinthians 2:14).

This is called habitual trust, or trust in first act.

The transformation of the sensitive appetite extends at least so far that the generation of saving faith in the intellect and will is not continually impeded by the desires of the flesh. A fuller change and perfection of the sensitive appetite belongs to renovation, of which in its proper place. See in the meantime Musaeus (same work, Disputation 2, section 19).

### 6 The principal efficient cause of regeneration is the triune God

The principal efficient cause of regeneration is the triune God.

Notes. This is a supernatural work of conferring spiritual life, accomplished by God's own infinite power.

Thus James says that the Father of lights, from whom every good gift descends, has "brought us forth" (James 1:18).

For it is a work ad extra, and it terminates in an effect really produced within the human being through a power common to the three persons. Hence it is also attributed to the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ (1 Peter 1:3) and to the Holy Spirit (Titus 3:5), when the "washing of regeneration of the Holy Spirit," that is, through which the Holy Spirit regenerates human beings, is mentioned.

### 7 The internal impulsive cause is the mercy of God

The internal impulsive cause is the mercy of God.

Notes. Moved by this, God willed not to allow us, wretched human beings dead in sins, to perish, but willed to call us back from the death of sin into spiritual life.

This is proved from 1 Peter 1:3, where God is said to have regenerated us κατὰ τὸ πολὺ αὐτοῦ ἔλεος (according to his great mercy); and from Ephesians 2:4 and 5, where we read that God, rich in mercy, on account of the great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead through trespasses, made us alive together with Christ. See also Titus 3:5.

### 8 The external and meritorious impulsive cause is Christ the Mediator

The external and meritorious impulsive cause is Christ the Mediator.

Notes. For in order that God might deal with us according to his mercy, with his justice preserved, and bring us who were dead in sins to spiritual life, this is owed not to our own merit but to the merit and satisfaction of another.

By virtue of his merit, passion, and death for us, grace is said to have come through Jesus Christ (John 1:17), given to us through Christ (1 Timothy 1:14), and we are called κτισθέντες ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ (created in Christ Jesus), as his workmanship (Ephesians 2:10).

### 9 The less principal cause consists in the Word and Baptism

The less principal cause consists in the Word and Baptism, and in their own way also the ministers of the Church.

Notes. Through these God effects conversion in a human being and concurs with them to produce a spiritual effect.

Thus we are said to be regenerated by the word of truth (James 1:18). And in 1 Peter 1:23, the word is said to serve as a kind of seed from which we are reborn.

This is what it means that we are said to be reborn of water and the Spirit (John 3:5). And baptism is called the "washing of regeneration" because regeneration takes place through it (Titus 3:5).

Ministers contribute insofar as they put the word and baptism into use and apply them to those who are to be regenerated, not by their own authority but by God's, and according to divine institution. In this sense Paul says (1 Corinthians 4:15): "I have begotten you in Christ Jesus through the Gospel."

### 10 The subject "which" is a human being lacking spiritual life

The subject "which" is a human being lacking spiritual life, one who does not contumaciously resist the operation of the Holy Spirit, without distinction of age, and whether he has never had spiritual life or has again lost through mortal sins the spiritual life that he once had.

Notes. That is, the subject of denomination, which in the nominative case is said to be reborn.

For otherwise, if he already possesses spiritual life, he will already have been reborn (cf. Musaeus, same work, sections 22 and 23, and Disputation 2, section 12).

For those who act otherwise, which indeed adult human beings can do and sometimes are accustomed to do, are not regenerated so long as they so resist; and they themselves are indeed the cause (cf. Musaeus, Disputation 2 on Conversion, Halle edition, sections 2 and 61 and following).

See what we said in section 2.

Thus infants conceived and born in original sin, and adult Gentiles and Jews, are reborn.

Concerning those, however, who have lost their spiritual life, it should be noted that even if they must be regenerated anew, baptism need not on that account be repeated; rather, they must be brought back to repentance through the word of the law and the Gospel, and thus faith must be kindled again in them. In this way, the fruit of baptism that had been interrupted for a time is also restored (cf. Musaeus, Disputation 5 on Conversion, Halle edition, section 58).

### 11 The subject "in which" is the human soul

The subject "in which" is the human soul: with respect to the intellect, the will, and in its own way the sensitive appetite.

Notes. Namely, with respect to those faculties in which faith resides as in a subject. Compare what we said in sections 4 and 5.

For the terms "from which" and "to which" readily indicate the subject of the change itself. See also Musaeus (same work, Disputation 2, sections 3 and 18).

As was said in section 5, final note.

### 12 As regards the mode by which the Holy Spirit acts upon the mind of an adult…

As regards the mode by which the Holy Spirit acts upon the mind of an adult human being when he regenerates it through the word, this is pertinent: that he confers habitual faith successively, through prior supernatural acts excited by himself.

Notes. For the regeneration of infants we have already said is less explicable (section 2, note e).

Regeneration does not occur in such a way that the habit of faith is immediately and instantaneously infused into the faculties of the soul. Musaeus teaches in his Disputation 1 on Faith, against the Scholastics, that just as natural habits are acquired through natural acts, so also supernatural habits of the mind are acquired through supernatural acts excited by the Holy Spirit through the word. Compare what we shall presently say concerning conversion (section 21).

Moreover, it must by no means be maintained that natural powers, and the acts depending on them, contribute anything efficiently to the production or acquisition of faith.

### 13 The word "conversion" is taken in two senses in the Scriptures

The word "conversion" is taken in two senses in the Scriptures: insofar as now God is said to convert a human being, and now a human being is said to convert himself, even though with respect to the thing itself it is one and the same action.

Notes. This terminology is drawn by analogy from local motion, just as the signification of "return" also obtains in Scripture (see Musaeus, Treatise on Conversion, Jena edition, Disputation 1, chapter 1, sections 5 and 6).

The former is called transitive conversion, because it does not terminate in the agent himself, God, but passes from Him into another subject, namely the human sinner; whence God is said "to convert" and the human being is said "to be converted." Thus what is said in Jeremiah 31:18, ינִ בֵ ישִ הֲ (which literally means "cause me to return"), is rendered by the Greek interpreters as ἐπίστρεψόν με, by the Vulgate as "convert me," and by Pagninus as "cause me to be converted" (cf. Musaeus, Treatise on Conversion, Jena edition, Disputation 1, chapter 1, sections 2 and 21).

The latter is called intransitive conversion. For although the acts through which a human being is said to convert himself depend efficiently upon the Holy Spirit, nevertheless because they are in their own way acts of the intellect and will, and do not pass from the faculties whose acts they are into another subject but terminate in those very faculties, in this respect they fall under the category of immanent or intransitive acts.

In every case, conversion implies a spiritual change in a human being, through which the human sinner is brought, not indeed by his own powers but by those of grace, to the point where he recognizes his sins, grieves over them, believes in Christ, and so forth.

### 14 First, then, two terms of conversion must be noted

First, then, two terms of conversion must be noted: one "from which" and another "to which," each of which is either formal or objective.

Notes. For in order to understand the nature of transitive conversion, which receives its specific character from its terminus (and which as regards the thing itself consists in intransitive conversion), it is necessary to begin with the consideration of the latter (see Musaeus, Disputation on Conversion 3).

For conversion, in its common notion and concept, is a certain change or spiritual motion of the soul, as the designations in the Scriptures also teach, such as "the return of the sinner" and "the return from sins to God" (see Musaeus, Disputations on Conversion 1 and 2). And since conversion taken transitively and intransitively is one and the same change with respect to the thing itself, it is necessary that the terms "from which" and "to which" are also the same on both sides with respect to the thing itself (Musaeus, Disputation 3, section 21).

The terminus "from which" is that from which the motion begins and which is abolished through it.

The terminus "to which" is that toward which the motion tends and which is acquired or obtained through it.

The formal terminus is so called because conversion by its very nature intrinsically attains it.

The objective terminus is the object of the formal terminus, constituted outside the intrinsic nature and definition of conversion (Musaeus, Disputation1, sections 7, 8, and 9; and Disputation 3, chapter 1, section 4).

### 15 The formal terminus "from which" consists in sins

The formal terminus "from which" consists in sins: both actual sins, whether of commission or omission, insofar as after they have been committed they morally persist as if ratified or unretracted, offend God, and incur for the sinner an obligation to punishment; and also habitual sins, both original or innate and acquired, not only insofar as they are habits of sinning but also by reason of the guilt and liability attached to them.

Notes. For the terms "to repent," "to change one's mind" (μεταμέλεσθαι, μετανοεῖν), and similar expressions that correspond to intransitive conversion, also imply a reference to past sins. Thus in 1 Kings 8:35, conversion is attributed to those who, having sinned against God, turn away from their sin. And in Ezekiel 18:26 and 27, conversion is attributed to him who "turns away from the iniquity or transgression that he committed" (cf. Musaeus, same work, section 9).

The same reasoning applies equally to sins of commission and omission, and it suffices that they share the common concept of sin.

These sins do not survive physically or really, nor need they be abolished in that manner, since they have already passed; just as sins of omission are not in themselves something positive but a negation (Musaeus, same work, sections 39, 59, 60, and 61).

For insofar as they are actions against the law and concern the right of a third party, they are considered to persist, like a contract, and to hold the agent bound under the state resulting from the action, until they are retracted (see Musaeus, same work, sections 42 and following).

Thus guilt and the liability to punishment are joined together (see Musaeus, same work, sections 46 and following).

Scripture certainly describes conversion through the removal of the heart of stone and the bestowal of a heart of flesh (Ezekiel 11:17; 36:24 and following), through the circumcision of the heart (Deuteronomy 30:6; Colossians 2:11), and through the softening of the heart (2 Kings 22:19 and following). By these expressions, a change of heart or mind with respect to the removal of habitual malice is plainly indicated (cf. Musaeus, same work, sections 15 and following; Disputation 4, chapter 3, sections 60 and following).

Concerning original sin, see what was said above in Part 2, Chapter 2. Here must be considered both the lack of original righteousness and the habitual propensity of all the faculties toward evil, both of which are innate, and both of which must in their own way be removed through conversion, as will presently appear. See in the meantime Musaeus (same work, Disputation 4, chapter 1, sections 4 and following).

Under the name of acquired habitual sin is comprehended not only the habitual propensity toward evil contracted through acts of sinning, but also the lack of that righteousness or grace, restored in the reborn through Christ, but cast off through graver sins (see Musaeus, same work, sections 3 and following).

That is, these habitual sins are considered both according to themselves, insofar as they imply the lack of habitual perfection that ought to be present and a habitual propensity toward evil, both of which must be removed; and also in respect of the guilt and liability attached to them, which indeed they share in common with actual sins (on which see the preceding note). For these attach to them insofar as they are sins, not precisely insofar as they are habitual.

### 16 The objective terminus "from which," generally speaking

The objective terminus "from which," generally speaking, consists in the things that are the objects of actual sins; more specifically, in those things to which sinners are especially devoted in mind and affection and to which they have, as it were, enslaved themselves, setting God aside.

Notes. The very name indicates this (cf. Musaeus, Disputation on Conversion 3, chapter 1, section 34).

For example, idols, from which human beings who are to be converted are said to turn away (Isaiah 31:6 and 7; Ezekiel 36:25; Acts 14:15; 1 Thessalonians 1:9); and Satan, or the power of Satan (Acts 26:18). In the same manner, the avaricious are commanded to turn from riches, and the intemperate from debaucheries (cf. Musaeus, same work, section 35).

### 17 The terminus "to which" of conversion

The terminus "to which" of conversion, the formal one, is faith in Christ, by which the human sinner is reconciled to God, who had been offended by sins.

Notes. This is the terminus by whose acquisition or attainment a person is said to be converted.

It is the terminus that conversion by its very nature and intrinsically attains, so that it might be produced. Thus in Acts 11:21, sinners are said to turn to the Lord πιστεύοντες (believing), that is, formally by the fact that they believe or become believers. And in Acts 26:16 and following, we read that Christ sent Paul to the Gentiles "to open their eyes, that they might turn from darkness to light," namely the light of faith, which also appears from what follows, where they are said to be about to receive "the forgiveness of sins and a share among those sanctified by faith in Christ" (cf. Musaeus, Disputation 1, chapter 3, section 44). Nor does this differ as to substance from what the same author says (same work, chapter 1, section 8): that the formal terminus "to which" of conversion is "the rectitude of mind to be restored, which either ought to have been present in a human being by virtue of the original creation and was lost in Adam, or, having once been restored by virtue of regeneration, was again cast off through sins against conscience." To this may be added what is found in the same place (section 9; Disputation 3, chapter 1, sections 22 and following; Disputation 5, chapter 1, sections 7 and 9).

It should be observed, according to what was just said from Acts 26:16, that the remission of sins, properly speaking, is not a part of conversion, even if conversion is taken in its entirety as encompassing contrition and faith, but is rather its consequence and fruit and belongs formally to justification (cf. Musaeus, same work, chapter 4, section 74).

### 18 The objective terminus "to which" is God

The objective terminus "to which" is God.

Notes. For the expression μετάνοια εἰς τὸν Θεόν (repentance or conversion toward God) is used (Acts 20:21), and human beings are commanded ἐπιστρέφειν ἐπὶ τὸν Θεόν (to turn to God) (Acts 14:15; 26:16) and πρὸς τὸν Θεόν (toward God) (1 Thessalonians 1:9); see Musaeus (Disputation 1, chapter 3, sections 43 and following). For faith, which conversion regards as its formal terminus, is rightly directed toward God as its object and reunites the sinner's soul with him (cf. Musaeus, chapter 1, section 9).

### 19 Accordingly, in order that actual sins may be abolished through conversion

Accordingly, in order that actual sins may be abolished through conversion, it is required, first, that they be retracted by the sinner; and that on the part of the intellect they be recognized, not only by a speculative judgment that they are truly sins, but also by a practical judgment that one must apply oneself to the abolition of sins and deliberate concerning the manner and means by which they may be abolished. On the part of the will, there is required a displeasure with sins, and indeed an efficacious displeasure, that is, a detestation conjoined with grief.

Notes. Sins can be abolished only morally, not physically, since they do not presently exist but have long since ceased to be, as we said at section 13, note c.

Retraction is opposed to ratification, by which it comes about that sins, even though past, morally persist and affect a person. Compare section 13, note d. Although sins cannot be abolished through retraction alone (cf. Musaeus, Disputation on Conversion 3, chapter 2, sections 49, 50, and 62 and following).

Recognition is a necessary condition without which retraction cannot take place, since the will, as a blind faculty, can ratify or annul nothing unless it has first been made known by the intellect. Moreover, Scripture shows us this practice: that when human beings were to be brought to conversion through the ministry of the word, a beginning was customarily made from the disclosure of sins, as in the example of David (2 Samuel 12:7 and following; Psalm 51:5; cf. Musaeus, same work, section 64).

By speculative judgment, sins are recognized as contrary to the divine law, hateful to God, and deserving of temporal and eternal punishments, whether they present themselves to the mind of their own accord (when they are graver) or are discovered through a more diligent examination and review of one's past life and a more careful comparison with the norm of divine law, by which means even those sins that otherwise go unnoticed because of carnal security, including sins of weakness, can be recognized. As it says (Romans 3:20), "through the Law comes the knowledge of sin." Compare Romans 7:7 and Musaeus (same work, sections 65 and 66).

By practical judgment, one must deliberate about the means of abolishing sins; otherwise, the saying of James would apply, concerning the man who looks at his face in a mirror but does not think about wiping away the blemish (James 1:23 and 24). It is clear from the examples of penitents in Scripture how, once their sins were recognized, they anxiously inquired by what means their sins might be abolished: for instance, Josiah (2 Kings 22:11 and following), and certain Jews at the time of John the Baptist (Matthew 3:6; Mark 1:6; cf. Musaeus, same work, section 67).

Even if the intellect were to recognize all sins and dictate that one must not persist in them, the sins would still not be retracted unless they had displeased the will. Through displeasure, however, sins cease to be voluntary and take on the character of involuntary actions (Musaeus, same work, sections 69 and 71).

A simple displeasure by which sins, recognized as evil in some respect, displease the will without an intention to flee from them, does not suffice for the retraction of sins; rather, it is necessary that we utterly turn from sins, desiring to undo them if it were possible, and abhorring the commission of similar ones (Musaeus, same work, section 70).

Grief is such that a passion, disturbance, and disquiet of mind arises from the apprehension of sin as a present evil and a cause of many evils to be endured in this life and the next. This grief is all the more severe the more distinctly and carefully the nature of the evil in sins is apprehended and recognized: for instance, the foulness of sin, the offense against God, the certainty and abundance and gravity of punishments. Hence it is evident that the pangs and terrors of conscience are contained under this grief. Examples are found especially in David (Psalm 6:3 and following; 32:3 and following; 38:4 and following; 88:17 and following) and in Peter, who wept πικρῶς (bitterly) (Matthew 26:75; Luke 22:62).

### 20 Furthermore, it is required that actual sins also be abolished with respect to…

Furthermore, it is required that actual sins also be abolished with respect to the offense against God and the obligation of sinners to render satisfaction to God, which indeed occurs in no other way than through faith in Christ the Mediator and in his merit and satisfaction for our sins. When faith apprehends this satisfaction, it simultaneously tends toward God, who, although offended by our sins, has nevertheless embraced us in his love and grace, and is now fully reconciled through the satisfaction of Christ.

Notes. For just as the cause why sins, after they have passed, morally persist and constitute a person in the state of sin is not merely ratification or non-retraction, but also the fact that sins are contrary to the divine law and offend God, so even if a sinner seriously retracts his past sins in his mind, he will nonetheless remain guilty on account of the violated law of God, and bound to render satisfaction for the offense and injury done to God. Just as the Savior. For the abolition of a sin by which one has injured a neighbor, requires not only the retraction of the sin but also that satisfaction be made to the neighbor or that the neighbor be induced to forgive the injury (Matthew 5:24; cf. Musaeus, same work, sections 49 and 50).

Sins considered as offenses, that is, insofar as they offend God, and the obligation or debt of rendering satisfaction to God for sins, stand to each other as the foundation of a relation and the relation itself; and therefore the offense and the obligation to render satisfaction are removed by the same acts (Musaeus, same work, section 76).

Contrition avails nothing here, to which nothing should be ascribed beyond the retraction of sins that have been committed. See what Musaeus adduces against the Scholastics (same work, sections 77 and following). Nor is the offense against God removed without satisfaction, by a mere pardon of sins. Rather, according to the Scriptures, the abolition of offenses and our reconciliation with God is ascribed partly to the grace or mercy of God, as the internal impulsive cause, and partly to Christ the Mediator, as the meritorious cause (Ephesians 1:5; 2:4 and following; Titus 3:4 and following; Romans 5:8). This is what is said in Romans 8:3: "the righteous requirement of the law is fulfilled in us through the Son of God," whom he himself sent, that is, through the fulfillment of the law and the satisfaction rendered by him on our behalf. And in Galatians 4:4, Christ was "made subject to the law, in order to redeem those who were under the law." And in 1 John 2:2, he is "the propitiation for our sins, and for those of the whole world." And in 2 Corinthians 5:18, "God reconciled us to himself through Christ." Therefore, since Scripture teaches no other satisfaction acceptable to God or valid in itself besides the satisfaction of Christ, conversion too can tend toward abolishing the offense of sins in no other way than through those acts by which it is first directed toward Christ the Mediator and through him toward God, reconciled by the merit of Christ. Compare what we said in Chapter 2 and Musaeus (same work, sections 81 and following).

For while faith is directed toward Christ as the cause of obtaining grace before God, that same faith is simultaneously directed toward God, whose grace is to be obtained through Christ.

God wills all to be saved (1 Timothy 2:4; compare our Disputation on the Universality of Divine Grace), and he loves us even when we were sinners and children of wrath, not indeed as such, but as his creatures (Romans 5:8).

Thus in 2 Corinthians 5:18 and 19, it is said that "God reconciled us and the world to himself in Christ," to which the words of Colossians 1:20 correspond: that God, "having made peace through the blood of the cross" of Christ, "reconciled all things to himself through him." These should be understood of reconciliation considered from the side of satisfaction, that is, that everything that could be required by way of satisfaction for reconciling human beings to God has truly been rendered. But it is certain that God is actually reconciled to the human sinner only through faith itself, which apprehends the satisfaction of Christ (cf. Musaeus, Disputation on Conversion, same work, section 91).

### 21 Conversion tends toward the abolition of habitual sins through the same acts by…

Conversion tends toward the abolition of habitual sins through the same acts by which it tends toward the abolition of actual sins, yet in such a manner that habitual sins must be abolished or expelled not only morally but also physically and really, if not entirely, then at least in a qualified sense and with respect to their dominion.

Notes. Namely, so that a person may recognize those sins and detest them with sorrow, and also believe in Christ the Mediator, according to what we have discussed in Sections XIX and XX.

Habitual sins must indeed be abolished morally no less than actual sins, with respect to guilt and offense. They must accordingly be retracted by means of a serious and efficacious recognition and displeasure, and the obligation to punishment contracted by those sins must be removed through those acts which are directed toward the satisfaction and merit by which God truly wills to be appeased and reconciled.

For the difference between actual and habitual sins is this: actual sins, after they have been committed, are not something intrinsic to the sinner; habitual sins, however, partly involve the lack of habitual justice or grace that ought to be present, and thus inhere in the person in the way that privations exist in subjects in which they remove the opposite perfection, and partly involve a habitual inclination toward evil, and thus import a certain positive entity. Hence, although actual sins are removed only morally, habitual sins can be expelled physically, just as privations or habits are otherwise expelled from their subjects.

As long as we live in this life, it must be acknowledged that in us, that is, in our flesh, there dwells no good thing (Romans 7:18), and that the flesh even in the converted lusts against the Spirit (Galatians 5:17). Compare what we have discussed concerning the tenacity of original sin (Part II, Chapter II, Section XIV).

For by divine grace sin can in a certain manner and with respect to its dominion be removed in us, even if it is not abolished entirely according to its whole being (Romans 6:12ff.; 7:6; 8:1ff.; 5:12ff.; Galatians 5:16ff., and other passages). That this occurs in conversion itself and through those very acts by which sin is morally removed will be evident from what follows. See in the meantime what Musaeus adduces (Musaeus, On Conversion, Disputation III, Chapter I, Sections XV ff., from Ezekiel 11:17ff. and 36:25, concerning the removal of the heart of stone).

### 22 Specifically, therefore

Specifically, therefore, on the part of the intellect, the lack of light and of powers for embracing and believing spiritual objects, together with the habitual inclination to judge rashly concerning them, is abolished in conversion through acts of faith produced in us by divine grace. Simple ignorance of the things to be believed is removed through the simple apprehension of those things to be believed. Errors, however, or false opinions in matters of faith and morals are removed through acts of assenting to true doctrine grounded upon divine revelation. The rash propensity of the intellect toward perverse judgment concerning the things that are of the Spirit of God is restrained through the pious affection of the will toward believing, an affection divinely excited by the power of the Word.

Notes. As discussed in Section XV, notes f and g, page 507.

Such as occurs in unbelievers being led to the Christian faith, who have not yet heard the dogmas of that faith.

Just as privatively opposed things mutually expel one another formally from a subject (Musaeus, On Conversion, Disputation X, Chapter I, Section IV).

Such as exist among those who, having heard the dogmas of faith, whether merely supernatural or naturally known, though referred to those supernatural things, are occupied with prejudices and judge otherwise, and either hold what is proposed to them to be fables, or in any manner maintain a divergent or contrary opinion.

Just as contrarily opposed things likewise mutually expel one another from a subject (Musaeus, On Conversion, same place). And so the act of the intellect by which assent is given to mysteries as divinely revealed excludes the perverted judgment of the intellect by which those same mysteries are held to be foolishness; and the recognition of sins together with the practical judgment by which the intellect commands that one must labor for their abolition as foul things, hateful to God and ruinous to us, removes that corrupt judgment by which the intellect determines that one should persist in sins as things pleasing to the flesh.

Which, such rashness of intellect is indeed innate to human beings through original sin, but is afterward increased by corrupt instruction, voluntary abuse of reason, and various prejudices.

In mysteries that are not self-evident, the intellect is subordinated to the will, and by the will, equipped with supernatural power, can be taken captive in obedience to Christ (2 Corinthians 10:4f.), so that, with thoughts opposing the faith restrained and judgment suspended, and further instruction admitted, the intellect at length by the grace of God gives full assent (Musaeus, On Conversion, same place).

(h) The lack of habitual light, or of the powers for believing, is removed efficiently through acts of faith; formally through the habit of believing, which is efficiently produced by means of repeated acts of believing. For acts of believing proceeding from the preaching of the Word leave behind in the mind of the person being converted a disposition toward eliciting further similar acts, which, augmented by the repetition of these acts, at length passes into a fixed and firm habit, and indeed a habit proportionate to the acts of believing and supernatural in substance (Musaeus, On Conversion, same place, Section VI).

Since this habit elevates the intellect beyond its natural condition for eliciting subsequent acts of believing, it receives on the part of the intellect the designation of habitual light and of the powers of believing, from which the eyes of our mind possess the quality of being habitually enlightened (Ephesians 1:17), or so that a person may be light in the Lord, a child of light, discerning what is acceptable to the Lord (Ephesians 5:8, 10). Hence it is evident that the lack of habitual light is removed formally by this very habitual light, just as privations are otherwise removed by their corresponding habits (Musaeus, On Conversion, same place, Sections VI and VII).

### 23 Similarly, on the part of the will

Similarly, on the part of the will, the inclination toward evil and the lack of powers for salvifically embracing spiritual goods is removed through acts of serious and efficacious displeasure at sins. This removal occurs partly and principally through acts of trust, which presuppose in the sinner a certain desire for grace and for the remission of sins, and which themselves import a security and certitude concerning the obtaining of God's grace and the remission of sins. These acts of trust are conjoined also with love of Christ the Mediator and of God reconciled through him; and they are joined with hope of obtaining grace and salvation. Thus they formally remove the opposite acts of the will, and tend efficiently toward the expulsion of habitual sins, until those sins are formally expelled by the spiritual habits born from these acts.

Notes. Namely, in a certain respect, as we have said (Section XX).

For when the will of a person who has recognized habitual sins turns away from them and intends to flee them, and meanwhile is distressed and grieves over what it discovers within itself, the contrary complacency and delight in sins, depraved desires, and the movements of concupiscence for persisting in them is inhibited or removed.

This desire is opposed to carnal security and the lusts of the flesh.

The confidence itself is opposed to timidity and distrust.

Which is contrary to love of the world and earthly things Which is opposed to despair.

The acts themselves indeed immediately leave behind dispositions that incline toward similar spiritual acts and movements; and then, with the grace of the Holy Spirit attending upon further acts, they tend toward a spiritual habit, in the manner in which we have said that acts of the intellect tend toward habits (Section XXII).

That is to say, the lack of powers for embracing spiritual goods is removed, as a privation, by the opposite form; while the habitual inclination toward evil is removed by the contrary habit.

### 24 In this way it is readily understood how conversion

In this way it is readily understood how conversion, while occupied in abolishing the terminus from which, simultaneously tends toward acquiring the formal terminus to which, namely habitual faith in Christ. This occurs through the very acts and movements of faith which are excited by divine power in the mind of the person being converted and brought to a sense and sorrow for sins: at first indeed more feeble or slight, then, as more frequently repeated, so also stronger and firmer, until, with powers augmented, habitual faith is produced.

Notes. Indeed the tendency of conversion toward acquiring the formal terminus to which differs only inadequately from its tendency toward abolishing the terminus from which, and is included in it.

For just as conversion tends toward the reunion with God of the person who has been turned away from God, so through the very acts of faith such a person begins to be joined with God, and is more and more joined, until, with the offense abolished, he is fully reconciled with God and reunited through faith.

That true faith presupposes contrition in the sinful person is readily established both from what has been said concerning the abolition of the terminus from which of conversion and from what will shortly be said concerning the parts of repentance.

Thus Chemnitz writes: "In the beginning of conversion the desire is more obscure, the assent more feeble, the obedience more slight" (Chemnitz, Loci Theologici, On Free Will, Chapter VII).

He then adds that these gifts must grow. In this way a distinction is customarily drawn in conversion between the willing and the accomplishing, both of which, however, God works (Philippians 2:13).

Nor can it be shown at any mathematical point where the liberated will begins to act, as Chemnitz observes in the same place. Moreover, that conversion does not occur in an instant but successively, and that faith is not entirely infused in a single moment but arises at length from antecedent acts of believing, Chemnitz taught at greater length in the same place, where he writes:

Conversion or renewal is not such a change as is completed and perfected in one moment with all its parts at once, but has its beginnings, its progressive steps, by which it is accomplished in great weakness.

Hence he distinguishes between the first beginnings of faith and faith itself. Similarly, Hutter writes:

The Holy Spirit excites good movements when He inspires pious thoughts, and by imparting the movement of good purpose, He by His grace prevents the person; He moves and impels the will, so that although, as still a slave, it is not yet fully liberated and still wavers and hangs in suspense, it nevertheless ceases to resist and begins to struggle with the flesh, until from unwilling it becomes willing and from a slave it is made free.

(Hutter, Prelections on the Formula of Concord, Article II, On Free Will)

From this it is also immediately clear that the conversion of the ungodly to God does not occur in the manner in which sometimes by the general action of divine power the hearts of people are changed and the counsels of the wicked are overturned, who do not even think about such a thing, and indeed often do not know what is happening to them, and are sometimes compelled to do what they do not wish, as Balaam was compelled to bless the people of Israel (Numbers 23:8). Rather, the grace of God in conversion progressively makes the unwilling more and more willing (Musaeus, Detailed Explanation, Question 47).

### 25 Meanwhile, when the first beginnings of faith and conversion are given to a person

Meanwhile, when the first beginnings of faith and conversion are given to a person, the struggle of the flesh and the Spirit immediately commences; and it is manifest that this struggle does not occur without the movement of our will.

Notes. These are the words of Chemnitz in the same place, where, having noted that those gifts conferred at the beginning of conversion must grow, he adds:

They grow in us not as a log is propelled by violent impulse, or as lilies that neither toil nor care grow; but by striving, struggling, seeking, asking, knocking. This is not of ourselves; it is the gift of God.

(Chemnitz, Loci Theologici, On Free Will, Chapter VII)

Moreover, according to the Formula of Concord, Article II, On Free Will: "This is most certain, that in true conversion a change, renewal, and movement must take place in the intellect, will, and heart of a person: namely, that the person's mind may recognize sins, fear the wrath of God, turn away from sin, recognize and apprehend the promise of grace in Christ, entertain pious thoughts in the mind, have a good purpose, and apply diligence in governing one's morals, and fight against the flesh." And the Formula pointedly adds: "For where none of these things takes place, there without doubt there is also no true conversion to God." See further materials on this matter in the Detailed Explanation at the cited passage.

So also Meisner, in his special Disputation on the Struggle of the Flesh and the Spirit, on Galatians 5:17, Section XXII, writes: "The time at which this struggle began can be determined as that very moment when a person first feels the powers of the Holy Spirit in regeneration, and it lasts until the end of life." However, just as these authors speak of a person placed under converting grace, and of the state in which the Holy Spirit works conversion in that person, so it is not to be concluded from this that in a person not yet regenerated, before the first conversion, there exist good movements, a pious desire, holy thoughts, the struggle of flesh and spirit (σαρκοπνευματομαχία, sarcopneumatomachia), and the beginnings of faith. As Musaeus also noted (Detailed Explanation).

### 26 Since intransitive conversion is the same as penitence or repentance

Since intransitive conversion is the same as penitence or repentance, it is manifest that its parts are rightly identified as contrition and faith.

Notes. So Musaeus writes (Musaeus, On Conversion, Disputation I, Section III). Repentance is understood here not in any general sense but taken specifically as that which belongs to the sinful person. According to the ecclesiastical writers, although it is sometimes taken more narrowly for that part of conversion called contrition, it is nevertheless frequently taken for the whole of conversion. In the Scriptures as well, the term μεταμέλεια (metameleia, solicitude or sorrow after the deed), or μεταμέλεσθαι (metamelesthai, to feel regret), which formally signifies care, displeasure, and sorrow after the fact, so that it properly signifies a part of conversion, namely contrition, nevertheless by synecdoche denotes the whole of conversion. The term μετάνοια (metanoia, repentance) or μετανοεῖν (metanoein, to repent), although it does not formally signify faith or believing in Christ, nevertheless implicitly and materially includes faith when it frequently denotes the whole of conversion in its proper signification (Musaeus, On Conversion, Disputation I, Chapter IV, and Disputation II, Chapter III).

Thus the meaning of the word μετανοεῖν (metanoein) is customarily rendered literally in Latin as "resipiscere" (to come to one's senses) (Musaeus, On Conversion, Disputation I, Chapter I, Section III, and Chapter IV, Sections LVI and LIX).

Certainly Musaeus also acknowledged that the essence of conversion (or repentance) consists in these two things, contrition and faith (Musaeus, On Conversion, Disputation I, Section III, Chapter IV, Section LXVI ff.; and Detailed Explanation, Book XII, Question 63).

By the name "contrition," the ecclesiastical writers customarily denote the entire retraction of sins. The designation is derived from the sorrow and terrors of conscience that are customarily joined with the serious displeasure at recognized sins, by which, as by a hammer, the hard heart of the sinner, obstinate in evil, is broken or crushed, according to the passages: Psalm 51:19; 142:3; Isaiah 61:1; 66:2; 57:15; 38:13 (Musaeus, On Conversion, Disputation III, Chapter II, Section LXXIV).

By "faith" is understood faith in Christ, explained above, by which contrite hearts are healed or raised up, and which is the principal part of conversion and its very soul, so to speak, and with which, once it is present, conversion itself is established (Musaeus, On Conversion, Disputation I, Chapter IV, Section LXXVI; Detailed Explanation).

### 27 Having understood the nature and parts of conversion

Having understood the nature and parts of conversion, it must now further be observed that the efficient cause of conversion, and indeed the principal cause, is the Triune God, and He alone.

Notes. And thus we enter upon the consideration of transitive conversion.

The principal cause is that which by its own and sufficient power works in a person the recognition of sins, serious displeasure and sorrow over them, and likewise the beginnings of faith and faith itself, together with the purpose of amending one's life.

For conversion, considered transitively, is formally an action of God, who is said to convert a person, or to bring it about that a person converts himself or is converted (compare Section XII above).

This is a work ad extra, that is, common to the whole Trinity. Specifically, however, the Father of Christ is said to draw people so that they come to Christ (John 6:44). The Son says of Himself that He wished to gather the Jews to Himself, and thus to work conversion in them (Matthew 23:37). The Holy Spirit is said to convict the world of sin, of righteousness, and of judgment (John 16:8).

Paul attributes both the willing and the accomplishing entirely to God working in us (Philippians 2:13), so as to deny them to all who are not God.

### 28 The internal impulsive cause is the mercy of God

The internal impulsive cause is the mercy of God. The external or meritorious cause is Christ the Mediator.

Notes. According to what we have said concerning regeneration in Sections VII and VIII.

### 29 The instrumental cause is the Word

The instrumental cause is the Word, namely that of the Law and of the Gospel. Through the former, the recognition of sins and sorrow over them is excited or produced in human beings; through the latter, faith in Christ.

Notes. By "instrumental cause" is meant the efficacious and operative medium to which God conjoins His infinite power for producing such an effect, and through which He exerts it.

To the Word, therefore, is to be attributed not a bare moral persuasion, but, on account of the concurrence of God, a far nobler and higher power than what can otherwise be attributed to any teaching or speech, however well suited to persuading (Musaeus, On Conversion, Halle edition, Disputation IV, Section LIV f.).

By "Law" we here understand the Word of God commanding or prohibiting something, with the force of binding to obedience and efficaciously denouncing the wrath of God to transgressors.

By "Gospel," when set in opposition to the Law, we understand the promises concerning the grace of God and the gratuitous remission of sins on account of Christ the Mediator and His merit apprehended by faith.

According to the statement of Paul: "Through the law comes the knowledge of sin" (Romans 3:20). And: "I would not have known sin except through the law; for I would not have known concupiscence unless the law had said, 'You shall not covet'" (Romans 7:7) (Musaeus, On Conversion, Jena edition, Disputation III, Chapter II, Sections LXV and LXVI). Moreover, the knowledge of the Law for the purpose of recognizing sins must be sought not from the light of nature alone after the fall, but from Scripture, as is evident from the corruption of our intellect that arose from the fall. Here also must be noted the divine power that God has added to the Word of the Law contained in the Scriptures, for producing in the person a supernatural assent and thus a recognition of those things that are found in the person to be at variance with the Law.

For when the foulness of sins and the offense against God arising therefrom, together with the liability to eternal damnation, are set before the intellect of a person by means of the Law, there is simultaneously presented to the will the very formal reason by which it may be moved to the detestation of sins, to sorrow over them, and to the fear of divine wrath and damnation. And so the Law itself, by divine power, works in the will of a person, through the mediation of the intellect's cognition, also displeasure and detestation of sins, terrors of conscience, and a certain horror of judgment, so that it is like a hammer crushing the rock (Jeremiah 23:29).

For the promises of the Gospel are general, under which a person can rightly subsume himself as an individual and by divine power conclude to the eliciting of the assent of faith. Hence the Gospel simultaneously on the part of the will (especially after the Law has made people anxious about a physician or mediator, or, as a terrifying pedagogue, has led them as if by an indirect path to Christ, according to Galatians 3:24) excites a desire for grace and then a fuller confidence, as we have previously indicated.

### 30 A human being, however

A human being, however, through his natural powers, can contribute nothing at all actively to the intrinsic commencement or completion of his own conversion, that is, to the exercise of spiritual acts; although with respect to the external use of means he can suitably exercise certain acts of the intellect and will.

Notes. For such a person is dead in sins (Ephesians 2:1; Colossians 2:13). Compare what we have said more fully concerning the terminus from which of regeneration and conversion (Sections IV and XV), where we have indicated that before regeneration or conversion a human being entirely lacks spiritual powers on the part of all the faculties of the soul, and on the contrary is inclined toward evil. Add Section XXVII and its note.

This pertains to the abolition of the terminus from which and the tendency toward the terminus to which.

For even the first holy thought and the pious willing or desire is from the Holy Spirit, not from ourselves (2 Corinthians 3:5; Philippians 2:13).

And He who has begun a good work in us must Himself also complete it (Philippians 1:6).

By "spiritual acts" are designated those acts that are occupied with the things of the Spirit of God (that is, things established above the order and light of nature, hidden in God who is Spirit) under their proper and spiritual aspect. On the part of the intellect, such acts deal with these things insofar as they can be known and believed under divine revelation as the proper ground of assent; on the part of the will, insofar as they can be desired and are customarily desired under the aspect of a good known through divine revelation. They are called spiritual acts both by reason of the object with which they are concerned and by reason of their efficient cause, since they come to a person from no other source than the supernatural operation of the Holy Spirit. (Conversely, those acts are called animal or natural which properly have for their material object things evident to the senses or things that bear a causal or other relation to sensible things, and for their formal object the light of nature as the ultimate ground of knowing, and a goodness known by the light of nature as the proper reason for moving the will.) Such spiritual acts on the part of the intellect include those by which the mysteries of the Trinity, the Incarnation, and the satisfaction of Christ are believed. On the part of the will, they include the desire for the beatific vision, the love of God reconciled through Christ, trust in Christ the Mediator, and the hope of eternal life to be obtained through Christ (Musaeus, On Conversion, Disputation IV, Chapter I, Section XXVI).

It must be acknowledged, moreover, that a person in his natural state is unfit and dead not only with respect to acts that are spiritual in themselves, but also with respect to those that are referred to spiritual things. The latter, although they are proximately occupied with things subject to the light of nature as their material object, nevertheless tend toward them under some spiritual aspect, or at least are ordered to the things of the Spirit of God and include or connote certain acts of a higher order that the Holy Spirit works. Such acts include those of mercy, temperance, the restraining of the lusts of the flesh, and the like, when they are performed with a view to a supernatural end and on account of God reconciled (Musaeus, On Conversion, same place, Sections XXXVIII and XXXIX).

As for the external use of means: a person can, for example, go to sacred places where the Word of God is taught, direct the ears and turn the thoughts to hearing and meditating upon the Word, or take in hand the book of Scripture, read it, and meditate upon it. Such acts are otherwise called pedagogical acts.

In this regard, people are said, even before they are converted by the Holy Spirit, to be able not only to hear the Gospel and in some fashion to meditate upon it, but also to discuss it (Solid Declaration of the Formula of Concord, Article II, On Free Will). Hence also the simple notion or simple apprehension of the bare literal sense of Scripture (without, however, salvific assent) may rightly be referred to pedagogical acts, as Musaeus showed (Detailed Explanation, Question XLIV).

Experience itself can testify to this: it teaches that even unregenerate people, such as Anabaptists and other fanatics, diligently examine the biblical writings, and indeed with a desire to learn, even while in their obstinacy in error they resist the Holy Spirit and His operation. These are the words of Hutter (Prelections on the Formula of Concord, Article II, Chapter II, Question III). He then adduces the zeal or pursuit of God on the part of the Jews (Romans 10:2), the hunger for hearing the Word of the Lord (Amos 8:11ff.), the example of Herod, who heard John the Baptist gladly (Mark 6:20), of Sergius the Proconsul (Acts 13:7) who desired to hear Paul, and of the Queen of Ethiopia (1 Kings 12:1) who traveled from the farthest bounds of her kingdom to Jerusalem to hear the wisdom of Solomon, of which the chief part was religion.

To these corresponds what Meisner showed (Meisner, Compendium of Theology, Disputation X, Thesis VIII), citing Mark 6:20 and Romans 10:2: that a person can naturally hear, read, and meditate upon the Word of God, and that not without a certain will or eagerness. And Kunadus writes (Kunadus, Theological Collegia, Disputation VIII, Thesis 16): "We do not deny that an unregenerate person can by his own instinct read the sacred Scriptures, hear the Word of God, and in some fashion meditate upon it, and likewise perform other pedagogical acts. But just as the instinct of nature and the instinct of grace differ as diverse principles, so also the end of each is different. For the end of the natural effort is the knowledge of a thing as new, wonderful, or delightful; but the instinct of grace produces a desire for salvation."

Musaeus, intending to explain these things more fully for the benefit of students in the schools, and to show how and to what extent acts concerning the Word of God itself and the things of the Spirit of God may be reckoned among the external or pedagogical acts of conversion, introduced distinctions between distinct and confused knowledge of spiritual goods, and similarly between acts of the will that are of simple complacency and those that are efficacious. He teaches that concerning spiritual goods known only confusedly, the will can naturally have an efficacious act (that is, it can desire and seek them as things to be acquired); but concerning spiritual goods known distinctly (that is, according to their specific and proper nature), the will can have only an act of simple complacency, not an efficacious one. Spiritual acts of the will, however, must be efficacious, tending toward things judged by a spiritual judgment of the intellect as truly given and as to the manner in which they can be obtained (Musaeus, Disputations on Conversion, held in 1649 and published at Halle in Saxony, Disputation II, Sections XXXVIII ff.; and Detailed Explanation, Question XLV).

### 31 And this is what is otherwise said

And this is what is otherwise said: that a human being, such as he is by nature, does not have free will in his own conversion.

Notes. That is, such as he is of himself after the fall and left to himself or to his natural powers.

See the Augsburg Confession, Article XVIII, and the Formula of Concord, Article II. The meaning is that the will of the person to be converted, with respect to purely spiritual goods known particularly and distinctly, is not indifferent, neither with respect to the specification nor with respect to the exercise of an act (Musaeus, On Conversion, Disputation III, Halle edition).

### 32 The operation of God by which He works conversion in a person through the Word…

The operation of God by which He works conversion in a person through the Word of Law and Gospel is customarily called by the name "grace," and is distinguished into prevenient, operating, and cooperating grace.

Notes. Not as though it were formally the gratuitous favor of God itself, but because it is His actual gift (Musaeus, On Conversion, Disputation IV, Halle edition, Sections XI ff.). The ancients employed the term "grace" in this doctrine, especially those who contended with Pelagius, among whom was Augustine.

This grace is variously distinguished by various authors, and the terms themselves are multiplied and taken in different senses. What must be observed concerning the substance of the matter can, however, be referred to the headings here indicated.

By "prevenient grace" is understood the first holy thought and pious desire inspired by God. It is called prevenient because it is prior to our free consent, that is, because the will of the person to be converted is thus prevented. Some add "exciting grace," by which a sinner is aroused from the sleep or death of sin and the security of the flesh. But this arousal seems to occur through that very holy thought and pious desire divinely inspired. Hence we also refer the name "preparatory grace" to the same category, because that thought and holy desire themselves in a certain way prepare the mind and will for embracing spiritual goods, or for further holy movements from which conversion may take increment. Although according to others, preparatory grace is said to be that by which a person, already prevented by the Holy Spirit, is further moved so as to begin gradually to consent to the calling and to struggle free from doubts.

By "operating grace" some designate the operation that immediately follows the beginning of conversion and pertains to its continuation, through which a person, with a certain effort, however feeble, now tends toward Christ the Mediator and the promises concerning the gratuitous remission of sins on account of Christ, and struggles against doubts. According to others, however, operating grace is also referred to the very beginning of conversion, and in substance coincides with prevenient and exciting grace. It is called "operating" because it operates in us without us, or without our free consent.

By "cooperating grace" is designated the operation that assists and strengthens or corroborates the mind already in some measure assenting to the promises of grace and the will already trusting in Christ, and thus cooperates with the will, which is now concurring through powers previously received, however weak. According to others, however, cooperating grace is said to be that by which God concurs with the person already converted, preserving and augmenting the powers conferred and assisting lest one fall from faith (Musaeus, On Conversion, Disputation V, Halle edition, Sections XXXII and XXXIII).

### 33 A human being at the beginning of conversion is rightly said to conduct himself…

A human being at the beginning of conversion is rightly said to conduct himself in a purely passive manner, although in the progress of conversion, through new powers previously received, he conducts himself actively.

Notes. So the Formula of Concord, Article II: "What Dr. Luther wrote, that the human will in conversion conducts itself purely passively, is to be rightly and properly understood, namely with respect to divine grace in kindling new movements." And further in the Solid Declaration. This is what Luther, and with him the Formula of Concord, deny to the person being converted: a natural active force, or an efficacious fitness, aptitude, or capacity. They attribute, however, a passive capacity: that is, the person can indeed be turned (unlike a log or a stone) toward the good through grace, and be made truly free for that for which he was created (Formula of Concord, Solid Declaration, same place).

The same view regarding passive capacity (which is present in unregenerate persons by nature, although in the terminology of the metaphysicians it might be called a passive obediential potency, and which does not require that new passive powers be supernaturally conferred in conversion to remove a natural passive incapacity and unfitness) was carefully taught not only by Chemnitz, Hutter, Gerhard, Lobechius, and Mylius (whose passages and words Musaeus adduced in the Detailed Explanation), but also by the theologians at the Colloquy of Quedlinburg (cited in Hutter, Concordia Concors, CXLV), the authors of the Apology of the Formula of Concord (Chapter XII), Meisner (Considerations on Photinian Theology, Chapter V), Steuber (on the Augsburg Confession, Article XVIII), Hannekenius (Synopsis of Theology, Sections 12 and 29), and Kromayer (Aphoristic Theology, Locus IX, Aphorism IX).

So also Kromayer writes (Kromayer, Positive Polemic Theology, Article IX, Thesis II): "A human being can contribute nothing to his own conversion, but at the beginning of conversion conducts himself purely passively; in the progress of conversion, however, he begins to cooperate with divine grace, not collaterally but subordinately."

And in his Aphoristic Theology (Locus V, Aphorism X).

Chemnitz had preceded him, writing in his Judgment on the Controversies of His Time (Chapter V):

Thus the subject (he indicates the will as the subject of conversion) receives the gifts and operations of the Holy Spirit, so that the will, which has begun to be renewed, after the first impulse and movement of the Spirit, is not idle; but as a new creature, to which the Holy Spirit has given the power to begin to operate, it acts by desiring, striving, struggling, and assenting.

And shortly after:

When the first beginnings of conversion are given to us through the Holy Spirit, immediately the struggle of the flesh and the Spirit arises, which it is manifest does not occur without the movement of our will. And this synergy of the will, not the old will but the one that has begun to be renewed, causes those beginnings to grow and be augmented in great weakness, not without the movement of our will. And so it is rightly said: with grace going before, the will accompanies. That synergy, however, always depends on the grace of God, from which, if it should depart, even the gifts cease and are lost.

And in his Loci Theologici, On Free Will (Chapter VII):

What is taught concerning prevenient, preparatory, and operating grace has this meaning: that it is not our part to take the initiative in conversion, but that God through the Word and the divine breath goes before us, moving and impelling the will. After this movement of the will divinely effected, however, the human will does not conduct itself purely passively, but, moved and assisted by the Holy Spirit, does not resist but assents, and becomes a fellow worker (σύνεργος, synergos) with God.

### 34 It must also be observed that the grace by which God works conversion is not…

It must also be observed that the grace by which God works conversion is not irresistible but resistible, inasmuch as human beings can, and frequently do, maliciously oppose not only the means of conversion and their external use, but also the grace of conversion itself as it operates intrinsically, and thus they impede their conversion whether in its commencement or its completion.

Notes. For although the power of God by which He works a person's conversion is infinite, nevertheless, because it ordinarily exerts itself only through certain means, it is not absurd that it can be resisted (Matthew 23:37) (Musaeus, Disputation on the Antecedent and Consequent Will of God, toward the end; and On Conversion, Disputation V, Halle edition, Sections XXXIX ff.).

Resistance to the external use of means occurs partly by omitting those acts required for the means to be put into use, such as hearing, reading, and meditating upon the Word, and partly by committing acts diametrically opposed to the legitimate use of the means, such as contradicting the Word of God, caviling at or contemptuously reviling or blaspheming the Word, repelling, defaming, or hostilely persecuting the preachers of the Word. See the example of the Jews (Acts 6:10ff.; 7:51, 54).

Resistance to the grace that operates intrinsically occurs on the part of the intellect when one indulges in prejudices or preconceived false opinions, whence the heavenly doctrine is rashly held to be foolish or scandalous, as Paul records happened to both Jews and Gentiles (1 Corinthians 1:23). On the part of the will, various disordered movements contrary to pious and holy movements, such as the desires of the flesh, the cares of riches, and the like (Luke 8:14).

We distinguish between malicious resistance and natural resistance. The latter indeed flows proximately from corrupt human nature and is common to all mortals. The former, however, is summoned by the person's particular fault and deliberate effort, proceeding from malice voluntarily contracted, and is in some persons greater and more obstinate, in others lesser and less obstinate, as the acquired malice itself varies. Natural resistance is gradually diminished through grace joined to the Word of God in conversion itself and is at length overcome; and so, taken precisely in itself, it does not impede conversion. The other resistance, the malicious one, which is superadded to the natural, since it is not equally common to all the unregenerate, people can abstain from by the powers of free will; or if they cannot now do so after having contracted vicious habits, they could previously have lacked it to some extent if right education and habituation to virtues had been present. See Musaeus discussing these matters more fully (Musaeus, Disputation on the Accommodation of the Eternal Decree, Chapter XI, Section CCCLXXX ff.).

### 35 The subject "which" of conversion is the adult human being

The subject "which" of conversion is the adult human being, who has been turned away from God through sin, and who does not obstinately resist the operation of the Holy Spirit.

Notes. That is, the supposit which is spiritually transformed, or in whom God works the acknowledgment of sins together with sorrow over them in earnest, and faith in Christ; and who accordingly, through the grace of the Holy Spirit, acknowledges his sins, grieves over them, and apprehends by faith the promises concerning the grace of God for the sake of Christ, and so forth.

For infants, when they receive faith through baptism, are indeed said to be regenerated, but are not equally or customarily said to be converted. Nor are they capable, by reason of their age, of hearing the Word and of the resulting acknowledgment of sins that arises therefrom.

In this way, the terminus "from which" of conversion is indicated (see above, § XV, p. 506 ff.). Those who are said to be turned away from God through sin include both those who have never previously had faith, such as persons born and raised outside the Church in paganism, Judaism, or Muhammadanism, whom they call unbelievers, and also those who have cast off the faith they once possessed through sins, whom some therefore call the lapsed, and others the relapsed. The conversion of the former group they call the first conversion, inasmuch as no other conversion has preceded it in that subject. The conversion of the latter group they call the second conversion, because another prior conversion, or regeneration, had already occurred in the same subject. There is indeed also a repentance of those who stand firm, that is, of persons who have been reborn and are believers, who still persist in the state of regeneration and grace; yet because they have sins which they ought daily to acknowledge, to pray against, and, having turned to God in faith, to deprecate, they are rightly said to be capable of conversion from sins to God in this respect. But it must be admitted that the term "conversion" is then taken in a more general sense, since in its more specific signification it has as its subject only the wicked person, who is constituted in potency toward conjunction with God but is not actually conjoined.

For those who, by obstinately resisting, place an obstacle before divine grace, so long as they conduct themselves in this way, not only are not converted, but are themselves the cause why they are not converted (see what we said at § XXXIV, note (d), p. 542).

### 36 The subject "by which" of conversion is the human soul

The subject "by which" of conversion is the human soul, with respect to the intellect and the will; and in its own manner, also with respect to the sensitive appetite.

Notes. For conversion is not received in the whole human being, but with respect to his nobler part, as the proximate and immediate subject, the person is said to be converted.

As is evident from what has been said concerning the termini of conversion, both "from which" and "to which" (§ XV ff., p. 506 ff.).

For although a fuller perfection of the sensitive appetite belongs to renovation, nevertheless it is here certain that the sensitive appetite must at least be subjected to the spirit to such a degree that the production of saving faith is not impeded by the lusts of the flesh. Compare what we said concerning regeneration at § IV and V, note (e), pp. 497, 498, 499.

### 37 The proximate end of regeneration and conversion is justification

The proximate end of regeneration and conversion is justification; the ultimate end on the part of human beings is eternal salvation; on the part of God, it is His glory.

Notes. Which God Himself intends, and for the sake of which He regenerates and converts human beings.

Whence human beings are commanded μετανοεῖν (metanoein), that is, to repent, εἰς ἄφεσιν ἁμαρτιῶν (eis aphesin hamartiōn), that is, for the forgiveness of sins (Acts 2:38).

Thus God is said to have regenerated us unto an inheritance of heavenly goods (1 Peter 1:3, 4, 5), and to have granted to the Gentiles τὴν μετάνοιαν εἰς ζωήν (tēn metanoian eis zōēn), that is, repentance unto life (Acts 11:18). And Paul teaches that there is a certain μετάνοια εἰς σωτηρίαν (metanoia eis sōtērian), that is, repentance unto salvation (2 Corinthians 7:9; compare Ezekiel 33:11).

See the passages cited at 1 Peter 1:3 and Acts 11:18.

### 38 The consequent or fruit of regeneration and conversion is new obedience

The consequent or fruit of regeneration and conversion is new obedience, and accordingly the resolve not to sin but to live piously; which resolve, if it is habitual, arises not so much from contrition as from faith.

Notes. Thus John commands that one bring forth fruits worthy of repentance (Matthew 3:8).

According to the saying in 1 John 3:9: "Whoever is born of God" (insofar as he is reborn and so long as he remains reborn) "does not commit sin" (that is, sin proceeding against conscience and from a deliberate purpose and intention of the mind). Indeed, "he cannot sin" (in the manner just explained, namely, that he should simultaneously sin and yet remain reborn; rather, as soon as he sins knowingly and willingly from deliberate purpose, he immediately ceases to be reborn), as the Blessed Aegidius Hunnius explains in his Commentary on this passage.

Just as we have shown that charity, the mother of holy works, is joined with faith in Christ by an indissoluble bond (Chapter II, § X, p. 491).
