For serious contrition and the resolve to sin cannot coexist together, since the former involves a serious displeasure with sins while the latter involves complacency in sins. Whence, by the force of their opposition, so long as contrition endures, the resolve to sin cannot have place in the same subject. But nevertheless it must be admitted that a constant resolve not to sin, that is, constancy of the will in fleeing sin, or habitual hatred of sin, depends upon the powers of grace and the special motive of charity, proceeding from faith kindled through the Gospel. Compare the Blessed Muse, German Treatise on Repentance against J. M. Stenger (Musaeus, German Treatise on Repentance against Stenger, Part I, Chapter I, pp. 12, 13; Part II, Chapter II, p. 205; Part III, Chapter IX, no. 1, pp. 709 ff., 711 ff.).

### 39 Meanwhile, it can happen

Meanwhile, it can happen, and sometimes does happen, that persons who have been reborn and converted fall from the state of regeneration and grace through sins, not only once but multiple times, and are restored to it through a conversion that is correspondingly repeated.

Notes. For not only after the first and second regeneration, but always, there remains within the reborn an evil concupiscence, which, although it is weakened through conversion so that it no longer reigns as it did before, is nevertheless not so completely subdued, whether by the first, the second, the third, or the fourth conversion, that it does not oppose the spirit or seek dominion. See Galatians 5:17 and Romans 7:18. Thus it can happen that concupiscence, having conceived, brings forth sin and death, according to James 1:15. Moreover, outside the reborn there always remain and lie in ambush the world and Satan, no less after the third and fourth conversion than after the first. And the will of the reborn in this life is not fully confirmed in good so as to be exempt from the danger of falling.

For God offers grace and the remission of sins without restriction to all sinners, without regard to whether they have fallen once or multiple times, and He asserts under oath that He does not desire the death of any sinner but wills that all should live by repentance, as the words in Ezekiel, chapters 18 and 33, set forth indefinitely, are to be understood in a universal sense, as Paul teaches (1 Timothy 2:4) and Peter teaches (2 Peter 3:9). Nor therefore can it be said that those who relapse after a repeated conversion are not converted except by an extraordinary grace, conferred from the hidden and inscrutable counsel of God beyond the common power of the Word. See in full the Blessed Musaeus (Musaeus, German Treatise on Repentance against Stenger, Part II, Chapter I, p. 126 ff., and Part III, Chapter VIII, p. 677 ff.). Thus also Chrysostom says: χιλιάκις μετανοήσας, χιλιάκις εἴσελθε (chiliakis metanoēsas, chiliakis eiselthe), that is, "Having repented a thousand times, enter a thousand times." Compare Kromayer (Kromayer, Aphoristic Theology, Book XII, Aphorism VII, p. 329).

### 40 True repentance

True repentance, even if it is late and occurs only at the end of life, can nevertheless be salutary; although to defer repentance for so long is most perilous.

Notes. For God offers grace to the penitent without restriction. And thus the ancients said: "True repentance is never too late." See Kromayer (Kromayer, Aphoristic Theology, Book XII, Aphorism V, p. 327). Compare also Musaeus (Musaeus, Treatise against Stenger, Part II, Chapter I, pp. 145 ff.; Chapter II, p. 185 f.; Part III, Chapter IV, pp. 479 ff.).

To this belong those sayings: "Late repentance is seldom true." "How shall one remember God in death who does not remember himself in life?" "Let one day be hidden, so that all may be observed." "He who promised pardon did not promise tomorrow." On which see Kromayer (Kromayer, Aphoristic Theology, Book XII, Aphorism VI, p. 318). Compare Musaeus (Musaeus, Treatise against Stenger, Part II, Chapter I, pp. 150, 151, and Part III, Chapter III, pp. 408, 409, and the passages cited there from Matthew 24:38, 42, 44, 50; Matthew 25:10, 13; Luke 21:34; likewise Chapter IV, pp. 479 ff.).

### 41 Regeneration may be defined as an action of God

Regeneration may be defined as an action of God, by which God endows and equips a human being who lacks spiritual powers but does not obstinately resist, out of pure grace, for the sake of Christ, through the Word and Baptism, with spiritual powers for believing in Christ and for beginning the spiritual life, for the purpose of obtaining justification and eternal life.

Conversion taken transitively may be described as an action of God, by which God works in an adult human being, who either has not previously been reborn or who after regeneration has been turned away from Him (God) through sins, out of pure grace, for the sake of Christ, through the word of the Law, an acknowledgment of sins together with serious sorrow over them, and through the word of the Gospel, faith in Christ together with the resolve to amend one's life, for the purpose of conferring upon him justification and eternal life.

Conversion taken intransitively, or repentance, is described as an immanent action of a human being, by which he, having been prevented by divine grace and further assisted by it, acknowledges his sins from the Law, grieves over them and detests them, apprehends by faith the promises of gratuitous remission of sins for the sake of Christ offered in the Gospel, and raises himself up by confidence placed in the merit of Christ, with the resolve of a better life, for the purpose of obtaining remission of sins and eternal salvation.

Notes. Who is the principal efficient cause (see § VI, p. 499).

The subject and the terminus "from which" of regeneration are indicated (see § IV and X, pp. 497, 501, 502).

This is the impulsive cause, both internal and external (see § VII, VIII, p. 500).

The less principal efficient cause is denoted (see § V, p. 501).

Thus the terminus "to which" is indicated, on which see § V, p. 498.

The end common to regeneration and conversion is denoted, on which see § XXXVII, p. 545.

See § XIII, note (c), p. 504.

Who is the principal efficient cause of conversion (see § XXVII, p. 528).

The subject of conversion and likewise the terminus "from which" are indicated, according to § XV and XXXV, pp. 506 and 542.

The impulsive cause, according to § XXVIII, p. 529.

The instrumental cause is denoted, on which see § XXIX, pp. 529, 530.

These pertain to the abolition of the terminus "from which" and to the terminus "to which" itself, according to § XVII ff., pp. 509 ff.

Which is necessarily conjoined with true conversion and faith (see § XXXVIII, p. 545).

The final cause of conversion, on which see § XXXVII, p. 545.

See § XIII, note (c), p. 504.

See the passage just cited.

See § XXX, XXXI, pp. 531 ff.

These pertain to the retractation of sins and the first part of repentance, which they call contrition (see § XIX, pp. 510 ff.; § XXVI, pp. 526, 527).

These things relate to the abolition, not only moral, of sins with respect to the offense, but also physical, and accordingly to the acquisition of the terminus "to which" of conversion itself; and thus to the second part of repentance (see § XVII, p. 509; § XX, pp. 513 ff.).

According to what we said at § XXXVIII, p. 545.

The final cause of conversion and repentance (see § XXXVII, p. 545).

## 21 On Justification

### 1 Justification, which immediately follows conversion

Justification, which immediately follows conversion, has a forensic signification and denotes that act by which God the judge pronounces a sinful human being, and therefore one guilty of both fault and punishment, yet believing in Christ, to be righteous.

Notes. For once faith has been posited, and through faith, which is kindled in conversion, a person is immediately justified, so that the act by which faith is conferred upon a person and the act by which that person is justified are simultaneous in time, even though the former is prior in nature and the latter posterior (Musaeus, Disputation on the Justification of the Sinful Person before God, 1650, §XII).

Although the Latin word "justificare" is composed of the noun "justus" and the verb "facere," nevertheless, according to established usage, especially in the Scriptures, when a sinful person is said to be justified before God, the term does not denote the infusion of habitual righteousness. Rather, in accordance with the character of the Hebrew term קידִ צְּ הִ (to declare righteous) (see 2 Samuel 15:4; Deuteronomy 25:1; Proverbs 17:15) and the Greek δικαιοῦν (to justify) (Romans 3 and 4), the Latin "justificare," which Luther correctly rendered as "rechtfertigen," has been transferred from the external court to the spiritual court, in which human beings are, as it were, placed before the divine tribunal, and, once the case has been examined and the sentence pronounced, they are absolved.

The doctrinal seat of this teaching is found in Romans chapters 3 and 4.

For it is God who is said to justify (Romans 8:33).

Every person stands as ὑπόδικος τῷ Θεῷ (guilty before God), as Paul declares of the whole world (Romans 3:19). The law, moreover, functions in the manner of a plaintiff and renders a person ὑπόδικον (liable to judgment) (see also John 5:45). The conscience, in turn, functions in the manner of a witness, confirming the accusation of the law and convicting the person (Romans 2:15).

Although the one who is justified has not been found innocent, he nevertheless has one who has made satisfaction for his offense and pleaded his cause before God the judge (Romans 3:25; 1 John 2:1).

For thus justification is set in opposition to condemnation (Romans 8:33, 34). This absolution of the person, or reckoning as righteous, takes place within the divine mind, not through an external act, as will occur in that final and solemn judgment, as will become clear from what follows.

### 2 The efficient cause of the act of justification is the triune God

The efficient cause of the act of justification is the triune God.

Notes. This is so called according to our mode of conceiving it, that is, it is the cause that virtually causes, because justification, with respect to the thing itself, is not an act really produced in God in the way that acts of our will are. Rather, in accordance with the character of other immanent acts of God, it is the very essence of God, conceived by way of an act on account of the connoted object (Musaeus, Disputation on the Justification of the Sinful Person before God, §XVI; and Musaeus, Detailed Explanation, book 13, pp. 584, 585).

The act of imputing righteousness to a person and of not imputing sin is ascribed to God (Romans 4:6, 8).

Thus justification is attributed to the Father, whose Son is Christ (Romans 8:33), to the Son himself (Luke 7:47, 48, 49; Matthew 9:6), and to the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:11). And it is otherwise established that the divine immanent acts are similar to the external works in this respect: that they too are undivided. Nevertheless, concerning the Son it must be observed that he relates to justification not only as an efficient cause, justifying us by one act together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, but also by way of a meritorious cause, inasmuch as, being the Mediator between God and human beings, he gave himself as the price of redemption for all (1 Timothy 2:5, 6).

### 3 The internal impulsive cause is the goodness or gratuitous favor of God

The internal impulsive cause is the goodness or gratuitous favor of God.

Notes. This too is a virtually causative principle, or so called according to our mode of conceiving, to which Scripture accommodates itself.

The Apostle calls this χάρις τοῦ Θεοῦ (the grace of God), by which he regards us who are unworthy (Romans 3:24), the riches of mercy and the great love with which God loved us (Ephesians 2:4, 5), and χρηστότης καὶ φιλανθρωπία (kindness and love toward humanity) (Titus 3:4).

### 4 The external impulsive cause

The external impulsive cause, which is also the principal and meritorious cause, is Christ the Mediator, by reason of his active and passive obedience.

Notes. This cause does not remove the gratuitous favor of God in the matter of justification, nor is it itself excluded by that favor, since it is owed precisely to divine grace that God sent his Son to make satisfaction on our behalf so that we might be justified, and that God accepts this merit of another as though it were our own (Musaeus, Disputation on the Justification of the Sinful Person before God, §§XXIII, XXIV, XXV).

This merit possesses a sufficient and therefore infinite power, worth, price, and value for moving God to pronounce us righteous.

As it is written, we are said to be justified through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus (Romans 3:25), meaning that God, in the act of justification, looks to the price of redemption that Christ paid for sinners, and, moved or impelled by it, remits our sins. And it says that God made Christ, who knew no sin (since he was innocent and supremely holy), to be sin for us (that is, a propitiatory sacrifice to be slaughtered and offered for sin), so that we might become the righteousness of God (righteous before God) through him (2 Corinthians 5:21). To the same point belongs the statement that Christ was made for us righteousness from God, namely, so that through him we might be made righteous before God (1 Corinthians 1:30).

For since we were obligated not only to fulfill the law of God but also to render for the transgression of the law the satisfaction that divine justice demands, neither of which lies within our power, and since Christ undertook and rendered both in our place, both therefore move God to pronounce us, for whose sake they were rendered, righteous, just as if we ourselves had fulfilled the law and rendered to him the satisfaction owed for sins. Hence that merit of Christ is called our righteousness.

### 5 The less principal impulsive cause is faith in Christ

The less principal impulsive cause is faith in Christ.

Notes. Faith indeed moves God to justify a person, yet not by its own proper worth, power, or value, but by the power and worth of the object that it apprehends. In the Solid Declaration of the Formula of Concord, this is expressed as follows: "Faith does not justify because it is itself so good a work and so excellent a virtue, but because in the promise of the Gospel it apprehends and embraces the merit of Christ" (Solid Declaration of the Formula of Concord, On the Justification of Faith, p. 648).

Others say that faith causes justification instrumentally or organically; still others, relatively. These positions, however, as far as the substance of the matter is concerned, agree with the view concerning the less principal impulsive cause, and this latter terminology expresses the matter most suitably. For those who speak of an instrumental cause, if they mean a physically efficient cause, do not so much express the relation of faith to the act of justification itself (which is established not to be a really produced act, much less one that might be produced through a physical instrumental cause) as the relation of habitual faith to the actual apprehension of the merit or righteousness of Christ. For faith, taken as the very act of believing, is not the cause of apprehension but is itself the apprehension of the merit of Christ. Yet it must further be admitted that faith, taken as the habit of believing, is rather the principal cause of its own acts than an instrumental one, just as other supernatural habits are physically efficient but principal causes of their own acts. Accordingly, when faith is called the instrumental cause of the apprehension of the merit of Christ, this seems to be understood in that sense in which any principle "by which" something is done is called an instrument, just as faith, apprehending the merit of Christ and the grace of God offered in the Gospel promises, is commonly compared to a hand stretched out to receive an alms. If, however, they call faith an instrumental cause in relation to the act of justification itself, it is necessarily understood as a morally moving cause, and one that moves not by its own worth, goodness, or merit, but by the goodness, worth, and merit of another principal cause. And so an instrumental cause in the moral order is the same as a less principal impulsive cause (Musaeus, Disputation on the Eternal Election Decree, ch. 2, §§LXVII ff., pp. 48 ff.).

Those, moreover, who say that faith justifies relatively or correlatively mean, of course, that faith, by virtue of its correlate, which is the merit of Christ, contributes something to our justification, and indeed morally, by moving the will of God by virtue of the merit of Christ toward our justification. Hence once again, the aspect under which faith concurs in our justification can be none other than that which belongs to an impulsive cause (Musaeus, Disputation on the Eternal Election Decree, ch. 2, §LXXVIII, pp. 54, 55).

That some of our theologians refused to call faith an impulsive cause arose from the fact that they were persuaded that every external impulsive cause implies some kind of merit, or at least a proper goodness, worth, and perfection by which the will of the efficient cause is moved to act, inasmuch as the distinction of causes into principal and less principal in the doctrine of the impulsive cause was not so thoroughly established among the older metaphysicians as it was in the doctrine of the efficient cause (Musaeus, Disputation on the Eternal Election Decree, ch. 2, §§LXII, LXIII, pp. 43, 44).

Thus we are said to be justified by faith, from faith, and through faith (Romans 3:28, 30; Galatians 3:24). When, however, it is said of faith in the nominative case that it justifies, the expression appears to be metonymic. For the sense is not that faith absolves a person from sins and reckons him righteous; rather, faith is said to justify because in consideration of it God reckons us righteous, or because it moves God (not indeed by its own worth, but by the worth of the merit of Christ) to justify us (Musaeus, Disputation on the Justification of the Sinful Person before God, §XXXVIII). Concerning the nature of faith, see the preceding chapter.

### 6 Besides this faith

Besides this faith, however, nothing else from our side can be considered a cause of justification.

Notes. See Romans 3:28, where Paul distinguishes faith from all works whatsoever, not only those that are done according to the law of nature by the powers of nature, but in general from works of the law, which are done according to the prescription of the law by whatever powers, in this respect: that through faith a person is justified, but through works not so. Hence it is rightly said that faith alone justifies; that is, that faith on our part is that in consideration of which God justifies us, and that whatever is not faith itself (even if it is conjoined with faith) ought not to be regarded on our part as a cause of justification (Musaeus, Disputation on the Justification of the Sinful Person before God, §XXXVIII; and Musaeus, Treatise on the Church, part 2, disputation 5, §LVI, pp. 377 ff., §§LXXV ff., pp. 395 ff.; Musaeus, Vindication of the Biblical Glosses against Erbermann, disputation 2, §XVIII ff., pp. 96 ff.).

For faith is not opposed to divine grace and the merit of Christ but is subordinated to them (Romans 3:24, 25).

Whether one should say it contributes to justification as much as faith contributes, or somewhat less.

### 7 The form, or formal reason

The form, or formal reason, of justification is the remission or non- imputation of sins.

Notes. Otherwise it would have to be admitted that justification is a substance composed of matter and form, which it is not.

Rather, God judges or wills that the sins of the person to be justified do not so pertain to that person that he should be afflicted with punishments on account of them (Romans 4:7, 8; 8:1). And so the guilt of sins, although it is not removed from the sins themselves (which, by the very fact that they are sins, are also worthy of punishment), is nevertheless removed from the sinful person.

We do not, however, exclude the imputation of the righteousness of Christ, that is, of his obedience both active and passive, nor the imputation of faith itself unto righteousness. We hold only that the imputation of the righteousness of Christ and of faith is, in the order of reason, prior to the forensic act of justification itself, that is, the absolution from the guilt of sins. For to the question, "Why does God justify a person?" the answer given by a priori reasoning is: "Because God imputes to the person the righteousness or merit of Christ apprehended by faith, or so judges it to pertain to the person that he is thereby absolved from the guilt of sins."

Hence a distinction can be made between the form of the righteous person, in consideration of which he is reckoned righteous in the act of justification, and the form of justification itself. As the Apology of the Augsburg Confession (article on Justification, p. 273) teaches, the word "justify" can be taken in two senses. In one sense, it means the same as to be made or constituted righteous from unrighteous, through the righteousness that avails before God, which is none other than the righteousness procured for us by the active and passive obedience of Christ. In the other sense, it means the same as to be pronounced or reckoned righteous. In the former sense, we are justified, or made righteous, when we apprehend by faith the righteousness of Christ as our own, and thus by the righteousness of Christ apprehended through faith we are formally constituted righteous before God. (For this reason it can also be said that the formal element of justification is the righteousness of Christ apprehended by faith.) In the latter sense, it must be acknowledged that the formal element of justification is the non-imputation or remission of sins, while the righteousness of Christ apprehended by faith and accepted by God as ours, or imputed to us by God, is its foundation and therefore prior in the order of nature (Musaeus, Detailed Explanation, book 13, question 73, pp. 586 ff.).

### 8 The subject of justification is a sinful person

The subject of justification is a sinful person, but one who has been converted or regenerated.

Notes. See Romans 3:23, 24 and 4:5, and compare Titus 3:5, 7. From this it is at the same time evident that God justifies the ungodly (Romans 4:5) not insofar as that person is and remains ungodly, but the ungodly person who, led by repentance, has retracted the sins committed and has presented to God the satisfaction of Christ for sins, apprehended by faith, as a λύτρον (ransom) for his own sins.

### 9 The end of justification

The end of justification, on the part of the human beings who are justified, is their eternal salvation; on the part of God who justifies, it is his glory.

Notes. Thus in Romans 4:6, 9, justification itself is called a μακαρισμός (a declaration of blessedness), namely, because it comes to human beings as the cause of eternal salvation, the inheritance of which it also confers.

See Ephesians 1:5.

### 10 The effects of justification are peace of conscience with God

The effects of justification are peace of conscience with God, adoption as children of God, the gift of the Holy Spirit, sanctification and renewal, and the hope of eternal life.

Notes. Peace of conscience means that the soul, though conscious of its sins, is nevertheless not distressed, nor does it dread and flee from an angry God, but is content in its strength and, secure in the grace of God, rests (Romans 5:1).

Indeed, by virtue of regeneration we are born children of God; yet, once regenerated and having received the remission of sins, we are adopted as children of God, or we obtain the right of the children of God through adoption (Ephesians 1:5; Galatians 4:5; John 1:12).

The gift of the Holy Spirit means that he himself, being substantially present in the justified, manifests his presence and, as it were, indwelling by conferring more abundant gifts of grace (Galatians 4:6; 1 Corinthians 3:16).

Sanctification (ἁγιασμός) is expressly called the fruit of emancipation from sin (Romans 6:22; see also vv. 18, 19). More will be said shortly concerning renewal.

Those who are justified are said to glory in the hope of the glory of God (Romans 5:2), namely, the glory to be obtained from God and in God. And not only the inheritance itself but also the hope and expectation of future salvation arising from it are attributed to them (Romans 8:17, 23, 24, 25; compare Galatians 3:29).

## 22 On Renewal and Good Works

### 1 The word "renewal" is sometimes taken so broadly that it encompasses conversion itself

The word "renewal" is sometimes taken so broadly that it encompasses conversion itself, or regeneration, and indeed even justification together with the subsequent work of sanctification. Here, however, it is taken more strictly, so that it may be distinguished from conversion and may itself also follow upon justification.

Note. Renewal in general denotes any action by which old things, or things worn out or weakened by age or otherwise, or things corrupted, are restored. And so in the spiritual renewal of a human being, taken broadly, the old man is understood to be abolished according to his entire nature, that is, the complete lack of spiritual powers, the guilt and dominion of sin; and the new man is understood to be produced according to his full extent, that is, the spiritual powers themselves, absolution from guilt, and the habitual gift by which the dominion of sin is suppressed. See 2 Corinthians 5:17 and following, where those who are in Christ are said to be a new creation; and to this is referred the reconciliation with God and justification through Christ (2 Corinthians 5:19, 21). Compare Musaeus (On Conversion, Jena edition, Disputation 3, ch. 1, section 29, p. 123), where he shows that the conversion of a human being is truly, and not unusually said to be, a kind of renewal. Add also Detailed Explanation, book 15, question 78, pp. 653 and following.

In the strict sense, we have reckoned renewal among the effects of justification in Chapter IV, final section. And the following discussion will set forth this special signification.

### 2 Renewal strictly so called imports a real and intrinsic change in the…

Renewal strictly so called imports a real and intrinsic change in the regenerate or converted person. Hence the terms of this change are to be noted: the term from which and the term to which.

Note. Thus Paul addresses his Romans in chapter 12, verse 2: "Be transformed (μεταμορφοῦσθε) by the renewal of your mind."

This is what occurs in every change, where one terminus must be abolished or abandoned, and the other must be produced or acquired.

### 3 The term from which consists of the remnants of sin which remain after conversion

The term from which consists of the remnants of sin which remain after conversion; namely, a certain defect of good powers: on the part of the intellect, for knowing spiritual things; on the part of the will, for pursuing spiritual goods; on the part of the sensitive appetite, for obeying the higher faculties; and at the same time also a proneness of these same faculties of the soul toward evil.

Note. This term is to be abolished, if not entirely and radically (which cannot happen in this life), then at least in a qualified sense, so that it may be diminished, weakened, or suppressed.

The old manner of living and sinning includes both innate sin itself and the vices contracted through evil living.

See the complaint of Paul (who was certainly regenerate and endowed with spiritual powers according to the inner man, as in verse 18 and 22), that he does not do the good that he wills, nor does he find sufficient powers to do good, but does the evil that he does not will, and this by the force of sin dwelling in him and clinging to him (Romans 7:15 and following).

This is not a complete lack of good powers (since in conversion itself something of good powers has already been obtained), yet there remains a certain deficiency.

For although some spiritual light is present after conversion, it is nevertheless joined with a lack of the fuller perfection that ought to be present.

For the powers conferred in conversion are feeble, so that the just or more perfect holiness that ought to be present is lacking.

See what we said in Chapter III on Regeneration and Conversion, section 5, final note, p. 499, whence it is clear that the lack of ready obedience owed to the higher faculties has not yet been removed through conversion.

Indeed, even in the regenerate, the flesh (that is, that which is carnal in a person, or what was transmitted to them after the fall through carnal generation, and by which one is inclined from spiritual things to sensible things) lusts against the spirit (that is, those new powers which the Holy Spirit began to confer in the act of conversion or regeneration), and in lusting resists the spirit (Galatians 5:17). Whence it is clear that in the intellect there remains a certain proneness (though not equally strong as before conversion) to rash judgments concerning spiritual things; in the will, a certain inclination to prefer perishable goods over spiritual ones; and in the sensitive appetite, a certain propensity toward goods pleasing to the senses, even if forbidden.

### 4 The term to which of renewal consists of those greater spiritual powers which…

The term to which of renewal consists of those greater spiritual powers which are to be acquired only after conversion: namely, on the part of the intellect, a fuller knowledge of spiritual things; on the part of the will, a more perfect holiness; and on the part of the sensitive appetite, a readier and more constant obedience to be rendered to the higher faculties.

Note. This is the term that must be acquired, and which renewal must attain by its acts.

These are not, however, full perfection without any defect, which does not befall human beings in the condition of this life after the fall, given the tenacity of original sin; though one must strive and aspire toward it through renewal itself.

Thus we are to grow up into Christ in all things, and arrive at the perfect man, at the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ (Ephesians 4:13, 15), that is, just as the Lord himself from infancy made certain advances, strengthened in Spirit, increasing in wisdom and age and grace before God and men, until he progressed from one stage of age to another into his full manhood; so too Christians should advance by the increase of the Spirit in faith and knowledge of Christ into the perfect man. Paul does not understand this of the complete perfection that is expected in the other age; rather, only that perfection is meant by which, with the roots of faith firmly established, a person cannot be moved from the foundation of salvation, Jesus Christ, by the cunning of heretics or by any frauds and deceits of Satan. This paraphrase is from Hunnius in his commentary (Aegidius Hunnius, Commentary on Ephesians).

Thus at Ephesians 4:13, the increase and perfection is referred to faith and the knowledge of the Son of God. And at Philippians 1:9, Paul prays for those already converted that they may abound in knowledge and all discernment. Compare Colossians 1:10 and 3:10, where in this latter passage we are expressly commanded to put on the new man, who is renewed unto knowledge and the image of him who created him.

This means that we are to be renewed in the spirit of our mind, putting on the new man, who according to God is created in righteousness and true (that is, genuine or sincere) holiness (Ephesians 4:24). By righteousness is understood a kind of universal righteousness, that is, the complex of all virtues pertaining to Christian morals, which are variously classified either according to the two tables of the Decalogue, or according to the method of moral theology, according to the duties of a person toward God with respect to internal and external worship, toward oneself (the regenerate person), and toward one's neighbor, concerning the neighbor's soul, body, reputation, possessions, and so forth. A brief catalogue of Christian virtues may be seen at Galatians 5:22-23; 1 Timothy 6:11; 2 Timothy 2:22; and 2 Peter 1:6-7.

The obedience of the sensitive appetite stands in opposition to the obedience rendered to the desires of the flesh (Romans 6:10).

### 5 The term from which of renewal is abolished in part when a person

The term from which of renewal is abolished in part when a person, having undertaken a diligent and careful examination of his life, more carefully observes and retracts sins committed or left unaddressed after conversion, through a serious displeasure and sorrow over them; and in part when he occupies himself in the exercise of spiritual acts of every kind, according to the various types of Christian virtues.

Note. Scripture uses the phrases: "Put off, according to the former manner of life, the old man" (Ephesians 4:22); "Strip off the old man with his deeds" (Colossians 3:9); "Crucify the flesh with its lusts" (Galatians 5:24); "Put to death your earthly members" (Colossians 3:5). But sin in this life is never entirely and radically extirpated in a person; it must, however, be diminished, weakened, and expelled as far as possible, as we said at section 2, note (a). Compare Musaeus (On Penance, Against Stenger, part 3, ch. 7, pp. 634-635).

This accords with what we said in Chapter III on conversion. Hence what was said about the penance of those who stand pertains here: that contrition cannot coexist with the intention of sinning (see section 34, p. 543, and section 37, p. 546). The more frequently and carefully, therefore, the regenerate person occupies himself in the chastening of himself or of his sins, the more frequently the dominion of sin is checked and thus diminished; although it has likewise been said that such more frequent or more constant contrition arises after conversion from the motive of love (section 37, p. 546, from Musaeus, Against Stenger, part 3, ch. 9, pp. 709 and following).

Concerning the exercise of spiritual acts, more will be said shortly. Thus, while one strives toward those greater perfections to which the term from which of renewal is opposed partly privatively and partly contrarily, it follows that one simultaneously tends toward the abolition of those opposites, that is, of the term from which itself.

### 6 And so at the same time one tends toward the acquisition of the term to which of renewal

And so at the same time one tends toward the acquisition of the term to which of renewal, when through more frequent spiritual acts of intellect and will, the spiritual powers previously conferred are augmented and receive increase, so that they may attain to a fuller habitual perfection.

Note. Thus Paul writes to Timothy: γύμναζε σεαυτόν (gymnaze seauton), "Exercise yourself, like an athlete, unto godliness" (1 Timothy 4:7). Elsewhere he compares Christians to runners (1 Corinthians 9:24 and following). And when he is about to set forth his own example for the Philippians to imitate, he says in chapter 3, verse 13: "I do not yet consider myself to have attained" (the requisite perfection, of which he speaks in verse 12), "but this one thing I do, forgetting those things which are behind and straining forward (ἐπεκτεινόμενος, as with body leaning or stretched forward toward what lies ahead, like runners pressing toward the goal). Namely, he does not rest content in what he has already attained, but continually presses on toward further progress and toward perfection," as Aegidius Hunnius explains (Hunnius, Commentary on Philippians). And in chapter 4, verses 8-9, he writes: "Whatever things are true, whatever things are honorable, whatever things are just, whatever things are pure, whatever things are fitting (προσφιλῆ), whatever things are of good report, if there is any virtue and if there is any praise, think on these things; do these things."

Here also belongs the parable in which Christ records that servants who received ten, or five, or two talents from their master acquired just as many additional talents; that is, persons who diligently used the gifts of grace first conferred upon them attained to greater perfection (Matthew 25:14 and following; Luke 19:12 and following).

### 7 The principal efficient cause of renewal is the Triune God

The principal efficient cause of renewal is the Triune God.

Note. This is equally true of regeneration. For just as the first powers of grace are conferred through the supernatural and infinite power of God, so too the increase and confirmation of those powers is owed to God. Hence Paul writes at Philippians 1:6: "I am persuaded that he who began a good work in you will perfect it until the day of Jesus Christ."

This is a work ad extra, which is nevertheless attributed by appropriation to the Holy Spirit (Titus 3:5), who is also therefore called the Spirit of sanctification (Romans 1:4), who dwells in the regenerate as in a temple (1 Corinthians 3:16), leads them (Romans 8:14), and assists their weaknesses (Romans 8:26).

### 8 The instrumental cause on God's part consists of the word of the Law and of the Gospel

The instrumental cause on God's part consists of the word of the Law and of the Gospel, and the Sacraments of Baptism and the Eucharist.

Note. The Law indeed throughout one's entire life dictates what is to be done, also for the regenerate (Psalm 1:2; Psalm 119 in its entirety). The same Law suppresses the remaining lusts of the flesh in the regenerate. See Galatians 5:15-16. We understand here the Law of Moses and of Christ, which is really one, and is to be observed by the regenerate for their renewal. Compare Musaeus (On Penance, Against Stenger, part 2, ch. 1, p. 160; ch. 2, p. 199; part 3, ch. 6, pp. 561 and following).

The Gospel not only arouses faith in the act of conversion but also preserves, confirms, and augments the faith already aroused. Hence at 1 Peter 1:22, the regenerate are said to purify their souls by obeying the truth. Compare Musaeus (Disputation on Renewal, sections 38-39).

Regarding Baptism, see Titus 3:5, where Baptism is expressly called the washing of renewal, because renewal depends upon it as upon a cause. For not only through Baptism, when it is actually received, does the Holy Spirit work in the heart of the person who does not place an obstacle the benefit of regeneration and renewal, which Baptism, as that for the sake of which it was instituted, outwardly signifies, and thus the powers of grace are efficiently conferred upon the person being baptized by the Holy Spirit through Baptism as an efficacious instrument, and these powers contribute something to subsequent spiritual acts; but also through Baptism once received and recalled to memory, the Holy Spirit similarly works and confers further spiritual powers or augments those already conferred. Compare Musaeus (Disputation on Renewal, section 42).

In the Eucharist we receive the body of Christ, which is the bread of life, or life- giving bread (John 6:54-55). And we are more closely united to Christ as to a vine, so that as branches in it we may bear fruit (John 15:1, 5). So also the many are said to have drunk of one Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:13). Compare Musaeus (Disputation on Renewal, section 43).

### 9 On the part of the human being

On the part of the human being, the powers of grace received in conversion contribute efficiently to renewal.

Note. For people are commanded to purify their hearts themselves (1 Peter 1:22), to put off the old man and put on the new (Ephesians 4:22 and following; Colossians 3:10). This nevertheless occurs dependently upon God, or the grace of God, as is clear from what has been said. Compare Detailed Explanation, book 15, question 79, pp. 663 and following. And this is what Scherzer teaches in his System of Theology, book 17, section 4, p. 458: that the justified person is a cause of renewal, for one is said to renew oneself (1 Peter 1:22); but that one is a secondary cause, because one is subordinated to God, and the grace of God by nature moves the person prior to the person acting through the grace by which he has been moved.

Not at all the natural powers, which are and remain always unfit for spiritual things.

The manner in which faith is called ἐνεργουμένη (energoumenē), efficaciously working (according to the analogy of Ephesians 3:20; Colossians 1:29; James 5:16), through love (Galatians 5:6), is especially to be noted. Hence it should be observed that faith performs a twofold function in relation to renewal. In one function, it determines the intellect to assent both in general to all things revealed in the Sacred Scriptures, and in particular to the promises of the gratuitous remission of sins on account of Christ; for thus, by deducing practical conclusions, faith prescribes what is to be done and what is to be avoided, adding reasons and motives by which the will is impelled to pursue the study of piety. In the other function, faith inclines the will itself (in which it also inheres as its subject) to resist the evil concupiscence of the flesh and to do what the intellect, concerning any spiritual object already believed, prescribes by way of a practical judgment. From these frequently repeated acts, the will is rendered daily more ready to act, and various Christian virtues are acquired, of which the principle and root is faith itself. Compare Musaeus (Disputation on Renewal, sections 10 and following).

### 10 The subject of renewal in the sense of "that which" is the converted and justified person

The subject of renewal in the sense of "that which" is the converted and justified person.

Note. That is, the entire supposit which is said to be renewed.

For we are speaking of renewal strictly so called. Otherwise the subject of renewal broadly so called coincides with the subject of regeneration, inasmuch as the same person who is born again is also said to be renewed.

### 11 The subject in the sense of "that by which" is the soul with respect to its faculties

The subject in the sense of "that by which" is the soul with respect to its faculties: the intellect, the will, and the sensitive appetite. Secondarily also the members of the body.

Note. This follows from what we said concerning the terms from which and to which in sections 3, 4, and following. For the subject of any change must be estimated from its terms.

The members of the body serve as instruments of the renewed or sanctified soul, necessary for carrying out holy actions. Here may be referred 1 Thessalonians 5:23, where Paul prays for his people that the God of peace may sanctify them wholly, so that their entire spirit, soul, and body may be preserved blameless. Compare Romans 6:12-13 and 19, where Paul demands that the regenerate present their members as weapons of righteousness unto sanctification. Compare Musaeus (Disputation on Renewal, section 14) and Detailed Explanation, book 15, question 80, p. 665.

### 12 The form, or formal nature

The form, or formal nature, of renewal therefore consists in the complex of many spiritual acts, through which a person strives more and more to tame evil concupiscence and to acquire an increase of the habitual gift, by which one is rendered more fit to perform those things that are conformed to the divine will.

Note. This accords with what we said in section 5 and following. This is what Paul teaches at 2 Corinthians 4:16: that renewal ought to take place ἡμέρᾳ καὶ ἡμέρᾳ (hēmera kai hēmera), day by day. Compare Ephesians 4:22, 25 and following; 2 Peter 1:5, 8. For the things there commanded require not the effort of a single hour or day, but a prolonged and continued study, so that daily we must be occupied in putting off the old man, and daily in putting on the new man and in the exercises of many virtues.

Neither in this life is sin entirely abolished in a person, nor is fully perfect holiness acquired (Romans 7:14 and following to the end; Galatians 5:17). Compare Musaeus (On Penance, Against Stenger, part 3, ch. 7, p. 634).

### 13 The proximate end of renewal coincides with its term to which

The proximate end of renewal coincides with its term to which. The ultimate end on the part of human beings is eternal life; on the part of God, his glory.

Note. For the sake of acquiring this term, renewal takes place.

Thus at Romans 6:22, it is said: "The end of our having been made servants of God, bearing fruit unto sanctification, is eternal life." But beware lest you infer from this that renewal is the efficient or meritorious cause of eternal life. For it is expressly added that this is χάρισμα τοῦ Θεοῦ (charisma tou Theou), the gift of God.

See Philippians 1:9-11, where Paul prays that they may be renewed and sanctified in mind and morals to the glory and praise of God. Compare Ephesians 1:13-14; Colossians 1:9- 12.

### 14 Renewal may be defined as the complex of spiritual acts which the regenerate person

Renewal may be defined as the complex of spiritual acts which the regenerate person, with God graciously concurring through the word and sacraments, exercises by means of the spiritual powers conferred upon him, with respect to the intellect, will, and sensitive appetite, for the abolishing of the remnants of sin and the acquiring of greater holiness, in the way of salvation, to the glory of God.

Note. See section 11, p. 575 The regenerate person is the subject of renewal according to section 10, p. 575, yet also acts efficiently according to section 9, p. 573.

God is the principal and primary cause according to section 7, p. 571.

The word and sacraments are the organic or instrumental causes according to section 8, p. 572.

The spiritual powers are the principle "by which" on the part of the human being, according to section 9, p. 573.

The intellect, will, and sensitive appetite signify the subject "by which" according to section 11, p. 575.

The remnants of sin denote the term from which, according to section 3, p. 565. Greater holiness is the term to which, according to section 4, p. 567.

The way of salvation indicates the ultimate end on the part of human beings, according to section 12, p. 576.

The glory of God is the absolutely ultimate end and the end on God's part, as noted in the same place.

### 15 To the doctrine of renewal belongs the doctrine of good works

To the doctrine of renewal belongs the doctrine of good works, which relate to renewal partly as its end and effect, and partly pertain to its formal nature.

Note. The nature of good works will presently be explained.

If we consider the works to be performed by means of the more perfect powers acquired through renewal, and intended and accomplished in this way, they relate to renewal as its end and effect.

For renewal formally consists in good and holy acts or works, which are performed by the powers of grace and through which one tends toward the increase of spiritual powers. Hence they also have the nature of a principle or cause in relation to the term to which of renewal. See Musaeus (On Renewal, sections 21 and following).

### 16 By good works are here understood the free actions of the regenerate person

By good works are here understood the free actions of the regenerate person, which he exercises by means of the powers of grace received in conversion and subsequently augmented, according to the norm of the divine word, to the glory of God.

Note. Not only positive works, performed according to the prescription of affirmative precepts, but also omissions of acts prohibited by negative precepts are included; these omissions, however, themselves involve or presuppose internal acts of the mind and a certain resolve to omit those acts.

For otherwise there are many holy impulses that the Holy Spirit brings about in a person in the very process of conversion; yet these are not, according to the customary usage of the theological schools, called good works in an absolute sense.

After conversion, the will, in relation to spiritual acts and the corresponding external works, behaves not only actively but also with indifference, so that it can act or not act, act in one way or in another.

These works are led or driven by the Spirit (Romans 8:9), whence they are also called the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22).

They are done according to divine laws, both the moral or natural law common to all people, and positive laws given to certain people and for a certain time. Although works done according to the prescription of human law, whether ecclesiastical or civil, insofar as it does not conflict with divine laws and tends rather toward edification and public utility, also pertain here. For those things are said to be commanded by God not only which are formally and immediately commanded, but also which are mediately and by consequence ordered to be done. Otherwise, if neither obtains, works of choice are not good, according to that saying (Matthew 15:9).

See also 1 Corinthians 10:31 and Colossians 3:17-23.

### 17 The works of the unregenerate

The works of the unregenerate, which are done in some fashion according to the prescription of the moral law, cannot equally be called good as can the works of the regenerate. And although not in themselves and simply, yet insofar as they lack the requisites of good works, they are rightly called sins.

Note. The moral law is known also by the light of nature.

Thus the Gentiles are said to do τὰ τοῦ νόμου (ta tou nomou), the things of the law (Romans 2:15). And the Apology of the Augsburg Confession, article 18, p. 218, teaches that the human will can in some measure accomplish civil righteousness or the righteousness of works: it can speak about God, render to God a certain outward worship, obey magistrates and parents in outward action, and refrain from murder, adultery, and theft. The unregenerate cannot, however, perform moral works exactly conformed to the law without any defect. Hence some have said that those works of the unregenerate, although with respect to the substance of the act they exhibit a conformity with the law and right reason, nevertheless fall short of the rule of rectitude in many ways as regards circumstances. See Detailed Explanation, book 8, question 62, p. 333.

They cannot be called good not only because they are not simply and in every way conformed to the law without any defect (which does not apply even to the regenerate), but because they are not done, as the works of the regenerate are, out of faith and with delight, to the glory of God. Rather, they are done under the compulsion of the law, without faith and inner pleasure, more for the sake of human beings than to be referred to God. Hence they are not equally pleasing to God. Nevertheless, insofar as they are congruent with the law, they can be called good in that respect; as Chemnitz says (Chemnitz, Examination of the Council of Trent, part 1, p. 200), that these actions are in their own kind honorable and good. He adds the reason: "Those things which nature still retains from the first creation, in formation, life, senses, mind, and so forth, are in themselves good, but through sin they are wounded, corrupted, and contaminated." Stegmann writes in his disputation against the Photinians (Joshua Stegmann, Photinian Disputations, disputation 40, question 2, p. 647): "That the good works of the pagans were in some way morally good we concede, because they were done according to the dictate of reason, however imperfectly that dictate may have functioned; but that they are spiritually good does not follow from this." And because some said that those works are good with respect to the substance of the act, which displeased others who included under the name of substance also those things pertaining to circumstances, Stegmann (p. 648) distinguished between the substance of the act with respect to genus and with respect to species, and refers to the latter signification the special causes from which the act proceeds.

This follows from what has been said. And it is indeed useful to distinguish between actions of the unregenerate that are evil in their kind and prohibited by the law of God, and those that are not evil in their kind, or whose very matter or substance is not evil, however else this may be expressed. Following Chemnitz, Gerhard writes (Johann Gerhard, Catholic Confession, book 2, part 3, article 22, ch. 3): "The outward works of the unregenerate, such as clothing the naked, aiding those in danger, and so forth, are not in themselves and by the kind of the act sins." And again: "Certain actions of unregenerate persons are not in themselves and with respect to the substance of the act evil. They are called sins not with respect to the substance of the act." Compare Musaeus (Detailed Explanation, book 8, question 42, pp. 336-337).

As is otherwise said, evil arises from any defect whatsoever. And this defect of actions is not supplied by the imputation of an alien righteousness that has not been apprehended by faith. Those actions are sins with respect to efficient cause, formal cause, and final cause, as Chemnitz and Gerhard teach in the cited passages.

### 18 The efficient cause of good works is the same as that of renewal

The efficient cause of good works is the same as that of renewal.

Note. According to what we said in section 14.

### 19 The form, or formal nature

The form, or formal nature, of good works, when considered in themselves, is their conformity with the law of God. But when they are considered insofar as, though not exactly congruent with the law, they nevertheless please God, their form is faith in Christ.

Note. For the goodness of any work done according to the prescription of a certain norm consists in its agreement with that norm.

Since these works do not exactly conform to the law, they cannot please God simply and absolutely on account of their agreement with the norm. Therefore the form by virtue of which they please God is not that imperfect ἐννομία (ennomia, conformity to law).

Through faith, however, when the merit of Christ is apprehended, it comes about that the infirmities adhering to the works of the faithful are covered.

### 20 The properties of good works are

The properties of good works are: first, that they are done freely; second, that they are imperfect; third, that they are necessary for those who are to be saved.

Note. First, the Law does not compel the regenerate by its threats and curses. Rather, it only directs, or teaches, by its precepts. In this sense, at 1 Timothy 1:9, the Law is said not to have been laid upon the just person, or to be incumbent upon the unwilling as a burden. And at Romans 7:6, the regenerate are said to serve God through the newness of the Spirit (that is, through new powers received from the Holy Spirit, readily and with a certain delight) and not through the oldness of the letter (that is, not by the force of the ancient law, pressing with its threats, driving forward even the reluctant and unwilling). The regenerate would serve God even if no coercive force or threat were annexed to the laws, since out of love for the God who is propitious to them they do all things gladly.

Second, since sin has entered the world and tenaciously clings even to the regenerate, so that the flesh always fights against the Spirit, we do not do all the things we will, as Paul testifies (Galatians 5:17). And thus sometimes in the very circumstances of good actions we err and stumble, or work more sluggishly than is fitting, not with the readiness and alacrity that is due; or by the accompaniment of disordered self-love we stain our works, however good they may otherwise be.

Third, there are various reasons requiring good works, pertaining either to God, to our neighbor, or to ourselves. God, by right of creation, redemption, regeneration, and adoption, holds us obligated to do his will (Malachi 1:6; 1 Corinthians 6:20; Ephesians 2:10; Titus 2:11-12), to glorify him, and to take care lest he be offended or his name spoken ill of; rather, we are bound to imitate him and his Son Jesus Christ (Matthew 5:6; 1 Peter 2:12; Romans 2:24; Titus 2:5; Ephesians 5:1-2; Matthew 11:29). We are obligated to our neighbor to assist them with our services (Romans 12:4 and following; 1 Corinthians 12:14-26; Galatians 6:2 and following), to go before them with a good example (Philippians 2:15), to avoid scandals (1 Corinthians 10:23-32; 2 Corinthians 6:3), and to exclude the calumnies of the wicked by doing good (Titus 2:8; 1 Peter 2:12; 3:16). With respect to ourselves, we must make our calling and election sure, namely, that from our works we may be made more certain of our faith, and from faith of our calling and election (2 Peter 1:10). We must beware lest by acting wickedly or living too carelessly we cast away faith, or grieve the Holy Spirit, and fall from eternal life (1 Timothy 1:19; Ephesians 4:30; Romans 8:13). We must strive rather to obtain the rewards promised to piety (1 Timothy 4:8).

Yet good works are not necessary by way of a cause in relation to salvation. And rightly one must abstain both from the phrase that says good works are destructive for salvation, and also from this one, that says good works are necessary for salvation. For whatever may be said of the interpretations or explanations by which either or both phrases might be drawn into a favorable sense, it is certain that both are ambiguous and have long been suspect, and have been rejected as seeds of dissension and scandal. Compare on the latter phrase Musaeus (Musaeus, Preface to the Treatise Against Stenger, quire F, 4b and following). Similarly, that it cannot properly be said either that faith is preserved through the pursuit of sanctification, or that life, or the right to eternal life once acquired, is guarded thereby, is shown by Musaeus (Detailed Explanation, book 13, question 70, p. 578).

## 23 On the Word of the Law and the Gospel

### 1 As has often been said

As has often been said, regeneration, conversion, and indeed renewal are accomplished by God through the medium of the Word. It is now necessary to treat more precisely of this very Word of God in relation to these operations.

Notes. See Chapter III, §IX, p. 501 See the same place, §XXIX, p. 529 See Chapter V, §VIII, p. 572 For above, in the Prolegomena (Chapter I, §XXV, pp. 38–39; §XXXV, pp. 56–57; and Chapter II, pp. 61 ff.), the Word of God was discussed insofar as it is contained in the Sacred Scriptures and constitutes the first principle of knowledge for revealed theology. But just as we indicated in that same place (Chapter I, §XXIV, p. 37) that the Word can be considered particularly as the instrument for kindling saving faith, which is faith in Christ, so it must now be examined more deeply under that relation and with respect to those matters which are connected to it.

### 2 The Word of God is divided into the Law and the Gospel

The Word of God is divided into the Law and the Gospel.

Notes. This division must be diligently understood and maintained, since it is well established that the confusion of Law and Gospel has given rise to many harmful errors.

To be sure, these terms are sometimes taken in a broader sense, so that "Law" includes the Gospel under its concept, or the Gospel in some manner embraces the Law. For example, "Law" is sometimes taken to mean the whole of Scripture (Psalm 1:2), or more specifically the Scriptures of the Old Testament (John 15:25; 1 Corinthians 14:21), and finally in a particular sense the writings of Moses (Luke 24:44). "Gospel" likewise is sometimes taken more broadly for the entire doctrine of the New Testament, handed down by Christ and the Apostles (Mark 1:14; 16:15; Luke 9:6). Here, however, the terms "Law" and "Gospel" are taken insofar as they are adequately contradistinguished from one another.

### 3 "Law" in the proper sense here denotes the Word of God by which certain things…

"Law" in the proper sense here denotes the Word of God by which certain things are commanded and others are forbidden, with binding force.

Notes. Thus Paul takes the term when he denies that a person is justified by the Law, in the Epistles to the Romans and to the Galatians. He specifically calls it "the law of works" (Romans 3:27).

Hence the precepts of the Law are called some affirmative and others negative.

The binding force extends in the first instance to obedience, but where obedience is lacking, it extends to most severe and eternal punishments.

### 4 The divine Law is divided into Moral

The divine Law is divided into Moral, Ceremonial, and Forensic.

Notes. This is not because all three kinds still remain in force today, but because God once enacted them in this threefold manner and they were in effect for a time, as will become clear from what follows.

To this pertains what is said in Deuteronomy 6:1: "These are the commandments and ceremonies and judgments which the Lord has commanded." The basis of the division is drawn from the object, which concerns either the morals of human beings in general, or the ceremonies and sacred rites of a particular people, or the courts and judgments of that same people.

### 5 The Moral Law is that which commands what is inherently fitting for rational…

The Moral Law is that which commands what is inherently fitting for rational creatures and forbids what is unfitting; it therefore obliges all human beings.

Notes. It is also called the Law of Nature, in accordance with what is found in Part II, Chapter I, §III, note c, p. 372.

"Inherently" means insofar as such a creature is what it is, and as it relates either to God, or to other creatures, or to the human being himself.

For from "insofar as" to "of all" the inference is valid (cf. Part II, Chapter I, §IV–VI, pp. 372 ff.), where we showed that this Law was not only implanted in all at the first creation, but also that, notwithstanding the Fall, some knowledge of it has been left remaining in the minds of all human beings.

### 6 The sum of the Moral Law is comprehended in the Decalogue

The sum of the Moral Law is comprehended in the Decalogue, whose precepts, just as they are reducible to the love of God and of neighbor (in which the love of oneself is also included), so if they are examined individually in their proper order, they yield the following:

The first commandment formally prohibits the worship of foreign gods, that is, of all those persons or things that are not the true God; at the same time it virtually commands the religious worship of the one true God, as He has revealed Himself (and therefore as triune: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit), consisting in sincere fear, love, and trust, such that we love God (fear Him and trust in Him) with our whole heart, with our whole soul, with our whole mind, and with all our strength (Matthew 22:38; Luke 10:27), setting all other things below God and in no way being drawn away from Him. For when the worship of foreign gods is prohibited, there is of course prohibited the worship of whatever is not God, that is, whatever is not the true God. Hence it is rightly concluded that in this very first commandment the worship of graven images and idols is prohibited, because they too are not God, so that the appendix added at Exodus 20:3 ff. is a fuller declaration of the preceding commandment rather than a new commandment. According to the interpretive rule of the Decalogue, negative precepts include the contrary affirmatives, and affirmative precepts include the contrary negatives, which is to be observed in all the commandments (cf. Musaeus, Treatise against Stenger, Part III, ch. VI, pp. 593, 595, 605).

The second commandment prohibits every abuse of the divine name, whether profane use without devotion, frivolous, rash, or habitual misuse. In particular, execrations, blasphemies, incantations, lies and deceptions in sacred matters are forbidden. At the same time it prescribes the genuine and holy use and celebration of God's name in preaching, hearing, reading, meditating upon, and confessing the Word; in adoring and praising God in view of His perfections and works; in invocation, by which we seek benefits from the divine power and goodness; and in thanksgiving for spiritual and bodily benefits which He has bestowed on us and on others whom we love.

The third commandment enjoins the sanctification of the Sabbath, that is, the consecration of a certain day for the exercise of divine worship, especially public worship. Not indeed precisely the seventh day in every week (for this pertains not to the moral but to the ceremonial element, and therefore at the beginning of the New Testament Church after the resurrection of Christ, it was freely changed, so that now the first day, or the Lord's Day, is celebrated), but rather some definite time and day to be specially set apart for divine worship. For, as Luther says in his explanation of the third commandment in the Large Catechism (p. 424 f.):

The Sabbath is observed among Christians chiefly for this reason, that on the Sabbath day, when one cannot otherwise attend to the matter, leisure and time may be taken for the service of divine worship, so that we may come together to hear and treat the Word of God, and thereafter praise God with hymns, psalms, canticles, and prayers. And indeed this ought to be done daily, but when the multitude, hindered by business, cannot be present, at least one day per week must be chosen and reserved for this purpose. Furthermore, since this day, the Lord's Day, has been appointed by our forebears for this end, this harmless custom of the ancients, now received, should not be changed rashly, so that a unanimous and consensual order may stand, lest anyone by an unnecessary innovation of his own disturb all things.

Not only works that formally constitute divine worship, but also works of charity, of necessity, and those pertaining to the sustenance of life are taught by our theologians to be lawful on this day. What is prohibited includes not only works otherwise sinful in themselves, but also works of ordinary civil occupation that either fatigue the body or distract the mind with cares and render it unfit for sacred duties, and finally works of untimely or disordered recreation by which the devotion of public or private worship is impeded.

The fourth commandment prescribes the honor and obedience to be rendered to parents and to those who stand in their place (for example, guardians and curators, masters and mistresses, magistrates, ministers of the Church, teachers, elders in age, and the like; for when a particular prominent species is commanded or forbidden, cognate species and indeed the whole genus is also commanded or forbidden, according to the ancient rule). It forbids contempt, whether declared by outward signs or suppressed in the mind, and offenses against them through disobedience or contumacy, though always saving the honor and obedience that is owed to God above all.

The fifth commandment prohibits homicide, whether committed in deed or intended in the mind, together with all injuries to the life or body of one's neighbor, whether friend or enemy, committed by deed, gesture, word, or conceived in the mind. Not, however, such injuries as charity commands and prudence directs toward the greater good of one's neighbor, such as those performed by surgeons, but those that harm one's neighbor. Hence rash and unjust wars, private duels, and all acts in which the intention, even indirect, of doing violence to one's neighbor is involved, are prohibited. Capital punishments inflicted by the magistrate on criminals and necessary wars are not prohibited here, since by common usage of language they are not homicides. The commandment enjoins that we render aid to our neighbor in necessities, and diligently perform works of mercy, humanity, and gentleness, by which human life and society may be made better or more agreeable. What pertains to the care of our own life and body also belongs here, whence it is clear that suicide is prohibited, while the care of one's soul, life, and health is commended.

The sixth commandment forbids adultery and all cognate impurities, whether of deed (such as fornication, incest, sodomy, and the like), of speech (obscene songs, poems, or jests), of gesture (including the lasciviousness of the eyes, the exposure of those parts of the body which ought to be covered to avoid the allurements of lust, and immodest kisses), and of the heart itself (obscene thoughts and delight in them), as well as whatever else conflicts with conjugal fidelity (malicious desertions, rash divorces, quarrels, and brawls between spouses). It demands chastity to be cultivated both within and outside of marriage, together with conjugal duties. For there exists not only virginal and widowed chastity, but also conjugal chastity; the former entails complete abstinence from carnal union and related pleasures, while the latter entails their moderate and holy use.

The seventh commandment prohibits theft and every seizure of another's possessions (including robbery, embezzlement, and the like), and all injustice in contracts of purchase, sale, loan, letting, hiring, and the rest, by which we attribute more than is fitting to ourselves and less to our neighbor. It is violated when magistrates impose excessive burdens, or subjects deny or sluggishly render what they owe; when workers or servants are unfaithful or negligent, or wages are not properly paid by those who owe them; when found items are not returned to their owners; when a livelihood is sought by dishonest arts or by reckless begging; when alms are either entirely denied to the needy or given grudgingly and sparingly. It commands that we give what is owed, to whom it is owed, and that we leave and preserve to each person what is theirs. In this way, what pertains to the honest acquisition and preservation of our own possessions is also to be observed, with idleness and prodigality excluded.

The eighth commandment prohibits false testimony and every lie that is customarily uttered against one's neighbor either in court (whereby not only a false witness sins, but also a plaintiff who accuses unjustly, a defendant who denies against his conscience, an advocate who defends a bad cause or prosecutes a good one by wicked arts, and a judge who renders an unjust sentence without sufficiently examining the case or according to his personal inclinations) or outside of it (when things are fabricated, or when things fabricated by others, or uncertain reports, are eagerly heard and more widely spread to the detriment of another's reputation; or conversely, when the unworthy are praised or commended). This includes insults, biting jests, and defamatory songs or pamphlets, even if what is said about another is true; indeed, even sinister judgments about another person contrary to the laws of charity. The commandment enjoins that we look after our neighbor's reputation as far as we can: not only gladly proclaiming what redounds to his praise, but also abstaining from unfair suspicions, interpreting doubtful matters in a more favorable light, covering or excusing errors and weaknesses as far as is permissible, hoping for his amendment, and promoting it by fraternally admonishing him or by seeing to it that he is admonished by others. The care of our own reputation is likewise commended to us in this commandment.

The ninth and tenth commandments, which our theologians rightly distinguish (since in Exodus the word דמחת ("you shall not covet") is placed twice, so that by the repetition of the prohibitory verb you may understand that two commandments are formally conveyed; while in Deuteronomy 5:21 the word דמחת is used once and in its place the word ואתת ("you shall not desire") is substituted once), prohibit not only actual concupiscence accompanied by delight, but specifically evil concupiscence considered in its first act, with its first movements: the latter formally, expressly, and directly; the former virtually, implicitly, and indirectly. Just as it is also certain that the disordered acts or motions of concupiscence that are formally prohibited in these last commandments are implicitly prohibited in the prior commandments (see Musaeus, Treatise against Stenger, Part III, ch. VI, pp. 593–594). It is certain that it is declared to be contrary to the Law, and that this evil concupiscence ought not to be present or have any place. In this sense it is rightly said to be prohibited, although if one considers the innate habitual evil that is already present inevitably, it seems to be accused and condemned rather than prohibited (see Musaeus, Treatise against Stenger, Part III, ch. VI, p. 594; cf. Chemnitz, On the Law, ch. II, at the beginning and in the section on the Ninth and Tenth Commandments, where he frequently admonishes that original concupiscence is accused, convicted, and censured, so that we may understand that "the chief end of the Law is to disclose the knowledge of sin and to accuse us because we do not have that conformity with the Law," which are his words at p. 24). On the contrary, a full and constant rectitude and purity of our desires and inclinations regarding those things that belong to our neighbor is required.

God, after the miraculous deliverance of His people, on the day of Pentecost, on Mount Sinai, amid thunder and lightning, publicly proclaimed the Ten Commandments and moreover inscribed them on two tablets of stone, which He delivered to human beings through Moses (see Exodus 19, 20, 31, 34; Deuteronomy 4, 5, 9, 10; cf. also Part II, Chapter I, §V, pp. 373–374). The sum of these commandments is, according to the word of Christ (Matthew 22:37–40), the love of God and the love of neighbor, the latter measured by the love of oneself, as it is said: "You shall love your neighbor as yourself." Although there is no reason to contend greatly about the order and enumeration of the commandments of the Decalogue, provided the commandments themselves are observed according to their genuine sense and force, it is nonetheless certain that the distinction which we Lutherans retain fully accords with the text of the words of the Decalogue and with the rules of interpretation.

### 7 The Ceremonial Law is that which prescribes the sacrifices and other sacred…

The Ceremonial Law is that which prescribes the sacrifices and other sacred rites to be celebrated in the people of God, with reference to the coming Messiah and His office and benefits, together with the persons and things pertaining thereto, with binding force.

Notes. By "sacrifices" are meant the offerings of certain gifts consecrated to God, whether from inanimate things, both solid (for example, bread, salt, frankincense, and the like) and liquid (for example, oil, wine), or from living creatures to be slain or immolated in honor of God. Hence arise the various species of sacrifices: burnt offerings, peace offerings (whether eucharistic, votive, or voluntary), and finally propitiatory offerings, either for sins of ignorance or for more serious offenses and crimes.

Among "other sacred rites" are included the sacraments of the Old Testament themselves, which, insofar as they were external rites sanctioned by divine law that had to be observed, certainly pertain to this category (cf. Gerhard, Locus XVI, On the Ceremonial and Forensic Laws, Section II, §II). (Concerning the requirements and manner of administering these, we shall speak specifically below.) Furthermore, festivities, inaugurations, washings, and various purifications are included.

These rites were also to serve as distinguishing marks of God's people from other nations.

They are called "a shadow of things to come" (not, certainly, by accident but by the very intention of the Author), while the body (the truth and fulfillment of the things prefigured by the shadows of the Law) is said to be Christ, or to be sought in Christ Himself (Colossians 2:16–17). In this sense it is also said (Hebrews 10:1) that "the Law had a shadow of good things to come, not the very image of the things," that is, not the things themselves that were foreshadowed or represented. And Augustine says beautifully: "The sacred rites, the priesthoods, the tabernacle or temple, the altars, the sacrifices, the ceremonies, the feast days, and whatever else pertains to that service which is owed to God and is properly called latreia in Greek: all these signified and foretold the things which, for the sake of the eternal life of the faithful in Christ, we believe to have been fulfilled, and which we see being fulfilled, and which we trust will yet be fulfilled" (Augustine, The City of God, Book VII, ch. 32; cf. also Part III, Chapter I, §VII, p. 466).

The Law also included prescriptions concerning the High Priest, the other priests, and the ministers of sacred things from the tribe of Levi.

Not only the things that were to be handled in a certain way in the sacrifices, but also the sacred vessels and utensils, vestments, places, and times were divinely determined.

And as with all divine law, these were accompanied by the threat of wrath and punishment.

### 8 The Forensic Law is that which contains the civil statutes prescribing the form…

The Forensic Law is that which contains the civil statutes prescribing the form of public judgments and of external discipline to be maintained in the Jewish people.

Notes. By this these laws are distinguished from the ceremonial laws, in that the latter pertained properly to the Church, while the former pertained to the Jewish commonwealth.

Under public judgments are included matters concerning magistrates, the process of judicial proceedings, contracts, the distinction of property rights, the division of inheritances, and penalties.

Beyond these, the laws that regulate domestic society also belong here, such as the laws concerning marriages, servants, parents and children, as well as those dealing with foreigners, military service, and the like.

All of these were thoroughly accommodated to the particular state of the Jewish people, and not equally suited to the form of every commonwealth.

### 9 The Ceremonial Laws were abrogated upon the appearance of the Messiah

The Ceremonial Laws were abrogated upon the appearance of the Messiah, and the Forensic Laws upon the dissolution of the Jewish commonwealth; but the Moral Law was not.

Notes. For God did not intend the Ceremonial and Forensic Laws to endure and to bind perpetually, but only for a time; hence, when the appointed time had elapsed, the binding force ceased.

It is said of the Ceremonial Laws (Hebrews 9:10) that they were imposed μέχρι καιροῦ διορθώσεως (until the time of reformation), when more perfect things would be substituted for the types. See also Hebrews 7:22 and 8:6.

Concerning the abrogation, see Acts 10:11 on the removal of the distinction of foods, and Galatians 2:13; 4:10; 5:2; Colossians 2:16 on the removal of the laws of circumcision, of festivals, and of similar observances. Moreover, once the Temple of Jerusalem and the Tabernacle, to which most of those sacred rites were tied, were destroyed, it is all the more clearly recognized that this very worship expired.

As for the Forensic Laws, they did not bind even in former times those who were converted from among the Gentiles, since these were left subject to their own ancestral laws.
