For neither Christ nor the Apostles imposed upon newly converted Gentiles the necessity of observing these laws; rather, they left them subject to the laws of whatever magistrates they lived under. See the examples of the Centurion (Matthew 8:13), Cornelius (Acts 10:1 ff.), and the Proconsul Sergius (Acts 13:12). And Paul wishes the Romans to be subject to imperial laws (Romans 13:1 ff.), and himself demands to be judged according to Roman laws (Acts 25:10, 25; cf. 1 Peter 2:13–14). When a republic is overthrown, its laws are obviously abolished at the same time. Nevertheless, not a few forensic laws of the Jewish state, to the extent and insofar as they are suitable for other commonwealths, may be freely introduced by a Christian magistrate and proposed for observance.

The Moral Law, however, was not abrogated, for it does not relate precisely to the Jewish Church or Synagogue, or to the Jewish commonwealth, but to human beings as rational creatures. Therefore, although the Moral Law is powerless and useless for justification on account of the corruption of human nature (Romans 8:3), and although its curses do not touch those who rely by faith on the satisfaction of another (Romans 8:1), the Law itself is not thereby abrogated. For it does not cease to bind all persons to exact and constant obedience, even if those who do not render such obedience are not therefore condemned, and even their imperfect obedience is pleasing to God (see Gerhard, On the Ceremonial and Forensic Laws, ch. IV, §43; Musaeus, Treatise against Stenger, Part II, ch. II, p. 204, and Part III, ch. VI, p. 618).

### 10 The Mosaic Moral Law

The Mosaic Moral Law, that is, the Law of the Decalogue, is the same as the Law of Christ. For Christ indeed purged it of Pharisaic corruptions and more correctly explained it, but He did not give believers entirely new moral precepts.

On both sides, perfect obedience and the rectitude of all human faculties and actions is required, and not only more serious and deliberate sins, but also those called sins of human weakness, and original sin itself, are prohibited on both sides (cf. Musaeus, Treatise against Stenger, Part II, ch. I, p. 160, and ch. II, p. 199; Part III, ch. VI, pp. 561 ff., 598 ff.).

See Matthew 5:20 ff., where the phrases "You have heard that it was said to those of old" and "But I say to you" are to be understood with reference to the righteousness of the Scribes and Pharisees, who clung to the letter of the Law while neglecting its true meaning, and who therefore stood in need of correction. This is especially clear if we attend to what Christ prefaced in verse 17: "I have not come to abolish the Law" (that is, to relax or remove its binding force), "but to fulfill it" (by My perfect obedience).

For the precepts that Christ emphasized are contained in the Decalogue, if not expressly, then at least implicitly.

### 11 The moral law was given for eternal life

The moral law was given for eternal life, but under the condition of perfect fulfillment. After the Fall, however, no one is able to render this perfect fulfillment. Therefore no one can be saved through the law.

Notes. Hence it is called ἡ ἐντολὴ ἡ εἰς ζωήν, "the commandment unto life," Romans 7:10, and "a good commandment," Romans 7:12, 13.

According to that saying: "Do this and you shall live" (Luke 10:28), and what is read in Galatians 3:12: "The one who does these things shall live by them."

For the rigor by which exact obedience is demanded and the natural incapacity contracted through the Fall, together with the habitual inclination toward evil, are mutually opposed to one another. Hence it is said that τὸ φρόνημα τῆς σαρκός, "the mind of the flesh," is not subject to the law, nor can it be subject (Romans 8:7; compare Romans 8:3 and Romans 7:15ff.). As for the fact that the commandments of Christ are said not to be burdensome (1 John 5:3), this is not to be understood in an unqualified sense or with respect to all persons whatsoever, but with respect to believers, who by the powers bestowed by Christ carry out their duties without being burdened, and whose imperfect obedience is accepted as though it were perfect on account of the perfect obedience of Christ, apprehended by faith and imputed by God (compare Musaeus, Treatise against Stenger, part 3, ch. 6, p. 588).

Thus it is said in Galatians 3:21: "The law was not given so as to be able to give life." And in Romans 7:10ff., Paul says that the commandment given for life turned to death for him, and so forth.

### 12 The Gospel, properly speaking

The Gospel, properly speaking, is the doctrine of the grace of God and the gratuitous remission of sins on account of Christ the Mediator and his merit apprehended by faith; a doctrine that was revealed not only in the New Testament but also in the Old Testament, in its own manner.

Notes. This definition stands in opposition to the Law, and the very etymology supports it, for εὐαγγέλιον (euangelion) signifies a good announcement. Thus the Gospel is said to be proclaimed to the poor (Matthew 11:5, 20).

It is, in other words, a body of promises that are welcome, joyful, and salutary for sinful human beings, the sum of which is contained in John 3:16.

It speaks of the gracious favor, the love, and the mercy by which God pursues human beings, even though they are sinners, and is intent on securing their salvation (see 1 Timothy 2:4).

In this gratuitous remission the justification of the sinful person consists, and from it flow peace with God, adoption as children of God, and the rest, as was taught above (part 3, ch. 4, §§ 7 and 10, pp. 560 and 562, 563; compare Romans 3:21ff., where it is declared that apart from the Law, and therefore through the Gospel, the righteousness of God, that is, the righteousness by which we are constituted just before God, has been made manifest).

Note the word of the angel to Joseph (Matthew 1:21), to Mary (Luke 1:31ff.), and to the shepherds (Luke 2:10, 11; compare Acts 4:12; John 1:12, 14, 16, 18, 29, 36).

Whence the Gospel itself is called "the law of faith" (Galatians 3:2), and there arises the phrase πιστεύειν εἰς τὸ εὐαγγέλιον, "to believe in the Gospel" (Mark 1:15).

That this doctrine pertains to the New Testament is plain from the passages cited thus far.

As for the Old Testament, the promises concerning the seed of the woman who would crush the head of the serpent, whose heel the serpent would meanwhile bruise, belong here: that is, concerning the true man to come from the posterity of Eve, who would destroy the kingdom and power of Satan (who through the serpent had persuaded humanity to sin, thereby casting them headlong into death and holding them captive under his power) by a power greater than Satan's own, a power that is truly divine, yet not without suffering or blood, and who would liberate the human race (Genesis 3:15). Likewise the promise concerning the seed of Abraham, in whom all the nations of the earth would be blessed with every spiritual blessing to be bestowed through faith in him (Genesis 12:2; 15:6; 22:18). Likewise concerning the Messiah, Shiloh, to be born from the tribe of Judah, to whom the nations would adhere (Genesis 49:10); concerning a Prophet like Moses (Deuteronomy 18:19); and what is found in the Psalms (Psalms 2, 8, 22, 45, 68, 110), in Isaiah (Isaiah 7:14; 53:4ff.; 61:1ff.), in Jeremiah (Jeremiah 23:5; 33:15), in Daniel (Daniel 9:24), in Hosea (Hosea 13:14), in Micah (Micah 5:2), in Haggai (Haggai 2:8), in Zechariah (Zechariah 9:9; 13:1), and in Malachi (Malachi 1:11; 3:1; 4:2). It is moreover certain that the things contained in the ceremonial laws, although insofar as they prescribed certain actions and rites they had the force of law, nevertheless insofar as they represented Christ the Mediator and his merit to be embraced by faith through certain rites, as through types or shadows, are rightly reckoned as belonging to the Gospel (compare Musaeus, Disputation against Curcellaeus on the Salvation of the Gentiles, §§ 46, 47).

Although the Gospel is one and the same in the Old and New Testaments, the evangelical promises were set forth and illustrated with increasing clarity over time, until at last the full light arose in the New Testament. Isaiah certainly possessed as great a light of knowledge as we can observe in none of his predecessors. Indeed, when considered in comparison with the light of the New Testament, the doctrine of the Messiah in the Old Testament is compared to night and darkness, that is, κατὰ σύγκρισιν (by comparison), for it was veiled in figures and shadows. With those coverings removed, the most brilliant splendor of knowledge shone forth in the New Testament, which is accordingly compared to the day (Gerhard, On the Gospel, disputation 37).

### 13 The Law and the Gospel therefore agree

The Law and the Gospel therefore agree: (1). With respect to their Author, who in both cases is God. (2). With respect to the Subject to whom they are given, namely all human beings. (3). With respect to the End intended in itself, which in both cases is eternal salvation. (4). With respect to the terminus of duration, which is the end of the world.

Notes. For each is the Word of God, as is clear from what has been said.

We are speaking here of the moral law, given to all, by which they are bound to obedience. The Gospel too, destined for the good of all, came to the whole human race at various times, especially with respect to its more notable periods: first in Adam, second in Noah, third through the Israelite Church, illustrious throughout the whole world, and fourth through the Apostles filling the entire globe with their preaching (Matthew 28:19; Mark 16:15; Romans 10:18; see Musaeus, Disputation against Curcellaeus, §§ 37ff.).

Concerning the Law this was stated in § 11 and its first note. Concerning the Gospel the matter is even more evident, and Romans 1:16 is to be noted, where the Gospel is called the power of God unto salvation for everyone who believes. It is, however, accidental that the Law results in death (according to Romans 7:10ff.) and that the Gospel is to some an odor of death unto death (2 Corinthians 2:16; compare 1 Corinthians 1:18ff.).

That the moral law is perpetual, and neither has been nor shall be abrogated, was stated in § 9 and its note (f). That the Gospel is to be preached until the end of the world is expressly stated in the final verse of the final chapter of Matthew.

### 14 The Law and the Gospel differ

The Law and the Gospel differ: (1). In the manner of their disclosure and cognition. For the Law is known by nature, even after the Fall to some degree. The Gospel, by contrast, is a mystery, knowable only by supernatural revelation. (2). In respect of their object. For the Law is concerned with things to be done and things to be omitted, whereas the Gospel delivers gratuitous promises to be embraced by faith. (3). In the diversity of their promises. The promises of the Law are compensatory. The promises of the Gospel, however, are entirely gratuitous. (4). In the diversity of their office. The Law prescribes perfect obedience, and accuses and terrifies all transgressors and condemns them. It does not, however, confer new powers for a spiritual and holy life. The Gospel, on the other hand, neither commands works, nor reproves sinners. Rather, the Gospel shows forth the Mediator, consoles, and promises grace and salvation. Therefore the Law is to be set before secure sinners, that they may be brought to contrition; the Gospel is to be set before the contrite, that they may conceive faith.

Notes. It was implanted by God, as the Author of nature, through creation and inscribed upon the hearts of human beings (compare Romans 2:14ff.).

(See part 2, ch. 1, §§ 4, 5, 6, pp. 372ff.) A fuller knowledge of the Law, however, on account of the corruption of the human intellect through the Fall, must be sought from the revelation contained in the Scriptures (compare Musaeus, Treatise against Stenger, part 2, ch. 1, p. 161).

See Romans 16:25; 1 Corinthians 2:6, 7ff.

See § 3 above, p. 588.

According to § 12, p. 605.

That is, under the condition of perfect obedience and of merits (see § 11, pp. 604, 605).

Excluding all regard for our works. (according to Romans 4:4 and Romans 11:6). Hence our theologians deny that the evangelical promises are conditional; they do not exclude every kind of condition, but specifically the condition of our merits, so that in this respect "conditional" is opposed to "gratuitous." "For the condition of faith differs from the condition of works" (Gerhard, On the Gospel, § 26; compare ibid. § 42).

See §§ 3, 5, 6, pp. 588ff. and § 11, pp. 604, 605.

See Romans 4:15; Galatians 3:10.

For it removes neither the anguish and stings of conscience, nor the blindness of the intellect in spiritual matters and the consequent resistance through doubts about the truth of revelation; nor does it kindle faith or charity (see Musaeus, Treatise against Stenger, part 3, ch. 9, pp. 712, 736).

For it is not the law of works but of faith, Galatians 3:2.

For although the Gospel, taken in a broader signification, may be called a sermon of repentance, this is not to be predicated of the Gospel strictly so called. For it does not, of itself and directly, treat of things to be done and things to be omitted, and consequently does not of itself and directly reveal or reprove sins. The Passion of Christ, insofar as it is a λύτρον (ransom) for sins and thus the cause of recovered divine grace, pertains to the Gospel; yet insofar as it arose from our sins and sets the wrath of God before our eyes, it pertains to the Law, as a real sermon of repentance (see the Formula of Concord, article on Law and Gospel, p. 593).

See John 1:17, where in opposition to the Law given through Moses, grace and truth are said to have come through Jesus Christ, and thus to be known from the Gospel; compare Romans 3:24ff.; add Isaiah 61:1; Luke 10:18, 19, 20; Matthew 11:5; 12:5).

Though the Law is not for secure sinners alone, as will shortly be taught. (See 1 Timothy 1:9).

See Matthew 11:5, 28.

### 15 Although the Law and the Gospel differ in these ways

Although the Law and the Gospel differ in these ways, in practice they must nevertheless be most closely conjoined. As regards the conversion of human beings, the Law, which teaches what is to be done and what is to be omitted, and obliges people to the most exacting observance thereof, denouncing the gravest guilt upon all transgressors whatsoever, by this very means brings human beings to the recognition of their sins and to sorrow over them, and thereby makes them anxious for a Mediator. The Gospel, in turn, shows forth the Mediator himself and the grace of God and remission of sins to be obtained through him. Thus the Law indeed prepares human minds for receiving faith; the Gospel, however, kindles faith itself, by which sinners are reconciled with God.

Notes. See Musaeus, Preface to the Treatise against Stenger, quire B, fol. 1a.

See part 3, ch. 3, § 29, note (g), p. 531.

The common first and perpetual function of the Law is that it teaches what is to be done and what is to be omitted. Hence, although a threefold use of the Law is customarily distinguished, and the first place is held by that which they call the political use, which aims at external discipline and the preservation of public tranquillity in civil society against unruly and ungovernable persons, for whom their own penalties are established, it is nevertheless certain that even here a didactic use is presupposed, by virtue of which the Law functions as a norm or rule for maintaining that discipline. For our purposes, however, the Law is to be considered in its relation to the spiritual conversion and renewal of human beings.

The second use of the Law commonly distinguished is called the pedagogical use, the occasion being taken from Galatians 3:24: namely, that the Law, like a rather stern pedagogue, reproaching human beings for their failings and rendering them terrified and anxious, causes them to desire a liberator and to look to every possible means by which they might be set free. Yet the Law itself neither knows nor is able to show or promise the Mediator; that the Mediator is anxiously sought is the effect of the Law, though the Law cannot itself supply what is sought.

See Romans 3:20; Romans 7:7; compare part 3, ch. 3, § 29, p. 530, note (c).

See note (f).

According to what was stated in § 12, p. 605.

The Law, however, does not efficiently contribute to the generation of faith, but only by removing the impediment of security and contempt arising from unrepented sins, and thus by disposing the subject in this manner, although the Law does not even adequately remove all impediments, as is clear from what was noted above (see Musaeus, Treatise against Stenger, p. 736).

### 16 In the business of renewal

In the business of renewal, the Law, by teaching what is to be done and what is to be omitted, directs the regenerate toward the performance of truly good works and the avoidance of sins. The Law, by means of its threatenings, also ensures that the desires of the flesh are more vigorously restrained. Moreover, by showing the imperfection of the new obedience, the Law leads to daily repentance. The Gospel, in turn, just as it preserves and increases the faith bestowed in conversion, so it continually supplies ever greater spiritual powers for acts of charity and other virtues. And the Gospel raises up the spirit that falters under the sense of imperfect obedience and sin.

Notes. See part 3, ch. 5, § 8, p. 572; compare Musaeus, Preface to the Treatise against Stenger, quire B, fol. 1b.

This is what they customarily designate the third use of the Law, which they call the didactic use.

Into these good works the regenerate are then carried by a willing spirit, possessing a rule and norm for rightly ordering their lives, as the example of David illustrates throughout the whole of Psalm 119.

The sins being known through the Law as sins, they are accordingly to be distinguished from the things that ought to be done.

For although the regenerate, insofar as they are such and with respect to their spiritual powers, desire to act rightly and do not await threats by which they might be compelled, nevertheless, since in them, besides the Spirit, the flesh also remains, the flesh must be terrified lest by resisting the Spirit it prevail.

For the Law always demands more and better things than we are able to render, as stated in § 11, pp. 604, 605, Which is customarily called the repentance of those who stand, and which the regenerate need, as is clear from chapter 3, § 35, note (c), p. 543.

For faith is preserved by the same causes by which it is generated; see the Detailed Explanation, article 13, question 70, p. 578.

For just as when faith, apprehending the merit of Christ, is kindled in the heart of the contrite person through the Gospel, there simultaneously arises love toward the gracious God, which inclines the will of the regenerate person to love God above all things, to do all that is pleasing to God, to hate and flee what is contrary, to trust in God, to hope for all good things from him, to endure all things that are sent, to love and help one's neighbor for God's sake, and so forth: so also when faith is increased and strengthened through the use of the Gospel, these things too certainly receive their growth simultaneously through the Gospel.

For it shows that our deficiencies are supplied and our sins are covered by the perfect obedience of Christ, imputed to believers.

## 24 On the Sacraments in General

### 1 Since, besides the Word of God

Since, besides the Word of God, the Sacraments are also instruments of regeneration, of conversion, and of renewal, and are thus instruments for conferring, sealing, and increasing faith, they too must be treated more distinctly.

Notes. See Chapter III, Section IX.

See Chapter I, Section XXIX.

See Chapter V, Section VIII.

### 2 The word "Sacrament" is an ecclesiastical term

The word "Sacrament" is an ecclesiastical term, taken to refer to sacred rites which are signs and means, or instruments, for conferring and sealing grace.

Notes. The word is not expressly found in the Scriptures. Since it is Latin in origin, no certain word has hitherto been found in Hebrew or Greek, nor specifically in the books of the Old and New Testaments, that corresponds to it exactly. And although the word "Sacrament" occurs in the Latin version of the Bible, it is not properly and specifically used there of those external and visible signs of grace about which we are treating here, but was only later transferred to them by ecclesiastical writers (Gerhard, On the Sacraments, section 5).

Among profane writers, the word is found to have signified not only money deposited by litigants before a judge, on the condition that the winner would recover his own while the loser's money would go to the treasury, but also a pledge for the payment of money by the one defeated in trial, and indeed an oath, especially a military oath. Tertullian appears to have had this last signification in mind. He was the first of the Latin Fathers to employ the word to denote the act by which those being baptized bind themselves to God and solemnly promise to fight faithfully and bravely under the banner of Christ against Satan (Tertullian, On the Soldier's Crown). From this it came about that not only the entire rite of Baptism, but also that of the Holy Supper, was called a Sacrament; although the name was also applied more broadly to any sacred and secret matters, and likewise to signs of sacred things, even those instituted by human beings (see Gerhard, On the Sacraments, sections 3 and 7).

### 3 For a Sacrament properly and strictly so called

For a Sacrament properly and strictly so called, it is required: (1). that it be an action commanded by God; (2). that it have an element visibly prescribed by divine authority; (3). that it have a promise of Evangelical grace.

Notes. Indeed, the requisites of a Sacrament in general, just like the name itself, are not expressly found in the Scriptures. But the general doctrine of the Sacraments must be deduced from what is found in Scripture concerning each one individually, as Blessed Gerhard advises (Gerhard, On the Sacraments, section 1), where he also for this reason first treats the requisites of true and properly so called Sacraments, and cites the words of Blessed Chemnitz:

Baptism and the Eucharist are by the confession of all truly and properly Sacraments; from these, therefore, we shall gather what is required as essential in order that something be truly and properly a Sacrament of the New Testament. For this will be the simplest and most certain demonstration.

Thus from the common concepts of those things which are without doubt Sacraments, and in which they agree, it is known that those things which are perhaps called Sacraments but do not possess those common requisites are not Sacraments of the same kind and essence as those which are properly so called, but are equivocally so named (Chemnitz, Examination of the Council of Trent, Part II, p. 14; see also Musaeus, Detailed Explanation, Book XVI, Question 81, pp. 667-668).

The command of this kind must expressly exist in the Scriptures.

The element means some thing or substance around which the external act or rite of the Sacrament is occupied.

The promise is of the remission of sins and the spiritual benefits connected with it.

### 4 The principal efficient cause of the Sacraments is the triune God

The principal efficient cause of the Sacraments is the triune God, and Christ in his assumed flesh.

Notes. That is, the cause which not only by its own authority institutes and determines what actions or rites are to be celebrated as means of grace, and in what manner or by what method they ought to be celebrated, and commands that they be celebrated (so that it is the cause both with respect to the species and with respect to the exercise of the act), but also elevates the Sacraments themselves, as instruments, to the conferring of spiritual grace.

God alone is this cause, since he alone is the author of grace, and therefore he alone can determine the means through which he wills to confer the grace that he freely bestows. He alone can also communicate to them the infinite power by which the Sacraments are rendered apt for conferring grace.

What we have said about the institution, command, and concurrence of God operates by way of an external work.

With respect to the Sacraments of the New Testament, of which we shall see distinctly in their proper place, this pertains to Christ in his assumed flesh.

### 5 The internal impelling cause is the goodness of God

The internal impelling cause is the goodness of God; the external or meritorious cause is the merit of Christ.

Notes. This is easily evident if we consider that the Sacraments are means of grace. Moreover, our theologians observe that God regarded our weakness (which some therefore call the inciting cause, prokataraktikē), on account of which we easily doubt the Evangelical promises, and therefore out of his love for us was not content with the revelation of the Gospel, but willed to confirm by external signs what is taught concerning our salvation in the Word (see Gerhard, On the Sacraments, sections 1 and 2).

For if "in Christ," that is, in Christ as Mediator, and thus on account of him, we are blessed with every spiritual blessing (Ephesians 1:3), it is rightly inferred that on his account also we are endowed with the sacramental means of grace.

### 6 The less principal cause is ordinarily a minister of the Church

The less principal cause is ordinarily a minister of the Church; in a case of necessity, however, a layperson or a woman.

Notes. That is, the cause which places the Sacrament in use and applies it to producing its effect, dependently indeed upon the authority of the principal cause, God, and exactly according to his institution. From this it is clear that the act must be celebrated not in jest and sport, but as something serious and holy, in order that it be sacramental; yet the dignity or intention of the one administering is not required for the truth and efficacy of the Sacrament.

Ministers are stewards of the mysteries of God (1 Corinthians 4:1), stewards not only of the Word but also of the Sacraments, in which the benefits of God are hidden. Moreover, Christ himself in the state of humiliation administered one Sacrament (the Holy Supper) when he instituted it, just as he otherwise performed the office of teaching.

If, however, a person cannot be without a Sacrament without danger of losing salvation, and the ordinary minister is absent, it is better that the act which cannot be omitted without danger be performed by another person, than that the one who ought to be granted the Sacrament should suffer harm. And God is efficacious through the Sacraments whoever it may be that administers, provided the administration is done rightly. What is to be said about Circumcision and Baptism will be discussed below.

### 7 The matter of the Sacrament involves two things

The matter of the Sacrament involves two things: first, a certain external and visible element; second, a certain action occupied with that element.

Notes. Indeed, the Sacrament is not a substance composed of matter and form, but a rite and action. Therefore "matter" here means the same as "material," that is, what is common, or can be common, to a sacramental action and to other actions which are not Sacraments; so that it must be determined to the being of a sacramental action by something else that is added.

Concerning the element, see Section III. Some call it the "thing" (res) of the Sacrament, distinguishing between the "thing" taken as the matter about which the action is occupied, and the "thing" taken as the fruit of the Sacrament; they hold that the former, not the latter, pertains to the present discussion. But this will be clear from what follows.

Now, the claim that some make, namely that in every Sacrament there is a twofold matter, earthly and heavenly, is not without difficulty. Nor can it be settled unless it has first been established from the proper foundation, that is, from the words of institution of each individual Sacrament, what the nature and essence of each is. This is acknowledged by both Gerhard (Gerhard, On the Sacraments, section 45) and Himmel (Himmel, Compendium, Disputation XIX, section 38). Certainly, if for each Sacrament there is granted, besides the earthly, also a heavenly matter, there must also be some union between the one and the other. And so, when we speak of Sacraments in general, something must also be determined about the union of the twofold matter of the Sacrament in general.

Yet Blessed Menzer, disputing against the Calvinists concerning the heavenly and earthly matter of the Sacraments and the union of both, writes:

To attempt to define a general mode and manner of that union common indiscriminately to all and each of the Sacraments of the Old and New Testaments is truly to fight against the very institution of each individual Sacrament (Menzer, Gießen Disputations, volume II, Disputation V, section 49, p. 164).

If this be admitted, it will be better to remain silent about the heavenly matter of the Sacrament in general than to say doubtful things. For the older teachers of our Church, when they set forth the doctrine of the Sacraments in general, did not teach that in every Sacrament there must be a heavenly matter sacramentally united to an earthly element. Certainly Blessed Chemnitz, in enumerating the essential components of a Sacrament, made no mention of a heavenly matter (Chemnitz, Examination of the Council of Trent, Part II, On the Number of the Sacraments, p. 14; see also Musaeus, Detailed Explanation, Book XVI, Questions 84 ff., p. 683).

Similarly, Blessed Aegidius Hunnius, in his book On the Sacraments, when asked "How many things are required for the substance or substantial integrity of each Sacrament?" replies: "Two, namely, the element, or the thing that strikes the eyes, and the word joined to it, according to Augustine's saying: 'Let the word come to the element, and a Sacrament is made.'" He is silent about a heavenly matter. So likewise Blessed Erasmus Sarcerius in his Examination of Ordinands, Blessed Jacob Heerbrand in his Compendium of Theology (Book On the Sacraments, pp. 511-512), Blessed Ambrosius Reudenius in his Catechetical Theology (Part V, Chapter II, pp. 178-179), Blessed Albert Graver in his Supplement to the Prelections on the Augsburg Confession (on Article IX, p. 78), Blessed Matthias Hafenreffer in his Books of Theology(Book III, State III, Book VII, p. 465), and Blessed Johann Gerhard in his Aphorisms of Theology (Book XVI, Aphorisms 37-38).

As for those who say that the other part of the Sacrament, namely the word of institution, from which together with the element treated by a certain action Baptism consists, is the heavenly and invisible matter of the Sacrament, it must be admitted that this is rather the form, or the formal element, of the Sacrament than its matter, as we shall see presently.

And those who by the name of heavenly matter understand a certain thing signified, relatively opposed to the element as a sign, not the fruit of the Sacrament itself, but the thing upon which the operation and fruit of the Sacrament depends, nonetheless concede that this very thing which they call the heavenly matter is sometimes not even really present (as we shall see concerning the Sacraments of the Old Testament). At other times, even if it is present, some nevertheless observe that the inference from presence to matter is invalid; for it is required that something be present by way of matter in order to be called matter. But what it means to be present by way of matter in a Sacrament, they themselves do not sufficiently explain with respect to the Sacrament in general, but leave it to be learned from the institution of each individual Sacrament. From this one may gather that the heavenly matter of a Sacrament in general cannot be acknowledged unless it has first been discovered in each individual Sacrament.

And since in the Holy Supper the body and blood of Christ are called heavenly matter for the reason that the act of distributing, eating, and drinking is occupied not only with bread and wine, but also truly and really with the very body and blood of Christ, so that when the bread is distributed and eaten, the body of Christ is simultaneously truly and really distributed and eaten, and when the wine is distributed and drunk, the blood of Christ is simultaneously truly and really distributed and drunk, it must be admitted that such a heavenly matter does not equally have a place in all Sacraments, especially those in which what is called by the name of heavenly matter is acknowledged not to be really present. Therefore, even if we posit some heavenly matter when treating of the Sacrament in general, the term "matter" would have to be so broadened that what is present by way of matter in one Sacrament would not be present as matter in another Sacrament in the same way. From this it would further follow that in one Sacrament something is present by way of matter properly speaking, and in another improperly speaking. Whether perspicuity and solidity of doctrine are served by this reasoning is not difficult to judge.

Meanwhile, we do not deny, but freely concede, that in the Sacraments there is, in its own way, a heavenly thing, understood not only as the fruit of the Sacrament, but also as the thing from which, as a cause, the fruit of the Sacrament depends, and which must be distinguished from the earthly thing. Yet we do not for that reason attribute to it the name and nature of matter, as we shall explain concerning each individual Sacrament in its proper place.

Some here use the distinction between remote and proximate matter, calling the element by the former name and the action occupied with it by the latter. They call it remote matter not because it is locally absent from the Sacrament, but because it does not have the nature of matter in the Sacrament except insofar as it is subject to a certain action and is treated by it.

The action is to be understood in a common sense, as being in itself indifferent to a common and a sacramental action. It is determined to the being of a sacramental action from another source (namely, by the addition of the word of institution, of which we shall see presently): for example, the act of washing with water, or the act of distributing, eating, and drinking bread and wine, of which we shall speak in their proper place. Otherwise, when the action is determined by the addition of the word of institution, it constitutes the very formal nature of the Sacrament, as we shall now say. In the meantime, see Gerhard (On the Sacraments, section 46).

### 8 The form of the Sacrament is the word of institution

The form of the Sacrament is the word of institution, which must be joined to the action occupied with the sensible element.

Notes. That is, the formal element, by whose coming to, or being united with, the action occupied with that element, the action formally has the character of being a Sacrament or a sacramental action.

Some say the form of the Sacrament is the action concerning the proper subject of the Sacrament, determined by the word of institution. And this indeed is the form of the whole, or the entire formal nature of the Sacrament, which they also sometimes call the essence of the Sacrament. But here we are treating of the formal as it is contradistinguished from the material.

The word, I say, is not the word of the promise, which pertains to the fruit or effect of the Sacrament, but of the institution, which enters altogether into the constitution of the Sacrament.

Therefore, although the word of institution in its own way pertains to the efficient cause, as its causality, namely that God through the word of institution efficiently determined what pertains to the nature of each Sacrament, nevertheless insofar as the word of institution must be added to the external sacramental action itself in such a way that by this very fact that action is distinguished from other common actions and is constituted in the being of a sacramental action, the word of institution altogether pertains to the form of the Sacrament.

### 9 The end "for whom" of the Sacraments consists of human beings who have been…

The end "for whom" of the Sacraments consists of human beings who have been born in a carnal manner and who are living.

Notes. That is, the subject for whose good the Sacrament has been divinely instituted and to whom it therefore ought to be applied. Some call this the object, meaning a personal object, which they distinguish from a real object, namely the thing itself which the sacramental action treats.

No other thing is this subject but human beings. This is evident partly from an induction of the individual Sacraments and their express institution, and partly from the common end, which will be treated in the following section. Meanwhile, not all Sacraments are equally destined for all persons, so that they could be admitted to them indiscriminately; this will be shown distinctly below.

The subject consists of those born in the flesh, not fetuses lying hidden in their mothers' wombs. Although salvation is not denied to the latter, these means nevertheless ought not to be applied to them for lack of a command, as we shall say below concerning Baptism. The fact that Christ himself made use of certain Sacraments took place through that dispensation by which he freely assumed for the benefit of others things that pertain to weak human beings.

Those who have died are no longer on the way of salvation, so that they could be helped by the means of grace; they are either blessed or damned.

### 10 The end "for which purpose" of the Sacraments

The end "for which purpose" of the Sacraments, which also has the nature of an effect, is proximately the conferring or sealing of Evangelical grace; ultimately, on the part of human beings, their eternal salvation.

Notes. That is, the thing for the effecting or obtaining of which the Sacrament was instituted by God its author, and for which reason it ought to be applied to human beings and received by them.

This is the effect insofar as it is conferred upon human beings through the Sacraments as efficacious instruments and means.

As to the question whether the efficacy of the Sacraments is physical or moral, Blessed Musaeus replied:

If this remains fixed and firm, that the Sacraments are efficacious instruments for conferring grace, and that God operates through them and confers grace by one indivisible action, which Sacred Scripture teaches sufficiently clearly, let us not be overly scrupulous about the mode of operating and conferring grace, but rather leave it to divine wisdom (Musaeus, Detailed Explanation, Book XVII, Question 83, p. 675).

It is manifest, however, that the opinion by which the Sacraments are said to be a moral but not a physical cause of conferring grace is not thereby approved, if it simultaneously denies that God and the Sacraments operate by one and indivisible action to confer Evangelical grace. Blessed Gerhard likewise, when he encountered this question, left it undecided (Gerhard, On the Sacraments, section 86; see also Gerhard, Catholic Confession, Book II, Part II, Article XI, Chapter II, p. 813, and Orthodox Witness against Bellarmine, Disputation XVIII, section 39; add also Cundisius, Notes on the Compendium of Hutter, Book XX, Question IV, p. 1065).

The Sacraments confer or seal Evangelical grace when they confer, or seal and confirm, faith. For thus human beings are regenerated, justified, and renewed, as we shall show below concerning each Sacrament individually. At the same time it is clear how the Sacraments do not profit unless faith intervenes.

The matter stands differently with respect to infants and adults. In the latter, faith must already be present in order for them to use the Sacraments profitably. In the former, however, faith is first produced through the Sacrament itself.

For God, in conferring Evangelical grace, always intends the salvation of human beings by this means.

### 11 A Sacrament in general can be defined as a divinely instituted action

A Sacrament in general can be defined as a divinely instituted action, occupied with an external and sensible element, through which, when the word of institution is added, there is conferred upon or sealed to human beings the Evangelical grace of the remission of sins unto eternal life.

Notes. A general definition of a Sacrament is nowhere to be found in Scripture. It must, however, be formed from an induction of all the Sacraments (properly so called) that have been divinely instituted, both in the Old and in the New Testament (Himmel, Compendium, Disputation XIX, section 18, p. 192).

It is not, however, one simple action, but an aggregate of several actions ordered to one another (see Cundisius, Notes on the Compendium of Hutter, Book XX, Question III, section 1, p. 1028).

In this way it is indicated not only that it is a serious and sacred action, but also what its principal efficient cause is (see Section IV above).

The matter or material is denoted (see Section VII).

The form which is granted to the sacramental action is indicated (see Section VIII).

The end "for whom" is signified (see Section IX).

The end "for which purpose," which is also the effect of the Sacraments, is contained herein (see Section X).

### 12 Some Sacraments belong to the Old Testament

Some Sacraments belong to the Old Testament, others to the New. The former are those which were instituted before the coming of Christ, pointed to him from afar, and foreshadowed him in certain figures, and which were abrogated once he had been manifested. The latter are those which were instituted by Christ himself, testify that he has been manifested, offer him as present, and are to endure in the Church until the end.

Notes. Both kinds agree in that they are both divinely instituted, both consist of the word and an element, and both are means for conferring or sealing grace.

The words given above are those of Blessed Himmel (Compendium, Disputation XIX, sections 66 and 68).

## 25 On the Sacraments of the Old Testament

### 1 After the human race had fallen into sins

After the human race had fallen into sins, and God, before the coming of the Messiah, willed to enter into a special covenant especially with Abraham and his posterity, and to endow them with his grace, it pleased him to exhibit his grace to human beings not only through the revealed Word, but also through the singular rite of Circumcision, instituted for this purpose.

Notes. In the state of integrity, Sacraments properly so called had no place, since sins were absent from the human race, and therefore there was no need for the remission of sins or its means.

Circumcision was the rite by which human beings were initiated, or inserted, into the divine covenant, and Circumcision itself is called berith (תירִ בְּ ), that is, covenant or pact (Genesis 17:4), and diathēkē peritomēs (διαθήκη περιτομῆς), that is, the covenant of circumcision (Acts 7:8).

The seat of this doctrine is found in Genesis 17.

### 2 The principal efficient cause of Circumcision is the triune God

The principal efficient cause of Circumcision is the triune God.

Notes. This is the cause which, by its own act of institution and sufficient authority, determined what pertains to the nature or essence of Circumcision, that is, to the species of the act, as they say. At the same time it commanded the exercise of the act, and not only annexed the promise of grace, but also conferred grace itself through this means.

See Genesis 17:1, 9.

Circumcision is a work directed outward (ad extra).

### 3 The internal impelling cause is the goodness and philanthrōpia (φιλανθρωπία)

The internal impelling cause is the goodness and philanthrōpia (φιλανθρωπία), that is, the love of God toward humankind; the external and meritorious cause is the merit of Christ.

Notes. God, impelled within himself by nothing other than his own goodness, instituted this Sacrament by which human beings would be so joined to God that, being reborn and having their sins forgiven, they would, as adopted children, enjoy God as their own.

His goodness was directed specifically toward the household and descendants of Abraham, to which pertains what will be discussed below concerning the end "for whom" or the subject.

As for the meritorious cause, not only does what we said about the Sacraments in general from Ephesians 1:3 apply here, but Circumcision itself also prefigured Christ who was to be born from this nation. From this one may infer that the type was instituted on account of this antitype, and that God, having regard to the Messiah and his merit, therefore willed also to be efficacious through Circumcision.

### 4 The ministerial cause of Circumcision was first Abraham

The ministerial cause of Circumcision was first Abraham, then the succeeding Patriarchs, afterward the Levitical priests. Extraordinarily, however, Circumcision was also performed by laypeople and women.

Notes. No express command about the ministerial cause is found either in the history of the institution of Circumcision (Genesis 17) or in the repeated institution (Leviticus 12). The example of the first act of Circumcision is rightly taken as the norm for the ministry of Circumcision to be carried out thereafter.

Abraham is to be considered (Genesis 17:25 ff.; 21:4) not precisely as a father of the family, but as a minister of sacred things in the church of his household. Abraham himself, however, seems not so much to have circumcised himself as to have been circumcised by Eliezer, the steward of his house and vicar of sacred rites.

The Patriarchs likewise acted not so much as heads of families, but rather as ministers of sacred things and teachers of the Church.

The priests claimed the remaining parts of the ecclesiastical ministry for themselves from divine institution and were therefore distributed through all the tribes of Israel, so that they could perform such offices everywhere (see 1 Maccabees 2:46).

Zipporah circumcised her son, with God's approval, removing the plague he was about to inflict on account of the omitted act of Circumcision (Exodus 4:25). Many women did the same during times of persecution (1 Maccabees 2:63; 2 Maccabees 6:10).

### 5 The material of Circumcision consisted of the foreskin

The material of Circumcision consisted of the foreskin, as the external element, and the cutting off of the same, as the action occupied with it.

Notes. The material is that which was common, or could be common, to that sacred or sacramental Circumcision and to other acts which are not of this kind.

The foreskin, which some derive from the Latin "praeputare" and others from the Greek propothion (προπόσθιον), is the anterior skin of the male member, to be cut off through Circumcision. By choosing this material for Circumcision, God seems to have intended to remind the Israelites partly of the coming of the Messiah, who was to be born from the posterity of Abraham (though not in a carnal manner); partly of original sin, propagated through carnal generation; and partly of spiritual regeneration, which was effected through Circumcision itself.

For the matter or element of a Sacrament, it is not precisely required that it be externally exhibited and distributed to the one using the Sacrament; it suffices if it is treated by the external sacramental action, or if the action is directly occupied with it. The cutting off is expressly delivered, along with the thing to be cut off (Genesis 17:11). The instrument by which the cutting was to be done is not specified. The cutting off of the foreskin considered in itself is in any case indifferent to a sacramental and a non-sacramental action, so that it is rightly regarded as the material of this Sacrament.

As for the heavenly matter which some seek here in addition to the earthly element, holding it to be the body and blood of Christ, we do not dare to assert this. (1). It is admitted by all that the body and blood of Christ were not really present in the administration of Circumcision in the Old Testament, since the Son of God had not yet become man. Yet it is difficult to assert a matter, and therefore an essential part of a Sacrament, which does not yet really exist. (2). Since the heavenly matter of the Sacraments can and ought to be judged rightly from no other source than from the divine institution, or what is the same thing, from the proper seat in which the divine institution is described, according to the accepted rule, nothing is found in the institution of Circumcision from which such a heavenly matter could be gathered. (3). The union between the earthly matter of this Sacrament and that heavenly matter which is proposed can be explained with difficulty, unless one has recourse to that relative union (schetikē, σχετική) which involves the relation of a sign to the thing signified, and to the fact that the merit of Christ's future passion was applied to human beings through this Sacrament. Whether these are sufficient for asserting a heavenly matter of the Sacrament is a matter of dispute. Therefore, with Blessed Gerhard in his Loci and Blessed Himmel in his Compendium, we have preferred to omit mention of a heavenly matter in this Sacrament.

### 6 The formal element of Circumcision was the word of institution itself

The formal element of Circumcision was the word of institution itself, to be employed in the act of Circumcision.

Notes. That is, the element by which the cutting off of the human foreskin was formally constituted in the being of a sacramental action.

The word is found in Genesis 17:11: "This is my covenant which you shall keep between me and you and your seed after you" (which he commands), "that every male among you be circumcised." The word of promise had been premised in verse 7.

For just as God through these words made Circumcision a Sacrament in its own species, as it were, and in the signified act, so in practice each individual act was to be performed through words grounded in that institution (Sebastian Schmidt, Treatise on Circumcision, p. 395). Schmidt also records among several ancient Jewish forms of blessing the following sacramental formula, which especially refers to the words of institution: "Blessed art thou, Lord our God, King of the world, who hast sanctified us by thy commandments and hast commanded that we initiate him into the covenant of Abraham our father" (Schmidt, Treatise on Circumcision, pp. 398-399).

### 7 The end "for whom" of Circumcision consisted of Israelite males

The end "for whom" of Circumcision consisted of Israelite males, together with their household servants and proselytes; and infants, when they had completed the eighth day of life.

Notes. These are the persons for whose good Circumcision was divinely instituted, and who were the subject to whom this rite, as a means of grace, was to be applied, that is, in a word, the subject to be circumcised.

Males alone were the subject, as is clear from the very seat of this doctrine, although women were not thereby deprived of covenantal grace.

The covenant made with Abraham was derived from him to Isaac, from Isaac to Jacob, and so to the Israelites, with the collateral lines not equally received into the covenant.

According to Genesis 17:12, express mention is made of aliens to be circumcised, if any were born in the household or bought with money, although they were not thereby to be compelled to Circumcision.

Proselytes too were to be circumcised if they wished to participate in the remaining sacred rites of the Israelites, especially the Sacrament of the Paschal Lamb.

Concerning the eighth day, see Leviticus 12:3. Infants dying before the eighth day could nonetheless be saved. By this deferral of Circumcision, God seems to have had regard for the tender bodies of newborns. It is also believed that he gave this comfort to parents, namely that he did not wish the Sacrament of initiation, by which their children would be received into the covenant of grace, to be deferred any longer. Otherwise, on account of dangerous illness or journeys, Circumcision was permitted to be deferred further, as God allowed it to be omitted for forty years while the people of Israel journeyed to the land of Canaan (Joshua 5:5-8). No fixed time was appointed for the circumcision of proselytes, but Circumcision had to precede admission to the remaining sacred rites of the Jews.

### 8 The proximate and principal end of the Sacrament of Circumcision was the…

The proximate and principal end of the Sacrament of Circumcision was the conferral of covenantal grace concerning the remission of sins. The less principal end was the segregation of the Israelites from other peoples, and the reminder of original sin and of the coming Messiah. The ultimate end was the eternal salvation of those circumcised.

Notes. The principal end was intended by God the author and was truly to be conferred or effected through Circumcision as an instrument.

See Genesis 17:7, where God promises that he will be the God of Abraham who is to be circumcised, and of his seed who are to be circumcised. This must be interpreted especially of spiritual benefits divinely conferred, and of adoption into the covenant of grace. Hence Circumcision is also said to have been a seal of righteousness (Romans 4:11). Thus, just as God in the first institution of Circumcision simultaneously promised that he would receive into the covenant of grace those who were circumcised, so also he concurred with Circumcision as it was placed in actual use in such a way that he excited or sealed the faith to be given to that promise in those who were circumcised, and made them certain of the grace of the covenant and of the righteousness obtained before God.

The very names "Circumcision" and "Uncircumcision" denote and distinguish the Jewish people from others (Romans 3:30).

For the reminder of original sin and of the coming Messiah, see what was said above at Section V.

The ultimate end of eternal salvation follows from the connection between the remission of sins and eternal life.

### 9 Circumcision may be defined as a sacred action divinely instituted

Circumcision may be defined as a sacred action divinely instituted, by which God in the Old Testament, through the cutting off of the foreskin, with the word of institution being added, conferred faith upon male Israelites, their household servants, and proselytes (upon infants, that is), while for believing adults he sealed and confirmed it, for the obtaining of the grace of the remission of sins and eternal salvation.

Notes. The genus is that which is common to all Sacraments.

The principal efficient cause is thus indicated (see Section III).

The material of Circumcision is contained herein (see Section IV).

The formal element is included (see Section V).

The subject, or end "for whom," is indicated (see Section VI).

The matters pertaining to the end of Circumcision are included (see Section VII).

### 10 The second Sacrament of the Old Testament is called by the name of the Passover

The second Sacrament of the Old Testament is called by the name of the Passover, or of the Paschal Lamb.

Notes. In Hebrew it is called Pesach (חסַ פֶּ ), which derives from the act of passing over or leaping over, such as was the act by which the destroying angel, slaying the firstborn of the Egyptians through all their houses, leaped over the houses of the Israelites. The Sacrament takes its name from this event, because it was to be celebrated so that the Israelites might be preserved when the angel passed over, and furthermore in memory of this passing over. See Exodus 12:11-13, 27.

That sacramental action was occupied with a lamb to be treated according to a certain rite, and hence it came about that the name, as well as the Greek Pascha (πάσχα), sometimes denoted by metonymy the sacrificial lamb itself.

The seat of this doctrine is found in Exodus 12.

### 11 The principal efficient cause of this Sacrament is the triune God

The principal efficient cause of this Sacrament is the triune God.

Notes. Instituting it by his own authority, commanding it, and efficaciously concurring with it according to the promise for its spiritual effect.

See Exodus 12:1.

### 12 The internal impelling cause is the goodness and gratuitous favor of God

The internal impelling cause is the goodness and gratuitous favor of God; the external or meritorious cause is Christ the Mediator.

Notes. God, moved by this goodness, both willed to spare the Israelites, though they were not entirely free from sin, and himself instituted and offered the means of grace for them to use for their salvation.

In Christ is contained the antitype of the Paschal Lamb, as we shall presently explain. Meanwhile, it is easily understood that this prefigurative Sacrament was divinely instituted in view of him.

### 13 The less principal cause consisted partly of Moses and Aaron

The less principal cause consisted partly of Moses and Aaron, partly of the fathers of families of the Israelite nation, and partly of the Levites.

Notes. These provided their ministry to God the author, so that this Sacrament might either first be introduced into the Church or subsequently be placed in use.

Moses and Aaron served as ministers for the promulgation of the divine institution (Exodus 12:1, 28).

The fathers of families undoubtedly administered the Sacrament when it was first to be celebrated in Egypt (Exodus 12:3, 6, 21, 28). Afterward, when the Levitical priesthood had been established, they still roasted the Paschal Lamb, even if they did not slaughter it.

Circumcised proselytes had the same right of sacred things as the Jewish fathers of families, as is taught elsewhere.

The Levites are known to have been ministers of sacred things in other respects. It is certain that in the case where the fathers of families labored under legal uncleanness, the Levites prepared the Passover for them (Ezra 6:20; 2 Chronicles 30:17-18). Whether, apart from this case, they performed the work of slaughter as ordinary ministers is disputed. The passage 2 Chronicles 35:10-11 is referred to this question. It is probable that after God tied the celebration of this Sacrament to the place where the Temple stood (Deuteronomy 16:5-7), the ministerial work of the Levites and priests was also more required than before.

### 14 The matter of this Sacrament was a lamb

The matter of this Sacrament was a lamb, whole and without blemish, male and of one year, and the acts performed upon it, namely: segregation from the flock, slaughter, and roasting; then eating; and finally the sprinkling of its blood upon the lintel and doorposts of the houses.

Notes. If not always, then most frequently the offering was a lamb, or in its place also a kid, as may be gathered from Exodus 12:5, where a common noun occurs and it is then added that it may be taken from various species of smaller livestock, that is, kevasim (םישִ בָ כְּ ), lambs, and izzim (םיזִ עִ ), goats. It is certain that not only the lamb but also the kid was a type of Christ, although it is not as customary to call Christ a kid as a lamb (see John 1:29, the words of which are thought to refer equally to the scapegoat and to all the lambs customarily offered in the Old Testament), along with twenty-eight passages in the Book of Revelation.

The lamb is called tamim (םימִ תָ ) in Exodus 12:5, which the Septuagint rendered as teleion (τέλειον), meaning perfect or without blemish. The antitype corresponds in 1 Peter 1:19, where Christ is called amnos amōmos kai aspilos (ἀμνὸς ἄμωμος καὶ ἄσπιλος), a lamb without blemish and without spot (see also 1 Peter 2:22; Hebrews 7:26).

The lamb was to be male, with reference to the preeminence which this sex possesses over the other. The antitype corresponds: the Son of Man, in whom is masculine strength and perfection.

It was to be one year old, that is, born in the previous year, so that it would either be about to complete or had already completed its first year of life, but had not so exceeded it as to be considered a two-year-old. The reference was to the flower of Christ's age at which he was to die.

The segregation from the flock and the two following acts were preparatory, yet necessary. The segregation appears to have prefigured the captivity of Christ.

The slaughter was to take place "between the two evenings" (Exodus 12:6), that is, around the third afternoon hour or shortly thereafter, before sunset. At this time Christ also willed to die. That Christ as our Passover has been slaughtered, Paul teaches (1 Corinthians 5:7).

The lamb was not to be boiled in water but was to be roasted and then eaten (Exodus 12:8-9). It also had to be roasted whole, with no part broken. In this way Christ too was, as it were, roasted by the fire partly of the divine wrath against the sins which he had taken upon himself, and partly by the fire of his love for us who were to be redeemed, and was deeply penetrated by it. Yet he remained whole with respect to the members of his body (John 19:36).

According to Jewish practice, which Maimonides records, the Paschal Lamb was roasted tied to a wooden spit. Justin Martyr writes in his Dialogue with Trypho (pp. 74- 75, Paris edition, 1575):

That lamb (the Paschal one) is roasted stretched out in the form of a cross. For one upright stake is thrust through from the lowest parts to the head; another likewise is transverse, across the back, to which the shoulders of the lamb are fastened.

Justin rightly observes that this signified Christ who was to be crucified.

The eating was the principal act of the Sacrament (Exodus 12:8). It should be noted that the whole lamb was to be eaten and nothing of it was to be left over. It is also certain that this signified the eating of Christ, both sacramentally in the Eucharist and spiritually through faith, in both of which the whole Christ is received. Unleavened bread and bitter herbs were to be added. To the former corresponds what Paul advises (1 Corinthians 5:8) about purging out the leaven of malice and using the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth in the Christian Passover. To the latter corresponds the fact that daily repentance is necessary for those who would profitably enjoy Christ.

The sprinkling of the blood (Exodus 12:7) was first employed so that, seeing the blood, the Lord would pass over the houses of the Israelites and not strike any of them (Exodus 12:13, 22-23). Whether afterward this act was also to be repeated at the appointed time annually in memory of what had occurred at the first Passover, some gather from Exodus 12:24 ff. If we look at Jewish practice, the smearing of the houses was discontinued, and all the blood of the Paschal animals was poured out at the base of the altar. In the meantime, both methods of religiously handling the blood of the Paschal Lamb undoubtedly prefigured the shedding of Christ's blood, upon which our redemption and the remission of sins depends (1 Peter 1:19; Revelation 13:8; Hebrews 9:22).

Concerning the heavenly matter of this Sacrament, which some seek here, those who acknowledge it hold it to be the body and blood of Christ. And it is certain that these are the thing signified by the earthly matter of the Sacrament as a sign, as is clear from what has been said. It is also certain that this is a thing of a higher order than the earthly matter, so that it altogether deserves to be called a heavenly thing, as it is also so called in the Sacrament of the Supper. It is certain, finally, that the efficacy of the Paschal Sacrament depended on the body of Christ to be given over to death and the blood to be shed, as its antitype. But whether those things which are not really present in the sacramental act, and indeed do not yet exist, let alone have been truly and really treated in the sacramental act, can properly speaking be called the matter of a Sacrament, is doubted by others. We, with Blessed Gerhard, are content with the earthly thing, or external element, of this Sacrament, and the sacramental action occupied with it (Gerhard, On Circumcision and the Paschal Lamb, Chapter IV, Section II, section 31).

### 15 The form of this Sacrament was the word of institution

The form of this Sacrament was the word of institution.

That is, the element by which the act of eating the slaughtered and roasted lamb, when applied to it, was to have the character of a sacramental act.

For thus the words of Exodus 12:11 read: Pesach hu laYHWH (הוָ הילַ אוּה חסַ פֶּ ), "It is the Passover to the Lord." And God commanded that these words also be used in the future, so that this rite might be distinguished from other similar non-sacramental acts (Exodus 12:27).

### 16 The end "for whom," which is also the subject to be admitted to the eating of…

The end "for whom," which is also the subject to be admitted to the eating of the Paschal Lamb, consisted of all the Israelites, without distinction of sex or age, as well as circumcised male slaves and proselytes.

Notes. These are those for whose good God instituted this Sacrament See Exodus 12:3-4, 21. Meanwhile, it is not denied that illness, or other impediments on account of which people could not eat meat, and indeed legal uncleanness and legitimate absence from home, excused those who did not use the Sacrament at the appointed time. But those who had been unclean, once purified, and travelers who had returned home, were nevertheless commanded to use the Sacrament, even if after the others and after the otherwise appointed time had elapsed (Numbers 9:10).

Boys and girls in whom the use of reason had manifested itself were also customarily admitted.

See Exodus 12:43-44, 48.

### 17 The end "for which purpose" of the Paschal Sacrament was first that those using…

The end "for which purpose" of the Paschal Sacrament was first that those using the Sacrament would have God propitious to them, passing over their houses while others were slain and averting all harm from them; second, that the memory of this benefit would be preserved and celebrated in subsequent times; and in both cases, the confirmation of faith in the promised Messiah, and finally eternal salvation.

Notes. This is the end which God, the author of the Sacrament, seriously intended, so that you may also call it the fruit or effect of the Sacrament.

With respect to the first celebration in Egypt, see Exodus 12:13-14. It is clear from verse 11 and verse 24 that the very name Pesach (חסַ פֶּ ) was divinely imposed upon this Sacrament because, in consideration of it, God was going to pass over the houses of the Israelites and grant his grace and the remission of sins.

With respect to the annual exercise of the sacramental act after that benefit of passing over and the miraculous deliverance, see Exodus 12:24 ff.

The Sacrament itself was a type of the Messiah and of the benefits to be expected through him and to be embraced by faith, according to what we have said at Section XIV. It is certain that God himself by his own power concurred with this sacramental rite, when placed in use, for the exciting and confirming of faith in the human beings using the Sacrament through it, so that this end also had the nature of an effect with respect to the Sacrament as an efficacious means or instrument.

The ultimate end of eternal salvation follows from the connection between faith, the remission of sins, and eternal life.

### 18 The Passover may be defined as a sacred action divinely instituted

The Passover may be defined as a sacred action divinely instituted, in which a lamb or kid, whole and one year old, segregated from the flock, was slaughtered, roasted, and eaten by the Israelites and circumcised proselytes, and its blood was sprinkled upon the doorposts and lintel of their houses, for the exciting of faith in the Messiah, and for the obtaining and celebrating of the grace of God and the remission of the plague, and for the attaining of eternal salvation.

Notes. The genus is that which, properly speaking and in the nominative case, is predicated of the Passover, according to Exodus 12:11 and 27, where not so much the passing over of the Lord itself, but rather that which was to be celebrated by the Israelites in view of that passing over, or the sacred action that was to be performed, is called Pesach (חסַ פֶּ ).

The efficient cause is indicated (see Section XI).

What pertains to the matter of the Sacrament is contained herein (see Section XIV).

The end "for whom," or the subject, is denoted (see Section XV).

What follows pertains to the end "for which purpose" (see Section XVI).

## 26 On Baptism

### 1 Among the two Sacraments of the New Testament

Among the two Sacraments of the New Testament, Baptism holds the first place.

Note. Besides these two (Baptism and the Lord's Supper), no other sacraments of the same order, nature, and essence are given. If there are others to which the word "sacrament" may be applied, the concept and definition of "sacrament" is nevertheless not the same in common; and accordingly the rest are not sacraments spoken of univocally. This can be taught from the Scriptures, inasmuch as these two special sacraments are found in Scripture, and the definition, essence, and nature of each can be taught from Scripture: namely, Baptism and the Sacrament of the Lord's Supper. From these a certain concept can be abstracted that is univocally common to both; and once it is shown that the remaining things which go by the name of sacraments do not agree with these two in their univocal and common concept, it readily follows that they are not sacraments in the equally proper sense. Blessed Musaeus also affirmed this (Musaeus, Detailed Explanation, lesson 16, question 81, p. 667).

### 2 The principal efficient cause of Baptism is Christ

The principal efficient cause of Baptism is Christ, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, who not only determined those things that pertain to the constitution of Baptism, but also commanded that this rite be regularly practiced, and rendered it efficacious for conferring its salutary fruit.

Notes. Both as God and as man. See Matthew 28:18-20, where Christ, in instituting Baptism, appeals to πᾶσαν ἐξουσίαν (all authority) given to him in time, and therefore given to him as man; which authority, however, as Son of God, he possessed from eternity.

For the authority and power that Christ there employed is common to the three persons, and their wisdom and will are one, as is established elsewhere. Hence Christ also commanded that one baptize in the name, and therefore as if by the authority, of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit (Matthew 28:19). Compare John 1:33, where John the Baptist mentions his divine mission to baptize, and Luke 7:30, where those who refused to be baptized are said to have rejected the counsel of God.

And thus he is the cause of Baptism considered with respect to the species of the act. See what will be said shortly concerning the matter and form of Baptism.

In this way he is considered as the cause of Baptism with respect to the exercise of the act.

Concerning which we shall see more when we treat of the end and effect of Baptism. See meanwhile Mark 16:16.

### 3 The internal impulsive cause is divine goodness

The internal impulsive cause is divine goodness; the external impulsive cause is the merit of Christ the Mediator.

Notes. Thus Paul writes to Titus (Titus 3:5), ascribing it to the goodness, love toward humanity, and mercy of God our Savior that we are saved through the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit.

Inasmuch as Christ is said to have given himself for the Church, in order to sanctify it, cleansing it by the washing of water through the word; and thus, by giving himself over to death, he merited that human beings should be cleansed by the washing of Baptism (Ephesians 5:26). Compare what we have said concerning the sacraments in general (chapter 7, section 5, pp. 619-620).

### 4 The less principal efficient cause is

The less principal efficient cause is, in the ordinary case, a minister of the Church; extraordinarily, in a case of necessity, even a layperson or a woman.

Notes. That is, the cause which puts Baptism into use by another's authority, namely that of a superior, and according to his institution, and applies it to human beings.

See Matthew 28:19, where Christ addresses the Apostles as ministers of the Church. And it is established that John the Baptist made mention of his mission as a minister (John 1:33). Add 1 Corinthians 4:1. Christ himself, however, abstained from the office of baptizing (John 4:2).

When, namely, it appears that a person, especially a weaker infant, must die without Baptism in the absence of an ordinary minister of the Church, it is better that another baptize him than that so necessary a means of regeneration and salvation (according to John 3:5) be omitted, not without peril. Especially since the one who administers Baptism does not bestow its efficacy upon it, but merely puts into use the means which, with God concurring, is efficacious. The administration has been specially entrusted to ministers of the Church for the sake of good order.

In this respect a lay man and a woman are equivalent. And since in the Old Testament circumcision was to be administered by women rather than omitted entirely (see chapter 8, section 4, p. 634), it is certain that no less is permitted in the New Testament with respect to Baptism.

### 5 The material element of Baptism is true and natural water

The material element of Baptism is true and natural water, together with the act of washing, which can be performed either by immersion or by sprinkling, once or three times.

Notes. This is what this sacrament has in common with other non-sacramental actions.

That is, the element, or earthly thing, with which some action is directly concerned and which it handles. Water was determined for Baptism by Christ himself (John 3:5), where it is certain that Nicodemus, anxious about the baptism of water already introduced by John, was more properly instructed by Christ. And the Apostles, baptizing with water, testified not obscurely that they were following Christ's institution (Acts 10:47; cf. Matthew 28:19; Acts 8:36ff.).

Not any other liquid or any other thing whatsoever, lest the substance of Baptism be altered. What kind of water it is, for example river water or spring water, cold or warm, makes no difference, because Christ determined nothing about this.

Some call this the proximate material, just as they call water the remote material, according to what we have said about sacraments in general (chapter 7, section 7, p. 625).

See Romans 6:4 and Colossians 2:12, where people are said to be buried together with Christ through Baptism; that is, because Baptism conferred by immersion in water represented the burial of Christ.

This is admitted not only by the force of the word "Baptism," as we showed above (section 1, note c), but also by the institution of the sacrament, which determined neither mode. Examples of sprinkling employed in Baptism are usually adduced from those passages where certain persons are recorded as having been baptized within their own houses (e.g., Acts 9:18; 10:48), of whom it can scarcely be reasonably affirmed, and certainly cannot be demonstrated, that they were plunged into water. In northern regions, moreover, and in colder weather, especially with respect to the tender bodies of infants, sprinkling is rightly employed in place of immersion.

For Scripture determines nothing on this point. In the Church, however, both customs formerly prevailed: the former, indeed, to indicate the unity or singularity of the divine essence, which the ancient Christians asserted against heretics; the latter, to denote and confess against other heretics the Trinity of the divine persons.

We omit mention of the heavenly matter in this sacrament, which some add at this point. It is certain, however, that even the older doctors of our Church made no mention of it when they were setting forth the substance or essential (or, as they say, principal) parts of Baptism. Blessed Luther writes in the Smalcald Articles (Luther, Smalcald Articles, part 3, article 5, p. 329, of the Book of Concord): "Baptism is nothing other than the Word of God with immersion in water, according to his own institution and command; or as Paul says, a washing in the word, just as Augustine also says: Let the word be joined to the element, and it becomes a sacrament." Here it is manifest that Luther taught that the entire essence of Baptism is comprised of: 1. water; 2. the act of immersion or washing; 3. the word of institution; in such a way that the water and the action performed upon it acquire the nature of a sacrament through the word of institution that is joined to them. This is the same as if he had said that the matter of the sacrament is the element of water together with the act of washing, while the form, which gives being to the thing (that is, to the sacrament), is the word of institution.

To these correspond what is found in the Large Catechism (Luther, Large Catechism, p. 537): "If you are asked what Baptism is, answer thus: It is not merely plain water, but water comprehended in God's word and command, and sanctified thereby, so that it is nothing other than God's own or divine water; not that the water itself is more excellent than other water, but that the word and command of God are added to it." Compare also the Small Catechism on the question "What is Baptism?" (Luther, Small Catechism, p. 376).

In this same simplicity the following also remained: Blessed Erasmus Sarcerius (Sarcerius, Examination of Ordinands, fol. 261b); Blessed Johann Wigand (Wigand, Syntagma of the Body of Doctrine from the New Testament, part 1, p. 240, and part 2, p. 854); Blessed Martin Chemnitz (Chemnitz, Loci, part 3, locus on Baptism, section 4, p. 161a); Blessed Nikolaus Selnecker (Selnecker, Examination of Ordinands, part 4, pp. 122, 124); Blessed Tilemann Heshusius, in the examination that he composed while engaged in ecclesiastical visitation under the auspices of Johann Wilhelm, Duke of Saxony, and dedicated first to that laudable prince and then to his son Johann, Duke of Saxony; Blessed Jakob Andreae, in the volume of disputations published jointly by Jakob Heerbrand (Andreae, Disputations, disputation 31, section 5, p. 452); and Blessed Jakob Heerbrand himself (Heerbrand, Compendium of Theology, locus on Baptism, p. 534). All of these taught that the substance of Baptism is comprised of water, the act of washing performed upon it, and the word of institution; and that the action by which the element of water is handled receives the nature or essence of a sacrament through the word of institution joining itself to it (so that the former is the material, and the latter the formal element of this sacrament), making no mention of a heavenly matter.

The occasion for the question concerning the heavenly matter of Baptism was provided by the Calvinists, especially Beza, who at the Colloquy of Montbeliard maintained that the blood of Christ pertains to the substance of Baptism as a second and indeed principal part.
