He accused Jakob Andreae and Lucas Osiander, who in their theses on Baptism (presented as beyond controversy) had placed this proposition first, namely that Baptism consists of water and the word, of not having correctly defined Baptism, inasmuch as they excluded the blood of Christ, which is a substantial part of Baptism (see Acts of the Colloquy of Montbeliard, pp. 428, 432, 437, 438, 442, 446, 448). But because Beza also introduced the distinction between external and internal Baptism, asserting that the former consists of the element and the word, while to the latter pertains the thing signified by the element as a sign, and that this thing is the blood of Christ, just as in the Sacrament of the Supper (pp. 437-438), Jakob Andreae therefore first of all attacked this distinction of a twofold baptism, showing from Ephesians 4 that there is one Baptism.

And since he remembered at the same time that what he chiefly needed to prove against Beza was that Baptism is not merely a sign, but a washing, that is, an efficacious means of regeneration and renewal (as is evident from theses 4 and 5, p. 419), and that regeneration and renewal cannot be efficaciously ascribed to Baptism except dependently upon the Holy Spirit, for this reason from John 3 he immediately added that this one Baptism consists of water and the Spirit; and that Christ in that passage joins water with the Spirit and attributes regeneration to both, because the Spirit regenerates through water unto eternal life (as he says, p. 444), or because the Spirit is the principal efficient cause of regeneration, which he works through the water of Baptism as through an instrument (as his words have it, p. 451).

On this occasion, however, while he was removing the opinion of Beza (who maintained that the blood of Christ, after the example of the Sacrament of the Supper, must also be referred to the substance of Baptism as material; on which point see pp. 439, 442, 445, and 450), and while he was showing how each individual sacrament has its own certain and mutually distinct characteristics, and while at the same time he wished to distinguish the effect of Baptism (which is regeneration) from the substance of Baptism, it happened that he said the substance of Baptism consists of water and the Spirit, and that these are the substantial elements of Baptism (p. 439). Yet immediately afterward (p. 441), repeating the same point, namely that the Holy Spirit is the principal and substantial part of Baptism, he notably added the words: "IF IT IS PERMITTED TO SPEAK THUS." From this it is manifest: 1. that the Blessed Doctor did not wish to lay down rules of ἀκριβολογία (strict precision of language) for others, but was occupied solely in teaching that the Holy Spirit, and the entire Most Holy Trinity, is substantially and ἀδιαστάτως (without separation) present in Baptism, and joins its infinite power as principal cause intimately with the water of Baptism as an instrument, for the production of one and the same effect of regeneration and renewal by one undivided action; so that this effect should be attributed neither to the water alone without the concurrence of the Holy Spirit or the Triune God, nor to God or the Holy Spirit acting separately outside the sacrament, but to both conjointly. This was indeed a true and orthodox opinion, diametrically opposed to the Calvinian or Bezian view of a twofold baptism (compare pp. 442-443).

2. It should be noted that the Blessed Doctor not only did not use the term "heavenly matter," but only asserted a "thing" (res) of the sacrament, an internal thing distinct from the external and visible one, though joined with it in its own manner. 3. It should also be observed that, when he was unwilling to call the blood of Christ a substantial part of Baptism or to say that Baptism consists of water and the blood of Christ, he gave this reason: that in the words of institution of Baptism there is absolutely no express mention of the blood of Christ, but only mention of the Trinity, in whose name one is to baptize (see p. 450). Meanwhile, he taught that the blood of Christ pertains to Baptism insofar as by its power human beings are regenerated in Baptism (p. 444), or insofar as through the water of Baptism, by the power of Christ's blood, the Holy Spirit works that which Christ merited for us by his blood (p. 445), or that the merit of Christ's shed blood is applied to the baptized person through the sprinkling of baptismal water, without which application the shedding of Christ's blood would profit an unbaptized and unregenerate infant nothing for the purgation of sins (p. 446).

4. Finally, since he referred now the Holy Spirit, now the entire Most Holy Trinity to the substantial elements of Baptism, he explained himself thus (p. 443): "Concerning each sacrament, one must both think and speak as the Word of God declares. Nor do we say the word is empty, but it truly contains what it declares. The word of Christ in Baptism is: Baptize them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. This word embraces the presence of the three persons of the Holy Trinity: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Therefore the work of regeneration in Baptism is the work of the entire Trinity. But because the Father and the Son work regeneration and renewal through the Holy Spirit, Christ therefore peculiarly attributes this work of regeneration to the Holy Spirit when he says: Unless one is born again of water and the Spirit. Wherefore we say that the thing of the sacrament in Baptism is the Holy Spirit, who by the power of the blood of Christ regenerates human beings unto eternal life."

From this it is again evident that Blessed Jakob Andreae uses the expression "thing of the sacrament" (res Sacramenti) to designate that from which the effect of the sacrament, namely regeneration and renewal, depends as from a cause; and that, besides the water, the Spirit also, or the entire Most Holy Trinity, is said to be the thing of the sacrament of Baptism, because in Baptism and in relation to the effect that is to be produced through Baptism, the Most Holy Trinity and the water are conjoined, or (since the work of regeneration is attributed by appropriation to the Holy Spirit) the Holy Spirit and the water are conjoined, as the principal efficient cause with its instrument or organ. As he adds on page 444: it is one thing for the Holy Spirit and water, or the Most Holy Trinity and water, to be conjoined in Baptism as subordinate efficient causes, a principal and an instrumental one, working by one undivided action and producing the same effect; it is quite another thing for them to be conjoined as a twofold matter, from which there arises one complete matter of Baptism. Certainly Blessed Doctor Andreae affirmed not the latter but the former, and for the rest, as to that manner of speaking by which he said these are joined as substantial parts of Baptism, he guarded himself and warned his readers by the appended formula: "IF IT IS PERMITTED TO SPEAK THUS."

Meanwhile, given this occasion, it came about that others among our theologians, wishing to distinguish their doctrine from the Calvinian view of a twofold baptism, made mention of a heavenly thing, and some even of a heavenly matter; but in setting it forth and explaining it, they pursued various paths.

Blessed Aegidius Hunnius, when in his locus on the sacraments (Hunnius, Works, vol. 1, fol. 1020) he had answered the question, "What then are the substantial parts of Baptism?," by saying, "There are two: the first is the word of institution with the annexed promise; the second is the visible element added to the word," he immediately noted that the Holy Spirit also pertains to the substance of Baptism, and indeed not only insofar as Baptism is administered in the name of the Most Holy Trinity, but also under that particular aspect insofar as he is the σφραγίς (seal), pledge, and earnest of the covenant between God and the persons who are baptized (Hunnius, Works, vol. 1, fol. 1023). It is clear, however, that Blessed Hunnius did not thereby teach that the Holy Spirit is, properly speaking, a substantial and indeed material part of Baptism. For not only does nothing appear in the cited passages to support this, but it also militates against it that on folios 1023 and 1024, when he proceeds to explain the sense in which it should be understood that the Holy Spirit pertains to the substance of Baptism, he teaches that one must first consider the formula of Matthew 28; then, that Baptism involves a covenant of God with the person who is baptized, and that God's covenant always has an earnest joined to it; and that this earnest in Baptism is the Holy Spirit, namely, substantially present in Baptism, who establishes the pact of eternal favor with the baptized person, of which the one who believes immediately becomes a partaker, while the hypocrite, who does not receive the fruit in the present, can nevertheless receive it whenever he returns through faith and repentance. And so the Holy Spirit is said to pertain to the substance of Baptism in the sense that, even if the fruit does not actually accrue, it nevertheless truly has its place when Baptism is administered, as that upon which the fruit of Baptism depends.

Others, moreover, while employing the term "invisible matter" distinct from the visible, said that by this name one should understand the word, containing the command (Matthew 28:19) and the promise (Mark 16:16). So Blessed Ambrosius Reudenius (Reudenius, Catechism, part 5, chapter 6, p. 283) and Blessed Petrus Piscator (Piscator, Twenty Disputations Embracing the Theological Loci Communes, disputation 14, sections 31- 32). But these men did not therefore judge that either the blood of Christ, or the Holy Spirit, or the Most Holy Trinity should be called the heavenly matter of Baptism, as is evident from the cited passages and will become more fully clear shortly, when we indicate what the opinion of Blessed Johann Himmel was, who at the same time appeals to Blessed Petrus Piscator.

Meanwhile, at the University of Wittenberg in 1596, on April 30, Blessed David Rungius, in a special disputation on Baptism (theses 4, 6, 32, 37ff.), when he was to set forth the constitutive parts of this sacrament, the matter and form of Baptism, said that the matter is the visible and external element, namely water, and the form is the word of institution. And he remained in this ancient simplicity, making no mention of a heavenly matter. But this disputation was also published a second time, inserted among the eight disputations of Blessed Rungius, published jointly in 1606, page 170ff. One may also join to these from the University of Tubingen Blessed Matthias Hafenreffer, who in his theological loci (Hafenreffer, Theological Loci, book 3, status 3, locus 7, p. 492), when setting forth the substantial elements of Baptism, mentions only the element and the word, and refers the word of institution to the form of Baptism (p. 493), being entirely silent about a heavenly matter.

Others, however, went somewhat further, and not only conceded but defended the position that the blood of Christ itself is the heavenly matter of Baptism. On this point Blessed Leonhard Hutter may especially be consulted, who in his Loci, when he had arrived at the question of the other essential part of Baptism, namely the heavenly and invisible thing, reviewed four opinions. The first, which substitutes the word in place of the heavenly thing, he openly attacked (holding that the word is not a constitutive principle, or a substantial part, but only a productive principle of Baptism). The remaining three, by which the heavenly substantial part is said to be the Holy Spirit, or the blood of Christ, or both together, he set forth in such a way as to leave it open which of the three each person might wish to follow; he himself, however, not obscurely maintained that the blood of Christ, either alone or together with the Holy Spirit, is the heavenly matter of Baptism (Hutter, Loci, pp. 580, 636, 637).

Notwithstanding all this, Blessed Johann Forster, at the same university, when in his Catechetical Thesaurus (Forster, Catechetical Thesaurus, chapter on Baptism, decade 2, problem 8 or 9) he descended to the doctrine of the substantial parts of Baptism, wrote in section 31: "Two constitutive or essential parts of Baptism are expressly designated in Scripture: the element and the word." And this, he said, was on solid and agreeable ground. But whether, just as the Sacrament of the Eucharist consists of a twofold and not a simple thing, namely a terrestrial and visible one and a heavenly and invisible one, so also in Baptism the same obtains, and besides the terrestrial and visible thing some heavenly thing, such as the blood of Christ or the Holy Spirit, sacramentally united to the water (just as the body of Christ is united to the bread and his blood to the wine), enters into and completes the constitutive material elements: this question, he says, so presents itself as to turn an abundance of resources into a perplexity (sections 34ff.).

Specifically, in problem 8, when he was about to set forth the Lutheran opinion concerning the blood of Christ in Baptism, he says in section 41 that nowhere in the Sacred Scriptures is it openly and expressly taught that the blood of Christ constitutes a substantial and indeed heavenly material part in the sacrament of initiation. He continues in section 42: Indeed there is absolutely no mention of it in the words of institution of Baptism, from which alone one must judge concerning its substance, as there is in the words of institution of the Supper. And in section 43: But we all hold to having ὑποτύπωσιν ὑγιαινόντων λόγων (a pattern of sound words), and to turn our whole mind away from those things that diverge from it (2 Timothy 1:13). In section 44 he adds: To which agree these truly golden words of Chrysostom (Chrysostom, Homily 49 on Matthew): "Christians wishing to receive firmness of faith ought to take refuge in nothing other than Sacred Scripture." Likewise in the Homily on the Progress of the Gospel: "Whatever is decreed contrary to Scripture is an error." And in section 45: Nor in the writings of Blessed Luther or the ancient fathers do such opinions anywhere occur by which the blood of Christ is presented as a material part of Baptism.

Similarly, in problem 9, "Whether the Holy Spirit is a substantial part of Baptism?," Forster answers in thesis 63: "The Holy Spirit pertains to the substance of Baptism, NOT however PROPERLY, as a heavenly MATERIAL PART, united to the water by a sacramental union." And in section 64: "What that heavenly part or thing of Baptism is, HAS NOT BEEN EXPRESSLY DEFINED IN SACRED SCRIPTURE. Therefore we prefer to confess a cautious ignorance rather than to profess a false knowledge," as Augustine admonishes (Augustine, Epistle 78). In section 65 he adds: "But by another rationale, and indeed a twofold one, one common and the other singular." In section 66: "By a common rationale, insofar as Baptism is administered in the name of the Most Holy Trinity, and a covenant is established between its persons (the third of whom is the Holy Spirit) and those who are baptized, which covenant from the side of the Most Holy Trinity always remains irrevocable and immovable" (Romans 11:29; 2 Timothy 2:13; Luther, Works, Jena German edition, vol. 4, fol. 284). In section 67: "By a special rationale, as the σφραγίς (seal), pledge, and earnest of the adoption, which the covenant in every Baptism always has joined to it and retains with respect to presence, even though by those who are baptized as hypocrites it is not received in the present with respect to fruit and efficacy."

Thus far Blessed Forster, from which it is clear that he believed the Holy Spirit and the entire Most Holy Trinity can be present in Baptism with respect to these rationales, and can pertain to the substance of Baptism, even though it is not properly a substantial material or heavenly material part. Indeed, he simultaneously teaches that what we have seen from Blessed Hunnius (with which these statements of Forster entirely correspond) should be understood in such a way that the opinion by which the Holy Spirit, or the Most Holy Trinity, is established as the heavenly matter of Baptism is not thereby proven. He himself rests, as we have seen, in the two constitutive or essential parts of Baptism expressly designated in Scripture: the element and the word.

In a similar manner, Blessed Zacharias Schilter treated the matter at the University of Leipzig. For against the opinion that maintains that the blood of Christ pertains to the substance of Baptism as the material from which it is constituted, he argued with several arguments. As for the Holy Spirit, he does indeed refer it to the substance of Baptism, but by that rationale which we have seen was also taught by Forster; he does not call it a heavenly matter, although he does call the word by this name. It should be noted, however, that he asserts that the "material from which" entirely corresponds with the substantial parts. But since it is otherwise certain that the substantial parts are matter and form (not matter alone, even if perhaps a twofold matter), and that from matter and form as parts the whole is constituted, which is called the essential whole or the composite of matter and form (of which the former bestows common being and the latter proper and determinate being), it readily follows that the word is called "matter" by Schilter in the sense of an essential part, which others would call the form or the formal element. Hence an argument for a heavenly matter, understood in the sense in which Forster and others deny it, cannot be drawn from Schilter (see Schilter, Catechetical Examination, theses on Baptism, pp. 440, 446, 485ff., and the disputations of Schilter and Blessed Burchard Harbart, published jointly, pp. 464ff.).

With these observations in mind, one can understand what Blessed Ambrosius Reudenius and Blessed Petrus Piscator taught in the cited passages concerning invisible matter, especially if we hear Blessed Johann Himmel, who, when he too had distinguished the matter of Baptism into visible and invisible (Himmel, Theological Syntagma, disputation 22, p. 220, section 47), and had taught that the former is the element of water and the latter is the Word of God (sections 48 and 51), immediately added in section 52: "It is therefore certain that water and the word, as the constitutive and essential (συστατικαί καὶ οὐσιώδεις) parts of this sacrament, are so conjoined by a sacramental union that without water the word, and vice versa, by no means obtains the nature of Baptism nor merits that name; but water and the word, joined together by a sacramental union (ἕνωσις), complete and constitute the being (τὸ εἶναι) of Baptism, that is, its total causes (τὰς ὁλικὰς αἰτίας)."

Indeed, Baptism has its being (τὸ εἶναι) through its form or formal element conjoined with its matter or material element; and the matter, although it is an essential part, does not by itself (even if it were perhaps twofold) complete the total causes without the form, but only together with the form does it do so. And so there is no reason here to seek a heavenly matter in Himmel, properly speaking, in the sense in which other theologians of ours are unwilling to assert a heavenly matter.

But it should be observed above all that Himmel continues in section 52: "There are those who maintain that the essential or material substantial part of Baptism is either the entire Most Holy Trinity, from Matthew 28:19, or the Holy Spirit, from John 3:5, or the blood of Christ, from 1 John 1:7. But whether any of these opinions can be solidly proven from the institution of Baptism (from which alone one must judge concerning any sacrament), we have doubts. See the disputation on Baptism publicly held here in 1666 by Blessed Petrus Piscator of pious memory, theses 113, 132; Gerhard, sections 82, 88."

Blessed Himmel therefore believed that the word of institution pertains to the essential and constitutive elements (τὰ οὐσιώδη καὶ συστατικά) of Baptism in such a way that nevertheless neither the Most Holy Trinity, nor the Holy Spirit, nor the blood of Christ is an essential or material part of Baptism, even though in the word of institution mention is made of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. This is because the word of institution is not, in the nominative case, the Most Holy Trinity itself, or the Holy Spirit, or the blood of Christ. And he affirmed that Petrus Piscator and Johann Gerhard agreed with him in this.

And indeed, to speak more precisely concerning Blessed Johann Gerhard, it is established that, although in his Aphorisms of Theology on Baptism he taught that the efficacious presence of the entire Most Holy Trinity in Baptism is to be gathered from the words of institution, and that Christ the God- man (θεάνθρωπος) is present with his blood and cleanses the human person, he nevertheless did not employ the designation "heavenly matter." Similarly, when he treated the institution of Baptism at greater length in his Harmony of the Gospel History of the Resurrection of Christ (Gerhard, Harmony of the Gospel History, chapter 12, p. 461ff.), he did not teach that the word of institution or the Most Holy Trinity is the other material part of Baptism.

In his Loci (Gerhard, Loci, vol. 4, locus on Holy Baptism, section 70), he treats the matter and the external element in Baptism as the same thing, as is clear from the marginal heading. Although in that chapter, which he entitled "On the Matter of Baptism," he treats in section 1 the earthly thing and in section 2 the heavenly thing of Baptism, nevertheless when he treats the heavenly thing he abstains from the designation "matter," and only teaches the conjunction of the heavenly thing with the earthly thing, or matter. That heavenly thing he says in section 80 is the Word of God, namely the word of divine ordination concerning the administration of Baptism in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. From this he further infers in section 83 that the entire Most Holy Trinity is present with its grace in Baptism; and in section 84 that the Spirit acts efficaciously in, with, and through the water; in such a way, according to section 85, that in every Baptism administered according to Christ's institution the Holy Spirit is present: 1. by reason of essence, as are also the remaining persons of the Trinity; 2. with respect to the offering of the salutary efficacy of the benefits of Christ; 3. with respect to the sealing of the covenant established between God and the baptized person, which is ratified at all times on God's part. Specially and beyond these, in the baptism of believers he concurs by reason of salutary efficacy in actual regeneration and renewal, and likewise by reason of the actual and reciprocal obligation of the covenant established between God and the baptized person. In the baptism of hypocrites, however, he concurs not only with respect to the offering of benefits and the sealing of the covenant on God's part, but also with respect to the judgment that the Holy Spirit exercises through Baptism upon unbelievers.

And in this sense he finally concludes in section 81: "Although the Most Holy Trinity is the efficient cause instituting and ordaining this sacrament, nothing prevents us from saying that the name of the Most Holy Trinity is the other substantial part, since the word of institution and promise testifies that God the Father, the Son, and the Spirit are present in Baptism with all the benefits of grace."

However, that Blessed Gerhard held that the Holy Spirit or the entire Most Holy Trinity is present in Baptism through a special approximation of its essence to the substance of the water, or that it is, properly speaking, the heavenly matter of Baptism, so that by the force of a sacramental union between the water and the Holy Spirit it could be said that those who are baptized are sprinkled not only with water but also, properly speaking, with the Holy Spirit (just as in the Lord's Supper, by the force of the sacramental union between the earthly and heavenly matter, all communicants, together with the blessed bread and wine, eat and drink the body and blood of Christ, not metaphorically but properly speaking and orally, though not in a natural manner): this we certainly cannot gather from the words of the Blessed Doctor.

Indeed, as for the blood of Christ, although Gerhard (section 86) maintains that it should not be excluded from Baptism, since it is present: 1. by reason of substance, inasmuch as Christ the God-man (θεάνθρωπος) is wholly present; 2. by reason of merit, because the fruit of Baptism comes from it; 3. by reason of efficacy, that is, the efficacious application of the merit of Christ's blood through faith conferred in Baptism; 4. because we are baptized into the death of Christ; nevertheless in section 87 he openly approves the opinion of those most weighty theologians who maintain that the blood of Christ cannot be conveniently called the other material part of Baptism, and he rests in their reasons, which he adduces.

For this reason, when it is acknowledged: 1. that besides water, the word of institution also pertains to the substance of Baptism; and 2. by the force of this word it is further acknowledged that the Holy Spirit and the entire Most Holy Trinity is the author of this sacrament as a means of grace; 3. it is acknowledged that the Holy Spirit and the Triune God, wherever and whenever Baptism is rightly administered, is present both by his immense essence and 4. by his grace, in such a way that not only does he seriously offer spiritual benefits through this sacrament, and 5. enters into a covenant of grace with the baptized person, never to be retracted on his part, and seals this through Baptism; but also 6. in the person who is baptized and does not resist divine grace, he actually accomplishes the work of regeneration or renewal through this sacrament, so that 7. not separately and by a peculiar action, but conjointly with the water of Baptism and through it, by one and undivided action, he kindles or confirms faith; and this 8. on account of the merit of Christ the God-man (θεάνθρωπος), really present according to both natures, and his blood shed for our sins; as also 9. when through Baptism faith is conferred, the blood of Christ is thereby sprinkled in the sense that its merit is applied through faith: when these things, I say, are acknowledged and taught, it shall be permitted for the rest, as to the name of "heavenly matter" and its scarcely explicable rationale, to remain silent with the older doctors, or to distinguish with Blessed Forster between the εὐπορία (abundance of resources) and the ἀπορία (perplexity), and to confess a cautious ignorance rather than to profess a false knowledge (Forster, cited above, sections 34 and 64).

We add nothing more here. For our purpose is not to dispute, but to set forth what pertains to positive theology. And just as elsewhere in those things that are adduced, so here, where what might seem worth adducing is omitted, we wished briefly to show the consensus of our theologians, which has nevertheless grown beyond expectation into these many pages.

### 6 The form of Baptism is the word of institution

The form of Baptism is the word of institution, that is, that the washing is performed in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.

Notes. That is to say, the form is that by which, when conjoined with the act of washing, the act itself formally possesses its character as sacramental, or as a sacrament.

This accords with the sense in which the blessed Luther, and the orthodox theologians who most closely followed him, understood the matter, as we indicated in the final note to the preceding section. Expressly also the blessed Aegidius Hunnius calls the word of institution the form of Baptism, as a substantial part (Hunnius, Works, vol. 1, fol. 1019–1020). Citing Ephesians 5:26, concerning the washing of water through the word, he says: "You see that the divine Apostle mentions both water and the word as substantial parts of Baptism. For water, without the word, would not have the power of sanctifying. But through the Word of the instituting God, it acquires this supernatural faculty of sanctifying." And the blessed David Rungius, in his disputation on Baptism held in 1596 (Rungius, Disputation on Baptism, theses 37–38), where he treats the form of Baptism and establishes that it is the very word of institution, adds: "This word is that by which the water of Baptism is truly sanctified, and by which Christ cleanses His Church with the washing of water, and which imparts, as it were, life and soul to it, so that it deservedly merits to be called the form of Baptism." And to this end he cites Luther's own words from the Small Catechism. However, that others refer the word of institution to the matter of Baptism (as we saw above) should be noted, since they believed that the twofold matter and the substantial parts of Baptism are equally broad in scope (see Rennecius, Piscator, Schilterus, and Himmel at the passages cited). Indeed, even those who reckon that word among the efficient principles nevertheless also refer it to the form of Baptism (see Hutterus at the passage cited).

Some call it the word of mandate or precept, understanding by this not so much that by which the exercise of the act is commanded, but that by which the act of washing is formally determined to a certain species of act. Hence others prefer to call it the word of ordination.

As Theophylact says on this passage, one name signifies one Deity, because to baptize in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit is to baptize by the authority and power of these three Persons. Since, therefore, there is one authority and power, and consequently one essence, of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, the Apostles are commanded to baptize not in the names but in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit (Gerhard, Harmony of the Gospels on the Resurrection of Christ, ch. 12, p. 463; and Gerhard, On Baptism, vol. 4, sections 81–82).

And we acknowledge that this full formula, just as it was constantly observed of old by the Apostles and their disciples, so must it be carefully and necessarily retained. Nevertheless, it is left to Christian liberty whether the one who baptizes, following the custom of the Latin Church, says actively, "I baptize you in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit," or, with the Greek Church, speaks in the third person passive, "Let this servant of the Lord be baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit," or finally, conjoins with the act of washing, which already of itself falls upon the senses, the invocation of the most holy Trinity, that is, the words "in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit," provided the Church is not disturbed by an untimely change.

### 7 The final cause

The final cause, which is also the subject of Baptism, consists of human beings who have been born according to the flesh and brought into the light of day; and indeed all of them, males and females alike, not only adults but also infants.

Notes. That is, those for whose benefit Baptism was instituted by God and is thus to be administered.

The subject is that to which Baptism, as a means of grace, ought to be applied. Others call it the object, which some further specify as the personal object.

Not, however, any other thing of whatever kind, nor indeed all human fetuses, unless it is established that they are alive and truly human beings.

This is so that they may be flesh of flesh, according to John 3:6. Christ, however, who had no need of Baptism, was baptized by the same economy by which He was circumcised (compare Matthew 3:14–15).

Those, moreover, who have not yet been fully born are not commanded to be reborn through Baptism.

For the saying of Christ is universal: "Unless someone, whoever he may be, is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God" (John 3:5). And in Matthew 28:19, Christ commands that all nations, πάντα τὰ ἔθνη (all the nations), be baptized: not only Gentiles as distinguished from Jews, but all peoples of the whole earth, whom Mark calls "every creature" (Mark 16:15). Nor did these things pertain only to the planting of the Church, but are to be preserved, just as the teaching or preaching of the Gospel and likewise Baptism, even until the consummation of the age (Matthew 28:20). Thus we know that Lydia was baptized (Acts 16:15).

That infants are to be baptized is rightly inferred from the passages of John 3:5 and Mark 10:14 taken together, in the following manner. All those whom Christ wills to come to salvation, but who cannot attain eternal life by the ordinary way except through Baptism, ought to receive Baptism as the ordinary means; it should not be denied them. But Christ wills that infants be saved (according to Mark 10:14), and they cannot attain eternal life by the ordinary way except through Baptism (by virtue of the universal saying of John 3:5). Therefore, Baptism ought to be conferred upon them.

Furthermore, secondly, the argument proceeds thus: all those whom Christ wills to be brought to Him, so that they may enjoy spiritual blessing, are to be brought to Christ through Baptism as the ordinary means. But Christ wills that infants be brought to Him so that they may enjoy spiritual blessing (according to Mark 10:14, which Luke, in explaining, indicates that βρέφη, that is, children of the most tender age, are meant). Therefore, infants are to be brought to Christ through Baptism.

Moreover, thirdly, the command of Matthew 28:19 to baptize all nations is rightly extended also to infants, who are included within the compass of the nations. And fourthly, the examples which teach that entire households were baptized, such as Acts 16:15, Acts 16:33, Acts 18:8, and 1 Corinthians 1:16, are rightly believed to include infants, who doubtless constituted a part of those households. To these are added, fifthly, the analogy of circumcision, which was conferred upon infants; and sixthly, that just as the promise of covenantal grace pertains to infants (Acts 2:39), so also does the seal of the covenant, namely Baptism. Finally, seventhly, since the whole Church throughout the world is to be cleansed by the washing of water through the word (according to Ephesians 5:26), this is rightly referred also to infants, seeing that they too, being unclean by nature, must nevertheless be grafted into the Church.

### 8 Meanwhile, we believe that infants of believing parents who happen to be…

Meanwhile, we believe that infants of believing parents who happen to be deprived of Baptism are regenerated and saved by the extraordinary grace of God. As for the unbaptized infants of unbelievers, we commit them to the divine judgment. Indeed, we do not even dare to seize them by force from unwilling parents and so baptize them.

Notes. For the necessity of Baptism is not absolute. On our part, we are obligated to receive Baptism; nevertheless, the extraordinary action of God in infants who have been offered to Christ by pious parents and by the Church through prayers, and who perished before the opportunity of Baptism could be given them, is not to be denied, since God has not so bound His grace and saving efficacy to Baptism that He cannot and does not will to act extraordinarily in the case of deprivation. These are indeed the words of the blessed Gerhard (Gerhard, On Baptism, section 237).

For although a determinate mode of acting with unbaptized infants of believers through extraordinary grace, and of working regeneration and faith in them and so applying the merit of Christ to them, is not expressly revealed in the Scriptures, nevertheless, relying upon theological reasons drawn from Scripture, we can conceive a hope that is neither rash nor doubtful concerning the extraordinary regeneration of those infants (see Musaeus, Detailed Explanation, question 61, pp. 358 ff.). Thus also the blessed Gerhard says at the same passage: "Concerning infants born in the Church, we hope for the better." And shortly after: "Those infants who are extinguished either in the womb of the mother or by some sudden accident before the reception of Baptism, we neither can nor ought to condemn rashly; rather, we maintain that the prayers of pious parents, or, if the parents have been negligent in this matter, the prayers of the Church poured out to God on behalf of these infants, are graciously heard, and that the same infants are received by God into grace and life." And to this end he adduces several arguments (sections 238– 239), though he does not equally address the determinate mode of action that God employs through His extraordinary grace.

Concerning the infants of unbelievers, we cannot equally conceive a hope of salvation from divine revelation. Indeed, when such children must be returned and entrusted to their parents so that the parents themselves may raise them, and when the parents will undoubtedly raise them in their own idolatry, there is reason to fear that by baptizing those children, holy things would be cast before dogs. However, if the infants of unbelievers have come into the power of Christians by a legitimate means, and can therefore justly be kept and educated in the true religion and faith, then just as Baptism can be conferred upon them once they have been educated, instructed, and thus converted and requesting Baptism, so also in their very infancy, if danger of death is imminent, it is permissible to baptize them.

### 9 The proximate final cause

The proximate final cause, which is also the effect of Baptism, is the regeneration or renewal of those to be baptized; the ultimate end is their eternal salvation.

Notes. This is the end to which Baptism, by the intention of its Author, has the character of a means.

For Baptism is an efficacious means and a cause of obtaining its end, as will presently be evident.

This is what is meant by saying that one must be born of water and the Spirit (John 3:5), where by water is understood true and properly so called baptismal water. Regeneration, however, which is not Baptism itself but that which is effected through Baptism as a divinely instituted instrument, is said to proceed ἐξ ὕδατος καὶ πνεύματος (from water and the Spirit), as from efficient causes, the less principal and the principal respectively (see Hunnius, On Baptism, vol. 1 of Works, fol. 1021). Similarly, in Titus 3:5, Baptism is called the washing of regeneration, a designation taken from its effect.

Baptism is likewise called the washing of renewal in Titus 3:5.

See also the aforementioned passages and Mark 16:16.

### 10 Here, however, with respect to the proximate end

Here, however, with respect to the proximate end, a diversity arises with regard to different subjects. For upon all infants equally, through Baptism there is first conferred and sealed faith, by which the merit of Christ is applied to them. But as for adults, only those who have conceived faith from the Word before the reception of Baptism receive through Baptism the sealing and confirmation of that faith. Nor does Baptism profit only at the time when it is received, but also afterward and throughout the whole of life, it efficaciously benefits believers for the confirmation of faith and for further renewal.

Notes. For infants cannot, on account of their age, place an obstacle or maliciously resist divine grace, and therefore, when the means of grace are set in use and are not impeded, they certainly obtain grace immediately.

For up to this point they are unclean by nature and children of wrath.

Baptism is the seal of the covenant of grace, just as circumcision formerly was, in whose place it has succeeded.

And this faith is proper to infants, consisting not in an idle habit but in spiritual acts and movements which, although not sufficiently explicable, are nonetheless certain (compare what we have said in Chapter 2, Section 2, note c).

For the faith of adults prior to Baptism, see Acts 2:41; 8:12, 36–38; 16:14–15, 31, 33; and 18:8.

But if adults lack faith, and thus resist divine grace, they will not receive the spiritual goods, nor will they be regenerated or renewed.

For the covenant of grace itself, of which Baptism is the seal, always remains ratified and firm on God's part (compare what we have said in Chapter 4, Section 8, note c; and Hunnius at the passage cited, fol. 1024).

For when Baptism renders believers certain of the covenant of grace of God through Christ, it assuredly consoles and uplifts their spirits, so that they may rest more securely in Christ.

Indeed, when it increases faith, it simultaneously stirs up greater love, hope, and the exercise of the other virtues.

Moreover, Baptism, once conferred, even when faith and the grace of God have been expelled through sins against conscience, nevertheless efficaciously benefits those who return to repentance for the confirmation of their faith (see Hunnius at the passage cited).

### 11 Baptism, once conferred according to the institution of Christ

Baptism, once conferred according to the institution of Christ, ought not to be repeated with respect to the same subject.

Notes. That is, provided nothing has been altered in its substantial elements, but these have been conformed to the institution.

This holds even if Baptism was administered by a heretic or a wicked person, so long as it is established that it was rightly administered.

This applies even though the baptized person may have fallen away from God through open denial or other sins and violated the covenant of grace.

For not only does no command or example exist for repeating Baptism, but neither does any necessity or solid reason appear. Indeed, the very nature of the sacrament of initiation excludes iteration rather than demands it.

### 12 Baptism may be defined as a sacred action instituted by Christ

Baptism may be defined as a sacred action instituted by Christ, in which human beings, without distinction of sex or age, are washed with water in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, so that they may thereby be regenerated and renewed, for the purpose of obtaining eternal salvation.

Notes. The genus common to all sacraments is that it is a sacred action.

The principal efficient cause is thus indicated (see Section 2).

The subject or the final cause for whose benefit Baptism is administered is denoted by the reference to human beings (see Section 7).

The matter of Baptism is water (see Section 5).

The form of Baptism is signified by the phrase "in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (see Section 6).

The things pertaining to the final cause for whose sake Baptism exists are regeneration and renewal (see Section 9).

## 27 On the Holy Supper

### 1 Upon Baptism there follows the other sacrament of the New Testament

Upon Baptism there follows the other sacrament of the New Testament, which we call the Supper of the Lord.

Notes. Baptism is not thereby abrogated, but rather, as a sacrament of confirmation, the Supper is to be conferred upon those who have already been initiated.

The designation follows the lead of Paul (1 Corinthians 11:26). Besides this, several other names have been received into common usage: the Table of the Lord, according to 1 Corinthians 10:21; the Eucharist, with respect to the particular act occurring therein (Mark 14:23; Luke 22:19; 1 Corinthians 11:24); Communion, from 1 Corinthians 10:16; Synaxis (σύναξις), with respect to the sacred assemblies in which it is customarily celebrated (cf. 1 Corinthians 11:20); the Mass, either from the rite of sending forth offerings and gifts, or from the formula of dismissing the people; and the Sacrament of the Altar, not indeed with a view to sacrifice properly so called, but with respect to the sacred table upon which the offerings were placed.

The doctrinal foundation for this sacrament is found in Matthew 26:26ff., Mark 14:22ff., Luke 22:19ff., and 1 Corinthians 11:23ff.

### 2 The principal efficient cause of this sacrament is Christ

The principal efficient cause of this sacrament is Christ, who instituted this sacrament, commanded that it be frequently observed, and even now brings it about that the action performed upon the outward symbols, administered according to his prescription, possesses the nature and power of a sacrament.

Notes. Christ determined each and every element pertaining to the substance or to the specific character of the sacramental act (cf. Matthew, Mark, Luke, and Paul in the passages cited above).

He so ordained it that he is also the cause with respect to the exercise of the act, inasmuch as he commanded it to be celebrated until his return for judgment, as Paul interprets (1 Corinthians 11:26).

For Christ himself joins his own body and blood with the blessed symbols, so that they may be received together, and thus he confirms and increases faith, as we shall see below.

Moreover, because the authority, power, and omnipotence that Christ employed in effecting this sacrament are shared in common with the Father and the Holy Spirit, it can rightly be said that the Triune God is the principal efficient cause of this sacrament.

### 3 The internal impulsive cause for the institution of this sacrament is the…

The internal impulsive cause for the institution of this sacrament is the goodness and love of Christ toward his own; the external cause is the very merit of his passion and death. Specifically, with regard to the real presence of the body and blood of Christ in each administration of the Supper, the institution of Christ itself has the nature of the principal impulsive cause; and the consecration of the symbols performed by the minister according to the institution of Christ is the less principal impulsive cause.

Notes. By goodness is meant that quality by which Christ is good toward others, that is, his gratuitous favor, as is evident from what follows.

To this pertains what we read in John 13:1 concerning the love with which Christ loved his own who were in the world, even to the end; to which love are also ascribed those things that were done at and after the Last Supper.

For although in the Holy Supper the very body of Christ, delivered unto death for us, and the blood of Christ, poured out for us, are exhibited to us, nevertheless, just as Christ, through that delivering of his body unto death and the pouring out of his blood, merited spiritual benefits for us, so also he merited that those benefits should be applied, sealed, and confirmed through this seal of the new covenant.

That is to say, the act by which the body and blood of Christ are rendered present in the Holy Supper and united with the earthly symbols depends upon the divine power and the free will of Christ together. After Christ determined to render his body and blood present and to unite them sacramentally with the bread and wine in the Holy Supper, whenever it is celebrated in conformity with his institution, and after he openly declared this in the words, "This is my body; this is my blood" (concerning which we shall see more distinctly below), it is certain that the will of Christ is moved by virtue of his own institution to effect that very thing which the words "This is my body; this is my blood" signify.

Concerning the consecration, we shall speak presently in the following section. In the meantime, it should be noted that the words of consecration move the will of Christ not by any power of their own or as they are uttered by the minister, but by virtue of the institution proceeding from Christ himself.

### 4 The ministerial cause is the ordinary minister of the Church

The ministerial cause is the ordinary minister of the Church, who consecrates the external elements and distributes them to the communicants.

Notes. That is, the cause which, by the authority of another as of a superior, puts the sacrament into use.

Indeed, Christ himself, on the night on which he was betrayed, first administered the Eucharist while still clothed in the form of a servant, although, as the God-man, he acted by his own authority. But after that first celebration of the Eucharist, this office belongs to the ministers of the Church (cf. 1 Corinthians 4:1; 11:23).

Unlike Baptism, this sacrament is not to be administered by a layperson at any time, nor by a woman, for the same necessity does not attach to both sacraments. However, when, in the absence of an ordinary minister, a faithful person anxiously desires this sacrament, it is better to persuade that person of the sufficiency of spiritual eating, and to point out the danger of other temptations that might arise if the sacrament were administered by another person without a legitimate calling, and therefore with a doubtful mind and outcome.

The earthly elements in question are bread and wine, concerning which more will be said presently.

The minister consecrates these elements; that is, having offered prayers to God, he sets apart the external symbols from common use and designates them for sacred use (which practice is also called Blessing or Thanksgiving, and among us is customarily performed with the Lord's Prayer). Then, by pronouncing the words of Christ that he used at the first institution of the Supper, speaking in the person of Christ, the minister brings it about that the body and blood of Christ, united with the symbols of bread and wine, are simultaneously dispensed, eaten, and drunk. This is Consecration strictly so called. The minister effects this not by any physical or intrinsic power of his own, whether principal or instrumental, but by moving the free will of Christ, so that Christ himself, through his own omnipotence as the physical efficient cause (that is, as the cause exerting real influence), renders his body and blood really present in the Holy Supper for true eating and drinking together with the earthly symbols. Indeed, those words of consecration, inasmuch as they are the words of the omnipotent Son of God, have a divine operation conjoined with them the very moment they are pronounced, by which what they declare is truly accomplished (cf. Musaeus, Disputation on the Holy Supper against J. Vorstius, section 75; and what we have said in notes d and e to Section III above).

The distribution may be made either by giving the blessed bread and cup into the hands of the communicants or by bringing both to their mouths, for nothing has been determined here; distribution can be done in either manner. Hence, there is no need for the breaking of bread in the very act of administration itself; it suffices if the bread is brought already broken or divided and prepared for distribution. For we know that Christ himself, at the first administration, broke the bread for no other purpose than that of distribution.

### 5 The matter of the Holy Supper is twofold

The matter of the Holy Supper is twofold: earthly and heavenly.

Note. So our theologians commonly hold, following the lead of Irenaeus, who writes: "The bread which is from the earth, receiving the invocation of God, is no longer common bread but the Eucharist, consisting of two things, an earthly and a heavenly" (Irenaeus, Against Heresies, book 4, ch. 34, p. 363, Feuardent edition). On the genuine sense of these words, see Musaeus, Disputation on the Holy Supper, sections 81ff., pp. 73-75.)

### 6 The earthly matter consists of true bread and true wine with respect to their substance

The earthly matter consists of true bread and true wine with respect to their substance; unleavened bread equally as leavened bread, and a thinner or finer bread equally as a coarser, common, or ordinary bread; not only wheat bread but also bread made from other grains. Likewise, red wine as well as white wine, and whether it be unmixed or slightly diluted with water.

Notes. The earthly matter is not abolished through consecration but retains its substance, for in 1 Corinthians 11:26-27 the communicants are said to eat bread, namely bread already blessed or consecrated; not something that was bread and has ceased to be so, but bread itself, still existing.

Other elements, foods, or drinks substantially different from these may not be substituted in their place.

The unleavened bread is of the kind that Christ is believed to have used, since he had just celebrated the sacrament of the paschal lamb.

The leavened bread is the kind that the Greek Church used from the most ancient times, and indeed the Latin Church as well, up to the time of Alexander I, Bishop of Rome.

The round breads, or small wafers, which are called Hosts or Oblates, are rightly used in our churches, for with respect to their material and form, and therefore with respect to their substance, they are true bread, since they consist of purer wheat flour mixed with water and baked by the heat of an oven. They can also serve for the nourishment of the body if taken in greater quantity, although in the Eucharist such a quantity is not required, since bodily nourishment is not to be sought therein.

Although grains of wheat may differ in their species, they nevertheless agree in having the nature of bread.

Christ determined only wine, that is, γέννημα τῆς ἀμπέλου (the fruit of the vine) (Matthew 26:29), leaving the rest to Christian liberty.

As for the admixture of water, in those regions where stronger wines are scarcely used in any other way than tempered with water for common use, it is established that the same practice was followed of old also in the Eucharist. In our regions, however, where wines are not so strong, there is no reason why they should be diluted with water. Certainly Christ, in the institution of the Holy Supper, made mention of wine but not of the admixture of water.

### 7 Bread and wine have the nature of matter in the Holy Supper insofar as they are…

Bread and wine have the nature of matter in the Holy Supper insofar as they are dispensed and received, eaten and drunk.

Notes. Hence some here also employ the distinction between remote and proximate matter. The remote matter, they say, consists of the symbols themselves; the proximate matter consists of the aforementioned acts performed upon those symbols.

These actions, however, as such, do not have the nature of form in this sacrament, for they are actions in themselves indifferent, and are determined to be sacramental actions only from another source, namely by the addition of the Word of Institution, as will be said shortly.

### 8 The heavenly matter of the Holy Supper is the true and substantial body

The heavenly matter of the Holy Supper is the true and substantial body, and likewise the true blood in its substance, of Christ. The former is sacramentally united with the bread, and the latter with the blessed wine, so that the body of Christ with the bread and the blood of Christ with the wine are truly and really dispensed and received equally by all communicants with the mouth of the body; the body is eaten and the blood is drunk.

Notes. The heavenly matter is so called not as though it remains only in heaven, or as though it were of a heavenly or ethereal substance, but because it is present in a heavenly, that is, supernatural manner, yet truly and really, and is conjoined with the earthly matter.

It is this very body that was delivered for us (Luke 22:19; 1 Corinthians 11:24), and that very blood which was poured out for us and for many for the remission of sins (Matthew 26:28; Mark 14:24; Luke 22:20).

The sacramental union is neither substantial, nor personal, nor merely local or juxtapositional, much less merely significative; rather it is such that each of the things said to be united remains in its own being, yet both are simultaneously, truly, and really received in one act by those who use the sacrament. Hence it is manifest that the Impanation and Consubstantiation, which adversaries have falsely attributed to the Lutherans, are rather excluded (cf. our special disputation On Impanation and Consubstantiation, held in the year 1677).

Although it is not necessary to define the precise moment at which the body and blood of Christ begin to be sacramentally united with the bread and wine, it is nevertheless certain that the sacramental union pertains to the use in such a way that, according to the rule of the ancients, nothing has the nature of a sacrament outside the use that was instituted by God. Hence we also believe that the symbols reserved after the consecration and placed outside the use do not retain the nature of a sacrament, and that the body and blood of Christ are not sacramentally united with them outside the use.

The body and blood of Christ are received not only by the worthy, that is, believers, but also by the unworthy, that is, unbelievers and the impious. Paul declares (1 Corinthians 11:27) that such persons are guilty not merely of abusing the sacred symbols but of sinning against the very body and blood of the Lord, and this because they do not discern the body (and blood) of the Lord; that is, because they eat the very body of the Lord unworthily, approaching this feast at which they receive the true body of the Lord without faith and reverent devotion, as though it were a common meal (cf. Musaeus, Disputation on the Holy Supper against J. Vorstius, section 10, pp. 6-7).

The sacramental eating encompasses in one act both the natural and sensible eating of the blessed bread and the eating, not indeed sensible and natural but nevertheless real, of the body of Christ sacramentally united with the bread. Similarly, the sacramental drinking, which is performed with the mouth of the body, encompasses both the sensible and natural drinking of the blessed wine and the drinking, not indeed sensible but nevertheless real, of the blood of Christ. For this reason, the sacramental eating and drinking is also customarily called oral, on account of the unity and identity of the act, or to denote the organ of the mouth by which the eating of bread and of the body, and likewise the drinking of wine and of the blood of Christ, is performed. The food and drink on each side are diverse, however, and the manner of eating the bread differs greatly from the manner of eating the body, and the manner of drinking the wine from the manner of drinking the blood of Christ. For it does not belong to the formal nature of eating as such (but only to the nature of natural eating) that food be received in a sensible manner, ground by the teeth, and sent down into the stomach; nor does it belong to the formal nature of drinking as such (but only to the nature of natural drinking) that we experience by tongue and palate the moisture and flavor of the drink. Here, the presence and the eating of the body and the drinking of the blood of Christ are insensible, supernatural, and unknown and incomprehensible to the human mind, yet so real that they truly exist whether or not anyone perceives them. We may confess our ignorance as to the determination of the manner in which the body and blood of the Lord are present and received in the Supper, even while we firmly hold to the reality itself (cf. Musaeus, Disputation on the Holy Supper against J. Vorstius, sections 91- 92, pp. 83ff.).

The true and real presence, eating, and drinking of the body and blood of Christ is proved from the very words of institution, where Christ, having extended the bread, said to the disciples: "Take, eat; this is my body"; and having extended the cup in which there was wine: "Drink; this is my blood." These words, inasmuch as they undoubtedly speak of oral eating and drinking, most clearly signify, when taken in their native force and character, that what Christ commands them to take and to eat with the mouth of the body, and therefore declares to be really present, is his very own body; and that what he likewise commands them to drink from the blessed cup is his very own blood. The sense of the declaration by which Christ, having extended the bread and pronounced the words "Take, eat," continues, "This is my body," when the words are taken properly and without trope, is this: "That which I give you, and which I command you to take and eat, is my body." Similarly, the sense of the words by which Christ, having extended the cup in which there was wine and added the words "Take, drink," then said, "This is my blood," is this: "That which I offer you, and command you to take and drink, is my blood." Although only bread and wine were shown to the senses, something else, namely the very body and blood of Christ, not equally apparent to the senses but nevertheless conjoined and united with what is shown to the senses, is declared by the added words to be really present and truly exhibited (cf. Musaeus, Disputation on the Holy Supper against J. Vorstius, sections 109ff., p. 103; section 140, p. 134; section 144, p. 137; section 158, p. 153).

That these words of Christ are to be taken in their native force and character, and that one must not deflect from their proper signification to a trope, is established on the following grounds. (1). From the common rule of interpretation, founded in reason itself, that the proper signification is to be retained unless an urgent necessity compels one to descend to an improper signification; a rule that must be observed with particular care in matters that contain supernatural realities and pertain to faith. (2). From the fact that although three Evangelists and Paul, writing at different times and in different places, commemorated the institution of the Holy Supper, none of them indicated by even a single word that a tropical signification of the words should be embraced to the effect that not the body but a sign of the body is eaten, and not the blood but a sign of the blood is drunk. (3). From the agreement of the passages in 1 Corinthians 11:27-28 and 10:16. (4). From the nature of testaments, in which the propriety and clarity of words is most especially required, and in which it is least of all to be supposed that Christ, most wise and most truthful, would have given occasion for disputes and quarrels by any impropriety of words in his testament (cf. Musaeus, Disputation on the Holy Supper against J. Vorstius, sections 4ff. to 13, pp. 2ff.).

### 9 The form of the Holy Supper consists in the words of institution

The form of the Holy Supper consists in the words of institution.

Notes. That is, the formal principle by which the action in which the symbols of bread and wine are dispensed to the communicants and received by them has the character of being the sacrament of the body and blood of Christ.

For the fact that the dispensation of the symbols is a sacramental dispensation of the body and blood of Christ derives from its being performed according to the institution of Christ and conjoined with the word of institution. And the fact that the eating of bread and the drinking of wine is formally the sacramental eating of the body and drinking of the blood of Christ derives from its being an eating and drinking of the symbols performed according to the institution of Christ and conjoined with the word of institution. Nor does it present an objection that the word of institution also pertains in part to the efficient cause. For just as it happens elsewhere in accidents and beings by aggregation, so also here it can and does happen that a thing (the action of the Holy Supper) is constituted in its specific being and receives its formal principle from that (the Word of Institution) which in its own way also pertains to the efficient cause.

### 10 The end for which

The end for which, or the subject to be admitted to participation in the Holy Supper, consists of Christian persons who are able to examine themselves.

Notes. These are those for whose benefit this sacrament was instituted by its Author.

To whom this sacrament, as a means of grace, ought to be applied. Some call this the personal Object, which is the correlate of the person administering the Holy Supper.

These are persons professing the Christian faith or religion, and endowed with, that is baptized by, the sacrament of initiation.

See cf. 1 Corinthians 11:28. To examine oneself here means to test oneself according to those things that ought to be absent from or present in a person who would rightly and profitably use the Holy Supper, so that sins that are adverse to the salutary use of the sacrament are retracted through repentance, while on the other hand, faith exercises itself in the contrite heart and is directed toward the body and blood of Christ as present and as the cause of the remission of sins.

### 11 To all those who are admitted to the communion of the Holy Supper

To all those who are admitted to the communion of the Holy Supper, both blessed symbols must without exception be given.

Notes. No distinction between clergy and laity is to be admitted, since it must be acknowledged that this sacrament, as a means of grace, was destined for the faithful as such, without distinction of ecclesiastical or secular estate; and that in the first administration, the Apostles themselves were regarded not as Apostles or ministers of the Church but as Christians and believers (see Musaeus, Disputation on Communion under Both Kinds, latter disputation, sections 15ff.).

Not only bread but also, in addition, the consecrated wine must be given; and this not for the ablution of the bread or host, but as the second part of the sacrament. The term "both kinds" is commonly used, not as though only the external appearance or bare accidents of the symbols, without the substance itself or in an alien substance, were present, but because the symbols of bread and wine themselves differ from each other in kind (see Musaeus, Disputation on Communion under Both Kinds, prior disputation, section 2).

This is required by the institution of Christ, which by its nature implies a precept concerning the specification of the act and does not leave the Church the liberty to administer this sacrament in one way or another (see Musaeus, Disputation on Communion under Both Kinds, prior disputation, sections 3ff.).

### 12 The end for the sake of which

The end for the sake of which, which is also the fruit or effect of this sacrament and which is the intermediate end, is as follows. (1). The remembrance and commemoration of the death of Christ, which is accomplished by faith. (2). The sealing of the promise of the remission of sins and the confirmation of our faith. (3). Our engrafting into Christ and spiritual nourishment unto life. (4). The mutual love of the communicants. The ultimate end is the eternal salvation of the communicants.

Notes. For the sake of obtaining this, this sacrament has been instituted to be celebrated.

Indeed, the sacraments are efficacious means in relation to the end; this also we will show here in detail.

So Christ himself says in Luke 22:19: "Do this εἰς τὴν ἐμὴν ἀνάμνησιν (in my remembrance)." Paul, repeating this in 1 Corinthians 11:24-25, adds in verse 26: "For as often as you eat this bread and drink of this cup, you proclaim the Lord's death until he comes." This sacrament, in which Christ himself really exhibits his own body and blood to us, assuredly possesses a mighty power to move the mind to remembrance of him.

This remembrance is to be exercised by faith, namely that we may consider and believe that Jesus Christ, the God-man, our King and Priest, himself offered his body to God the Father as a sacrifice for us on the altar of the cross, and poured out his blood for us, in order to obtain for us the grace of God and the remission of sins. Faith, insofar as it is directed toward the body of Christ delivered unto death for us, is called the spiritual eating of the body of Christ; and insofar as it is directed toward the blood of Christ poured out for us, it is called the spiritual drinking of the blood of Christ; concerning both of which, see John 6:35, 53ff.

Since we eat that very body of Christ which was delivered unto death for us by means of the blessed bread, and drink that very blood of Christ which was poured out for our sins by means of the wine, we are thereby made certain (and Christ wills that we be made certain by this means) that by grace through faith there are bestowed upon us all the benefits that Christ merited on the altar of the cross by the delivery of his body and the pouring out of his blood, namely the remission of sins, the grace of God, and eternal life (so Gerhard, combining the end and the fruit of the Holy Supper, in his Theological Commonplaces, vol. 5, Locus on the Holy Supper, section 212).

Although the promise of the Gospel, that everyone who believes in Christ should not perish but have eternal life, is universal, nevertheless, because anxious consciences, terrified by the sense of sin, divine wrath, and their own unworthiness, frequently doubt whether this promise pertains also to them as individuals, so that they might by true faith rest upon it before the judgment of God and by it raise themselves against the accusation of the law, of sin, and of Satan, therefore Christ distributes to them individually his body and blood, so that, as ὁ μάρτυρ ὁ πιστός (the faithful witness) (Revelation 1:5), he may confirm them against all the assaults of various temptations: namely, that the promises of the Gospel and the blessings offered therein truly pertain also to them, since in the Holy Supper they are fed and given drink with the body of Christ delivered unto death and his blood poured out for sins, which are the source and foundation of the Gospel promise. These are the words of Gerhard in the same passage.

Nothing is more closely and intimately conjoined with the Son of God than the assumed human nature, which he united to himself by a personal bond; conversely, nothing is more closely conjoined with us than what we eat and drink, since it is converted into the substance of our flesh. Christ, therefore, desiring to unite himself most closely with us and us with himself, instituted this sacrament in which, by means of the blessed bread, we eat his body, and by means of the blessed wine, we drink his blood (so Gerhard again, following the observation of Tauler, in section 213). Gerhard cautions, however, that he does not maintain that this spiritual food is altered and transmuted in us, but rather that it transmutes and alters us, so that we become partakers of the divine nature (2 Peter 1:4) and members of the mystical body of which Christ is the head (Ephesians 5:30). Thus it is evident that not only does the intention of Christ as the author look to this engrafting as its end, but also that our engrafting into Christ is efficiently conferred through the sacrament itself.

When the sacramental eating and drinking is conjoined with the spiritual eating and drinking, and the body and blood of Christ are received in both ways, then the contrite heart, burdened by sins, is refreshed, the fearful mind is raised up, sustained, and nourished unto eternal life, so that it neither hungers nor thirsts but has life in itself, has eternal life (John 6:33, 54ff.). Gerhard teaches in the same place that from this union with Christ it comes about that we, as branches from the vine, receive new strength for fighting against Satan, resisting the desires of the flesh, and growing in grace.

To this end, among other things, pertains the administration of the Holy Supper in the public assemblies of the Church, as the bond and sinew of ecclesiastical gatherings (1 Corinthians 11:20). And when Paul exhorts to Christian charity and concord, with the exclusion of schisms and divisions, among his other arguments he says: πάντες εἰς ἓν πνεῦμα ἐποτίσθημεν ("we were all made to drink of one Spirit") (1 Corinthians 12:13).

The further fruits of the Supper may be seen in Gerhard at the same place.

For all sacraments, as means and instruments of evangelical grace, tend ultimately toward this end.

We deny, however, that the celebration of this sacrament, when performed by others, benefits those who are absent or dead, whether by virtue of the work performed (ex opere operato) or by way of a sacrifice properly so called. For neither can the celebration of the Holy Supper be called a commemorative sacrifice, if it is distinguished from the Eucharistic genus of sacrifice (see the Detailed Explanation, book 18, question 90, pp. 695ff.; cf. Chemnitz, Examination of the Council of Trent, part 2, p. 250f., where he teaches in what sense the liturgical action can rightly be called a sacrifice according to Scripture; and p. 275ff., where he explains in what sense the ancients called the liturgy a sacrifice).

### 13 The Holy Supper may be defined as a sacred action instituted by Christ

The Holy Supper may be defined as a sacred action instituted by Christ, in which, together with the blessed bread, his body is given to Christian communicants to be eaten, and together with the blessed wine, his blood is given to be drunk; and both are received by them: the body is eaten with the bread, and the blood is drunk with the wine, in commemoration of the death of Christ, for the sealing of the remission of sins, and for the confirmation of faith unto eternal life.

Notes. In this definition, the genus common to all sacraments is denoted by "sacred action."

The principal efficient cause is indicated by "instituted by Christ" (cf. Section 2, p. 684).

The earthly matter is the bread and wine (cf. Section 6).

The consecration performed with the words of institution constitutes the form of the Holy Supper (cf. Section 9).

The heavenly matter is the body and blood of Christ (cf. Section 8).

The end for which, or the subject of the Holy Supper, is denoted by "Christian communicants" (cf. Section 10).

And the final end is indicated by the commemorative, sealing, and confirmatory purposes described (cf. Section 12).

## 28 On Predestination and Reprobation

### 1 Those same persons whom God in time leads to salvation

Those same persons whom God in time leads to salvation, and by the same method, He also decreed from eternity that He would lead to salvation in time by that same method. To this end pertain the terms "predestination" (in Greek, προορισμός (proorismos)) and "election" (in Greek, ἐκλογή (eklogē)), by which is denoted sometimes the decree concerning the entire work of leading human beings to salvation, and sometimes more specifically the decree concerning certain human beings, known under a certain description to the divine intellect, who are to be saved with certainty.

Notes. Here indeed is summed up all that we have thus far discussed concerning the causes and means of obtaining salvation.

For God does nothing in time that He did not decree from eternity He would do in time. And so the acts that God exercises in time stand as the execution of God's eternal decree; therefore an exact correspondence between the two must be acknowledged. And concerning the eternal decrees, which might otherwise remain hidden, we can most correctly be informed if we have come to know, according to revelation, what and by what method God does in time. Hence, having recognized the method and way by which God leads human beings to salvation in time, we shall all the more easily be taught concerning the eternal decree of saving human beings.

The term "predestination" is used in accordance with Ephesians 1:5 and Romans 8:29, 30. What is denoted here is the destination of a certain subject, and indeed, by virtue of the particle πρό (pro) or "pre," the destination of a subject before it itself exists, toward a certain end. And here indeed, following in the footsteps of Scripture, which nowhere employs the verb προορίζειν (proorizein), "to predestine," concerning human beings in a negative sense, we take predestination as predestination to life only (see Musaeus, Inaugural Disputation on the Eternal Decree of Predestination, ch. 1, sections 2 and 8).

The term "election" (ἐκλογή (eklogē) in Greek) is used in accordance with Ephesians 1:4 and Romans 8:33. Regard is had for the number of those who are saved and who have accordingly been destined by the eternal decree to salvation: these are few, chosen out of the great number of human beings and separated from the rest. Some call this election, with the added qualifier, "election to glory," distinguishing it from what they call election "to grace" or "to the means of salvation." But according to the received custom in our churches, the word "election," spoken absolutely, denotes that which pertains to eternal life itself. And so election as to the substance of the matter is the same as predestination, although on account of the diverse connotations, namely here referring to the priority of the ordination and there to the mixed mass of sinful human beings, some distinction of reason may be admitted (see Musaeus, Inaugural Disputation on the Eternal Decree of Predestination, ch. 1, section 11).

This is indeed the broader acceptation of the terms, by which the entire process of God, so to speak, in the matter of salvation, which is to take place in time, is conceived as having been decreed from eternity. In this sense, predestination or the eternal election of God is said to procure the salvation of the children of God and to dispose those things that pertain to it (see the Formula of Concord, art. 11, no. 4, p. 618). And certain definite steps, in which election or predestination consists, are enumerated (see the Solid Declaration of the Formula of Concord, art. 11, p. 802; also Musaeus, Disputation on the Eternal Election Decree, published 1668, section 266 ff., pp. 205, 206).

More strictly, the term "predestination" is taken either broadly or narrowly (see Gundisch, Notes on Hutter's Compendium, book 13, question 5, section 1, p. 797). Taken broadly, it comprehends the entire apparatus of the means of salvation; in this sense the Formula of Concord uses the same word in the Solid Declaration, article 11. Taken narrowly, this word signifies the ordination itself of the faithful to salvation, instituted according to God's purpose. In this sense, πρόθεσις (prothesis), or "purpose," and προορισμός (proorismos), or "predestination," ought to be considered here as distinct. The same narrower acceptation was also recognized by Balthasar Meisner (Anthropology, decade 2, disputation 4, question 3, no. 4, section 31), when he writes: "First God ordained the means for all; but because not all were going to accept them, therefore He did not elect all. Thus the decree of the means is prior in order to the decree of election, and therefore the merit of Christ apprehended by faith and considered from eternity is not a means of the decree but a cause." But more will be said about these matters in what follows (see also Musaeus, Inaugural Disputation on the Eternal Decree of Predestination, at the same location).

### 3 For recognizing the decree of predestination

For recognizing the decree of predestination, insofar as it concerns the entire matter of human salvation, the order of the divine acts must be carefully observed, as in a sign of reason, according to divine revelation, some follow upon others.

Notes. Here belong those steps of which predestination consists, according to the Formula of Concord at the cited location, and concerning which we shall presently see.
