For as to the matter itself, it must be confessed that within God there are no really distinct and mutually successive acts of intellect or will, on account of the supreme simplicity and immutability of God.

Nor is it permissible to invent either the acts themselves or their series and order according to our own ingenuity; rather, one must attend to what God Himself teaches us concerning the acts of His intellect and will, and how, according to the Scriptures, this act presupposes that one and not that one this one. Especially we must take care lest we attribute some act to God in such a way that we exclude or pervert another act which ought no less, indeed even more so, to be acknowledged as prior.

### 4 And so, since God out of His supreme goodness

And so, since God out of His supreme goodness, embraces all human beings, even though sinners, with such love that for the sake of procuring their salvation He gave His Son as Redeemer for all, it must also be acknowledged that when God from all eternity foresaw that human beings would be corrupted by sin, He nevertheless decreed, for the sake of procuring their salvation, to give the Son who would pay the price of redemption for all.

Notes. In which He is good not only in Himself but also to others, to His creatures, and intends to lead them to their ends for which they were created For thus Paul testifies (1 Timothy 2:4) that God wills all human beings (for whom the faithful ought to pray, all and every one, who exist, not in the state of integrity but after the fall, and therefore sinners, with no one excluded, not even tyrants under whom they lived, and Nero himself, who was never converted) to be saved (not merely to signify by an external word, as if He willed it, but truly and earnestly to will) and to attain true and eternal salvation. Compare our disputation On the Universality of Divine Grace, delivered on this passage in the year 1675. However, we do not call that will which terminates upon the salvation of all a "decree," properly speaking; but the word "will" has a wider extension. And here also pertains the distinction between the antecedent and consequent will, concerning which see the special disputation of Musaeus, and what we cited from it in part 1, chapter 1, sections 19 and 20, pp. 188 ff.

To this pertains what Christ said (John 3:16): "God so loved the world" (that is, with such great, earnest, and efficacious love God loved the world, the entire multitude of the inhabitants of the earth, or the universal human race), which comprehends believers and non-believers, as afterward in verse 18 it is divided into the former and the latter; but here it is considered as the antitype of the promiscuous multitude of Israelites who formerly, struck by the bites of fiery serpents on account of their rebellion against God, were near death (according to verses 14 and 15), "that He gave His only-begotten Son" (namely, He gave Him to the world itself, or to the human race otherwise destined to perish, as the antitype of the bronze serpent, to be raised up on the cross, according to verse 15, so that it would not be necessary for sinful human beings to perish, but) "that the world might be saved through Him," that is, so that all human beings contained in the world might have one through whom, by the earnest intention of God, who loves them most dearly, they could be saved, and would be saved, if they did not reject Him; just as the bronze serpent was raised up for the good of all the wounded, so that all might have something from which they could be healed (according to verses 14, 15, and 17).

Compare Romans 8:2, 3, where it is said that God saw that human beings could not be saved through the law, since through carnal generation and the contracted stain of original sin they had been made unfit for fulfilling the law; and therefore God, wishing to come to the aid of human weakness and to supply that deficiency, sent His own Son, who in the place of wretched human beings would fulfill the law and in the assumed flesh satisfy the law. See also what we said at chapter 1, section 3, paragraph 10, pp. 469, 470; and Musaeus, Disputation on the Insufficiency of the Light of Nature for Salvation against Lord Herbert, section 87 ff., pp. 54 ff.

For God knew from eternity all things that would come to pass in time, even contingently, and He knew them immediately in themselves (see part 1, chapter 1, section 14, note b, p. 184). And it is certain that the will of God concerning the sending of a Redeemer for the sins of human beings presupposes the knowledge of those human sins themselves.

Nor did the act of will that terminates upon the sending of the Redeemer begin in time in God; rather, it must be confessed that God, who sent the Mediator in time, sent Him according to an eternal decree. And so, when it is established that He was sent for the good of all sinful human beings, it must be confessed that it was formerly decreed that He should be sent not for the good of a few pre-elected out of a mere good pleasure, but for the good of all.

### 5 Furthermore, just as God in time declares that only those shall obtain…

Furthermore, just as God in time declares that only those shall obtain salvation through the merit of Christ who believe in Christ, but so that all might be able to believe in Christ, God Himself so promulgated the doctrine of faith that it could reach the ears and minds of all; so it must be acknowledged that God willed from eternity that all human beings should believe, and decreed that the Mediator, whom He had determined to send, should, through the promulgation of the doctrine concerning Him, be offered to all for their embrace.

Notes. Here pertains what we said in part 3, chapter 2, on faith in Christ, section 1, pp. 476, 477. And in the cited passage of John 3:16, the love of God is referred to all human beings, yet so that actual deliverance from destruction and the attainment of eternal life is restricted to believers; as in the following verse 18, once the division of human beings into believers and non-believers has been made, it is said of the former that they are not condemned, and of the latter that by virtue of their very unbelief they are liable to damnation.

This accords with the saying: "How shall they believe in Him of whom they have not heard?" (Romans 10:14); and "Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of God" (Romans 10:17).

See also above, chapter 6, section 13, note b, p. 608; and Musaeus, Disputation against Lord Herbert, section 90 ff., pp. 55 ff.; and what we discussed in the German treatise Fundamental Demonstration against the Quakers, sections 25 and 49, pp. 27 and 105. From this it is also established that for a universal calling it is not necessary that the doctrine of the Gospel be immediately announced to each and every person in their presence by special preachers sent by God; rather, it suffices that the doctrine be so promulgated, or have been so promulgated, that all who are obligated to inquire after the true and saving religion, and who through the use of reason can recognize that there exists somewhere a certain and saving religion divinely revealed, are able to come to the knowledge of it, and are not barred from it by God, who out of absolute good pleasure refuses to grant them access to that doctrine and denies them every way by which they might attain to its knowledge.

For although it is rightly said that God willed all to be saved if they believe, it must nevertheless also be confessed that God willed that all should believe, or that all should come to the knowledge of the truth (that is, of the true, divinely revealed doctrine), which He testifies He wills (1 Timothy 2:4). Compare Musaeus, Disputation on the Eternal Election Decree, section 279, p. 207.

Indeed, we do not call that will by which God wills that all should believe (nor that by which God wills that all should be saved, concerning which see the note at section 4) a "decree." However, that act of the divine will by which God determined to promulgate the doctrine of the Mediator between God and human beings in such a way that it could come to the knowledge of all and obtain faith is rightly called a decree.

### 6 And just as God in time conjoins divine power with His word

And just as God in time conjoins divine power with His word, by which the supernatural assent of faith to be rendered to the word itself, and thus faith in Christ, can be excited and is excited whenever a person without malicious resistance admits the word itself; so it is certain that God decreed from eternity to concur powerfully and graciously with the word to be promulgated in time for the production of the effect of faith, in such a way that no one would lack faith unless he had despised the means of conferring faith.

Notes. See Prolegomena, chapter 2, section 39, p. 121 ff.; and part 3, chapter 3, section 29, p. 529 ff.; See also Prolegomena, chapter 2, section 39, note l, p. 128; and part 3, chapter 3, sections 34 and 35, p. 540 ff. And here pertains what is said in 1 Timothy 2:4, that God wills all to come to the knowledge of the truth, through which they may be saved, and therefore to saving faith. From this it absolutely follows that God, as far as it is in Him, is prepared and ready to confer the powers of arriving at that saving knowledge or powers of believing, so that no one is excluded by God as if out of a mere or absolute good pleasure; but if any do not attain to it, the cause and blame must lie with themselves. And so Christ also expressly teaches (Matthew 23:37) that it is not absurd, but happens very frequently, although wrongly, that those whom He Himself earnestly wills to gather to Himself, or, as far as it is in Him, to contribute to their conversion and faith by which they might be joined with their Mediator and obtain grace and salvation, the human beings themselves nevertheless refuse to be converted, and they impede and exclude the faith that could otherwise have been obtained.

For if God in time willingly gives faith through the word to all who do not resist, and gives it according to an eternal decree of His will, then it must be confessed that this very eternal decree of God terminates upon faith to be conferred in time through the word upon all who do not resist.

### 7 Moreover, just as God in time justifies all who believe in Christ

Moreover, just as God in time justifies all who believe in Christ, and, unless they themselves cast off faith and the Holy Spirit by sins against conscience, He increasingly renews or sanctifies them and preserves and confirms their faith even to the end of life; so it must be acknowledged that God decreed from eternity to confer the grace of justification and renewal upon all who would believe in Christ in time, and to further sanctify those making right use of the means, and to preserve and confirm their faith even to the end of their life.

Notes. See part 3, chapter 4, section 1, p. 152; and section 7, pp. 561, 562.

That they can indeed cast off faith is clear from part 3, chapter 2, section 11, pp. 492, 493.

See also part 3, chapter 5, p. 563 ff., and chapter 6, section 16, pp. 614, 615.

For when God in time justifies all believers, sanctifies them, and in all who continue to use the means of grace preserves and confirms faith, and does so willingly and according to His eternal decree, it must be confessed that God's eternal decree terminates upon the justification of all believers, upon the renewal of all the justified who will continue to make right use of the means of grace and are foreseen as such, and upon the preservation and final confirmation of the faith of all of them.

### 8 Finally, just as God in time actually saves all who finally believe in Christ

Finally, just as God in time actually saves all who finally believe in Christ, it must also be acknowledged that there exists an eternal decree of God concerning all who will finally believe in time to be certainly saved.

Notes. Or, as others express it, glorifies them, from Romans 8:30 For God in time willingly confers blessedness upon those who finally believe, and does so by virtue of an eternal decree (according to Matthew 25:34), and therefore His eternal decree concerning the saving of certain human beings terminated upon them as those who would finally believe.

### 9 And because God foresaw from eternity

And because God foresaw from eternity, which human beings would finally believe, and determined to save these as such, the eternal decree of bestowing eternal salvation upon those who would finally believe, in view of the merit of Christ and of foreseen faith in Christ, when considered precisely, is called by the name of predestination or election in the specific sense.

Note. By virtue of His omniscience by which He knows all things, even contingently future, immediately in themselves.

### 10 Conversely, just as God in time punishes with eternal damnation those human…

Conversely, just as God in time punishes with eternal damnation those human beings who either never believed or who cast off their faith again and end their lives without faith, so it must be confessed that God decreed from eternity to damn eternally those who will have lacked final faith.

Note. This follows from the reasoning of opposites, in the same way as we have stated the matter stands concerning the decree of God in the business of procuring salvation.

### 11 And just as God foresaw from eternity which human beings would depart in time…

And just as God foresaw from eternity which human beings would depart in time without faith in Christ, so He decreed to damn eternally those same persons, as such and distinctly known. And this decree is called reprobation.

Note. That is, the rejection and repudiation of human beings. In Greek one might say ἀποδοκιμασία (apodokimasia), although this word does not occur in Sacred Scripture in opposition to predestination. It suffices, however, that the sense is found. And it is more correctly called reprobation than predestination to death.

### 12 To the causes virtually causing election in the stricter sense pertains

To the causes virtually causing election in the stricter sense pertains, first, the efficient cause, which is the triune God.

Notes. For election in the stricter sense is what must now be considered more distinctly. And although certain causes can also be assigned to election taken in the broader sense, it is nevertheless certain that in the schools, when the causes of election are treated, the stricter signification of the term is attended to, as will be clear from what follows.

For acts of the divine will, such as election, do not really differ from the divine essence; and so, just as the divine essence itself, they are not really produced, nor do they acknowledge causes of themselves in the strict sense, that is, formally causing, which would flow being into another (see Musaeus, On the Eternal Predestination Decree, ch. 1, section 22; and Disputation on the Eternal Election Decree, ch. 1, sections 4 ff.). In this way, our theologians have long since taught against Conrad Vorstius, for example, Johann Gerhard (Theological Exegesis, book 2, On the Attributes of God, section 277): "God does not produce in Himself new actions of intellect and will, as human beings and angels do, which would be accidents distinct from His essence, but the acts of intellect and will are the very essence of God" (see also Christoph Scheibler, Metaphysics, book 3, ch. 3, section 264 ff.). The distinction between a formally causing cause and a virtually causing cause in this matter was also used by Scherzer (System, book 18, pp. 511, 512).

To God, as agent, election or predestination is attributed, so that you may call Him the one who predestines or elects.

God is customarily called the cause of the acts of His will.

Indeed, in Ephesians 1:5, it is ascribed to the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ that He predestined or elected us; but the remaining persons are not excluded, whose essence, as it is one, so the acts of will equally belong to all. However, at the cited passage, there is a special regard of the one who elects to the one in whom He elected, as we shall presently state.

### 13 The internal impulsive cause is the goodness or mercy and gratuitous favor of God

The internal impulsive cause is the goodness or mercy and gratuitous favor of God.

Notes. This is not a formally causing but a virtually causing cause, or the reason a priori which, according to our manner of knowing, in the genus of impulsive cause, relates to that act of the divine will in the manner of a cause, so that if that act were caused or really produced, this would truly and in reality, in the genus of impulsive cause, be the cause of that act (see Musaeus and Scherzer at the cited locations).

For Paul conjoins the πρόθεσις (prothesis), "purpose," and χάρις (charis), "grace," of God, in opposition to our works, and says that this was given to us before eternal times (2 Timothy 1:9). And when he writes in Ephesians 1:5 and 9 that God predestined us so that the glory of His grace might be praised, he manifestly indicates that predestination proceeded from or took its origin from that grace of God as from an impulsive cause or reason. And if the act by which believers are saved in time acknowledges the grace of God as its impulsive cause, it must be confessed that the decree of saving believers also rests upon the same reason or impulsive cause. Compare what we said at section 1, note b, and what we shall say at greater length in the following section.

This is the antecedent will, as they call it, the fountain and origin of our salvation (see Musaeus, Inaugural Disputation on the Eternal Predestination Decree, ch. 3, sections 31 ff.).

### 14 The external impulsive cause

The external impulsive cause, and indeed the principal one, is the merit of Christ.

Notes. This is a virtually causing cause, as we indicated in the notes to sections 12 and 13.

It is the cause which, by virtue of its own dignity, perfection, and value, relates to the decree of predestination as an impulsive reason, in view of which God decreed eternal life for us from eternity (see Musaeus, Disputation on the Eternal Election Decree, published 1668, ch. 2, section 37, pp. 23, 24). It is otherwise called meritorious, because under the aspect of merit it moves the will of God to decree salvation for us; by this very fact, however, it must be acknowledged as a cause or impulsive reason, namely importing a twofold relation: one indeed to the thing merited, and another to the will of the efficient cause or the one decreeing (see Musaeus, Disputation on the Eternal Election Decree, ch. 5, sections 109, 110, pp. 76 ff.).

For the merit of Christ, just as it is the cause of every spiritual blessing that is divinely bestowed upon us, so also it is taught to be the impulsive cause of our predestination or election to eternal life (Ephesians 1:3, 4), where it is also expressly said that God elected us ἐν Χριστῷ (en Christō), "in Christ"; and ἐν (en) is used for διά (dia), as frequently elsewhere, so that God is said to elect us on account of Christ, or in view of Christ, as the impulsive cause. That this is the only explanation conformable to the context, while all others that are circulated are either forced or, rightly understood, ultimately coincide with this one, Musaeus demonstrates at length (Inaugural Disputation, ch. 5, sections 74 ff.). And here especially pertains the argument drawn from the execution, in the following manner: "That which is the impulsive cause why God in time confers salvation upon us is also the cause why He elected us to salvation. But the merit of Christ is the impulsive cause why God in time confers salvation upon us. Therefore the merit of Christ is also the cause why God elected us." The major proposition can be proved both a posteriori, that is, because we commonly so judge concerning things that are done from a preceding decree of the will, and we do not doubt the impulsive cause of the decree when we are certain of the impulsive cause of the execution, since we acknowledge the impulsive causes to be the same on both sides; and also a priori, that is, from the nature and formal reason of the impulsive cause, through which it imports a relation to the will of the efficient cause, by alluring or moving it (formally or virtually) to the act of willing or decreeing to do that which it is said to do at its impulse, so that a contradiction must be incurred if anyone, admitting the impulsive cause of the execution, denies the same to be the cause of the decree, when the decree corresponds exactly to the execution and the execution to the decree, and no change intervenes on the part of the will of the one who decrees and executes (see Musaeus, Inaugural Disputation on the Eternal Predestination Decree, ch. 4, sections 51 ff.; and Disputation on the Eternal Election Decree, published 1668, ch. 3, sections 82 ff., pp. 59 ff.; and ch. 7, sections 166 ff., pp. 123 ff.). The minor proposition of the argument is confirmed by those passages of Scripture that teach that we are saved on account of Christ, and accordingly they teach that just as the merit of Christ is the meritorious cause of salvation actually conferred, so the same has the character of an impulsive cause with respect to the divine will (see also Musaeus, Disputation on Election, published 1668, ch. 5, sections 102 ff.).

Nor does the acceptance of another's merit conflict with the fact that election is ascribed to the gratuitous favor of God (see 2 Timothy 1:9), especially if we remember how God Himself gave us a Mediator who would perform on our behalf what we owed (Romans 8:3; John 3:16). And the merit of Christ, although rendered in time, could nevertheless have the character of an impulsive cause in relation to the eternal decree of God; for it suffices that it was objectively present, or foreseen by God as something to be rendered in its own time (see Musaeus, Disputation on the Eternal Election Decree, ch. 7, sections 177, 178, pp. 132, 133).

### 15 The external impulsive cause

The external impulsive cause, less principal, of the decree of election is faith in Christ, and indeed final faith.

Notes. This is a virtually causing cause, or reason a priori, as we said the term should be taken in the preceding sections as well.

By "less principal" is meant that which, according to our manner of conceiving, is prior to the decree of election and relates to it as that in view of which we were elected, so that when one asks why these particular persons who are saved, and precisely not others, were elected from eternity to life, by adducing or expressing that factor (namely, here, faith, as we shall see) one answers appropriately. And yet this factor does not possess any proper merit, goodness, dignity, or perfection of its own by which the will of the agent or the one electing would be moved to act or to elect; rather, it is elevated by the merit, goodness, or perfection of another as the principal impulsive cause, or by virtue of another's merit, goodness, or dignity, it functions as the reason in view of which the will of God determines and from eternity determined itself to decree salvation for us (see Musaeus, Disputation on Election, published 1668, ch. 2, sections 18 ff., pp. 24, 25; and section 63, p. 45).

Here the reference is to the decree or act of election itself, which is clear from the formal reason of the impulsive cause (see the note at section 14, p. 720). The impulsive cause or reason is understood here not in relation to the decree concerning the entire process or business of procuring salvation, or concerning predestination taken more broadly, but more strictly, as we have already noted at section 12, p. 717.

For the merit of Christ, considered absolutely in itself without respect to the human beings who apply it to themselves by faith, is universal and extends even to the reprobate; but it moves God to decree salvation for certain human beings insofar as it is apprehended by them through faith. And so faith also must here be considered not in itself, as it is a supernatural habit or act (in which respect, even though it possesses some proper dignity, it does not in the least move God by that dignity to decree salvation for us), but rather from the standpoint of the merit of Christ which it apprehends and includes by way of object (see Musaeus, Disputation on Election, ch. 2, sections 40 to 44).

Moreover, among our theologians, some have called faith in Christ the instrumental cause of the decree of election, others the condition of it, some the condition on the part of the object to be elected, and others a part of the predestinatory order; but the meaning is the same among all of them and with those who call it the less principal impulsive cause. For all acknowledge that faith is not a bare condition exercising no causality; rather, just as it relates to the act of saving, so it relates to the act of decreeing salvation by way of a cause (at least virtually causing) as that in view of which we were elected. And yet faith could not, by its own dignity, have moved God to elect us so as to be a principal cause. Hence, when faith is elsewhere said to function in the manner of a hand or instrument by which the grace of the electing God and the merit of Christ are apprehended as the cause of salvation, and for this reason is customarily called an instrument here as well, it must nevertheless be indicated how faith relates to the decree of election itself. In this regard, our theologians do not say that it functions by way of an instrument by which the principal efficient cause, God the elector, uses it to produce the act of election by a real influx. Those who have called it a moral instrumental cause can mean nothing other than a less principal impulsive cause.

Furthermore, when faith is called a part of the predestinatory order, it must be added what relation it has (within the things that the entire order of acts of predestination more broadly understood contains) to the very act of decreeing salvation for certain human beings, namely for those who will finally believe. And so there remains in the end that manner of speaking in which faith is called the impulsive cause or reason, not however the principal one in the eminent sense, but, with an addition to avoid ambiguity, the less principal one, in relation to the very act of election. And those who formerly were unwilling to call faith the impulsive cause of election had in view the principal impulsive cause, not thinking of a less principal impulsive cause (see throughout Musaeus, Disputation on Election, sections 50 ff., pp. 32 ff., whom Scherzer entirely follows in System, book 18, p. 488 ff., especially p. 510, where he proposes and presses the argument from the execution of the decree of election in exactly the same manner, and expressly teaches that the merit of Christ is the principal and meritorious external impulsive cause of the decree of election, while faith is the less principal and organic external impulsive cause; see also pp. 512, 513, 514).

Indeed, even Balthasar Meisner (Anthropology, decade 2, disputation 4, member 3, section 36), after he had said, "When faith is called the cause of election, do not understand it as the principal, impelling, or meritorious cause, but only as the instrumental, and indeed not of the whole decree but rather of a part, namely the merit of Christ, which faith apprehends; for since it is the cause of a part of the decree, by popular manner of speaking it is called the cause of the decree itself"; and after he had added, "It is more fitting, however, to call faith either the condition of election, lest it be imagined to be absolute, or a part of the predestinatory order, which God no less regarded from eternity than the merit of Christ"; he notably concludes: "Most fitting of all, it seems, is that faith not be considered separately as a peculiar cause of election distinct from the merit of Christ, but conjointly together with the apprehended merit itself, so that both conjoined together constitute one impelling cause of election. For neither merit without application nor faith by itself moved God to elect; but both conjoined in divine foreknowledge, that is, merit apprehended by faith or faith apprehending merit."

In this way, faith's relation to election is such as an impulsive cause or reason has to that of which it is said to be the cause; not, however, insofar as it is considered separately or absolutely in itself, but insofar as it is considered from the standpoint of the merit of Christ that it apprehends, so that not as two coordinate or partial causes (if it is permissible to speak thus here), but after the manner of a principal and instrumental cause (which, just as in the genus of efficient cause they produce an effect by one influx, though otherwise distinguished from each other, so in the genus of impulsive cause they move, as it were by one impulse, the will of the agent to will to act or to decree), the merit of Christ and faith relate to the decree of election. This is the very position explained thus far.

It is proved, moreover, that faith is the less principal impulsive cause of the decree of election by the argument drawn from the execution, in this manner: "That in view of which, as a less principal impulsive cause or reason, God saves us in time, is also that in view of which, as a less principal impulsive cause or reason, He decreed from eternity to confer salvation upon us in time. But faith in Christ is that in view of which, as a less principal impulsive cause or reason, God saves us in time. Therefore faith in Christ is that in view of which, as an impulsive cause or reason, God decreed from eternity to confer salvation upon us in time." The major rests upon the same proof by which we showed the argument for the principal impulsive cause of election to rest (see the note at section 14). For with regard to the correspondence of the decree and the execution, not only in the case of the principal impulsive cause but also of the less principal cause or reason, the reasoning must be the same on both sides.

The minor proposition is proved from those passages of Scripture in which we are said to be saved by faith, from faith, through faith (Romans 3:28; Ephesians 2:8), where a certain causality of faith in relation to our salvation is ascribed, and that not of a principal cause, whether efficient or impulsive, but of a less principal one, and yet not physically efficient but impulsive; that is, God, who saves, is moved to will to save through faith, not indeed considered by reason of its own dignity (for we are not said to be saved "on account of" faith), but insofar as it apprehends the merit of Christ and includes it by way of object, so that in view of it God wills to save and does save (see Musaeus and Scherzer at the cited locations).

Moreover, faith has the character of an impulsive cause in relation to the eternal decree of election because it was foreseen in God's foreknowledge from eternity. Here pertains that passage in Romans 8:29: οὓς προέγνω, καὶ προώρισε (hous proegnō, kai proōrise), "those whom He foreknew" (as those who would be in Christ Jesus through faith, according to verse 1) "He also predestined." Hence it is otherwise said that the foresight of the merit of Christ to be apprehended by faith, or the foresight of faith in Christ, is the reason or impulsive cause of the decree of election (see Musaeus, Inaugural Disputation on the Eternal Predestination Decree, ch. 3, section 50).

And "final faith" is specified because we are not saved except through final faith (see above, chapter 2, last section, pp. 493, 494).

### 16 The object of predestination is sinful human beings

The object of predestination is sinful human beings, but those finally believing, and all and only those.

Notes. Some call it the subject of election, and it coincides with section 6.

For the predestination of angels, since it was not made in Christ, does not pertain to the present discussion (see part 1, chapter 3, section 32, pp. 261, 262).

All finally believing human beings are included because the impulsive cause or reason of election extends to all of them.

And only they are included because the merit of Christ does not move God to save us or to decree salvation for us except insofar as it is apprehended or is to be apprehended by final faith; therefore, the decree of predestination does not terminate upon human beings lacking final faith.

### 17 The end of election is salvation itself

The end of election is salvation itself, to be conferred upon the elect in time; but the ultimate end is the glory of the divine goodness.

Notes. The end is that for the sake of which the decree of election was made, from eternity, according to our manner of understanding.

See Matthew 25:34, where the faithful are commanded to occupy the kingdom prepared or destined for them by divine decree from the foundation of the world, and therefore destined so that they might one day obtain it.

See also Ephesians 1:5, 6, where we are said to have been elected by God for this purpose, or for the sake of this end, that the glory of His grace might be praised.

### 18 The decree of election

The decree of election, according to what has been said thus far, is established to be, first, particular, and second, immutable.

Notes. As to the first point: not all human beings are predestined or elected to salvation, as is manifest from section 16 and the last note there. Moreover, the very word "election," by which the few chosen or separated from the many are denoted, indicates that particularity.

As to the second point, the decree is irrevocable, yet not with an absolute but only a hypothetical immutability. For those who were elected in view of foreseen final faith, just as they could have not finally believed, so they could have not been saved but damned, and accordingly could have not been elected but reprobated. But when, as those who would finally believe, they were foreseen by God and so elected, just as they cannot be both finally believing and not finally believing, so, since they are elected, by hypothetical necessity they cannot be not- elected. And on account of the immutability of the divine will, when the object does not change, and God foresaw that it would not change, it comes about that the elect are necessarily saved, although absolutely speaking they could fall from salvation. Hence, although the elect can fall from the grace of God, and sometimes do fall, yet none of the elect ever falls from it finally.

### 19 Predestination or election in the broader sense can be defined as the eternal…

Predestination or election in the broader sense can be defined as the eternal decree of God by which God, out of His immense mercy, determined to send a Mediator to all human beings whom He foresaw would fall into sin, and to offer Him for their embrace through universal preaching; also to confer faith through the word and sacraments upon all who would not resist; to justify all believers, and to renew those making further use of the means of grace, and to preserve and confirm faith in them even to the end of life, and finally to save those who finally believe, to the glory of His goodness.

Predestination or election in the stricter sense can be defined as the eternal decree of God by which God, out of His immense mercy, determined to bestow eternal salvation upon all and only those human beings whom He foresaw would finally believe in Christ, on account of the merit of Christ itself, to be apprehended by final faith and so foreseen, for the sake of their salvation and His own glory.

Notes. The broader definition concerns the entire business or process of our salvation, according to section 2, p. 705. From sections 3 through 9. In it the efficient cause, God; the internal impulsive cause, the mercy of God; and the end, namely the salvation of human beings and the glory of God, can be discerned. The remaining elements concern the acts themselves to which the decree terminates.

For the stricter definition, see section 1, pp. 704, 706, and section 12, p. 716. The efficient cause is according to section 12; the internal impulsive cause according to section 13, p. 718; the object of election according to section 16, p. 727; the principal external impulsive cause according to section 14, p. 719; the less principal external impulsive cause according to section 15, p. 721; and the end is indicated according to section 17, p. 728.

### 20 Reprobation, is likewise a decree of God

Reprobation, is likewise a decree of God, and accordingly acknowledges the triune God as its efficient cause.

Notes. Which is opposed to election or predestination in the stricter sense, according to section 11.

This decree indeed presupposes the universality of divine grace, the merit of Christ, and the earnest calling to embrace the Mediator; but it also presupposes, on the part of human beings, the divinely foreseen contempt of divine grace, of the merit of Christ, and of the means of grace. For otherwise, given the universal grace of God, the merit of Christ, and the universal calling, no one would have been condemned if no one had despised the means of grace.

The efficient cause is a virtually causing one, as we said of the decree of predestination.

God is the one who decrees or reprobates.

It is an act of the divine will, and therefore common to the three persons.

### 21 The internal impulsive cause is the vindicative justice of God

The internal impulsive cause is the vindicative justice of God.

Notes. This is the reason a priori by which a proper answer is given to the question of why God willed not to save but to damn certain human beings.

This is the wrath of God against sins (Romans 2:5, 8; 9:22, 23). For just as in the cited passage of Romans 2, the damnation of the impenitent is referred to the wrath of God, namely because His wrath against sinners, or His justice by which He is inclined to avenge the violation of His law, moves Him to will to punish them; so, since it is certain that God formerly decreed the things that He does in time, it must similarly be acknowledged that when God decreed to damn certain human beings, the reason for so decreeing was that justice of God, on account of the necessary correspondence of the decree and the execution. And so also, when in Romans 9 the reprobate are called vessels of wrath, that is, objects of divine wrath from which their destruction and damnation proceeds, the same is rightly referred also to reprobation, which is founded upon that wrath or vindicative justice.

### 22 The external impulsive cause consists in the sins of human beings

The external impulsive cause consists in the sins of human beings, insofar as they are conjoined with final unbelief.

Notes. God, in ordaining just punishment, does not act as supreme Lord but according to His ordained power and as Judge (compare Musaeus, Dissertation on the Eternity of the Decree of Election, ch. 8, section 186).

Nor is it necessary here to distinguish between a principal and a less principal cause, since the sins themselves, by the very fact that they violate the law of God, are worthy not only of temporal but also of eternal punishment (see Part 2, ch. 1, section 13).

For just as in the act of damnation, understood as the execution of the decree of reprobation, regard is had to not believing in the only-begotten Son of God as that on account of which, as a meritorious cause (or demeritorious, as some express it), God who damns wills to condemn (John 3:18, 36), so also in the decree itself, final unbelief functions as an impulsive cause, moving the will of God to reprobate, that is, to decree damnation. Similarly, just as in Romans 11:20 certain spiritual branches are said to have been broken off in time, or human beings who had been for a while in a state of grace are said to have been cast off through unbelief, meaning that their unbelief moved God to cast them off, so also it must be acknowledged that those who were once rejected or reprobated by the eternal decree of God were so decreed because God, according to our mode of understanding, was moved to issue that decree in view of their unbelief as the impulsive reason.

For otherwise, if faith in Christ intervenes, sins can be abolished with respect to guilt, so that human beings are not condemned on account of them. Hence, unless faith is absent, they will not be reprobate.

And although these things come to pass contingently in time, they are nevertheless represented to the divine will through the eternal foreknowledge of God, not by the force of a predetermining decree, but as determinately, though contingently, future, and therefore determinately knowable immediately in themselves.

### 23 The object of reprobation consists of impious human beings who are finally unbelieving

The object of reprobation consists of impious human beings who are finally unbelieving.

Notes. That is, the subject which is reprobated.

Namely, such persons in whom that which constitutes the cause or impulsive reason of reprobation has a place. But toward human beings considered merely as human beings, without sins and final unbelief being yet foreseen according to our mode of understanding, the will of God, which is otherwise most benign, does not terminate as toward those to be condemned.

### 24 The end of reprobation is the vindication of sins and the glory of God's…

The end of reprobation is the vindication of sins and the glory of God's vindicatory justice.

Notes. For human beings are destined to punishment by the decree so that punishment may actually be inflicted upon them in time.

For just as it is said in Romans 9:22 that God, willing to display His wrath or vindicatory justice and to make known His power, bore with much patience the vessels of wrath fitted (not indeed by an absolute decree of God, for otherwise there would be no need for much patience to tolerate that which God Himself had made such by absolute good pleasure, but fitted by themselves or by their own fault) for destruction, so that nevertheless, as vessels of wrath, they might at last be cast off and the justice of God might be made manifest, whose executive act had been delayed for some time, so also, because God foresaw how those human beings would fit themselves for destruction, He decreed to reject them, and this tended toward the glorious display of divine justice as its end.

### 25 The decree of reprobation is not only particular but also immutable

The decree of reprobation is not only particular but also immutable.

Notes. For since some human beings are elect, and only the finally unbelieving are reprobate, the particularity of the decree is readily evident.

It is immutable in the same way in which we said the decree of predestination is immutable: not by absolute but by hypothetical necessity.

### 26 Reprobation may be defined as the eternal decree of God

Reprobation may be defined as the eternal decree of God, by which God, out of His vindicatory justice, decreed to condemn sinful human beings who are finally unbelieving, on account of their sins conjoined with final unbelief, for the punishment of their sins and the glory of His divine justice.

Notes. The genus common to predestination and reprobation is that it is a decree.

God is the efficient cause, virtually causing (see section 20).

Vindicatory justice is the internal impulsive cause or reason (see section 21).

The object of reprobation is indicated as sinful human beings who are finally unbelieving (see section 23).

The sins conjoined with final unbelief constitute the external impulsive cause (according to section 22).

The end of reprobation is denoted as the punishment of sins and the glory of divine justice (see section 25).

## 29 On the Church

### 1 All those human beings whom God

All those human beings whom God, according to His eternal decree, has endowed with faith and His grace, taken collectively, are called the Church. And indeed, considered with respect to the present life, they are called the Church Militant; but with respect to the other or future life, the Church Triumphant, although sometimes the name "Church" embraces both assemblies, while at other times, used absolutely, it signifies precisely the Church Militant.

Notes. Not all human beings, but some from the indiscriminate multitude, so that the words eklegein (to choose out), whence eklektoi (the elect), and ekkalein (to call out), whence ekklēsia (the Church), have a certain kinship.

For those whom God calls out of the indiscriminate multitude in time, so that they might constitute one peculiar assembly, He decreed to call out from eternity. And those whom He saves or glorifies in time, He decreed to save or glorify from eternity. From this the reason for the connection of this doctrine with the preceding is evident.

Indeed ekklēsia is a collective noun and properly denotes an assembly of a few, convoked from a larger number by public authority; but by extension it denotes any assembly, even a disorderly and confused one (see Acts 19:37, 39, 40; compare Musaeus, Treatise on the Church, Part 1, Disputation 1, section 2).

This is said with regard to the spiritual warfare in which, under the leadership and banner of Christ, believers are stationed against Satan, the world, and carnal concupiscence, and must fight in this life (see Ephesians 6:10 and following; 1 Peter 5:8, 9; 1 John 5:4; Romans 7:14 and following; Galatians 5:17 and following).

Namely, having completed their warfare and overcome their enemies, they live and rejoice with Christ in the heavens (see Revelation 2:10, 26, 27; 4:4; 7:9; 21:10).

To this may be referred the passage in Hebrews 12:22, 23, and Ephesians 1:22; 5:23 and following.

See also Acts 20:28; Romans 16:4; 1 Corinthians 12:28; 14:4, 5; 16:19; 2 Corinthians 8:11.

### 2 The Church Militant itself is also taken in two ways

The Church Militant itself is also taken in two ways. In one way, properly and precisely, for the congregation of the truly believing and holy, who are engrafted into Christ the Head through faith and, as living members, constitute one mystical body with Him. In the other way, improperly and by synecdoche, for the entire aggregate assembly composed of the truly believing and holy together with admixed hypocrites and wicked persons.

Notes. Concerning which we must now proceed further, setting aside the other significations.

As is also the customary manner of speaking in the Scriptures, that what is proper to the part is attributed to the whole, or conversely.

Indeed it might seem immaterial whether the name "Church" is said to properly denote the assembly of the truly believing, and by synecdoche of the part for the whole to denote the mixed assembly aggregated from holy and unholy persons, or conversely, whether you call the latter signification proper and the former synecdochical, by synecdoche of the whole for the part, since the foundations for both significations are contained in the Scriptures. Nevertheless it matters greatly to know to which assembly the privileges and promises that Holy Scripture attributes to the Church properly belong: to that which, precisely insofar as it consists of the truly believing and holy, is the Church, or to the mixed and visible assembly? This is demonstrated by the contentions of our theologians with the Papists (compare Musaeus, Disputations on the Church, first edition of 1657, section 46).

By faith is understood such faith as we described in Part 3, chapter 2, for which is required: (1). On the part of the formal object, that it rest precisely upon divine revelation as the proper reason for assent, and thus be supernatural in its substance. (2). On the part of the material object, that besides other things divinely revealed, it specifically tend toward Christ as the Mediator and the cause of obtaining grace and the remission of sins before God; whence it must also be conjoined with trust in Christ, indeed this trust must be included within it (compare Musaeus, Treatise on the Church, 1671 edition, Part 1, Disputation 1, sections 9 and following).

This is understood first of all with respect to the holiness which is Christ's and is imputed to believers (according to 1 Corinthians 1:30), but simultaneously also with respect to the inherent holiness which pertains to Renewal and draws its origin from faith as from a root, and consists in love and other virtues, although it is not perfect in every respect (compare Musaeus, same work, sections 19 and following).

And indeed all these persons are not only elect or predestined but also those who believe for a time, provided their faith is true and living. For as long as they are in Christ through faith, so long do they belong to the Church as its parts or members.

For dead members are members of a living body only equivocally. Hence hypocrites and the unholy are excluded here.

And thus it is proved that the Church properly so called is precisely the assembly of the truly believing and holy. For in Ephesians 4:16, the Church is described as a spiritual body which depends entirely upon Christ, according to all its joints and ligaments (by which it is compacted and constituted as one body), as upon the Head, that is, through an influx such as is owed to members from the head, so that they may receive growth befitting the body, and this through love. Whence it is rightly concluded that all and only those are true members of the Church properly so called who live a spiritual life, from the supernatural grace and influx of Christ the Head and His Spirit, and thus possess faith not of any sort, but supernatural and conjoined with love (compare Musaeus, sections 49 and following; also section 56).

To this belongs, (2)., the fact that the Church is described in 1 Peter 2:4 and following as a spiritual house, built from living stones upon the chief cornerstone, Christ, so that it is a holy temple of the Lord, a dwelling place of God through the Spirit, which does not happen except through faith in Christ, by which human beings rely upon Christ as the cause of salvation in an act of trust, conjoined with love (see Musaeus, same work, section 57). To the same effect, (3)., the Church is compared to an olive tree; and its branches, in the spiritual sense, are said to be engrafted through faith and to remain in it through the same faith (Romans 11:16 and following). And (4)., the Church is the assembly of the children of God; but they become and are children of God through faith in Christ (see Galatians 3:26, 28; Ephesians 2:19, 20).

Namely, the faithful and holy in this life always have admixed with them, with respect to external ecclesial society, wicked and unholy persons, as we shall see below.

### 3 The Head of the Church properly understood is Christ the θεάνθρωπος (God- man)

The Head of the Church properly understood is Christ the θεάνθρωπος (God- man), not only by reason of dignity and perfection above the members of the body, but also and principally with respect to power and influx, not only moral but also physical.

Notes. For we must now proceed further concerning the Church properly so called. The other synecdochical signification will be examined more distinctly shortly thereafter.

For the Church is a being through aggregation with order, where someone is supreme and the rest depend upon him. He upon whom the assembly of the Church depends is called the Head; and this indeed not with respect to the material concept of the head, insofar as it is an integral part of the body and has the same relation to the whole body as the other members (for Christ cannot suitably be called a member of the Church, since He in no way depends upon it), but formally, insofar as the head is the governing principle of the body, and by its influx rules, nourishes, and assists the whole body and all its members (compare Musaeus, Treatise on the Church, Part 1, Disputation 2, section 5).

So He is expressly called in Ephesians 1:22; 4:15, 16; 5:23; Colossians 1:16; 2:19.

According to both natures, divine and human: according to the human nature, indeed, by which He is conformed to the members (Ephesians 4:30), but exalted above all things and constituted head of the Church (Ephesians 1:20 and following); according to the divine nature, because the influx which He bestows upon individual members and upon the body of the Church is of infinite power, such that it could not proceed from a mere human being (compare Musaeus, Treatise on the Church, Part 1, Disputation 2, section 7).

For assuredly the God-man, who according to His divine nature is infinitely perfect and Lord of all, and according to His human nature, by virtue of the personal union, has been truly made partaker of the divine αὐχήματα (prerogatives) and exalted to the right hand of God, possesses the highest perfection and dignity above mere human beings who constitute the Church (compare Ephesians 1:20 and following; 4:15, 16; Colossians 1:16).

The moral influx consists in His infinitely valid merit, through which all spiritual goods are obtained for the Church (Ephesians 1:3; Romans 5:15; compare Musaeus, same work, section 9).

The physical influx He effectively bestows upon the body of the Church and its individual members, through actions terminated in them toward supernatural acts and habits of grace (Musaeus, same work, section 10).

### 4 And just as in the human body there are various joints through which the animal…

And just as in the human body there are various joints through which the animal spirits are conveyed from the head into the members, so the manifold influx of Christ the Head diffuses itself into the Church, partly through the various functions established by Him in the Church, and partly through the gifts granted to the Church, both ministerial and sanctifying.

Notes. Paul himself uses this similitude in Ephesians 4:16 (compare Musaeus, same work, sections 38, 39).

For thus Christ gave to the Church some as Apostles (who, as ambassadors of Christ, travelling hither and thither, were occupied in planting and propagating the Church through the preaching of the word and the appointment of other Teachers and Pastors), others as Prophets (divinely appointed for the interpretation of the Scriptures and sometimes for predicting future things), others as Evangelists (assistants of the Apostles who taught the first rudiments of evangelical doctrine, as catechists), others as Pastors (who publicly preached, dispensed the sacraments, and governed the churches), and Teachers (dedicated, as it were, to the theological school for the more accurate explanation, confirmation, and defense of sacred doctrine), "for the equipping of the saints, for the work of ministry, for the building up of the body of Christ" (Ephesians 4:11, 12). And indeed the first three offices were temporary, while the latter two are perpetual.

Add 1 Corinthians 12:28, where to Apostles, Prophets, and Teachers are subjoined Powers (that is, concretely, those who performed miracles), Gifts of healings (in the concrete sense, those who devoted themselves to healing the sick without natural means), Helps (such as Deacons and Deaconesses), Governments (the order of elders who were custodians of ecclesiastical discipline and polity), and Kinds of tongues (persons speaking foreign languages for the instruction of various peoples; compare Musaeus, same work, sections 41 and following).

These are called in Greek χαρίσματα (charismata), certainly given gratuitously (compare 1 Corinthians 12:4; Ephesians 4:7, 8, from Psalm 68:19).

The ministerial gifts are necessary for performing the functions we have seen, and were therefore conferred upon members of the Church not as considered absolutely in themselves, but in order and respect to other members and the whole body of the Church, and thus for the benefit of individuals and of the whole body. They are also for a good part involved in the functions enumerated, such as the gift of healings, the gift of miracles, the gift of tongues, the gift of prophecy, and so forth (see 1 Corinthians 12:8, 9, 10; Ephesians 4:29).

The sanctifying gifts are common to all members of the Church as such, of which the first is faith itself in Christ, by which they draw nourishment from Christ, as branches from a vine (John 15:5). To this is added love, through which they grow, according to Ephesians 4:16 (compare Colossians 3:14). And upon this follow other Christian virtues, concerning which see Ephesians 4:24 and following (compare Musaeus, same work, sections 52 and following).

### 5 But besides Christ

But besides Christ, another Head of the Church, which would visibly govern the entire Church in Christ's stead, is to be acknowledged neither from necessity nor from the free will and institution of Christ.

Notes. Not even after Christ ascended into heaven and the Apostles departed from this life.

Much less if such a head should arrogate to itself the power of changing what Christ instituted or of introducing new dogmas, sacraments, and forms of worship into the Church.

So that its decrees and decisions in matters of the Church would bind all the faithful to hear and acquiesce in them without hesitation.

That is, it is not the case that the Church of Christ is by its nature such that it cannot be preserved and governed without such a Head.

Nor is any such will of Christ revealed anywhere; rather, the Scriptures teach that Christ set over His Church several Ministers simultaneously, among whom none holds primacy of power and jurisdiction over the universal Church above all the rest.

Thus, (1)., Christ in Matthew 28:19 and Mark 16:15 commits equal power to plant and govern the Church to several ministers, and attributes nothing of power to one that would not equally belong to all the Apostles. And (2)., if at times He might seem to have attributed superiority and peculiar power to Peter, for example in Matthew 16:19, elsewhere He teaches that these things are common to several (see Matthew 18:18 and John 20:23; compare John 21:15 and following with Acts 20:28 and 1 Peter 5:2). Similarly, (3)., in 1 Corinthians 12:28 and Ephesians 4:11, Paul, reviewing the entire hierarchical order instituted by Christ, makes no mention in either place of a visible head presiding over the universal Church. And (4)., when he distinguishes the body of the Church from Christ the Head, he says that all the faithful are members not only in relation to Christ but also to one another, ἀλλήλων μέλη (members of one another; Romans 12:5). Indeed, (5)., although he frequently discusses the head and members of the Church, nowhere does he indicate by any sign that a vicarial head of the Church has a place.

### 6 The efficient cause of the Church is the triune God and Christ the θεάνθρωπος (God- man)

The efficient cause of the Church is the triune God and Christ the θεάνθρωπος (God- man).

Notes. That is, the cause which gathers human beings into one assembly by efficiently conferring faith, through which they are united to one another and to Christ for the constitution of the Church.

Hence the Church is called the Church of God, the people of God, whom He Himself established or called (see Psalm 95:7; 1 Peter 2:9, 10; 1:15).

For the conferral of faith, and therefore the gathering of the Church, is an external work of the Trinity.

Namely, Christ, not only as God, by the power proper and essential to Himself, that is, His omnipotence which He has in common with the Father and the Holy Spirit, efficiently produces faith in human beings and thus continually exerts His influence from the beginning of the Church to plant it, and always sustains, nourishes, and governs it; but also as man, by the same divine power communicated to Him by virtue of the personal union, He employed it in the state of humiliation more rarely and extraordinarily, but in the state of exaltation by an unceasing influx, making human beings believers, gathering the Church to Himself, sustaining and preserving it (see Musaeus, Treatise on the Church, Part 1, Disputation 2, sections 22 and following; also sections 31, 32).

### 7 The internal impulsive cause is the goodness or gratuitous favor of God

The internal impulsive cause is the goodness or gratuitous favor of God; the external or meritorious impulsive cause is Christ the Mediator.

Notes. The goodness of God is the impulsive cause of conferring faith upon human beings, through which they become members of the Church, and of the remission of sins and eternal salvation.

For this reason Christ is said to have acquired the Church for Himself by His own blood (Acts 20:28). And His merit, performed in the fullness of time, nevertheless had sufficient power with respect to the gathering of the Church of both the Old and New Testaments and the transfusion of grace into its members, and was able to move God and does move Him (see what Musaeus discusses concerning the moral influx of Christ into the Church, same work, Disputation 2, section 34).

### 8 The matter of the Church is constituted by truly believing and holy human beings

The matter of the Church is constituted by truly believing and holy human beings.

Notes. The term "matter" is used here in the sense in which beings through aggregation are said to have matter, namely, the things of which they consist.

We are here considering the Church Militant, and indeed the Church properly so called, according to what we said in section 2 (compare Musaeus, same work, Disputation 3, section 9).

### 9 The form of the Church consists in the union of the truly believing and holy with Christ

The form of the Church consists in the union of the truly believing and holy with Christ, through true and living faith.

Notes. That is, the formal reason by which that assembly of human beings is constituted in the being of the Church properly so called.

This union is not an external and local union of bodies, but an internal and spiritual conjunction of souls. For although the faithful also hold local sacred gatherings, these are not of the essence of the Church (see Musaeus, same work, sections 11, 12, 13).

For the Church is a being through aggregation with order, where one person placed in the supreme position rules the others who are inferior, and, as the head, sustains and governs the rest of the body; they are therefore united with him in this way (see Musaeus, same work, sections 10 and 14).

This faith depends efficiently upon Christ and tends toward Him as the cause of grace and the remission of sins, and thus unites believers with Christ (see Musaeus, same work).

### 10 The end of the Church

The end of the Church, and indeed the proximate end, is the edification both of the whole body and of each individual member; the ultimate end is their eternal salvation.

Notes. This is the end for which God gathers and preserves the assembly of the Church.

See Ephesians 4:12, 16; 1 Corinthians 12:4 and following. And to this pertains what is elsewhere taught, that the Church is the mother of the faithful, from whom spiritual children are born to Christ, by whose accession the Church itself is preserved and vindicated from destruction (compare Musaeus, same work, sections 17; also Disputation 2, sections 81 and following). See also Ephesians 5:27.

And this indeed is the proper end of the Church. The ultimate common end, to which all human things are ultimately directed, is the glory of God (compare Ephesians 1:11, 12).

### 11 The attributes of the Church are commonly established as four

The attributes of the Church are commonly established as four: namely, that it is (1). One, (2). Holy, (3). Catholic, and (4). Apostolic.

Notes. For so the Fathers at Constantinople, in the appendix added to the Nicene Creed, professed that they believed in One, Holy, Catholic, and Apostolic Church, whose footsteps theologians have followed down to this age.

### 12 The Church is One

The Church is One, partly absolutely and in itself, through the internal unity of faith in Christ, which is conjoined by an inseparable bond with love not only of God but also of neighbor; and partly exclusively, in opposition to several assemblies of the same species or kind, whether coexisting or succeeding one another.

Notes. Inasmuch as to be one is to be undivided.

This unity is called internal because the reason for uniting belongs to the intrinsic nature of the parts as such, so that it does not fall under the external senses, except perhaps accidentally, insofar as it can be known in some fashion a posteriori and from its operations (Musaeus, Treatise on the Church, Part 2, Disputation 1, section 100). And this unity is absolutely necessary and essential to the Church (same work, section 101; also Part 1, Disputation 3, section 23).

For through faith, just as they are united with Christ, so also among themselves in Christ, so that they are one body of one head, members of one another (see Romans 12:4, 5; compare Musaeus, Disputation 3, sections 20 and following; also Part 2, Disputation 1, section 101).

According to what we said in chapter 2, section 10, the hearts of the faithful, after they have been united with Christ the Head through faith, are also immediately conjoined among themselves (Musaeus, Part 2, Disputation 1, section 103). Here is understood the fraternal and reciprocal love of the faithful (same work, sections 106, 107), in such a way that the union through love in the first act, or φιλαδελφία (brotherly love), has a place among all as absolutely necessary; but the conjunction through love in the second act does not equally so, since it finds a place only among those who are known to each other, as members of the household of faith; nor is it perpetual, but can be impeded or destroyed by various hindrances, arising partly from the weakness of the faithful themselves, partly from hypocrites and wicked persons admixed from without (same work, sections 114 and following).

In this sense, to be one is the same as to be unique, that is, that to which nothing coexists that is of the same species or kind with it.

For inasmuch as the Church, as the body of Christ, embraces all the faithful within itself as its members, there assuredly does not exist outside it another true Church, let alone several. As for the distinction between the universal Church and particular churches, we shall see it shortly; here it is certain that the universal Church is meant, that is, the whole mystical body of Christ.

In this sense, that the Church is one means that it is perpetual, that is, that it has never perished nor will perish, but has endured from its first beginning and will endure until the end of the world, according to the divine promises (Psalm 48:9; 72:5 and following; Daniel 2:44; Matthew 16:18; 28:20). And thus it can also be said that the Church remains numerically one on earth always: namely, as a moral entity, because it never entirely perishes, on account of the perpetual succession of the faithful (compare Musaeus, same work, sections 28 and following).

### 13 External unity, with respect to the profession of the same doctrine of faith…

External unity, with respect to the profession of the same doctrine of faith and the participation in the same sacraments, as well as fellowship and communion of life through mutual offices of fraternal love, does not equally belong to the attributes of the Church, for it is not perpetual. Moreover, unity by reason of one visible head, a vicar of Christ, has absolutely no place.

Notes. This external unity formally consists in the external acts and signs by which the internal conjunction manifests itself.

And this is twofold: one is of individual believers, by which each one gives an account of his faith in particular; the other is of entire assemblies, which occurs through the voice of the pastors, at stated times, or through some formula of doctrine, committed to writing and published under a public name. The former profession is extraordinary; the latter is ordinary (see Musaeus, same work, sections 133 and following).

For besides the word, that is, Christian doctrine, the sacraments also are means of grace through which persons become believers and members of the body of Christ (compare Musaeus, same work, section 140). That is, so that, as members of one body, they may be of assistance to one another for their own edification and that of the whole body (same work, section 141).

Namely, attributes, as essential properties, are necessary and perpetual. But what is not perpetual cannot be essential.

Indeed, the external profession of faith or of believed doctrine ought everywhere to be one and the same (see Musaeus, same work, section 132). But dissensions in religion arise very frequently, not only from the weakness of the faithful, but much more through the work of Satan operating through hypocrites and wicked persons, when false doctrines are spread and sometimes cruelty and fraud are added, by which true doctrine and its profession are suppressed (Musaeus, same work, sections 121 and following, to 128). And when the consensus of doctrine is removed, fraternal communion in the external fellowship of life is usually also destroyed (same work, section 142).

For that vicariate is a mere fiction (compare what we said in section 5; also Musaeus, same work, section 144).

### 14 The Church properly so called is Holy

The Church properly so called is Holy: first, because its Head is holy; then, because all its members are also holy, with holiness both imputed and inherent, though this latter holiness is imperfect.

Notes. Concerning the holiness of Christ, see Hebrews 4:15; 7:26; 1 Peter 2:22.

According to what we said in section 2, note (e).

For it suffices that "there is no condemnation" (ouden katakrima) "for those who are in Christ Jesus, who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit" (Romans 8:1; compare Musaeus, Treatise on the Church, Part 1, Disputation 3, sections 44 and following).

And this holiness which we have described is assuredly an inseparable property of the Church, for it is posterior to the concept of the Church and flows necessarily from its intrinsic form. There are, moreover, additional reasons for denominating the Church as holy, for example, from its doctrine, laws, sacraments, and the entire worship to which it is devoted (see Musaeus, same work, sections 50 and 54).

### 15 The Church is and is called Catholic

The Church is and is called Catholic, not only insofar as it is orthodox, but with respect to universality: (1). of places, peoples, and nations; (2). with respect to persons, namely, all the faithful; (3). by reason of time.

Notes. The term katholikon is the same as kath' holon (according to the whole or universal; see Musaeus, citing Augustine, same work, section 56; also Part 2, Disputation 1, sections 9 and following).

Namely, orthodox doctrine, insofar as it proceeded from Christ and the Apostles, was commended to all the faithful, and was received and believed by their unanimous consent, is customarily called Catholic in this respect. Hence also the Church embracing that doctrine is accustomed to be called Catholic, in opposition to a heterodox and false church. But thus it is also immediately clear that any particular assembly whatsoever, which, agreeing with others, retains and professes the entire Catholic faith, can be called the Catholic Church (compare Musaeus, Part 1, Disputation 3, sections 59 to 62; also Part 2, Disputation 1, section 10 and section 26).

That is, by virtue of its institution it is not bound to any particular place, people, or nation, but is spread or at least to be spread throughout the whole world among all peoples and nations (Musaeus, Part 1, Disputation 3, section 66; Part 2, Disputation 1, section 28).

Or, that it extends universally to all the faithful of all nations and peoples (Musaeus, same passages).

That from its first beginning it has endured and will endure until the end of the world, which in substance is the perpetuity of the Church, of which we have already seen (compare Musaeus, same work).

And this Catholicity of places, persons, and times is a property of the Church of the New Testament, and indeed of the whole Church, by which it differs from the Israelite Church of the Old Testament and from any particular assemblies whatsoever (Musaeus, Part 1, Disputation 3, sections 67 and following; Part 2, Disputation 1, sections 29 and following).

### 16 The Church is finally called Apostolic because it embraces and holds intact the…

The Church is finally called Apostolic because it embraces and holds intact the Apostolic doctrine by faith.

Notes. For it is said to be "built upon the foundation of the Apostles, of which the chief cornerstone is Christ" (Ephesians 2:20; compare Musaeus, same work, sections 71, 72).

### 17 The effect of the Church properly so called is the vivification of those who…

The effect of the Church properly so called is the vivification of those who are already in it, and the generation or regeneration of others.

Notes. This in a certain way coincides with the end, concerning which see section 10.

Indeed the effects of the Church are manifold; but here we must especially consider that which the Church produces for its own preservation from the influx of Christ (see Musaeus, same work, section 16).

That is, the sanctification of those who are already believers, whom the Church, as it were, nourishes in her bosom.

For the Church is a successive being, some of whose members or parts continually depart while others are generated, by whose accession the Church vindicates itself from destruction (Musaeus, same work). And in this respect the Church is said to be in travail and to give birth, as the mother of the faithful (Isaiah 54:1 and following; Galatians 4:27; compare Musaeus, Disputation 2, sections 80 and following).

### 18 The Church properly so called may be defined as the assembly of the truly…

The Church properly so called may be defined as the assembly of the truly believing and holy, collected by God and Christ the God-man out of gratuitous favor toward human beings, on account of the merit of Christ, united to Christ their Lord and Redeemer through true faith, in which Christ is efficacious through the word and sacraments, and continually regenerates some, and those engrafted into Himself through faith, together with others already previously regenerated, He vivifies and sanctifies, for the edification and salvation of the whole body and of each individual member.

Notes. Otherwise, according to the well- known allegory, the Church may be described as a mystical or spiritual body, aggregated and united from the truly believing and holy in Christ as Head through faith, from whom, by the influx imparted through the ministry of the word and sacraments, it draws life, sense, and motion, and by the continual generation of new members receives growth befitting itself, for its own preservation, edification, and salvation (concerning which, and how it agrees in substance with the other description, see Musaeus, Treatise on the Church, Part 1, Disputation 3, sections 1 and following).

The word "assembly" holds the place of genus, for the Church is a being through aggregation, as we said in section 1 and section 11.

The additional qualifications of "truly believing" and "holy" pertain to the differentia, which is here drawn from the matter (see section 8).

God is indicated as the principal efficient cause (see section 6).

The gratuitous favor of God is the internal impulsive cause (according to section 7).

The merit of Christ is the external or meritorious impulsive cause (see section 7).

The form of the Church consists in union through faith (according to section 9).

The vivification and regeneration represent the effect of the Church (see section 17).

Edification and salvation pertain to the end of the Church (according to section 10).

### 19 The Church of Christ

The Church of Christ, spread throughout the world, contains several partial assemblies, which also claim for themselves the name and definition of the Church. And the well-known distinction between the universal Church and particular churches is to be noted. Although particular churches may be further subdivided into simple ones, which do not consist of other churches, and composite ones, which consist of other churches.

Notes. Concerning the universal Church we have dealt thus far, as with the whole body of Christ.

For the faithful themselves are so spread throughout the world that nevertheless, here and there, united by certain bonds, they coalesce into and constitute certain congregations, insofar as they make use of one ordinary and complete ministry that is distinct from the ministries of other congregations (see Musaeus, Treatise on the Church, Part 2, Disputation 1, section 38).

In the plural number indeed, as several distinct among themselves, according to Acts 15:41; 16:5; 1 Corinthians 16:19; 2 Corinthians 8:1; Galatians 1:2. Otherwise also in the singular number, if the discourse concerns some one particular church taken determinately, but with some added restriction, for example, "the church that is in Jerusalem" (Acts 8:1), "the Church of God that is in Corinth" (1 Corinthians 1:2), "the church of the Thessalonians" (1 Thessalonians 1:1; compare Musaeus, same work, sections 7; also Disputation 2, section 7).

For the whole Church stands in relation to the partial congregations of the faithful in the manner of a homogeneous whole, which is of the same nature or essence as its parts (Musaeus, same work, section 3).

This distinction is nevertheless not an adequate division of the whole into its parts, but an inadequate distinction, because the universal and particular Church stand to each other as whole and part, including and included (Musaeus, same work, section 95).

Simple churches are said to be simple not absolutely and in every respect, as though they were devoid of all composition (for then they would not be churches), but in a qualified sense and in a certain genus, as is clear from the words added.

Namely, composite churches are so especially by reason of ecclesiastical government: as formerly the churches, distinct according to places, which with respect to individual major cities were subject to individual bishops, were nevertheless, when subject in the same province to one Metropolitan, constituting one provincial church (see more in Musaeus, sections 46 and following). Furthermore, (2)., by reason of secular government, when the princes in whose territories the Church was hosted had become devoted to the Christian religion, to which pertain the names of the Eastern and Western Church, and the Greek and Latin Church (see Musaeus, same work, sections 70 and following). Indeed (3)., by reason of the unity of doctrine which otherwise distinct churches profess (same work, sections 81 and following).

### 20 Meanwhile, those more notable commendations and promises of perpetual duration…

Meanwhile, those more notable commendations and promises of perpetual duration which are attributed to the Church in the Scriptures must be referred not to any particular church but to the Church of Christ considered absolutely.

Notes. For example, that it is "the house of God, the pillar and ground of the truth" (1 Timothy 3:15; compare 1 Peter 2:4 and following); that it is "the body of Christ" (Romans 12:4 and following; Ephesians 4:7, 12 and following).
