For example, that "the gates of hell shall not prevail against it" (Matthew 16:18).

For these passages do not speak determinately of this or that particular church.

This is in substance the universal Church itself (compare Musaeus, Part 2, Disputation 2, sections 5, 6). Therefore it suffices for the perpetuity of the Church that it never entirely perishes, even if no particular church of a definite place remains perpetually uncorrupted.

### 21 The truly believing and holy

The truly believing and holy, who constitute the Church properly so called, everywhere on earth have admixed with them unholy persons or sinners, both hidden and manifest, not only with respect to cohabitation and merely civil society, but also in such a way that these have some ecclesiastical fellowship and external communion with the truly believing; and when this is the case, the name "Church" is customarily attributed to such mixed assemblies by synecdoche.

Notes. For those who wish to be entirely remote and separated from sinners would need to go out of the world, according to 1 Corinthians 5:10.

Just as in the time of the Apostles, Gentiles and Jews were mixed with the truly believing and holy, and today in the Turkish Empire Muslims are mixed with Christians, who nevertheless have no ecclesiastical fellowship among themselves whatsoever.

Namely, the unholy, although they are not true members of the Church, nevertheless feign the appearance of members, either through a mere profession of faith, or also through a simulation of holiness and a fictitious form of piety (see Musaeus, Treatise on the Church, Part 1, Disputation 5, section 2).

That this happens in such a way that within the boundaries of the same Church there are contained, besides the truly believing and holy, also wicked persons, not indeed as true members, but who are admixed to its members accidentally and contrary to the intention of Christ, eventually to be separated from the good, is clear from the parables of the field in which wheat and tares grow together (Matthew 13:24 and following), of the net in which good and bad fish are enclosed (Matthew 3:12; Luke 3:17; compare Musaeus, Disputation 4, sections 4 and following; also Disputation 5, section 16).

### 22 Since it happens that when the holy and the unholy are gathered together

Since it happens that when the holy and the unholy are gathered together, sometimes the former and at other times the latter predominate, and the holy are considered to predominate both with respect to doctrine (when, with harmful errors excluded, pure doctrine is publicly preached) and with respect to integrity of morals (when good examples of Christian virtues flourish and vices are suppressed), while the unholy prevail with respect to morals when vices run rampant with impunity, and with respect to doctrine when false dogmas are publicly spread and true doctrine and its confessors are oppressed: accordingly, a church together with its admixed unholy persons is called the Church of Christ simply and absolutely only when the holy predominate with respect to doctrine and morals. But when the unholy predominate, especially with respect to doctrine and public profession, in the Church, then that mixed assembly aggregated from holy and unholy is not called the Church absolutely, but in a qualified sense, or with an addition, a "corrupt Church."

Notes. That is, when the public ministry of the word and sacraments is pure and uncorrupted, and in the assemblies of the Church the word of God is taught purely according to the norm of the Scriptures and without corruptions contrary to the Catholic faith or good morals, just as the truly believing hold it purely fixed in their hearts, so that the unholy, erring in faith, are either compelled to dissemble their errors or to abandon them, unless they wish to be excluded from the ecclesiastical fellowship (see Musaeus, Part 1, Disputation 5, section 10).

Or when enormous and notorious sins are not tolerated in the assembly of the Church, and the teachers of the Church, civil magistrates, and other good persons, each in their own station, shine before others by their zeal for piety, virtue, and honesty of morals, setting an example for the pursuit of a holy life, while the unholy, either overcome by shame or terrified by the severity of ecclesiastical censure, abstain from enormous sins and put on the appearance of piety and honesty (Musaeus, same work, section 8).

Such a state of the Church existed in the time of the Prophets (see Isaiah 1:7; 5:7 and following; Jeremiah 5:8; 9:4 and following; Ezekiel 22). And Christ predicted such a state toward the end of the world (Luke 18:8; Matthew 24:38 and following), as did Paul (2 Timothy 3:1 and following; compare Musaeus, same work, section 9).

Such was the state of the Church in the East when the Arians dominated, and in the West before Luther (see Musaeus, same work, sections 10 and 29).

Such a mixed assembly is not called the Church absolutely because in itself, taken as a whole, it is the mystical body of Christ or the Church, but by a synecdochical manner of speaking, on account of the preponderant part, though not preponderant in number, yet such that the remaining part rather conceals itself (see Musaeus, same work, section 12).

Namely, the Church, which is the congregation of the truly believing and holy, does not immediately perish entirely when the unholy dominate; but in the meantime, because those who predominate, considered in themselves separately, are rather the synagogue of Satan than the Church of Christ, and the truly believing and holy lie hidden under their oppression, therefore the name of the Church can indeed be attributed by synecdoche, but not absolutely, to such an assembly (see Musaeus, same work, section 30).

That is, from the corruptions of doctrine and morals that prevail in it, although some parts of the doctrine of faith, and likewise Baptism in its essentials, are preserved intact (compare Musaeus, same work, and following sections).

### 23 And here belongs the distinction between a true or pure Church

And here belongs the distinction between a true or pure Church, in which the truly believing and holy constitute the stronger part, and a false or impure Church, in which the unholy, erring in the doctrine of faith, constitute the stronger part.

Notes. Indeed, a true and false Church can be spoken of in a twofold sense. In one sense, as the word "true" added to the word "Church" says nothing more than "Church" and a relation of reason to the knowing power, to which it appears to be a Church. In this signification, a true and false Church are opposed to each other contradictorily, and every Church that is not a non-Church is called a true Church, that is, any Church whatsoever. In the other sense, a true Church is spoken of insofar as the word "true" denotes the negation of admixed foreign matter, and a true Church is the same as a pure, not false Church; a false Church, conversely, is one that is impure, falsified, corrupted. So Musaeus (same work, sections 31 and following), where he also shows that both meanings had long been accepted among our theologians and that the diversity of significations is rightly to be noted. Here the latter meaning is intended, so that the true or pure Church coincides with the Church absolutely so called, while the false or impure Church coincides with the Church said to be such only in a qualified sense.

The stronger part is here said to be not so much the one that is greater in number, but the one in whose hands it lies to constitute the public ministry in conformity with the doctrine it holds in mind, and through that ministry to profess, teach, defend, and propagate it in public assemblies (Musaeus, same work, sections 48 and following).

That is, when according to the desire of the truly believing and holy, preachers of the word are appointed who are sincere and free from errors, who teach the doctrine of faith and morals conformably to the word of God as they hold it fixed in their hearts, defend it from corruptions, and propagate it (Musaeus, same work, section 50).

Or, conversely, when it lies in the hands of the unholy to appoint preachers and teachers in conformity with their doctrine, which they hold fixed in their minds, that is, impure ones devoted to false doctrines, through whom they teach, defend, and propagate the corruptions they embrace in public assemblies (Musaeus, same work, section 51).

### 24 The true or pure Church can be described as a congregation of human beings in…

The true or pure Church can be described as a congregation of human beings in which all things that are necessary to believe for salvation and to do for holiness of life are taught from the Word of God without the admixture of harmful errors, and in which the sacraments are administered according to the institution of Christ; and thus the spiritual children of God are begotten, who are joined to Christ their Head through true faith and become one body in Him.

Notes. Though taken synecdochically, for we have already described the Church properly so called above in Section XVIII.

Musaeus, German Treatise: Defense of the Immovable Foundation, against Jodocus Keddius, part 2, ch. 1, pp. 91ff., and ch. 11, pp. 197-198.

The term "congregation" here does not refer precisely to the faithful alone (Musaeus, same work, p. 91).

For it is in this manner that faith is generated and preserved, as we have discussed in the Prolegomena concerning the fundamental articles (ch. 1, sections 29ff., pp. 42ff.).

As for the exclusion of harmful errors: otherwise, when a Church is not free from doctrinal errors, even if it retains enough doctrine that the faithful can still be generated within it (about which we shall speak shortly), that Church itself will not be pure but impure.

The sacraments likewise are means and instruments for conferring and sealing faith.

Accordingly, as the Church spoken of synecdochically is also called the Mother of the faithful.

So the mixed assembly has the name "Church" on account of those true believers contained within it.

### 25 And so it customarily happens that to the Church designated by synecdoche there…

And so it customarily happens that to the Church designated by synecdoche there are also attributed, in their own manner, the properties of the Church properly so called, so that it is called One, Holy, Catholic, and Apostolic.

Notes. These properties, however, do not belong to it in entirely the same way, as will readily be apparent from what follows.

Unity, by which something is called one absolutely and in itself, belongs to that Church internally, that is, as a unity of faith and charity, on account of the true believers and saints contained in it, who in this respect are one among themselves. External unity, however, that is, of the profession of the same doctrine of faith, belongs essentially to such an assembly, which is constituted in its being by the fact that it professes the entire and pure doctrine of faith by public consent.

Holiness, which properly belongs to the faithful, can be and customarily is attributed to the Church of which we speak, because the saints are preeminent in it; just as Paul, in the openings of his various Epistles, addresses the entire assembly, for example the Roman, Corinthian, and Ephesian, calling them saints.

The designation "Catholic" applies insofar as it is understood as the catholicity or orthodoxy of doctrine; otherwise a certain difficulty arises, which we shall examine shortly.

And it is called "Apostolic" because the doctrine that publicly resounds within it is Apostolic.

### 26 Although several assemblies of the called

Although several assemblies of the called, considered individually, are rightly called several Churches of Christ, nevertheless all those assemblies taken together do not constitute one Catholic or universal Church, which, on account of the entire multitude of true believers and saints contained in them, is rightly called the Catholic or universal Church of Christ.

Notes. Namely, on account of the partial congregations of true believers and saints contained within them.

Indeed, if all the assemblies of the called throughout the entire world were to profess the catholic faith purely and without corruption, and were joined together by the bond of charity and peace, one would not hesitate to assert that they, taken together, constitute the Catholic or universal Church so called by synecdoche, within whose compass the entire multitude of true believers and saints is contained, and outside which there is no salvation. But this appearance of a catholic Church is more to be desired than hoped for. For we never read that, from the time of the Fathers onward, it has ever happened that throughout the entire world all assemblies of the called simultaneously professed the catholic faith sincerely and without corruptions, in true charity and peace. And so, when one or another assembly of the called has been contaminated by heresy or torn from the rest by schism, the remaining ones no longer constitute that one Catholic Church outside which there are no true believers and saints, and no salvation; since outside them the Word of God and Baptism can be and are given, from which faith and salvation are conferred upon human beings (Musaeus, On the Church, part 2, disp. 2, sections 40ff., p. 104ff.).

For, according to what has been said thus far, there are true believers and saints outside those assemblies that agree in the public doctrine of faith and in the use of the sacraments in true charity and peace: namely, those who lie hidden in the assemblies of the heterodox or schismatics.

### 27 For even in a corrupt Church

For even in a corrupt Church, spiritual children can be and are born to God through the Word of God, which is still preached there, and through Baptism that remains substantially intact.

Notes. We prefer to speak this way rather than to say that they are born "from" a corrupt Church. For it is certainly true that a corrupt Church, insofar as it is corrupt, does not bear spiritual children for God, that is, true believers (Musaeus, On the Church, part 1, disp. 5, section 98, p. 265).

For just as, according to the parable of Christ (Matthew 13), in the field where the Master of the household sowed good seed and the Enemy sowed tares, good wheat can still grow from the good seed, so also in those assemblies where errors are joined with true doctrines, faith can nevertheless be conceived from the Word of God, since the errors do not penetrate the minds of men equally, or are cast out again; just as the faithful, by the grace of God, are able to distinguish between the precious and the vile (Musaeus, same work, sections 53ff., pp. 23ff., and disp. 6, in its entirety).

### 28 Moreover, the Church properly so called is indeed not distinctly visible

Moreover, the Church properly so called is indeed not distinctly visible, but only confusedly so. The Church spoken of synecdochically, however, that is, a particular Church, is visible in such a way that it can be distinctly recognized as true with respect to its members, and can be discerned from false or corrupt Churches.

Notes. The Church properly so called precisely denotes the assembly of true believers and saints, insofar as they are united among themselves and with Christ their Head through faith, as we have shown above.

It is not distinctly visible or knowable in such a way that we could know distinctly and individually who they are, of whom it truly consists as members. For faith neither falls under the senses, nor can the faith that is in others be known by us with sufficient certainty. God alone knows the hearts of the children of men (1 Kings 8:39) and those who are His (2 Timothy 2:19).

But where there are congregations, especially larger ones, in which the Word of God is rightly taught and the sacraments are duly administered, it is rightly inferred that there are some true believers and saints there who constitute a part of the Church of Christ; and this by virtue of the divine promises concerning the fruit of the preached Word (Isaiah 55:10ff.; see also Musaeus, On the Church, part 1, disp. 10, sections 7ff., pp. 636ff.). Which particular individuals are truly faithful, however, we discern only with probability.

A particular Church is thus considered together with its admixed hypocrites and wicked persons, and with respect to its external profession.

The universal Church, moreover, because it consists of the aggregation of particular Churches, cannot be known by us except in the parts of which it consists. And since the true believers and saints who constitute the Church properly so called do not everywhere stand out above the non-saints with whom they are joined, they therefore do not constitute one Catholic Church that would be visible (Musaeus, On the Church, part 2, disp. 7, sections 20ff., p. 496).

Those, however, who outwardly profess the catholic faith whole and uncorrupted, and rightly use the sacraments of Christ, can indeed be distinctly and individually known.

### 29 It can happen, however

It can happen, however, and has been divinely predicted, that the Church may for some time be visible in no part of itself, that is, that the visible Church may entirely fail.

Notes. This can occur if the non-saints predominate everywhere, and the pure preaching of the Word entirely ceases. That this can happen is evident from the fact that Christ, although He promised perpetuity to the Church properly so called, did not promise immunity from the dominion of admixed evil persons.

It has been foretold, moreover, especially that in the time of Antichrist, wicked men devoted to his deceitful doctrines would dominate, and the Church of Christ would lie hidden (Revelation 12:14ff.; 13:12ff.; 17:2ff.; 18:3; Luke 18:8; 2 Thessalonians 2:12).

We do not, however, thereby maintain that the entire Church of Christ has perished or will perish, since we acknowledge that some true believers and saints, immune from pernicious errors and from fellowship in wickedness, have always survived and will always survive, even if hidden.

### 30 Meanwhile, for a true or pure particular Church

Meanwhile, for a true or pure particular Church, as such, to be recognized by a person learned in the Scriptures, that is, by a Christian, two marks suffice: namely, the pure preaching of the Word, and the legitimate administration of the sacraments.

Notes. This follows from what we said in Section XXVIII. If it should happen that the Church has no uncorrupted public ministry anywhere, and thus lies entirely hidden, then by that very fact of being hidden it will have no sensible marks.

For a person who is an unbeliever and a pagan, ignorant of the Scriptures, the divine origin of Scripture itself must first be demonstrated (by the arguments mentioned in the Prolegomena, ch. 2, sections 17ff., pp. 84ff.), along with the true Christian doctrine contained in the Scriptures, from which the Church has what makes it true; before such a person can be taught to discern the true from the false Church among Churches divided by schism (Musaeus, Defense of the Immovable Foundation, against Keddius, part 2, ch. 4, pp. 129ff.).

These marks are indeed, first, better known than the Church itself, both to us and by nature or absolutely (Musaeus, same work, pp. 128ff.). They are also, second, proper to the true Church and not common to false ones. For although false Churches also claim these marks for themselves, their misuse or false arrogation does not remove the genuine use and certainty, so that some other special foundation would be needed (Musaeus, same work, chs. 6ff., pp. 162ff.).

### 31 The Church is represented

The Church is represented, in its own way, by the Ecclesiastical Ministry, and likewise by Councils, that is, sacred Congregations of men learned in sacred doctrine, convoked by public authority, and occupied, in a suitable order, with examining and judging controversies of faith and Christian doctrine according to the Scriptures, and with instituting or amending those things that pertain to the external government of the Church and to good order, for the edification of the Church and the glory of God.

Notes. From this the name "Representative Church" has taken its origin.

This representational character holds insofar as what is done publicly in the name of all by a few, and is ratified by the rest, is considered to have been done by all.

Thus the common confession of the entire Church and of its individual members is considered to be that which the voice of the pastor delivers when he instills the doctrine of Christ in public assemblies and explains it to the capacity of the hearers (Musaeus, On the Church, part 2, disp. 1, section 136, p. 73). Especially to be understood here is the complete ministry, which has full authority to perform the entire worship prescribed by God (Musaeus, same work, section 41, p. 19). We shall say more about the Ecclesiastical Ministry in the following chapter.

Councils are also called Synods, a term used by both Greeks and Latins.

They consist not only of clerics, that is, those endowed with ecclesiastical dignity and more splendid title (though such persons, if they are qualified, should undoubtedly be admitted first), but also others whom they call laypersons, provided they are learned in sacred matters, diligent, pious, and lovers of peace.

They are convoked by the authority of those to whom external ecclesiastical jurisdiction belongs; and where there is a Christian magistrate, this authority also pertains to him, as we shall discuss in the section on the Magistrate.

A Council is an entity constituted by aggregation with order. Hence the presider, or moderator of the discussion, is particularly relevant here, and is commonly held to be twofold: ecclesiastical, whose duty it is rightly to propose the questions for deliberation, to request and collect opinions, and to record the decrees; and political, whose task it is to provide the participants security from external violence, to prevent internal tumults and contentions, to confirm and promulgate the decrees, and to carry them out.

The true and sole norm of councils, as of all religion, is Scripture.

The matter or object of a council is thus indicated: and at the same time it is apparent that in councils, new dogmas are not to be established, but ancient ones are to be declared, confirmed, and defended by fitting formulations of words and phrases.

The end of all councils ought to be edification.

### 32 Councils are divided into Ecumenical or Universal

Councils are divided into Ecumenical or Universal, which either contained some bishops or learned men from all or nearly all the Churches throughout the Roman world, or at least whose decrees were approved and received by all those Churches universally; and Particular, which were convoked from only one or another part of the Church. Those composed of learned men from one nation were called National; those from the learned men of one province, Provincial; and those consisting of the learned men of one diocese were called Diocesan.

Notes. The term "ecumenical" is used in the sense in which the Roman world is called πᾶσα οἰκουμένη (the whole inhabited earth), by synecdoche (Luke 2:1; see also Musaeus, On the Church, part 2, disp. 7, section 117, p. 583).

These councils were not universal absolutely and simply, as though they contained the bishops and learned men of the entire Church Militant, or perfectly represented the universal Church Militant; for we have never had such a universal council. Rather, they are called universal comparatively (συγκριτικῶς), in relation to councils of the latter class: national, provincial, and so forth (Musaeus, same work, section 112, p. 376, and section 119, p. 583).

Thus concerning the Council of Nicaea, Eusebius (book 3 of the Life of Constantine, chs. 7-8) and Theodoret (book 1, ch. 9) report its breadth (see also our disputation in defense of the Council of Nicaea against Daniel Zwicker and Christoph Sandius, held in 1671).

Regarding the Council of Constantinople, we know that from the Western Churches and from those outside the Roman Empire no one was present, while from the Eastern Churches only 150 bishops attended. And yet it is regarded as Ecumenical, the designation being taken from a later reception (Musaeus, same work, section 112, p. 376, and section 120, p. 584).

Particular councils are otherwise called μερικά (partial) or τοπικά (local).

The term "diocese," though it otherwise refers to the administration of certain provinces governed by the Praetorian Prefects and their vicars, is used here in the ecclesiastical sense as the complex of Churches subject to one bishop.

### 33 Those councils that have undoubted authority do not have it from the fact that…

Those councils that have undoubted authority do not have it from the fact that they represented the Church, which is the pillar of truth, but dependently on the sacred Scriptures, and from the agreement of their decrees with them; although from a posterior consideration, from the consent of the Churches existing throughout the world, a certain authority is added.

Notes. Not all councils, not even those called universal, have undoubted authority, since some of them are known to have gravely erred (Musaeus, On the Church, part 2, disp. 7, section 123, p. 586).

Nor is the Church called the pillar of truth in 1 Timothy 3:15 in the sense that it always appears as such by its own power to someone wavering in faith (Musaeus, same work, sections 81ff., p. 550). Nor has any council been seen that perfectly represented the universal Church, since not all bishops of all Churches have ever been gathered together after the time of the Apostles; and those who did convene often did not sufficiently represent their own Church, and frequently those more capable were absent compared to those who had attended (Musaeus, same work, section 112, p. 577).

The authority of councils rests, then, on the fact that, although they could err, they did not in fact err, but followed the guidance of Scripture and sincerely declared the catholic faith in all things (Musaeus, same work, section 125, p. 588).

The posterior confirmation from the consent of the Churches is further discussed (Musaeus, same work, section 126, pp. 588- 589, and disp. 6, sections 11ff., pp. 419ff.).

### 34 Opposed to the unity of the Church is

Opposed to the unity of the Church is, first, Schism, that is, the division of the Church into parties, with mutual charity and peace removed, as regards actual ecclesiastical or fraternal communion, that is, the communion of those of the household of faith.

Notes. This is a violent separation. For otherwise Churches can be divided as to the distinction of ministries and of ecclesiastical or secular government, yet on account of the unity of faith and charity, and because they preserve communion of duties, they are considered to constitute one Church.

Civil concord, moreover, can remain even among assemblies torn apart by schism, not only in one larger empire but even in one city.

Thus formerly the exchange of letters, which they called Encyclical, was suspended between Churches when their union was dissolved (Musaeus, On the Church, part 2, disp. 1, section 118, p. 63).

### 35 Schism arises partly from disagreement in doctrine on the foundation of faith

Schism arises partly from disagreement in doctrine on the foundation of faith, especially if cruelty and deceptions are added to the corruptions of doctrine; partly from disagreement on less necessary parts of doctrine, or on ceremonies, or on matters pertaining to ecclesiastical government, if some impose upon others, under the pretense of necessity, things from which those others, holding fast to their liberty, prefer to abstain, and do abstain.

Notes. Just as union through faith is prior to union through fraternal charity, so when the union of faith fails through disparity of external profession of faith, actual conjunction as among blood-relatives of the faith does not equally have a place. And the obstinate defense of error conflicting with the foundation of faith, that is, of heresy, necessarily also entails the guilt of schism; just as formerly heretics were excommunicated by the orthodox Church, and having gathered a crowd of followers, constituted separate assemblies (Musaeus, On the Church, part 2, disp. 1, sections 84ff., pp. 43-44, section 91, p. 49, section 118, p. 62, section 126, pp. 68ff.). It is moreover the same here whether dogmas necessary to believe are obstinately denied, or whether unrevealed and false dogmas are obstinately defended as if they were revealed and necessary to believe. For both are rightly called by the name of heresy (Musaeus, On the Church, part 2, disp. 5, sections 5-12, pp. 334-339).

When, for example, the followers of the true faith, who are prepared as far as it lies in them to preserve the bond of unity and peace, are neither heard nor convicted of error but are condemned, then by this cruelty, which is diametrically opposed to charity, the unity of the Church is itself torn asunder (Musaeus, same work, section 128, p. 69, and disp. 4, section 87, p. 266).

Such was the schism between the Roman Church and the African Churches in the time of Stephen, Bishop of Rome, and Cyprian (Musaeus, Defense of the Biblical Glosses, disp. 1, section 16, pp. 16-17).

Similarly, Victor of Rome gave occasion for schism between the Roman Church and the Asian Churches, disagreeing about the day of Easter (Musaeus, same work, section 15, pp. 15-16, and On the Church, part 2, disp. 4, section 109, p. 288).

To the same category belongs the schism between Julius I, Bishop of Rome, and the Eastern bishops, over whom he had sought dominion (Musaeus, same work, section 17, p. 19, and diss. 3, section 48, pp. 212-213).

### 36 But those who, having been unjustly excommunicated from a Church

But those who, having been unjustly excommunicated from a Church, depart from it and cease to communicate with it, cannot be charged with the guilt of schism; and the hatred with which they pursue the authors of the schism is not contrary to charity.

Notes. This applies, for example, when they refuse to accept errors imposed as articles of faith, with their conscience protesting (Musaeus, On the Church, part 2, disp. 4, sections 143-144, p. 327).

And so, properly speaking, they do not withdraw of their own accord but are expelled, since they would otherwise prefer to remain in communion (Musaeus, same work, section 35, p. 221, section 56, p. 237, section 145, p. 327). Indeed, the Church unjustly excommunicated remains, as regards internal unity, most closely joined with the faithful in the excommunicating Church (Musaeus, same work, section 135, p. 319).

But they celebrate separate assemblies, inasmuch as the Church unjustly excommunicated nonetheless retains the right of teaching the Word of God, administering the sacraments, and ordering all other things that pertain to divine worship (Musaeus, same work, section 135, p. 319).

For they suffer schism; they do not make it. And thus Musaeus showed at length that the guilt of the schism between the Papists and the Protestants does not lie with the latter but with the former (Musaeus, same work, sections 33ff., pp. 218ff., sections 53ff., pp. 236ff.).

Nor is this a hatred directed at brothers, but at those who, by their fraternal hatred and the cruelty born from it against the brothers, have cut themselves off from the Church (Musaeus, same work, section 88, p. 267).

### 37 Opposed, second

Opposed, second, to ecclesiastical unity is Syncretism, that is, the coalition of parties dissenting in religion into fraternal and ecclesiastical concord, notwithstanding their dissension; so that either the doctrinal errors of the dissenting party are tolerated, or at least the erring persons themselves are tolerated within the ecclesiastical fellowship as brothers in Christ and co-heirs of eternal life. Both forms of toleration, however, are vicious.

Notes. The term "Syncretism" sometimes assumes the name of peace or ecclesiastical concord.

By the force of its origin and primary signification, it denotes a profane peace that dissenting parties enter into against a common enemy for a time, while hatreds and injuries, the causes of war, remain. From this it is apparent that the word, when transferred to ecclesiastical peace, is more rightly applied in a bad sense than a good one (Musaeus, Detailed Explanation, question 15, pp. 144ff., and Treatise on Syncretism and Sacred Scripture, question 1, sections 1ff.).

The description given is that of Haberkorn, whom Musaeus follows (Musaeus, Detailed Explanation, question 16, p. 148, and Treatise on Syncretism, question 2, section 7, pp. 9-10).

The word "religion" here refers to the Christian doctrine of faith and morals; yet by this term one must understand not precisely only those parts of Christian doctrine without knowledge of which no one can be saved while retaining faith and salvation, but the entire Christian doctrine in all its parts, whether they constitute the foundation of faith or have a necessary connection with it: that is, all fundamental articles, whether they are such positively and directly in themselves, or indirectly and negatively by reason of another. For in all of these, agreement is required for legitimate ecclesiastical peace; and if disagreement exists in such matters, there will be no true ecclesiastical peace (Musaeus, Treatise on Syncretism, question 3, sections 7-8, pp. 16- 18, and question 4, section 21, pp. 36-38).

If, however, the disagreement pertains only to adiaphora, or to questions that have arisen incidentally alongside matters of faith, it must be admitted that a true and pious concord can be entered into even while disagreement persists; unless it happens incidentally, as it sometimes does, that one party imposes its ceremonies or opinions on the other under the pretense of necessity, in which case it is better to retain Christian liberty than to confirm the dissenting party in a false opinion through an untimely peace (Musaeus, same work, question 3, sections 2- 5, pp. 11-14).

Where the religious dissension between the parties has been removed and agreement in true doctrine has been reached, then the concord or coalition of the parties is not Syncretism but true, pious, and Christian concord (Musaeus, same work, question 2, section 7, p. 10). It sometimes happens, however, that a certain "temperament of religion," as they call it, is sought, and that each dissenting party yields to the other to some degree in its own doctrine, while in the remaining controverted articles they tolerate one another; as the book called the Interim in the previous century was seen to aim at. But this manner of entering into concord, which some call "mitigating Syncretism," is not only rightly regarded as vicious but also differs from the matter under discussion here (Musaeus, same work, appendix to the questions on Syncretism, section 7, pp. 137- 138). Furthermore, that errors, even non- fundamental ones, of whose falsity one is convinced in conscience, may not be received as true dogmas, is also taught (Musaeus, On the Church, part 2, disp. 5, section 10, pp. 336-337).

The coalition of parties dissenting in religion into a political concord can be made without the stigma and vice of Syncretism (Musaeus, same work, section 3, pp. 134-135, and question 2, section 7, p. 10). Nevertheless, heterodox persons who have not held the rights of citizenship should not easily be received into a commonwealth, on account of various disadvantages to be feared (Musaeus, same work, question 5, section 11, p. 77).

We are said to "tolerate" those things which, although they are troublesome, we nevertheless do not avoid or remove (Musaeus, same work, question 5, sections 1ff., pp. 72-73).

Errors of doctrine are tolerated when they are not attacked or condemned (Musaeus, same work, section 5, p. 74).

Persons are tolerated when they are regarded as weak and erring, yet still as brothers, partakers of the same sacred rites. It is indeed certain that simpler persons, who through invincible ignorance are so attached to certain errors that they yet retain saving faith by the grace of God, would have to be tolerated as weak brothers, if they were distinctly known to us. But the discussion here concerns a dissenting party with respect to its public ministry and the doctrine of faith and morals as publicly preached, and the sacraments as administered, that is, corruptly; so that the members of such a visible assembly are considered in themselves, as they are members of it, and not according to what may incidentally apply to this or that individual (Musaeus, same work, sections 13 and 16, pp. 78 and 80, and appendix, section 9, pp. 139-140).

The toleration of errors, first, conflicts with the passages of Scripture that command the entire Christian doctrine to be preserved pure from corruptions (2 Thessalonians 2:15; 2 Timothy 1:13; 3:14). Second, it conflicts with the elenctic office, by which false doctrines are rebuked and condemned, an office enjoined by God upon faithful teachers (Titus 1:9, 11, 13; 2 Timothy 4:2; 3:16), to which the examples of Christ (Matthew 5:12ff.; 16:6) and of Paul (Galatians 1ff.) correspond. Third, it is very dangerous, because errors and corruptions, unless they are restrained, attacked, and condemned, spread further; the truth of doctrine is rendered doubtful and suspect, or at least is regarded as a matter of indifferent opinion; the erring themselves are hardened in their errors; and occasion is given to seducers to infect more people.

The toleration of erring persons, moreover, since it involves respect not only for the simpler folk but for entire assemblies, and thus also for the public ministry itself and for heterodox teachers, conflicts with the precepts concerning the rebuking, admonishing, and avoiding of false teachers and defenders of error (Romans 16:17; 2 Corinthians 6:14, 17; Galatians 1:8; 5:12; 2 Thessalonians 3:6; 1 Timothy 6:3; Titus 3:10; see Musaeus, On Syncretism, question 5, sections 8ff., pp. 75ff., and appendix, sections 30, 32ff.).

And thus, specifically as regards concord to be entered into with the Papists and the Calvinists while the dissension remains, Musaeus often and solicitously taught that there is indeed a dissension on the foundation of faith, in various parts of doctrine necessary to believe and needed for the edification of the faithful, that is, the children of God; and therefore that such concord is unlawful and is studiously to be avoided. This is set forth not only in his cited Treatise on the Questions of Syncretism and the appended Appendix, but also in his Treatise on the Church (part 2, disps. 5 and 6), in the preface to his Treatise on Repentance against Stenger, and in the preface to his Detailed Explanation. It is also well known how Musaeus not only endeavored to dissuade our people from the concord attempted at the Colloquy of Kassel by grave and timely admonitions (see the preface to his Treatise against Stenger), but also openly declared his dissent from that conciliation and the unfavorable outcome he had long foreseen (in the preface to his Dissertation on the Eternal Decree of Election, near the beginning); although, in most dutiful obedience to the commands of the Most Serene Princes, he refrained from publishing writings against those who seemed too intemperate in their attachment to such conciliations (see the preface to his Treatise against Stenger).

### 38 Finally, third, and above all

Finally, third, and above all, the Antichrist opposes the Christian Church: that is, a series and complex of several human beings succeeding one another in the same impiety, arrogating to themselves in the Church of Christ a peculiar kingdom and, as it were, a divine power over all, having their seat principally in the city of Rome, introducing various corruptions of doctrine and of public sacred rites, and propagating them by deceits and much violence, with the confessors of the true faith oppressed; yet in such a way that this impiety is at last to be publicly revealed and reproved, and that Antichrist is to be abolished when Christ comes to judgment.

Notes. The name "Antichrist," taken generally, denotes any heretics who spread and defend false dogmas conflicting with the doctrine of Christ; in which sense they are called in the plural ἀντίχριστοι πολλοί (many antichrists) (1 John 2:18). But specially and preeminently, ὁ Ἀντίχριστος (the Antichrist) denotes the notable adversary of Christ, of whom the same passage and 2 Thessalonians 2:3ff. treat at greater length; and it is this signification that is to be considered here.

This Antichrist is not one single determined human individual. For, first, Antichrist was to come when that which obstructed the erection of his kingdom (namely, the old Western Roman Empire, whose seat was at Rome) had been removed, and he was to endure until the glorious advent of Christ; a duration spanning so many centuries that it utterly exceeds the lifespan of one man (Musaeus, preface to the Treatise on Conversion, p. 63, and Defense of the Biblical Glosses, disp. 3, sections 10ff., pp. 179ff.). Second, the Scriptures describe the origin or planting of the kingdom of Antichrist and the affairs to be conducted in it in such a way that it is impossible for everything to occur within one man's lifetime: namely, if we consider that the kingdom was to be erected by hidden beginnings, not so much by arms and open force as by insidious arts, by which the minds of men would be gradually occupied and drawn to his side, and this not in one people and nation but throughout the greatest part of the earth; and that kings and peoples would use his fellowship to the point of satiety and disgust, and would furnish him aid for persecuting the saints, and so forth, according to Revelation 13, 14, and 17, concerning the beast and the great harlot (Musaeus, preface to the Treatise on Conversion, p. 63, and Defense of the Biblical Glosses, disp. 3, sections 20ff., pp. 188ff.).

That he is said to sit in the temple of God (2 Thessalonians 2:4) means in the Church, and not in some small part of the Church, but in Churches, according to the Greek interpreters and Estius himself (Musaeus, On the Church, part 1, disp. 6, sections 51-52, pp. 309-310).

This sitting denotes one who reigns, and it is rightly concluded that he is foretold to present himself as the head of the Church (see Revelation 17, last verse).

He is described as ὑπεραιρόμενος ἐπὶ πάντα λεγόμενον θεόν (exalting himself above everyone who is called God), that is, above all kings and princes, arrogating to himself power over all kingdoms, whether direct or indirect; indeed, while sitting in the temple of God, displaying himself as being God, as if acting in the place of God, having full power over all the faithful and likewise over the ministers of the Churches (2 Thessalonians 2:4).

As it is said in Revelation 17:3, the woman (that great harlot) sits upon the beast having seven heads, by which seven mountains are denoted according to verse 9; which is a manifest description of seven-hilled Rome. And so in 2 Thessalonians 2:6-7, Paul teaches that there is a τὸ κατέχον (the thing restraining) or a ὁ κατέχων (the one restraining), preventing the kingdom of Antichrist from being erected: namely, the Roman Empire, not the present one, but the ancient one that had Rome as its jewel; or the Emperors who presided at Rome with authority. When these were removed, the impious one was to come, who until then could not have his throne in the same seat that the Emperors actually occupied (Musaeus, preface to the Treatise on Conversion, pp. 60ff., and Defense of the Biblical Glosses, disp. 3, sections 9ff., pp. 178ff.).

Thus a great ἀποστασία (apostasy) or defection from the truth is said to come, so that men would believe a lie (2 Thessalonians 2:3, 11). And in 1 John 4:3 and 6, the spirit of Antichrist is called the spirit of error.

His operation is described as "according to the working of Satan, with all power and signs and lying wonders, and with all deception of unrighteousness" (2 Thessalonians 2:9-10; see also Revelation 13:13-14).

The beast is said to be drunk with the blood of the saints and with the blood of the martyrs of Jesus (Revelation 17:6; see also 13:15-17), where it is taught how it establishes its kingdom by force, so that those who do not worship the image of the beast are killed, and no one can buy or sell except one who has the mark or the name of the beast or the number of its name.

The abolition of Antichrist is foretold (2 Thessalonians 2:8; Revelation 17-18).

That the aforementioned properties of Antichrist are found in the Roman Pontiffs was shown by Musaeus (preface to the Treatise on Conversion, and disp. 3 of the Defense of the Biblical Glosses). That this doctrine of the Protestants is compatible with religious peace, and is not injurious to the Roman Empire or the Roman Emperor, and indeed that if the Papists were to cease doing what the Scriptures predict would be done by Antichrist and his satellites, no Protestant would easily raise a dispute with them about Antichrist or call the Pope Antichrist, was also taught by Musaeus (preface to the Defense of the Biblical Glosses, and disp. 1, section 46, pp. 43-44, and disp. 54ff., pp. 13ff.). Finally, how, under the kingdom of Antichrist, the assembly of true believers could be preserved, and was preserved and continues to be preserved, even though, once Antichrist is recognized, the faithful are commanded to separate themselves from his fellowship, may be seen in Musaeus (On the Church, part 1, disp. 6, sections 58ff., pp. 317ff.).

## 30 On the Ecclesiastical Ministry

### 1 For the gathering and preservation of the Church

For the gathering and preservation of the Church, it is necessary that certain men discharge the office of preaching the Word and administering the sacraments, so that through these means faith may be conferred upon people, and once conferred, may be confirmed and increased. This is the function that is called the ecclesiastical ministry.

Notes. Indeed, God could have immediately illuminated any persons and conferred faith upon them, preserving and increasing what had been conferred. Yet it pleased Him to prescribe a certain order and certain means, along with their use, for the attainment of faith by His grace. Therefore He willed that the revelation made immediately to a few should not only be conveyed and promulgated to many through the ministry of these persons and their successors, but also that it should be declared and inculcated, and that what was to be believed and done should be set forth, confirmed, and defended from corruptions according to the capacity and condition of various persons. Hence, and especially because the doctrine of faith exceeds the grasp of human reason and is to be learned from Sacred Scripture alone, the necessity of the ecclesiastical ministry is easily recognized, although the light of nature also teaches it in a certain manner, and the gentiles acknowledged it to some extent (see Musaeus, Refutation of the Objections of the Sect of Conscience, pp. 54, 66; also the Treatise on the Church, part 2, disputation 1, §36, pp. 16-17).

That is to say, the means of salvation are to be put into use, and the seed of the Word is to be sown in the field of the Church. Baptism, as the sacrament of initiation, is to be conferred upon the spiritual children of Christ and of the Church who are about to be born; and the sacrament of the body and blood of Christ is to be conferred upon those who have been born and have grown, for the confirmation of faith and the spiritual nourishment of the soul (see Musaeus, On the Church, at the same place).

Thus the office of the apostolate is called διακονία (ministry) (Acts 1:16; 6:4; 21:19; Romans 11:13; 2 Corinthians 3:2). And Paul calls himself and others ὑπηρέτας Χριστοῦ, καὶ οἰκονόμους μυστηρίων Θεοῦ (servants of Christ, and stewards of the mysteries of God) (1 Corinthians 4:1). Elsewhere he calls himself δοῦλον Χριστοῦ (a servant of Christ) (Titus 1:1).

### 2 The principal efficient cause of the ecclesiastical ministry

The principal efficient cause of the ecclesiastical ministry, both in itself and with respect to the ministers who discharge it, is the triune God, and Christ the θεάνθρωπος (God-man).

Notes. That is to say, the sufficient power or virtue to institute this ministry and to entrust it to certain persons, indeed to grant success and to produce spiritual fruit through it, belongs to God.

The ministry considered in itself is the condition of ministers, instituted and established in a certain manner, which is regarded abstractly.

Considered concretely, it refers to the human persons by whom this office is to be undertaken and administered.

For He who is the author of grace is also the one who ordains the office by which the means of grace are applied to people. To this end pertains, first, that God has revealed what pertains to the right conduct of this ministry: for example, what doctrine is to be preached (Galatians 1:8-9, 12), what pertains to teaching, reproving, and correcting and forming morals (2 Timothy 3:14 ff.), what sacraments are to be administered and how (see 1 Corinthians 11:23 ff.). Second, that God imposes this office upon certain persons, or sends people to discharge it (see Psalm 68:12; Matthew 9:38; Luke 10:2), which others call vocation, according to Romans 1:1 and Hebrews 5:4. Third, that He cooperates with the actions of the ministers (see 1 Corinthians 3:5 ff.).

For this is a work directed outward. And so Paul attributes his vocation to God the Father and Jesus Christ (Galatians 1:1), while elsewhere he teaches that the Holy Spirit appoints bishops to shepherd the Church of God (Acts 20:28; compare 1 Corinthians 8:4 ff. to 11).

That is, Christ determines the functions of this office and commits it to certain persons and effectively cooperates, not only as God but also as man (see Matthew 28:19 ff. to the end; Mark 16:15 to the end; Ephesians 4:11- 12).

### 3 God calls people to the ecclesiastical office sometimes immediately

God calls people to the ecclesiastical office sometimes immediately, that is, without any intervening voluntary action of other persons, and sometimes mediately, namely through the Church, which in the name of God commits that office to certain persons. When this occurs, the Church can be called a less principal cause of the vocation of ministers.

Notes. As Moses (Exodus 4:10) and very many prophets in the Old Testament, and likewise the Apostles in the New Testament, were called, so that God Himself named the persons upon whom the sacred office was to be conferred.

Moreover, when ministers of the Church are called through human agents acting upon a singular and express divine command, and not relying on their own judgment and choice, the vocation can nevertheless be called immediate. To this category belongs the example of Aaron, whom God called through Moses indeed, but by express name (Exodus 5:14 ff.; 28:1 ff.).

To the Church, after it has been planted, belongs the right and power of appointing ministers. For the Church, as a bride, holds the keys of the kingdom of heaven given to her by her bridegroom Christ (Matthew 16:18; 18:17). Therefore, just as it is hers to open and close the kingdom of heaven, so it is hers to appoint ministers through whom she may open and close. And if we observe that the Church is a certain commonwealth, and that ministers of the Word are like magistrates or administrators of public affairs to whom the care of the whole commonwealth is committed, it is easily understood that the power of appointing them resides by its own nature in the whole Church, and does not belong to any single part unless it has been transferred from the common consent of all to some particular part.

It is also established that this was the practice of the primitive Church from the time of the Apostles, so that public ministers were appointed by the consent of the whole body. See Acts 6:5, where deacons (though particularly assigned to the care of the ecclesiastical treasury, yet not strangers to the office of teaching, and rather to be chosen above others on account of their expertise in sacred doctrine, so that they might teach) were called by the collected votes of those who constituted the Church. And Acts 14:23, where Paul and Barnabas are said to have appointed presbyters in each church by the collected votes of the faithful (χειροτονήσαντες, so that individuals cast their votes by extending their hands). And so after the time of the Apostles, over the course of many centuries, ministers of the Church were customarily appointed in this way, as, among others, Marco Antonio de Dominis has taught at length (On the Christian Commonwealth, book 3, chapter 3).

The Church does not act on its own authority, however. For this is a matter belonging to God and pertaining to the salvation of souls. And so we know that prayers were formerly joined with the act of calling (see Acts 4:6; 14:23), and more recent practice teaches that the formula "In the name of the Most Holy Trinity" is customarily inserted into letters of vocation.

### 4 This right or power of appointing ministers belongs also to particular churches…

This right or power of appointing ministers belongs also to particular churches that have been separated from the fellowship of the rest by unjust excommunication.

Notes. For those things which have been granted to the Catholic Church with respect to the common end, which is spiritual edification, are rightly claimed by particular churches, through which the Catholic Church must edify, and insofar as they belong to the Catholic Church (see Musaeus, On the Church, part 2, disputation 3, §7 ff., p. 166 ff.).

For by the unjust excommunication which they suffer, they do not cease to be true churches; and therefore they do not lose the rights that belong to all true churches of Christ (see Musaeus, On the Church, disputation 4, §35, pp. 318-319).

### 5 Three things concur in the vocation of ministers that takes place through the Church

Three things concur in the vocation of ministers that takes place through the Church: 1. Election, that is, the judgment concerning the worthiness of a person to be advanced to the sacred ministry, with respect to learning and gifts necessary for rightly discharging the acts of office, and the designation of that person for the ministry. 2. Ordination, that is, the solemn inauguration of the elected person to the sacred office, performed through certain rites. 3. Vocation in the specific sense, that is, the granting of authority to teach the Word of God in public assemblies and to administer the sacraments, and the assignment of the function.

Notes. As the Apostles said to the multitude of disciples or the faithful: "Look among yourselves, brothers, for men of proven integrity, full of the Holy Spirit and wisdom, to whom we may delegate this business" (Acts 6:3; also verse 5). And Paul enumerates at length the requirements of a bishop (1 Timothy 3:2 ff.; Titus 1:6 ff.).

Ordination is most rightly performed, after the apostolic manner, through prayers and the laying on of hands (Acts 6:6; compare 1 Timothy 4:14; 5:22).

The vocation in the specific sense is customarily carried out today through what are called letters of vocation.

### 6 To these matters the ecclesiastical order and the secular order contribute in…

To these matters the ecclesiastical order and the secular order contribute in different ways. It is the task of the ecclesiastical order to examine the learning and other necessary gifts of the person to be elected and to render judgment concerning them; then to ordain the designated or elected person by a solemn rite, both of which it does in the name of the Church. The secular order generally acquiesces in the judgment of the ecclesiastical order concerning the fitness of the person, except that if, having heard the sermon, it has rightly observed something concerning external gifts, the sincerity of doctrine, or the manner of life, this ought justly to be heeded. The same secular order, jointly with the ecclesiastical order, designates or elects the person for the ministry, and thus by unanimous consent confers upon the elected person the authority to teach the Word and administer the sacraments.

Notes. For although the appointment of ministers belongs by its own nature to the whole Church, nevertheless, since the parts of which the Church consists are diverse, each part should be left with what belongs to it in respect of the requirements for the appointment of ministers.

The ecclesiastical order is commonly called the clergy, not so much by the force of the words of Scripture (which designates the Church itself or the faithful by this name, 1 Peter 5:3) as by ecclesiastical custom.

The secular or political order, in this context, embraces in its scope both the magistracy and the people.

To this end, examinations of candidates for ordination are held, which are more properly set before the vocation than made to follow it.

Moreover, it is the same whether a bishop or a presbyter performs the rite of ordination. For by divine right a bishop and a presbyter do not differ, as is evident from Acts 20:17 and 28, and 1 Peter 5:1-2. It can also happen that a minister of a church in which there are no other ministers, or for other reasons, is ordained elsewhere; in which case it suffices that clear testimonies of proven competence and completed ordination be presented to the church which he is to serve.

The ordination is performed by authority granted by the Church. Hence ordination is customarily performed in the assembly of the Church, with the faithful people joining in prayer.

The sermon is for this reason called δοκιμαστική (a trial sermon).

Not only ecclesiastical persons but also other people are able to distinguish suitable from unsuitable delivery and manner, and to test whether the spirits are from God (see 1 John 5:1).

For sometimes the morals and actions of those who seek the ministry are more known to the people than to ecclesiastical persons.

Thus in Protestant churches, by more frequent custom, it has been accepted that the right of electing, or of nominating and presenting, belongs to the patron of the church, that is, to the one who at some time founded or endowed the church, or who has succeeded to his place. The right of examining the nominee and of judging whether he is fit for the ministry is attributed to the bishop and is exercised through consistories or theological colleges. Once the worthiness or aptitude of the examined person has been recognized, he is presented to the whole church so that he may be publicly heard. And so he is called either by the church or by the patron with the consent of the church, ordained by the bishop, or by his command through ministers of the Church who hold episcopal rights, and finally confirmed.

### 7 The ecclesiastical ministry involves the authority and office of

The ecclesiastical ministry involves the authority and office of: (1). publicly teaching and ordinarily administering the sacraments; (2). the authority and duty of remitting and retaining sins.

Notes. This is commonly distinguished into the power of order and the power of jurisdiction. And those things which we have stated in the thesis are sometimes referred to under these headings, although in the Papacy the terms are explained differently.

Here one must distinguish between public and private instruction in doctrine (that is, the public and private presentation of faith, as they call it). Outside public assemblies, any of the faithful may instruct others in Christian doctrine, according to the laws (Acts 18:26; Ephesians 6:4; Colossians 3:16; 1 Peter 2:9).

But the public office of teaching is appropriate neither to women, according to 1 Corinthians 14:34 and 1 Timothy 2:12 ff., nor to any and all faithful men, but to those specially chosen for this office (see Musaeus, On the Church, part 1, disputation 7, §17-19, pp. 391-392).

Baptism, indeed, in a case of necessity, even a layperson or a woman may administer (see above, chapter 9, §4, notes c and d, p. 653). But this is extraordinary. Hence it is not permitted for anyone other than an ordinary minister to administer the Lord's Supper, the necessity of which is not of the same kind (see chapter 10, §4, note c, pp. 686-687).

This is otherwise called the power of the keys, of binding and loosing (see Matthew 16:19; John 20:23).

### 8 To the office of teaching it pertains that the doctrines of faith divinely…

To the office of teaching it pertains that the doctrines of faith divinely revealed should be clearly set forth according to the capacity of the hearers, and solidly confirmed; that opposing errors, against which there is reason to fear that they may insinuate themselves into souls from elsewhere, should be distinctly identified and refuted as contrary to the Word of God and harmful; similarly, that what is to be done according to the Law and the duties of Christians in every condition of life should be explicitly taught, and that people should be roused and moved to fulfill them by strong and persuasive arguments; that sins and vices to be avoided should be exhibited with regard to the guilt of fault and the liability to punishment, and that the minds of people should be drawn away from them and corrected; finally, that the minds of the afflicted and anxious should be raised up and strengthened with consolation suited to their condition and divinely offered.

Notes. This accords with the words of 2 Timothy 3:15-16, where the good works of a man of God or minister of the Church are enumerated (see also Prolegomena, chapter 2, §11, pp. 77-78).

To this belongs the term διδασκαλία (teaching) at the same place.

For the minister must not invent new doctrines, but present what has been sincerely drawn from the Scriptures as the principle of knowledge. And so he is commanded to hold fast to the faithful word which is in accordance with doctrine, that is, which having proceeded from divine inspiration, is of certain and proven trustworthiness (Titus 1:9; see Musaeus, preface to Introduction to Theology, at the beginning).

It is necessary, indeed, that the minister be διδακτικός (apt to teach) (1 Timothy 3:2; 2 Timothy 2:24). And so one method of teaching must be employed for the mixed multitude of the faithful in church assemblies from the pulpit, and another for select youth devoted to the liberal arts and the study of theology, to be instructed in the doctrine of faith and morals from the academic chair in theological lecture halls (see Musaeus more extensively at the same place).

What is otherwise called explaining, resolving any ambiguities of terms that may arise, is παραφράζειν (paraphrasing); indeed ὀρθοτομεῖν (rightly dividing) the word of truth (2 Timothy 2:15).

This is so that hearers may not, like children, be tossed about and carried around by every wind of doctrine (Ephesians 4:14), but rather grow in the knowledge of Christ (2 Peter 3:18; Colossians 1:9; see Musaeus at the same place, pp. 9-10). From this it is also evident that no part of doctrine should be set forth as necessary for belief unto salvation (or for practice unto holiness of life) that is not derived from the Scriptures, nor should anything be adduced for its explanation or confirmation that is not conformable to them (Musaeus, at the same place, p. 5).

For not all errors, however obsolete or buried, are to be recounted out of season, lest they appear to be taught.

To this pertains ἔλεγχος (refutation), which is mentioned in 2 Timothy 3:16 and Titus 1:9. For sacred doctrine must be defended against the enemies of truth; and therefore it must be vindicated from their objections and exceptions, and they themselves must be driven to be silent, having nothing further to oppose under the appearance of truth. And this is ἐπιστομίζειν τοὺς ματαιολόγους, καὶ φρεναπάτας (to silence the vain talkers and deceivers of minds) (Titus 1:10-11; see Musaeus at the same place).

Among the works of a minister is also numbered ἡ παιδεία ἡ ἐν τῇ δικαιοσύνῃ (instruction, as of a child, in righteousness, or holiness of life) (2 Timothy 3:16).

For the intellect must be taught in such a way that the will is simultaneously bent toward action.

To this pertains that ἐπανόρθωσις (correction) of 2 Timothy 3:16, that is, the correction of morals, by which things that had fallen or become distorted are restored, set upright or bent back, to their proper rectitude.

See 2 Corinthians 1:4. Consolation itself, moreover, is to be referred either to παιδεία (instruction) or to διδασκαλία (teaching), as Gerhard teaches (Gerhard, Commentary on Romans 15:4; compare what we have said in the Compendium of Homiletical Theology, part 1, chapter 7, §3, p. 128).

### 9 In the administration of the sacraments

In the administration of the sacraments, ministers ought to attend not only to observing accurately the tenor of the institution of each sacrament, but also to conferring those means of grace in a timely manner upon those who need them and are not unworthy, while not admitting the unworthy without discrimination.

Notes. As Paul writes concerning the Eucharist: "I received from the Lord what I also delivered to you" (1 Corinthians 11:23).

Ministers must therefore take care that no infant dies without Baptism through their own fault, nor an adult person, contrite and desirous, without the conferral of the Eucharist.

Let not holy things be given to dogs, nor pearls cast before swine (Matthew 7:6). We speak, however, of those who are openly known to be unworthy and who can be turned away, as is taught more extensively in moral theology.

### 10 With respect to the office of remitting and retaining sins

With respect to the office of remitting and retaining sins, it should be observed that the remission of sins is to be announced not only universally and indeterminately to all who repent and believe in Christ, but also determinately and individually to those who, having made confession, have given probable signs of penitence and faith, and who ask to be absolved from their sins. Nor is this a mere declaration, but it is efficacious for the confirmation of the remission of sins made by God.

Notes. It is certain that the authority and power itself of formally remitting sins belongs to none other than God (see Isaiah 43:25; Mark 2:7). But God, and Christ the God-man, exercises this power through the ministry, by announcing it to people with an audible voice, though this announcement is not without effect, as we shall presently say.

Thus in our churches, on each Lord's Day, after a general formula of confession has been read, a general absolution is likewise appended.

The private absolution, as they call it, is that in which a person confesses sins in general before a minister of the Church, or, if certain sins particularly trouble the conscience, confesses them specifically and determinately. Sins are also to be confessed before God (Psalm 32:5; 51:5-6) and before the neighbor whom we have harmed (James 5:16). But here we particularly consider the confession required for obtaining absolution or the remission of sins by virtue of the office of the keys.

This private confession before the minister of the Church, which they call auricular confession, although it does not have an express and special command and therefore is not of absolute necessity, nevertheless since it provides very many benefits and is a not insignificant part of ecclesiastical discipline, received by the public consent of the Church, it is by no means to be rashly neglected or abolished, but is to be employed piously and in true fear of God, especially by those who approach the Holy Communion. These are the words of Gerhard (Theological Commonplaces, vol. 3, On Penance, §99).

For sins are to be confessed with respect to the guilt of fault and punishment, and therefore as things that displease us, that trouble us, and from which we desire to be freed through Christ.

For what is signified by the voice of the minister is truly bestowed and exhibited or confirmed by God upon the contrite and believing through that voice, as firmly as if Christ Himself in person said to the penitent what He said to the paralytic: "Take heart, your sins are forgiven" (Matthew 9:2). To this pertains the saying: "Whose sins you shall remit, they are remitted" (John 20:23).

### 11 Similarly, with respect to the retention of sins

Similarly, with respect to the retention of sins, it is the task of the minister of the Church not only to declare universally to all unbelieving and impenitent persons the wrath of God and His punishments, but also in particular or individually to deny the remission of sins to notorious and flagrant sinners, and by the consent of the Church either merely to bar them from the use of the Lord's Supper or wholly to cast them out of the fellowship of the Church and deliver them to Satan. This again is not a mere declaration but an efficacious sentence.

Notes. As Paul pronounces an anathema upon all who bring a false doctrine (Galatians 1:8- 9) and upon all who do not love Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 16:22). And in this way a general formula of the retention of sins is appended to the general absolution read in our churches in public assemblies.

For just as absolution from sins involves the announcement of grace, so the retention of sins involves the announcement of divine wrath. And the minister retains the sins of people not by his own authority, but by the authority and in the name of Christ and of the Church.

This involves determining a specific person, as Paul did with the incestuous man (1 Corinthians 5:3), and with Hymenaeus and Alexander (1 Timothy 1:20).

For the one who has sinned out of ignorance or weakness, a gentle admonition with an exhortation to guard against future lapses suffices, as Gerhard says (On the Ecclesiastical Ministry, §286).

Where a public scandal has arisen from a lapse, such persons are to be rebuked before all, so that the rest may have fear, as the Apostle warns (1 Timothy 6:14).

To this is referred the saying: "Tell it to the Church" (Matthew 18:17), that is, to the presbytery and assembly of elders who represent the Church. "If he will not hear the Church, let him be to you as a Gentile and a tax collector." For although that passage treats of cases of private offenses and the pursuit of reconciliation, it is rightly applied also to the administration of ecclesiastical discipline with respect to any sinners, regarding certain degrees of admonition and the final sentence to be observed (see Johannes Major, preface to the Treatise against Valerianus, of the Capuchin Order).

This refers to the lesser excommunication, so that holy things are not given to dogs (Matthew 7:6). This lesser excommunication, they teach, is not to be undertaken by the minister of the Church alone without the consent of the ecclesiastical senate or consistory.

The greater excommunication is that to which 1 Corinthians 5:3 ff. pertains, where Paul commands the incestuous man to be cast out of the communion of the Church in a solemn act, in the assembly of the whole Church, at which he himself would be present in spirit though absent in body, in the name and with the power of our Lord Jesus Christ, and to be delivered to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus. For not even the damnation of the excommunicated, but their eternal salvation, is to be sought.

For the very application of legal threats to guilty persons carries immense weight. Moreover, sinners who have sinned not only against God but also against the Church can certainly also be bound by the Church; nor will they obtain grace from God unless they have been restored to favor with the Church and loosed by her. The case of those unjustly excommunicated, however, is different.

For the restoration of collapsed ecclesiastical discipline, ministers of the Church alone do not suffice, but the assistance of those who hold episcopal rights is required, which ministers cannot arrogate to themselves. In the meantime, ministers of the Church are not lacking in what they can do toward the conversion of sinners, or to render them inexcusable (see Musaeus, preface to Treatise on Penance against Stenger, quaestio D.3, a-b).

### 12 Finally, ministers of the Church are also occupied with the external affairs of the Church

Finally, ministers of the Church are also occupied with the external affairs of the Church, that is, rites and ceremonies, which are in themselves indifferent, but are nevertheless destined for the edification of the Church; they are to be instituted by the public authority of the Church, not however as a form of worship or of merit before God, but for external pedagogy; they are to be maintained and observed so long as the use of the Church warrants, and are not to be changed or abolished except prudently and in accordance with the benefit of the Church.

Notes. Hence also the term external jurisdiction originated, to which some also refer excommunication itself, suspension from participation in sacred things, and indeed the enactment of ecclesiastical laws and constitutions, ecclesiastical visitations, and so forth, which are customarily referred to episcopal rights, concerning which we shall see more in the chapter on the magistrate.

To this belong certain prescribed forms of hymns, the use of musical instruments, certain feast days, fasts, nuptial rites, baptismal rites (among which is exorcism), rites of the Lord's Supper, funeral rites, and the like.

These are matters not defined in Scripture but established by positive human law.

They serve, for example, the good order, the arousing of attention and devotion in sacred things, and indeed the representation of spiritual realities. Useless, idle, and scandalous ceremonies, however, do not even deserve the name of ecclesiastical matters.

These things do not belong to the ministry as precisely as the office of teaching and administering the sacraments does, but rather by their own nature belong to the whole Church, or to those who hold ecclesiastical rights (which are called episcopal rights), as in our churches they have been transferred to the civil magistrate through the Peace of Passau. Yet ministers of the Church should participate in this care; certain things should be exercised or put into practice through them, and the people should be informed by them concerning the rationale and use of such matters.

For those things which belong in themselves to the worship of God must necessarily be commanded by God, if not expressly, then at least by necessary consequence. Hence care must be taken that consciences are not burdened, according to the admonition of the Augsburg Confession, article 15.

Whether the merit in question be understood as condign or congruous.

That is, rites are to be observed where, when, and so long as the use of the Church requires.

They are therefore not to be changed without gravity and scandal, without tumult and petulance, nor except for sound reasons, and only when the people have been sufficiently informed about the reasons for the change and about the change of ceremonies itself.

In particular, it should be observed that one does not untimely yield to adversaries in the cause of religion who demand a change of rites. For in a case of confession, adiaphora change their nature, as it were, and from indifferent things become necessary (see the Formula of Concord, article 10).

### 13 The correlate of the ministers of the Church

The correlate of the ministers of the Church, and likewise the end for whose sake the ministry exists, is the assembly of those who hear the ministers as they teach and who are made partakers of the sacraments through their ministry and dispensation.

Notes. For the term "minister" is relative and looks to certain persons to whom one ministers.

The ministry was instituted for their good and benefit.

Scripture calls them the flock, with reference to the name of pastor, by which ministers of the Church are designated (Acts 20:28-29; 1 Peter 5:2-3). Otherwise the assembly is called the Church (Acts 20:28), although the Church in the strict sense includes in its concept both teachers and hearers (see Musaeus, On the Church, part 2, disputation 1, §36-37, pp. 16- 17).

Hence the assembly of hearers is sometimes so called, being those obligated to hear.

They are also made partakers of absolution itself, having made confession as is fitting. In German, the terms "Beichtkinder" and "Pfarrkinder" (children of confession, parish children) are used.

### 14 The proximate end of the ecclesiastical ministry is the reconciliation of…

The proximate end of the ecclesiastical ministry is the reconciliation of people with God through faith in Christ and their growth in faith and the other Christian virtues. The ultimate end is the eternal salvation of those same persons.

Notes. This is the end which the Author of the sacred ministry Himself intends, as that which is to be obtained through the acts of this office, yet to be produced by His own divine power. Hence it is also rightly called the effect (see 1 Corinthians 3:5, where the Corinthians are said to have believed through the ministers; also verses 6 ff.). Although the efficacy of the Word does not depend upon the legitimate mission of the one who presents or teaches it (see Musaeus, Treatise on the Church, part 1, disputation 7, p. 383 ff.).

The ministry is thus called the ministry of reconciliation (2 Corinthians 5:18; compare verses 19-20).

See Ephesians 4:12 ff., where it is said that ministers were given to the Church for the καταρτισμόν (fitting together, that is, the ordered arrangement, as in a certain proportion or symmetry) of the saints, for the building up of the body of Christ, in which each member receives growth fitting to the body through love.

So Paul, having commanded Timothy to attend to himself and to doctrine (1 Timothy 4:16), adds: "For if you do this, you will save both yourself and those who hear you."

### 15 The ecclesiastical ministry is defined as the public office

The ecclesiastical ministry is defined as the public office, ordained by God, in which certain persons, legitimately called and ordained, teach the Word of God, administer the sacraments, remit and retain sins, and take care of and direct all else that pertains to the Church, for the conversion, sanctification, and eternal salvation of people.

Notes. This definition shares in common with the office of the magistrate that it is a public office, and this rightly occupies the place of the genus.

The efficient cause is thus indicated (see §2, p. 794).

The office formally consists in the specific functions described (see §7, p. 802 ff.).

The end for whose sake and for whose benefit the ministry exists is indicated (see §14-15, pp. 813 ff.).

## 31 On the Political Magistracy

### 1 The other estate which has its place in the Church consists of those who

The other estate which has its place in the Church consists of those who, endowed with civil power, preside over the rest and thus have the care of the public welfare committed to them; these are commonly called magistrates.
