Notes. Thus indeed here we consider magistrates chiefly; although elsewhere, even outside the Church, among all nations the wiser men are recognized: since nature itself demands an order of rulers and subjects in the common society.

By this term we understand it here in its broader signification, insofar as it denotes any power of command, and therefore also, and indeed principally, the supreme power itself, although in the schools of political theorists it is more strictly taken to mean inferior power.

### 2 The efficient cause of the office of magistracy

The efficient cause of the office of magistracy, both considered in itself and insofar as it is exercised and administered by certain persons, is the Triune God and Christ according to his human nature.

Notes. Or in its abstract and formal aspect, as it is instituted and determined by certain laws toward a certain end.

Or considered concretely, with respect to the subject to whom that power and office are granted and belong.

For this author must be referred to that impulse of nature, by which all peoples are drawn to establish and preserve such a condition in public societies, so that by the guidance of the light of nature they have recognized the necessity of this condition for preserving public decency and tranquility. See Musaeus, Refutation of the Claims of the Conscientious Sect, pp. 56, 65, 66. To this are added the testimonies of Scripture: Proverbs 8:15; Romans 13:1; Deuteronomy 1:17; as well as the examples of magistrates established by God himself, Exodus 3:10, and the many signs of divine providence in the preservation of magistrates.

No distinction among the divine persons is applicable here, since the wisdom, authority, goodness, and power of God, from which human magistracy draws its origin, is common to all three persons.

For Christ approved the office of magistracy not only during the days of his flesh as something befitting even a Christian man, as we read in Mark 15:43 that Joseph of Arimathea, although a friend of Christ and awaiting the kingdom of God, nevertheless served simultaneously in the office of a senator; and in John 4:46, 53, when Christ praised the faith of the royal official, he did not command him to resign his post. Moreover, even after his exaltation to the right hand of God, just as he governs and rules the entire world, so also within it he protects and governs the magistracy.

### 3 The office of magistracy is committed to certain persons by God either immediately

The office of magistracy is committed to certain persons by God either immediately, with no arbitrary human intervention; or mediately, through the deliberations and voluntary action of human beings: whether by election, or by succession, or by legitimate conquest.

Notes. Thus Moses, Exodus 3:10; Joshua, Numbers 27:18; Deuteronomy 3:28; Saul, 1 Samuel 9:15 and following; and David, 1 Samuel 16:12, attained to rule immediately.

This mediate manner alone is valid today, and it is comprehended also in the passage of Paul, Romans 13:1, which was written at a time when the magistracy was pagan. The manner of attaining to rule, insofar as it depends upon the free will of human beings, is accustomed to vary; yet that there should be some magistracy at all is determined by the natural dictate of reason, and thus by God himself.

That is, through the votes of those who hold the right of election, under which is also included the case when inferior magistrates are chosen or appointed by superior ones.

Hereditary rule occurs when children receive dominion from their parents by right of inheritance, or kinsmen from their agnates.

Conquest occurs when enemies defeated in a just war are subjected to the victor, by whom they are thereafter preserved.

### 4 The power and office of the magistracy extends to all things upon which the…

The power and office of the magistracy extends to all things upon which the welfare of the commonwealth depends, and therefore encompasses both civil and sacred matters, though in a different manner in each case.

Notes. This is evident from consideration of the end, which we shall examine below.

Civil matters are those pertaining to the moral conduct of individuals and of all collectively, to the security of citizens, and to the abundance of the goods of this life.

Sacred matters are those pertaining to the worship of God and the eternal salvation of souls. That sacred matters belong to the care of the magistracy was recognized in some measure even by the Gentiles. Aristotle himself taught in his Politics, book VII, chapter 8, that religion is the principal concern among those things in which the welfare of the commonwealth consists, and that it ought therefore to be commended above all else to those who hold authority. In the Old Testament, the custody of the entire law, with respect to both tables of the Decalogue, was committed to the ruler.

See Deuteronomy 17:18, 19; Joshua 1:7; 2 Kings 11:12; 2 Chronicles 23:1.)

### 5 Civil matters of themselves are subject to the authority of the magistrate

Civil matters of themselves are subject to the authority of the magistrate, so that he may command and dispose concerning all things at his own discretion, provided only that he does not act contrary to natural or divine law.

Notes. We speak here of the supreme magistrate, that is, of Majesty, which is commonly said to denote a power unbound by laws. It is otherwise certain that inferior magistrates depend also, in those matters not defined by natural law, upon the superior power, and do not have full freedom of action.

For the magistrate is bound by the laws of nature, which are identical with the eternal and immutable law of God, both by reason of the nature of the subject matter and by the will of God as the supreme Lord; this obligation tends proximately toward obedience, and in the failure of obedience, toward guilt and punishment. If this punishment does not come in the present life through another superior on earth, it will nonetheless be incurred without doubt after this life, where repentance has not intervened.

The positive divine laws as well, which have been prescribed for magistrates, bind them by virtue of God's supreme dominion over all human beings.

In all other matters, that is, with respect to merely positive human laws, Majesty is entirely free, since neither can the subject matter of a law bind it, nor does Majesty acknowledge any superior on earth. It therefore rather gives laws to others, and can not only press the claims of natural and divine law, but also define, command, and dispose concerning those things which are not determined in those laws.

### 6 With respect to sacred matters

With respect to sacred matters, the dogmas of faith are not subject in themselves to the power of the magistrate. Of the actions divinely prescribed, the magistrate himself must observe and exercise those which are common to all Christians, while those which are proper to the ministers of the Church must be left to them and must not be claimed by the magistrate for himself. Now since all things that are ordered to the worship of God, and that serve either for the preservation of true religion or for the restoration of a collapsed religion, are ordinarily numbered among sacred matters, it must be acknowledged that such things fall in their own way under the power of the magistrate.

Notes. For by the very fact that the dogmas of faith have been determined by God and revealed to human beings as things to be believed, they oblige the magistrate himself as well, and leave him no license to alter anything. See Galatians 1:9; Deuteronomy 4:2; 5:32; 12:32.

For example, the actions of whatever Christian virtues, and likewise those pertaining to public worship and to the use of the sacraments.

For example, public teaching in the Church, and the administration of the sacraments.

As it is said in 1 Timothy 2:2 that the care of the magistracy tends to this end, that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty. And so it must be acknowledged that the rights of supreme powers are engaged in the matters of leading subjects to the knowledge and exercise of true religion in such a way that they have regard proximately for external acts, yet at a distance they are also aimed at the internal acts that pertain to religion. See Musaeus, Disputation Against the Theological-Political Treatise of an Anonymous Writer on Philosophical Liberty, sections 104 and following.)

### 7 And thus it belongs to the magistrate to appoint suitable ministers for the Church

And thus it belongs to the magistrate to appoint suitable ministers for the Church; to erect and maintain schools and temples; to provide on both sides for the honorable sustenance of ministers; to institute visitations and councils; to enact and defend ecclesiastical laws; to administer the goods of the Church; to preserve ecclesiastical discipline; to inquire into heretics as well as depraved ministers of churches and schools equally with any other like persons, and to compel them to submit to judgment; to punish those convicted of heresy or crimes; to abrogate manifest and Church-condemned heresies and idolatrous cults, and to take care that the Church be purged of them; and so forth.

Notes. The right to appoint ministers belongs to the entire Church in the manner described above when we treated the ecclesiastical ministry; for the magistrate cannot claim it for himself alone against the resistance of the remaining orders.

Schools are to be erected in order that those may be educated who can thereafter teach in the Church and serve the Christian commonwealth; from which it is understood that the founding, erection, and care of academies also pertains hereto.

Temples serve the exercise of divine worship in public assemblies.

Thus magistrates are called the nursing fathers of the Church in Isaiah 49:23.

In accordance with the example of the pious kings of the Old Testament, for example David, 1 Chronicles 28 and following; Jehoshaphat, 2 Chronicles 17:7 and following; Hezekiah, chapter 29:4.

Although the power to enact ecclesiastical laws belongs of itself to the Church, it belongs most especially to the magistrate insofar as he is a Christian and therefore a principal member of the Church. Laws may be enacted concerning the exercise of external divine worship, concerning ceremonies and fasts, and concerning the orders and functions of ministers. See the example of David, 1 Chronicles 24 and following; of Jehoshaphat, 2 Chronicles 19:8 and chapter 20:3.

See the example of Joash, 2 Kings 12:4 and following; of Josiah, 2 Kings 22:4.

See the examples of Solomon removing Abiathar from the priesthood, 1 Kings 2:26, 27; of Asa, who expelled the effeminate from the land and removed the filth of idols, 1 Kings 15:12; of Jehoshaphat, who removed the high places, 2 Chronicles 17:6; of Hezekiah, who restored sacred worship more fully by removing corruptions and abominations, 2 Kings 18:4 and 2 Chronicles 29:5 and following; and of Josiah, accomplishing similar deeds, 2 Kings 23:4 and following; 2 Chronicles 34:3 and following.

These ecclesiastical rights were rightly transferred in the Protestant churches through the Peace of Religion to the princes and estates of the Empire, rights which before the Reformation the papal bishops, and especially the Roman bishop, had wrongly arrogated to themselves, to the exclusion of the magistrate.

### 8 Furthermore, it is clear from what has been said that the Christian magistrate…

Furthermore, it is clear from what has been said that the Christian magistrate possesses not only legislative and judicial power, but also vindicative power, that is, the power to punish the recalcitrant; and it is certain that this power extends even to capital punishment of offenders.

Notes. Partly because the public welfare cannot be promoted and the authority of the Decalogue maintained intact unless evil persons are restrained by penalties; and partly because of what we have said specifically concerning the punishment of heretics and depraved members of the Church.

The power of the magistrate is commonly divided into the legislative (nomothetike), the judicial (dikastike), and the punitive (kolastike); and where the authority of the legislator is violated and the definitive sentence of the judge is held in contempt, one must indeed proceed to the imposition of penalties.

See Romans 13:4, where bearing the sword unto wrath means having the power, by means of the sword, to remove from life the wicked and the contumacious. And in Genesis 9:6 a decree is set forth concerning the shedding of the blood of a murderer, and thus concerning the infliction of capital punishment upon murderers by those who bear the place of God on earth.

### 9 The magistrate may also wage war in order to repel the unjust force of enemies…

The magistrate may also wage war in order to repel the unjust force of enemies from innocent subjects and from the whole commonwealth, and to defend religion, liberty, and property.

Notes. That this is permitted by the law of nature is established. And in Scripture itself, not only did God more than once in the Old Testament command his people to wage war and himself prescribe the manner of waging it; but also in the New Testament we read that no soldier who embraced the Christian faith was compelled to abandon military service. And when John the Baptist replied to soldiers asking what they ought to do, in Luke 3:14, "Be content with your wages," he presupposed that they earned wages, and thus that it was lawful to serve as soldiers. Christ also, in Matthew 8:9, 10, 13 and Luke, Acts 10:1 and following, praises the faith of soldiers and declares them acceptable to God, notwithstanding their military station.

We say pointedly that the magistrate is permitted to use arms for the defense of religion. But we deny that military force is to be used for the spreading of religion, or for correcting the religion of unbelievers, as if it were a means of conversion; just as we likewise do not enjoin upon subjects, who do not hold the right of making war, that religion is to be defended by arms against the magistrate.

Indeed, arms may also be taken up to recover things that have been taken away, when satisfaction cannot otherwise be obtained.)

### 10 Careful heed must be taken

Careful heed must be taken, however, that resort to war not be made so long as milder means are available, nor to gratify passion, but for the sake of the public welfare and tranquility; and finally that war be waged only by legitimate means and methods.

Notes. These conditions pertain to the justice of war with respect to its moving cause.

These pertain to the justice of war with respect to its final cause.

So that divine assistance is sought without vain reliance on human strength; military discipline is scrupulously observed; and what is done against the law of nations or of nature, or what argues only notorious fraud or cruelty, is not practiced under the guise of honorable stratagems.

### 11 The correlate of the supreme magistrate is the body of subjects

The correlate of the supreme magistrate is the body of subjects; and by this name are understood all those who are contained within the commonwealth, yet are not themselves the magistrate. No distinction exists between laymen and clergy in this regard.

Notes. For the very word "magistrate" is relational and regards those over whom authority is exercised.

As Paul writes in Romans 13:1, "Let every soul be subject to the authority of the magistrate." And Bernard states elegantly in his Epistle XLII: "If anyone attempts to make an exception, he is attempting to deceive."

Insofar as both laymen and clergy are regarded as members of the commonwealth. See the example of Christ himself, who submitted to the magistrate, Matthew 17:27; John 19:11; and of Paul, Acts 25:10, 11, 12; chapter 26:32.)

### 12 Subjects are indeed obligated to render to the magistrate honor

Subjects are indeed obligated to render to the magistrate honor, obedience, tribute, and prayers for his welfare.

Notes. See 1 Peter 2:17; Romans 13:7. Pertaining hereto are both the interior reverence of the soul and the outward signs of honor.

See Romans 13:1. This obedience extends to all things that are not contrary to the will of God, but no further. See Acts 4:19; 5:29. Indeed, if the magistrate demands something unjust, obedience must nonetheless be refused with modesty.

See Romans 13:6, 7.

See 1 Timothy 2:2.

All these duties must be rendered not only to a faithful and pious magistrate, but also to a wicked and unbelieving one, as may be manifestly gathered from the passages cited.

### 13 The end of the civil magistracy is the public welfare

The end of the civil magistracy is the public welfare.

Notes. To this end the magistracy is ordered by its nature and by the will of God as efficient cause, although those who hold power do not always by accident intend or achieve it.

Indeed, this same end ought to be the end of the subjects as well.

That is, that human beings under the magistracy may live a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty, as stated in 1 Timothy 2:2.

### 14 The magistracy may be defined as a public office

The magistracy may be defined as a public office, ordained by God, in which certain legitimately called persons, endowed with power over both civil and sacred matters, enact laws in the commonwealth, exercise judicial functions, punish transgressors, and defend the commonwealth against external enemies, for the sake of the public welfare.

Notes. By this characteristic it agrees with the ecclesiastical ministry, so that this term rightly occupies the place of a genus.

What follows pertains to the specific difference, and indicates first of all the efficient cause, as treated in section II.

This is the causality of the efficient cause with respect to this office considered concretely. See section III.

What has been indicated up to this point pertains to the very form of this office, even if its actual exercise may and customarily does vary according to the diversity of circumstances. See section IV and following.

Thus the final cause, which also includes the subjective end, is indicated. See section XIII.)

## 32 On the Domestic Estate and Society

### 1 The third estate occurring within the Church

The third estate occurring within the Church, which is as it were the seedbed of the ecclesiastical and political order, is the domestic estate, which encompasses conjugal, paternal, and household society.

Notes. For from domestic society come forth in part those who are to be admitted to the ecclesiastical ministry, and in part those who are to be advanced to the office of the civil magistrate.

It is also called elsewhere the economic estate.

As a composite society made up of several simpler ones, though each of those simpler societies can exist without the others.

### 2 The efficient cause of conjugal society is God

The efficient cause of conjugal society is God, whether you consider marriage as it is in itself and by its own nature, or with respect to the contracting parties themselves.

Notes. Conjugal society rightly holds first place, since it is also the cause of paternal society. It is called in a single word "conjugium," from the common yoke which husband and wife bear together; it is likewise called "matrimonium," from the end of marriage or the procreation of children, through which a woman becomes a mother. See Musaeus, Theses on Marriage, section III, pp. 1, 2.

Considered abstractly, God alone is the cause of marriage; for he not only created the first human beings with a certain inclination toward marital union, and endowed them with the principles of right reason, by whose guidance they could understand the difference between the union of bodies as it exists among themselves and as it exists among brutes; but he also solemnly instituted marriage, Genesis 2:21, confirmed in Matthew 19:4, 5. Moreover, he gave many other laws pertaining to the same state, for example, concerning degrees of consanguinity that impede marriage, concerning the punishment of adultery, and so forth. See Musaeus, Theses on Marriage, sections V through IX, pp. 2, 3.

Considered concretely, with respect to marriage as it is being contracted or has been contracted, God is the cause of marriage partly by reason of the instinct of nature given for entering into marriage, partly by reason of his general influence, and partly by reason of the special influence by which he bends the hearts of the contracting parties, or at least suggests the occasion for contracting marriage. See Proverbs 18:22; 19:14. And so it is also evident that God, considered concretely as the cause of marriage, is either the remote, first, and universal cause, or at least an inadequate cause. See Musaeus, Theses on Marriage, sections XV, XVI, p. 5.

### 3 The causes of marriage in the act of contracting it are also the spouses themselves

The causes of marriage in the act of contracting it are also the spouses themselves, and their parents, in whose power the spouses are.

Notes. They are the proximate cause.

Insofar as they contract with one another. See Musaeus, Theses on Marriage, section XI, pp. 3, 4.

Parental consent is therefore required not merely for contracting marriage honorably, but for contracting it validly; so that children together with their parents constitute the adequate and complete cause. Pertinent here is, in part, the fact that the very nature of the contract requires the contracting parties to be masters of their own persons, whereas children are by natural law subject to parental authority; and, in part, the fact that Scripture itself grants parents the power of directing the marriages of their children, Deuteronomy 7:3. And it also teaches that a father may deny his deflowered daughter to the one who violated her and seeks her as his wife, Exodus 22:16, 17.

### 4 The internal moving cause on the part of the spouses is that natural…

The internal moving cause on the part of the spouses is that natural inclination toward the procreation of offspring and toward mutual companionship in life.

Notes. On the part of God, the moving cause for the institution of marriage is the divine goodness.

To these also belong, after the fall, disordered concupiscence and the necessary flight from fornication, according to 1 Corinthians 7:2, as treated in Musaeus, Theses on Marriage, section XIII, p. 4. That the desire for wealth or lust sometimes moves human beings to enter into marriage is something that arises from a peculiar human vice and therefore cannot equally be considered here.

### 5 The external moving cause is the need of human beings of either sex and the…

The external moving cause is the need of human beings of either sex and the necessity of mutual assistance, both for the procreation of offspring and for living well.

Note. See Genesis 2:18 and Musaeus, Theses on Marriage, section XIV, pp. 4, 5.

### 6 The causality of the efficient cause of marriage on the part of the spouses is consent

The causality of the efficient cause of marriage on the part of the spouses is consent, which is manifested through external acts of mutual and free promise concerning conjugal cohabitation.

Notes. As with other contracts as well.

For although consent formally consists in internal acts of the will, and commonly denotes the will of two or more persons directed equally toward the same thing, it must nonetheless be acknowledged that internal acts alone are insufficient for contracting marriage. See Musaeus, Theses on Marriage, section XX, p. 7.

If, however, the promise is extorted from either party by force or fear, or if ignorance of the person intervenes, or of a circumstance directly contrary to the primary end of marriage, there will be no true and valid consent. See Musaeus, Theses on Marriage, section XVII, p. 6.

The promise is expressed in significant words, or signified and confirmed by other signs, for example by an earnest pledge. Pertaining hereto are betrothals, of which some are called betrothals of present intent and others of future intent: the former simply introduce the character of a contracted, though not yet consummated, marriage; the latter do not have the character of a contracted marriage in the absolute sense, unless a new consent is added, expressed in words of present intent. For the conjugal bond between the contracting parties is thus finally established, concerning which more will be said presently.

### 7 There also belongs to the efficient cause of marriage in its own way the…

There also belongs to the efficient cause of marriage in its own way the sacerdotal blessing, or the solemnization of the union, instituted by the Christian Church.

Notes. For by the very custom of speaking in the Church, the contracting parties are called betrothed rather than spouses before the priestly solemnization, and the contract entered into between them is called not so much a marriage or nuptials as a betrothal. See Musaeus, Theses on Marriage, section XXI, pp. 7, 8.

Not so much for the contracting as for the consummating of marriage. See Musaeus, Theses on Marriage, section XXII, p. 8.

For very weighty reasons: partly so that the contracting parties may be admonished concerning the Author, sanctity, and indissolubility of marriage, concerning the divine blessing and conjugal duties, and concerning the bearing of hardships; partly so that public record may be established of their legitimate union; and so that all things may be done decently and in order; and partly finally so that the new spouses themselves may be commended to God through prayers. See Musaeus, Theses on Marriage, section XXII, p. 8.

### 8 The matter of marriage is the persons themselves who are joined in marriage

The matter of marriage is the persons themselves who are joined in marriage: one man and one woman, capable of rendering the conjugal debt, and between whose union consanguinity or affinity does not stand as an obstacle.

Notes. Insofar as they are joined in marriage, they are as it were the parts and members of conjugal society; otherwise they pertain to the efficient cause, as we have seen above. See Musaeus, Theses on Marriage, section XLVII, p. 22.

Not a plurality of men with one woman, nor a plurality of women with one man. See Matthew 19:4, 5, 9, where Christ, by virtue of the primeval institution described in Genesis 2:24, teaches that two persons are to be joined in matrimony, and adds at the same time that the man who takes another wife while his first wife still lives is guilty of adultery. From this it is entirely rightly concluded that the conjugal union of one man with several wives, since it imports adultery of itself and by its own nature, also conflicts with the primeval institution and with the very law of nature; and is therefore both illicit and null by that same law. See Musaeus, Theses on Marriage, sections XLIX and following, pp.

23 and following; and his special dissertation vindicating that passage of Matthew against the Discourse on Polygamy by the author writing under the pseudonym Theophilus Alethaeus, published in 1675. See also 1 Corinthians 7:3, where it is said that the man joined to one woman, equally as the woman joined to one man, no longer has power over his own body; and thus it is denied that he has the right to admit another woman to bodily union with him through marriage. See further Musaeus, Theses on Marriage, sections LVI and following, pp. 28 and following. Moreover, right reason can also conclude from the very end of marriage that simultaneous polygamy, not only of one woman with several men but also of one man with several women (which some call polygyny), is not in accord with natural reason; namely, because the procreation of offspring from wandering lust, and immoderate use of the generative faculty, and the kind of union that is an obstacle to conjugal love and peace, are incompatible with it. See Musaeus, Theses on Marriage, section LXII, pp. 33, 34.

Both with respect to age, and also with respect to the natural power itself of generating, or of extinguishing in the other the flames of passion. See 1 Corinthians 7:3 and Musaeus, Theses on Marriage, section LXIV, pp. 34, 35. In the meantime, the marriages of elderly persons, which are reasonably entered into for the sake of mutual assistance in life, are not condemned universally.

Whether the impediment arises from the modesty and decency grounded in closeness of flesh resulting from generation or from marriage; concerning these we must now treat in greater detail. In the meantime see Leviticus 18:6, where it is forbidden to join to oneself in marriage a person close to oneself in flesh, that is, in body; and noteworthy is the universality with respect to the subject, expressed as "any man" (ish ish, meaning "each man"), so that every human being is bound; and the universality with respect to the object, namely that no one may take any woman close to him in flesh as a wife. See Musaeus, Theses on Marriage, section LXVI, pp. 35, 36.

### 9 Consanguinity is described as the relation of persons of whom one descends from another

Consanguinity is described as the relation of persons of whom one descends from another, or who, being two or more, descend from one common ancestor through carnal generation.

Notes. It is a certain unity of blood with respect to the seed into which blood is converted and from which generation proceeds. See Musaeus, Theses on Marriage, section LXXII, p. 39.

Following Johannes Andreae, the jurist of Bologna, whom Musaeus follows in his Theses on Marriage, section LXXIII, p. 40.

### 10 Affinity is the closeness of persons arising from marriage

Affinity is the closeness of persons arising from marriage, such that those who are one flesh with either spouse by reason of a blood relationship between themselves are thereby also carnally close to the other spouse, inasmuch as spouses have been made one flesh with each other.

Notes. So called not so much because it denotes a unity of two persons toward a single end, as because one party approaches the boundaries of the other's kinship, as Musaeus explains in his work cited at section LXXXII, page 45.

With respect to the Civil Law, only legitimate marriages are understood to produce this bond; but with respect to Canon Law, and accordingly here as well, any carnal union whatsoever generates that closeness.

Furthermore, the blood relatives of each spouse become thereby the affines of the other spouse; however, the blood relatives of one spouse do not become blood relatives of the other spouse's kindred in such a way as to render marriage between them impossible.

### 11 For the purpose of assessing the closeness between persons concerning whose…

For the purpose of assessing the closeness between persons concerning whose lawful marriage inquiry is made, the Lines and Degrees of Consanguinity and Affinity must be observed.

Note. For not every degree of kinship or affinity, however remote, impedes marriage.

### 12 A Line is a collection of persons descending from the same stock

A Line is a collection of persons descending from the same stock, containing degrees.

Notes. A term applied to this doctrine by metaphor drawn from the mathematical line, which consists of points and a certain continuous flow of them, as Musaeus explains at section LXXIII, page 41.

That is, from a common ancestor, or the person from whom, as branches from a tree, those whose kinship is in question derive.

### 13 The Line is divided into the Straight Line

The Line is divided into the Straight Line, which exists between persons of whom one descends from the other, and which is called Ascending when traced from children to parents, or Descending when traced from parents to children (for in substance it is one and the same line, as Musaeus notes at section LXXVI, pages 42 and 43); and the Collateral Line, which exists between persons of whom neither descends from the other, but both descend from some one third person. This line is called Collateral because the persons within it are not subordinated to one another as generators and generated, but are joined side by side under one common ancestor; it is otherwise called the Transverse Line.

### 14 The Collateral Line is subdivided into the Equal Collateral Line

The Collateral Line is subdivided into the Equal Collateral Line, which exists between persons equally distant from the common stock; and the Unequal Collateral Line, when one of the related persons is closer and the other more remote from the common stock.

Notes. That is, in the same degree.

With respect to the difference and number of degrees.

### 15 A Degree is the relational measure between distant persons

A Degree is the relational measure between distant persons, by which one may determine by how many removes of agnation or cognation two persons differ from each other.

Notes. So called by metaphor drawn from the steps of a staircase or of a sloping place.

As defined by John of Andrea and Musaeus at section LXXIII, page 41.

### 16 The method of computing the degree of closeness or distance between persons in…

The method of computing the degree of closeness or distance between persons in this doctrine is comprehended in three distinct rules corresponding to the different lines.

Notes. As derived from Canon Law and customarily observed in the schools and consistories of our churches. The other method of reckoning, which rests upon a single rule alone, namely: as many generations as there are, so many degrees; is prescribed in Civil Law and pertains to matters of succession and the entering upon an inheritance. This latter method agrees with the canonical method in the Straight Line, but differs considerably from it with respect to the Collateral Line, as Musaeus shows at sections LXXIX and following, pages 43 through 45.

### 17 The first rule, which pertains to the Straight Line

The first rule, which pertains to the Straight Line, is this: as many persons as are counted among those whose kinship is in question, including intermediate persons where they exist, less one, so many degrees lie between them.

Notes. Expressed more briefly and clearly thus: as many generations as intervene in the straight line between the persons whose closeness or distance is in question, so many degrees lie between them, as Musaeus sets out at section LXXIX, page 43.

Thus, for example, looking to the families of the Patriarchs in the sacred text, Jacob and Dinah are related in the first degree of consanguinity in the straight line; Isaac and Dinah are distant by two degrees (or in the second degree); and Abraham and Dinah are distant by three degrees, or in the third degree.

### 18 The second rule

The second rule, which applies to the Equal Collateral Line, is this: by as many degrees as the persons whose kinship is in question are distant from the common stock, by so many degrees are they distant from each other.

Note. Thus, for example, Laban and Rebekah, both born of Bethuel, are blood relatives in the first degree, since each of them is distant from Bethuel in the first degree of cognation in the straight line. But Jacob, the son of Rebekah, and Rachel, the daughter of Laban, are distant in the second degree, because each of them is distant from Bethuel, their grandfather and common stock, in the second degree of consanguinity.

### 19 The third rule, which pertains to the Unequal Collateral Line

The third rule, which pertains to the Unequal Collateral Line, is this: by as many degrees as the more remote of the persons whose closeness is in question is distant from the common stock, by so many degrees are those persons distant from each other.

Notes. For otherwise, if we were to reckon the degrees according to the nearer person, the result would be that very distant persons were judged to be equally close.

Thus, for example, Esau, the son of Isaac, and Dinah, the granddaughter of Isaac through Jacob, are joined in the second degree of the unequal collateral line; because, although Esau is one degree removed from Isaac, who is the common stock, Dinah is nevertheless distant from him by the second degree.

### 20 Concerning the prohibition of marriage between blood relatives

Concerning the prohibition of marriage between blood relatives, it is to be known that in the Straight Line marriages are prohibited absolutely and without limit; and this prohibition rests upon Divine and Natural (that is, Moral) Law.

Notes. For between parents and children the closeness of flesh impedes marriage, partly through physical identity of blood, by reason of which it is not lawful for a son to pour back into his mother the blood derived in him from his parents, nor for a father to transfuse his own blood into a daughter who is his own part and his own flesh; and partly by reason of the respect owed to parents and children, insofar as nature has granted to parents a superiority and authority over children, and conversely enjoins upon children submission, reverence, and deference toward parents, with which it is incompatible that parents and children should be carnally mingled, as Musaeus explains at section XLIV, page 52.

For although the physical closeness and identity of flesh is less in more remote degrees than in nearer ones, yet the respect arising from the act of generation never expires (Musaeus, section XCVI, page 54).

This is expressed in the primeval constitution of marriage found in Genesis 2:24, by virtue of which a man is commanded to leave his father and his mother, with whom he is already one flesh, and to become one flesh with his wife, with whom he was not previously one flesh. Furthermore, in Leviticus 18:10, although only the first and second degrees are expressly and explicitly prohibited, yet it is certain that the remaining degrees are also prohibited implicitly and by reason of the parental respect owed therein.

This law is natural in the sense that it possesses binding force in and of itself, by virtue of the underlying subject matter, even setting aside the will of the legislator; for the bond contracted through generation is altogether natural, and accordingly the reason for the prohibition is drawn in Leviticus 18:7 from the very subject matter itself (Musaeus, section XCVII, page 54).

### 21 In the Equal Collateral Line

In the Equal Collateral Line, marriages are prohibited in the first degree by Divine and Natural Law. By positive Ecclesiastical Law, however, marriages are also prohibited in the second degree.

Notes. That is, between brothers and sisters, whether fully related or united in only one parent.

See Leviticus 18:9; 20:17.

Since children are something of their parents and a part of their flesh, and therefore just as they are fully one flesh with their parents, so among themselves they are one flesh, though not immediately but as flesh united in the parents (Musaeus, section CI).

Though not equally by Divine and Natural Law, since Scripture is silent on this point, and as regards the matter itself, it must be conceded that the unity of flesh in one common parent is not found among first cousins except in a remote sense, which, speaking absolutely, is not unity at all (Musaeus, section XCV, page 53). The Church prohibits marriages in degrees not prohibited by Divine Law in order to uphold greater reverence for the divine laws and to keep persons further removed from marriages prohibited by Divine and Natural Law.

### 22 In the Unequal Collateral Line

In the Unequal Collateral Line, marriages are prohibited in the second degree by Divine and Natural Law. By Ecclesiastical Law, however, marriages are also prohibited in the third degree, and indeed in the fourth degree as well, if one of the persons is only one degree removed from the common stock.

Notes. (Leviticus 18:12, 13; 20:19), since persons of this kind are indeed one flesh with the common stock, though in an imperfect sense (Musaeus, section XCV, page 53). It is accordingly to be observed simultaneously that this prohibition is valid not only with respect to the persons expressly named, but also with respect to others equally distant, by reason of the identity of the underlying ground (Musaeus, section CXXV, pages 77 and 78).

For such a person stands to the descendants of a brother or sister in the place of a father or mother, inasmuch as she is one flesh with the brother or sister through one common parent.

### 23 Three genera of affinity are customarily distinguished

Three genera of affinity are customarily distinguished. The first genus of affinity is that which is contracted through the mediation of one person joined by carnal union. The second genus is that contracted through the mediation of two persons and a corresponding number of marriages. The third genus is that contracted through the mediation of three persons and a corresponding number of marriages. Today, however, the second and third genera of affinity do not impede marriage; although formerly the first degree of the second genus was prohibited by Ecclesiastical Law.

Notes. According to the Canonists' rule: a person added to a person through carnal union changes the genus but not the degree.

For example, Nahor, the brother of Abraham, and Sarah, the wife of Abraham, were affines through the mediation of Abraham alone and through his marriage to Sarah.

For example, Keturah, the wife of Abraham after Sarah's death, and the blood relatives of Sarah were affines through the mediation of Abraham and Sarah, and through the first marriage between Abraham and Sarah and the second between Abraham and Keturah.

For example, if Keturah, after the death of Abraham, had married another man, the blood relatives of Sarah would thereby have become affines of Keturah's second husband.

In the first genus, however, certain degrees are prohibited with respect to marriage. (Musaeus, section LXXXIV, page 46).

### 24 The Lines and Degrees of affinity are assessed and computed in proportion to…

The Lines and Degrees of affinity are assessed and computed in proportion to the Lines and Degrees of consanguinity, so that by whatever degree and in whatever line of consanguinity the person through whom affinity is contracted (through the intervention of marriage) is connected to his or her blood relatives, by that same degree and in that same line those blood relatives are counted and are affines of the other person to whom the former is joined in matrimony.

Notes. For otherwise in affinity, properly and in itself, there are no degrees, since one affine does not descend from another, as Musaeus notes at sections LXXXV and LXXXVI, page 47.

Thus, for example, since Abraham and Terah are blood relatives in the first degree of the straight line, Sarah, the wife of Abraham, and Terah are affines in the same first degree of the straight line. That same Sarah is an affine of Nahor in the first degree of the equal collateral line, because Abraham and Nahor are brothers. Again, Sarah is an affine of Lot in the second degree of the unequal collateral line, because Lot is the son of Haran, who was Abraham's brother.

### 25 Accordingly, in whatever degree and in whatever line blood relatives are not…

Accordingly, in whatever degree and in whatever line blood relatives are not permitted to contract marriage, in that same line and degree of affinity, affines are prohibited from contracting marriage.

Note. It is indeed true that the bond of consanguinity, contracted through natural generation, is by its very nature closer than the bond of affinity, which is contracted only through marriage, and that there is a greater ground of impropriety and baseness in marriages of blood relatives than in marriages of affines; yet it is nonetheless certain that degrees of affinity are also divinely prohibited, and that the reason for the prohibition is grounded in the very nature and underlying subject matter of the relationship (Musaeus, section CIV, page 61, and sections CXII and following, pages 67 and following).

### 26 Specifically, in the Straight Line of affinity

Specifically, in the Straight Line of affinity, marriages are prohibited by Divine and Natural Law absolutely and without limit.

Notes. This is demonstrated by Leviticus 18:8, where marriage with a stepmother is prohibited; verse 15, where marriage with a daughter-in-law is prohibited; and verse 17, where marriage with a stepdaughter and with the daughter of a stepson or stepdaughter is prohibited; see also Leviticus 20:11, 20:12, and 1 Corinthians 5:1.

The reasons for these prohibitions, cited in the passages mentioned, are drawn from the very underlying subject matter (Musaeus, sections XCVII and CIV, pages 54, 55, and 62).

As the first and second degrees only are expressed in Leviticus, yet in the remaining degrees of this line the respect owed to parents and children remains.

### 27 In the Equal Collateral Line of affinity

In the Equal Collateral Line of affinity, affines are prohibited from marriage in the first degree by Divine and Natural Law.

Notes. See Leviticus 18:16; 20:21, where marriage with the widow of a deceased brother is forbidden.

This is a matter of Natural Law because in marriage with a sister-in-law, the deceased brother transfuses his own blood into one who is one flesh with him with whom he himself received his flesh from one common parent, so that she thereby stands to him in the place of a sister (Musaeus, section CIV, page 62).

To this prohibition also belongs marriage with the sister of a deceased wife, which is forbidden in Leviticus 18:18, not only when aggravating circumstances are present, such as simultaneous polygamy and the objection of the first wife still living, but also insofar as it falls equally with that other marriage (with a deceased brother's widow) under the general law by which it is prohibited that a man approach any woman close to him in flesh (verse 6). See Musaeus, sections CXXIV and following, pages 77 and following.

### 28 In the Unequal Collateral Line of affinity

In the Unequal Collateral Line of affinity, marriages between affines in the second degree are prohibited by Divine and Natural Law

Notes. See Leviticus 18:14; 20:20, where marriage with the wife of a paternal uncle or maternal uncle is forbidden.

The respect owed to parents and children remains operative here, together with the unity of flesh with the person with whom the other party is one flesh in respect of one common ancestor.

Here again, beyond the persons expressly named, we hold that the law must be extended to others standing in the same degrees of relationship (Musaeus, section CXXV, pages 77 and following).

### 29 Among those marriages contracted in prohibited degrees

Among those marriages contracted in prohibited degrees, there appears to be the following distinction: some must be altogether dissolved; others may be tolerated upon the infliction of an arbitrary penalty.

Notes. Those that must be dissolved are those for which God in Leviticus 20 expressly appointed capital punishment, because they are so base and abominable that it is unlawful for the spouses to persist in them. These include marriages between blood relatives and affines in the straight line between ascendants and descendants, and marriages between blood relatives in the first degree of the collateral line, which Carpzov in his work on consistorial jurisprudence (Carpzov, Jurisprudence of the Consistory, book II, definition XCIX) likewise judges must be dissolved on account of the flagrant and detestable scandal they occasion (see also Musaeus, section CXIX, page 74). Indeed, such unions are only equivocally called marriages, since the conjugal and indissoluble bond finds no place in them, as will be said below at section XXXIV.

Those marriages that may be tolerated upon the infliction of an arbitrary penalty are those for which Leviticus 20 has not appointed capital punishment: for example, those contracted and consummated in consanguinity in the second degree of the unequal collateral line, and those contracted in affinity in the first degree of the equal collateral line and likewise in the second degree of the unequal collateral line. For in these cases it appears that the spouses are left in the contracted and consummated marriage by the laws contained in Leviticus 18 and 20, yet are subjected to the arbitrary penalty of the magistrate along with the threat of childlessness, as Carpzov and Musaeus note in their respective passages.

Such toleration on the part of the Church and the Magistrate will not, however, be equivalent to a dispensation properly speaking from the laws prohibited in Leviticus 18 and 20. For a dispensation properly speaking is a relaxation of a law with respect to its binding force in those matters which it prescribes or prohibits. But when the Church and the Magistrate tolerate, that is, do not dissolve, those marriages which God has not commanded to be dissolved, they do not thereby relax the prohibiting law; rather, they leave it in its full force (Carpzov in the place cited, and Musaeus, pages 74 and 75).

### 30 In those degrees

In those degrees, however, in which marriages are prohibited only by positive Ecclesiastical Law, the Church is also able, properly speaking, to grant a dispensation

Notes. For example, in the equal collateral line in the third degree, according to sections XXI and XXII above.

Yet care must be taken lest dispensations be granted too frequently and made on trivial grounds, thereby causing scandal.

### 31 The form, or formal principle

The form, or formal principle, of marriage consists in the mutual obligation of the spouses to fidelity and the conjugal duties. It is commonly called the Conjugal Bond.

Notes. That is, that by which a man is formally constituted in the being of a husband, and a woman in the being of a wife, as Musaeus explains at sections XXIV and CXLI, pages 9 and 85.

For it is a relation of a kind, since spouses are thereby constituted in the being of correlatives: the husband regards that woman as his own wife, and the wife regards that man as her own husband, and each regards the other mutually as one who, by mutual consent, has bound himself or herself to an indivisible companionship of life and to mutual duties, with the husband discharging his marital duties toward the wife, and the wife her wifely duties toward the husband, as Musaeus explains at section XXVIII, pages 11 and 12.

The mutual obligation of the spouses and the conjugal bond do not in reality differ from each other (Musaeus, section XXV, pages 9 and following).

The conjugal bond is a moral bond, not a physical one; not something transitory but permanent; founded indeed in the act of consenting on the part of the contracting parties, yet also at the same time grounded in the divine institution (Musaeus, sections XXIV and XXIX, pages 9 and 12).

Furthermore, carnal union is rather a consequence and effect of marriage than something pertaining to its formal principle; for the formal principle and the conjugal bond itself endures even when carnal union and bodily cohabitation have ceased (Musaeus, section XXIV, page 9).

### 32 The conjugal bond is indissoluble

The conjugal bond is indissoluble, partly by virtue of its object, and partly, and indeed principally, by virtue of the divine institution.

Notes. So that it endures perpetually as long as both spouses are living, and cannot morally be rescinded or abolished even by the mutual dissent of the contracting parties.

That is, because marriage is contracted by consent directed to a fellowship of life to be continued perpetually and throughout all of life, to be dissolved only by death.

For if marriage derived its specific being from the consent of the spouses alone, then upon the retraction of that consent by the mutual dissent of both parties the marriage itself would likewise cease; but by virtue of the divine institution, the man and woman are bound to enter into marriage in no other way than by a consent directed to perpetual cohabitation or fellowship, and that consent irrevocable and irretractable (Musaeus, sections XXXI and XLI, pages 15 and 20).

This institution is expressed in Genesis 2:24 in these words: "Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and shall cleave (proskollethesetai, as the Seventy interpreters and Christ in Matthew 19:5 and Mark 10:7 render it, meaning joined as with glue and not to be separated) to his wife." And Christ adds pointedly in Matthew 19:6: "What therefore God has joined together, let no man put asunder." This law is grounded in the very nature and end of marriage, both in the procreation of offspring and in the mutual fellowship of life, each of which requires the fellowship of male and female throughout the whole of life (Musaeus, sections XXXIII through XL, pages 14 through 20).

### 33 Nevertheless, in two cases it can happen that there is a Divorce

Nevertheless, in two cases it can happen that there is a Divorce, that is, a legitimate and valid dissolution of marriage with respect to the conjugal bond itself. The first is the case of Adultery, in which the marriage may be and is dissolved by the law itself, and it is lawful for the innocent party to enter into another marriage. The second case is that of Malicious Desertion, provided that the innocent party was prepared to continue cohabitation and it was not through any fault of theirs that the marriage was not continued, and provided that the desertion has been declared by a competent judge, whose declaration gives the deserted party the right to enter a new marriage.

Notes. For these things are required for a divorce properly so called. Otherwise, even if the spouses seem to be separated to the greatest degree, if nevertheless there has not been a true and valid marriage between them, or if the marital bond itself is not dissolved, then a divorce, properly speaking, does not occur.

This follows from Matthew 19:9 and 5:32, where by the force of the exceptive proposition ("Whoever puts away his wife, except for fornication, and marries another, commits adultery") two things are stated: first, that the man who puts away a wife who has not committed adultery and marries another commits adultery; and second, that the man who puts away a wife who has committed adultery and marries another does not commit adultery; from which it is rightly concluded that in the case of fornication or adultery it is lawful to dismiss one's wife or to be separated from her by divorce and to marry another (Musaeus, section XLIV, page 21).

Even if the spouse who committed adultery wishes to continue cohabiting.

For the bond with the former spouse has truly been dissolved, and the obligation to conjugal fellowship has ceased.

According to the saying of Paul in 1 Corinthians 7:15: "If the unbelieving spouse departs (that is, separates himself or herself and makes a divorce from the other faithful spouse), let him depart. The brother or sister is not bound in such a case" (so that it is not unlawful to marry another or to remarry, but the deserted party is free from the bond and obligation to conjugal fellowship with the deserter or the one who has deserted).

When the innocent party was prepared to continue cohabitating, and it was not through him (or her) that the continuation of the marriage was prevented.

### 34 When, however, persons unlawfully joined are separated

When, however, persons unlawfully joined are separated, this is not so much a divorce, as a declaration that in that union there was no conjugal bond.

Notes. For example, in degrees of consanguinity prohibited by natural law, as noted above at section XXIX, or where an error of person or the incapacity of one of the spouses has intervened.

For the definition of divorce given in section XXXIII above does not apply.

The separation occurs because either one of the parties could not validly contract with the other as with a person close in flesh, or one did not in truth contract with that person but with another, or one of the parties is utterly incapable of entering into sexual union and thus of contracting matrimony.

### 35 Similarly, when spouses are separated only as to bed and board

Similarly, when spouses are separated only as to bed and board, this is not properly a divorce, but a suspension of the acts of cohabitation and of conjugal duty.

Notes. With the conjugal bond remaining intact, so that neither spouse may enter into another marriage.

And indeed the husband may on occasion be required to provide maintenance to the wife. Such separation may occur on account of graver enmities that appear incorrigible and even attended with danger to the life of one of the spouses.

### 36 When one of the spouses dies

When one of the spouses dies, however, the conjugal bond is truly dissolved, and it is lawful for the surviving spouse to enter into marriage again with some other person.

Notes. See Romans 7:2, 3; 1 Corinthians 7:39.

This is commonly called Successive Polygamy, and is distinguished from Simultaneous Polygamy, which is what is meant by Polygamy in the absolute sense.

### 37 The parties for whom marriage is ordained are persons of both sexes whom nature…

The parties for whom marriage is ordained are persons of both sexes whom nature has made fit for marriage, without distinction of ecclesiastical or secular estate.

Notes. That is, those for whose benefit it was instituted by God and who are permitted to enter into it.

According to those thongs which we have said concerning the matter of marriage.

For the impulsive cause of marriage (treated above at sections IV and V) applies also to those in the ecclesiastical estate; and accordingly the saying of 1 Corinthians 7:7, 8, 9 pertains to them as well. To this may be added 1 Timothy 3:2, 12; Titus 1:6; and 1 Corinthians 9:5, where the honorableness of the marriage of clergy is plainly set forth. Regarding that last passage, and the point that by "a sister as a wife" (adelphen gynaika) is to be understood a believing woman joined in marriage, see Musaeus in his Biblical Vindication of the Gloss, disputation V, sections 1 and following, page 299 and following.

Nevertheless, celibacy freely and chastely maintained must not be deprived of its proper praise (1 Corinthians 7:1, 8, 32 and following).

### 38 The proximate end of marriage

The proximate end of marriage, to which it is ordered in and of itself, is the procreation of offspring and mutual assistance in life. The more remote end is the preservation of the Church and of the commonwealth.

Notes. For the union of male and female in one flesh is ordered in and of itself and proximately toward the generation of progeny, as the Author of Marriage himself indicates in Genesis 1:28 (Musaeus, section CXXXII, page 83); and this end of marriage endures even after the human race has been multiplied, for the purpose of its conservation (Musaeus, section CXXXIX, page 85).

The end of mutual assistance consists in each caring for the other as for his or her own flesh, and in their mutual support in domestic affairs, in the raising of children, and in the whole of life, as indicated in Genesis 2:18 (Musaeus, section CXXXIV, page 83).

See Musaeus, section CXXXV, page 83.

### 39 The intermediate and accessory end

The intermediate and accessory end, is that marriage be a remedy against depraved lusts.

Notes. Which is accordingly an end of marriage by accident and not in itself, in the state of the fall, though intended by God for the benefit of human beings in their present condition, Musaeus, sections CXXXVI and CXXXVII, pages 83 and 84.

See 1 Corinthians 7:2, 9.

As for the fact that the spouses themselves not infrequently intend other ends, such as pleasure, wealth, glory, and the like, we leave that aside in its place; for the end of marriage itself, whether in its essential or its accidental aspect, is to be judged not so much from the intention of these or those individuals as from the intention of God and Nature (Musaeus, section CXXXVIII and following, pages 84 and 85).

### 40 The duties of spouses are some common to both

The duties of spouses are some common to both, and others proper to the husband or wife.

### 41 To the common duties belongs the union of souls

To the common duties belongs the union of souls, of bodies, and of material goods.

Notes. That is, mutual love and the earnest desire to help one another, as shown in Ephesians 5:28-29 and 1 Corinthians 7:10, 33-34.

As in 1 Corinthians 7:7 and following; and that this union of bodies must be conducted in sanctification and honor is taught in 1 Thessalonians 4:4).

Certainly with respect to their use, and for the relief of the other's need, as in Ephesians 5:29).

### 42 The duties of the husband are

The duties of the husband are: to protect his wife, to govern her with counsel and admonition, to supply the necessities of this life, and to refresh her with gentle companionship.

Notes. As seen in the example of Jacob, Genesis 32:13 and following, and of David, 1 Samuel 30:3 and following.

Ephesians 5:23.

Ephesians 5:29.

Colossians 3:19.

### 43 It is the wife's duty to honor her husband and to obey him

It is the wife's duty to honor her husband and to obey him, and to take care of the household.

Notes. Ephesians 5:33.

1 Peter 3:16; Colossians 3:18; Ephesians 5:2.

Proverbs 31:10 and following.

### 44 Marriage may be defined as a society or union of one man and one woman

Marriage may be defined as a society or union of one man and one woman, indissoluble according to divine institution, arising from the mutual consent of both parties, for the purpose of the generation of offspring and mutual assistance in life.

Notes. Understood not as the act of joining, but as the state of those joined, so as to designate the very form or formal character of marriage, as treated above.

Here the matter is indicated, as discussed earlier.

Which pertains to the efficient cause, as is evident from earlier sections.

Which is the end of marriage, as treated in the preceding sections.

### 45 The Paternal Society has God as its efficient cause

The Paternal Society has God as its efficient cause, whether that society is considered in itself or from the perspective of parents and children alike.

Notes. Which arises directly from the conjugal society and is therefore most properly subjoined to it; and if children are sometimes born from an illegitimate union, this is incidental and results from human vice.

For God is not only the cause of the conjugal society from which the paternal society proceeds, and the one who granted the first human beings the faculty of generation so that they might become parents; but he also always concurs with generating spouses (Psalm 127:3). He has impressed upon parents and children a mutual inclination toward one another; he has laid down laws for both parties (Exodus 20:12; Ephesians 6:1-4; Colossians 3:20-21); and he aids this society with his blessing (Exodus 20:12; Ephesians 6:2).

This consideration applies whether the society is viewed abstractly or concretely: to the former belong the divine laws mentioned; to the latter belong that natural instinct, the influence of God toward generation, and the many specific arguments of Providence.

### 46 The parents themselves also pertain to the efficient cause of the paternal society

The parents themselves also pertain to the efficient cause of the paternal society, insofar as they beget children from themselves.

Notes. Considered concretely, not abstractly.

For when children are produced through generation, a society and relation between parents and children simultaneously arises, even though it is also true, as the common saying has it, that children are not chosen by the will of parents but are received from nature, and thus from God, the author of nature (Psalm 127:3).

### 47 The impulsive cause on the part of the parents is the natural desire to…

The impulsive cause on the part of the parents is the natural desire to generate and to have someone like themselves.

Note. According to nature, though children are sometimes born even when parents do not directly intend it.

### 48 The causality of the efficient cause on the part of the parents is Generation

The causality of the efficient cause on the part of the parents is Generation.

Note. How God is in act the cause of this society has been stated above, in the notes to Section XLV.

### 49 The matter of the Paternal Society consists of parents and children

The matter of the Paternal Society consists of parents and children. Although a father alone, or a mother alone, together with a son or daughter, may suffice.

Notes. Regarded here as parts or members of this society.

Namely, if one parent has been taken away by death. And although the society is named "paternal" from the father, as the more dignified person, the mother too truly belongs to it.

### 50 The formal character consists in that mutual relation by which parents

The formal character consists in that mutual relation by which parents, as such, regard children as their children, and these in turn regard them as their parents; and being joined in a single society, they are bound to mutual duties.

Notes. Which is elsewhere called paternity and filiation.

Thus here too a certain moral bond, though founded in nature, obtains.

### 51 That relation and bond of society endures so long as parents and children live

That relation and bond of society endures so long as parents and children live.

Notes. The relevant passages of Scripture command children, without restriction of time and therefore absolutely, to be mindful of their obligation as long as their parents live (Exodus 20:12; Sirach 3:14; Tobit 4:3).

We do not deny, however, that duties cannot always be exhibited in the same manner by both parties, nor do we deny that a parent may repel an incorrigibly wicked son and disinherit him, just as we have said that marriage can also be dissolved in a certain case.

### 52 The proximate end is partly the education of the offspring

The proximate end is partly the education of the offspring, and the welfare of the family. The ultimate end is that the Church and the Commonwealth may be preserved.

Notes. A point acknowledged by Aristotle himself, in the eighth book of the Nicomachean Ethics, chapter thirteen; and toward this end is directed that natural affection which God, as author of nature, has impressed upon parents.

Just as all natural societies tend toward the common welfare of those very societies; and to this also look the divine laws by which duties are prescribed equally to parents and to children.

For from marriage, through this society, the Church and the Commonwealth are increased and adorned with citizens and ministers.

### 53 The duties of Parents consist in supplying children with food and clothing

The duties of Parents consist in supplying children with food and clothing, and likewise in taking care that they are educated in all piety, in learning and in the arts, so that both their temporal and eternal welfare may be advanced.

Notes. 1 Timothy 5:8; Matthew 7:9; and this must be done until children are able to provide necessities for themselves.

Ephesians 6:4; Colossians 3:21.

Proverbs 29:17.

### 54 The duties of children consist in showing love

The duties of children consist in showing love, honor, and obedience to their parents. Likewise, if necessity so demands, in supporting them, and also in bearing their faults with an equable spirit.

Notes. Proverbs 10:1; Proverbs 15:20.

Exodus 20:12; Ephesians 6:2-3.

Ephesians 6:1; Colossians 3:20.

1 Timothy 5:4; Matthew 15:4-6.

Proverbs 23:22; Sirach 3:14.

### 55 The Paternal Society may be described as a society or union of parents and children

The Paternal Society may be described as a society or union of parents and children, divinely instituted, for the purpose of the education of children and the welfare of the whole society.

Notes. In this it agrees with marriage and with other unions or associations; although this also pertains to its form.

Which is the matter of this society, as treated above.

Indicating the efficient cause, as established above.

Which is its end, as treated above.

### 56 The Herile Society likewise has God as its efficient cause

The Herile Society likewise has God as its efficient cause, whether one considers it in itself or with respect to those who enter into and hold it.

Notes. Namely, such as is upright and befitting the faithful; it is called "herile" from the more important party, though it exists between master and servant.

See 1 Corinthians 7:20; Colossians 3:23-24.

For as regards the nature of servitude, although it is such as to have had its origin only after the Fall, it is well known how God, the author of all good order, has also fortified the herile state with certain laws (Exodus 21:1 and following; Ephesians 6:5 and following; Colossians 3:23-24), and has promised various goods to those who observe those laws (1 Peter 2:19; Colossians 3:24; Colossians 4:1; Ephesians 6:8).

This likewise extends to divine Providence occupied about the persons of this society, insofar as legitimate modes are given for entering into it, of which the following section treats.

### 57 The masters themselves

The masters themselves, and sometimes also the servants themselves, pertain to the efficient cause of this society.

Notes. Considered concretely.

Who make captives taken in war, or purchased men, or men hired for a price, into their servants.

Who accept a price and consent to servitude.

### 58 The impulsive cause on the part of human beings is the need of this life

The impulsive cause on the part of human beings is the need of this life, which obtains not only on the part of servants, but also on the part of masters.

Notes. That men are often driven by luxury or pride to acquire servants is a fault, and is therefore largely disregarded here.

So that by servile labors they may acquire the necessities they would otherwise lack.

Who are themselves insufficient to accomplish the tasks of the household without the help of attendants or servants.

### 59 The causality of the efficient cause on the part of human beings consists in this

The causality of the efficient cause on the part of human beings consists in this: that a servant is either led away as a captive in a just war, or is purchased, or a free contract is made with him.

Notes. From which some wish the word "servant" to be derived, from "preserving".

Exodus 21:7; Leviticus 25:39; and to this also formerly belonged the fact that those born of servants in the master's household contracted servitude by that very fact.

And in this way this society is today for the most part constituted between master and servant.

### 60 The matter of this society consists of the master and the servant

The matter of this society consists of the master and the servant, and likewise the mistress and the maidservant.

Notes. Insofar as they enter into and maintain this association.

Or also several servants according to the scale of the household and the degree of need.

Since difference of sex makes no distinction here (Genesis 16:6, 9).

### 61 The formal character of this society consists in the mutual relation and…

The formal character of this society consists in the mutual relation and obligation of master and servant.

Notes. In accordance with the analogy of the conjugal and paternal societies.

That this bond is dissoluble is not difficult to establish: for a master can manumit a servant who was captured or purchased; and if a contract has intervened, it ordinarily binds for a limited time only; indeed the society, which was entered by mutual consent, can also be dissolved by mutual dissent.

There is truly not only an obligation of servants toward masters, but also of masters toward servants, by reason of the divine law, and specifically also if a voluntary contract has been entered between them.

### 62 The proximate end is the mutual utility of those who govern and those who are…

The proximate end is the mutual utility of those who govern and those who are governed in this society; the more remote end is the benefit of the public society.

Notes. Namely for the satisfaction of the needs of this life.

Insofar as simple societies tend toward the happiness of the whole city.

### 63 The duty of Masters consists in the fair imposition of labors

The duty of Masters consists in the fair imposition of labors; in the supply of the necessities of this life or in the payment of the promised wage; and finally in prudent and moderate direction and correction.

Notes. And likewise of mistresses.

Exodus 20:10; Deuteronomy 5:14.

According to the different modes of this society. Matthew 10:10; Deuteronomy 24:14-15; James 5:4; and to this also belongs care for the sick, Matthew 8:6.

See Ephesians 6:9.

### 64 The duty of Servants consists in showing honor

The duty of Servants consists in showing honor, obedience, fidelity, and patience to their masters.

Notes. And likewise of maidservants.

See Ephesians 6:5-7; Colossians 3:22; Titus 2:9-10.

See 1 Peter 2:18.

### 65 The Herile Society may be described as a society or union between a master and a servant

The Herile Society may be described as a society or union between a master and a servant, and likewise between a mistress and a maidservant, ordered according to the divine will, for the purpose of mutual utility.

Notes. This is the genus, which, however, with attention to what follows, also designates the form.

This is the matter of that society.

Indicating the efficient cause.

Which is the end of this society.

SOLI DEO GLORIA.
